en: Preface to the Supplement to the Biographies of Eminent Monks:

In former times, the Great Master Xuelang overturned the stagnant conventions of scholastic learning; among his disciples, those who were like dragons and elephants were too numerous to easily enumerate.
Master Yunru was the one with white eyebrows; Master Daoru was his eminent disciple under Master He. Daoru propagated and clarified the teachings of the Vehicle, becoming a model for his time.
Last year, he traveled to the White Gate (Nanjing) with his staff, preaching the sutras at Ba’en Chan Monastery. Ten thousand people gathered to hear the Dharma.

At that time, I went to his mountain retreat in a sedan chair wearing informal clothes, engaging in a long conversation. I regretted that we had not met earlier to clasp arms in friendship. Before long, he returned home.
At Wumen, I presented him with a poem containing the lines: "The disciple’s teaching brings forth flowers that fall like rain;

Vimalakīrti has returned, his tongue now blunt. I did not expect this to become a poetic prophecy. Within but a few days, he suddenly fell ill and passed away. Among those who heard of it, there was none who did not weep and pine for him in longing.
This autumn, his disciple Daokai brought the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (Gaoseng zhuan) composed by the Master and entrusted [it to me].
I have composed this preface and shall here recount the words of Master He: "This old monk has labored for thirty years compiling [this work] to transmit the Dharma-eye treasury of the robe.
It must now be committed to the carving blocks; I specifically sought out Sima of Wucheng Bridge to provide a preface for its opening.
I, however, reflect that since the time of Dahui, the *Lamp Records* have been sparse and scattered, making them difficult to verify. How could it be otherwise?
This is no small omission regarding the vehicle of dhyāna. Master He’s withered staff pointed the way for my travels, as I journeyed across famous mountains and ancient monasteries.
I searched out and unearthed inscribed stone tablets, climbing through vines and ivy to trace those that had been eroded by time. I collected them one by one in chronological order.

Later, the Scholar Cao Xueshi further brought forth the collection held in his library at Ye, emptying his chests to assist me. After thirty years of toil, this work was completed. From Zhao... [text ends].

From the Song dynasty to the present Zhaodai era, more than four hundred years have passed. Without distinguishing between specific lineages, this work has roughly encompassed all true sons of the Buddha.

Following the precedent of Jiyin’s *Biographies of the Jewel of the Sangha*, I have appended critical essays and praises; this is truly a magnificent undertaking for the Garden of Dharma and a secret record from the Dragon Palace.
In the intervals of my meditative contemplation, I have frequently delved into the scriptural teachings, often sighing over those who merely chase after clods of earth.
They vied with one another to rush toward the seventeen hundred sites of clamor, readily disparaging the masters of the teaching as being more talkative than a single phrase from a bamboo staff.

Alas! Regarding this great matter of the external world, how could there be anything further of mystery or essentiality? Master He kindled this lamp of wisdom and continued the cultivation of the stages of fruition;
formerly his tongue turned forth rain and dew, and his hands reached out to touch the sun and stars—a single expanse of fervor.

The intestines [of this work] have been completed. Through these three births, I have attained realization; this single volume serves as a succession of the lineage. It fully exhausts the great principles of both Chan and the Teachings (Dharma).
From the tip of a hair, light is emitted, causing those who unroll this scroll to see, as if with their own eyes, the dragon-elephants treading upon the earth.

As for all you worldly men of dull faculties, how could you possibly contribute even a single word? Master Daokai Gong personally received the transmission of the seal of entrustment; may he not let the legacy of his family fall into ruin, and thus edited this work.
Written by the Layman Sir Ren, Fan Jingwen, at the end of autumn in the year Xinsi of the Chongzhen era, while dining in the White Gate (Baimen).

This record not only serves as a response to the Master’s kindness through three turns of discourse, but because my bonds of fellowship within the Lotus Society have endured for more than a few days or nights, I have informed my fellow practitioners and thus had it carved into woodblocks for circulation. Written at the Can [Hall] in Baimen.
Bingzhai.

In the preface to the *Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks*, it is recorded that the Tathāgata’s Treasury of the True Dharma Eye was entrusted to the Arhats. Some attained enlightenment through the mind-ground, while others did so through the ear.

The fundamental entry into the assembly is the wisdom of wondrous observation; it is spiritually pervasive in every place. Although the paths by which one arrives may differ slightly, the gate through which one enters is fundamentally one and the same.
Having once read the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*, I have long reflected upon them with deep emotion.

Since their features remain vividly present and their spiritual essence is mysteriously resonant, what the mind encounters seems as if it were being transmitted by hand, and what the eyes behold seems as if it were being pursued by foot.
With a bright mirror before one, the Dharma is revealed in its entirety. How profoundly the former sages have enlightened me!
Master He traveled to the four quarters to inquire about the Way and refined his mastery of the Three Studies. Thereupon, he gathered eminent monks at the Dharma Cave to engage in discourse.

Since the influence of his lifelong teachings has pervaded the entire realm of *sāhasra-lokadhātu*, none but those whose bodies and minds are simultaneously perfected, and whose hands and eyes act in unison, could have achieved this.
How could such excellence and erudition be anything other than marvelous? Master Hóng held the complete manuscript to visit me.
In Bái Xià, I have only just opened this precious treasury, its radiance illuminating the entire world; only then did I come to appreciate the divine discernment of Master Hé.
The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom reflects through both past and present—is this not what is meant by "this literature"? Written by Huang Duānbo of Xī Jiāng.

In the preface to the *Continuation of the Biographies of Eminent Monks*, I have classified eminent monks into ten categories, much as the disciples of Confucius were ranked according to the four sages.

Just as there were further disciples recorded after the accounts of those four sages, how could it be that there are no more eminent monks after the establishment of these ten biographical categories? It is not that there are none.

Seng was a person whose lofty character as a monk could not be transmitted [by others]. Furthermore, among his disciples, there was none who possessed the brush of Sima Qian and yet failed to transmit [his life].
What is called a "biography" (zhuan) is indeed a transmission. It values transmitting the spirit so that one sees it as if meeting an old friend;

upon opening the portrait once, without even waiting for a question, one immediately knows it is such-and-such a person. This is due to nothing other than encountering him through the spirit, rather than attaining knowledge through words. Alas!

This is not merely the portrait of a single eminent monk from a great monastic history; rather, the ancient, refined, and austere countenances—majestic and imposing—are all contained within these volumes.

Were it not for one possessing the hand of Monk You who adds the final dot to the dragon’s eye, who has traversed tigers’ dens and eagles’ nests in exhaustive pursuit, and who possesses the talent of a Sima Qian or Dong Guo as a virtuous chronicler, how could one possibly have compiled this?
Picking up someone else's spittle; what enters the basket is but grass. Sometimes "yi" is substituted for "jia," or the great is omitted for the small.

Thus, the arrangements of the ancients' courtyards and the mechanisms of their "killing and enlivening" through the hanging of the hand can no longer be discerned. After the *Song Ningzan Zhuan* was completed, [the errors were thus introduced].
Zhang Wujin, Lü Xiangqing, and other gentlemen of integrity deliberated upon this with the Venerable Jiyin;
indeed, there were inevitably some points left unsatisfactory. My friend, Lord Gaosong He, once lamented before me the deficiency in the official monastic history of our enlightened era.
Thinking, "Now that he has departed from our circle, who else could [complete it]? he locked himself away by the East Sea for three years to sharpen his tools.

He did not begrudge the effort of "trampling through iron shoes," traveling between Qi, Lu, Yan, and Zhao. Only then did he begin to trace out the fragmented steles and scattered ruins, searching them out until he had exhausted every possibility.
Regarding those famous mountains in the southeast that he had not yet been able to visit, he made an agreement with me to share the responsibility. I recall the spring of the year Jiayin.
I saw you off by the lake as you departed for a journey through the Eight Min regions; I, too, shall take up my staff and travel to the two provinces of Yue, taking the route via Zangke.

Upon returning to his former mountain, between Mount Jizu and Mount Xiong’er, he frequently encountered the Great Being in his physical body, much like the ancient pavilion of the coiled dragon in Shengguo.
To this day, he remains in meditative absorption, with nails growing and hair lengthening; others, such as Nian’an, have likewise re-illuminated the Meditation Hall.
This is comparable to the deep orchid that thrives in empty valleys: though its fragrance is peerless, there is no one to appreciate it. Unfinished.

I am able to lift them all up. I vow to search for them until the end of my life so that this public case may be resolved. At that time, the remaining snow covers the roads; the hungry crows have lost their luster. As the traveler looks toward home, solitary thoughts bind him in desolation. You, sir, must go; do not fail to return.

[The original text concludes with a poetic lament regarding the departure of a seeker. **Translation:** "I can lift them all up. I swear to exhaust my life in searching for them, so that this public case may be fully understood. At that moment, the remnants of snow lay thick upon the paths; the hungry crows were devoid of color. The traveler looked back toward home, his solitary thoughts bound in sorrowful longing. "Go forth, sir! Before long, you shall return."
When they met, [Xiangjien] said, "First, the Iron Mountains; next, the Lengkong. The Master rejoiced at these lines:
"Wooden clogs with teeth that have chewed through the snows of Min, and the patchwork robe hood that has brushed against the clouds of Zhejiang.

He did not know how many ancestral masters had already been gathered into a single sack, nor how many old monks throughout the world had all been weighed and sifted, each one measured on the scale. What a pity! From this point on...
Both men fell into the conventional molds of the lecture halls; they had no leisure to reach this level.

As for the chronology of these masters across past and present, the evaluation of their merits and defects, and the arrangement of their sequence, these still await further deliberation and may be called incomplete works. Alas! You have now passed away.
What can be done when a person is gone and it becomes difficult to recover [the truth]? I too am approaching old age; though I might pack my provisions and take up my staff, how could I—?
I shall not harbor the lament of one who has lost his way. This book was intended to be placed upon a high shelf; yet the lifelong toil of its author has ultimately become as if it never existed.
When I sought to present it to the world, I found that much remained unrefined. Having read it over and over again, I concluded that it would be better to preserve it than to let it vanish.
Thus, I consulted with the layman Mao Zijin and committed it to print. Should I incur the censure of others for this, [I ask for their forbearance].
As for this matter, I truly cannot escape my responsibility. In the realm of the unseen, I have failed my good friend no small amount;
what more need be said? Fortunately, at the moment he drew his last breath, he entrusted Dao-kai with his final instructions, and Dao-kai exhausted every effort in his arduous task.
Now that this work is finally completed, I shall present it to you, O Master, within the realm of the Constantly Quiescent Light.
Among all my disciples, he alone who can read his father’s letter and fulfill his father’s will is surely Dao-kai.
Written later while residing at Zhongfeng by Du Che, in homage.

Preface to the *Supplementary Continuation of the Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Buxu gaoseng zhuan*). This work was compiled by my friend, Dharma Master He Tairu. The biographies are arranged as follows:
From the Song and Yuan dynasties down to the Ming era, the various eminent Chan masters were prefixed with "Da Ming" (Great Ming).

If this work were merely a monastic history of a single dynasty, then the title would not have been established based on the person being recorded, but rather derived from the name of the compilers themselves.
This also follows the principles and precedents established by Master Zanning; it is intended to signify that this is not a "Continuation" (Xu) but rather a record of the Song dynasty.

In the past, my late teacher, the Elder Zibai, once considered the failure to continue the *Chuan Deng Lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp) to be a major failing regarding the life-force of wisdom (*hui-ming*).

This was spoken specifically with regard to the single gate of Chan practice. However, if one does not merely propagate the Five Lamps in succession, but also fully records the ten categories [of Buddhist learning], then...

The task of compiling and arranging this collection has required even greater toil and diligence. Therefore, I have often said that the difficulty in recording the *Chuan Deng Lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp) lies in possessing the discerning eye to verify the mind;
the difficulty in transmitting the biographies of eminent monks lies in possessing broad learning to make precise selections, and furthermore, it requires the skill of one’s own hand in writing.
Master He, through half a lifetime of labor and exertion, has extensively hunted and gathered these materials in minute detail.
Furthermore, he delved deeply into the matter. Regarding human physiognomy, facial hair, and family lineages, he examined the original manuscripts and transcribed them all with his own hand.
After several rounds of verification and refinement, it is clear that his painstaking efforts cannot be adequately matched by the ordinary labor of pen and paper.
Since you, sir, have been my companion in the style of Zhi Dun and Xu Xun, and your eminent disciple, Wumen Gong, has likewise... [text continues]

I have a close bond with the Left Minister Jiao Ran; therefore, I present this draft of the biographies for his examination and consultation, and request that he provide a preface for its opening fascicle.
In my observation of those who composed histories in antiquity, it began with Mr. Cui Yanluan, who compiled separate biographies for figures such as Fotudeng and Kumārajīva.
Thus, within the annals and records, there are those who may be separated out to form the "Biographies of Monks" (Sengzhuan).
He served as the Director of the Bureau of Sacrifices (Dongxu).

However, apart from the compilations by the three masters Liang Jiao, Tang Xuan, and Song Ning, even Zhiyan’s *Shengbao zhuan* (Biographies of the Jewel of the Sangha) was specifically intended only for the Chan school;

it generally never once addressed matters such as the translation of scriptures or the various miscellaneous liturgical rites. Therefore, from the Song dynasty onwards, this vast [work] could by no means be omitted.
Furthermore,
when the August Emperor of the Ming Dynasty ascended the Golden Wheel to rule over the realm,
those declarations concerning the Śākya school contained within his Imperial Compositions shine with a brilliance equal to the sun and stars; yet as his years drew on...

Out of these three hundred [monks], could there not be at least one who would compose a written record to illuminate the Dharma-vehicle? It was for this reason that Master He (Heshang) resolutely undertook the compilation of this biography.
I recall once when a Chan master asked Su Dongpo what his surname was; Dongpo replied, "My surname is Cheng (Scale).

[He explained that he] weighed the lightness and heaviness of all the elders under heaven. I suggest that those who compose biographies should establish for themselves the office of a historian based on this principle. Furthermore, I recall once...
Prime Minister Pei saw the portraits of eminent monks on the walls of Da’an Temple and remarked, "The true likenesses are worthy of contemplation, yet where are the eminent monks themselves?
I request that this be used as an opening gateway for those who read their biographies.
I do not know whether you, Master, would be willing to present my words to your teacher within the realm of eternal quiescent light."

Biographies of the Three Masters Tianxizai, Fatian, and Shihu of the Song Dynasty: Section on the Translation of Scriptures.
Tian Xizai was a native of Kaśmīra in North India. During the Taiping Xingguo era, he arrived at the capital together with the Tripiṭaka Master Śīladharma from Oḍḍiyāna.
At that time, various Indian scholars had arrived in succession, each presenting palm-leaf manuscripts;

these were collected and stored in great abundance. The Emperor was then keenly intent upon translating and transmitting these works, desiring to find someone who was thoroughly versed in both the Indic and Chinese languages.

One of eminent virtue and great achievement served as the Chief Translator. By imperial decree, the Institute for the Translation of Buddhist Scriptures (Yijing Chuanfa Yuan) was established to the west of Taiping Xingguo Temple to accommodate him.
Previously, there had been one named Fanta (Dharmadeva), a native of Central India who possessed profound mastery of the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*) and deep penetration into the Tripiṭaka.
Having first arrived at Putong Pass, he collaborated with the śramaṇa Fajin, who was well-versed in Indic studies, to translate the *Amoghapāśahṛdayadhāraṇīsūtra*.

The *Pramāṇasamuccaya* was praised by the seven Buddhas; the local governor submitted it as a memorial to the Emperor. Upon reading it, the Emperor was greatly pleased and said, "A great achievement has been accomplished.
He summoned Tian Xizai, Shi Hu, and Shihu [sic] to an audience and questioned them on the general meaning of the Buddha-dharma.

Their responses were in accord with His Majesty's intentions, and they were each granted purple square-cut robes and appointed to the Translation Court (Chuanfa Yuan). The Master Tian Xizai was conferred the title of Great Master Mingjiao (Master of Enlightened Teaching). [This was recorded by] Fatian.
The State Preceptor Shi Hu was appointed as the Great Master for Revealing the Teachings. He was commanded to first translate one sutra each from the Sanskrit manuscripts he had brought.

The Sanskrit scholars-monks Fa Jin, Chang Jin, and Qing Zhao were ordered to receive the oral transmission and compose the prose; Yang Shuo, Court Gentleman for Splendid Happiness, and Zhang Ji, Vice Director of the Ministry of War, were to polish the literary style;
and Liu Su, Palace Attendant, was to oversee the project. All necessary provisions and requisites were to be supplied from the state treasury.

The government provided the necessary supplies. The Three Masters submitted a description of the translation ritual for imperial review and made this request: "In the translated texts, there may be words that coincide with the Imperial name or the temple names of the ancestors.
In previous dynasties, these were not avoided. If the text were altered to circumvent them, we fear it would obstruct the essential meaning of the scriptures.

The Emperor replied by decree: "Regarding the characters used in Buddhist scriptures, they should follow the original text. There is no need to avoid temple names or the Imperial name. Less than a month later, the newly translated scriptures [were completed].

The *Tian xizai shangsheng fomujing* (Sūtra of the Holy Mother of the Celestial Dispeller of Calamities), the *Fashang tianshijixiang chishijing* (Sūtra of the World-Protecting Auspiciousness of the Dharma-Heaven), and the *Shihu shang rulai zhuangyanjing* (Sūtra of the Tathāgata’s Adornments by Śīladharma) were each completed in one fascicle.
An imperial edict was issued for the two monastic districts to select one hundred śramaṇas learned in the doctrines to thoroughly determine the meaning of these scriptures.

At that time, Shen Yao, the Head Registrar of the Left Monastic District, and others submitted a memorial stating: "The translation bureaus have long been neglected; the transmission and translation of scriptures have become extremely difficult. Three...
The Master then took up the Sanskrit text and first translated its meaning; he then corroborated it with the Chinese language, whereupon the assembly was convinced.
When the Emperor examined the new scriptures, he showed them to his ministers, saying: "The teaching of the Buddha is beneficial to governance and brings universal benefit to all living beings.

Those who are enlightened realize its profound source for themselves, while the ignorant give rise to groundless slanders. Regarding this Way, I have a slight understanding of its essence. As for all those who..."

"Your Majesty, to rectify the mind and be free from private interest is the practice of self-benefit (*svārtha-caryā*). To perform even a single act of goodness for the peace of the world is the practice of benefiting others (*parārtha-caryā*).
For instance, Emperor Wu of Liang’s sacrifice of himself as a slave was a biased view of the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*);

it is not a method suitable for later generations. The imperial carriage visited the Translation Institute (*Yijingyuan*). The Emperor granted him a seat and offered words of consolation. He increased his personal effects and provided additional attendants, all of which were drawn from within the imperial palace.

The Tibetan and Sanskrit manuscripts were commissioned for translation. Furthermore, śramaṇas learned in Sanskrit were selected as scribes (bi-shou), and ten śramaṇas learned in doctrine (yi-xue) served as proofreaders of the meaning (zheng-yi).
From then on, on each anniversary of his birth, new scriptures were invariably presented; he would summon them all to sit and bestow upon them a vegetarian feast.
The scripture was entrusted to the Tripitaka and promulgated. At that time, a Mahāyāna scripture for the consecration of the imperial treasury arrived from the Western Regions.
An edict was issued for Fǎtiān to examine and finalize it. Fǎtiān memorialized: "This scripture is written in the script of Khotan; it is not in Sanskrit.

Furthermore, throughout sixty-five passages from beginning to end, there is no one who poses questions nor any assembly listening to the Dharma, and the phrasing and meaning are incorrect. The Emperor summoned Fǎtiān and addressed him, saying:

To allow such heterodox and false practices to prevail is not the way to honor the Buddha-dharma. It is appropriate that this original text be burned and discarded to eliminate future delusions. An imperial edict was issued, stating:
"I am currently promoting the teachings of the Dharma to bring blessings upon the state and the family. Let all novice monks and nuns from both the inner and outer provinces be ordained.
At that time, newly arrived scriptures were presented in succession; as the Emperor examined them one by one, he said to his ministers:

Tian Xizai and others had mastered the principles of translation. By imperial decree, Tian Xizai was appointed as Chao-san Dafu (Court Dispersing Grand Master) and Shi Guanglu Qing (Provisional Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices), while Fata (later renamed Faxian) was appointed as Chaofeng Dafu (Court Venerating Grand Master) and Shi Honglu Qing (Provisional Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial).

Both were granted monthly stipends of ghee, curd, and cash according to their respective ranks. The Emperor personally composed the "Preface to the Holy Teachings of the Tripitaka" to bestow upon them.

This is placed at the beginning of the new translations. Within it, it says: "The Dharma Masters Tian Xizai and others constantly maintained the four patiences and early on awakened to the three voids.
They translated the true expositions from the palm leaves and continued the holy teachings of devas and humans. Their noble path was reopened, coinciding with the fortunes of the times.

They enriched the five tones within their literary compositions and gave full expression to the four beginnings within the rules of wind and pitch. Their dignified deportment was majestic and serene."

Radiant and glorious, after eons of obscurity and slumber, there was a profound re-illumination. The Gate of Mystery was made manifest, and the sublime Dharma was gloriously propagated as a model for all.

The sound of this resounded throughout the Pure Realm. When the True Sovereign ascended the throne, Chen Shu, Minister of Rites, remarked that the Translation Institute had long been a drain on state resources;
however, the Emperor would not hear him. Furthermore, the Emperor composed a preface and ordered it to be placed after the preface of the late Emperor, following the precedent of Dharmadeva.

I respectfully submit this. In the eighth month of the third year of the Xiǎnpíng era, Tiānxīzāi passed away; he was posthumously titled Huìbiàn, and the relevant authorities were ordered by imperial decree to prepare the rites for his funeral and burial.
The following year, Fǎxián died; he was posthumously titled Xuánjué, and the funeral rites accorded to him were identical to those of Huìbiàn. Shīhù had already passed away earlier.

These three masters encountered a sagely age and were the first to flourish the translation bureau, continuing the resonance of the lion’s lute and bringing forth the sound from the empty valley. They propagated [the Dharma].
In proclaiming this merit, he did not disgrace the sages of old.
As for the two masters Fahu and Weijing, they transmitted the Dharma of Fahu.
They were natives of Central India. In the first year of the Jingde era, they brought Sanskrit manuscripts to the capital and were granted purple robes and a staff.

[He] was provided with silk [robes] and accommodated at the Chuanfa Temple. At that time, Tian Xizai and Faxian had passed away one after the other. Although the work of translation did not cease, there was a lack of personnel to direct it.
After general deliberation, it was concluded that none but Dharma-rakṣita would suffice; he was consequently summoned by imperial decree to fill their positions.

Furthermore, the Emperor issued an edict appointing the Great Master of Sanskrit, Weijing, as Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments to participate in the translation of the scriptures alongside him. Zhao Anren, who served in the administration, [was also involved].
The imperial edicts were equally gracious, and his ceremonial honors increased. He translated over two hundred fascicles of scriptures, including the *Buddhasvayambhū-sūtra* and others.
Together with the translations produced since the Taiping Xingguo era, the combined total of sutras, vinayas, and śāstras amounted to four hundred and thirteen fascicles.

Jing, along with Yang Yi, Director of the Bureau of Secretaries, compiled and arranged these works. Furthermore, he collaborated with Anren and others to compile the *Great Canon Catalogue* (*Dazangjing lu*), totaling two [volumes].

It consists of eleven fascicles. Emperor Renzong bestowed upon it the title *Dazhong Xiangfu Fabao Lu* (Record of the Dharma Treasures of the Great Zhongxiangfu Era) and composed a preface by imperial decree, which was placed at the beginning of the record.
After Renzong ascended the throne, Jing, together with the Hanlin Academician Xia Song, presented a seventy-fascicle work on the phonology and meanings of newly translated scriptures.

Jing further presented two volumes of a catalog for the Tripitaka, which was bestowed the title *Tiansheng Shijiao Lu* (Record of the Buddhist Teachings of the Tiansheng Era). In total, there were six [works].
One thousand one hundred and ninety-seven fascicles. An envoy from the country of Zhulian in the South Seas presented a Sanskrit scripture on gold-leafed tablets.
By imperial decree, Dharmapāla was commissioned to translate it. The Emperor composed a verse in praise of the translated scriptures as a gift.

In the first year of the Zhìhé era, an edict was issued appointing the Silver Light Luòdàfú (Silver Light Luòdàfú), acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmapāla, whose preceptual virtue is lofty and eminent, to be specially granted the title of "Six-Syllable Master."
He was titled Great Master Puming Cijue Chuanfan. At that time, the translation hall had been open for a long duration;

as for the officials who polished the texts, those whose rank and virtue were not both eminent were not permitted to participate. Such as Lü Yijian and Song Shou, and such as Fu Bi, Wen Yanbo, and Han Qi—all were selected from among the chief ministers.
The grandeur of this extensive propagation was unprecedented in antiquity, let alone regarding the Sanskrit manuscripts themselves.
It is extremely voluminous and cannot be translated in its entirety. Yijian and Chou Shou were commissioned by imperial decree to continue compiling the *Fǎbǎo lù* (Record of the Dharma-Jewels).

From the Xiángfú era through the Jǐngyòu era, they had already completed one hundred and sixty fascicles. Upon reaching this point, Jìng submitted a memorial stating that scriptures had been presented from the Western Regions.
The tens of thousands of scrolls, both new and old, and the establishment of the Court of State Ceremonial (Honglu) entail expenses for stipends and salaries; I request that these be discontinued.

Grand Councilor Kong Fudao also spoke to this effect. The Emperor produced the *Jingshu* (Pure Preface) and showed it to them, admonishing that the grand ceremonies of the former reign must not be rashly abolished.
Although the translations did not cease, from then on the momentum slowed considerably and was no longer as vigorous as before. This continued until the reign of Emperor Hui.
During the Zongda era, there was still the Tripiṭaka Master Jin Zongchi, who had struck the *qing* to awaken the monk Ding of Jiazhou;
he served as the oral translator (*yanyu*), while Renyi acted as the scribe (*bishou*). When Zongzheng traveled south to Jiangzhe, it can be known that his translation center had fallen into decline.
Hu passed away in the third year of the Jiayu era; Jing’s place of death remains unknown.
The Biography of Suvarṇasrī (with the appended biography of Master Baohong Huihong).
Suvarṇasrī was a monk from Nālandā Monastery in Central India in the Western Regions. He was thoroughly versed in the Tripiṭaka.
He had mastered the five sciences and was able to recite the *Saṃpuṭa-sūtra*.

Having long admired Mount Qingliang in this land, the dwelling place of ten thousand bodhisattvas, at the age of eighty-five, he set out across the sea with seven disciples. Of these seven, three returned and three perished.
Only Buddhāśrī followed him alone for six years before they finally reached Qingliang.
Whenever they reached the summit of a terrace, he would recite ten sections of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra and practice meditative stillness for seven days, neither resting nor eating.

Each time he entered samādhi, he beheld a city of purple-golden walls, a deep-blue palace of crystal, fragrant waters with precious lotuses, and a shimmering lattice of pearls—an inexhaustible array of adornments.
The youths of the devas played within it. Later, he passed away at the Gṛdhrakūṭa Monastery. The Buddha collected eight *he* of his *śarīra*, which were as brilliantly radiant as pearls;
these he brought back to the Western Land (China). Tang Kuō praised their authenticity, saying: "It is like it; it is indeed it."
Sudāśrī traveled from Western India; he was one hundred and eight years old. His complexion was as white as snow reaching his cheeks, and a verdant luster overflowed from his arms.

While inwardly harboring true compassion, he outwardly manifested a formidable appearance. During the reign of Emperor Min, the skies remained overcast and did not clear; the Emperor specially issued an edict for him to ascend the ritual platform.

The dragon was compelled by incantations to descend to the ground. A saffron-colored *kāṣāya* robe, personally crafted by the Empress, was bestowed as a treasure within the inner treasury. Monks were ordained and a temple was established;

half the people were filled with both doubt and faith. Buddhatabhāra returned once more, seeking passage through the land, to travel and pay homage at the Five Peaks, where he donned the crown of the five Buddhas.
Mañjuśrī, what difference is there? Your face is like the full moon; your complexion is not merely crimson.

The True Man Xiao gazed from afar and prostrated himself (The Immortal True Man Xiao’s skills were difficult to fathom, yet all submitted to his teacher; he bowed his head in gratitude, hence these words).
As for Master Bao and Master Huihong, both possessed a transcendent spiritual nature. Master Bao was born into the Wu clan of Cizhou.

At the beginning of the Dading era, he built Yangshan Temple in Fuyang; its halls and buildings were magnificent and grand, with two pillars carved with coiling golden dragons that left onlookers staring in awe.
Suddenly, someone inscribed a poem upon one of the pillars, which said: "People say the *banjiu* (turtledove) is clumsy; I say the *banjiu* is clever."
"A single piece of firewood, two pieces of firewood—this is the household's property. Upon seeing this, Master Baowu attained great enlightenment;

he immediately retired to the Western Mountains, where he thatched a hut to dwell in and never emerged for the rest of his life. Huìhóng, whose courtesy name was Zǐfàn, while reading the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, came upon the passage:

"When one person gives rise to the truth and returns to the source, the voids of the ten directions all vanish away. He suddenly attained awakening and said: "The Mind-Seal of all Buddhas is originally non-existent..."
"Profound and wondrous! Today I have finally become a man of no affairs. He then went to the Chan master Wen at Heshuo and presented his realization.
Wen approved of it. At the time of his death, he spoke a verse: Sixty years of springtime, now eight years past;
The floating clouds have cleared away, revealing the blue sky. As I depart, I kick over Mount Sumeru; In the night that follows, the moon atop the mountain is even more full.
HŪṂ HALOŚRĪTVAṂ HŪṂ HALOŚRĪTVAṂ.
He was originally from the country of Makutabandhana in Northern India and resided on Mount Kukkuṭapāda.
He recited the secret mantras of all the Buddhas and possessed great supernatural powers; he could dispel illnesses, subdue fierce tigers, and summon wind and rain, which would respond immediately.
Huangtong, together with his paternal cousin Samayasiri and seven others, arrived at the frontier and requested to travel to Mount Qingliang to pay homage to Mañjuśrī.
The court granted their request. Having visited Mount Qingliang, they also traveled to Lingyan Mountain to worship the Avalokiteśvara statue.
They would not cease until they had circumambulated it a thousand times; at every circuit they prostrated, and in every prostration they showed the utmost reverence.
Every day he consumed only one cup of rice. Whenever guests were seated with him, he would distribute his portion until everyone was served, eating only what remained.

He would invariably observe the fast (*upavāsa*) even when there were but a few grains left. Upon first arriving in Jinan, he established the Mañjuśrī-Zhenrong Temple and remained there for three years, presiding over it.
When he reached Di, he further established Sanxue Temple. In the fourth month of the fifth year of the Dading era, he passed away at Sanxue at the age of... (year missing).
63. Yuan: The Imperial Preceptor Phags-pa transmitted [the teachings] to Phags-pa.
He was the one whom the Yuan Shizu (Emperor Kublai) honored as Imperial Preceptor. He was a native of the country of Tubo (Tibet), of the 'Bum clan.
At the time of his birth, many auspicious omens occurred. Formerly, in the land of T'u-pa, there was a state preceptor named Śāntarakṣita who possessed great majestic power;
for generations his lineage was honored by the kings of that realm for seventeen successive reigns until it reached Sa-zhi-sga-ba, who was the master’s paternal uncle.
The master studied under him and, at only seven years of age, could recite hundreds of thousands of words.
He thoroughly mastered the great principles; from his youth, he was richly learned in the five sciences (*pañcavidyā*) and had investigated the subtle nuances of the three baskets (*tripiṭaka*).

At the age of fifteen, he visited the Shizu at the imperial residence before his accession; the Emperor was greatly pleased by their conversation and personally led the Crown Prince and others to receive the precepts from him, treating him with exceptional honor and respect.

In the year Wumu, when the Master was twenty years old, Daoist practitioners propagated the claim that [the Buddha] had converted the barbarians for the Emperor Xuanzong; the Emperor then issued an edict for the Master to refute them.

He was unable to respond, and the heterodox teachings were consequently extinguished. When Shizu ascended the throne, he honored him as State Preceptor (*guoshi*), conferred upon him a jade seal, and appointed him as the Dharma Lord of Central China with authority over all Buddhist schools throughout the realm.
Shortly thereafter, he returned to the West; however, before a month had passed, he was welcomed back again. In the year Gengwu—
When the Master was thirty-one years of age, he was commanded to create new Mongolian characters. These characters numbered no more than a little over one thousand.
Regarding their formation, those composed by combining up to forty-two basic components possessed the method of "rhyme-relations" (*yun-guan*);
those formed by the conjunction of two, three, or four components possessed the method of "syllabic rhyme" (*yu-yun*). As for the essential principle, it was as follows:

The principle of associative phonetics (*xiéshēng*) was taken as the foundation. All [the characters] were created by the Master through his solitary genius, modeled and drawn by hand. Upon reviewing them, the Emperor attained great enlightenment and was deeply pleased;

he immediately issued an edict for their promulgation throughout the empire for universal adoption. Eventually, they became the standard script for a generation. His posthumous title was proclaimed as:

"The One Above All Under the August Heaven, the Great Sage of Supreme Virtue and Universal Enlightenment Who Opens the Way, Proclaims Civilization, Assists Governance, and Protects the State with Wish-Fulfilling Wisdom."
The Great Treasure Dharma King, Son of Buddha from the Western Heaven, Imperial Preceptor of the Great Yuan, was further granted a jade seal to preside over the Buddhist teachings of all nations.
He subsequently returned to the West. In the eleventh year of Zhizhi, an envoy was specially dispatched to welcome him back; he arrived at the capital at the end of that year.
From the princes and dukes downward, all departed from the city by one *śā* to prepare incense altars and pure offerings, bowing in rows to welcome him.
Along every street and thoroughfare he passed, five-colored banners were tied on both sides; ten thousand people gazed upon and paid homage to him as if a Buddha had appeared in the world.
He further expounded the *Tattvasaṃgraha* for Prince Zhenjin, elucidating the treatise on the objects of knowledge (*jñeyālaṃkāra*). Its phrasing was rigorous and its meaning magnificent.
The Tripiṭaka Master Śaraba translated and disseminated it. Before long, [the Prince] again earnestly declined the invitation to return to the West; the Emperor pressed him firmly to remain.
It was not permitted. On the day of Gengchen, when the Master was forty-two years of age, he passed away on a certain day of the eleventh month in the seventeenth year of the Zhiyuan era.
Upon hearing the news, the Emperor was struck with profound grief; his remembrance of the Master’s virtue remained inexhaustible.

He subsequently erected a great stūpa in the capital to enshrine the Master’s true-body relics, adorned with peerless magnificence. During the reign of Emperor Yingzong, an imperial decree was issued for each administrative region to construct a Hall of the Imperial Preceptor (Dishi). It was established there.
The inscription eulogizing his virtue reads as follows: "Now, those who are clever tend to grow negligent in broad learning; those who are noble feel ashamed to ask questions of inferiors.

When one’s talent is high and rank is weighty, they praise themselves and treat others with arrogance—this is the constant nature of men. Yet our Master, possessing the clarity of innate knowledge, served as the Teacher to the Son of Heaven;
he may indeed be called both clever and noble. Nevertheless, he pursued broad learning without satiety and inquired of others without hesitation."
The Elder has a method for which he will travel thousands of *li* without regard for distance.

Whether it be one of stubborn integrity or one of outstanding common ability, if there is anything worthy of being adopted, he leaves nothing out. He possesses talent that transcends the world—talent more magnificent than any other.

He occupies the station of Imperial Preceptor—a position more honorable than any other. Yet, he examines himself against the Way and guides all beings with steady patience, fearing only lest his virtue...
He did not cultivate [the path]. His Way was not expansive; he never considered his many abilities to be saintly, nor did he display any air of self-satisfaction.
He was as vast as a valley, as still as a deep abyss, as distant as clouds and mists, and as weighty as a mountain.
Is this not the Ultimate Virtue? Who else could attain such a state? As for the reach of his Way and the extent of his virtue, they were like the bright sun shining brilliantly.
Heaven’s brilliance leaves nothing unilluminated; its warm and harmonious yin-and-yang energy permeates all things without exception. Its height is like that of heaven—unclimbable by means of steps;
its vastness is like that of the ocean—uncrossable by boat or ford. Yet, without speaking, the people place their trust in it.

Without being exhorted, all things followed him; wherever he passed, there was transformation; wherever he remained, there was spiritual resonance. Were it not for one whose sagehood was as if bestowed by Heaven, who could have achieved this?
The Master’s attendant was named Da-yi-ba. He served as the master of affairs for thirteen years; he followed him when going out and attended him when entering.
He listened to his discourses at his side and observed his virtue and conduct before and behind him. Having been refined and nurtured over such a long period, he emerged as a vessel of great beauty.

Regarding all the Vinaya and Śāstras of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, as well as the secret scriptures, [Ba] received them through oral transmission from the master’s ears and visual instruction from his hands;
thus he attained the ultimate destination of their principles and the direction of their practice. When the Master returned to the West, Ba was unable to attend him due to long-standing exhaustion.
He remained in Tāo, where the people of Tāo were transformed by him. When Emperor Wuzong ascended the throne, the Dharma flourished greatly in Bā and Dào.

Initially, while the Master was in Tāo, he had resided at an ancient Buddhist temple. Upon arriving there, he expanded the temple buildings with imperial donations and intended to spend his final years in Wenshang;

however, imperial edicts arrived repeatedly, bestowing upon him a golden seal with a camel-shaped knob and conferring the title "Great Master Hongfa Pujie (Extensive Dharma and Universal Salvation) Tripitaka. Thus, he remained.
In the fifth year of the Yu era, he passed away in the capital. He was granted state-sponsored funeral rites and burial, and posthumously conferred the title of State Preceptor Wusheng (佑圣国师).

The Vajra Master Champa—translated as "Subtle and Wondrous"—was a native of Tugan Sidamapa in the Western Regions (Xifan). Having lost his father at a young age, he relied upon his paternal uncle. [He] heard...
The sound of the sutras silenced his crying. At fifteen or sixteen years of age, he had mastered all the various sections of both the Exoteric and Esoteric teachings.

When the Great Ancestor was residing at his private palace, he heard that there was a man of great virtue named Chöjé Zangpo (Chos rje bzang po) in the Western Regions and dispatched an envoy to invite him.

At that time, Chöjé had already passed away, so King Kordän (Kor ldan) sent the Master [Sakya Paṇḍita] in his stead. Upon his arrival, the Emperor asked, "How does the Buddha-dharma of your teacher compare to that of my uncle? He replied:

He said, "My uncle’s Buddha-dharma is like the great ocean; what I have received is but a drop upon its surface. The Emperor laughed and looked to his attendants, saying, "His spiritual lineage is extraordinary.
He then prostrated himself and took him as his teacher. From the princes and dukes down to the commoners, all held him in reverence as their preceptor.

Possessing a numinous mind from his youth, his incantations were precise and profound; whenever he offered prayers for petitions, the responses were as swift as a rushing wind or a flashing bolt of lightning.
Inconceivable! At that time, Huai and Meng suffered from a great drought; when he recited mantras over them, it rained immediately. Once, he recited mantras over food and cast it into a dragon pool.
After a short while, extraordinary flowers and strange fruits surged up from the surface of the waves. He took these and presented them for the Emperor’s consumption.

When Yue Moli (Yue Lishi), the Vice Director of the Bureau of Military Affairs, was stationed in Chao, his wife contracted a strange illness for which no remedy was effective despite a hundred methods. The Master simply recited mantras over his prayer beads and applied them to her.
He did not even notice when his illness had departed. During the Yuanzhen era, when Hai-du invaded the borders of the Western Regions, Chengzong consulted the Master;

he performed incantations and achieved victory. Furthermore, by consecrating water with mantras, he raised the Emperor from the brink of death. When the Emperor went on a northern hunt, the Master preceded him in an elephant-drawn carriage.
Upon passing through Yunzhou, he said to his disciples, "There are spirits and monsters here; when the Emperor arrives, there will surely be some slight alarm."

"One should overcome them with mantras. Subsequently, a violent storm of wind and rain indeed arrived; the multitude were all struck with terror and prostrated themselves amidst the grass, yet the one who traveled alone under his canopy suffered not the slightest setback or distress.
Initially, Phagpa had received the precepts from the Master and subsequently became a disciple of the Imperial Preceptor (Ti-shih).

He was by nature arrogant and unrestrained; when the Master rebuked him, he did not reform. Consequently, he harbored a grudge against him. Upon ascending to the position of State Councilor (Xiang-wei), he feared the Master’s upright and forthright character.
Because he was slandered to the Emperor, the Master subsequently went to Chaoyang. Once Xiangge had been executed for his crimes, the Emperor suffered from an ailment in his thighs.
He summoned the Master back to the capital to establish a Siṃhanāda (Lion’s Roar) ritual site within the inner palace; after seven days, the Emperor recovered.
When the Emperor mentioned Xiangge, the Master replied that it was due to past karma. The Emperor, as the state treasury was insufficient, wished to levy taxes upon the monks.
The Master petitioned, saying: "In the past, when Emperor Genghis held the realm, his territories were not yet vast, yet he still exempted monks from taxation.
Now that the four seas are unified and the myriad states present tribute, how could we abandon established regulations for the sake of minor profit?

If their taxes were remitted, they would have peace of body and single-mindedness of will, and might thus diligently cultivate themselves to repay the state. The Emperor was pleased and ceased the matter. (Section B)
No. He was summoned by imperial decree to reside at Daehoguk Inwangsa Temple. In the summer of the *gimyo* year, he manifested illness. The Emperor dispatched physicians to attend to him.
The Master smiled and said, "The physical body is finite; how could medicine possibly preserve it? He then asked those around him, "What time is it now? They replied, "It is noon.

Thereupon, he composed his countenance, sat upright, and passed away. Upon hearing this, the Emperor was moved by grief and sorrow, bestowing upon him agarwood, sandalwood, and various incenses, and a stupa was erected.
He was cremated. After the fire had subsided, when the remains were opened for inspection, his cranial bone remained unburnt, and the number of *śarīra* relics was beyond counting.
A stūpa was erected at Renwang Temple. Regarding the secret teachings of the Western Regions, Mahāvairocana (Dàchí Jīngāng) is regarded as the progenitor;
these were transmitted through successive generations until they reached this Master, by whom they were further made prominent. Thus, he received the title "Vajra Guru" (*Vajrācārya*).
The Biography of Tripitaka Master Fozhi.
Tripitaka Master Fozhi was born into the Jin family. Of four brothers, he was the youngest. From his early childhood, he...

He received ordination as a monk under the Imperial Preceptor Phags pa and mastered the methods of initiation for all the Buddhist tantras. When the Great Ancestor (Kublai Khan) received instruction from the Imperial Preceptor, he resolved to undertake translations with great vigor.
The Master served as the chief editor of the translation team; his phrasing was clear and eloquent, fully satisfying the Emperor’s intentions.

By imperial decree, he was bestowed the title of Dharma Master of Great Eloquence and Vast Wisdom (*Mahāpratibhāna-viśālajñāna*). Commentators have remarked that since the decline of the final age, the translation bureaus had long been neglected.
Those capable [of such a task] were indeed few. Who would have thought that in an age of declining humanity, one would encounter a master such as you?
Beholding his translations, one must call him truly capable. The Master’s Way was widely propagated; the people of Hexi revered him so much that they did not dare address him by name.
Even when referring to his own kinsmen, they would all say, "This is the family of Dharma Master Jining. Such was the degree to which he was esteemed. At that time, the monks...

The offices for the administration of offerings were established, yet the discipline of the monastic order gradually fell into decay. Being unable to serve as a bulwark for the legacy of the Dharma to resist external insults, they instead became a source of harassment and disturbance to the various monks.
Driven by this surging tide of decline, the situation was particularly severe in Jiangnan. The imperial court wished to select capable individuals to rectify this state of affairs.
All agreed that only one with refined insight who understood the affairs of the times, such as the Master, would be suitable for the post.

By imperial decree, the Master was appointed as the General Superintendent of the Buddhist Teachings for the regions of Jiangzhe and elsewhere. Upon his arrival, he abolished cumbersome regulations and strove for leniency and magnanimity; the monastic community found peace under him.
Subsequently, he was transferred to the regions of Fujian and elsewhere. His upright spirit, however, frequently clashed with his colleagues. The Master sighed and said: "Heaven..."
What need is there to speak of worldly affairs, let alone the gates of the Dharma? It is simply that ordinary people disturb themselves through their own ignorance.

Now, the more officials are appointed, the more chaotic the affairs become; with ten sheep and nine herdsmen, who can possibly manage them? Thus, he proposed that they be abolished, and those who discussed the matter praised his lofty insight.

Having obtained this request, the Master retired from his post and withdrew to the hills and mounds, where he built a cottage and planted trees, intending thereby— (Note: The original text appears to be incomplete at the end.)

Thus it ended. Not long thereafter, he was reinstated as a Grand Master of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Guanglu Daifu). When Renzong was still the Crown Prince, he had once approached the Master to inquire about the Dharma.
Once he ascended the Great Jewel Throne, his favor toward the Master became even more profound. The Master was lodged at Qingshou Monastery and provided with a stipend of grain and provisions.

By imperial decree, all the translations produced by the Master were carved onto woodblocks for publication. From childhood, the Master had been exceptionally brilliant; he was able to master the languages of various nations without having studied them. Thus...

In the end, he was indeed able to establish himself. As for his studies, he would recite the words and contemplate their meaning; having traversed the shallows, he eventually ventured into the depths.

Furthermore, he cherished the worthy and loved the capable, being especially adept at adopting the virtues of others. During discussions, he would initiate the topic, and once he had grasped more than half of the underlying thought, he would proceed.
Thus, everything he possessed was achieved through his love of inquiry; it was for this reason that his reputation surpassed that of others.
All who encountered him delighted in following him in his travels. In the tenth month of the first year of the Yanʼyou era, he manifested parinirvāṇa at the age of fifty-six.
When he first fell ill, an imperial edict granted ten thousand *zhongtong* cash notes to assist with his medical treatment. Prince Shen, the Grand Marshal, went to visit him in his illness.
After his passing, another ten thousand cash notes were bestowed to provide for the funeral rites, and an envoy was dispatched to escort his remains back for burial.
The *Guli* states:
"Bilanashi-li transmits Bilanashi-li.
Initially, his name was Jilalavami-di-li. He was from Beiting, [originally] of the state of Ganbenlu.
This person was proficient in Uyghur and Indic scripts from childhood. By adulthood, he had mastered the Tripitaka as well as the languages of various nations.

In the sixth year of the Dade era, by imperial decree, he followed the Imperial Preceptor (Di-shi) to receive the precepts at the Guanghan Hall and entered the monastic order on behalf of the Emperor, being granted his current name.
During the Huangqing era, he was commissioned to translate various Sanskrit scriptures. In the Yanwu period, he was granted a silver seal and appointed [to office].
Guanglu Dafu. At that time, various foreign tribes presented tribute, yet there was no one capable of reading the texts of their memorials and correspondence.
Consequently, Bilana Shili was ordered to interpret and present them all. Once, someone submitted a memorial inscribed with characters in gold;
the Emperor sent for it to be examined, and those in the court were struck with astonishment as they awaited his response. Bilana Shili immediately took ink from the desk.

Having gilded the leaves and carefully examined the characters, he commanded his attendants to take up brushes. He orally dictated the wording of the memorial, the names and surnames of the envoys, and the number of tribute items.
These were written and submitted. The following day, when the officials conducted their inspection, everything matched exactly what had been written.
None among the assembly failed to be awed by his vast learning, yet no one could fathom from whom he had received it.
Some considered it a divine intuition. Later, however, he was beset by misfortune.
The Biography of Fazheng.
Fazheng’s courtesy name was Mengyin, and his style name was Xuejian. His surname was Jiang; his ancestors were from Dingtao in Cao.

For generations, his family had held high rank and official standing. During the Jingkang era of the Song dynasty, his great-grandfather and grandfather fled the Jin troops and moved to Shouchun in Huaixi, where they settled.
His father, De-sheng, had distinguished himself by leading troops to capture Xiangyang and was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Jiyin. His mother was Lady Lu, who was both strict and virtuous.
From birth, the Master possessed an extraordinary intelligence; at the age of seven, he studied poetry, rhapsodies, and prosody, memorizing several thousand words daily.

However, his constitution was frail and he suffered from chronic illness; whenever he fell ill, he would nearly die. A diviner declared that he did not possess the physiognomy of longevity, and so his parents sent him away.
At home, he received the tonsure from the Great Lecturer Wugong at Tuian Monastery. At the age of seventeen, he entered the lecture halls and mastered the essential tenets of the sutras and śāstras.

He established an official lecture series in Jianye, where his reputation eclipsed that of his peers. Subsequently, he went to the capital and informed the Grand Marshal Qin Shengqing and the Prince of Shen;
they invited him daily to enter their residence to preach the Dharma. In the *bingchen* year of the Yuan-ying era, he was summoned by imperial decree to reside at Qingshou Monastery.

He opened the hall for formal preaching. He was transferred to Xingguo Monastery in Yizhou, where, after more than a year, he twice received imperial edicts to translate the twenty-seven fascicles of the *Bodhicaryāvatāra-ṭīkā*.
The Xixia monk Huiceng served as the oral translator, while the Master transcribed the text and composed the literary version. He examined every word three times with meticulous detail.

The editing and revision were entirely the work of the Master. The relevant authorities provided all necessary supplies, and the Master further directed the painters to depict eighty-eight niches of eminent monks within the Baoyun Hall of the Imperial Palace.
The Master composed eighty-eight biographies for them, which were inscribed in gold characters upon the portraits.

Initially, when the examination halls were opened during the Huangqing era, the Mongols and Semu people practiced the three-part civil service examination curriculum, gradually becoming influenced by the teachings of Zhu Xi.
Regarding these doctrines, they claimed that the Buddha’s words were false and delusory.

An imperial edict was issued for the Grand Secretary of the Hanlin Academy, Hu Chengzhi, the Tripiṭaka Master Miaozhao, and the Master [Wang]—three men in total—to translate Zhang Tiantuo’s *Treatise on Protecting the Dharma* into the national language in order to convert them.

When Emperor Yingzong ascended the throne, he intended to cast copper plates for the Tripitaka; however, as the texts contained many errors and discrepancies, he summoned and selected six eminent monks from throughout the empire.
There were ten members for the collation. The Master, along with Zhantang and Xigu—three individuals in total—served as supervisors.

They re-examined the collations made by the various masters and compiled a new catalog. Their rewards were exceptionally generous. During the transition between the Taiding and Zhishun reigns, there were major affairs within the Buddhist community;

the Master invariably participated in deliberations and took up the pen. Later, in the Bingzi year of the Zhizhi era, he received imperial edicts from both palaces and presided over the Southern Monastery.
At the Great Bamboo Grove Monastery, in the fifth year of the Zhèng period (1358), an imperial edict was issued to retranslate the *Bodhicaryāvatāra*.
The Emperor received him at the Dàkǒu Imperial Lodge and addressed him in person, calling him by his title in the vernacular Chinese language.

That same year, the Confucian scholars Wáng Pǔ and Zhāng Láng submitted a memorial detailing dozens of abuses among the monastics and Daoists; the provincial ministries followed their proposals and were about to issue formal documents and proclamations.

The Master refuted their heterodox arguments to refute them, and the proposal was consequently shelved. Furthermore, Tu Yiyi, an official of Confucian studies in Jiangxi, submitted several thousand words;

its main thesis sought to completely demolish all temples and monasteries throughout the empire, requiring monks and Daoists to return to secular life and their property to be confiscated by the government.
The Master drafted an official petition to the provincial ministry to rebut these heterodox views, whereupon the matter ceased. In the year Jiawu, he was transferred to Tan.
At Zhezhong Longquan, Master [Fayan] opened the hall and entered the world; for over forty years, he received the favor and patronage of successive reigns.
At all imperial assemblies, the Dharma Master was regarded as a preeminent leader. Men of noble rank and discerning great figures alike paid him reverence from afar, even before they had seen him.

His fame resounded throughout the world; his inscriptions and commemorative writings nearly filled the realm. By nature, he was brilliant and quick-witted; upon reading a scripture or book once, he could recite it from memory.

Regarding the doctrines of *Dharmalakṣaṇa* and *Dharmatā*, the teachings of Chan and Esoteric Buddhism, as well as the Confucian, Laoist, and various other schools—including the Classics, Apocrypha, Histories, and Records—there was nothing he did not survey.
When he composed literary works, they were refined, elegant, and vigorous, ensuring that he never followed in the footsteps of his predecessors.
This man emerged from his own loom with a flourishing brilliance, establishing a school of thought all his own. His mind was noble and magnanimous, free from the slightest trace of resentment.
Since he took office, although he has administered rewards and punishments with impartiality, he has never harbored anger or nursed grudges. By nature, he is devoid of suspicion or duplicity;
when he encounters someone who speaks a word of inspiration, he pours out his very heart and soul. Upon hearing of the virtues of those junior to him, he rejoices as if they were his own.
Whenever he saw what was unwholesome, he would invariably offer stern admonitions. He studied the Great Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra five times and read through the Tripitaka twice.

Though his age exceeded seventy, he remained self-exerting and tireless; his practice of meditation and recitation became even more diligent. While presiding over Tanzhe Monastery, he strove to restore its dilapidated ruins, bringing the entire monastic complex to new life.
He personally donated over thirteen thousand and five hundred strings of cash from his own clothing and assets.

The records of alms offered from the ten directions total more than four thousand four hundred strings of cash. Through the mutual support of various causes and conditions, this was brought to completion.

Furthermore, he accumulated there provisions for several years’ grain and gathered together monks from all quarters. His single-minded sincerity moved the divine, and within five years, auspicious light appeared seven times;

yet the Master took no notice of these signs, feeling only profound regret that while he propagated the Buddha’s Mind-Source with lofty teachings, those who harmonized with him were so few. The Master—

His writings did not survive as drafts; most were lost and never published. Ge Tianlin, a jinshi degree holder, composed an account of the Master’s deeds and had it engraved upon stone, though the details of his final years remain unclear.
Biography of Ming Xitian Guoshi Zhiguang (with the appended biography of Rouke Balala).
Zhiguang, whose courtesy name was Wuyin, was the son of the Wang family in Wuding Prefecture, Shandong Province. His father was Quan and his mother was Lady Dong.

From childhood, he was exceptionally intelligent; whatever he read, he never forgot. At the age of fifteen, he took leave of his parents to enter the monastic life. He subsequently paid homage to the Indian master Ka... [text fragment ends]
The State Preceptor Bandida Sakya Shri of the kingdom of Śrīmiḷa transmitted the principles of the Indian treatises on grammar and logic.
In the *jiyou* year of the Hongwu era, because his realization was boundless and difficult to fathom, he resolved to travel abroad in search of further instruction;
he journeyed to Mount Wutai and was moved by the manifestation of Mañjuśrī. When the Great Emperor Taizu heard of his reputation, he summoned him.
Upon arriving at Mount Zhong, he was commissioned to translate his teacher Padma dkar po’s *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* for the fourfold assembly of disciples;

its phrasing was concise and its principles clear, earning him the respect and admiration of all. In the year Bingchen, he received an imperial decree to visit Mount Potalaka among the various famous mountains of Jiangnan.
His travels nearly covered every region. In the spring of the Jiazi year, he accompanied his disciple Huiben and others on an imperial mission to the Western Regions.
Crossing a single-log rope bridge, they reached the country of Nepāla (Nepal) in India to propagate the Sage’s transformation.

Subsequently, he paid homage to the Master Makhapūti and received the transmission of the forty-two assemblies of the Vajramālā Maṇḍala. He also worshipped the Jewel Stupa that emerged from the earth. To the west...
The people of the realm held him in high esteem. The Master traveled to the Western Regions twice.

Emperor Taizong Wenhuang, mindful of the toil and hardship of his journeys back and forth, engaged him again in discussions on the teachings of the Tripitaka. Having grasped their profound depths, the Emperor was greatly pleased.

In the year of Yiyou, he was promoted to the rank of Right Director of the Monastic Registry (Senglü You Chanjiao). The following year, he was dispatched to welcome the Great Dharma King; upon his return, he provided extensive counsel and assistance during his audiences with the Emperor.

He was granted books, paintings, carriages, robes, and ritual offerings. By imperial decree, he was assigned to reside at Xitian Temple and promoted to the rank of Right Shanshi. In the year Dingyou, he was summoned to Beijing;
his discourse on the Dharma met with the Emperor’s approval, and he was ordered to reside at Chongguo Temple, where he was presented with the crown of a National Preceptor (Guoshi).
When Emperor Shao of the Renzong reign succeeded to the throne, he conferred upon him the title of State Preceptor of Universal Harmony,
Sublime Wisdom, Pure Enlightenment, Great Salvation, Aiding the State, Radiant Model, Spreading the Teachings, Consecrated, and Vast Goodness. He bestowed upon him a golden seal and ceremonial robes,
and further granted him a peacock-canopied umbrella with gold-embroidered silk, banners and streamers, as well as a silver-plated gold incense burner, basins, jars, and ritual vessels.
He provided him with a desk, a couch, a palanquin, horses, and all necessary articles. The imperial edict stated (as follows). Furthermore, he was settled at Guangnengren Temple.

When Emperor Xuanzong Zhang ascended the throne, he drew from the inner treasury to establish Dajue Temple on Mount Yangtai in Beijing, assigning [the master] to reside there so that he might enjoy his retirement in leisure.
He also issued an imperial decree to the officials of the Court of Ceremonies to ordain over one hundred monks.
He served as his disciple; the master’s kindness was so profound that nothing could surpass it.

The Master then took the gold and silk bestowed by successive reigns, as well as the offerings from the faithful, and commissioned artisans to stack stones and construct a stupa beside the temple, intending to enshrine his spirit therein on another day.
At the beginning of Emperor Yingzong’s reign, the Master’s title was posthumously conferred and he was granted a jade seal and a precious crown.

A golden-woven *kāṣāya*, meditation robes, seasonal garments, a palanquin made of *būrja* palm, a horse with its saddle, and various types of ritual implements. The imperial edict stated (as follows):

"Throughout successive reigns, from the time we encountered the various sagely emperors, the favor and treatment bestowed upon you have been as grand as this. The Master’s character and conduct were pure and simple.

Whenever the imperial court commissioned the performance of great *zhāi* (purificatory rites), he was always sincere and reverent. Each time he entered the presence of the Emperor, he spoke only of benefiting and saving all living beings.

Regarding the ceremonial regalia bestowed upon him by Renzong, he did not use them when entering or leaving the palace. When the Emperor learned of this, he dispatched a eunuch of high rank to inquire about the reason.
He replied that throughout his life he had merely upheld the scriptures and precepts, and possessed no merit from military service on the battlefield.
"As for the honors and gifts bestowed upon me, it is sufficient that I respectfully receive and preserve them; would it not be excessive to put them to use?
The Emperor marveled at this and praised him with words of extreme laudation. As for the Master, he was profoundly proficient in the profound mysteries of the teachings and doctrines.

Among his works were translations of both exoteric and esoteric sūtras, as well as the transmission of the *Heart Sūtra*, the *Eight Branches of Definitive Meaning: The Sūtra of True Names*, and the *Benevolent Kings’ Sūtra for the Protection of the State*.
The *Mahāsitātapatrā-sūtra* was circulated throughout the world. Among his disciples, numbering several thousand, each was guided and supported according to their individual capacities;
those whose reputation for the Way was renowned in the age numbered several dozen. As his years grew old, his wisdom became increasingly refined and acute.

Whenever anyone sought instruction and questioned him, he would explain it with earnest devotion, never wearying nor indolent. Were it not for such long-standing cultivation, how could he have achieved this?

It was indeed so. On the thirteenth day of the sixth month in the tenth year of the Xuande era, he manifested his passing. He exhorted his disciples, each urging them to strive with diligent progress.
When the news of his death reached the Emperor, he expressed deep sorrow and admiration.

He dispatched an official to present sacrificial offerings and further commanded the relevant authorities to prepare the funeral rites, enlarge his stupa, and establish a temple, which was granted the name Xizhu (Western India). Through cremation, he obtained śarīra relics filling both palms, pure and lustrous.
Upon his interment, which was like that of a precious jewel, his disciple Sangke Balai presented his funerary portrait. The Emperor personally composed a eulogy and inscribed it upon it, saying:
"Born in the East, he studied the Dharma in the West. His resolve was firm and steadfast; he maintained the precepts with singular devotion.

His practice was matured in the Vinaya, and his realization was thorough in the Prajñāpāramitā. He attained spontaneous verification of the truth, remaining serene and detached. He served my imperial ancestors."

Traversing four successive reigns and traveling ten thousand *li* on imperial missions, he achieved meritorious service and displayed tireless devotion. He expounded the profound mysteries, for which his jade-like voice was praised by the Emperor, whose brilliance shone like the sun and stars.
His life reached its full span in peaceful extinction; his wisdom was as brilliant as foresight, and like clouds vanishing over the vast ocean, he has passed away.
The moon shone brightly in the midst of the sky.
Sangke Baraza was a man from Central India. While the Master was in the West, Baraza devoted his heart to serving him and never left his side.
The Master took pity on him and brought him along to the East. Emperor Taizong, discerning the Master’s intention, commanded that he be...
He served as a professor at the Bureau of Translated Scriptures. Whenever there were state-sponsored Buddhist rites at the imperial court, the Master invariably accompanied Balaha;

sometimes he presided over the ritual altar, and at other times he assisted in its propagation, thereby exalting the Secret Vehicle (Guhyayāna) and bringing immense benefit to many. By nature, however, he was upright and firm, possessing little inclination toward yielding or deference.
He alone maintained the utmost reverence for his teacher, from west to east, without interruption from beginning to end. In the eleventh year of the Zhengtong era...
At Shangsheng Monastery in Dingzhou, he passed away while seated; his lifespan was seventy years.
[This concludes] the Biography of the Great Master Jusheng Jixiang (with the appended biography of Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna).
As for the Great Master Jusheng Jixiang, his Sanskrit name was Padmasaṃbhavaśrī; he was from Kāmarūpa in Central India.
The people of Vīra were of the Kṣatriya caste. Initially, he studied both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna Piṭakas;

soon, however, realizing that linguistic analysis was not the ultimate Dharma, he abandoned it to practice meditative concentration (*samādhi*) in the Snow Mountains. After twelve years, he attained the realization of *śamatha*.

At the beginning of his reign, he struck his mendicant’s staff and traveled eastward, crossing the Indus River and passing through Gaochang. In all the kingdoms he traversed, kings and ministers alike revered him with awe. All...
Traveling through four seasons of both winter and summer, he finally reached Gansu. Entering Mount Wutai, he stayed at the Shouan Chan Monastery;

the people of Hengshan revered and served him as if a Buddha from antiquity had appeared in the world. In the seventh year of the Hongwu era, the Emperor heard of this and issued an imperial decree for him to reside at Jiangshan.
When those seeking refuge gathered like wind and rain, the Master’s virtue was profound and his demeanor serene;

at the mere sight of him, people were transformed without waiting for him to utter the "kalaviṅka" voice. Although offerings of alms accumulated like mountains, he never once looked upon them, saying, "I have no need for these;

they shall all be dedicated to the two fields of compassion and reverence. The Emperor praised him with admiration and bestowed a poem upon him, which contained the line: "Laughing and conversing as if in the realm of the *Pāñcika* gods..."

When he reached the verse beginning with "If one gives birth to the red lotus," he happened to suffer from a foot ailment that made walking difficult. The Emperor ordered him to receive medical treatment, yet it could not be cured.
One day, he suddenly petitioned to return to Wutai Mountain; the Emperor suspected this was a ruse and thus granted his request.
The Master addressed the assembly, saying, "As for today’s journey to Wutai Mountain, is there anyone who can follow me? A disciple replied, "I will follow."
The Master Qiao, suffering from his foot ailment, said, "Without this one foot, how can you follow me? At noon, he washed himself, changed his robes, and sat upright.
His disciples, understanding his intention, wailed in grief and requested that he bestow some final instruction. The Master held up his prayer beads and showed them to them.
A disciple wiped away his tears and asked, "Does the Master wish for us to recite the Buddha’s name? The Master threw the prayer beads to the ground and sighed deeply.
Upon his cremation, wherever the smoke reached, all became śarīra relics. Those that adhered to the pine branches were like strung pearls.

A stupa was erected at Xilin Hermitage to enshrine them. He left behind three fascicles of discourse for the assembly, as well as a translation of the *Aṣṭāṅga-prātimokṣa-sūtra*, both of which have been transmitted to the world.
Dīwadāsi was a man from Eastern India. At the age of eight, he served his teacher as a disciple, enduring hunger, cold, and toil; his teacher held him in high regard.
Following his teacher, he entered the Middle Kingdom and had an audience at the Shǎng Fǎtiān Gate (Palace of Heavenly Laws).

He was granted a *duòdié* (ordination certificate) and commanded to propagate the teachings wherever he went. After his teacher passed away, Dāsi traveled north. During the Xuāndé era, he resided at Qìngshòu Monastery in Běijīng. Xǐtán...
The Zhe region was secluded and magnificent; to its right, at Longquan (Dragon Spring), he built a hermitage to dwell in. From then on, his footsteps never entered the city or marketplace.
His conduct was extraordinary, and his spiritual realization was vast and profound. On the day of his passing, the hermitage where he lived manifested light of five colors.
Upon cremation, a great many *śarīra* relics were obtained. It is impossible to exhaustively record all the miraculous events of his life; he was truly a magnificent *śramaṇa*.
[End of] Volume One of the Supplement to the Biographies of Eminent Monks;
[Beginning of] Volume Two of the Supplement to the Biographies of Eminent Monks.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Minghe of Huashan Monastery in Wu Commandery during the Ming Dynasty.
Section on Exegesis:
Biography of Dharma Master Zhili of Siming in the Song Dynasty (with the appended biography of Shangxian).

Zhili, whose courtesy name was Yueyan, was the son of the Jin family of Siming. His parents prayed to the Buddha for his birth, and he possessed a spirit and countenance that were pure and refined, setting him apart from the common crowd.
Upon leaving home, he received full ordination and studied the teachings and contemplation under Baoyun, attaining profound understanding and insight.
