He formed a bond with Ciyun that was as close as that between brothers. In the first year of the Duan-gong era, when Baoyun passed away, Zhili succeeded him on the seat and propagated the teachings.
The assembly of students gathered like clouds. During the Shaoping era, the prefecture suffered a great drought. He and Ciyun together performed the *Guangming* Repentance ritual to pray for rain.

They had agreed that if there were no response within three days, they would stop; however, while he was single-handedly making offerings to the Buddha, before the repentance was even finished, it rained heavily and thoroughly. In that year...

He dispatched his disciple, who was like the second son of Kumārajīva, carrying the *Ten Meanings* (*Shiyi*) and the *Two Hundred Questions on Contemplating the Mind* (*Guansin*), to the quarters of Master Zhao at Qiantang.

Initially, regarding the *Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra* (*Fahua Xuanyi*), there were both extensive and abridged versions. Prior to the Jingde era, Master En of Qiantang composed the *Huifui Ji*, which specialized in explaining the abridged version.
He maintained that the ten sets of three dharmas discussed therein spoke exclusively of the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) and thus required no further establishment [of categories].
Regarding the statement that "the *Guānxīn* (Contemplation of the Mind) exists in the *Guǎngshū* (Extensive Record)," this was added arbitrarily by later generations.

The Master [Zhiyuan] thereupon composed the *Fuzōki* (Record for Supporting the School), clearly elucidating the meaning of the *Guǎngshū*'s inclusion of the *guānxīn* according to the Dharma. He asserted that his late teacher’s abolition of *guānxīn* meant that while the teachings existed, contemplation did not.
Both Fàntiánzhào and Gùshān Yuán, who both followed the learning of their predecessors, authored the *Biànyé* (Discerning Errors) to assist [in this matter].

A brief record: This exchange of mutual challenges and refutations spanned seven years. I have now synthesized the preceding and succeeding arguments into two volumes comprising ten chapters, titled the *Ten Meanings* (*Shi-yi-shu*).
Furthermore, I have formulated two hundred questions to further examine them. At that time, Master Juzhao was seated at the head of the assembly on Mount Gu;
observing the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* (the "Ten Stages Treatise") without ceasing, he suddenly informed the Prefect that there had been no official [imperial] decree.

According to the dispatch, he was ordered to return; no further reply was sent, and the matter was thus concluded. In the sixth year of the Xiangfu era, he established an assembly for the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha and the bestowal of precepts, which became an annual tradition.
Furthermore, he composed the *Rongxin jie* (Explanation of Melting the Mind), clarifying the three contemplations within the one mind and elucidating the principles of the four pure lands.
At the beginning of the Tianxi era, he said to his disciples: "For half a verse, one would lose one's body; for a single phrase, one would cast oneself into fire. This is the way of the Sage."
"This is the nature of the Dharma. I shall sacrifice my body to warn against indolence. He then gathered ten like-minded companions and performed the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* repentance ritual.
When the three-year period was complete, he intended to cremate his body as an offering to the sublime scripture.

Yang Dainian, the Librarian, requested that the permanent endowment be used for the propagation of the Dharma; furthermore, various gentlemen collectively exhorted him with great effort to desist. Thereupon, he again formed [a new group].
Ten monks practiced the Great Compassion Repentance Rite for three years to fulfill their long-held vow.

In that year, he composed the *Zhaoyu San-yong Zhang* (Chapter on the Three Uses of Extinguishing and Restoring) and, in response to Gu Shan, expounded the *Chanyi Chao* (Commentary on the Repentance Rite). In the fourth year, Prince Li Zunxu memorialized the Emperor regarding the Master’s lofty conduct and self-sacrifice.

The Emperor praised him with admiration and bestowed upon him the title Fazi (Dharma-Wisdom). Furthermore, he dispatched an inner attendant to Yanqing Temple, commanding that the Three-Day Lotus Repentance be performed for the sake of praying for the prosperity of the nation.
Consequently, [the Master] composed the *Xuanyi* (Profound Record) on the *Avalokiteśvara-bodhisattva-pṛthak-caryā-sūtra* and the *Miaozongchao* (Exquisite Commentary) on the *Amitābha-sūtra-śāstra*.

In the first year of the Tiānshèng era, Tiantóng Néng Chánshī sent a letter discussing the *Zhǐyào chāo*, pointing out that it was incorrect to distinguish between the depth of realization attained by the three disciples under Bodhidharma;
the Master revised this for him. In the third year, he greatly propagated the practice of releasing living beings.
In the fifth year, he composed the *Gōngmíng wénjù jì*, but as his end drew near, he did not complete the entire volume. In the sixth year—
On New Year’s Day, he established a seven-day *Guanming* (Light-Pervading) repentance ritual for the occasion of his passing.

On the fifth day, sitting in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), he summoned the assembly to preach the Dharma and recite the Buddha’s name; then, suddenly, he passed away. He was sixty-nine years old, having completed fifty-four years of summer retreats.

After being left in an open niche for fourteen days, his countenance remained as if alive, and his nails and hair had both grown long. His stupa was erected to the left of Chongfa Monastery in the southern city wall.
The Master composed several dozen works that fully elucidated the tenets of the Tiantai school, leaving no meaning unexpounded.

He was truly a meritorious official among his predecessors and a model for later students. He alone attained profound realization and entry into the *Awakening of Faith*, and thus cited it extensively.
Later generations named his hall "Awakening of Faith" (*Qixin*) to show that they did not forget him.

The disciples in his school were very numerous, yet Shangxian was preeminent among them. He succeeded Fazhi as the head of Yanqing Monastery, and his spiritual influence spread widely. Once, at dawn...
He entered the hall of repentance and saw a tiger crouching before a desk. Xian walked straight forward, spread his *niśīdana* mat upon the tiger’s back, and prostrated to it.
Suddenly, nothing was to be seen. How extraordinary! Thus, one may know the character of that man.
The biography of Zunshi, the Patriarch of Ciyun Chan Temple:
Zunshi’s courtesy name was Zhibai. He was the son of the Ye family of Ninghai in Tiantai; his mother was Lady Wang. She had prayed to Guanyin for a son.
The Great Being was born having swallowed a bright pearl in a dream. When he had grown slightly, he went secretly to Mount Dongshan to rely on Master Yiquan for ordination.

He received the full precepts and studied the Vinaya. Subsequently, he entered Guoqing Temple, where, before the statue of Samantabhadra, he burned off a finger, vowing to propagate the teachings and the practice of contemplation.
In the first year of the Yongxi era, he met Baoyun, from whom he received instruction. Before long, his wisdom and understanding became preeminent.
On the anniversary of Zhiyi’s death, Zhizhe observed the four samādhis as vowed by his master. When Baoyun entered into meditative stillness, the Master returned to Tiantai.
Due to his arduous studies, he fell ill to the point of vomiting blood; he was cured after having a miraculous dream. Subsequently, the crown of his head rose more than an inch.

His hands hung down past his knees, and his voice was like a great bell. At that time, he was twenty-eight years old. The assembly requested that he reside at Baoyun Monastery, where he lectured on such sutras as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the *Vimalakīrti*, and the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*.
In the second year of the Taiping Dao era, he gathered both monastics and laypeople to cultivate the practice of purity with single-minded devotion.
He composed the *Record of Vowing to Be Born in the Western Land*. During the Xianping era, he returned to Tiantai and presided over Dongye Monastery.

Because his disciples were so numerous, he immediately constructed additional vihāras in the western corner and led the assembly in the practice of the *nienfo samādhi*. There was a temple dedicated to a white crane; the local residents held it in great awe.

The Master conferred the precepts upon the deity and changed its sacrificial offerings to vegetarian feasts. In the fourth year of the Xiangfu era, he lectured on the *Mohe Zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation).
At Jingde Temple, while Dao was traveling through Huangyan, a pig ran and prostrated itself before him.
Upon investigating its origin, he found it had escaped from a butcher’s stall; he paid its value and raised it as a pet.

At Chishan Temple, situated by the sea on high ground, there had previously been a strange light at the summit of the mountain, within which appeared the form of a seven-storied pagoda. For forty *li* around the mountain, all were the dwellings of fishermen.

Liang. He sometimes spoke to his teacher, who rejoiced that there were such auspicious omens and subsequently erected a stupa for him. Thereupon, the local inhabitants were moved by his transformative influence and ceased fishing altogether.

At that time, a repentance assembly was being held at Mount Dongshan when a great drought occurred; the Master thrust his mendicant’s staff into a crevice in the rock, and a spring immediately gushed forth.
For seven years, he accepted the invitation from Zhaokong Temple in Hangzhou and extensively propagated the Dharma, drawing a vast multitude of followers. From this point on—

He resided in Hangzhou for eight years. In the eighth year, the people of Suzhou, bearing the official seal of the commandery, went to Kaiyuan Temple to welcome the Master and establish a lecture series.

Monastics and laypeople gathered in full; those who abstained from meat and alcohol filled the entire district. Butchers and wine-sellers could not sell their goods, leading the government inspectors to remark that they had failed to meet their tax quotas.
The Master addressed his disciples, saying: "In the letter left by the Venerable Zhi to the Prince of Jin, there are six grievances mentioned. The first states: 'Because of the *Dharmasaṃgraha*...'"

"Agitating the masses and obstructing official business, I have become an object of resentment for others. My virtue is now meager; how can I remain here for long? He then turned back and returned to Hangzhou.
The Regional Inspector (Cishi) Xue Yan first invited the Master to reside at Mount Ling, which was the Tianzhu Monastery originally established by Zhen Guan of the Sui dynasty.
In the third year of the Tianxi era, Wang Qinruo governed Hangzhou and, finding his spiritual resonance with the Master, petitioned the throne to grant him the title "Tianzhu."

He restored the old name of the temple and re-established it as a center for teaching. Furthermore, he petitioned the throne to designate West Lake as a *fangsheng chi* (a pond for the release of living beings), whereupon the Emperor bestowed upon him the title Ciyun (Cloud of Compassion).
In the first year of the Qianxing era, Empress Dowager Zhangyi, recognizing the Master’s diligent cultivation and spiritual progress, dispatched an envoy bearing white silver.
He was summoned to the mountains to perform repentance rites for the state; thus, the Tiantai teachings were subsequently included in the Tripitaka.
On the night of the full moon during the Mid-Autumn Festival in the fourth year of the Tiānshèng era, cassia seeds descended into the palace courtyard.

The Master gathered their fruit and sowed them beneath the grove, then composed a poem on the cassia seeds. In the ninth year, while lecturing on the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, he suddenly said to his disciples: "In the past..."
While lecturing on this sutra at Dongye, he dreamed that Jingxi handed him a scroll. Upon leaving his room, he saw that the sun had already set.

He thought, "Is it likely that my lectures here have reached their end? Thereupon, he took leave of the assembly and composed a poem titled "Expressing Gratitude to the Three Conditions," in which he spoke of severing ties with his disciples, parting from his friends, and burning his brushes and inkstones.
He subsequently moved to the thatched hall on East Ridge. On the eighth day of the tenth month of the first year of the Mingdao era, he passed away.
He manifested illness and declined medical treatment; he passed away while preaching the Dharma to encourage the assembly. He was sixty-nine years of age and fifty years since his ordination.
On the evening of his passing, those among the mountain folk saw a great star fall upon Vulture Peak.

Four days into the second month of the following year, his remains were escorted to their final resting place and interred at the foot of Moon-Plum Peak to the east of the monastery. When the Master first left the household life, he was a student in the local school.

Admiring the teacher’s brilliance and talent, he was encouraged to turn his studies toward Confucianism. He composed a poem in response to Lu Ji, which contained the lines: "The True Void is the field of selection;
Great Enlightenment is the official rank. Many people recited these words. He frequently practiced *samādhi*, setting a period of ninety days as his limit.
During his practice, he placed heated pans with glowing coals at the four corners. Whenever he felt weary or drowsy, he would dip his hands into the pans until all ten fingers were singed.

Only three [volumes] remain. In the third year of the Chongning era, he was granted the title of Dharma Treasure Great Master (Fǎbǎo Dàshī). During the Shaoxing era, he was further posthumously titled Chanhui (Chan-Wisdom) Confessional Master.
This concludes the biography of Dharma Master Changshui.
Zixuan was a native of Xiuzhou. Since his tonsure, he had recited the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* without ceasing.

Following Master Hongmin’s lectures, when they reached the passage on the two aspects of motion and stillness—“they are clearly seen as not arising”—he attained an awakening. He said to Min: “Beating the air or striking wood still falls within the realm of the trap and the snare;

raising an eye or lifting a brow has already become a matter of conceptual deliberation. Only by departing from these two paths can one accord with this essential principle. Min patted [him on the back].

Thus he sought realization. Yet, wishing to explore the source of Chan, he was at a loss as to where to turn. Hearing that Master Jue of Langye’s Way was preeminent in his time, he immediately went to attend his lectures.
Arriving just as the Master was ascending the hall, he asked: "The nature is fundamentally pure;

how is it that mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise? Master Jue responded with a commanding presence: "The nature is fundamentally pure; how is it that mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise?"
Dizang bowed in gratitude and said, "I wish to serve as your attendant, carrying your robe and bowl. Huairang said to him, "The tradition of your school has long been in decline;
you should rouse your resolve to support it and repay the Buddha's kindness. Do not let the difference in our lineages be a source of hesitation. The Master followed these instructions.
Later, he resided at Changshui, where his community numbered nearly one thousand. He propagated the teachings of the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* and composed a ten-fascicle commentary on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
Wang Sui, the Vice Director of the Imperial Chancellery, wrote a preface for its circulation, which caused the price of paper to rise. He was granted the honorary title "Great Master Śūraṅgama.

He once addressed the assembly, saying: "The Way is not attained through words or images; Chan is not known through analogy or deliberation. To realize the meaning and penetrate the source, there is never any other artifice."
Both schools held him in high esteem. Later, he sat in the lotus posture and manifested illness; he was then interred in a double-layered urn at Zhenru Monastery.
When Wudu entered as an invader, he opened the grave to inspect it and found that his fingernails and toenails had grown around his body; he reburied the remains and departed.
Cong Ya Shaoxiang transmitted the lineage of Cong Ya.
He was a native of Qiantang and was granted the honorary title Fabao. Having initially studied under Haiyue, his mastery of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* (calm abiding and insight) was thorough.

He then said to himself, "To speak of purity while one's conduct is turbid is what the sages and saints condemn. Thereupon, he entered the Tianwang Monastery on Mount Nan and recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

Up to the Five Collections (*pañcanikāya*): the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* constitutes four collections; the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* constitutes ten collections (totaling 5,048 units, which constitute one collection).

Prostrate ten times before a Śarīra stūpa (totaling 84,000 prostrations, which constitute one round). Prostrate 300,000 times before Śākyamuni; prostrate 1,000,000 times before Amitābha; recite the name of the Buddha 50,000,000 times.
Prostrate before the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, performing three prostrations for each character, three times over. This is the aspiration of the mind.

In this single lifetime in the Pure Land, one sits without turning away from the west. The Commissioner of the Circuit, Yang Jie of Wúwéi, composed thirty stanzas of praise for the Land of Ultimate Bliss (*Anle guo zan*) to extol it.
The first stanza says: "The Pure Land pervades the entire realm of sand-grains; why labor to point specifically toward the west?

If one can enter through a single gate, every place is *bodhi*. The Master, wishing to widely transform the secular world, subsequently [established] the [practice] at his own ordination site in Jing...
He resided at the monastery, where he depicted the nine grades and three classes of rebirth and carved their hymns upon stone. All who beheld them were moved to spiritual transformation.
One day, without prior illness, he sat cross-legged and passed away, accompanied by the auspicious omens of celestial music resounding in the sky and extraordinary fragrances filling his chamber.
Shaokang was a man of unknown origins. His surname was Zhou, and he was granted the honorary title of Chan Master Guangdao.

While traveling to propagate the Dharma, he arrived at Jiangling and encountered a monk who said to him, "Your karmic affinity lies in Muzhou. Having spoken, the monk vanished. Shaokang subsequently went to Muzhou, where he begged for food in the city every day.
He would entice small children with money, telling them to recite the name of Amitābha Buddha; for each utterance, he gave them one coin, rewarding them more if they recited many times.
He never lacked for anything. Later, he established a *dharmapūjā* site on a mountain peak; when he recited the name of the Buddha, the sound could be heard for several *li*.
Every time he recited the Buddha’s name once, the assembly saw a Buddha emerge from his mouth. On the evening of his passing away, a light illuminated Mount Wulong.
The mountain colors turned white. Regarding Benru:
the biographies of the two masters, Benru and Zilin, state that Benru was a native of Juchang in Siming.
Initially, he relied upon Fazi to study the Dharma; among a multitude of a thousand followers, he had a reputation for being exceptionally talented.
Once he requested further instruction on the meaning of the scriptures. Fazhi said, "Serve me as the administrator for three years, and then I shall speak to you.
When the service was completed, he requested it again. Fazhi let out a sharp shout and called out, "Benru!

At that moment, the Master attained sudden enlightenment and composed a verse, saying: "Everywhere I encounter the path home, At every turn I return to my native land. That which has been so from the beginning is now fully manifest."
"Why must one wait for deliberation? Fazhi approved, saying, "If I had spoken to you about this earlier, how could there be a day like today?
During the Xiangfu era, Ciyun moved to Mount Ling. He asked Fazhi for someone who could succeed him.
Fazhi said, "You should choose from among the assembly yourself. When Ciyun reviewed the candidates and came to the Master, he said, "This man will do. The Master then arrived at Cheng...
The Venerable Tian greatly propagated the Way of the Dharma for thirty years. His assembly often numbered five or six hundred people.

He manifested the Dharma beyond words, employing the lightning-like faculty of Dharma-wisdom to continue his teachings while seeking out disciples. The Compassionate Cloud (Ciyun) possessed the eye that discerns the Dharma;

there was never a time when his teaching was not Chan, nor was there ever Chan that was not teaching—such as those like Yongming and Changshui. Later, there was Master Gong, who [continued this tradition]. One hundred [years passed].
In his later years, he had a son named Lin. Lin ascended the hall of Master Fuzhi Yu and attained the meaning beyond words.
Consequently, in his lectures, he would only present the general purport and reveal the fundamental principles;

he did not get mired in names and forms, causing those who heard him to suddenly realize for themselves that the Way resides within oneself and is not dependent on texts, yet is also not outside of texts. Although...

Among the veteran Chan masters of great virtue, there were none who did not submit to his influence; upon hearing his cough or his voice, they all marveled at his eloquence and were satisfied by his mind.

Master Dahui Zonggao was particularly devoted to him and once said to the Master, "People of this age know only that my elder nephew has the Teaching (Jiao), yet Jingshan allows that my elder nephew also possesses Chan.
Dahui and Yu were both dharma-heirs of Foguo, which is why he addressed the Master as "nephew."
He remained as the Master. He inscribed his own portrait with these words: "Having realized the *svādhiṣṭhāna-dhāraṇī-samādhi*, I have attained great mastery over all phenomena.
Upon the tip of my tongue, the waves of the ocean surge; I do not deviate from the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

In the spring of the first year of the Qiandao era of Emperor Xiaozong, the Emperor summoned the Master to inquire about the Way. The Emperor said, "I wish to read the scriptures; what is their essential point? The Master replied:
"Vajra-yuga-avataṃsaka (The Diamond Perfect Enlightenment) is the most essential path. [The student] asked, "How does one practice Chan? The Master said, "Chan must be realized by oneself.

[The student] asked, "What constitutes its practice? The Master said, "Purify and quiet the body and mind; after a long time, you will naturally accord with it. Later, on one day, he told his disciples:
"I have served as the head seat for eighteen years, reciting one volume of the Lotus Sūtra daily. In my dreams, I have often seen..."
Since Xian became the abbot, he has not seen such a dream again; one can truly know that his words regarding the harm to himself from leading disciples were prophetic.
After another half-year, he wrote a verse and passed away.
Siyu (Si-wu). His lineage was transmitted from Siyu.
A native of Qiantang, he served Ciyun for the longest period and attained a profound realization of the Way. He once healed the illnesses of others by consecrating water with mantras;

those who came to seek his aid were as numerous as those at a marketplace. During his recitations, both his body and the sacred image he venerated emitted *śarīra* relics. In the third year of the Tiānshèng era...

In that year, Ciyun wished to have the scrolls of Zhiyi’s teachings included in the Imperial Canon (*Dazangjing*). Before Wenmu Wang Gong could report this to the court, Guowu said, "This is no ordinary matter;

I, your humble servant, shall assist you. He then painted an image of the Thousand-Armed Great Compassionate One and recited mantras with a vow, saying, "If this undertaking is successfully fulfilled, I shall burn my body as an offering.
When the Duke passed away, Guowu’s recitation of the mantras became even more diligent and clear.
In that year, he received the imperial decree. The Master was overjoyed; he piled firewood to form a tower and requested a source of flame from Ciyun.

Ciyun took a glowing charcoal from his brazier and gave it to him. The Master reached out his hand to receive it, showing no sign of distress. He then entered the wooden tower. After the fire had died down—
His *kāṣāya* robe covered his body; he appeared as solemn as if alive. Yun then added fragrant wood and performed incantations and prayers as he cremated him.
He was transformed along with the flames, leaving behind countless śarīra relics of five colors. Ciyun composed a eulogy and inscribed it upon stone, saying:

"We, the disciples, have received the Dharma and sacrificed our bodies. The flames were magnificent; the joy was profound. Even as the fire was about to die out, he remained as solemn as if [still living]."
His legs were severed, and when the bones were later crushed, they shattered into fragments as bright as perfect pearls. One may believe such things existed in antiquity, but today they are no more.
At the age of thirty, he was truly a man of integrity.
Huizhou was a native of Danqiu. He abandoned his family to enter the path of the Way and diligently practiced the four *samādhis*.

At the beginning of the Tiansheng era, he gathered ten fellow students to practice the Dharma of Great Compassion for three years; he then gathered fourteen people to practice the Dharma of Samantabhadra for another three years.
At the commencement of the first period, he made a vow before an image, saying: "If these *samādhis* are successfully accomplished, I shall burn my body."
He made offerings as a demonstration of his devotion. Having completed his religious practices, he returned to his hometown to seek the divine sanction of Shen Zhao.

Desiring to fulfill his profound vow, Zhao exhorted both the clergy and the laity to contribute fragrant wood, which was piled into a great mountain. On the final day of the sixth lunar month, Zhao charged him, saying:
"The noble gift of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, you must cultivate; the clarity and obscurity of the *Brahmajāla-sūtra*, you must observe. Let your mind be bound solely to the Dharma-realm."
The body was like fire; thus, this single heap of ashes was the very essence of samādhi. With joyful diligence, he offered a pure and luminous true offering. "Only you, my son, must perform this.
Zhou, having received these instructions, expressed his gratitude and sat upright within the pyre of firewood.

The flames reached toward the heavens, yet the body remained perfectly still without leaning or tilting. The śarīra were crystalline and radiant; all who sought them had their wishes fulfilled. After the fire had subsided, the remaining bones were collected.
He was buried there.
Renyue’s lineage was passed on to Renyue, the son of the Jiang family of Xiachuan, who styled himself Qianfu. Having heard of Fazhi’s transformation of Nanhu, he went to rely upon him.
While studying, he reached Suiryō Bridge (Water-Moon Bridge) and cast his straw hat into the water, saying, "If what I have studied does not bear fruit, I shall never cross this bridge again.
Hōchi recognized his potential and provided him with a residence in the eastern wing of the monastery. During the day, he burned oil lamps to focus exclusively on detailed exegesis;

when the provincial examination results arrived, he threw them all into the storeroom and never once opened them to look. Consequently, he traveled abroad to beg for alms, traveling by boat upon the water, where he lay down and reclined at ease.

He attained a state of sudden enlightenment, as if opening up empty space; even the masts of ships were broken by his presence. Whenever he requested further instruction from his teacher, he grasped the great slipper and turned the great lock.
The assembly stood in awe of him at the mere sight of him. He once practiced the Avalokiteśvara Samādhi together with ten like-minded companions.

Due to his illness, he had intervals of recovery during which he sat in meditation in a quiet room. He felt as if he had awakened from a dream and declared that all he had previously studied was incorrect.
He then composed the *San-shen shou-liang jie* (Explanation of the Lifespan of the Three Bodies) to challenge the *Miao-zong* (Wondrous Doctrine).

As his arguments did not accord with the established views, he returned to Mount Ling in Zheyang, where Ciyun received him as a successor in the Dharma lineage. Subsequently, at Siming, [Zhiyuan] added thirteen "critical examinations" (*liao-jian*) to refute him; the Master, in turn, [responded].

The aforementioned ten admonitions were offered to clear his reputation of slander; this exchange continued without end. It happened that there was an invitation from Zhaokong, and Ciyun composed a poem to see him off.
Half of his disciples followed him on the journey, and Ciyun did not stop them. After he moved to Shibi, he relocated again to Lingzhi.

At that time, Fazhi had already passed away, and the Master, presiding over the assembly, remarked with self-congratulation: "It was precisely because it was difficult to kill the Master of Siming that [the Dharma] flourished—who else could have done so?"

Lingzhi dared to speak out. A benevolent man from Yongjia invited him to reside at the Pure Society (Jingshe), where he stayed for ten years, extensively propagating the Dharma and its transformation.

Upon reaching an advanced age, he returned to his hometown. The Governor of Xie invited him to preside over Xiangfu Temple. Liu Chongguang, the Regional Inspector, submitted a memorial requesting that he be granted the rank of a nobleman’s robe.
Hu Su, the Director of the Bureau of Military Affairs, petitioned for the title "Pure Enlightenment" (Jingjue). In his later years, he devoted himself exclusively to cultivation.
He purified his karma by making offerings with three fingers to the Buddha and maintained the Vinaya with the utmost rigor, never compromising his principles for worldly affairs.
He established the Yilun Hall as a private chamber for his leisure. In the spring of the first year of the Zhizheng era, he said to his disciples, "I shall depart at noon tomorrow.
When that time arrived, he recited a verse and passed away while sitting peacefully. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa to the west of Heshan. This was the Master.
His writings were extensive; he was particularly proficient in the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, for which reason he applied himself diligently to its commentary.

He produced the *Huìjiě* (Commentary on the Essential Meaning) in ten fascicles, the *Xūnwénjì* (Record of Perfuming the Hearing) in five fascicles, and the *Wénjù* (Phrasing and Sentences) in three fascicles. Furthermore, he composed works such as the *Shuōtí* (Explanation of the Title) and various liturgical manuals for repentance (*chānyí*).
For those who follow the lineage of Master Shishi, there are separate records by Kējǔ and Língzhào.
Wéiyǐchuánwéiyǐ, whose courtesy name was Yāxiū, was a native of Púdùn in Qióngzhōu. His surname was Qiú. From childhood, his aspirations were lofty and far-reaching;

he had no worldly attachments or personal indulgences, but took sole delight in Buddhist affairs. He followed these practices spontaneously without being exhorted, and his parents recognized that his spiritual faculties were extraordinary.
He was thus enrolled into the monastic registers of Da-yi Jing-lin Temple and took Ren-putu as his teacher.

He shaved his head and received full ordination, then entered Chengdu to attend lectures at the academy, where he studied the sūtras and śāstras until he had mastered their profound meanings. After seven years, he returned to his former residence;
it was entirely dilapidated and neglected, consisting of only a few old rooms with rotten rafters and broken walls, leaning and leaking, yet he dwelt there with complete serenity.
Among them was Wu Yanse, a man from the local district named Hu Weiyue, who was a man of lofty character and a close associate with whom he shared a deep friendship, exchanging poems between them.
[Wu] had once presented a poem to the district magistrate, Secretary-Chamberlain Sheng Qiao.

When Qiao came to express his thanks, he saw that the courtyards and corridors were dilapidated and cracked, such that they were hardly fit for sitting; he rose to propose that the local people repair them. [Wu’s] virtue and achievements—
After Dayuan passed away, [Huiji] would also compose poems whenever he encountered objects or felt inspired while outside his affairs. His poetic lines were serene, refined, and essential;

his speech was harmonious and gentle, and he never once acted in opposition to others. For sixty years, whether entering or leaving the county seat, he never allowed likes or dislikes to influence matters of benefit or harm between them.
By nature robust and seldom ill, his appearance was tall and imposing, and he was compassionate and forgiving.
He was gentle and magnanimous. People, regardless of their age, all wished to see him. Upon seeing him, they would invariably prostrate themselves with joy;

he would then speak to them with earnest and lingering kindness, offering instruction and exhortation until they were fully comforted before departing. One day, he admonished his disciples: "Do not do evil; do not lose what is good.

Having spoken these words, he drew up his legs into the full lotus posture and passed away. Though they shook and pulled at him, he did not move, remaining as motionless as a carved statue. He was eighty years old.

6. The tenth month of the first year of the Zhiping era. The fourfold assembly constructed a *sūtī* (stūpa) for the True Body and enshrined it within, so that those who come might behold its form and give rise to wholesome roots.
Wen Yuke wrote this elegy for him, saying: "In years past, I once served in the provincial administration and knew the Master very well.
Later, I returned to take up temporary office in the prefecture, and by then the Master had already passed away. On my way home, I detoured [to pay my respects]."
He passed through the town and went beneath the teacher’s stupa. He circumambulated it, gazing upon it with reverence, mourning and sighing in lamentation.
Although the teacher’s countenance was as if alive, the teacher’s voice could no longer be heard. He then composed an inscription for the stupa.
Yuanjing’s Biography.
Yuanjing, styled Wuxiang, was the son of the Xu family of Yushan in Hangzhou. At birth, a fleshy protuberance appeared on his left shoulder, resembling the cord of a *kāṣāya* robe;
it disappeared after eighty-one days. He entered the monastic order at the age of ten and, at eighteen, went to study under Ciyun. He did not... [text continues]
After several years, he attained a high rank among his peers. He subsequently visited Mingzhi, where, during a lecture, he heard the Dharma and was so moved by realization that tears fell like rain;

he recounted this experience on his behalf. In the fifteenth year [of the reign], Lü Zhen, the Governor of Hangzhou, invited him to reside at Beigé. An imperial edict was issued granting him purple robes and the title "Discerning Talent" (Biàn Cái).
During the Jiàyù era, when Shen Gou, a Grand Secretary, governed Hangzhou, he deemed Shangzhushan suitable for the propagation of the teachings and requested [the Master’s presence].
The Master resided there, and his disciples gathered in great numbers. He excavated the mountain and expanded the dwellings until nearly ten thousand foundations were established.

In the third year of the Xining era, the Governor of Hangzhou, Zu Wuzhe, was imprisoned at Jueli; the Master was subsequently summoned for interrogation on the grounds of having cast a bell for him. He was later released and returned to the mountain.
Furthermore, there was a donor with vast resources who, relying on his power, sought to seize the property of Lishan Monastery; the community likewise...
They dispersed accordingly. More than a year later, that person was defeated. Hearing that the imperial court had again summoned the Master, the assembly gathered once more.
Lord Zhao Qingxian, who was a friend of the Master beyond the secular world, composed a eulogy for him, saying: "When the Master departed from India, the mountains were empty and ghosts wailed;
when the Master returned to India, the site of enlightenment shone with renewed splendor. Not long after, he retired to Longjing on South Mountain. Thereafter, at intervals...
He departed, intending to go to Nanping and the ancestral site of Ling Shan to comply with the sincere requests of the assembly; yet in all cases, he returned before his seat had even grown warm.
In the fourth year of the Yuanyou era, when Dongpo was governing Hangzhou, he once asked the Master, "How many practitioners like you are there on the Northern Mountain?
The Master replied, "The secret practices of śramaṇas are numerous and cannot be fully known. Dongpo’s son Tai was four years old at the time and could not... [text ends]

He was able to walk. He requested the Master to shave his head; after the Master had rubbed his crown for several days, he could walk well. Tao Tan, the Magistrate of Jiaxing, had a son who suffered from a demonic affliction. When the Master arrived in Xiu, Tao Tan respectfully invited him with incense tucked in his sleeve. Consequently, the Master followed him on foot to the man’s home. The boy’s illness was at its most severe; the Master sat cross-legged and beckoned him, asking: "Where do you dwell, and why have you come here? The boy replied: [The boy] replied: "I am the Prince of the Eastern Sea. The Master asked, "What is your name? He replied, "My name is Long. The Master said, "Why do you torment this child? He replied, "This child has committed many transgressions in his past lives; I am merely following his karmic retribution. The Master said, "If that is so, you should depart immediately. He replied, "I am not yet finished with my tasks. The Master said, "If you do not leave, I shall summon the King of Hell to bind you and cast you into the boiling cauldron. Upon hearing this, the boy suddenly vanished. The Master then returned to the temple. The next day, the boy was cured. Later, when the Master traveled to Guangzhou, he encountered a great storm. He boarded a boat with some merchants. Suddenly, the wind and waves rose violently, and the boat was about to capsize. The merchants were terrified and prayed to various deities, but it was of no avail. One merchant said, "We have heard that the monk Daoyi can subdue demons and spirits. Let us pray to him. They all knelt and prayed together. The Master then recited the *Heart Sutra* and chanted the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. Immediately, the wind and waves subsided, and they reached their destination safely. The merchants presented him with gold and silk, which the Master would not accept. He said, "I am a monk; I have no need for these things. The merchants said, "We have already come a long way. We wish to offer this to you as a token of our gratitude for saving our lives. The Master finally accepted a small portion of the offerings. He then took his leave and returned to the capital. Along the way, he passed through the territory of the Qiang tribes. The Qiang people were fierce and violent by nature. Hearing that the Master was coming, they all came out to meet him. The Master ascended a high mountain peak and preached the Dharma to them. The Qiang people were moved and submitted. They subsequently sent envoys to the court to report the matter. The Emperor granted them titles and bestowed upon them Buddhist scriptures and images. From that time on, the Qiang people became peaceful and harmonious. The Master then returned to the capital and resided at the Great Zhihui Temple. His reputation spread throughout the land, and disciples from all quarters flocked to him. The Master taught them according to their capacities, never failing to lead them toward the Way. He lived for over sixty years. During the Kaiyuan era, he passed away peacefully at the age of seventy-two. The Emperor issued an imperial decree bestowing upon him the posthumous title "Great Master of Universal Wisdom" (Guanghui Dashi). His remains were enshrined in a stupa at the temple. His disciples erected a stele to record his deeds. His legacy continues to inspire practitioners to this day.
To the east of Kuaiji, on the southern slope of Mount Bian, lies my dwelling. The ancient trees stand in a deep, verdant green. [The Master] asks: "What is your surname? She replies:
"On the mountain of King Wu of Wu, in a place where no one dwells, how many times have I practiced the movements of a dancing waist in the breeze?

He asks: "Are you surnamed Liu? Thereupon she laughs heartily. After a long while, the Master rebukes her, saying: "Since beginningless time, you have been deluded regarding yourself and have pursued..."
Beings are turned by things; they sink into lustful depravity and wander through a thousand kalpas without attaining liberation on their own.
Entering the realms of Māra, they recklessly bring about calamities that extend even to the innocent. You should now know that Māra is not Māra; Māra is the Dharma-realm.
I shall now proclaim for you the secret divine mantra of Śūraṅgama. Listen attentively and take it deeply to heart.

He felt regret and remorse, lamenting his past transgressions and returning to his original state of purity. Having finished speaking, he wept aloud and said no more. From that time on, the boy became peaceful and composed.
Whenever ordinary people suffered from illness or were afflicted by demons, the Master would chant mantras over water and sprinkle it upon them; there was none who did not recover instantly.
All of this was brought about by the profound sincerity of his virtue and conduct. When he was about to pass away, he entered the Fangyuan Hermitage and sat in meditation.
He declined visitors and ceased all speech and food. On the seventh day, he recited a verse to the assembly and then lay down in the auspicious posture on his right side.

He passed away suddenly; it was the final day of the ninth month in the sixth year of the Yuanyou era. He was eighty-one years old, which coincided exactly with the number of days he had worn his monk’s sash.
His stupa was erected at the mountain where he resided. Su Dongpo commissioned his younger brother Su You to compose the inscription for it. The Master’s lectures and expositions...
Without ceasing day or night, he once said: "As for ghosts and spirits, those who do not possess full majestic power cannot come during the day;

only when the night falls and all is quiet can they perhaps hear. He burned his fingers as an offering to the Buddha—three on the left and two on the right. When someone wished to imitate him, the Master stopped them, saying:
"Only one such as I may cultivate the Pure Land practices of the Western Paradise. He never abandoned these for even a moment. On occasion, he would pray to the Great Being (Avalokiteśvara).
He requested the manifestation of light, and the light appeared accordingly. While the śramaṇa Xizhong was facing his meal, he observed that light emanated from between the Master’s eyebrows;
he rose abruptly and grasped it, obtaining several grains of śarīra. Later, people frequently found them at the Master’s place of rest.

There was a man surnamed Li who was eloquent but lacked virtuous conduct; wishing to leave home under the Master, Dongpo requested him on his behalf. Before the name had been mentioned, [the Master] firmly refused.
"Agreed. If he had known this beforehand, the mad monk from Xiuzhou, known as Houtou, would have used heterodox ways to delude the masses.
He proclaimed his desire to build a great stupa to plant blessings for the people of Wu; offerings poured in like clouds.

Fearing that the Master could not be deceived and dreading entry into Hangzhou, the monk first dispatched an envoy with a request to provide one hundred thousand coins for the monks. The Master replied, "I accept these funds for the construction of the stupa as pure merit."
He wished to provide a meal for the Sangha; as the teachings contain explicit instructions, he was not permitted to use the funds interchangeably.
The madman felt great shame and desisted. Regarding Jizhong (繼忠):
his courtesy name was Facheng (法臣), and he was the son of the Qiu family of Yongjia. His parents sought an heir at a Buddhist shrine, and they both dreamed of a monk.
He was given a fine son, saying, "Venerable Luoxi has entrusted him to you; raise him. Upon becoming pregnant, the mother immediately grew weary of meat and blood.
When the child was young, he would invariably pay respectful homage upon seeing a Buddha image. At the age of eight, he received ordination and went directly to Nanhu to study under Guangzhi.

Having become exhausted and ill from his labors, he then practiced the invocation of Avalokiteśvara Samādhi. He was moved by the Great Being’s emission of light, which poured water over his head, and thus his illness—

He was immediately healed. Subsequently, he attained profound insight into both the teachings and contemplative practice (*jiaoguan*). Guangzhi deeply accorded with him and frequently commissioned him to lecture on his behalf.

Upon seeing him, Chan Master Xuedou Xian sighed in admiration, saying, "The Way of Siming now has a successor. The gentry and commoners of Yongjia requested that he reside at the Eastern Pavilion of Kaiyuan Temple;
later, he moved to Miaoguo Temple. When Huian retired into seclusion, Jixian succeeded him and subsequently emerged to preside over the Dharma at West Lake.

In the Ming dynasty, scholars gathered there suddenly in great numbers. Some wished to renovate and enlarge the monastery’s buildings, but the Master said, "The donors are currently receiving their blessings;

how could I bear to destroy them? Every year on the eighth day of the first lunar month, he bestowed the Bodhisattva precepts within the commandery and carried out the rite of releasing living beings.
The gentry and commoners who attended often numbered in the tens of thousands. He would always exhort the assembly, saying: "Upon entering my place of practice, you must take refuge..."

Regarding the entrustment to the Three Jewels: even if one has not yet attained the Way, may one, in life after life and age after age, never lose the human body; may one leave the household life with right view to seek the unsurpassed path;
and may one practice the Samādhis of the Lotus Sutra’s Radiance, Amitābha, and Avalokiteśvara, so that not a single day passes in vain.
He recited mantras to cure illnesses, and his divine responses were unfathomable. Whenever he entered a marketplace, those sitting would rise from their seats and those walking would clear the path;

all raised their heads in reverence, addressing him as "Preceptor of the Precepts. On the eighth day of the tenth month in the fifth year of the Yuanfeng era, he bathed, changed his robes, and passed away while seated.
People saw a crimson light shining through the void, and birds and sparrows cried out in grief, not descending for three days.
Zuoshen was a native of Linhai. He received the Bodhisattva precepts and the essential teachings of the Mahāyāna from Dongye Shenzhao, attaining profound realization.
Shenzhao, before the assembly, rubbed his head and bestowed a prophecy upon him. From then on, he strictly observed the monastic rules and never altered his conduct regardless of the circumstances.
He carved images of the Three Holy Ones of the West and served them with devotion day and night, reciting the Lotus Sūtra three thousand four hundred times.

[He recited] the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* twenty thousand times. In the autumn of the second year of the Shaosheng era, while lying ill, he instructed the monks to chant the title of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* and received the Bodhisattva precepts in addition to his existing vows.
Soon thereafter, he dreamed of three eminent figures standing on a riverbank who called for him to board a boat;
they departed toward the west in an instant. Knowing that the time for his rebirth was near, the Master then ordered the monks to recite the *Amitābha Sūtra*. Before it was finished, he said:
"I have already seen the Buddha’s light," he said. He then bathed and changed his clothes, and instructed those around him: "Do not weep; do not crowd before me.
Invoking the Buddha's name and forming mudrās, he passed away.
Congjian (From Jian). He was a disciple in the lineage of the two masters Xihui and Zuoxian.
Born into the Mao family of Songyang, he was able to recite Buddhist scriptures from memory as soon as he saw them as a child. His father remarked, "This is one who has returned for a second birth.

At nineteen, he underwent the ordination examination on the *Lotus Sūtra* and received the precepts. He visited Biancai, listening to his teachings day and night, and subsequently relied upon Nan... [text fragment].
He secluded himself at Jinshan, where his eloquence in debate flowed like a stream. Nanping sighed in admiration, saying, "The Way shall be propagated through you.

During the Xining era, he lectured at Mingqing, where his disciples increased daily; he subsequently moved to Jingzhu. At the beginning of the Yuanfeng era, Chengru established Shoujing Temple and invited him to reside there.
Three years later, Biancai took charge of Nanping and, considering himself advanced in age, retired to let the Master preside over it.

The assembly subsequently proposed him to take his own place. In the fifth year of the Yuanyou era, when the seat at Upper Zhi (Shangzhu) was vacant, he petitioned the Prefect, Pu Zongmeng, saying, "This site of miraculous inspiration cannot be managed by anyone other than Congjian.
The prefect followed this advice and again submitted a memorial to grant him the title Cidian (Compassionate Eloquence).
In the second year of the Daguan era, he took leave to return to Shousheng. Ten of his disciples, including Chexi and Puming, went to [visit him].

The Master went to inquire after his health. The Master said, "You disciples have come from afar, and there will be no time for a future meeting. It would be better for this old monk to depart while the inspiration lasts.
He then ascended the seat to preach the Dharma, wrote a verse, and passed away.
Xihui was a disciple of the Shi family of Xiechuan. He entered the monastic order at the age of four and, at fifteen, transmitted the teachings and contemplations of the Tiantai school to Guangci.

His fellow disciples both revered and feared him, bestowing upon him the title "Tiger of Meaning" (Yi Hu). During the Zhiping era, he first began to lecture on the sutras at Longping in Jiahe, subsequently moving his residence to Shengguo.
There was an empty room where a malevolent spirit resided; the Master took earth, cast it with incantations, and recovered a fragment of paper upon which was written: "Now I am possessed..."

The Dharma expels it; the power of the Dharma causes it to vanish. It shall surely return again. For several days, it struck objects and flared up fire, manifesting hundreds of strange and monstrous transformations.

The Master rebuked it, saying: "Have you not heard that those who disturb a Dharma Master shall have their heads split into seven pieces? He then extensively explained for them the causes and conditions of saṃsāra.
The assembly of monks recited incantations to break the obstacle. Suddenly, there was a thunderous roar from the air, and a document written in vermilion was cast down, which read: "Han..."
The late hero Shen Guang now knows his error and offers his apologies, saying: "By the power of my teacher’s Dharma, I shall be reborn in the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.
From this point on, he has ceased all activity. Because Jingjue had turned his back on the school's tenets, the Master sent him a letter of admonition in ten points.
Fazhi composed a "Refutation of Slander," to which Jingjue replied with a "Defense Against Slander. At that time, Fazhi was ill and did not respond further. Jingjue remained...
Lingzhi addressed the assembly in astonishment, saying: "It is only because it is difficult to kill Master Siming that who would dare to speak out against Lingzhi?
The Master (Siming) was not satisfied and thus composed a critique and refutation to argue his case to the utmost. Its general outline states:

"Recently I have observed the extensive composition titled *Dispelling Slander*, which purports to 'dispel the two slanders of adding and subtracting' regarding the two bodies of the Dharma and the Response. However, this book, taken as a whole..."

It is worth examining. To speak [of it] again is a mistake. Although your refutation of the slander has already been made clear, your own stubborn adherence to that very slander remains as icy as before.
Now, judging the Venerable’s erroneous interpretation according to the standard of our Patriarch, Jingjue observed: "As for the teachings of Siming..."

He eventually set out on his travels. In the autumn of the Gengwu year of the Yuanyou era, he passed away while seated in meditation. Upon cremation, several hundred *śarīra* relics were recovered. The colophon states:
Although Cibian taught others, he frequently associated with Chan monks. He once sought the Way from Datong, who sent him a letter.
Upon opening the seal, he beheld two circular symbols, one black and one white, and was suddenly enlightened. He replied with a verse: "The black symbol, the white..."
The signs: bearing the shackles and confessing one’s transgressions. Whether it is realized or not, waves arise where there is no wind.
If you ask how the ultimate matter is, Mount Dongting stands upon Lake Tai. The eye of Compassionate Discernment transcends all boundaries.
From this, one may know that those who grasp the true essence of the Tiantai school do not find it within the realm of verbal expression.
Lingzhao’s Biography:
Lingzhao was born into the Lu clan of Lanxi. Having lost both parents at a young age, she requested her elder brother to allow her to leave the household life.

Her brother tested her resolve, saying, "If you can take a rattan vine and tie yourself to it until we both break, I will grant your wish. The Master joyfully entered the forest, gathered rattan vines, and fashioned them into a bundle, which she then placed [around her body].

He went before his elder brother and said, "If you truly allow me to enter the Way, let this [robe] bind me; I shall have no regrets even if both are shattered. Since his brother could not take it back, he subsequently entered Bao-hui Temple.

He vowed to never use pillows or bedding again, instead offering incense, lighting lamps, and performing recitations. Before a month had passed, he had mastered the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Prabhāsa-sūtra*.
After receiving full ordination, he went to rely upon Jingjue at Wuxing. There was nothing, from the doors to the windows of that entire household, that he did not master. At first...
The Master [Zhao] was the Abbot of Wushan Jiekong. He succeeded [to the abbacy] at Jingde Temple. During the Xining era, he moved to Chaoguo Temple in Yunjian.
From the Yuanfeng era onward, every year at the beginning of spring, he established a seven-day Pure Practice Society. Those who participated numbered twenty thousand;

those who attained realization through the practice of *nianfo* were beyond record. He once dreamed of the majestic forms of the Three Holy Ones, who knelt before him and paid homage, saying: "Lingzhao."

Throughout his life, he recited Mahāyāna sūtras, vowing to be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang). When asked whether this was his ultimate aspiration, Guanyin pointed and said, "The Pure Land is not far;

if you have the vow, you shall be born there immediately. He continued to recite the sūtras. One night deep in the stillness, he suddenly dreamed that Samantabhadra manifested his form to him, whereupon he fashioned an image of the Bodhisattva.
He recited the sūtras ten thousand times to adorn and purify his karmic retribution. In the winter of the fifth year of the Yuanfeng era, while lying ill, he said to his attendant:
"The time for my rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss has arrived," he said. Thereupon, facing west and placing his feet one upon the other, he passed away.
During the cremation, a wondrous fragrance pervaded the air, and śarīra relics were scattered abroad. A stupa was erected in the southeast corner of the monastery courtyard.
Ji’er, who could serve as a master for the two aforementioned masters, was a native of Ning in Mingzhou.
He received his training at Yan-shou Monastery on Mount Fuquan under Master Ming-zhi.

Residing at Nanhu, he followed his teacher’s instruction and attained realization regarding the principles of the teachings and contemplation (*jiaoguan*). At the beginning of the Yuanfeng era, he devoted himself exclusively to the practice of Pure Land, saying to his fellow practitioners:
The Samādhi of Buddha-Recollection is the essential method for rebirth in the Pure Land.

He then burned three fingers and constructed the Hall of the Sixteen Contemplations, wherein he installed the Three Sages of the Western Paradise surrounded by lotus ponds. Once this work was completed, he again burned three fingers; thus, those practitioners who cultivate the contemplations...

There was something upon which he relied. In the fourth year of the Jianyan era, the Jurchen invaders attacked Mingzhou. The monks of the temple fled in all directions, but the Master alone did not leave.
When the raiders suddenly arrived, they rebuked him, saying, "Are you not afraid of death? The Master replied, "This poor monk’s lifelong vow."
He built this meditation hall; now that he is old, he cannot bear to leave it behind in his search for life.

The chieftain of the barbarians admired him and said to him, "For my sake, go back to the northern lands and build a meditation hall according to these same regulations. He then compelled the Master to depart.

Later generations, mourning his memory, established the day of his departure as an anniversary of remembrance (*jì*). They honored him from afar as "Venerable Dhyāna-Wisdom" (*Dinghui Zunzhe*), though the details of his [subsequent] life remain unclear.

Zhongneng, the Master, was a native of Jiahe. From his youth, he studied under the Buddha (Nengren). He entered the hall of repentance for forty years, practicing the path during the six periods of the day without ceasing even when ill.
It was only after several days of fasting that his illness healed spontaneously. Consequently, his reputation as a practitioner spread throughout Jiangzhe.
As he grew old, he read texts as if he were a beginner. Cao’an teased him, saying, "Have you not yet forgotten the trap? The Master replied, "What trap should I forget?
Cao’an was deeply ashamed. Once, while sunning his clothes during the summer heat, he sighed, "A man of such noble spirit, yet reduced to being like a slave."

Thereupon, he dispersed his remaining belongings and retained only a single tattered cotton robe. In the summer, he would hang it between the beams and rafters, and enter the forest bare-shouldered to ward off mosquitoes.

One day, he encountered two tigers; he approached them with his body, and the tigers lowered their heads and departed. A mountain deity frequently provided offerings for him, and they were often seen interacting.
Once, when the Xiangji Monastery was short of supplies, the administrative official came to inform him, but the Master resolutely refused.

The next morning, Shi arrived of his own accord. Everyone said, "Last night, a traveler passed by our door and informed us; we have only now learned that the mountain deity has taken the Master to Yuanjue Monastery.
Master Ci has received the command of Cien, and the Master, together with Wen the Head Seat, burned their fingers to request [his presence].
When he arrived, they requested instruction day and night, and there was great awakening and development. It is not known how it ended.
Regarding the masters Chuxian and Chuxian: Master Chuxian was transmitted [the lineage] by [Master] Chuxian.

He was born into the Wang family of Tiantai. At the age of seven, he entered Guoqing Monastery; at fourteen, he received full ordination. He studied with great diligence until there was no one who could rival him.
In the third year of the Tianfeng era, he had finished reading the entire Tripitaka. He visited Shenzhao and attained a profound realization of the doctrinal principles. By nature, he was respectful.

He remained silent and withdrew in humility. Shenzhao then feigned illness, and the command was passed to Xuanshuang. As soon as the assembly heard this, they were won over in their hearts. Initially, he resided at Chongshan on Mount Chicheng.
When Li Tingzhi was the governor of Tai, he dreamed of a divine being who said: "You govern Tiantai; beneath the Five Patriarchs’ Terrace there is a monk named Longtou Jiujiu.
You should go to see him. Li consulted his advisors but could not understand the meaning. A man of discernment said to Li:

The fifth patriarch of Tiantai once resided at Mount Chicheng; now Master Xian resides here. He was born on the ninth day of the ninth month of the Bingchen year—is this not what is meant by the "nine-heads of the dragon"?
Li Da’uo immediately ordered his carriage to visit the Master and engaged him in conversation regarding the supramundane path, finding profound resonance with his teachings.
As the temple buildings were cramped and dilapidated, he planned to relocate them; Li donated ten *jin* of gold for the purpose.

The ground opened up toward the southeast, and a bronze *qing* gong was recovered from within the earth. He succeeded [his predecessor] as the master of the White Lotus Society. The Master resided in the mountains for fifty years;
those who came to his gate to receive the Way numbered in the tens of thousands. In the first month of the first year of the Yuanyou era, when the Dharma drum was struck, it did not sound.
The Master said, "I am about to depart. At the hour of the morning bell, he passed away peacefully.
Chuchu was born into the Pan family of Yongjia. He remained in the womb for three years and entered the monastic life at the age of nine.

He visited Shenzhao, through whom he clearly understood the principles of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching. Thereupon, he burned off three fingers as an offering to the Buddha, praying for wondrous enlightenment. Before long, he was promoted to the position of First Seat.

Shenzhao presented him with a volume of the *Zhi guan* (Stopping and Contemplation) and said to him, "You shall establish the great banner of the Dharma; it is my regret that I shall not live to see it."

Later, he presided over several major monasteries (*mahāvihāra*), and his spiritual influence flourished and spread far and wide. The Emperor bestowed upon him the title "Divine Enlightenment" (*Shenwu*).

Prime Minister Wang Anshi and the eminent officials of the time vied with one another to compose songs and poems to praise his virtue. During a severe drought in the prefecture, the Master went to the Dragon Pool (*nāga-taṭāka*).
He spoke in the language of dragons. Suddenly, a great wind and black clouds rose from the pond, and torrential rain poured down.
Throughout forty years, the Master sat in the Dharma hall ten times, preaching and chanting without weariness. Those who entered his gate to receive the Dharma numbered three thousand.

In the fourth month of the year Yimao of the Xining era, he gathered the assembly to recite the *Samantabhadra-caryā-praṇidhāna* and the *Sukhāvatī-vyūha Sūtra*. He then said, "I have attained the state of non-arising."

He had practiced for a long time. Now, through the realization of non-arising (*anutpāda*), he was born into the Pure Land and subsequently entered quiescence. His disciples enshrined his entire body in a stupa.
Yang Wuweī composed an inscription for it. The Master and Xian were both disciples of Shenzhao; people called them "the two from the same body within the gate of Shenzhao."
Huiben (Hui-bian),名思義 (Siyi), was known as Hui-bian.
His courtesy name was Nüweng, and his style name was Haiyue. He was the son of the Fu family of Huating. From birth, he was exceptionally gifted;

his parents sent him to Puzhao Monastery to enter the monastic order. Initially, he traveled to study at Tianzhu, where he sought instruction from the master Mingzhi. He devoted himself wholeheartedly to the teachings and contemplative practices (*jiaoguan*).
When Zhijiang was about to grow old, he entrusted the succession to Shu for eight years and subsequently passed on his seat to him.

It happened that Shen Shiqing of the Hanlin Academy was governing Hangzhou with such severity and ferocity that all who saw him were struck with terror and lost their composure. Yet when the Master faced him, he remained as relaxed and composed as if they were old acquaintances.

Shen Yizhi marveled at him and appointed him as the Metropolitan Superintendent of Monks (*du-sengzheng*). At that time, Dongpo, serving as Vice-Governor of Hangzhou, composed a preface to see him off.

The Master’s deportment was upright and serene; he did not accumulate any superfluous possessions. When thieves entered his quarters at night, he stripped off his robes and gave them away, directing them to take a side path to escape.
He lectured and taught for twenty-five years, with students often numbering over a thousand. In his later years, weary of the bustle, he [addressed] the six matters...
He followed his belongings back to hide away in the thatched hall. As he was about to pass into nirvana, he left a final instruction stating that the coffin must not be closed until Dongpo arrived.
Four days later, when Dongpo arrived, he saw him sitting upright as if alive, with the crown of his head still warm. He then composed three verses to mourn him, saying:
Seeking his traces, I force my robes to dampen; originally unborn, there is nothing to be forgotten.
Tonight, on Master Seng’s lecture hall, the moon fills the courtyard, cold as ever like frost. Birth and death are like the bending and stretching of an arm;
our deep attachment to this world brings but a single pang of bitterness. I am no guest of Penglai; I rely upon the Western Paradise as my host. I wish to visit the drifting clouds...
The cause of arising and ceasing is non-existent; yet one sees the body within a dream. Rest your mind and dwell well, Wang Wendu;
why need you ask others about this principle?
Siyi, whose courtesy name was Hefu, emerged from the gate of Mingzhi together with Haiyue; they were brothers in the Dharma. Zhi once...

He drew back the curtain and presented ten questions; the Master answered them all, and they were in accord with the essential meaning. When Huizhi retired to the thatched hall, the assembly escorted the Master into his room.

Once the crowd had dispersed, the Master remained standing in attendance. Huizhi asked, "What did you just see? He replied, "I saw the great assembly bowing and then withdrawing. Huizhi said, "Come, let me tell you:
you shall travel, but you must eventually dwell on this mountain and propagate the Great Teaching. You too shall come here in the future."

While residing in this chamber, it was not long before Chancellor Su Song, as Governor of Hangzhou, invited him to reside at Tiantzhu. He propagated the Way for twenty-three years and then retired to the Cottage of Grass;
all these events occurred exactly as recorded in Zhi’s chronicle. In the fourth year of the Xining era, he was granted purple robes and the title Jinghui (Pure Wisdom).
On the eighteenth day of the second month in the third year of the Yuanyou era, he took leave of the assembly and passed away while sitting peacefully.

After the community had been chanting for a long time, he suddenly spoke again, saying: "I was accompanying Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva when I saw a śramaṇa with a golden complexion and a tall, long body whose arms hung down to his knees.
He said to me, 'Your karmic conditions are not yet exhausted; after seven days have passed, I shall send someone to welcome you. On the twenty-fifth day, [he spoke] again."
He passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture.
The two masters Jingfan and Qiyu transmitted the lineage from Jingfan. Jingfan was a native of Jiahe;

his surname was Zhu (written with the radical for "grass" [竺], "two" [二], and "dàn" [亶]). His mother was Lady Gong. She dreamed that the light of the Buddha filled her room, and she subsequently conceived. Upon his birth...

He was named Fohu because of this. At the age of ten, he left home to become a monk. He would often meditate on Amitābha Buddha. When someone asked him, "At such a young age, why do you act so urgently?
the Master replied, "I wish to go to another region to seek lodging. At eighteen, he received full ordination and followed Master Zhan of Chaoguo.
He later visited Shenwu, attending his lectures repeatedly; these deeply accorded with his long-held aspirations. At the beginning of the Yuanyou era, he presided over...
Gucuo Daci lectured on the Three Great Treatises more than ten times; other records state the same. Those who received the precepts from his teacher nearly filled the city and its suburbs.
He once led twenty-seven people to practice the Lotus Samādhi for a period of twenty-eight days, doing so three times in succession.
He was moved by the Great Being Samantabhadra bestowing the *karmavācanā* for the precepts, which reached the point of being compared to the Pure Brahmā.

At Mount Qiu, his great voice resounded like the striking of a massive bell. At the place where Master [Fahai] practiced dhyāna and contemplation, the assembly often saw a deity in golden armor kneeling before his seat.
On one occasion, while performing a rite of repentance at a certain location, they saw the Deity Wei (Weitian) inspecting the hall of confession.
Whenever a practitioner was scrutinized by him, the deity would immediately shield them and withdraw. During the Zhenghe era, a maidservant of Governor Ying...
He was afflicted by a malevolent spirit that caused him to sing and laugh incessantly. When he requested the Master to bestow the precepts, his spirit immediately became settled.
A laywoman named Ge invited the Master to bestow the precepts for her deceased husband; she then saw her husband circumambulate the Master’s seat, proclaiming that he had attained liberation.

Once, while staying at the Western Monastery during the peak of summer, the heat was so intense that the assembly could not sleep peacefully. The Master was just then wearing his three robes and sitting atop a water pavilion when suddenly a wind and snow began to blow.
They flew and gathered together, their coolness overwhelming those nearby. In the morning, he said to the assembly, "The seasonal influence of winter is prevailing during the summer.

The assembly all sighed in admiration, realizing that a divine dragon had provided protection, transforming the heat into coolness. At the beginning of the Xuanhua era, the Prefectural Governor, Lord Jia, revered the Master’s noble conduct.
Bǔ served as the Dharma Master of Guǎnzhōng.
Qíyù was a native of Xièchuān and a descendant of the Minister Mò Gōng. From an early age, he devoted himself to Buddhist studies, memorizing several thousand words daily.

He frequently attended upon enlightened masters. One day, when it was his turn to serve as the presiding monk (*sēngcì*), he declined the honor. When someone asked him the reason for this, he replied:

Truly, he did not wish to sacrifice a day’s worth of spiritual merit for the sake of five thousand in profit. Residing at Baozang on Mount Tiao, he regularly established a society for the cultivation of pure karma at the end of each year.
Later, moving to Mount Xiangshan, he erected a sixteen-foot statue and led both monastics and laypeople in spiritual practice.
In the middle of the night, he addressed the assembly, saying: "Before we practiced the mindfulness of the Buddha, our minds followed after sensory objects and committed various unwholesome deeds.

For even a single *dūṣaṇa* offense (*duṣkṛta*), one must undergo the sufferings of hell for nine hundred thousand years; how much more so for the grave offenses of the various categories and clusters [of precepts]?"
If one now recollects the Buddha, a single thought-moment can extinguish the sins of birth and death accumulated over eighty-one kalpas;

how much more so when one’s own parents have given birth to them and enabled them to leave the household life? By principle, they ought to deliver and liberate their parents to repay such profound kindness.

If one now breaks the precepts and falls into ruin, would not one’s parents be filled with disappointment? Upon hearing this, the great assembly all responded with sincere repentance. Thus it was raised.

He threw himself down so violently that he injured his forehead and lost his voice. Once, in the middle of the night, while circumambulating an image with his head bowed, he happened to encounter a monk who had violated the rules.
He rebuked him, saying, "You are ignorant; you are nothing but a beast. Later, he repented, saying, "Although he was unworthy, to curse him as a beast brings disgrace upon the Triple Gem.
From then on, for three years, he confessed his transgression before the Buddha. During a great drought that year, the wells ran dry.
The Master performed secret prayers. He dreamed that water emerged from the western slope; at dawn, he dug there and a clear stream gushed forth. Consequently, it was named Dream Spring (Mèngquán).
The two masters passed away together in the first year of the Jiàn'ān era.
Congyi (with Rui appended). Congyi was a native of Pingyang in Wenzhou. His surname was Ye.
At the age of seventeen, he mastered the sutras and received ordination. He studied to support the school and attained a profound understanding of its tenets.

Throughout his career, he successively presided over several major monasteries. In his later years, he took charge of Shousheng Monastery in Xiuzhou, where he extensively propagated the school’s teachings. This was the Master.

Although he took the Perfect and Sudden [Teachings] as his gateway, he remained scrupulously earnest regarding the precepts. During the six periods of the day and throughout the three modes of action, he ensured that every detail was performed in accordance with the Dharma.
The Imperial Commissioner Liu Tao recorded the Master’s conduct, saying: "His precepts were upright and pure; he did not associate with others frivolously.

He contemplated the Three Contemplations while awake and asleep, and was devoted to the savoring of his writings. He did not eat after noon, and he spoke nothing that was not in accord with the Dharma."
He did not lie on his right side. He would not drink water that had not been filtered. He was mindful as he walked. He sat and stood like a tree planted in the earth.
He never sought the recognition of high officials; he may truly be called a worthy man. Xiu belonged to the gentry class and requested the Master to pray for his illness.

The Master commanded his disciple Liao Rui to attend him on the journey. Upon his return, the Master assumed a stern expression and rebuked him, saying: "You are pure and sincere; it is for this reason that I..."

"I shall take you with me. Why do you look left and right at the houses of the laity? Zhirui merely apologized for his transgression. Such was his rigorous and cautious conduct in governing himself and regulating others.
In the spring of the sixth year of the Yuanyou era, he passed away. His śarīra were enshrined as relics in the Baozang Stūpa in Qiantang.
He was posthumously titled Shen-zhi (Divine Wisdom). The Master composed more than ten works totaling tens of thousands of words, all of which were exegeses on doctrinal meanings.
Liao Rui was a man of outstanding talent. There was also a Daoist from the Wang family of Sishi who requested Rui to perform a ritual for his deceased daughter’s consecrated food.

It happened that the river ice prevented a boat from crossing; the Daoist then sent someone to inform him, instructing him to set up the seat before the *hu* (measuring vessel) and [perform the rite] from the boat at a distance.

He performed a prayer of benediction for her. When he had finished, a woman suddenly appeared at the boat. She prostrated at his feet in thanks and said, "I have already attained rebirth in a higher realm;

therefore, I leave this object as a token. Suddenly, she vanished. The next day, when Master Wang arrived at the boat, he saw the object and said in astonishment, "This was the very item used by the deceased girl when she was placed in her coffin."
The Biography of Master Yuanming Yan: Yan was the son of the Zhang family of Tianpeng. From childhood, he was valiant and heroic; he could not endure remaining in the secular world.
At fifteen, he left home and served Master Baofan Zhaofu of Chengtian Monastery. Zhaofu prophesied of him, saying: "This boy shall one day become a dragon-elephant within the Dharma."
At twenty, he recited the sutras, shaved his head, and received the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra* from Jìjìng. After Jìjìng passed away, he completed his studies under Wéifèng Wénzhāo.
He received the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, the *Awakening of Faith*, and the *Treatise on the Awakening of Faith* from Xuǎngān;
the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and the *Treatise on the Hundred Dharmas* from Yǎnqìng. All of these masters were renowned for their fame.
It was said that the Master would not rest until he had perfectly mastered the essential style of his tradition. Furthermore, he studied under various Confucian scholars;

there were no scriptures he did not examine and no literary compositions he could not master. When Lord Zhao Qingxian invited the Master to ascend the Dharma seat, he expounded upon the definitive meaning of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* with such clarity as if pointing at one's palm.
Those who heard him were like those drinking fine wine—there was none who did not become intoxicated. Having thus...

In this sutra, his mind merged with its form and interpretation; he further delved into both internal and external classics as freely as the wind blowing or lightning flashing, reaching his destination according to his will.

Furthermore, he once sought the Way from the Chan masters Weidi and Weisheng. The masters remained silent but granted him their approval in their hearts, saying, "This person is naturally within our own sphere of practice.
He also fashioned a transformative image of Mahākāruṇika Avalokiteśvara and enshrined it within a majestic pavilion that reached toward the heavens.
