Using inferior craftsmen and precious materials, it took more than twenty years to complete. People regarded it as the pinnacle of magnificent adornment, unaware that it was merely the Master’s playful diversion.

In his middle years, he took delight in Ge Hong’s *Baopuzi Neipian* and invited men of extraordinary and eccentric talents, intending to use cinnabar and minerals to subjugate substances and transform them all into gold.
Some would take the gold and desert him; the Master neither regretted nor became angry. At other times...
Whenever he encountered him, he treated him as he had at first; through this, one may observe his virtuous nature.

After Bao Fan had passed away and his two parents had grown old, he anticipated their departure from this world and traveled south, saying: "I have heard that in the South there is a Great Being who is like Zu Xin."
There was Ruo Ke and Ruo Shanben; both were men of extraordinary character and near-sages. One must certainly go to observe their realization of the Way.
In the third month of the third year of the Yuánfú era, while traveling through Róngzhōu, he stayed at Juelín Chányuàn in Yúzhōu.
He transformed others without haste. He had thirty-seven years of seniority as a monk. His dharma-sons enshrined their master’s remains to the west of the Baofan Pagoda;
though they were resolute, their purpose was not fulfilled, for he was suddenly cut short by his allotted lifespan. How lamentable!

He was instructed to practice contemplation after contemplation. He was the son of the Huang family of Putian; he left home at the age of thirteen at Guanghua Temple and received full ordination at eighteen.

He mastered various texts such as the *Book of Changes*, the works of Mencius, and those of Zhuangzi and Laozi, but subsequently set them aside. Thereafter, he listened to lectures on Mahāyāna sūtras and śāstras. One day, while reading the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*...

Upon reading the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, he was struck with a sudden and profound awakening and exclaimed: "The world merely transmits that in former years there was a Guifeng of the *Awakening of Mahāyāna* (Yuánjué);

who would have known that today there might not be a 'Me' of the *Śūraṅgama*? Not long after, he obtained the An-yang Cloister of the monastery; there he broke his staff, walled up his door, and took up residence.
He maintained a standard of simple and unadorned purity, and throughout the day his speech never strayed from the truth. Unless driven by necessity, he would often remain in silence until the end.
Throughout his life, he never leaned against the gatepost waiting for his son’s return. He perused the Tripitaka several times; though advanced in years, he applied himself with even greater vigor.

By nature, he was profoundly compassionate, taking pity on the sick and hastening to aid those in distress or poverty. Whether it was consecrating food or releasing captive creatures, there was nothing he would not do.

When his resources were insufficient, he would readily pawn his own clothes without a hint of reluctance. For fifty years, he served the Buddha with morning incense and evening lamps, never driving away mosquitoes.
He would not scratch away the lice that were starving, nor did he take it upon himself to correct the assembly. Someone once teased him, saying, "How weary you are!
Look at what you are doing. The Master replied, "I am not weary; I am simply afraid that by sitting here, I shall become weary.
His subtle intentions for warning others were like this. Suddenly, one day, he manifested illness and said to his disciples, "The Six Honored Ones will soon pass by."

I hurriedly prepared tea and fruit. The assembly suspected that the Master was delirious with illness, yet his words were clear and unconfused. Shortly thereafter, a person arrived from afar carrying a statue;
upon examining its features, it was precisely the Sixth Patriarch, the Golden-Robed Arhat. That night he bathed;

at dawn, having changed his robes and spread his seat, he took leave of the assembly, exhorting them not to fail the Buddhas and Patriarchs. Having finished speaking, he struck his palms together and passed into stillness. This was indeed...
This was in the eighth month of the third year of the Yuanyou era. He lived to the age of ninety-one, with seventy-three years of monastic seniority (*bhikṣu-vaṣa*).
Three days after his passing, the crown of his head remained warm. He was cremated on a northern ridge of the monastery; as the fire spread, a wondrous fragrance issued forth.

Among the ashes, they recovered his tongue-root, which had not been destroyed. His disciples enshrined it in a stupa. At night, there was a brilliant light that shone from the site of the cremation all the way to the stupa, appearing as if it were traveling back and forth between them.

Three days later, silver and gold-colored śarīra appeared for a circumference of over five li. Every blade of grass and every piece of wood, even a foot or an inch in size, all emitted brilliant light.

Whether it was uprooted stones or excavated earth, there was nothing that did not partake of this phenomenon, yet it was inexhaustible. Neighboring residents went so far as to take them to sell for their own use.
How extraordinary! How magnificent! From this, one can know the reality of the Master’s lifelong meritorious conduct and the substance of his spiritual cultivation.
Chengjue (Huiwu) was a native of the Zhang family of Dazhou.
While still learning to speak, he was able to recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*; his parents marveled at this.
He escorted him to Sahnju Hermitage. Master Hei was a youth at that time; his reputation for the Way was already brilliant, and he was granted the honorary title of Great Master Ciui.
He later moved to Qingliang Temple. Because Master Ciui had personally attended to him for a long time, he recognized in his heart that he was a vessel of the Dharma.
One day he said to him: "The ancients called those who leave the household life 'great men' (*mahāsattva*). There are four matters by which one becomes a great man:
drawing near to virtuous friends, inquiring about the True Dharma, contemplating its principles, and practicing according to the teachings.
The future is to be feared; do not, because I am old, remain stagnant and confined to a single corner. You must go forth. Following this, he traveled everywhere to seek out masters and teachers.
He followed Mingjiao Dashi for the longest period; thus, he thoroughly mastered the profound depths of the single school of *Vijñaptimātra*.

Later, he widely propagated its teachings. People of the time said: "Ciyi [possessed] the wisdom to recognize a worthy son, while Mingjiao [possessed] the wisdom to find a worthy successor to transmit the Dharma.
The Master once instructed his students, saying: "For those who study the Way, there are three essentials for maintaining the mind: greatness, concentration, and distance. Greatness—"
"Then I shall certainly attain that which the Buddhas and Patriarchs attained. I will not be led astray by the minor benefits of gods and men.
To be 'single-minded' means to investigate only one matter and not be drawn away by names and appearances. To be 'distant' means to take realization as my goal, ceasing only after death.
Possessing such a mind, one will surely reach the Way. Strive for the substance and discard the ornament. Such were his words in general. He was eighty years old.
She passed away.
As for Huiwu, she was born into the Li family of Xingtang. Her elder brother would daily recite verses from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
When he died and was cremated, his tongue remained intact. Wu’s mother once dreamed that her elder brother’s wife held a single lotus stalk and bestowed it upon her; consequently...
He was pregnant and gave birth to a son. His countenance was dignified and well-proportioned; his tongue was long enough to cover his nose, and his voice was resonant and clear.

He served as a monk at the Zhenrong Monastery on Mount Wutai, where his discipline and wisdom were so brilliant that none could equal him. At the beginning of the Yuanyou era, he was summoned to the inner court by imperial decree.

His expositions of the Dharma were highly praised, and he was granted purple robes and the office of *Sengzheng*. The Master declined the honors with great earnestness and was thus spared from accepting them. In the first year of the Chongning era, he was again summoned.
An imperial edict summoned him to the capital, but he firmly declined on account of his old age and illness. Only after messengers had traveled back and forth did he finally set out.
Upon reaching Fudao Dian, he said to the messengers, "Since I have encountered the Way of the Buddha, I shall now return. Having finished speaking, he passed away while standing upright.
Biography of Dharma Master Jìnshuǐ (Appendix: Dharma Master Chéng and Sengtǒng Yìtiān).
Jìngyuán, courtesy name Bózhǎng, was the son of the Yáng family. From birth, he was quick-witted and intelligent; he received the full precepts under Grand Master Hǎidá of Bào cí Temple in Tōngjīng.
Resolute in his ambition, he set out on a journey of study and inquiry. Initially, he received the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* from Chéngqiān of Wú tái, and subsequently visited Héng...
Haiming Tan later visited Dharma Master Changshui Xuan, from whom he fully mastered the profound essentials of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Scholars from all quarters recognized him as a "Dragon of Meaning," and his reputation became exceedingly great.

He frequently presided over great seats of the Dharma to propagate the ultimate Perfect and Sudden teachings at Qingliang in Kaifeng, Guanyin in Suzhou, Xiangfu in Hangzhou, Baoge in Lake District, and Shanzhu in Xiuzhou.

The Imperial Decree stated: "Pu Gong, the Vice President of the Left, is governing Hangzhou. He honors the Way and has requested that you, Master, reside at Huìyīn Monastery, changing its practice from Chan to the Exoteric Teachings (Jiào).

Your reputation for the Way shall thus flourish greatly. The Master’s calligraphy was powerful and vigorous; he combined the two commentaries on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* composed during the Zhengshèng and Zhèngyuán eras into a single work to facilitate study.
He also composed the ritual methods for repentance (*chǎnfǎ*) for the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Śūraṅgama*, and the *Awakening of Faith*, as well as the ritual for the *Lotus Sūtra*.
He compiled the *Jiyi tongyao* (Essentials of Collected Meanings) in fourteen fascicles. He also composed commentaries on the *Benevolent Kings Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and other scriptures.

Uichon was the fourth son of the King of Goryeo; he renounced his royal splendor to enter the monastic order and was invested with the title of State Preceptor for the Protection of the World (*Yuse Saengtong*).

At the beginning of the Yuanyou era, he traveled to China and submitted a memorial requesting permission to transmit the teachings of Xianshou and return to his own country to propagate them. An imperial decree was issued to the relevant authorities to nominate [a successor].
As for those worthy of receiving the Dharma, they were matched with the Dharma Master Cheng.
Dharma Master Cheng resided at Jueyan Temple in Dongjing and lectured on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Having occupied the lecture seat for many years, scholars relied upon him to achieve renown.
As a man, he was pure and free from artifice; his conduct was lofty and his insight far-reaching. Among lecturers in recent times, he was peerless.

There was no one who could stand to his right. He submitted a memorial to recommend himself as a successor, stating: "Though I have applied myself diligently to study, my understanding and insight are shallow and incomplete.
It is only because my years have advanced that I am unworthily esteemed by students. Now, there is a renowned monk from a foreign land..."
In seeking a teacher for my maritime journey, it is appropriate to find one of lofty insight and broad learning to serve as my master.

I have observed that the monk Jingyuan of Huizhen Monastery in Hangzhou has mastered the Buddhist teachings and is well-versed in secular studies; I propose him as my successor, a choice that truly accords with public consensus.
The Emperor approved his petition and dispatched Yao Fenglang Yang Yi to serve as his guest-master. They traveled together to Huìyīn Temple and other monasteries where he received the Dharma;

they welcomed and saw him off with the etiquette due to an honored visitor. Previously, the commentaries and sub-commentaries on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* had long been lost and scattered; Yitian brought them with him to seek clarification and resolution.

He was thus able to recover his full health. Yitian, having completed his work, returned to his country, leaving behind one hundred and eighty fascicles of the three translations of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* written in gold.
Yu Huiyin subsequently constructed a pavilion to enshrine them; at that time, he was acclaimed as the patriarch who revived the *Avataṃsaka* tradition.
Thus, the Master’s Way spread widely abroad. In the winter of the third year of the Yuanyou era, he manifested parinirvāṇa. [Tea.]
He obtained countless śarīra relics, which were enshrined in a stūpa to the northwest of the courtyard.

At the age of seventy-eight, Uicheon, mindful of the Master’s milk of the Dharma, dispatched his attendant monk Sujae and others across the sea to offer sacrifices. The Master was originally from Jinshui in Quan Prefecture.
Therefore, scholars refer to him as Dharma Master Jinshui (Jin Water).
He was known as Zhìyán.
Zhìyán was the son of the Hu family of Linhai in Tai Commandery. When his mother was about to conceive, she suffered intense and sudden pain. His elder brother was a śramaṇa.
Zongben said, "There must certainly be something extraordinary about this child. If a son is born, he shall leave the household life. Upon hearing this, the mother joined her palms in assent.
Soon thereafter, the pain ceased, and indeed a boy was born. At six years of age, he followed a teacher; at fourteen, he received full ordination under Master Yue-shou Chan.

While reading the *Xin fu* (Treatise on the Mind), he felt as though he had attained some realization and immediately went to Dongshan to visit Shenzhao. There, regarding the Way of the Three Contemplations within One Mind... [the Dharma]... (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly with "法" [Dharma], which appears to be the beginning of a new section or a citation marker.)

Regarding the practice of the Flower Samādhi, there was none who did not attain spiritual liberation; he personally put it into practice. Once, while reading the *Mohe Zhiguan*, upon reaching the section on the "Inconceivable Realm," he remarked:
"The myriad dharmas are but the one mind; outside the mind, there is not a single dharma. Since neither mind nor dharmas can be apprehended, this is called the 'Marvelous Three Thousand.
Initially, he took non-substantiality as his primary focus, and his wisdom arose from the reality of dharmas. Later, moving from Mount Chicheng to Dongye, he elevated the Master [Zhiyi] as his guide.

Daishi once remarked, "Since the Buddha passed away long ago, people have become deluded regarding their own nature. Whenever I preach and expound the Dharma, I invariably point directly to the One Mind so that it may be easily understood;
thus, those who hear me are all able to attain entry [into realization]. During the Shaoxing era, the local administration requested that he take charge of Dongye Monastery.
The Master said, "When Zhiyi was not yet fifty years old, he already dispersed his assembly of disciples. I am old now; how could I possibly endure this? Ultimately, he did not accept.
He retired to the Eastern Peak of Mount Song, where he built a hut beside a jujube tree and thus styled himself the "Jujube Hermitage.

Possessing nothing beyond a single alms bowl, he personally gathered firewood and drew water; his diet consisted solely of the "three whites. For twenty years, he devoted himself exclusively to the practice of pure karma.
Regarding An-yang as his native land, he composed eight stanzas of a poem on cherishing the Pure Land; the diction and sentiment were so poignant that many people delighted in reciting it.
When his mother suffered from eye disease, the Master faced Avalokiteśvara and visualized the *sūryakānta-maṇi* (sun-essence jewel) in her hand;

his mother then dreamed of a deity holding the sun before her, and upon waking, her vision was restored. Within samādhi, the Master experienced many auspicious responses that cannot be enumerated. He established... [text ends]
In the first year of the Kansei era, while in a state of meditative concentration, he beheld a celestial deity who told him, "Master, your pure karma has been perfected.

Furthermore, he dreamed that a great lotus flower grew from a pond, surrounded on all four sides by celestial music. Thereupon, he composed a poem bidding farewell to return to the Pure Land. Seven days later—

He passed away while sitting in the lotus posture. He was enshrined in a stupa made of earthenware to the north of his hermitage. A light appeared over the stupa, shaped like the moon, and only vanished after three nights.
— Zhiyuan.
Zhìyuán (智圓), whose courtesy name was Wúwài (無外), was the son of the Xu family of Qiántáng. From the time he could speak, he understood filial piety and fraternal duty.

As he grew older, he would sometimes split wood and moisten it with water, then carve characters upon the stone; he would arrange flowers and plants like the ritual cords used for sacrificial altars, playfully enacting the manner of delivering lectures and exhortations.

His parents marveled at this and sent him to enter the Buddhist order to receive full ordination. At the age of twenty-one, he heard that Master Qīng of Fèngxiān had transmitted the teachings of [Tiantai] Tiān.
He traveled to the Three Contemplations (San Guan) school on Mount Tai, carrying his books upon a bamboo staff. Two years later, the Qing dynasty fell.

He subsequently went to reside on Gushan Island in West Lake, closing his doors to delight in the Way and styling himself "The Hidden Man" (Qianfu). As a neighbor and friend to the Recluse Lin (Bushi), he was naturally prone to illness and thus also styled himself "The Sick Man" (Bingfu).
The Master often lamented that since the passing of Jingxi, the subtle teachings had fallen into ruin, saying: "What kind of person am I..."
Thereupon, he composed ten commentaries (*śū*) to elucidate the sutras and wrote various sub-commentaries (*cāo*) to explain those commentaries, thereby supporting and propagating the teachings;
his merit was truly magnificent. With a mind as pure as snow and ice, the Master remained aloof from worldly affairs, regarding the mundane world as no more than a speck of dust.
He did not pay the slightest heed once he had seen it. At that time, Emperor Qinruo was governing Qiantang.
Ciyun sent a messenger to invite the Master to go together to welcome him. The Master smiled and said to the messenger, "Convey my regards to Ciyun in Qiantang;

please station one monk there for now. Those who heard this sighed in admiration and submission. Beyond his lecturing on the Way, he delighted himself with poetry and prose; there are five miscellaneous compositions.

It consists of ten fascicles and is titled *The Collected Works of Leisurely Dwelling* (*Kanjūhen*). On the seventeenth day of the second month of the first year of the Qiánxìng era, he himself composed a sacrificial text and elegies.
Two days later, he entered parinirvāṇa at the age of only forty-seven. He had previously instructed his disciples, saying:
"After my death, do not perform an elaborate burial to wrong me; do not erect a stupa to misrepresent me;
and do not petition those in high office for an inscription to falsely glorify me. Simply use two joined earthenware vessels to inter me, and set up a stone marking only my name, dates, and year.
Upon my passing, the disciples followed these instructions: they enshrouded me in earthenware and excavated the rock where I lived to bury me."
He did not build a house but used an altar. Fifteen years later, two mountains collapsed upon it. His disciples opened the site to examine the earthenware vessel;
the physical body was undecayed, with his nails and hair having grown long. His lips were slightly parted, revealing teeth as white as jade.

They then dressed him in new robes, scattered various powdered incenses over him, and reinterred him. In the third year of the Chongning era, he was posthumously granted the title of Dharma-Wisdom (Fahui) Great Master.
Continuation of the Biographies of Eminent Monks, Volume Three.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Minghe of Huashan Temple in Wu Commandery during the Ming Dynasty.
Section on Exegesis and Interpretation (Yijie).
Song Zhongli Zhuan:
Zhongli was the son of the Chen family of Ningbo. His mother dreamed that a solar disc entered her breast, whereupon she became pregnant. She did not bathe more than three times during the night.
He wept and wailed incessantly. At the age of nine, he left home to become a monk; having received the scriptures, he recited them once and remembered them forever without forgetting.
During the Zhìpíng era, he passed the scriptural examination in Kaifeng and received ordination. He followed Shénzhì at Nánshú Dù;

when Shénzhì opened the curtains for instruction, two hundred people posed questions and answers, yet none could surpass the Master. When Shénzhì retired from his duties, he appointed the Master as his successor. Yuánxiù...

First, the State Preceptor of Goryeo traveled to China to seek the Way. As soon as he reached the shore, he encountered the Master ascending the hall and sighed, saying, "Truly there is such a person here!

He then paid his respects with the etiquette due to a teacher. The Master ordered his disciples to maintain strict silence and began constructing a chamber for the Sixteen Contemplations to welcome those devoted to the practice of pure karma.
Afterward, the visitor took his leave, saying, "At the age of sixty, I shall return. Thereupon, he withdrew to his quarters.
While living in seclusion at Donghu for several years, the Prefectural Governor, Lord Wang, urged him to take charge of Baoyun Temple, whereupon he renovated the buildings and halls.

Within the belly of the temple’s guardian deity (the *gaolanshen*), they discovered a prayer text which stated: "A hundred years hence, there shall be an incarnate Bodhisattva who will restore this site.

Those who heard this were struck with wonder. Later, he retired to Baiyun Hermitage, where he daily expounded upon *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calm abiding and insight) until reaching the stage of the inconceivable (*acintya*).
He sighed and said, "My Way has reached its ultimate limit here. Since there is the inconceivable realm, there must be the inconceivable mind;
thus he composed the *Inconceivable Discourse on Rectification* (*Fǎzhèng wén*), as well as the *Commentary on the Net-Shredding and Pointing to the Return*, and the *Text for Resolving Doubts*.

After Master Huizheng passed away, the local administration invited him to once again take charge of Yanqing Monastery, which truly fulfilled the prophecy that he would return in his sixtieth year. He once ascended the seat to preach the Dharma.
His compassionate grace was inexhaustible. Once, while descending from his seat, he asked an attendant, "What words did I just say? The attendant replied with what he had heard.

The Master said, "I perceived my body and mind as being identical to the great void; I was not even aware of where my speech originated. On the fourth month of the fifth year of the Zhenghe era, he passed away.
The Master had lectured on the *Three Great Treatises*, the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, and the *Prabhāsa Sūtra* dozens of times, and had recited...

The *Lotus Sūtra* exceeds ten thousand sections; [Dunhuang] bestowed it upon others to eliminate illnesses, repel demons, and avert disasters such as droughts, such that his miraculous responses cannot be fully recorded.
He read all the texts of Confucius and Laozi without exception. When lecturing to Confucian scholars, he would instead question them, saying:
Regarding this Way, how does it stand in relation to the Sage Confucius? How does it appear in the *Odes* and the *Books*?
When a Confucian scholar could not provide an answer, the Master cited various arguments to explain it, saying, "Is it not indeed like this? Those who heard this were moved to heartfelt conviction.

While the Master was supporting the school in Yongjia, he said, "I once saw Mārīcī and Vajrapāṇi in a dream, requesting that they protect the Dharma. It is fortunate that one day [this shall come to pass] in the South."
At the Hu Chan Hall, his seat and the master’s presiding chair were established; it was from the Master that the practice of erecting statues began. Chen Yingzhong once praised the Master, saying:
"He reverently upheld the *vinaya* and steadfastly maintained pure contemplation; using his body as a tongue, he expounded upon ten billion matters.
The Master’s posthumous title was Mingzhi (Wisdom-Enlightened).

Youpeng Chuan was a native of the Jiang clan from Nanan County, Quanzhou. Having passed the scriptural examinations at the age of seven, he shaved his head and studied successively at various lecture halls.
He became renowned as a scholar under the lineage of Master Zongyi of Baolin Temple. He frequently harbored doubts regarding the doctrine of direct pointing of the Chan school; thus, he [often]...
He traveled with Zen monks. One day, he went to visit Chan Master Kaiyuan Qi. Before his feet had even crossed the threshold, he suddenly attained realization.
As Qi came out to meet him, he asked, "Why have you, a Dharma master, come here? He replied, "I do not dare to hold my ears in high esteem while disparaging my eyes.
Qi said, "Though you are old and venerable, why must you be like this? He replied, "He who considers himself self-sufficient does not grow. Qi said, "In the morning, look..."
Huayan was reading the *Prajñāpāramitā* at night. [Zhaozhou] did not ask how it was; rather, this was a single phrase for the present moment.
Huayan replied, "The sun is exactly at midday. Qiji said, "Speak further of idle words. He replied, "Throughout my life I have relied on loyalty and trust;
today I leave myself to the wind and waves. Although it is thus, as for the Master speaking in such a manner, what connection does it have? One must...
Xinjie was wearing straw sandals. Qiji said, "I will let you pass for now. But if you encounter Bodhidharma and he asks you how you would answer, what will you say?
Fung immediately shouted. Qiji said, "This lecturer! Today, meeting this old monk, your spirit has pierced the Ox and Dipper constellations.

Fung said, "A second offense will not be tolerated. Qiji clapped his hands and laughed heartily. Fung thought that saving sentient beings is no small matter, and that all quarters were pulling him back.
None of these efforts succeeded. Chan Master Donglin Zong sent him a letter saying: "To suddenly cast aside the dregs and refuse them is already to say they are flavorless;

only now do I realize that the sun and moon are a different sky altogether. Not only has the blue-eyed barbarian not come east in vain, but our own ancestral lineage is seen to be vast and far-reaching.
Or again, someone urged him forward, saying: "How can you claim to be so lofty when you have not yet found harmony?"
He had previously requested [to be left alone]. Although the style of solitary cultivation may be admirable, the principle of engaging with others has not been heard.
When his companions would not comply, in the sixth year of the Xuandehé era, he passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture.
The person below is from Jinhua; this one is from Quanzhou. Their times of passing away were also different: the former was during the Qiandao era, while this one was during the Xuanhe era.
Since the *Chuan deng lu* refers to him as a "Lecturer" (jiangshi), I have recorded this here for fear that they might be confused.
Biography of Zongtan.
Zongtan was a native of Licheng in Xiangyang. He entered the monastic order at Yanxiang Monastery and took Daogong as his teacher.

After receiving full ordination, he traveled extensively among the lecture halls, mastering the sutras and śāstras, and was highly esteemed by his contemporaries for his expertise in such works as the *Awakening of Faith*, the *Sixteen Contemplations*, and other scriptures.

He provided detailed commentaries for all of them. For fifty years, he used the Perfect and Sudden teachings as his gateway; practicing meditation by night and lecturing by day, he brought great enlightenment to many.
In his later years, he settled at Xiangyang, where he devoted himself exclusively to the practice of Pure Land.

He frequently expounded upon the contemplative methods of the Pure Land to instruct the common people of the village, and those who listened gathered like clouds. Furthermore, at Qingtai in Tangzhou, he closed his quarters to practice contemplation, becoming increasingly diligent with each passing day.

Throughout his three modes of action and four modes of conduct, he never for a moment forgot [the Buddha]. For the most part, when the Great Master transformed people, those who followed his transformation did so by observing his practice rather than merely his words.
On the twenty-seventh day of the fourth month in the fourth year of the Zhenghe era, a Buddha suddenly appeared in a dream and told him:
"The Pure Land is already prepared; you have only six days remaining of your remaining karmic conditions. Do not be indolent. The following day...

He was not yet prepared. He continued to chant the *jingce* (exhortations). On the fourth day of the fifth month, he struck the bell to inform the assembly, saying, "The auspicious opportunity is near;
it depends solely upon the appointed hour. I pray that the great assembly will assist me by reciting the Buddha’s name as I depart. Suddenly, thunder rolled and white clouds covered the hermitage.
He assumed the form of tula-cotton and passed away in stillness; a wondrous fragrance lingered for three days before it finally dissipated.
Daocheng transmitted the Dharma to Daochen.
Wen was the son of the Peng family of Leqing; his mother dreamed that purple vapors coiled around her body when he was born. He was eighteen years old [at the time of this event].
He was fully ordained and studied under Xian’an; having heard the subtle words and profound principles but once, he immediately grasped them. Upon returning to his hometown, he propagated the Dharma.

It happened that Emperor Gaozong visited Yongjia, where an imperial decree was issued to establish Lin Lingsu’s former residence as Zifuyuan Monastery. Prime Minister Lü Yihao recommended the Master in response to this summons.
He presided over the monastic centers on three occasions in total, and his efforts in gathering merit and transforming others never waned. Regarding meditative concentration...

In the interim, he saw the instructions bestowed by Siming [Zhiyi]. He performed the Lotus Repentance and was moved by the manifestation of Samantabhadra’s radiance. From that time on, his wisdom and eloquence progressed further.
One day, while lecturing on the meaning of the six arhats, a student requested him to explain it further; he dismissed the request, saying, "These are the dharma-characteristics of the Hīnayāna."
What benefit would there be in speaking further? I shall now explain the meaning of the King of Sutras for you. Let us proceed for three days, with not a single word repeated.
He manifested his passing on the twenty-third year of the Xianxing era, uttering this verse: "The Pure Land is but the mind; fundamentally, there is neither delusion nor enlightenment.

When not a single thought arises, one immediately enters the first stage. He was posthumously titled Yuanbian (Perfect Eloquence). This Master’s noble character and vast conduct were equal to those of Xuedou Dayuan.

Master Yuyang Chen was a Chan master of the second dhyāna. He was a close friend of the two elders, who held him in deep respect; indeed, he moved them profoundly, for his influence went beyond mere eloquence.
When the Master resided in the mountains and his provisions ran short, he once pawned his saṃghāṭī robe for rice at the market.

At night, he saw a brilliant light streaming forth; when he returned the robe, the light ceased. Suffering from a lack of water, he pointed to a workman to dig a well, and a spring followed the excavation.
Yong enjoyed staying on the banks of the Qing River, yet he was constantly troubled by its collapsing embankments. Everyone attributed this to the interference of malevolent spirits.

The Master conferred the precepts upon the deity, after which the river subsequently remained still and free from harm. Later, when he was about to take charge of Nanhu, his disciple Qingshun dreamed that the various patriarchs of Yanqing Monastery came to visit him.
An attendant stood by holding a diagram of their seating positions, but the eighth seat was missing. Qingshun pointed to it and asked about it.
He replied, "Your teacher was about to fill that position. Later, when [Renyue] resided at Nanhu, he indeed became the eighth generation. Alas!
How could this be a mere coincidence? (Liaoran’s lineage, including Zhixian).
Liaoran was the son of the Xue family of Tai in Linhai. He was born after being in the womb for thirteen months. At the age of sixteen, he received full ordination.

Following Master Hui of Anguo, he studied the teachings and contemplation (*jiaoguan*), grasping their essential points. Once, he dreamed that he sat upon a flat rock while floating upon the great ocean;

looking toward a mountain, he saw a Great Being (Bodhisattva) sitting amidst a bamboo grove. The Master stood upright and recited a hundred verses in praise of him. Upon waking, Liaoran remembered half of them. From then on...

He suddenly manifested eloquence and served under An Guo at Bai Lian Monastery. Before long, he departed to visit Mingzhi; whenever Mingzhi discussed matters with him, he would nod his head in approval.
Consequently, Mingzhi appointed him to reside at Guangyan. The Master said, "I must not fail the legacy I have received," and eventually became the successor to An Guo.
He dwelt in the mountains for twenty-four years, and his students often numbered between five and six hundred. In the Wuma year of the Xiangshu era...
A great assembly was being held at Ninghai when a messenger arrived bearing a decree, saying: "The Tuṣita Heaven requests the Master to preach the Dharma.

The Master replied: "The Dharma assembly here has not yet concluded. The messenger said: "The imperial edict cannot be delayed; you must attend to that first and then attend to this. He then tore up the Master’s name and departed.
In the fifth month of the year Xinyou, he dreamed of two dragons sporting in the air; one transformed into a divine person, whose sleeves...

He issued a statement saying, "The Master shall depart in seven days. The Master responded with a simple "Yes, yes. Upon awakening, he gathered the assembly to preach the Dharma, saying, "By the power of mindfulness of the Buddha, I have attained rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss;
you, my disciples, must strive diligently. He then bathed and changed his robes, and together with the assembly, recited the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*.
When they reached the passage on the Western World, he passed away. The assembly heard celestial music resound through the air, and auspicious light radiated in all directions.

The funeral was held at Donggang. He was posthumously granted the title Zhizhong. Throughout his life, the Master performed many miraculous deeds. When the commandery prayed for rain at Yuxi, the multitude suffered from the treacherousness of the path;
the Master invoked the dragon to relocate it. That night, wind and rain broke out violently, and by dawn, the dragon pool was seen to have moved to a level and open location.
He studied under Master An with one named Zhixian, who was also a man of refined mind and stillness.

As for the monk Linzhong, when he was about to pass away, the multitude heard the sound of the Buddha filling the heavens, and celestial music resounded in their ears; it may truly be called a "difficult brother" [a rare and auspicious coincidence].

As for the monk Ruzhan, according to his biography: Ruzhan was born into the Jiao family of Yongjia. In his youth, he underwent the scriptural examination and received ordination. He applied himself with vigor to the study of the *Śāstras* and traveled to rely upon Master Che.
Master Xiqing. At that time, the assembly had already grown so large there was no room for them; yet, in a small chamber no larger than a peck-measure, he settled them without finding it cramped.
During the intense heat of summer, they buried a large jar and filled it with cold spring water. He and his four companions sat back-to-back around the jar to draw in its coolness.
For several years they did this, until the crowd jokingly named the small chamber the "Hall of the Five Plagues. Later, he attended upon Master Huijiao day and night.
He immersed himself in his studies until he fully mastered the subtleties of both doctrinal teaching and meditative contemplation. Initially, he presided over Chuxi Shousheng Temple.

After his lectures, he would recite one copy of the *Lotus Sūtra* and chant the name of the Buddha twenty thousand times. There was once a person who sought to serve as the temple administrator; because [Zhili] perceived him to be an unsuitable vessel, he did not grant the position, which left the man resentful.
One night, while he was carrying a blade and entering the room, he saw official guests filling the seats. On the following night, he entered again, but it was pitch black and he lost his way.
When he finally reached the room, he saw ten or more people, all of whom had the same appearance as his teacher; the man, filled with shame and fear, fled. He usually slept very little;
during the summer months, he would sit amidst the thickets and grasses, reciting the *Lotus Sūtra* aloud, baring his body to offer himself to the mosquitoes. His disciples said:
The Master was advanced in years and should have rested from his ascetic practices. He said, "As for those that fly about, how could they obtain a sublime vehicle?

I merely hope that they may feast on my blood and hear my scriptures; let this serve as a causal condition. Later, people designated that place as the "Mosquito Feeding Terrace" (Weiwen Tai) in commemoration of him.

In his later years, he retired from public affairs and lived in a small hermitage. Daily, he cultivated the pure practices of the Buddha. In the Gengshen year of the Shaoxing era, he sat upright reciting the Buddha’s name and passed away.
Upon cremation, five-colored śarīras were obtained.
Fajiu: Shi Faxi and Shi Yan transmitted the Dharma to Fajiu.
He was born into the Shao family of Yaocheng. Having long roamed the gardens of the teachings, he later sought the essentials of the mind from Chan Master Dahui of Mount Jing.
Dahui once had him expound upon the principles of contemplation regarding objects, for which he was repeatedly praised. Thereupon, Dahui said to him, "The garden of the teachings..."

The population was sparse; he should have exerted himself to propagate [the teachings] and thereby glorify the ancestral Way. Subsequently, Lu of Cixi invited him with a request for "perfect stillness," and the assembly of students gathered from the four directions.
In the thirteenth year of the Shaoxing era, the local administration ordered him to reside at Qingxiu. There, the spring water was pure and the rocks were pristine.

Both the person and the environment were preeminent. He once lamented that later generations living in single quarters suffered from many faults, so he cleared out the communal hall and arranged beds with continuous mats according to the regulations of the Zen groves (*cān-lín*).
Taking the lead by his own example, none among the assembly dared to be negligent. His eloquence in expounding the Dharma possessed the spirit of Mahāmati;
yet there were those who could not grasp it, and they claimed the Master was merely "talking Zen. To the left of the temple was Lion Rock (*śi-zǐ-yán*), where he established a hall.
His name was Wuwe (Fearless). He resided there daily, reciting seven sutras including the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, without ceasing for nineteen years.
He passed away peacefully and without illness. While the Master was at Mount Jing, the daughter of Imperial Censor Wang had died young;

she frequently sent messages through a medium requesting that eminent monks recite the *Lotus Sutra* to ensure her rebirth in a superior realm. Dahuì summoned the Master, who went to the hall and ascended the seat to expound the scripture. The Censor’s...

Suddenly, the Imperial Attendant experienced a profound realization. That night, his deceased daughter appeared in a dream and said to her father, "By the power of the Dharma Master’s exposition of the sutra, I have already secured a place of rebirth.
Consequently, the Attendant composed the *Record of the Response of the One Vehicle*. As for those who succeeded the Master in the Dharma, it is said:

Xiyan, whose courtesy name was Shengtú, was a native of Fènghuà. Whether in monastic schools or Chan centers, there were none who did not seek his counsel. He had thoroughly mastered the Three Teachings and the hundred schools of thought.
Before his passing, he composed his own funerary inscription, using the text to convey the intent of transmitting the Dharma.

The Master’s will and character were upright and firm; the broad masses feared and submitted to him. Furthermore, his literary style was sublime and exquisite, such that those of later generations admired him. Thus, his fame spread far and wide.

Before he was free from worldly delusions, wherever he stayed, he would surely occupy the position of secretary. After he attained the knowledge of destiny, wherever he went, he would invariably sit at the head of the assembly.

Although various regions repeatedly offered him positions of spiritual leadership, he consistently declined and did not accept them. Once, while walking through a vegetable garden, he saw the abundance of uprooting, killing, and injury;
consequently, he ceased eating vegetables altogether. He purchased only three hundred and sixty catties of sea kelp, taking a portion of it each day.
He provided one *jin* of grain for his morning porridge and midday meal. In his later years, he reflected that his lingering habit for literary pursuits offered no benefit to the Way.

He consequently resided at the Hermitage of the Li family in Taoyuan, where he devoted himself exclusively to the recitation of the Buddha’s name. For ten years he sat in meditation without ceasing, practicing with diligent perseverance.

He said to his friend Zhang Hanqing: "As for the Way of the Pure Land, how could there be any single dharma to be attained? [Therein lie] the precious pavilions and jeweled nets, and the *kalaviṅka*..."

"Ga! This is merely the Buddha’s skillful means of guidance and encouragement. However, within the practice, if one does not perceive even a single dharma, then the supreme grade of the *Sāmbhogakāya* (Peaceful Light) is realized without realization.
On the days when the Master lived in seclusion, the local authorities attempted to conscript him as a laborer (*mianding*). Those who understood him derided this, saying:
"How can there be anyone in the world who has read ten thousand scrolls of books and yet, while practicing the conduct of a high-minded scholar, still wishes to be drafted for labor?"
Qian reprimanded him, and upon hearing this, the presiding official dropped the matter, whereupon it was finally settled.
Sishao inherited the lineage from Juexian.

Sishao was born into the Yang family of Qiantang. From his youth, he listened to the *Lotus Sūtra* and attained a profound realization; he drew blood to transcribe the scripture, devoting himself exclusively to its practice.
He practiced the *nien-fo* samādhi and constructed a small hermitage called De-yun. Later, he added a small gate to it, using it as a place to contemplate the setting sun.

Every evening after noon, he would rise and practice the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*), continuing for thirty years as if it were a single day. This was in the first year of the Xuanhua era.
Suddenly, he dreamed that the Buddha came to welcome him. Seven days later, sitting upright and counting his fingers while forming mudrās, he passed away.
Throughout his life, the Master was most diligent and earnest in the practice of recitation and prostration.

For each character of the seven Pure Land sutras—namely, the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Śūraṅgama*, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha*, the *Bhadracaryā-praṇidhāna*, the *Śāriputraparipṛcchā*, the *Brahmajāla*, and the *Anantamukhanirhāra*—he performed one prostration.
It is so for all of them. Only for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, ten recitations amount to a total of two hundred and seventy fascicles.
It is said that one who has recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* one thousand times, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* five hundred times, and the *Amitābha-sūtra* ten hundred times [attains this].
Juexian was the son of the Chen family of Siming; his style name was Chengzhao. At the age of seven, he received the scriptures, and upon reading them once, he could recite them from memory.

Later, he resided at Baolin Monastery in Fenghua. During a period of drought, the local district requested him to lecture on the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*. When he finished the final fascicle, it rained for three days.
He exhorted the local people to erect a *prabhāsa-dhvaja* (Glorious Banner) and recite ten thousand sections of sutras to serve as a protection for the district.

Next, he resided at Yanqing Monastery, where his Way flourished greatly. After a long time, he returned once more to Baolin, where he built a dwelling called Miaolian. There, he again recited ten thousand sections of sutras and maintained forty-eight *kṣetra* (collections) of Buddha-name chanting.
He extracted significant phrases from the commentaries on the sutras to support his contemplative practice, titling this work *Xinyao* (Essentials of the Mind). He succeeded...
In the first month of the sixteenth year of Xinghe, he preached the Dharma while sitting peacefully and passed away. A stupa was erected beside his quarters.
On another day, someone heard the sound of chanting sutras at night; tracing the source of the voice, it emerged from within the stupa.

Later, Yue Tang resided at Nanhu and remarked that although Master [Fahai] had rendered meritorious service in preserving the teachings at Yanqing, his stupa remained amidst the weeds. He therefore ordered it to be relocated to the ancestral burial mound. And...
The Vision of Opening the Earth. The tethering rope remains indestructible;
his bones are like cast bronze. Regarding Zongli (with Ruoshui appended):
Zongli was the son of the Gao family of Kuaiji. At the age of seven, he received instruction from Tianhua. He dreamed of traveling to Lingzhi to pay homage to the Great [Master].
Master Zhì received the precepts according to the ritual; Zhì called out the name Zōnglì and caused him to swallow a white pearl that issued from his mouth.
Furthermore, while once in a state of pure meditative concentration, he traveled spiritually to a Pure Land sanctuary. Later, upon returning to Tiānhuá, he constructed a pavilion for Amitābha Buddha.

He received guests from all quarters. During a drought, he went to the shrine of Emperor Shun on Mount Rizhu to pray for rain; a dragon was moved to manifest its golden body, and sweet rain fell in sufficient abundance.
At the end of the Jianyan era, he entered Daowei Mountain and named his dwelling "The Hermitage of One Mark" (Yixiang-an).

The monastics and laypeople of Kuaiji requested that the Master preside over the *xiennian* (commemoration) rites. On the third night, the pearl atop the painted image emitted a light as large as [the sun].
Ji. On the final day of the first month in the fourteenth year of the Xiangshu era, he told his disciples, "The Buddha has come to welcome me.
He then wrote this verse: "My age is ninety and my head is already white; In this world, there should be no guest who reaches a hundred years. O man of the One Appearance, return!
Seated upon the Golden Terrace, heaven and earth are cut off and grow narrow. Having cast down his brush, he passed away.

Rushi was a native of Sanqu who possessed divine powers through his diligent recitation of mantras. As the anniversary of his master’s忌 (jì—memorial day) approached, he instructed the cook to prepare sprouts and bamboo shoots.
The cook mocked him, saying that these were out of season. When evening fell, the Master sprinkled water from his bowl into the rear garden. That night, a loud crackling sound was heard.

When they inspected it at dawn, the bamboo shoots were growing in dense clusters across the ground. Furthermore, he was able to cure illnesses by consecrating water with incantations, saving many lives.
They were numerous, and their ultimate end is unknown.
Among them, he transmitted [the teachings] to the two masters Xian and Yuanzhi.

Master Xian, whose courtesy name was Xuzhong, was the son of the Zhang family of Huangyan. He resided at Upper Zhuchi Monastery; he maintained the precepts and cultivated his person, and was at that time acclaimed as foremost.
First: He took the Pure Land as his ultimate refuge and often said, "The Buddha-land lies beyond ten trillion lands, yet its boundaries do not exceed a square inch.
If one can diligently follow the path of contemplation, then it is not far to go there. Later, he moved to Chicheng.
Once, while bestowing the precepts at Falun Temple, he invited the Holy Master; the assembly beheld a precious light shining down from above, and a foreign monk appeared standing there.

As for Kongbiao: in the intervals between his meditative retreats, he would constantly recite the "Chapter on Emptiness. When he reached the passage on the "intrinsic emptiness and stillness" (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*), he would enter samādhi for several days.
Upon reaching the section on the "boundlessness of birth and death," he would weep with great sorrow without ceasing. His embodiment of the Dharma was as sincere and earnest as this.
One day, a Chan master came to visit him and saw a small booklet on the bed recording his purchases; it noted that he had never kept even a single coin of property for himself.
Upon his passing, [the Master] sighed and said, "In the Way, I have no cause for shame; yet in my practice, I did not equal my teacher.
When the Prefectural Governor entered the mountains and saw red lotuses in the pond, he asked, "Since these are the causes of white lotuses, why do they instead bloom as red flowers?

The Master replied, "In the mountains, we are equally delighted by your arrival, O Lord. Even that which is insentient changes its appearance. He then pointed to an Arhat reading a scripture and said, "Since this one is already..."
Xue asked, "How does one read the sutras? The Master patted the Arhat’s back and said, "Why do you not respond with reverence?
His wisdom, talent, and eloquence were likewise marvelous. In the first year of the Longxing era, he entered parinirvāṇa. Upon cremation, countless five-colored śarīra relics were obtained.

He authored a commentary on the Bodhisattva Precepts. The Master was proficient in the *I Ching* (Book of Changes); thus his name was derived from a hexagram, and his pen-name was Zeshan Sou (The Old Man of Mount Ze).
Yuanzhi was born into the Lin family; he was also a native of Huangyan. He transmitted the teachings and contemplations of Tiantai and resided at Dongshan for fourteen years.
Two monasteries and a thousand followers ranked him among their foremost leaders. Nevertheless, he was devoted to the Vinaya rules; every half-month, he invariably performed the *poṣadha* ceremony.

Someone remarked, "In the school of Perfect and Sudden Enlightenment, why is it necessary to act in this way? The Master replied, "The Perfect Dharma integrates phenomena and principle within a single thought-moment."
It is sufficient. How could one ever reject phenomena to seek the principle? Throughout my life, there has never been a time when I have not taken the *Prātimokṣa* as my teacher.
To uphold the Vinaya while discussing the eternal truth is precisely what is required today. During the Shaoxing era, I was commissioned by imperial decree to preside over Upper Zhi.

Amidst the ruins of the conflagration, only the Hall of the Great Being (Mahāsattva) remained. There were those who pooled their gold to construct gates and corridors for it; however, the astrologers declared that the presiding star...
It was unfavorable. The Master said, "The Buddha and the heavenly stars share the same creative transformation.

If the precious monastery is magnificent and grand, I shall have no regrets even in my death. Before long, he indeed suffered from a slight ailment; he dreamed of an immortal who gave him celestial nectar, and his illness was immediately cured.

During a summer drought, the Emperor issued an edict for the Master to preach the sutras at Mingqing Monastery; as soon as the assembly dispersed, rain fell in abundance. Once, while visiting the monastery’s estate, he heard that livestock were being used for sacrifices to the local earth deity.
Dizi said, "How can one violate the Buddha's prohibitions? He then preached the precepts for the deity and substituted plain vegetarian food for the offerings.
Later, he manifested illness, wrote a gatha, and passed away while sitting upright. Those who sought auspicious signs took his dream as evidence that he was one of the five hundred arhats of Tiantai;
perhaps this is indeed so.
Zhili transmitted the lineage to Zhilian.

His courtesy name was Wenshou, and he was a native of Siming. At the age of eighteen, he received full ordination. He possessed an ancient appearance and a tall, slender stature, bearing the air of a long pine tree or a wild crane.

Later, Zhiyong attained sudden enlightenment regarding the perfect teachings (*yuanzhi*). He entered the world and successively presided over five monasteries, all of which were situated amidst military conflict.

From the ashes of the conflagration, he transformed rubble into gold and azure tiles at the mere movement of a finger. At that time, Yuanbian was restoring Yanqing Monastery; before his work was complete, he passed away.
The Master happened to visit Hongzhi, and they ascended the Qianfo Pavilion together. Hongzhi asked, "I have heard you of Siming speak of 'form within emptiness.
Is this so? The Master replied, "Indeed. Hongzhi pointed with his finger and said, "The great void is fundamentally without a single thing."
The Master pointed to the mountains, rivers, pavilions, and towers and said, "As for these various phenomena, what exactly are they?

Zhidai was deeply moved by these words and immediately recommended him to the prefecture. He presided over the affairs there for ten years, lecturing every single day until all the monasteries were completed.

The Grand Master Shi Zhenyin, who had retired from public life to live as an elder in his hometown, would frequently visit him to inquire about the essentials of the Dharma. Zhenyin remarked, "Regarding both Chan and the Vinaya, you, Master..."
"Does it penetrate through? The Master said, "When the ice melts and the snow dissolves, it is but one water. He asked again, "The *Avataṃsaka* and the *Prajñāpāramitā* seem too fragmented.
The Master said, "It is precisely because they are fragmented that they are simple and easy. Zhenyin was solemnly moved to submission.

The Provincial Commander and Chancellor, Lord Shen, invited him to hold a monastic office, but he declined on account of old age and illness. The Lord sent a handwritten note to exhort him, saying: "Your practice..."

His conduct was pure and his cultivation refined; he bore the burden of the religious teachings with great vigor. It was fitting that he should manifest the correct path and serve as a governing authority for the monasteries of this region;

I trust you will not decline this out of stubbornness, but rather purify your own resolve. The Master then accepted the command, and those from all quarters were moved by his integrity and discipline. One day, he was stricken with illness and said to his attendant:
"The person who is unimpeded in all things transcends birth and death through the Single Path. He then clapped his hands and laughed loudly, saying: "I..."
"I am fortunate to have been born here. When the bell tolls, I shall depart. This was on the eighteenth day of the eleventh month of the first year of the Longxing era.
He was cremated, and śarīra were obtained and enshrined. Commentators remarked that on the day the Master passed away, he seemed to know his destination;
consequently, they identified him as the later incarnation of Shi Miyuan.
Daoyin (with the minor biography appended).
Daoyin’s style name was Ca’ān. He was of the Xue clan of Siming. Regarding his relationship to Master Can, who sat at the feet of Fazhi, he was Can’s great-uncle.

During her pregnancy, his mother dreamed that a radiant figure entered her chamber while lifting the curtain; she awoke and gave birth. At dawn the next day, news of his death arrived, and everyone knew him to be the latter incarnation [of the deceased].
His palms bore circular marks that appeared like rings when cupped; beneath the soles of his feet, the auspicious signs of twin fish were clearly visible.

At the age of seventeen, he received full ordination and spent the summer retreat at Nanhu. Whenever anyone questioned him regarding the meaning of the teachings, he would explain them to them with deliberate composure and correctness.

His writings harmonized with the [original] texts. Those who understood him recognized his past karmic predispositions (*pūrvābhyāsa*). Mingzhi resided at Baoyun Monastery and studied there; subsequently, within the monastic school and meditation halls, there was nothing he lacked.
Upon reading the *Zhijyao chao* (Essential Excerpts), he attained a profound realization and insight. He declared, "While I live, I am the person; when I die, I am the book.

Consequently, he directly succeeded the Fourth Patriarch Zhizhe as a transmitter of the Tiantai teachings. Because of this, some looked down upon him. Throughout his career, he moved from one monastery to another several times.
At his lecture seat, he later presided over Yanqing Monastery. In the third year of the Qiandao era, he passed away while reciting the Buddha’s name and speaking a verse.

His entire body was interred at the ancestral stūpa. The Master’s countenance was solemn and majestic, and his eloquence flowed like a torrent; those who encountered his sharp wit were said to have "ascended the Dragon Gate.
Xue Qingqing Cheng was the Master’s secular nephew. He offered this eulogy for the Master: "He reached the highest pinnacle of the Way; he tore his robes..."
He wore his cap even in times of mourning and did not resolve matters when doubts arose; he kept prisoners in the jail while awaiting a dispute. His teachings can be clearly perceived.
He once resided in a thatched hermitage south of the city, and thus took it as his own title. Among those who studied under him, the one who fully grasped his essential meaning was said to be:

Fah Yin shared the same name as his teacher; thus, he was known at the time as "Little Yin. He presided over Guangshou Monastery for thirty years, lecturing day and night without ever once visiting the gates of donors.
Whenever a donor arrived, he would immediately stand up in shame and sigh to himself, saying, "The dharma of a bhikṣu is to sustain one's life by begging for food.
What kind of person am I, sitting here and depriving others of the fruits of their diligent toil? He would then decline the gift and send the donor away.

Having no choice but to accept a small portion [of offerings], his dwelling was dilapidated and leaking. He intended to renovate it, saying: "This very body is impermanent; why concern myself with external things?
One day, as the assembly gathered for a lecture, the attendant reported that the guests had not yet returned from their invitation.

The Master said: "The devas in the void wish to hear the Dharma right now; why wait for the assembly to gather? He immediately struck the drum and ascended the seat. This was in the fourth year of the Shaohsi era.

He manifested illness. While in a state of meditative concentration, he had a vision and said to those around him, "I behold the Dharma Flower (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka) Bodhimanda, which is vastly different from what I have seen at other times.
I am about to depart. He then invoked the name of the Buddha, sat upright, and passed away. His remains were enshrined to the east of the temple.
The Biography of Huixun:
Huixun’s courtesy name was Moudao, and his style name was Yuetang. His ancestors were of the Chen clan from Yongjia; he resided at Qushan on Changguo Island in Siming.
His mother conceived him after dreaming of an extraordinary monk. At the age of eight, he entered the monastic life at Zuyin Monastery, where he was first instructed in the *Lotus Sūtra*.

He was able to master the recitation after only a few repetitions. Once, while returning home for a visit, his grandmother instructed him, saying, "Now that you have left home, you should emulate the Buddhist disciples of our region who were devoted to the Buddha.

Initially, he went to pay his respects to Nanhu Chengzhao, who praised him for his steadfast resolve. Later, when he reached Dongye, some who were jealous of him incited a mob to shout insults at him.
The Master said, "Regarding the great principles of the Buddha-dharma, if one has doubts, one simply asks; why must one be subject to such jealousy? Thus he remained.
In his youth, he relied upon Yuanbian to hear the profound principle that the nature of evil is itself replete with enlightenment and the subtle teaching that names and essences do not shift.

He attained a deep realization of the perfect and sudden (yuantun) doctrine of this single school. At the end of the Shaoxing era, he emerged as the abbot of Fachang, later moving to Jingming and Puhua.

Once, while carrying his alms bowl along the seashore, he encountered bandits. The Master assumed a solemn expression and said, "What you desire is wealth; I give it all to you. Thereupon, he exhorted them.

Regarding the retribution for good and evil karma, he took it upon himself to move others through his conduct; he would return stolen goods and depart after repenting his errors. His purity was peerless.
Whenever he faced the sea and mountains, he lectured on the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* for spirits and deities, frequently eliciting divine responses.

In the fifth year of the Qiandao era, he was appointed as the abbot of Nanhu. Students carrying their satchels arrived from afar, nearly beyond the capacity of the monastery to accommodate them. The Chancellor Wei Shu was a disciple of the Master.

He was a spiritual peer. Once he asked about the meaning of "the marks of the world are eternally abiding. The Master said, "Is it not that you harbor doubts regarding the succession of the four seasons?
He replied, "Indeed. The Master said, "From the furthest reaches of the past to the limits of the future, although there is succession, this principle remains eternally abiding.
In the winter of the sixth year of the Chunxi era, he suddenly informed the assembly that he was ill. Those who came to inquire after him arrived in great numbers; upon entering the gate, they saw—

To those who studied, he urged them to advance in virtue; to those holding official rank, he exhorted them to protect the Dharma. Those who heard this were struck with awe. He sat cross-legged and passed away in a state of serene stillness.
According to the custom of successive generations, his entire body was to be interred; however, he had only his hair shaved as a fulfillment of his master’s intention.

Over a month later, when his hair was examined, it was full of *śarīra* relics that could be gathered in one's hands. Throughout his life, the Master sat always upright and walked without looking to the side, even when in a quiet, private room.
He invariably donned the *kāṣāya* robe when lecturing and did not engage in literary composition; his students mostly recorded his teachings in notes during the course of their listening.

His Zen practice followed a regular routine, and he never allowed secular affairs to disrupt his established discipline. He would not permit those who had not completed twenty years of training (*śīla-varga*) to emerge from the monastery to teach, whereby the trend of impetuous advancement was for the first time brought under control.
The commentary states: Master Yuetang’s transmission of the Way was intended to match that of the ancients; it was not merely to fulfill his duties. He often said:
"To verify one's words based on their similarity of phrasing, or to mount one's own theories based on a good memory for resources—neither of these constitutes the true method of preaching the Dharma.
Only by personally awakening to the heart-source (citta-tattva) and then proclaiming and expounding it can one truly inherit the lineage of the Patriarchs. This is what I seek.
The Gate of Awakening is most urgent; do not let yourself be self-limiting. This is the great sickness of those who study the Tiantai school, fully expressed in these few words.
Yuetang Zhiben understood this. Recorded by Ruone.

Ruona, whose courtesy name was Xiyan, was the son of the Sun family of Jiaxing. He first relied upon Zhuan’an and subsequently visited Zhengwu at Chicheng, where he was appointed as the head of the assembly under him.
Following Wu’s passing, he succeeded to his master’s Way. His teachings spread widely. In the third year of the Qiandao era,

Emperor Xiaozong visited Shangzhu Monastery to pay his respects to the Great Being (Avalokiteśvara). The Master received him with such propriety that he pleased the Emperor’s mind, who subsequently appointed him as the Right Street Monk-Registrar (Youjie Senglü).
Thereupon, by imperial decree, a Hall of the Sixteen Contemplations was constructed within the mountain monastery; furthermore, a hall modeled after it was built within the Imperial Palace.

The Emperor then commanded the Master to lead fifty disciples into the Inner Hall of Contemplation on the eighth day of the fourth month to perform the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* ritual for the protection of the nation.
The Emperor asked, "The Buddha-dharma is indeed wondrous. How could there be such a vast number of scriptural volumes? The Master replied, "That which has its source is thus.

The Emperor approved of this and promoted him to the rank of Left Street Monk Registrar (Zuōjiē Sēnglù). In the ninth year, he was summoned for an audience at Xuǎndé Hall, where the Emperor questioned him regarding the miraculous traces of Great Beings throughout the ages and the essential meaning of the *Lotus Sūtra*.
The Emperor said, "From the very beginning, I have relied upon you, Master, to clarify this matter," and subsequently [bestowed honors upon him].

The *Complete Enlightenment* (Yuánjué) is a Dharma-gate that, when realized, is like playing chess. Once victory or defeat has been decided, not only must the chess pieces be removed, but the chessboard itself must also be discarded at once.

The Master said, "Even 'discarding them both' cannot be attained. The Emperor remarked, "One who is proficient in both the fundamental principle (*zōng*) and its exposition (*shuō*) is truly what is meant by a teacher.

An imperial edict was issued ordering him to lecture on the *Complete Enlightenment*; when he reached the passage concerning the "illusory mind" (*xūwàng xīn*), [the Emperor] asked, "If it does not exist..."

Regarding the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*), the Master said: "The mind is fundamentally formless; it acquires characteristics because of sense objects. When the objects cease, the mind ceases; the true mind remains serene.

The Emperor had this statement written by hand and bestowed it upon him. Furthermore, when asked about the meaning of the *Vajra*, his answers were all to the Emperor's satisfaction. The Emperor said:
"I read this sutra daily. I now further command the assembly to recite it thirty thousand scrolls together. He then issued an edict stating:
"In the past, among the birds and fish I have consumed, there has been much injury caused. Now, relying upon the Prajñā, I shall eliminate these transgressions."

He hoped that all living beings might together receive liberation. At that time, Prince Yi was still young; the Emperor summoned the Master into the inner palace to preach the Dharma for the prince and bestow a blessing by stroking his head.
Thereupon, the Master requested leave on account of illness. The Emperor said, "First, grant him land to build a residence; after several more years..."
They became companions in leisure; by the water’s edge and upon the rocks, they spoke together of non-arising (*anutpāda*).

In the eleventh year of the Chunxi era, he retired to Xingfu Temple and was specially appointed as the Chief Registrar of the Two Streets. At that time, Emperor Guangzong was still the Crown Prince, who inscribed the plaque for his seclusion: "Returning to Seclusion."

The Emperor granted him this honor and further composed a eulogy to extol his virtue. When the Emperor retired to the Chonghua Palace for rest, he summoned [the Master] to lecture on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

The Master was carried to the hall in a sedan chair and stayed overnight in the palace quarters. Upon the completion of the commentary, he presented it; the Emperor perused it and gained even greater insight and inspiration.

On the first day of the tenth month in the second year of the Xiangshu era, he said to his attendants, "My lineage has mastered the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*; it is fitting that I conclude my life with this.
He then assembled the community to perform the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* repentance ritual. Taking his ritual implements, he presented them to the two imperial palaces, sat upright, and passed away.
He was eighty-two years old. His stupa was erected in the main quarters and granted the posthumous title of Master Guangci of the Religious Teaching, named Puzhao.
Zheqing was a man of distinguished appearance who had three masters as his teachers.
A native of Tiantai, he possessed a naturally keen intellect and was both widely learned and possessed of a powerful memory. He received instruction from Cibian of Shangzhu.

He once said, "I have already grasped the essential meaning of the Four Teachings; only regarding the 'Arousing of Teaching and Contemplation' (qijiao guan) do I not yet fully believe it, yet I dare not fail to believe.
Initially presiding over Chexi Shousheng Monastery, he never bowed his head before the powerful or the wealthy, and his assembly numbered three hundred.

The donor came in person. At the age of thirty, [Tanying] subsequently set aside his scrolls and sat in meditation. Whenever he encountered a lecture, he would simply have his attendant provide him daily with the lecture texts;
his eloquent exposition flowed like a stream, and those who listened were convinced and attained insight.

When Tanying led his disciples to Chexi, he happened upon a recitation of the *Anantamukha-sādhaka-nirdeśa-sūtra* (Wuliangyi jing). Upon hearing it, he said to his companions, "This master’s words possess canonical authority."
He was fully capable of inquiring about the Way and immediately sought to become his disciple. There was one who did not follow the formal rules and took pleasure in this;

when the assembly heard of it and inquired after his name, they were told, "There is a friend named Ke-guan. The Master set him aside and said nothing further. Guan’s courtesy name was Yi-weng; he was the son of the Qi family from Huating.

At the age of sixteen, he received full ordination. Having heard that the reputation of Che-xi resounded throughout Jiang-zhe, he carried his book-case to follow him. One day, he heard [the Master] raise a koan.
Yun said, "Prajñā is silent and desolate; suddenly there is awakening and entry [into its truth]. It is like taking a cup of qi-subduing decoction.
Upon hearing this, the Master was inwardly convinced. Yu Huijue of Hengshan invited the Master to travel with him to study the *Zhijyao*.

When they reached the passage, "If one does not say that the iron bed is suffering, nor that transformation is migration," he sighed and said, "Words and letters are all nothing but chaff. This was at the beginning of the Jianyan era.
The Master [resided at] Jiàhé Shòushèng Temple and later moved to Dēngcáng Temple in Dāng hú, where he dwelt in the Yuèshì Hall. There he composed a supplementary commentary to the *Śūraṃgama Sūtra*.
Xiá fù invited him to stay for two years due to auspicious signs, but because of illness, he returned to the Southern Forest of Dāng hú. His single room was desolate and sparse;
others could not bear it, yet he said, "The sound of pines in the wind and the mountain moon—these are my inexhaustible robes and bowl. In the seventh year of the Qiándào era, the Vice-Minister...
Wang Wei was appointed as the military governor of Gusu and invited [the Master] to preside over Beichan Monastery. Upon entering the gate, it happened to be the ninth day of the month;
pointing to the seat, the Master said: "An inch of ash within my breast has long since grown cold; a thousand strands of snow upon my head have not yet melted.

My aged steps are fit only for level ground; I know not for what reason I must ascend this height again. Lord Wang struck his palm-boards incessantly in approval. He subsequently appointed the Crown Prince, Prince Wei, to succeed him.
His life was blessed with longevity; at eighty-nine years of age, his travel gear was meager, a sight that moved all who beheld it to admiration.
After two years, he returned once more to Danghu. He inscribed his own portrait, saying: "Vimalakīrti did not destroy his body, yet he conformed to the single mark of aging.

In the Bamboo Hut, whether there is destruction or non-destruction, from the outset there is neither deficiency nor excess. Everywhere, the mountains, rivers, wind, and moon are nothing other than [this].
This was his skillful means. In the second month of the ninth year of the Chunxi era, he passed away without illness.

The Master had resided five times at Danghu, and each time he retired into seclusion at Zhuan-an (Bamboo Hermitage), adopting it as his own title. Dahui Zonggao once visited him and conversed with him all day long;

upon leaving, he sighed in admiration, saying, "An old dragon in the ocean of the teachings. When the Master saw that an image had been installed in the refectory, he immediately cautioned him, saying, "In your daily conduct..."
To be disrespectful and speak useless words—this brief act of offering incense does not compensate for the sin of a whole day’s familiarity with irreverence.
Such was his meticulousness regarding even the most minute details. My friend, a native of Jin Hua, styled himself Mukan (Pastoral Hermitage).

He had recited nearly half of the entire Buddhist canon from memory and attained the Way of Cheokkeum. He presided over Seontam and later moved to Neungnim, where his lectures on the Way flourished daily until his later years.
Master Yanqing renamed a room in the abbot’s quarters "The Hall of the Six Classics. He placed a single table inside it but kept no books or writings there at all.
The scholar-officials found this preposterous; they gathered at the temple intending to challenge him. The Master instructed his attendant to speak to them first, saying:
"Gentlemen, what do you wish for our meeting? If it is to be as guests, we shall sit facing one another. If it is to discuss matters or seek instruction, then..."
He stood in attendance. When questions were posed or difficult points sought, the guest would first extend three inquiries, all saying, "I beg you to follow the etiquette of a host.
Yet as they conversed, he would cite passages without end; thus it was known that the Six Classics resided within his breast. Whenever he approached a lecture, he would not pre-examine the text.
He once said, "In my seven lectures on *Zhiguan*, throughout the actual practice of cultivation, I have never uttered a single word [of mere theory]. Furthermore—
[The interlocutor] said: "In the Great Treatise (*Mahāśāstra*), one might wish to raise a single objection as small as a scrap of paper, yet it cannot even be established.

This is because 'the nature of letters is detached; all are liberation. Someone asked: 'The ten objects and ten vehicles must be fully established before they constitute the method of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*);

why then did Jingxi say that one need not wait for the objects of contemplation to be called the cultivation of contemplation? The Master replied: 'I have already told you: this refers to the subsuming of phenomena into principle (*li*). He asked again."
"In the Perfect and Sudden Teaching, is the establishment of the aggregates (skandhas) affirmed or not? The Master raised his voice and gave a single shout, saying:

"The heavy burden of the aggregates and sense-bases is constantly manifest before you; why ask again whether they are established or not? Furthermore, he was stern in governing the assembly and was selective toward those around him.

Whenever anyone wished for the Master to announce the time for the hall and to assemble the multitude, the Master would say: "The reason I do not repeatedly inform the multitude is that I have a specific intention. He did not.

Upon seeing the Way, the thunder of heaven lost its majesty. In the twelfth month of the fourth year of the Qiandao era, while seated in the Green Jade Pavilion, he gathered the assembly to recite the Buddha’s name;

sitting upright, he passed away. His disciples who received the Dharma from him were very numerous. The Master himself was broad-minded and possessed a powerful memory, yet he did not keep formal lecture notes or outlines.
He once said to his fellow student Zhuan’an, “In the world there is only one and a half patriarchs; you, my elder brother, are only half.”
"One person. A question was asked: "What is meant by 'half a person'? The Master said, "It is not right to have several extra sheets of paper [in the commentary].

While at Xiantan, Zhuan’an came to visit him. For the sake of the lecture, the Master finished reading the major sections of the text and immediately closed his case, saying, "The Master of the School is present in the seat."
I do not dare to be overly ornate. Even in his conduct toward venerable elders, his humility was such as this.
