When the two masters were studying, while Chexi sat in the night at the abbot’s quarters, he heard the sound of celestial music in the corridors and galleries. He sent someone to trace it, and the sound emerged from the masters’ room.
Che-xi peered through a crack in the wall and saw the two masters playing together before the lamp, raising their hands to perform silent music.
Che-xi marveled at this all the more; thus, at the time of his death, he entrusted the path of the Dharma to them.
The Pagoda of Contemplation (Guantapa) was located at the northwest corner of Dezang Temple; it had been leveled by the construction of the city walls.
County Magistrate Xie Liangbi dreamed of an elderly monk dressed in purple robes who said to him, "I am Zhuanan; I entrust my pagoda to you.
Xie subsequently searched for it and indeed found the pagoda, whereupon he renovated it and erected a stone monument to mark its restoration.
Biographies of the Two Dharma Masters Huiding and Ziyou.
Dharma Master Huiding, whose courtesy name was Ningdao, was surnamed Wang. His family had been natives of Shaoxing’s Shan-yin for generations.
In his youth, he received the tonsure from Dao-ren Yao at the Bao’an Monastery in Qianqing. He traveled throughout the four quarters and studied under Master Daolong.
He followed the Three Masters as their disciple and was fully instructed in the meaning of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, until he attained a state of transcendent self-realization.

Moving freely between the teachings of the past and present, he neither followed them blindly nor deviated from them arbitrarily; indeed, the Three Masters could not bend him to their will. When the assembly requested that he reside at the Jie-zhu Provincial Monastery, he departed before long.
At that time, Dahui Zonggao was preaching the Dharma at Ayuwang Mountain, and the Master went there with a sense of profound resolve.

His residence was a place where learning flourished; scholars took him as their master. He moved from Zhizhao Temple to Guanyin Temple, and later returned to Shengyuan Temple—all of which were modest, secluded monasteries.
There he lived on wild herbs and beans, his austerity such that others could not endure it. Nevertheless, he never ceased his literary output;

his works include the *Commentary on the Diamond Sutra*, the *Illustrated Compendium of the Contemplation of the Dharma-realm*, the "Chapter on the Three Refuges," and the *Treatise on Zhuang and Yue*. All of these...

It flourished throughout the world. On the twenty-fourth day of the twelfth month in the eighth year of the Chunxi era, he burned incense, recited a verse, and manifested his passing at the age of sixty-eight. He was buried in Qianqing.
Dharma Master Ziyou, whose courtesy name was Xiuzhong, later styled himself the Elder Xiaoyun. He was born into the Chen family and was also a native of Shanyin.
At the age of seven, he became a novice; at twelve, he shaved his head and received full ordination.

He studied the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and its commentaries at Guangfu Monastery under Zhejiao, from whom he acquired his learning. He also traveled to Qiantang, where he visited Master Huiyin of Huayin Monastery and thoroughly resolved all his doubts.

The two masters both considered themselves to have reached their limit and subsequently returned to Shanyin. There, they preached the Dharma at Miaoxiang Monastery to the east of the city for nearly twenty years.
At times there were over a hundred students, but the masters grew weary of the proximity to the city and longed to dwell in the mountain forests.
He then left the assembly and withdrew to the upper reaches of Mount Meishang.

His disciples were unwilling to disperse, but as the monastery was too cramped to accommodate them all, they petitioned the local administration, requesting that the Master be invited back to Miaochang Temple. Thereupon, the Dharma seat became even more flourishing than it had been before.
The works he authored circulated widely throughout the world, and the monastery was further renovated until it was renowned as a magnificent temple.
When Dahui Zonggao passed by, he marveled at it and left a verse upon the wall; nevertheless, the Master eventually abandoned it and departed. His disciples, however, did not let him go.
He preached the Dharma three times more, finally residing at Jiangshan for three years. There, he sighed deeply and said, "I am old; where shall I return?"
He hurriedly packed his books and returned to Meishi. There he built a hermitage to spend his final years.

On the twenty-sixth day of the eighth month in the sixteenth year of the Chunxi era, he suddenly ordered a boat and took leave of all those with whom he had previously come and gone. Rising the following morning, he preached the Dharma and then passed away while seated.
He was sixty-nine years old. Three days later, his body was cremated, and five-colored śarīra were obtained, brilliant and resplendent. His younger brother...
The Master’s son immediately constructed a stupa to the west of the hermitage and enshrined the remains and śarīra therein for burial. The Master possessed vast talent and extensive learning;
his noble conduct and profound insight were preeminent, standing far above his contemporaries.

Although he took the Avataṃsaka as his primary school, he exhaustively explored the teachings of Tiantai in the south, Ci’en in the north, the mind-dharma of Shaolin, and the Vinaya section of Nanshan—there was nothing he did not investigate. Throughout his life...
He sought out their subtleties to assist his own discourse. As for the books of the hundred schools, there were none he did not read.

Upon hearing of renowned scholars and virtuous men, even if they were a thousand *li* away, he would certainly go to associate with them. He was earnest in practicing righteousness and diligent in cultivating his character;

he was strict in matters of taking and giving, and treated gain and loss as one. His manner of engaging with others was simple yet dignified; he did not bow before wealth or nobility, and he possessed the means to provide for and bestow upon others.
As for his conduct at the gate: if the ritual propriety was insufficient, he would invariably refuse to accept even a hundred pieces of gold.

How truly worthy! Huishi’s successor was named Guangzhao; he was the son of a certain family in Zhen ding. From birth, he was compassionate and obedient. When he was seven or eight years old, his mother sent him to cook.
While eating, he saw a swarm of ants gathered inside a cauldron; he immediately ceased cooking and devoted himself to the study of the *jǔzǐ* (preparatory) curriculum.

He soon became renowned among his fellow villagers. One day, while composing a literary work, he was unable to find the right inspiration. Consequently, he went out for a stroll in the wilds and encountered an extraordinary monk, who enlightened him with the teachings of world-transcendence (*lokottara-dharma*).

He was profoundly moved and attained great awakening. He followed this teacher to shave his head, traveled to the academies to study the sutras and treatises, and applied himself day and night without ceasing.

He was weary [of worldly affairs] and his discourse on integrity and conduct far surpassed that of his contemporaries. Throughout the regions of Yan, Zhao, Song, and Wei, his Dharma teachings flourished greatly.

He once said to people: "Those who study the Buddha-dharma must practice with earnestness. If one does not practice with earnestness, even the worldly dharmas will not be accomplished, let alone transcending birth and death.
Someone asked: "To transcend birth and death, one must necessarily break through attachments; how can this be achieved through earnestness? [The Master replied: "Earnestness..."
"Do you not have attachments? The Master said, "To recognize the True is precisely what breaks attachment. You, however, do not take the True as real because of your minor attachments;

you indulge your passions and are negligent. Thus, this attachment will never be broken, and you will never escape from birth and death. Furthermore, regarding the vessel-world, the body, and the mind—"
These are all the dual attachments to self and dharmas. They run directly as warp and cross as woof, interwoven with firm tenacity.

Even if one were to apply oneself with earnestness and perform this arduous labor for twenty or thirty years, one might still fear being unable to extricate oneself; how much more so if one does not apply oneself earnestly?
As you have said, this is precisely what the Tathāgata calls "clinging to worldly toil," and he regards such people as objects of pity.

Emperor Shenzong, having heard of the Master’s lofty conduct, bestowed upon him a golden-embroidered robe. The Master said, "I have nothing to replace my saffron-colored *kāṣāya*, yet I cannot disobey the imperial decree.
He accepted it upon his head but did not wear it for the rest of his life. This was in the first year of the Yuanfeng era.
He resided at Mount Jue. At the age of seventy-eight, he did not allow his efforts to benefit himself and others to decline due to old age; rather, he applied himself with even greater vigor.

Later, while presiding over a lecture assembly, he passed away while seated upon the dais. A month later, his countenance remained as if alive, his beard and hair had grown longer, and he possessed no belongings beyond what was necessary for his person.
His reputation left behind a lingering fragrance. That he could depart so serenely at the moment of death truly makes him an "old dragon" within the ocean of the Teaching.
Such individuals are not easily found.
The two masters Jingwu and Liaoxuan transmitted [the lineage].

Master Jingwu, whose courtesy name was Jixian, was born into the Li clan of Leqing. At nineteen, he received full ordination; whether in monastic schools or Zen hermitages, there were none where he did not [attain mastery].
Looking at him as a whole, his aspirations were lofty and outstanding; he granted few favors to others. He would often admonish himself, saying:

"Cooking my rice in a broken cauldron, resting in the midst of the forest, borrowing the mouth of empty space to speak to the myriad phenomena—what cause for shame should I have? Only if my learning were not sufficient would there be reason for regret."

To achieve one's purpose by relying on others; to cling to the words written on scraps of paper while gathering together a hundred or ten disciples; to dwell in grand mansions and covet a space of only a few square feet—these are things I shall not do.
Master, you first began by building halls at Feiquan, and in the middle of your career, you personally engaged in lecturing and instruction.
In his later years, he devoted himself exclusively to the practice of Pure Land. When he fell ill, he wrote a large inscription to show the assembly, saying:
"Seeking physicians and inquiring about medicines would disturb my final transformation. I shall silently observe its changes. The next morning, he sat upright and passed away.

This was in the ninth month of the Dingmao year of the Kaixi era. After his cremation, his ears and teeth remained intact and undamaged. His stupa was erected at the western foot of the mountain at the temple. —Recorded by Master Jian of Beijian.
For it, I have composed this inscription: This is Huo’an; his eloquent exposition of the *Dhāraṇī-saṃgraha* constitutes two indestructible treasuries.

Valued by the Way and its Virtue, though he remained in seclusion, his influence was manifest. Knowing that those of different eras share the same heart, I shed tears upon the southern slopes of Mount Yan.

Liaoxuan was a native of Siming. He practiced the Lotus Samādhi for twenty-seven successive periods, never eating after noon and never failing to observe the passage of time according to the sun’s shadow.
He shared a spiritual friendship with his fellow practitioner Shanrong; whenever he encountered doubts while reading the sutras, he would invariably visit Shanrong’s quarters to resolve them.
One day, after sitting in silence for a very long time, Shanrong asked, "What are you doing today? The Master replied, "I am waiting for the time of my return."
"We have already drawn near. The meaning of the Way is difficult to forget; I did not realize it would come to this. I pray that you will devote yourself single-mindedly to advancing on the Path;

we shall meet again in the Pure Land. Rong smiled and said, "I was precisely wishing to see your strategic skill. From that time forward, the Master manifested illness. As he approached his end, he requested the assembly to gather.
He recited the *Amitābha Sūtra* and chanted the Buddha’s name. Suddenly rising, he sat upright and wrote a verse: "Nature and characteristics, emotion and thought—all forgotten;
one and three, no longer dependent. The winds of breath cease to move; Mahāsiddhi. He then joined his palms, closed his eyes, and passed away. This was in the first year of the Jiatai era.
Three years later, Rong also passed away while sitting in the lotus posture. People said that he had gone to fulfill his master’s appointment.
The two masters Shan Yue (Good Moon) and Jing Hui (Pure Wisdom) transmitted the lineage to Shan Yue.
His courtesy name was Guangyuan. He was the son of the Fang family of Dinghai. His mother conceived him after dreaming of the moon; he was given this name because of that dream.

At fifteen, he received full ordination and went to attend upon Yuetang, from whom he gained a profound understanding of the doctrinal teachings. After Yuetang passed away, he again relied upon Ca’An. Regarding his [further] studies...
Dwelling among ancient cypress trees, he stood out in solitary beauty; thus, he styled his own residence "Cypress Court" (Bótíng). The Grand Preceptor Shì Zhēnyǐn invited him to reside at Yuèbō.

When scholars came seeking him out, the provisions for their sustenance were insufficient. Zhēnyǐn said, "The Master invites the assembly for the sake of the Way; if they wish to eat, let them come and take it. I am not stingy. He succeeded to the position of South Lake (Nánhú).
The Master governed the community with discipline, maintaining his integrity without wavering for thirteen years. Both the monastic and the lay...
On this basis, he believed it. The Master received imperial summons and resided twice at Upper Zhushan. He was subsequently appointed as the Director of the Left Street Monastic Registry.
Everyone congratulated him, citing the verse by Su Shi: "The master has gone and suddenly returns; the birds' songs and mountain countenances open in welcome."
The Master remained as serene as ever, appearing unaware. In the third year of the Duanping era, he suffered from an eye ailment and requested to retire to his eastern hermitage.

As he was about to enter nirvana, he looked to those around him and said, "People suffer from a lack of genuine virtue to be praised by future generations; if one merely pursues empty fame, I have no time for it.
A thousand years hence, if I am called the 'Old Man of Baiting,' then these withered bones of mine will have no cause for shame."
"I pray you do not trouble yourself by requesting a posthumous title for me, which would only hinder my lifelong practice. Having spoken thus, he placed his feet together and passed away.

He was ninety-three years old, having attained seventy-eight summer retreats. The Master’s writings were very numerous; they primarily elucidated the tenets of his own school and were of great service to the Dharma gate.
Jinghui, whose style name was Yue’an, was also a fellow disciple of Yuetang and Bating.
After Bating moved from Nanhu to Shangzhu, the Master succeeded him in that position. While Bating delighted in nurturing talent, his junior disciples were preoccupied with literary composition.

He was fond of dissenting opinions. When the presiding officials were somewhat dissatisfied with the assembly, the crowd would inevitably rise up in a body to shout and drive them away. When the Master arrived, he governed affairs with gravity and resolve;

his regulations were particularly strict, and people dared not offend him upon merely catching sight of his demeanor. The local customs were thereby transformed. He never locked the door of his study (*vimala-śālā*);

those who came to seek further instruction were never turned away, even after nightfall. As one walked along the two corridors, the sound of recitation and chanting could always be heard. He would invariably—
He accepted this with joy. In the ninth month of the first year of the Jiading era, he gathered the great assembly to chant the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra*.

Sitting cross-legged upon his couch, he suddenly passed away. Throughout his life, the Master had no fondness for secular books; whenever he presided over a lecture and saw citations from commentaries or records, he would stop and not read them.
He said to his disciples, "These are external texts; you should examine them yourselves. Whenever he was selected for a public appointment, he [would act accordingly].
If it was not the right person, he would immediately confront the various mountain monasteries, saying, "The so-called lecture halls exist for the purpose of transmitting and upholding the teachings.
Can this person truly shoulder such a responsibility? He ultimately refused to grant permission; his strict integrity was like this.
Zongyin succeeded to the lineage.
His courtesy name was Yuanshi; he was a native of Yanguan and a disciple of Zhuanan. He possessed a profound understanding and a resolute spirit.

Regarding the aphorisms of the various patriarchs, he would invariably recite them one thousand times before moving on. He entered Nanhu to practice the long-term *chán* (repentance), where the Zhou family invited him to reside at their hermitage.
While residing there, he used the monastery's grain rations to encourage the reform of illegal practices, reducing the annual consumption by five hundred *hu*.

He went to visit Xiangtian Yuanwu Yan, who cross-examined him on the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West. The Master replied, "There is a place of humiliation where there is no place to cry out. Yan approved of this.

On the anniversary of Zhiyi’s death, the Master lit incense in the hall at night and wept so bitterly that his voice failed him. Moved by his sincerity, Yan saw him off with generous gifts upon his return home.

Nanhu. Subsequently, the head of the assembly, Sūnyatā-anusārin (From Emptiness), was invited to occupy the Vast Hall. In that hall, he authored the *Zongji lun* (Treatise on the Ultimate Principle), supporting Zhiyong;
therein, he established the doctrine of a single nature for both phenomena and principle. The Master [Wonhyo] proposed nine objections, and Zongji was defeated in his arguments.
Tongshou Su Bian, who had inherited the Master’s Dharma, requested him to reside at Posoksa. At that time, a great hurricane arose, uprooting trees.
A drifting tile: all the other buildings were destroyed, leaving only the Scripture Hall intact. The Master resolved to die there and would not leave.

Baen summoned him back, requesting that he travel with him to the West to propagate and promote the teachings together. Having resided in the East for twenty-four years, he returned once more to the region south of the Zhe River.

There, he lectured on *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* at Upper Zhuchi Temple. The presiding authorities, jealous that he had gained such a follower, drove him away, and he went into seclusion at Maoshan on Leifeng Peak.
He took the style name Shian (Shi-an). Those who came to seek the Way arrived in great numbers. He successively held positions at Dezang, Yuantong, and Chaoguo.

Once his reputation for virtue and wisdom had spread throughout Beichan, his achievements in temple construction were also completed. Hai-kong departed from Ling-shan and recommended him to succeed him; the Emperor granted this by imperial decree.

He was summoned to the private audience hall, where the Emperor inquired about the fundamental principles of the Buddha-dharma. His responses were concise yet profound in their reasoning, which greatly pleased the Sovereign. Consequently, he was conferred a posthumous title.
Dharma Master Huìqǐng later traveled to Sōngjiāng to propagate the teachings. Addressing his disciples, he said, "My karmic conditions for transformation have ended here.

He then passed away peacefully in the right-side reclining posture. This was on the eighth day of the twelfth month in the sixth year of the Jiàdì era. His remains were enshrined in a stupa beside Cíyún Tà.
The Master’s robes conformed to the Vinaya, and he strictly prohibited the five pungent roots; his spiritual power was so pure and ultimate that both the unseen and visible worlds were moved by him.

Furthermore, he rectified the deviant and rescued those who were stagnant; he eliminated chronic ailments and quelled epidemics. Whenever there was a prayer or supplication, there was none that did not result in recovery.

He often said: "A lecturer must be equipped with three methods: maintaining solemn deportment when facing the great assembly; grasping the main framework to exhaustively elucidate the textual meanings;
and possessing the 'eye of the school' to demonstrate the meditative objects and contemplations. Only when these three are complete is one truly without shame in proclaiming the teaching."
The Biography of the Great Being Huairu (Huaiji) of Jinhua.

Huairu’s secular surname was Wang, and he was a native of Xihe. When he was a youth, he petitioned his father to leave the household life; however, because he was their only son, his father found it difficult to grant his request.
Upon reaching adulthood, there were no Buddhist scriptures that he had not read. He was subsequently entrusted with the *Huayan fajie guan* (Contemplation of the Dharma-realm of the Avataṃsaka).
Regarding Master Bao of Tianning Monastery in Fenzhou: after his father passed away, he shaved his head and resided at Shousheng Monastery; at that time, he was already fifty-one years old.
In the first year of the Chongning era, he finally obtained monastic robes by virtue of imperial favor, and shortly thereafter was bestowed the purple robe.
He subsequently presided over the lecture hall of Master Xin, and students daily filled his gate. To avoid the military turmoil, he traveled south and resided at Puzhao Monastery in Ruzhou.
He later moved to Echeng in Nanyang. Taking the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* as his primary study, he transcribed the entire scripture by hand and made it his fixed daily practice to recite four fascicles.
Having become a guest in that place, his followers dispersed; yet, dwelling alone in an earthen cell, he did not cease his lecturing.

When someone questioned him about this, he replied, "I am merely preaching for the sake of the dragons and devas. Before his meditation niche stood a tree that had long been withered, yet it blossomed with flowers.
As it was gathered, it grew. People took this to be a response to their firm and sincere devotion to the Way.

On the fifth night of the ninth month of the year Wuchen (1206), he preached the "Chapter on the Formation of the World. The following day, he revealed it to the assembly and declared it with the intent of profound stillness and extinction.
He further asked, "From where do you come? To where do you go? Thereupon, he passed away while reclining on his right side at the age of seventy-nine.
Ten thousand people attended his funeral. The śarīra relics obtained, as well as other miraculous manifestations, were exceedingly numerous.
Stūpas were erected at Puzhao Huayan, Dasheng at Guangyang, and Hongjiao at Wuyang. Yuan Yishan inscribed a stele for him, which begins: "That one above..."

This person is a transmitter of the teachings beyond words; within the ocean of the *Avataṃsaka*, he serves as a great Dharma vessel. Dwelling in quietude within a single cell, the numinous deities fill the space before him.
What was once a withered stump now stands with flourishing and luxuriant sprouts. Sacred stupas stand in mutual view, their radiance illuminating the heavens.
The sound of the bells expounds the Dharma for the sake of the entire trichiliocosm. This is indeed a record of actual events.
Fen Yun transmitted the Dharma Cloud.
He resided at Mount Ling in Nanyang. In his youth, while still living in his hometown, he abandoned his family to become a son of the Buddha.
During a year of famine, he harnessed a cart to travel a thousand li for the sake of his parents to seek food. When his mother passed away, he lived in a grass hut beside her grave for three years.
He wailed and wept without ceasing; he did the same when his father passed away. The people of the mountains called this "the cloud over the tomb.

In the winter of the second year of the Yuanguang era, a monk came to the Master at night to request a lecture on the *Fajie guan* (Contemplation of the Dharma Realm). As dawn broke and he was about to leave the gate, he saw [the monk] nearby the hermitage.
The falling snow and rain all turned into flowers, as large as cups and bowls in shape. When the residents heard of this, the old and the young gathered together;
those flowers that had landed on bricks and tiles were all taken away by them. A literary scholar composed a poem to record these events.

Furthermore, to the east of the mountain, the water sources were insufficient, causing distress to the students of the lecture hall. One day, a spring emerged from among the rocks at the western cliff of the temple, its water sweet and delicious.
His tastes were extraordinary; his use of resources was inexhaustible. The Master was a native of Linhai, surnamed Liu. At the age of seven, he abstained from meat and pungent roots.
At eleven, he entered the monastic order at Hongdong. At twenty-five, he received full ordination. He studied doctrinal learning under Guanghua and practiced Chan under Shaoshan.
He came to Nanyang, where he presided over the Guanyin Cloister of Chongsheng Temple. He resided at Mount Ling and founded Ba’en Temple. Thus, with rectitude—
He was sixty-four years old when he passed away after manifesting illness. Liu Guangfu, the Governor of Dengzhou, was a fellow townsman of the Master and knew him well;

he requested Yuan Yishan to compose an inscription for his stupa, which read: "Among the śramaṇas of the world, taking the severance of affection as their fundamental principle, they regard even their own flesh and bones as strangers.
Yet now, this Master’s filial piety toward his parents was such as this. Thus, as for learning..."
As for the Buddha, why must one necessarily abandon all people and flee from them before it can be called "leaving home"?

I, having been granted permission by Liu Buwang, have therefore composed this inscription for him. When the monk Yuncheng came to Linfen in Jin, he dwelt at his father’s grave for six years, wailing in mourning.
There, the spring water gushed forth and celestial flowers fell in profusion; the fame of his filial piety was like incense, universally perfuming the world. How else could this be manifested?
