Exegesis Section, Part One:
The Biography of Dharma Master Shang of Yuanpu.
Pu Shang, courtesy name Xigu, was a native of Zili. His mother dreamed of a monk riding a white horse entering her door before she conceived him.

At the age of seven, his mother taught him the *Xiaojing* (Classic of Filial Piety); he recited it from memory after a single reading and never forgot it. He took a fondness for Buddhist scriptures. At twelve, he met Master Haili of Huili Temple on Mount Ziwai;
he informed his parents of his wish to follow him as a disciple, and they granted permission. He then shaved his head and became a śrāmaṇera.

Upon reaching adulthood, he heard that Master Jingyan Fu was residing at Changle in Chongde, so he went there to seek instruction. Day and night, he investigated the *Huayan guan* (Contemplation of the Avatamsaka).
The Master, pleased by his brilliant understanding, remarked, "In the future, the one who shall establish the teaching in the southeast will surely be you.

Later, while serving the Master at Gaoli in Hangzhou, he took over the Master’s duties as instructor; the assembly submitted to him with respect, and they unanimously elected him as the Head Lecturer (*dugang*).

In the *tiānlì* year Wùchén (1388), he received a decree from the Xuanzheng Yuan and took up residence at Changle Monastery. Since the departure of Master Fú, Changle had been in ruins for a long time;
the Master renovated it and restored it to new splendor. Students came from as far as a thousand *lǐ*, and there was no room to accommodate them all.
In the fourth year of Zhìyuán (1339), he moved to Chōngxiān on Gāotíng Mountain, where he further propagated his profound secrets. His fame reached the imperial court.
The Emperor bestowed upon him the title Great Master Cifeng Miaobian. After seven years, he retired to the Lanya Hermitage on Mount Yuxi.

In the tenth year of the Zhizheng era, the Chancellor of the Provincial Administration, honoring his Way, dispatched an envoy to invite him to Goryeo and specially presented him with a golden-embroidered *kāṣāya* robe composed by imperial decree.
When Zhang Shicheng occupied Gusu, he repeatedly extended invitations, but [the Master] did not comply. As his illness grew critical, he arose and sought—
He wrote a verse with his brush, saying: "For seventy-three years I have dwelt in this world, solely to give voice to the Buddhas and patriarchs.
Today I strike the final blow; I startle the void until it falls to the ground. Having cast down his brush, he passed away. This was the ninth month of autumn in the twenty-second year.
The cremation was attended by more than twenty thousand people. Over a thousand śarīras were recovered; his cranial bone, tongue, teeth, and rosary remained unburned.
After burning the ground for three nights, a light shot toward the heavens. People considered this a sign of the Master’s pure conduct.
The Master was of imposing stature and vast capacity. He was courageous in his pursuit of the Way, reciting the Buddha’s name incessantly.

When guests arrived, he engaged them in profound conversation until dusk without showing the slightest sign of weariness. His ability to explore the depths and unravel the secrets was not something derived from the superficial leaks of language and written characters;
those who received his Dharma transmission and came to be renowned in the world numbered no fewer than several dozen. Xuegu Hai resided at Chongxian, providing nourishment and benefit.

The Elder resided at Miaoxin on West Lake; he was most renowned during his twentieth decade. In his later years, the Master styled himself the "Man of the Avataṃsaka" (Zahua Daoren), for he never forgot his devotion to the Huayan school.
Goodness begets goodness.
His courtesy name was Zizhi, and his style name was Yuexi. He was the son of the Zhu family of Dinghai. Having first taken the tonsure at Jingju Temple, he studied the Vinaya at Huxin.

Later, while traveling to Daxiong Temple in Hangzhou, he became a disciple of Master Wankong. Upon hearing the words of Master Jue, they harmonized with his own realization, and he was appointed to maintain the lecture seat.

He once sighed with profound lamentation, saying: "The scriptural teachings are vast and expansive; their essential points are difficult to discern. It is as if one who has been mute has regained the power of speech, or one who has been blind has regained sight. If not me, then who?
Thereupon, he applied himself with keen diligence to composing his words, arranging them so that they were orderly and unconfused, and explaining them as clearly as pointing at one's palm.

He titled this work *Jiaoguan cuoyao* (Essentials of Teaching and Contemplation), which was convenient for those studying the Tiantai school. Later, while traveling to Jingci Monastery, he visited Master Lianchi and was instructed by him to strike [the bell].

As the various discourses on meditation were being debated, they emerged in an instant, leaving the listeners’ minds clear and bright. The Master [Zhi] clung to names and appearances and was easily deluded.
The Master [Zhili] then said slowly, "The essential principle of the Three Contemplations does not lie outside of this. He bowed in gratitude and said, "Its ultimate aim is to revitalize your school.

When Jiqing Temple was completed, the imperial court ordered that the abbot of the Upper Zhi (Upper Tianzhu) be selected from among the candidates; the Master was included in this selection and lectured on the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.

The *Pán jīng* (Discourse on the Bowl). Listeners arrived like clouds. The Master’s eloquence was suspended like a scale, seizing upon the vital pivot; his discourse was orderly, expansive, and reached the underlying principle.

However, the Master ultimately clung to a stubborn emptiness (*śūnyatā*), which the Patriarch of Upper Zhù could not persuade him away from. Zhǔ Chán Huìzé presided over Yángbào Guóyàoshī during the Zhìpíng era. Daily, he received visitors as numerous as those treading upon the threshold.
He established a separate hall to accommodate them, where oil lamps were arrayed like stars. Subsequently, by public consensus, he was appointed to lead Yánqìng during the Zhìyuán era.
In the twenty-sixth year [of the reign], the temple was destroyed by fire. He resided in a thatched hut of reeds, yet his lectures and discussions continued without interruption.

In the first year of the Dade era, he entered nirvana at the age of seventy-nine, having observed sixty years of monastic seniority (*śrāmaṇerī*). The Layman Qingrong, Jue, lived near the Southern Lake.
I visited Qixin Hall and heard the sound of recitation reaching my seat. I took up the book and read it, but I could not understand it at all.
Master Tai said to me, "Take up the *Zhiyue shuo* (Direct Exposition) and read it; then you will understand. Later, when the Master came to Nanhu, I went to pay my respects to him.
Observing his countenance, which was harmonious yet dignified, and his discourse, which was straightforward and clear, I finally realized: [It was Master Cao.]
The Master’s words were not in vain.
Jōen succeeded to Jōen.

A scion of the Prince family of the Three Rivers, he possessed latent roots from past lives; when a child, he was taught Buddhist scriptures and mastered them at the mere sound of the teacher’s voice.
[Seng]song was a disciple of the Venerable Master Chongguo Long’an. He studied the profound and essential principles of the Perfect and Sudden teachings (*yuan-dun jiaozhi*).
Long’an entrusted him with the responsibility of transmitting and illuminating [the Dharma]. He presided over Qinghui and the Great Master Jizhao, the Master Zhigong, who was his senior brother.

When the Master [Sengsong] emerged into the world, [Zhigong] praised him and presented him with a fly-whisk (*chushi*), exhorting him, saying: "The True Dharma cannot remain without a transmitter; the beings of the human and celestial realms look toward it with earnest longing."

Having found someone to rely upon as a teacher, he simply responded with "yes, yes" and immediately entered Mount Wutai, where he resided at Shangfang Temple. There he explored the ocean of the Tripiṭaka, paying particular attention to the Vinaya.
His water for purification and his incense and lamps were such that no one could even peer into his room. When Falingong passed away, An followed suit.

The seat of the Chongguo Monastery was vacant, and at the earnest request of the assembly, he was invited to fill it. Students gathered in great numbers, and he lectured upon the *Zahua* (Miscellaneous Flowers) every day.

He applied himself tirelessly to its exegesis, never once showing signs of weariness or aversion to the labor involved. When Emperor Shizu heard of this, he praised him and bestowed upon him the title "Great Master Chongjiao of Perfectly Harmonious Buddhahood" (*Foxing Yuanrong Chongjiao Dashi*).
In the Dinghai year of the Zhiyuan era, the Emperor specially granted land in Dadu; thereupon, he collaborated with his disciples [to establish the monastery].
He diligently undertook its construction, transforming rubble and pebbles into a precious monastery (*ratnāvāsa*) and conjuring weeds and wasteland into a golden realm (*suvarṇadhātu*).
Whatever was appropriate for a forest monastery (*araṇya*), he established in due order; thus, there were both the Northern and Southern Temples at Chongfu.

At that time, the Great Master Xiongbian, a man of profound virtue from the past who served Emperor Haotian, bestowed upon the Master the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* written in blood with gold ink by the Liao Emperor Daozong. With more than ten thousand disciples, the entire assembly bowed their heads in reverence.
Seated below, he maintained the discourse on the observance and transgression of the precepts. Since the Master first took his seat, he had been manifestly favored by imperial patronage;

whatever gifts and offerings from pure donors he received, on every June nineteenth, he would exhaustively distribute them to feed the monks, recite sutras, and provide offerings until everything was completely empty, only then ceasing.
He offered this prayer: "May the state be peaceful and secure, and may all sentient beings..."

He received such merit; I had no part in it. At the age of seventy-four, he passed away without illness. When the Emperor was informed, he issued a special decree for the government officials to provide funeral subsidies.
According to the old regulations, cremation was prohibited within the vicinity of the capital. The Master was cremated at Jingtu Monastery west of the city.
Some raised objections, but the Emperor said, "Yuan is no ordinary man; what harm is there in being near? More than a hundred śarīras were obtained, which were perfectly round and pure.
It was like a jewel. The stupa stood in the wilds of Luguokuo. Two years later, when Emperor Renzong ascended the throne, his chief disciple petitioned the court, saying:
"Our late master entered nirvana, and we have already enshrined his remains as śarīra within this stupa.

Given that our late master’s spiritual conduct was so highly esteemed by successive sovereigns, it would not be fitting for this to remain unrecorded in writing if we wish to ensure its endurance for all time. [The request was granted] by those in the court.
"Among his disciples, who is most worthy to compose this inscription? May Your Majesty choose. Emperor Renzong commanded Zhao Mengfu of the Hanlin Academy to write the text, stating:
"The Master’s precepts and conduct were as pure and clean as clear lapis lazuli; yet when he ascended the great altar and presided over vast assemblies,"
When his profound voice reached those below, it was like a great general swearing an oath to his troops; there were none who did not tremble with awe and receive it with reverence.
Were it not for one whose Way is perfected and virtue complete, who else could have attained such a state?
The Biography of Master Xiyuan Yi.
Master Xiyuan Yi was the son of the Liu family of Zhengzhou. While he was still in the womb, his mother dreamed that she had gone out into the wilds and found a golden seal.
A person in the wild said to her, "Present this immediately to the Buddha; do not delay. She then beheld from afar a stupa and temple that were most magnificent.
Sheng, carrying the seal with him, fell asleep and was born as the master’s son. His parents regarded this as extraordinary.
When he reached the age of five, they sent him out to rely upon Master Fei at Tianning Monastery in Zhenyang. When his parents returned south, they took him along again because of his young age.
At fifteen or sixteen, wearing a monastic robe, he traveled north to study at Baoji Temple in Yanzhong, and further studied the Huayan teachings of the Perfect and Sudden Vehicle in Zhending.
Master Jing studied the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* under Master Wen Xiaoyan of Daliang. As the years passed, his understanding of the principles of the mind deepened.
Whenever Wen established a doctrinal argument, he would beat the drums and ascend the hall; as the sharp points of his arguments rose on all sides, the Master would simply raise a single finger.

Wherever that finger reached, it was as if mist were dispersed and ice were melted; there was no one who did not roll their tongue and lower their brows to take their place among the listeners. Subsequently, he withdrew to cultivate the "wall-contemplation" (*bhittidhyāna*).

At Mount Mingyue, the great bhikṣus led by Quan Gong declared, "Now that both the dust-like world and its lands are empty, and the Dharma has no place of abiding, the lamp grows dim while the night is long;
who can fathom the way through the mazes of delusion? They thus requested the Master to emerge from seclusion within the mountains.

The Master accepted their words and went forth to reside at Dahong Jisi Temple in Xuzhou, where he expounded the principles of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Consciousness-Only) school and purchased thirty commentaries and records.
The remaining sections totaled more than one thousand three hundred fascicles. As the Master expounded their meanings in succession, his voice resounded far and near.
Those who leaned forward with rapt attention from the lowest ranks numbered constantly over a thousand. From south of the River, all who wished to study flocked to him.

When he first arrived, there were no more than four or five dilapidated dwellings and monks; yet before long, what was ruined was renewed, what was lacking was provided, and the monastery was magnificently adorned.
It was truly extraordinary, like a celestial palace. The overflowing abundance of the Buddhist fields in the Indus region was entirely due to the Master’s transformative virtue.
The Master maintained the precepts with rigorous discipline; throughout his life, he wore tattered robes and ate coarse food, refining his mind through the practice of the "four-finger" austerity.

For over forty years, he lectured on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* some thirty times. Throughout the regions of the Yellow River and Luo, those who prepared seats to await him were filled with anxious longing.
From the kings, dukes, and nobles above to the woodcutters and herdsmen below, there were none who did not pay him respectful homage and turn toward him with faith.
Those from all quarters who sought to exhaustively investigate the definitive meaning (nītārtha) all took the Master as their refuge.

Yet, who could have known that what the Master called "definitive meaning" did not reside merely in words? He was bestowed the title *Dafoming Yuanming Puzhao Dashi* (Great Master of the Perfectly Illuminating Universal Radiance of Buddha-nature).
He entered parinirvāṇa in the fourth month of the second year of the Yanyou era. He was seventy-three years of age and had fifty-five years of monastic seniority (*bhikṣu-vaṣa*).
His entire body was enshrined in a stupa to the south of the city.

Shanru Shanru (literally: "Skillfully Entering, Skillfully Entering"). His surname was Fu, and his family had resided in Dinghai for generations. The Dharma Master Da Pengyin saw him and marveled at his extraordinary qualities.

In the eleventh year of the Chunyou era, he received full ordination from Master Bin of Ban-shan. He traveled through various regions, where his analytical understanding reached profound depths, and he stayed as a guest at Dongye.
Shan composed four books on the teachings of the school. Relying on the essential principles and adhering to the core tenets, he did not allow himself to be mired in mere words;

his instructions were earnest and direct, and those who followed him delighted in their simplicity and ease. Initially, Dharma Master Fuguang resided at Upper Zhushan and led all his disciples to follow him.
At that time, there was a man of virtuous character who studied with the Master; they each established their own positions and refused to conform or align themselves with him.
The Master consulted with Liang, saying, "My teacher was Dapeng; you, brother, are capable of succeeding him. I wish for you to pay your respects once more and await his instructions.

Later, Liang succeeded Yuanjue Wankong, while the Master ultimately succeeded in flourishing the lineage of Dapeng. He first served as the attendant at Nanming, later presided over the seat of instruction, and became the abbot of Donggao on Mount Zhe.
His secular name was Shizhong. His teaching held that the primary illness is the assertion of individuality, while fragmentation is but a secondary consequence.

His discourse flowed freely without overflowing, concise yet never abrupt. Monastics and scholars alike revered him. Where the Dharma had declined, he restored it; where the community was disordered, he brought peace without weariness.

During the Zhizheng era, an imperial edict was issued to the Xuanzheng Yuan, instructing them to be diligent in their selection of candidates and not to yield to favoritism or greed for personal gain.
Those who convened the discussion said, "Nanhu was absent; who else but Master She could have done this?

They then deeply reflected upon what had been transmitted to them in the past and secretly revealed the refutation of emptiness and conventionality, establishing the clarity and stillness of the single nature. As they deliberated and critiqued one another, they eventually forgot their words.
Da-peng indeed became renowned in the world, and Chong-ben took up his resolve; thus, the Master achieved success therein. This is the "Great" [section].
Thus it was. Regarding his cultivation and practice, he no longer clung to worldly affairs.

He was bestowed the honorary title of Master Huiguan Hongjiao (Wisdom-Contemplation Propagator of the Dharma), while he styled himself Qiuxu (Autumn Void). During the Yanyou era, he manifested parinirvāṇa. He had been a monk for sixty-three periods.
At the age of seventy-eight, Master Ne appeared as if unable to speak; yet when one listened to his seated lectures, they were vast and boundless.
His conduct was pure and refined, his emaciated countenance solemn and cultivated—truly a sublime ancient worthy who was sufficient to inspire and uplift others.
The Biography of Dharma Master Pujue of Qinzhou.
He was renowned for his brilliant eloquence and bore the surname Zhao. At the age of seven, he followed a teacher and received full ordination.

At twenty-five, he relied upon Master Tan of Bo-lin to study the teachings, eventually becoming the presiding master of Ci'en Monastery. Wherever he went, he made the transmission and preservation of the Dharma his primary task. By nature, the Master was sincere and pure, like fine jade.
Jade contains its raw essence; though it is not further carved or painted, people naturally hold it in high esteem. Even fierce soldiers and martial men can show it respect.
People say that in an age without a Buddha, he was sufficient to serve as one.

Whenever he obtained money or worn-out currency, he used it all to establish Buddhist shrines and provide food for those who observe the Way. Thus, gentlemen held his character in high regard, and many followed his transformation. [Year]...
He was sixty-eight years old. On the sixth month of the first year of the Yanyou era, he passed away at Jingfu Temple amidst extraordinary and wondrous signs.
On the evening of his death, he manifested miraculous traces. Following his cremation, he was interred in a stupa behind Pujue Temple.
Chōen Fukuen Kōshu Tōden Ken was the son of Yang [surname] from Dingping in Ningzhou. In his youth, he followed monks to study Buddhist scriptures.
Upon reaching maturity, he traveled through Qin, Luo, Bian, and Ru to consult with former masters and study the way of the *bhikṣu*. It was there that his hair was shorn. Thereupon, he crossed...
Crossing the river to the north, he visited various great Dharma masters. The scriptures he heard totaled six sutras, four treatises, and one vinaya;

all were vast in expression and profound in meaning, exhausting the depths of the Tripitaka. These elders were all renowned far and wide for their mastery of the Dharma and their ability to explain its principles.

The Master personally studied under them, absorbing their teachings as if by incense-smoke and being warmed by their presence, entering their halls and partaking of their finest portions. Thus, before his years had even exceeded those of the *li* (the age of thirty), he had completed his training.

He had already attained great renown during his time. Later, he went to the capital, where he received the teachings of the Perfect and Sudden *Avataṃsaka* school under the master Jian, the presiding abbot of Wannian Temple.
Jian held him in high esteem for his vast learning and many talents. Initially, by imperial decree, he resided at Wanningsi;
subsequently, he was transferred to Dachongensi. He served as the abbot of these two great monasteries for a total of twelve years, and his virtue and character were highly esteemed.
His imperial sincerity caused his reputation to spread even to the corners of the sea. Yet he never allowed the honors and glory of imperial favor to alter his original character.
He once said to others: "A scholar clad in hempen robes stands apart from the mundane world; if one is not ashamed before the morning, then dying at evening is sufficient.
What more could one desire from the outside? From then on, he withdrew from human affairs and confined himself within a single room, keeping his conduct as secret as a closed bag.

Delighting in the Way, he passed away at his secluded retreat on the first month of the fourth year of the Yanyou era. He was fifty-one years of age and had forty-three years of monastic seniority (*śrāmaṇera*).

When the ministers reported this to the throne, an imperial edict was issued for the relevant authorities to prepare ceremonial guards and to assemble the banners, canopies, drums, and music from the various temples of the capital region to escort him.
After the cremation, *śarīra* relics were obtained, and a stupa was erected to the south of the city.
The biography of Dharma Master Miaowen:

Miaowen was the son of the Sun family from Weizhou. He became a monk at the age of nine. At eighteen, he donned the monastic robes and traveled abroad for study, traversing the regions of Yun, Shuo, Yan, and Zhao.
After receiving full ordination, he reached the capital and relied upon the Great Virtue Master Ming to study the Perfect and Sudden teachings.
He fully grasped the essential meaning of the Way. For thirty-two years, he remained submerged among the common crowd.

Only when the exhortations of the assembly became insistent did he finally don the crimson robes and ascend the lion throne to join the ranks of those who transmit and propagate the teachings. His cultivation was characterized by humility and restraint;

he had no desire for rapid fame or success, nor did he act with impetuosity to seek advancement. Such was his nature. He served as the abbot of Yunquan in Ji, where he practiced diligence and frugality.
The elderly cherished his virtue, while the youth respected his teachings; thus, the community was harmonious and the monastery was well-ordered.
After two successive years of good harvests, the granaries were filled with surplus grain, which he used during times of famine to relieve the hungry. The people of Ji praised him.

When Emperor Shizu heard of his Way, he summoned him for an audience and, turning to his attendants, remarked, "This is a monk of great merit. By imperial decree, he was appointed to reside at Baoji Temple. At that time, the study of Chan was gradually declining.
The teachings of the various vehicles flourished even more, and both the Xing (Nature) and Xiang (Characteristics) schools drove side by side as Mahayana traditions.

Those within the realm who studied these doctrines were confined by mere categories and numbers, stalled by divergent paths, and obscured by views born of emotional attachment; they were deluded regarding the purport of the Perfect and Sudden.

The Master alone extensively propagated the Vaipulya (Vaipulya-sūtras), rousing the perfect capacity [of sentient beings] and providing a means for those who clung to the stump of literal words to cleanse their emotional attachments.
Dust and phenomena are fused in tranquil illumination. Thus, like dragons and elephants treading the path, they vied to mount the carriage of the One Vehicle.

When he exceeded eighty years of age, wearying of his labors, he entrusted the affairs of the monastery to his disciples and retired to live as a recluse in leisure. He devoted himself exclusively to the samādhi of Buddha-recitation.
In the sixth year of the Yan-you era, he passed away while seated, at the age of eighty-three. On the day of his death, he exhorted the assembly to chant the name of the Buddha with a loud voice.
Ming suddenly rose, sat in the full lotus posture, and formed the *samādhi* mudrā; he became profoundly still and tranquil. Huizhen (Huiyin) transmitted [the dharma] to Huizhen.
He was the son of the Zhang family from Guansi; having believed in the Buddha-vehicle since childhood, he left the household life and later followed Pujiu of Hedong.

Master Yue studied the definitive meaning of the *Awakening of Faith* (*Jué jīng*). He further studied the teachings of the perfect and ultimate *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* under National Teacher Dahui of Baima Monastery in Henan.
Later, he studied the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* under Master Yi of Xiyuan. At the age of twenty-two, he received full ordination.

A person of the Ge clan established an assembly for one hundred monks; the Master served as the First Seat (*prathama-pīṭhika*) and was requested to preach the Dharma, whereupon he manifested the form of a lion.

He raised a lion’s roar. Subsequently, he followed Master Xiu to lecture on the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, studied the treatises on *Hetuvidyā* (Logic) and other subjects under Master He Xin-yi, and further studied the *Avatamsaka-sūtra-śāstra* under Master Da-tong Yan. For twenty years, he sported within the ocean of the teachings;

there was no gate he did not knock upon and no principle he did not exhaustively investigate. Yet, when it came to leaving the world, he alone chose to dwell among the crags and burn incense—a true ascetic. Indeed...

He took Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*) as his ultimate refuge. Later, he entered Mount Taihang and practiced the Samādhi of Mind-Only Consciousness for seven years, until the sense faculties and their objects became empty and still.
In the second year of the Zhizhi era, Emperor Yingzong visited Mount Tai; he invited the Master to accompany him to the Southern Peak and commanded the Master to pray for auspicious omens.
The Master immediately entered meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). The Emperor beheld a white light like water, filling the expanse of space. The Great Being [appeared]...
A circular halo appeared within the light, which brought him great joy. Consequently, he commanded the Crown Prince and various nobles to receive the Bodhisattva precepts from the Master.

The Emperor issued an edict bestowing upon him the rank of Grand Minister (Situ) of the first grade; however, the Master firmly declined, and the matter was thus dropped. In the third year of the Zhizhi era, he passed away at the age of sixty-seven.
Biography of Dharma Master Yudang of Jin’an Temple (with his younger brother Jinbao), whose courtesy name was Shiwei.
“Yudang” was his style name. He was the son of the Kang family of Chengji. From his youth, he possessed a transcendent spirit and took no pleasure in worldly affairs.
Together with his younger brother Jin, he shaved his head and donned the robes of a monk to follow a teacher, seeking the Way that transcends the mundane. Whenever he encountered those of renown...
Whenever a virtuous teacher began a lecture, he would invariably go to attend. He once remarked: "To study without reflecting, or to reflect without studying—this is what the gentleman fears.
Though one may master the explanations, if one does not penetrate the fundamental principle, this is 'studying without reflecting. How can such a person be called a man of true understanding?

Moreover, as for the study of words and letters, it is like守着 the stump or following the tracks of an elephant; deluded by the many divergent paths, how could one possibly traverse toward the single destination?"
"Is this not the profound depth of the Ocean-Seal Sudden Teaching? To listen to his discourse is indeed eloquent; yet, when observing what he has attained, it is still not sufficient.
Thereupon, having questioned him, I studied under him to broaden my understanding and further refine my contemplation.

It is by this means that his realization was achieved—attaining it beyond the realm of conceptual bonds. Therefore, his expositions possess a profound lineage, penetration, and essential flavor, which his successors..."
National Preceptor Zhenjue inherited the teachings of the Xianshou school. Because his lineage was so exalted, his insight became even more lucid;
the realm of his mind was as still as calm water and as polished as a clear mirror.

Although he possessed such innate talent and a refined capacity for learning, it was also due to the refinement of his teachers and friends—like jade being carved and orchids being perfumed—that he reached the state of Zhenjue, and was thus commissioned to reside at Dabai.
Master Ma was accompanied by Jin. They traveled together to Mount Tai, where Zhengjue passed away. By imperial decree, Master Ma succeeded him in his position.
Later, by the command of the Empress Dowager, he resided at Dapu'an Temple. He entered parinirvāṇa in the seventh month of the second year of the Zhi-zhi era at the age of fifty-one.
He was buried in Dongfeng Valley. Jin also possessed noble conduct; he previously resided at Youguo and later moved to Puxian.
"Peaceful. All these served as the Master's successors. To serve one's teacher as one would a father, remaining consistent from beginning to end without any lapse—this is indeed difficult.
The Biography of Daliang, the Great Master Hongjiao of Puning on Mount Wutai:
His courtesy name was Dalin; his secular surname was Wu. From youth, he possessed a love for learning and a nature of keen intelligence, which seemed almost divinely bestowed.

The venerable and virtuous Master An served as his preceptor and shaved his head for him. Once he had received full ordination, he traveled through various monastic academies, probing the depths of the sutras and śāstras.
There he encountered Master Zhengjue Yuan, who awakened his initial resolve. He then journeyed north and south for nearly ten thousand li, exhaustively visiting secluded and magnificent sites;
wherever he went, he invariably sought out eminent persons and inquired into the essentials of the Ultimate Way. These were the ones whom he took as teachers and from whom he studied.
For instance, Master Tan of Beilin, Master Hui of Guanzhong, and Master Ci of Nanyang were all renowned for their expertise in the study of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.

Upon returning, they beheld the True Awakening at Longdi once more; there, they perceived even more clearly the towering height of its walls and the profound depth of its inner chambers, whereupon they said: [...]* *(Note: The original text contains an ellipsis indicating an omitted portion of the quote.)*
The Buddhist Dharma is the compass for all; is it not found here? After the passing of the True Awakened One, he traveled north to Yan and Ji.
He concealed his traces beneath the gates of Wei, remaining as carefree as one dwelling upon the rivers and seas, as if having forgotten the world.

Yet, because the beauty of his inner gem could not be hidden though he wore coarse cloth, his fame eventually spread through the mouths of the multitude, and his reputation reached the imperial court. Thus, he encountered [the Emperor] at Wan...

It was better that he first fall [into obscurity]. The Emperor summoned the Master to reside there. During the Dazhong era, the Empress Dowager founded a temple on Mount Tai, naming it Puning (Universal Peace).
Because this site possessed the preeminent beauty of the world, the responsibility of serving as its abbot could not be borne by anyone other than one of the most eminent reputations in the realm;

thus, the Master was appointed to the post. The Master resided there for over ten years before passing away. By nature, he was firm and resolute, and he possessed a considerable sense of integrity and principle.

He was unable to bow and nod in conformity with worldly customs. Although he resided in a monastic office, he never once visited the provincial or capital government offices to seek the doors of the powerful and noble.
Some remarked that the Master lacked a genial air, to which he replied: "I am but a single monk;

the Son of Heaven did not disregard my lowly status and instead placed me in this great monastery. I shall simply exhaust my sincerity without slackening, seeking only to repay the state. What else should I seek?"
Ah! There must have been slanderous words from someone like Zang Cang against me. This was likely just the buzzing of a bluebottle fly alighting upon the thorny hedge.
Considering that my destiny has not met with fortune and my Way cannot be realized, I shall put on my shoes and depart; where could I go that I would not find fulfillment in the Way?

At that time, the state held Western monks in high honor and patronage, and their followers were extremely numerous; they entered and exited with mounted retinues, matching the imperial entourage in their tracks.
O King, this man has reddish-brown hair and wears a towering crown; he dwells with such haughty self-assurance that none among the ranks of renowned virtuous ones fail to pay him homage.
Some bow deeply forward, tucking up their robes to touch his feet, begging him to place his hand upon their heads—an act they call "bestowing grace."
The Master alone performed a long bow and was silent. Some said of him, "He is arrogant. The Master replied, "How could I dare to treat others with contempt?
I have heard that a gentleman loves others according to propriety. How could I arbitrarily bend my principles to kowtow at their feet and thereby invite humiliation for myself?
Furthermore, what do I seek from them regarding the Way? They are haughty and insolent because of their power; if I were to [yield]..."
This was his yielding. It was neither flattery nor sycophancy; how could a gentleman engage in such acts of flattery and sycophancy?

Those who discerned the truth praised Master Shi’s spirit, saying that his meeting with the Prince of Goryeo—like that of Master Foyin Yuan—may be called an understanding of the great principle and an attainment of propriety.
He passed away in the ninth month of the first year of the Zhizhi era. His stupa and śarīra were enshrined at Zhu.
The Ruins of the Forest:
The Biography of Dharma Master Hongji (with an appended note to Gu’an).
Hongji, whose courtesy name was Tongzhou and also Tian’an, was the son of the Yao family of Yuyao. He entered the monastic order at Baoji Temple in his native village.
Shun received the full precepts from Master Man. Master Man was his paternal uncle. The Master was exceptionally brilliant and peerless;
whenever he was taught the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he was immediately able to memorize it. At the age of sixteen, he received ordination and became a *bhikṣu*.

He upheld the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, and in every step and movement, he did not dare to transgress its precise measurements. Later, he sighed and said: "The precepts must certainly not be treated with laxity; one must refine the teachings."

He multiplied his efforts to support his practice and understanding; how could he afford to delay? Thereupon, he went to Yīn and relied upon Master Quán of Bānshān to study the texts of the Tiantai school.

After a long time, he thoroughly mastered their doctrines. He frequently performed the ritual repentances of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, and the Pure Land, concentrating his essence and spirit with unwavering sincerity.
Within a state of meditative visualization, he had a vision of the Venerable [Tiantai Zhiyi], who bestowed upon him—
With a rhinoceros-horn *ruyi* [ceremonial scepter], his eloquence increased daily from that point on; like a river flowing or a spring gushing forth, it was entirely without obstruction.
Before long, with the commencement of the Taiding era, he began teaching the Dharma at Wanshou Yuanjue Temple.

Distinguished scholars from both sides of the Zhejiang River flocked to his quarters, fearing only to be left behind. Commentators remarked that he had initiated the Way of Fohai and spread its fragrance.
The name You (Yǒu) truly originated with the Master himself.

He revealed his name Gù'ān (Blind Hermit) after receiving the tonsure from Yìshān Yuán-gōng. Yìshān ordained four disciples, naming them according to the "opening, showing, awakening, and entering" (*kai-shì-wù-rù*) of the *Lotus Sūtra*.
The Master was the second, named Xiànshì (Manifesting), and his style-name was Gù'ān; he was from Níng-hǎi in Tái.
The son of the Lu clan possessed an ancient countenance and a tall stature. He was reticent in speech and laughter, maintaining himself with pure frugality.
For twenty years he occupied but a single mat, appearing as carefree as if staying in a guesthouse. He practiced the teachings of *śikṣā* and *vipaśyanā*, following his master at Wanshou Monastery.

Upon seeing that his natural endowment was sharp and keen, possessing a momentum like water flowing a thousand li in a single rush, the master said: "Have you not followed my teacher to study? In the future, you shall be great..."
"To manifest the single school of Nanyue—upon you, my son, I have high hopes. Having been thus instructed, he subsequently served at Fohai [Monastery].

At the beginning of the Zhizheng era, he emerged into the world at Longshou Jiaoshe, loudly proclaiming the teachings of the Tiantai and Jingxiu schools, thereby becoming a renowned Buddhist master throughout the realm; this was truly due to the inspiration of his teacher.
The coastal cliffs of Yanguan collapsed, leaving the people trembling with fear day and night, dreading they would become fish and turtles.
The Provincial Governor, Duke Tuohan, was deeply concerned and requested that the Master personally visit the site to convene a seven-day and seven-night *shuilu* (water-land) assembly.

The Master focused his mind in contemplation, took sand from the sea, consecrated it with mantras, and led his disciples to scatter it everywhere across the area. Wherever their footsteps reached, the cliffs were restored.
He did not collapse [in spirit]. All people marveled at him. When the Tianli era was inaugurated, he was promoted to the two monasteries of Zhuxian and Ciji in Jiqing;
both were famous Buddhist sites in Hangzhou. The Master dwelt there with utter detachment. In the seventh year of the Zhizheng era, the Master was eighty years old.
Among the renowned mountains of Qiantang, as the elder statesmen had passed away one by one, the Master alone remained towering like the Lingguang Pavilion of Lu. Furthermore, because the Great Fu...

Fuxi invited him. The Master lay firm in his reclining and did not respond. A disciple stepped forward and said, "While it is certainly well for the Master to make such plans for himself, what will become of this Way?
The Master was compelled to go. Not long after he arrived, he finally brushed off his robes and returned to his old mountain retreat.

There he opened the Jingqing Pavilion and lived in deep seclusion. Subsequently, he examined the commentaries on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* produced by various schools and found that they were unbalanced, being either too prolix or too terse. Just then—

He intended to synthesize these various doctrines and compose a commentary upon them. Suddenly, his illness flared up. He summoned the fourfold assembly and earnestly exhorted them with the teaching of the Pure Land as Mind-Only.
Some among them did not yet understand the Master’s intent; the Master spoke in a stern voice, saying, "Difficult is birth and death!

Difficult is birth and death! He then immediately sought a brush to write a verse and passed away. He was eighty-six years old, with seventy-one years of monastic seniority. Seven days after his passing...
On that day, his disciples used earthenware vessels to enshrine his remains and buried them at Songhwawu on Mount Omei within the village—the site the Master had chosen for himself.
The Master possessed a majestic and imposing appearance and spoke with refined elegance. Having read any book but once, he never forgot it for the rest of his life.
Throughout his life, he regarded the propagation of the Dharma as his primary duty; whenever he was summoned, he never...

It was not so; he frequently experienced the auspicious omen of heavenly flowers raining down. Nevertheless, regarding the textual matters of the Buddha-vehicle (*buddhayāna*), he did not neglect either of them.
Whether in public office or in retirement, whether speaking or remaining silent, he never departed from *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.

The books he authored—including the *Siji zhengyi*, the *Tian'an waiji*, and others—circulate together in the world. To Shigu’an: he passed away at the age of sixty-nine, having entered our [tradition].

This is clear. The two masters were diligent in their propagation of the teaching; in their extensive exposition and transformative guidance, they followed the treatises of the various masters of the Shanjia school as their sole foundation, never daring to deviate from them.
Thus, they may truly be called those who knew the venerable one’s merit in aiding the Way and who were exemplary successors and continuators of his legacy.
Biography of Dàyòng Cáifǎshī:
Cáì, styled Dàyòng, was the son of Qū of Línhǎi in Tāizhōu. His father, Zhémíng, was a scholar of the *kēmù* system who was well-versed in the great classics.

His mother, née Zhào, was devoted to goodness and venerated the Buddha with great diligence. When the Master was just able to speak, he could already recite the *Xiàojīng* (Classic of Filial Piety) by heart.
In his seventh year, he was skilled at composing verses; they flowed from his mouth spontaneously, harmonious and imbued with profound thought. He shaved his head and received full ordination.

Traveling to Wulin, he went to pay his respects to Master Zhantang Cheng. Upon seeing that the Master’s countenance was strikingly noble and that his speech always struck the essential point, the Master immediately expected him to become a vessel of the Dharma.
At that time, Runyugang served as the First Seat; the Master humbled himself to serve him.
Thus he studied. Even during the heat that could melt gold or the cold that could snap leather, he did not step beyond the threshold of his door for ten years.

Regarding all the profound mysteries of the Tiantai school’s categories of flavor (*wei*) and the essentials of its teachings and contemplation (*jiaoguan*), once he was instructed in them, his understanding was liberated and his mind harmonized;

there was nothing he failed to master in its innermost depths. Yugang sighed and said, "If this youth had not already practiced these matters at the assembly on Vulture Peak, how could he have attained such realization?"
"It has come to this! When Yugang went forth to preside over Desheng in Haiyan, the Master sat on his seat as an assistant.

Later, when Yugang moved to Yanfu, the Imperial Secretariat (Xuanzheng Yuan) invited the Master to succeed him in the teaching seat. At that time, the reputation of Zantang was spreading far and wide both within and without the realm, and the general consensus was that the Master would surely wish to become his dharma heir.
Yet, upon ascending the seat, the Master offered incense to succeed Yugang. The gentlemen of the age remarked:"
As for Zhiji: in the second year of the Zhizheng era, he moved to Xingfu Temple in Hangzhou. Before long, he was promoted to the abbacy of Yanfu.

The Chancellor, Prince Kangli, visited him repeatedly, presenting incense and ceremonial offerings while seeking his counsel on the essentials of the mind. The temple had long been in ruins; the Master restored it step by step.
He constructed the Ten Thousand Buddhas Pavilion (*Wanfo Ge*), which was over one hundred and thirty *chi* in height. As for the Master’s character, he was grave, dignified, simple, and taciturn.
His contemplative practice was diligent and ardent; he strove tirelessly in his cultivation without a moment’s laxity.

Whenever the summer retreat concluded and the period of seclusion ended, while his fellow practitioners all packed their robes and departed at their convenience, the Master alone remained behind, closing his door to refuse visitors, further refining himself through rigorous discipline. People...
Unable to endure such purity and austerity, he dwelt therein with joyful serenity. One day, he suddenly felt his head and eyes ache;
he immediately said to the assembly, "My karmic conditions have come to an end. He then sat upright facing west, reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha for an entire day and night.
Thereupon, he addressed the assembly, saying, "Do not say that the practice of cultivation yields no results; my conditions for the Pure Land have ripened through samādhi."

He appeared before them. He immediately requested a bath and changed his robes, then wrote a farewell letter to his acquaintances. Joining his palms, he passed away. During the cremation, light of five colors emanated from the interior of the coffin.
After the fire subsided, his tongue was like a red lotus and his teeth were like white conch shells.

Relics as large as soybeans filled the ground; tens of thousands of people vied with one another to collect them until they were all gone at once. Those who arrived later dug the earth for more than a foot deep.
He also attained this. To the south of Takan-ji Temple, he lived for sixty-eight years and sat in meditation for fifty-six summer retreats.

Master Jixian of Gu'an said: "With his vast and inclusive capacity and far-reaching insight, the Master achieved the efficacy of establishing and maintaining [the Dharma] amidst the kalpa of emptiness and destruction;
yet there may be those who can equal him. As for the subtle point of the inherent nature, however, when it comes to expounding upon it with full license—"
He was a hero who illuminated the true lamp when it had already grown dim and cemented the harmony of wisdom when it was about to fall.
How could this have been achieved by mere human effort? These words are well-founded.
Shanjì. My master Ān inherited the lineage from Shanjì.

His courtesy name was Juézōng. His mother dreamed that a deity bestowed upon her a white lotus, and he was born therefrom. Initially, he studied for the civil service examinations, but suddenly exclaimed, "This body is illusory;
it will ultimately undergo transformation and extinction. He then realized that attaining high office through mere words is like a spark from a flint.

A flash of lightning vanishes into emptiness in the blink of an eye; what wise person would be so attached to it? He then departed to seek the Dharma from Master Zantang Cheng, under whom he grasped the essential meaning.
He practiced the Lotus Sūtra Repentance and frequently attained spiritual responses. At that time, many men of talent and refinement gathered at his teaching site;
there were none who came empty-handed but returned with true realization. Upon returning to Huading, he stayed in a place where the ponds were deep and the woods were cold.

He practiced the sixteen contemplations and set his mind single-mindedly on the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang). Later, he sat in meditation until death according to his appointed time. Upon cremation, the śarīra relics were piled up like bricks.
Benwu, whose courtesy name was Wuan, was a native of Huangyan in Tai prefecture. He received the tonsure at Jingci Monastery under Fashan and relied upon Jizhao as his teacher.
In Central India, there was a maternal uncle who served as a director of the monastic community. He urged [the master] to convert to the Buddhist faith.

The Master joyfully agreed and went to see Master Tancheng at Yanfu Temple, where he diligently studied the scriptural divisions (*śāstra*). He said, "If it is for the purpose of propagating the Way and benefiting sentient beings, whether one is there or here makes no difference;
what harm is there? Jizhao lamented his departure and sent him a verse, which said: "Entering Chan by way of the Teachings."

There have been those who followed from Chan into the Teachings in both ancient and modern times; such cases have never occurred before. Although the gates of the "One Mind and Three Contemplations" differ, the moon remains solitary even as it fills a thousand rivers.
Having become the successor to Master Cheng for the sake of transcending the world, he nevertheless burned a single incense stick to pay homage to Master Jizhao.

He did not allow their differences in outward traces to create a duality in his heart. When Jizhao manifested his entry into nirvana, the Master was at Yanqing in Siming, where he sent a letter entrusting him with [the lineage].

There is no other way to propagate the great essence of the Sūtra’s ultimate intent than through this power. When the Master received the letter, he prepared a memorial service and offered incense, saying:
"The fifth transmission of Miaoxi is the most brilliant flame; Jizhao’s life-work is the gate of ambrosia. To casually touch it is to have one's liver and brain split asunder."
Frost and ice suddenly turn into the warmth of spring. I think back to the day my nostrils were struck away; what kind of breath remained then that it still exists today?
The celestial wind blows from the north as the year draws to a close; why seek traces in the void with a flash of lightning? Subsequently, I resided at Jiqing Temple.
The pagoda poles of the Upper Tianzhu Monastery stand facing one another; all were established by Master Tancheng. It is said that "one lamp divided its light.
Regarding the biography of Dharma Master Yunruo:
his courtesy name was Jiheng, and he styled himself Fuxiuzi. His clan was the Xiangli, and he was a native of Yue. For generations, his family had served as high officials.
Ying. From his youth, he possessed a disposition that transcended the mundane. Initially, as a young boy, he served the Venerable Yunmen Yuan.
At fifteen, he received full ordination and became a bhikṣu. He traveled to Hulin to pay respects to Da Shan at Xingfu Temple; from then on, he studied the Tiantai teachings.
When Master Zhantang Cheng presided over Nan-Tianzhu, the Master joined him there. His hearing penetrated his heart, and his understanding flourished day by day.

When he arrived, Zhantang held him in high esteem. After he had already emerged into the world as a master at Jingxing Temple, Zhantang could not cease thinking of him and summoned him back to return.

He requested that he occupy the position of the First Seat (Dìyīzuò). He led a community of over a thousand people with strict and orderly regulations; those who received his instruction were transformed.
He attained profound realization and insight. During the Tai Ding era, the Xingzheng Yuan (Bureau of Buddhist and Tibetan Affairs) requested him to take charge of Xinghua Monastery.
At that time, those who propagated the Way on the Northern and Southern Hills of Hangzhou—including Tian’an Ji, Wú Ān, and Yùtíng Hǎn—each possessed great reputations;
people referred to them as the "Four Heavenly Kings within the Assembly of Buddha-Oceans. Not long after, he retired to Yunmen.
Regarding honor, profit, fame, and offerings, he regarded them with such equanimity that he felt no inclination toward them.

He roamed freely among the crags and gullies, occasionally joining Master Duanjiang En and Master Xiugeng Yi to laugh and sing in the breeze, unaware that the setting sun was already hanging over the trees. The Gentleman also observed this.

He served as the abbot of Yunmen for three successive masters. Over the course of his career, he presided over four monastic centers in total. Wherever the rain of his teaching fell, it was like nectar or clarified butter;
those who drank of it found their minds at peace, ultimately taking Yunmen as their final refuge.

He constructed a secluded hermitage and, in his later years, took the Lotus Sūtra, the wisdom of contemplation, and samādhi as his pure practice. However, as the world fell into great chaos and the turmoil of war raged, the Dharma...

The Master gave it to him. When he encountered Wei with a blade held to his side, the Master remained resolute and did not yield; his words and expression were both stern. Consequently, he was killed, and white milk overflowed onto the ground.
He was eighty years of age and had been a monk for sixty-five years. After the soldiers withdrew, he was cremated, and countless *śarīra* relics, the size of soybeans, were obtained.
They were interred at the foot of Mount Yunmen. The Master’s demeanor was simple and profound. At the end of his life...
In his later years, his spirit and vital energy remained complete and firm. Liu Bowen praised his poetry and prose as being ancient, elegant, lofty, and pure, possessing a singular style;
consequently, he became famous at the time, and high officials and nobles alike were deeply impressed by him.

Although we cannot fully examine the beauty of the Master’s lifelong conduct, it remains that what is determined by one's final destiny is something even the sages of antiquity could not entirely avoid; this does not in the least detract from his moral integrity.
Chonggao (Venerable Chonggao).
Shanyou (Master Shanyou).
The Dong family. A native of Yongxing in Dexing. At the age of seven, he served Master Guangxing of Yong’an. He remained silent...
He recited the *Vajraśekhara* and various other sutras. At twenty, he entered the Perfect and Sudden Dharma-gate of the *Avataṃsaka*.

He received the precepts from the Great Master Guangyan, the transmitter of the Vinaya, and thereafter discarded worldly flavors and severed all attachment to finery. Daily, he recited one scroll of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* and performed one hundred prostrations before the Buddha.
He contemplated deeply and remained in silent meditation, traveling alone and reaching solitary heights; no one could gauge the depth of his realization. Emperor Xianzong...
Upon hearing his name, he was granted the title Great Master Hongjiao Tongli (弘教通理大師) and ordered to preside over the Qingliang Assembly at Mount Tai.
Master Xiu, the General Superintendent of the Buddhist Teachings and Head of the Baoji Altar, admired his virtue and invited him to preside over the Huayan lecture seat in the capital.
Furthermore, he transmitted the Bodhisattva Precepts at Fuzi Mountain, as well as at the various monasteries of Weiruo and Huanglou. From then on—
His disciples made further progress, and the Way of the Dharma spread across half the world. The Master’s realization was profound and far-reaching;
he was courageous in doing good, striving with such urgency as if he could never catch up.

He codified and supplemented the omissions in the scriptures, demolished and renovated ruined temples, and repaired broken embankments and dilapidated bridges—his deeds were too numerous to list. As for his own person, he subsisted on vegetarian food and...
As for his water and tattered robes, they were sufficient merely to house his body. Commentators say that the Master was as profound as the void and as humble as one in concealment;
he was desolate, serene, and deep, having no desires for anything external. Yet, when it came to guiding others and providing compassionate relief, he was diligent and tireless.

It was like embracing a leaking jar to pour water into a parched cauldron; those who attained his Dharma were all satisfied and comforted with joy, as if returning home after traveling ten thousand li.
How could the Way of this Master not be worthy of contemplation? In his later years, he resided at Fayun Aranya in Fengsheng Prefecture, where he eventually passed away.
He was seventy-two years old and had thirty-eight years of seniority as a monk (*bhikṣu*). His stupa [was erected].
Beside the temple, there was Minghui Jin’s biography of Huijin.
Huijin, whose courtesy name was Qiyuan and pen-name Zhiweng, was a native of Lingshi in Huozhou, Shanxi. His surname was Song, and he was born in...
In the year of Yiwu (1355) of the Yuan Zhi Zheng era, while still a youth and already proficient in the Buddhist language, he lost both parents at the age of nine due to the chaos of war.
He wove reeds to provide filial care for his grandparents, but they too perished amidst the weeds.

With a mind set on renouncing the world, he paid homage to Master Jian of Dayun Temple in the district, shaved his head, and took up the scriptures. Through the new grace of the Hongwu Emperor, he received full ordination and entered [the monastic order].

Fanyi relied upon the ancient peaks to investigate and master the fundamental tenets of the *Avataṃsaka* school, while also attaining a thorough understanding of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, the *Śata-dharmaka-śāstra*, and various other treatises.

His comprehension was profound and his mind harmonized with the Dharma, earning him the respect and admiration of all, whereby he attained the title of "Dharma Master. Emperor Taizong took notice of this and dispatched an eunuch on an express courier to summon him to the Southern Capital (Nanjing).
There, the Emperor questioned him extensively on the great meaning of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*; his responses were in perfect accord with the Imperial will, and he was subsequently granted [honors].
He was invested with the purple robe and commanded to reside at Cheonhae-sa Temple, where he was ordered to select outstanding and talented monks to study under him.

Furthermore, he was commissioned to lead eminent monks at Ingyung-sa to compile the *Samjang palsa su* (A Compendium of the Three Pitakas). Later, accompanying the imperial entourage to Beijing, he resided at Haerin-sa Temple.
He received an imperial decree to lead the monastic community of the realm outside the Daming Gate to perform a Great Universal Salvation Retreat (*pudu daizhai*).

After a month had passed, he expounded upon the Threefold Pure Precepts (*sanju jingjie*), benefiting beings both in the hidden realms and the manifest world. At that time, the *huoding* (the ritual vessel) and the banner-pole both emitted extraordinary light.
He was granted an imperial edict and a gold-embroidered robe, and promoted to the rank of Left Jueyi.

He presided over the eminent scholars and monks of the realm at the Haiyin Sutra Hall to collate the Great Tripitaka; consequently, he memorialized that the canon should be carved and published to assist in the governance and transformation of the people.

He was instructed to compose various prefaces to clarify the teachings for distant lands. The Emperor followed this advice and personally authored thirteen prefaces to the scriptures and twelve eulogies and colophons for the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
The Emperor summoned him to the Incense Hall (*Xiangdian*), where he was granted a seat.

He bestowed upon him a statue of Śākyamuni with a Brahmanical appearance, a silk-thread embroidered image of Avalokiteśvara, a crystal rosary, and the verses of the Seven Buddhas. The Emperor exhorted him, saying: "Practice according to these; you shall be promoted to the Left [Rank]."
He propagated the teachings, and from his first encounter with the Emperor until his last, a total of seventeen years elapsed.
In the first year of the Hongxi era, Emperor Renzong reformed the ecclesiastical offices; the Master alone was singled out for commendation. The Imperial Edict stated:

"The Buddhists take Benevolence as their teaching to transform and guide the ignorant masses, thereby providing secret support to the imperial governance and bringing benefit and peace to all classes of beings. Those who preside over these religious affairs must necessarily..."

I have found a worthy person, yet I do not bestow office lightly. You, Zuo Chanjiao Huijin, have thoroughly investigated and clarified our fundamental tenets and maintained pure and rigorous observance of the precepts;
thus, you are appointed to this position. As your cultivation becomes ever more diligent, I am pleased with you and grant you this imperial decree.
You must further cultivate your vigor and diligence, revitalize the tradition of your school, and thereby respond to my command. Be reverent! The First Year of Xuande, Emperor Xuanzong.
The Emperor treated him as a state elder and bestowed upon him a *vairocana* crown and a gold-embroidered *mohana* robe. By imperial decree, he was appointed to the Inner Academy (*neihan*).

Thereupon, together with many officials and the monastic community, he transcribed the four great sections of the sutras—the *Avataṃsaka*, *Prajñāpāramitā*, *Ratnakūṭa*, and *Mahāparinirvāṇa*—in golden characters.
A sumptuous banquet was provided, and upon the completion of the work, the Great State Preceptor Jingjue was granted the title of Longshan. He then submitted a petition [to the Emperor].
He opened [the assembly] and lectured on the *Lengyan jing huijie* (Commentary on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra). Over ten thousand monastics and laypeople attended and received his teachings.
As his years advanced, his virtue grew even more eminent. His hearing and sight were clear and lucid; his countenance was extraordinary and ancient-looking. By nature he was upright and frugal.

Among his venerable dharma friends were the State Preceptor Yao Gong of Rongguo and Jingjing, the Chief Translator Guang Gong, the lecturer Yin-feng Cong Gong, Du-fang Lian Gong, and Yue-ting Lang Gong. With his own hands...

He surpassed his senior and junior brothers: Zhanjiao (who concurrently resided at Daxinglong), Guangtong of Wanshou Mountain, Guangbian of Jiming Mountain, Guangzai of Jietan, the patriarch Guangyan, the disciple Guangyi (Left Shanshi), Guangming (Right Jueyi), and Daoshen who lectured on the sutras by imperial decree;
these are but a few examples, as there are many others not fully enumerated. His worldly lifespan was eight [years].
He was seventy-three years of monastic seniority. In the intercalary sixth month of the first year of the Zhengtong era, he passed away in his quarters at Qingshou Monastery.
Upon receipt of the news, the Emperor dispatched an official from the Ministry of Rites to offer a ceremonial memorial service.

His remains were cremated at Fucheng, and his relics and sacred bones were enshrined in a stupa west of the Hun River. By imperial decree, the site of Wannfo Shan was granted to him as a mark of exceptional honor.
Yirushi (with the appended meaning of "Capable")—Yirushi was a man whose courtesy name was Yizan.
Having grown old, he adopted the pen-name Tuweng. He was the son of the Sun family of Shangyu.
At the age of thirteen, he took leave of his parents and enrolled at Changqing as a monk, following Master Juyan Xi at Baokui Temple on Mount Wu. There he sharpened [his practice].

He devoted himself to his vocation, never flagging even during the bitter cold or intense heat. If a single principle was not fully penetrated or a single doubt remained unresolved, he would pursue it until he had reached the ultimate conclusion.
He subjected himself to rigorous austerity and lived on plain fare; as the years passed, his resolve grew ever more steadfast, and he eventually attained profound mastery of the innermost mysteries.

In the eighteenth year of the Hongwu era, he emerged from seclusion to reside at Chongqing in Songjiang, and subsequently moved to Beichen in Suzhou, where both monastics and laypeople turned to him for refuge.

Those who were converted increased by the day. In the twenty-seventh year, Master Qiacha of the Southern Continent served as Director of the Office of Monastic Records and concurrently presided over Dabao’en Temple.
He invited the Master to serve as the Chief Lecturer (*dujiang*). At that time, the Buddhist teachings were being reformed and administrative affairs were manifold;

yet while Master Qiacha managed the responses of both superiors and subordinates, his lectures continued without interruption. This was largely due to the Master’s assistance. In the twenty-eighth year, he resided at Hangzhou.
At Ling Shan Temple in India, in the thirty-first year [of his life], he resided at Upper Zhu.

He took it as his personal mission to further revitalize the school and inspire future generations, and those who followed him as disciples increased ever more. At the beginning of the Yongle era, he retired to Da Ba’en Temple;

considering that the profound and secret purport of the Lotus Sūtra was not easily entered by ordinary scholars, he assembled the community and expounded it, subsequently composing a commentary upon it. Great...
His junior master, Master Yao, wrote a preface for it, praising him as "the one man in the Two Zhe regions.

The Emperor once perused it and commended him repeatedly, bestowing upon him generous rewards. Over twelve years, he was summoned to compile and edit the Great Canon (*Tripitaka*), serving as the general supervisor of the project.
He was appointed as Right Jueyi of the Senglu Si, and subsequently promoted to Right Chanjiao. (The first year of the Hongxi era...)
In the third month of that year, he passed away at Haerin Temple in the capital. He was seventy-four years of age and had completed sixty-one summer retreats.
After his cremation, his tongue remained unburnt; it was enshrined in a stupa.
Regarding those capable of this task: the four eminent monks were of equal reputation and standing at that time;
they were all appointed as officials of the Senglusi (Bureau of Monastic Records) and enjoyed the patronage of His Majesty. Yang Dongli’s preface to the *Rutapu* states:

"In my travels throughout the four quarters, I have encountered men whose capacity and insight, as well as their discourse, are truly magnificent, surpassing those of the common crowd, and who are diligently engaged in promoting what is neglected and restoring what has fallen into ruin."
As for those who have inherited the mantle of the Great Master’s school, they are by no means few. Thus, was it only in former times that such was the case?

When one seeks for those who are profound in their inner being, serene in their composure, and whose conduct appears to others as if they were incapable, yet who possess a rich flavor when approached closely—such individuals were already not easily found in antiquity; how much less so could they be found today alone? —Emperor Taizong.

The Emperor—whose fame as a sovereign over the four quarters was such that eminent monks from all directions had once entered his presence for audience—placed his singular weight upon Yi of Siming and Ruru of Kuaiji. Alas! How could this have been by mere chance? Furthermore, it is said:
the two masters were humble and reverent, their speech rarely venturing forth; Ruru was profound in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, while Yi was profound in the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra*.
Dàtóng was the successor of Dàtóng.
His courtesy name was Yīyún, and his title was Biéfēng. He was the son of Wáng Shìzǐ of the Upper Yú district in Yuè; his family was traditionally esteemed as a lineage of scholar-officials.
His father was Yǒuqiáo and his mother was of the Chén clan. When the Master had been carried in her womb for ten months, his father saw a monk with a long, bushy beard shaking a monk’s staff.
He departed. When asked where the monk had come from, he replied, "From Mount Kunlun," and then pushed open the door and entered.

His father hurriedly pursued him, but found him silent and gone. Upon exiting, he heard the sound of a child crying in the room. He laughed and said, "Could this child not have been that Buddhist monk just now?
From childhood, he was exceptionally bright and spirited; whenever he perused various records and texts, he immediately grasped their profound mysteries. His father then instructed him...

Regarding the secrets of literary composition, he would grasp his brush with graceful ease, and his works were invariably worthy of admiration. Consequently, [his father] entrusted him with the continuation of the family’s scholarly tradition.
His mother alone sighed, saying, "This son possesses the seeds of *prajñā*. How could we allow him to be entangled in the toils of worldly existence?

She then commanded him to leave the household life and enter Chongsheng Monastery in Kuaiji to follow the monk Senggui. Subsequently, he shaved his head, received the Bodhisattva precepts, and joined the assembly.
Master Jingde of Chuntang lectured on the sutras, and [the Master] went to rely upon him once more, obtaining the two texts *Wujiaoyi* and *Xuantan*.
He also visited Master Haigu Zhao and received the *Sichong fajie guan*. Both Haigu and Chuntang were great disciples of Nanshan and were scholars deeply versed in the Huayan teachings.
Since the Master’s innate aptitude was already high, he further applied himself with diligent effort.
[This was] the merit. All the commentaries and chapters of the Qingliang school were fully encompassed within this work, which synthesized their integrations and grasped their essential pivot.
Its meanings dissolved away, and the light of wisdom shone forth; those who understood it were moved to sincere admiration.

When Chūngu ascended to the position of Head of the Baolin Huayan Teaching Institute, he summoned the Master and said to him, "Your learning is both refined and vast, yet I fear you may become stagnant within your mind and heart, thereby forming coarse attachments."
