While the Renzong Emperor was still in the position of Crown Prince, he intended for the Master to fill that post and ordered him to enter the imperial court. Upon seeing the Master’s dignified appearance, the Emperor was greatly pleased and appointed him as the Left Jueyi of the Office of Buddhist Records (*Senglü*).
He bestowed upon him a set of brocade robes, a sable fur cloak, a warm hat, boots, and stockings, along with paper currency.

He was granted two hundred taels of silver and sent back to Nanjing by an imperial eunuch. There, at the foremost Chan monastery on Mount Zhongshan, he proclaimed the Dharma of the Zen school, winning the admiration and submission of both monastics and laypeople.
Before long, he returned to court and was promoted to the rank of Left Lecturer on the Sutras. While residing at Qingshou Temple, he fell ill.
The Emperor heard of this and bestowed medicine upon him. Imperial messengers appeared one after another along the roads. He gathered the assembly and spoke a verse, saying:
"Having dwelt in Jambudvīpa for seventy years, The imperial grace is like the ocean, vast and boundless. Now I cast off my hands and return to the West;

Ten thousand li of cloudless sky, the moon is perfectly full. He threw down his brush and passed away. When the Emperor read the verse, he was moved to deep admiration and issued an edict in his honor.
A memorial service was held. An order was issued to the Ministry of Works to construct a shrine, and the cremation took place outside the Pingze Gate.
Five-colored clouds appeared above. Upon collecting the remains, dozens of *śarīra* relics were obtained. His disciples requested that they be returned to Mount Zhongshan.

When Emperor Renzong ascended the throne, he again dispatched an envoy with orders for a memorial service, returning the sacred remains and *śarīra* to Jingshan. A stupa was erected beside the ancestral grave of Master Jizhao. The Master—
His countenance was pure and dignified; those who beheld him found their worldly thoughts dissolved. He was skilled in rhythmic verse and composed poems in response to imperial rhymes.
Among his works was one sent to the Great Dharma King, which included the lines: "When at times the discourse reaches the realm beyond words, the mind merges with the spirit and Yao’s brows open.
This was widely circulated and recited by people.
Regarding Qingtian Chuan:
Qingtian was a native of Luling in Jiangyou. His courtesy name was Jiezhu, and he belonged to the Ouyang clan.

From childhood, he was exceptionally intelligent and deeply weary of the mundane world; he followed Master Zhong of Duobao Zhengzong to receive his instruction. This was in the first year of the Xuande era.

The Dharma Master Yunhai of the Right Street shaved his head for him and entered the Great Heaven Realm (Dajie). There he met Chan Master Hongci Puying, who appointed him as attendant for the incense and entrusted him with the keys to the storehouse.
He was subsequently promoted to the position of First Seat. At the beginning of the Zhengtong era, he discovered the ruins of an ancient monastery at the foot of the western mountains of the capital.
Moved by a profound resolve to restore it, he exhausted the proceeds from the sale of his robes and property to recruit a community of followers.
As for the construction: when the work was undertaken and materials were being prepared, even a single tile or a solitary rafter was handled by the Master’s own hand.

When this matter was reported to the Emperor, he granted the temple the name Hongqing Chan Temple. The Master served as its founding first patriarch; this refers to the Black Pagoda that stands today.
The Master excelled above his peers, standing out preeminently like a solitary crane amidst a flock of chickens. He initially presided over Suimyeo Temple, and subsequently moved to Nongam Temple.
The Dharma arrived. Subsequently, he opened Mount Hongqing, from which point his spiritual influence spread far and wide, becoming renowned throughout both the court and the common world.
In the year Bingyin, the Right Street Chan Master Lian’an was recommended by the Minister of Education;

Grand Chancellor Hu Gong and various eminent officials and dignitaries all praised and commended him. Consequently, he set out for Mount Shuangjing. Feng Ning of Jue Mountain sponsored and printed [the text].

Regarding the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and its accompanying embroidered banners, as well as the various offerings for the golden altar—such as those provided by Shen Fucheng, Du Hongzhen, and others—all joyfully gave rise to the aspiration for enlightenment.
They cast three iron Buddha statues along with various ritual implements and followed the Master. In the following year, the Year of Dingmao, they entered the monastery.
Far and near, all looked up to them with reverence; there were none who did not praise their efforts and provide encouragement and assistance. These are the matters concerning the Master’s conduct.
There was indeed a vast difference. Zhang Gongyi of the Hanlin Academy remarked: "The Master’s spiritual capacity is firm and sharp, and his resolve and diligence are earnest and sincere.

Thus, by means of his teacher’s instruction, he was able to awaken to the profound meaning within the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, and by observing his teacher’s conduct, he brought the three karmas to complete cessation.
This is truly a factual record."
Honglian. His courtesy name was Dufang. He was the son of the Wu family of Taiyuan in Shanxi. By nature he was stern and perceptive; even as a young child, he acted as if he were an adult.
He left the household life at Raoyi Temple and received full ordination at the age of twenty. There he met Xiuyun, from whom he received the seal of approval and was bestowed with [the dharma].
Wearing his religious robes, he entered the Dragon Cave to sit in meditation and, drawing blood from his ten fingers, transcribed the five great divisions of the scriptures.
Furthermore, at Myeonsan-dong (Famous Immortal Cave), he established a maṇḍala seat and performed the *yankou* (flaming-mouth) ritual for three years to provide relief to those in the dark realms.
When the Prince of Jin heard of this, he invited him to inquire after the Way, provided him with robes and food, and requested that he reside at Hongyou Temple.

From then on, his reputation and virtue spread far and wide. During the Yongle era, by imperial decree, he annotated the *Daming Sanzang Fashu* (The Three Pitaka Dharma-numerals of the Great Ming) and collated the Tripitaka.
Furthermore, he was summoned to enter the Incense Hall, where he engaged in a dialogue with Jin Fazhu on the essential principles of the *Śūraṃgama Sūtra*.
He was also commanded to oversee the collation and transcription of the Tripiṭaka at Haerin Temple; in all his successive duties, he attained the Emperor’s favor.

Having inherited the patronage and affection of the two reigns of Renzong and Xuanzong, he was appointed as the Right Lecturer of the Office of Monastic Records (*Senglusi*). In the seventh year of the Zhengtong era, he was promoted to the position of Left Lecturer.

Due to his advanced age, he submitted a petition to retire from official duties; consequently, he was exempted from attending court audiences, though his administrative responsibilities remained as before.

On the fourth day of the seventh month in the seventh year of the Jingtai era, he passed away while sitting upright and writing a verse. Upon hearing the news, the Emperor expressed profound sorrow and ordered the Minister of Rites to present a sacrificial offering.
He was posthumously bestowed the title of Chan Master Jingfan Yijiao. He was ninety-one years of age and had seventy-one years of monastic seniority (*śramaṇa-varṣa*). His body was cremated.
He obtained one hundred *śarīra* relics. By imperial decree, they were returned to Wanfo Temple on Mount Xi (West Mountain), where a stupa was constructed to enshrine them.

The Master’s appearance was majestic and distinguished; his character was expansive and serene. His discourse was磊落 (*lěiluò*, lofty and brilliant), issuing entirely from the orthodox. Possessing both theoretical understanding and spiritual practice, he took the Way upon himself as his personal responsibility;
thus, successive emperors treated him with the utmost courtesy and honor. In the fourth year of the Jingtai era, a Japanese monk entered the capital to present tribute. His...
Seng was a great master of Chan in his native land. Few were those whom he deemed worthy; he alone had devoted himself to his teacher.

Those who came with him each had their own questions, and though their words differed from one another, the Master responded to them as fluidly as a flowing stream, granting everyone their requests. They withdrew, marveling at what they had never experienced before.
His eloquence and ability to persuade others were thus like this. I have briefly recorded the general outline of his manifestations to serve as a basis for his biography. Its...
His hidden virtues and secret practices, as well as the extent of his realization, can be envisioned beyond the reach of words.
The ancestral master Fēngtóu transmitted the Way to Fú, whose courtesy name was Xìnān.
He was the son of the Liú family of Jiāngpǔ; his skillful training was evident even in childhood play, and his sharp faculties were manifested from an early age.
As a child, at the age of seven, he entered a schoolhouse. When his teacher gave him a book to read, he was unwilling to do so; even when he did read, he would not finish it.
He said, "This book is not what I enjoy, nor is this teacher my master. Thereupon, he became a disciple of the venerable Qing from Linggu Temple.

He shaved his head and donned black robes. Morning and evening he paid homage to Avalokiteśvara, whereby his intelligence was awakened and he mastered the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.

Regarding the Mahāyāna sūtras and śāstras, he surveyed all that they encompassed at a single glance without omission; their refined essentials and subtle meanings were gathered within him like rivers pouring forth, so vast and flowing that none could fathom their limits.
He was further honored by Tianlong and Guanzhong. At that time, Master Guan’s reputation for public esteem was high throughout the world.
When King Seon was still in the rank of crown prince, he frequently received the king’s inquiries. In the year of Bingwu during the Xuande era, he was summoned to court.

In the capital, he stayed in the *vimalā* (丈室) of Qingshou Monastery. The Master served him with the utmost diligence. The Emperor praised him and bestowed upon him a western-style robe of cinnabar red;
the Master firmly declined it and would not wear it. Subsequently, he traveled through Jiangzhe to receive the full ordination (*pūrṇa-saṃvara*).

He entered Mount Wutai and beheld a sacred image within a body of light, from which hundreds of miraculous manifestations emerged. In the space of a single thought-moment, they suddenly vanished. He sighed and said, "Ancient..."
As people say: "When a single speck of film is in the eye, empty flowers fall in confusion. For this reason, he styled himself the "Son Who Knows Illusions" (Jihwan-ja).

King Yeong-myo, having heard the Master’s reputation, summoned him for an audience and was greatly pleased; he called him "Phoenix-Head Monk" (Pungdu Hwasang), because the front of the Master’s head rose to a sharp point.

Shortly thereafter, the Master was appointed as a *Sengluk* (Monastic Registrar) and lectured on the sutras. Before long, however, he requested to retire and retired to the mountains, where he built a thatched hut which he named "Pine Grove" (Songyeok).
He stilled all external conditions and did not engage in idle social intercourse; only those who were earnest and sincere could rely upon him.
Consuming and wearing things of remote antiquity, he lived in tranquil self-contentment as if for the rest of his life.

Previously, Lord阮 (阮公) Jian of the Ministry of Rites had acquired the abandoned temple at Mount Ma’an to the west of the capital and wished to restore it, intending to consult with a great master of knowledge to lead its religious tradition.

"It cannot be done without a master. He composed a petition with utmost sincerity, repeating his request four times, yet it was still not granted. Later, he excavated the earth and discovered a broken stele.
Holding the stele, Yuan wept and pleaded, saying, "Though the stele is incomplete, it is still legible; I only ask that you, Master, deign to look upon it.
The Master read it and first learned that this temple had been built by the Great Master Puxian of the Liao dynasty and was a place where the fourfold assembly received the precepts. The Master...
He sighed deeply and said, "The bequeathed teachings of Śākyamuni Tathāgata have nearly vanished after more than three thousand years.
As a disciple of the Buddha, how could I bear to witness their decline without restoring them? Thereupon, he rose with renewed resolve.

He cleared away the overgrowth and leveled the rugged terrain, erecting a series of tiered structures. He distributed his own wealth to assemble the craftsmen and selected capable monks to supervise the labor. Thus, the artisans completed the work.
He took the principles for his heart and received the instructions with his hands. In the daytime he did not wear a sunshade, and in the rain he did not wear wooden clogs.

Those who rushed toward him in the wind and gazed upon his presence arrived like a flock of birds. A monastery that had been in ruins for a century was restored in an instant; its corridors and galleries were resplendent as if newly built.
The full account from beginning to end is recorded in the inscription composed by Grand Secretary Yang Shiqi. Furthermore, Prince Qinning Zhaojing...
He converted his residence at Xuanwu Gate into a Buddhist monastery, which was granted the name Cheng'en. It served as a place for the Master to rest during his travels.
The Master was skilled in calligraphy; his brushwork was powerful and vigorous. He once inscribed large characters for a plaque at Wenhua Palace.
The Emperor bent down to examine it closely and praised it as excellent, bestowing upon him a poem that contained the line: "The calligraphy of this eminent monk surpasses that of the Secretariat.
Furthermore, the Emperor once personally witnessed his distribution of food within the inner court and heard him expound the Dharma in the secret palace;

on every occasion, he clapped his hands in approval and expressed his admiration. At that time, as the elder masters were passing away one by one, the Master alone was renowned throughout the four quarters, and disciples [flocked to him].
He hurried to attend the assembly, fearing only that he might be late; he was truly the most outstanding figure among the monks.

By virtue of such extraordinary merit and wondrous conduct, he was fully capable of acting as a compassionate vessel across the ocean of suffering and leading those lost on the path to the shore of enlightenment.

On the tenth day of the sixth month in the summer of the Bingzi year of the Jingtai era, he gathered the assembly and ascended the hall, where he spoke this verse: "In the past, there was originally no birth; now, likewise, there is no..."

He passed away. Like clouds dispersing across the vast sky, beneath a azure firmament and bright moon, he sat upright and departed this life. Upon hearing the news, the Emperor was deeply grieved and dispatched an imperial decree for a memorial service;

dukes and marquises below him all followed to pay their respects at his funeral. His body was cremated, and śarīra were obtained, which were enshrined in a stupa on the southern plain of the monastery.
He was fifty-five years of age in secular years and forty-nine years in the monastic order (śrāmaṇera-vaṣa). His younger brother succeeded him in the lineage.

His disciples numbered in the tens of thousands; those who received the precepts from the fourfold assembly reached ten billion. His lineage disciples numbered over a thousand, all of whom were bound by meditation and upheld the Vinaya, propagating the teachings in their respective regions.

Among his writings were the *Zhiding jieben* (The Established Text of the Precepts) and the *Jiedie* (Precept Certificates), along with several volumes of verses, hymns, and poetic compositions that have been transmitted through the monastic communities.
Lord Hu Zhongan Ying praised the Master for the breadth of his learning, the refinement of his conduct, and the merit of his [achievements].
Sheng remarked, "He is able to glorify and expand the Dharma-gate.
Wansong Qian-song Bai-song was a successor of Huilin;
his courtesy name was Wansong. A native of Renhe in Hangzhou, he was born with an extraordinary nature and, as he grew older, became deeply devoted to the study of Buddhist scriptures.

He was given secular classics to study and abandoned the contemplation of the Buddha. When his parents observed that his resolve was thus, they allowed him to leave home and become a monk at Falun Temple.

Seeing that what the other monks practiced was base and vulgar, the Master was displeased and sighed with a somber expression, saying, "How can this possibly resolve the great matter of birth and death?
Having long heard of the spiritual conduct of the Elder of Tianmu Pingshu, he went to rely upon him. One day, during a banquet...

While sitting among the trees, he heard the calls of monkeys and birds and attained a sudden, expansive realization. At that time, the recluse Konghuan of Funiu was residing at the Chan Forest of Guangde;
the Master went to see him and recounted his insights. He subsequently became a successor in the lineage of Konghuan and traveled through various regions.

He returned to Hangzhou and secluded himself at Mount Jing. He withdrew from the city and its administrative centers. The Master maintained his person with restraint and observed the Vinaya with strict rigor.

He was fundamentally well-versed in the Tripiṭaka and was particularly proficient in various sūtras such as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the *Awakening of Faith*, and the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*. He excelled at inspiring and guiding others;

in analyzing meanings and proclaiming the essential teachings, he was like a compassionate parent instructing their child, never ceasing until the student had attained full understanding. His Way grew increasingly sublime day by day.

His cultivation flourished daily, and those who came from the four quarters to study under him increased in number day by day. In the Ding-si year of the Jiajing era, he suddenly said to his disciples, "The time has come.
He ceased taking grain, drinking only several cups of mountain stream water each day for over a month, and then passed away.
He reached the age of seventy-six.
He attained enlightenment and was named Yuetting (Moon Pavilion). He succeeded Master Wansong in the Dharma and was also called Chiansong (Thousand Pines).

He was the son of the Zhou family of Wucheng. From childhood, he was precocious and extraordinary. Once, while accompanying his father to a Buddhist assembly for the Western Offering (*xīzī*), he pointed to a portrait and asked, "Is this not a monk?
His father replied, "Yes. Thereupon, he sought to leave the household life and received the tonsure at Qingshan Hermitage. Initially, he studied *Yogācāra*.

Regarding Buddhist practice, he realized its futility and abandoned it. Seeking transcendence, he visited the various seas and hundreds of rivers, yet his spiritual faculties did not harmonize with the Dharma.

He traveled extensively to consult renowned masters, undergoing every kind of hardship; this only served to further intensify his indignation and resolve. He then went to Upper Zhushan in Wulin to offer earnest supplications to the Great Being (Avalokiteśvara).
Seeking an enlightened master, he encountered Wansong at Zhongzhu. When asked about his purpose in coming, the Master replied with the *Pumenpin* (Universal Gate Chapter).
Wansong held up one finger and said, "Go; you have come to see Avalokiteśvara. Only then did the Master suddenly attain a profound realization.
He prostrated twice and sought the secret instruction for resolving birth and death. Wansong bestowed upon him the method of "Mind-Gathering Buddha-Recitation.
Consequently, he remained in attendance by his side, seeking guidance morning and evening for ten years. One day, while reading the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, he reached the passage:

"The fundamental nature is pure and still; how can mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise? At this, he attained sudden enlightenment. He then entered Mount Jing, where he built a thatched hut on Mount Lingxiao.

He reached the summit and sat in solitary meditation for three years. Zen practitioners from all directions arrived one after another; the Master responded to them according to their capacities, resolving every doubt as easily as slicing through meat with a blade.
He later moved to Yian Hermitage, where he lectured on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. Having traveled to Tiantai, the monastics and laypeople there—
The heterodox and the orthodox were intermingled and confused. The Master lectured on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and other scriptures, converting non-Buddhists by the thousands.
As soon as the lecture concluded, precious lotuses sprang up everywhere within the hall; it is now known as the Yonglian Hall (Lotus-Sprouting Hall).

Upon his return, Wu Gong, the Vice Minister of Justice Yun’an, who was then the Governor of Hangzhou, invited the Master to expound the Dharma at Lingyin Monastery. Guan Jun, the Provincial Surveillance Commissioner Dongming, [invited him] because of the... (text fragment)
He was invited by the Ministry of Rites to visit the esteemed Mr. Shen. He was subsequently invited by Lord Lu of Wutai to serve as the abbot of Yuanzheng Temple.

Later, he was further invited by Lord Lu to lecture on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* at Dongchan Temple in Xiushui. The Master delighted in its secluded elegance and, together with him, renovated the Fayun Hall to reside there;
it thus became the place where the Master passed away. As for the Master’s character, his tall, slender frame stood like a jade pillar, and his temperament was lofty.
He was simple, upright, and straightforward, honoring himself through the Way. When encountering high officials and ministers, he never lowered his dignity or assumed an air of servility or flattery.

Though the petty and vulgar might detest and revile him, he remained unbending despite a hundred setbacks. He protected the True Dharma with resolute determination, never acting for his own personal gain.

During his stay at Tianchi, a man of noble rank arrived with courtesans to visit the monks' quarters; the Master assembled the community to drive them away, showing no hesitation or regard for their status.
At that time, the world was devotedly serving Zhenwu. The Master remarked, "He is merely the presiding deity of Xuanwu, governing but one corner of the realm.
How can he cause people throughout the world to run about like madmen? Our Bhagavān is the Teacher of Gods and Humans; why not abandon the former and serve the latter?
Consequently, he frequently altered the images and changed the temple layouts. By nature, he delighted in drawing in and guiding those who were still learning. And so...

He regarded non-Buddhists as enemies; when his fellow monks committed faults, he did not hesitate to criticize them severely. For this reason, he incurred the resentment of those who harbored jealousy.
Had it not been for the support of various scholars who acted as his protective ramparts, he would likely have met with misfortune.
He entered nirvana in the sixteenth year of the Wanli era at the age of fifty-eight. The Master shared a profound affinity of Dharma-joy with Wutai Gong, and...
The Inscription for the Stupa at Mingwang Village: It is said that our Master attained the stages of realization through ascetic practice and upheld the eternal Dharma with steadfast resolve.
I had the honor of associating with him for thirty years, and the benefits of his teachings were manifold. We hoped that in our later years we might together revive the traditions of Donglin;
yet, the Master passed away first. Who now shall act as my guiding chariot toward the Land of Lotuses? [Stupa] Postscript.
He moved to Mount Jing.
His name was Zhenjue, and he was styled Baisong. He was a native of Kunshan in Suzhou and surnamed Wang.

Having already taken a wife, he happened to follow a traveling monk to Hangzhou, whereupon he entered Guozishan to shave his head. After residing there for over a month, he went to Wumen to receive full ordination. His...

At that time, his debating prowess was already irresistible. Not long after, he went to Huzhou to pay his respects to Qiansong. During the lecture session, he emerged with such brilliance that he was suppressed by the assembly.
The Head Seat, Daoyuan, took pity on him and spoke of the matter to Qiansong, who then recorded him as a member of the lower seat.
Later, when [Daoyuan] entered the world [as a master], he eventually offered incense to Qiansong and became his dharma heir. In the Jiazi year of the Jiajing era, he received the [imperial] decree.
His invitation from Tiantai was such that people from near and far were drawn by his reputation, hastening to attend as if they could not wait long enough.
He lectured on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* several times, the *Lotus Sūtra* several times, and the *Miaozongchao* several times; however, he lectured on the *Fahua Xuanyi* only once.
Whatever offerings he received were immediately exhausted upon his hands. The layman Zhenshi remarked: "Master Miaofeng’s physical appearance is extraordinary and ancient; his body..."
He did not exceed the level of an ordinary person in appearance; yet his discourse and bearing were like a great wheel of fire, impossible to touch.
At that time, there were two Dharma masters in Jiangnan: Master [Shi] and Dongchan Yeting Deshi.

Master Shi emerged from the lineage of Dongchan, who did not specialize exclusively in the Xianshou (Huayan) school, whereas Master Shi alone was refined in the Tiantai school; thus, differences arose between them. Nevertheless, his subtle eloquence was unrestrained.
He was formidable, overwhelming the thousands of the assembly; he was the Southeastern Vajra Banner of Fearless Radiance.
Master Zhuzhu of Luting resided there;
his courtesy name was Hanyi, and Luting was his sobriquet. He was born into the Yang family of Dantu; he was profound, meticulous, and free from greed.

He had seventeen worldly connections. At nineteen, he received the full precepts (*upasampadā*). He thoroughly mastered the great meanings of the various sutras. He traveled to Shaoshi to rely upon Dazhang;
then he went to Funiu to rely upon Gaolian, where he spent twelve summer retreats in total. Subsequently, he went to the capital to pay his respects to the two masters Song and Xiu.
Upon arriving in Nanjing, he visited the elder Wuji and served as a West Hall Attendant (*xitang*). During the intervals between the striking of the *ghanṭā* and the *dundubhi*, he...
He entered into manual labor, working day and night without rest. He subsequently expounded the *Huayan chao* (Commentary on the Avatamsaka Sutra) at Wanshou Temple in Jingkou.
Monastics and laypeople who came to listen numbered in the thousands daily; the Elder led his disciples there to observe him. Later, he said to the assembly, "I am likely not his equal.
Nevertheless, there is one thing in which he is inferior to me: previously, when that Superior Man was my Western [Preceptor]..."
"Is there currently such a superior person in the West Hall? From that time on, his reputation for the Way flourished, and the monastic communities vied to honor him.

The Master honored wisdom and humbled himself in etiquette, just like the monk Aniruddha (Changbuling). He tirelessly exhorted and guided others, with those who ascended the Dharma seat under him numbering in the tens.
Wherever he went, he was able to establish magnificent monasteries (*ratnagṛha*). However, as for his three robes—

Externally, he wore a single robe that covered his entire body and sustained himself on mere vegetable soup and gruel, yet he maintained the five contemplations (pañca-vipaśyanā). As for various offerings and gifts, he would not even cast an eye upon them.

Furthermore, he upheld the Vinaya with rigorous precision, committing no transgression, however minute. In the *jiashen* year of the Wanli era, he entered Mount Wushan to Lotus Peak, where he ascended the lecture seat of Zhi Daolin.
The seclusion and beauty of the mountain forests gave rise to his intention to remain there for the rest of his life; before long, he moved on.

Biography of Dharma Master Suanan (Appendix: The Two Bhikṣus Wuzhai and Huanzai). Dharma Master Suanan’s name was [Name].
He was born into the Zhong family in Xiangyang. In his prime, he renounced Confucian studies and traveled extensively to seek out learned masters.

He arrived at Liushan Temple in Nanyang and received the tonsure from Master Xiugong of Min’an. Carrying only a gourd and a single alms bowl, he traveled to Funiu and Qingliang Mountains to receive full ordination.
There he relied upon Master Xiu to study the sutras and śāstras for eleven years, mastering their contents thoroughly.

He then traveled south to pay homage at Putuo Mountain and passed through Baixia, where his affinity with the local luminaries was like the meeting of a needle and its eye; they invited him to remain at the lecture seat of Sheshan.
The fame of his Way resounded far and wide. The Master, likewise delighted by the seclusion and depth of this mountain, cleared away the weeds and built a dwelling, where he remained for ten years.
One day, leaning on his staff as he prepared to depart, he left a verse at Jingye Hall, saying: "Since entering Qixia, ten years have passed; Eastward I repaired, westward I mended, never idling.
I overturned rubble and debris to form a Chan temple; I cleared away briars and thorns to create a vegetable garden."

"Whenever I prepare vegetable soups to provide for the assembly of monks, I must always ensure that the Great Teaching continues the legacy of the former sages. If one does not act in this way, it will not be a true undertaking for the sake of one's descendants;

rather, it should be left as a tradition passed down through the ages to one's fellow practitioners. One can imagine the spirit and resonance of these words. Subsequently, he remained among the assembly once more.
The Master was seven feet tall; his skull was square and upright, and his face and eyes possessed a radiant luster. He had a prominent forehead and full cheeks, and his voice was like a bell.
Throughout his life, his conduct was as pure as ice and snow, yet his responses to others were as warm as spring and as bright as the rising sun, causing people’s stubbornness to melt away naturally.

His preaching of the Dharma was direct, straightforward, and simple, avoiding harsh or severe language, yet he was able to transform the obstinate and guide the ignorant. Those far and near alike held him in reverence and joy.
Throughout his life, he lectured on the *Huayan dashao*, the *Lotus Sūtra*, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, and various other Mahāyāna sūtras and śāstras, totaling several dozen sessions.
On the night of the thirteenth day of the eleventh month in the *Guisi* year of the Wanli era, he sat upright in meditation reciting the Buddha’s name and passed away.
Three days later, at midnight, fires filled the mountains like rows of torches. He had lived for seventy-five years and maintained the precepts for fifty years. Such was the Master’s life.

The auspicious traces [of his presence] were numerous. When he first arrived at Sheshan to expound the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, upon reaching the "Entering the Dharma Realm" chapter (*Dharmadhātupraveśa-parivarta*), the stupa emitted light of five colors.
On another day, while lecturing on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, when he reached the "Jeweled Stupa" chapter (*Ratnakoṭi-parivarta*), he beheld a solemn manifestation of light in the sky.
Sima Wang Daojun composed an inscription to commemorate these events. Sima Gong twice convened the Great Unrestricted Assembly (*wu-zhe da-hui*) at Jiao in Xin'an.
At Mount [Shan], he saw several dozen people prostrating before the Master to express their gratitude for being delivered from suffering. Sima witnessed this with his own eyes.
In the year Bingxu, a great famine occurred and the assembly of monks was deprived of food; however, the Hao family of Wuyin arrived carrying a hundred hu of rice.

Empress Dowager Xiaoding Cisheng, who held the Triple Gem in high esteem, happened to see the Master’s text on the release of living beings and marveled at it greatly.
She dispatched an inner attendant with a purple *kāṣāya* robe and provisions for a vegetarian feast to present as an offering and to inquire about the Dharma.

The Master received it with a prostration and replied with a verse. He was deeply moved by the suffering of the dark realms of existence and personally practiced the *Yankou* (Feeding the Hungry Ghosts) rite;
he would often arrange the offerings himself. There were those who saw the form of the Tathāgata manifest upon the Master’s seat, which was due to the power of his contemplative vision (*vipaśyanā*).

By nature, the Master was simple and sincere; he lived in plainness and lacked any ornamental affectations. He responded to things with an open mind and possessed a gentle and refined countenance, yet his heart was free from [worldly attachments].

The cliffs and embankments were guarded like a formidable fortress. He delineated groves and measured daily provisions; he scrutinized the gravity of benefits bestowed and weighed the causes and effects of transgressions and blessings.
Even for a grain of rice or a stalk of vegetable, he never allowed anything to go to waste. For fifty years, he did not appoint a presiding ritual master.

He supported the elderly and the infirm and provided for the assembly of monks. Monastics from throughout the land arrived with their staffs and bundles upon their backs, crowding shoulder to shoulder and axle to axle;
those counted by the finger each day numbered in the thousands. Whenever there was even a slight surplus, he immediately distributed it among the various mountains, leaving no stores in the treasury.
There were others who provided offerings for the Master; he accepted them all, using them as clothing, medicine, and alms for the poor and sick, with scarcely a day passing without such distribution.

According to my private records, during the last seven years alone, over five thousand *jin* (gold coins) were actually spent. Throughout his life, the Master was frugal with his blessings; he once composed thirty-two articles of self-admonition.
Even in his old age, he personally washed his own robes and cleaned his chamber-pot. To the end of his life, he wore only plain cloth and undyed silk. First...

The hempen curtain was an item used during the period of mourning for his mother; it still exists today, and by this, all other matters may be understood. The Master, through impartial great compassion, gathered and transformed those of his time.
He spoke nothing that was not the Buddha’s word, performed no action that was not the Buddha’s practice, and undertook no task that was not the Buddha’s work.

Regarding those entrusted by the Buddha in the final age to protect and uphold the True Dharma, he was instructed to rely upon the four practices of peaceful dwelling (*catvāraḥ sukha-vihārāḥ*); the Master truly applied himself to these. —Hàn [Shàng].
The Master said: "I have observed all the patriarchs of antiquity; while they single-mindedly upheld the true command, it was not necessarily the case that they fully cultivated the myriad practices.
As for those who manifest the one mind through the myriad practices and perceive the Buddha-nature within worldly toil, from ancient times to the present, there has been none other than Yongming."
There was only the Master alone. Former scholars praised Jiyin as the Ban Gu and Sima Qian among the monastics; I, however, maintain that the Master was the Zhou and Confucius of the Dharma-gate.

In the sixth month of the Yimao year of the Wanli era, he entered the city and took leave of his disciples, headed by Song Shouyi and others, as well as his old friends, saying only: "I am about to depart elsewhere. No one could fathom this.
He returned to the mountain and prepared tea and soup to offer as a memorial feast. Addressing the assembly to bid them farewell, he said, "I shall not remain in this place;

I am departing elsewhere. The assembly was at a loss to understand his meaning. On the first day of the seventh month, in the evening, he entered the hall and sat down, instructing the great assembly:

"The assembly does not listen to my words; I am like a candle in the wind—my lamp is spent and its oil is exhausted. That following night, he entered his private quarters and manifested a slight illness. He closed his eyes and passed away.
He spoke. His disciples gathered around him. The Master opened his eyes again and said, "Great assembly, recite the Buddha’s name with sincerity;

do not indulge in eccentricities, and do not violate my regulations. The assembly asked, "Who is fit to lead this monastic community? The Master replied, "One whose understanding and practice are both complete. They asked again, "Who is currently present?

The Master replied, "For now, follow the order of seniority according to the precepts. Having finished speaking, he faced west, recited the Buddha’s name, and passed away peacefully. Thus ended the life of the Master.
In the year Jiājìng Bǐwèi (1535), at the age of eighty-one and fifty years since his ordination, the Master chose a site on the slope below the mountain to the left of the temple.
He was subsequently interred in a full-body stupa there. His former consort, née Táng, had also taken the tonsure after the Master;
she established Xiàoyì Ān as a nunnery for women and passed away one year prior to him. She too was interred in a stupa on the right-hand mountain outside the temple. The Master—
His disciples who attained ordination, with Guangxiao as the foremost among them, numbered no fewer than several thousand;
those among the laity who were counted among his followers were none. Among the gentry and scholars who entered his gate, they likewise numbered in the thousands;
yet those who benefited from his private instruction were none. As for his writings, apart from his commentaries on the sutras, there is also [his work on] the precepts.

*Shu shi yi wen bian* (Commentary on the Questions and Debates on the Meaning of Affairs), *Shu chao shi yi* (Excerpts from the Commentary on the Meaning of Affairs), *Leng yan mo xiang ji* (Record of the Blind Men Touching the Elephant of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra), *Yi jiao jie yao* (Essential Sections of the Teaching of the Last Days),

*Shui lu yi wen* (Ritual Texts for the Water and Land Assemblies), *Zhu chuang sui bi* (Random Notes from the Bamboo Window), *Er bi san bi* (Two and Three Brushes), *Si shi ba wen da* (Forty-eight Questions and Answers), *Jing tu yi bian* (Discrimination of Doubts Concerning the Pure Land),

*Wang sheng ji* (Collection on Rebirth), *Chong xing lu* (Record of Venerable Conduct), *Ming seng ji lüe* (Compendium of Eminent Monks), *Zheng e ji* (Compilation of Correcting Errors), *Zi zhi lu* (Record of Self-Knowledge), *Yun qi ji shi* (Chronicle of Yunqi), and *Shan*... [text truncated]
The *Fangzalu* and other such works, numbering more than twenty varieties, circulate in the world.
*Supplement to the Biographies of Eminent Monks*, Volume Five;
*Supplement to the Biographies of Eminent Monks*, Volume Six.
The Chapter on Practicing Chan, containing the Biographies of the Two Masters Guiyang and Foshouyan,
composed by the Śramaṇa Minghe of Huashan Temple in Wu Commandery during the Ming Dynasty.
Master Guiyang Huizhong was the son of the Chen family of Xianyou in Quanzhou. He left home at the age of nine.

After receiving full ordination, he traveled with his staff to visit various regions and went to call upon Cao’an. Cao’an asked, “Where have you come from? The Master replied, “From Mount Liubou. Cao’an asked, “Do you see the six eyes?
The Master said, “I am simply troubled by not having double pupils. Cao’an approved of him. He remained at Cao’an’s hermitage for ten years before returning.

Regarding his mountain hermitage: it was during the reign of Emperor Wuzong of the Tang that the Buddhist teachings were suppressed. When Emperor Xuanzong issued an edict to restore them, the Master said, "Those who ascend to the realm of the immortals do not necessarily receive the registers of initiation;
those who depart as Buddhas do not necessarily require the status of a monk. Thereupon, he ceased eating after midday and practiced meditation without sitting upright.
He did not leave the mountain for over thirty years. He composed three verses to express his realization, saying: "Only after the snow has fallen Does one truly know the pine."
The clouds part and the river is revealed; had it not been for the Imperial Preceptor’s instruction to return to lay life, how could one distinguish the flock of chickens from the flock of cranes?
For many years you have wandered aimlessly amidst the dust and soil; though you wear the square robe, you are not yet a monk.

Today, practicing according to the teachings of Shanhui, you leave your hair intact to await the lighting of the lamps. Though your outward appearance has changed, the Way remains ever-present as you blend with the mundane world.
The source of the mind is likewise never obscured. Try reading the verses on Sudhana’s pilgrimage. At that time, how could he have been merely an ordinary śramaṇa? He often said to his disciples:
"That sentient beings cannot attain liberation is due to the fetters of their own emotions. To awaken to the Way is easy; to clarify the Way is difficult."

Now, the word "enlightenment" (*ming*) signifies "faith" (*xin*). It is like a snake-handler who, by virtue of his faith in the power of his medicinal herbs and incantations, can coil and play with snakes, even holding them within the folds of his sleeves without difficulty.
Those who do not yet know this are terrified and flee. However, once one clearly perceives one's own mind, emotional views are immediately shattered;

at that time, a thousand doubts and ten thousand anxieties find no place to function. This state of being unable to employ such thoughts is precisely because one has not yet seen one's own mind. One day, he suddenly sought it out.
After the incense had been burned, he sat upright and passed away. His entire body was interred two hundred paces to the east of the stupa of Chan Master Wuliao;
it was called the East Stupa. Several years later, the stupa suddenly cracked open. The custodian of the stupa intended to excavate it to see what was inside.
Seeing Wuliao in the stillness of the night, [Zhaozhou] said, "There is no need to seek him further. I shall now serve as the true body for the two masters, Shen and Chen.
Shen’s surname was Wuliao; he had studied under Mazu.

Regarding Xingyin of Foshouyan: he was a native of Yanmen whose family name and given name are unknown. In his youth, he studied Confucianism; later, he renounced secular life to become a monk and began traveling as a wandering mendicant.
He first visited Master Zhen of Lumenguan, under whom he attained realization. Subsequently, he traveled to the Jianghuai region and ascended Mount Lu.
To the north of the mountain was a rock formation resembling five fingers; beneath it was a stone grotto about three zhang in depth, where the Master dwelt in seclusion.

Consequently, he was known as the "Fingers of the Buddha Rock" (Foshou Yan) Monk. He did not ordain disciples, but a monk from a neighboring hermitage served him. There were always extraordinary deer and blackbirds with scarlet pouches that would circle and tame themselves by his side.
When the Ruler of Jiangnan issued three successive summons, he did not arise to comply; yet when the ruler pressed his invitation firmly, he finally went to reside there.

Within less than a month, Xiankai departed and once again returned secretly to his mountain retreat. Jiyin composed a eulogy for him, which says: "In the depths of the Huai mountains, he found a place to plant his staff.
He practiced walking meditation beneath the trees and dwelt in tranquil stillness among the crags. For over sixty years, his side never touched the mat.

Though the Son of Heaven issued three summons, he shook his head and did not respond. Knowing he could not be brought forth, the Emperor turned southward and increased his reverence. Mountains trembled and the seas surged."

How startling! The heavens, earth, and the vast distances are all overturned for the descendants of later generations; they act quite the opposite, like worms in milk, greedily attached to worldly flavors.
As I trace their tracks, I shed tears of grief. After the Master descended from his meditation seat and walked several paces, he stood upright and passed away.
A single pine tree atop the cliff withered on that same day. He was over seventy years of age. To the north of the cliff is his bone stupa.
Cunyan (both masters were the direct grandsons of Caoshan).
Regarding Chan Master Ruilong Zang of Huangbo: his childhood name was Zang;
he was the younger cousin of the Tang Prime Minister Xiahou Zizhi. At the beginning of the Dazhong era, his paternal uncle...

When the Minister of Works went out to serve as a regional commander at Guangling, the Master was seven years old. While wandering through Huizhao Temple, he heard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* being recited.

Thereupon, he knelt before his paternal uncle and requested to leave the household life. His uncle hesitated, so the Master ceased eating and drinking. Having no other choice, his uncle granted his request.
He followed the Chan Master Huiyuan to have his hair shaved, and ten years later, at the age of [twelve], he received full ordination. At age two...

In his fifteenth year, he traveled abroad and reached Gao'an, where he visited Bai-shui. He also paid his respects to the two great elders of Shu-shan, both of whom recognized his potential and gave him their approval.
In the thirteenth year of the Xian-tong era, he met Master Teng-teng at Jiangling;
Teng-teng instructed him, saying, "Go to Tiantai and seek a quiet place to dwell. When you meet An, stop there. Shortly thereafter, he again met Master Han-han.
Hanshan patted him and said, "Forty years from now, there will be a Bodhisattva under Mount Jingshan who shall rule over Jiangnan;
at that time, my Dharma will flourish. He then departed for Tiantai Mountain, where he established the Fudang Monastery in Jing’an Township.
This fulfilled his earlier prophetic words. He subsequently resided at Yilong Monastery. In the fourth year of the Zhonghe era, famine and pestilence ravaged the region of Zhedong.

The Master collected and buried thousands of exposed remains throughout the three prefectures of Wenzhou, Taizhou, and Mingzhou; at that time, he was called the Great Being Pibei (Increasing Compassion).
During the Qianning era, Xuefeng once met him and bestowed upon the Master a *zōnglǚ* whisk before departing. In the third year of the Tianyou era...
The Senior Uncle Qian dispatched his messenger Tong Jian, carrying robes, incense, and medicinal herbs, to enter the mountains and extend an invitation.

Upon arriving at the capital, [the Master] was appointed as the Great Master Zhide and lodged in the Gongchen (Meritorious Subject) Courtyard. Day and night, the Senior Uncle sought the Way from him. When [the Master] took his leave to return to the mountains, the Senior Uncle would not permit it;
he therefore constructed Rui Long Monastery within the city to welcome him. Zen practitioners flocked there like clouds, and they also attained the "Dumb-Dumb" realization.
Regarding these words, he once said to his disciples: "In recent years, this old monk has traveled abroad through the regions beyond the Yangtze River, including Lingnan, Jing, and Hu.
There was no monastery where I found a teacher of wisdom that I did not visit to seek instruction. This was solely for the purpose of gathering with you all today."

Each must know this point of departure. Yet, throughout all quarters, there is ultimately no divergent teaching; it simply instructs people to let their frantic minds rest and cease seeking from others.
Simply follow the situation and act authentically, yet there is no "authenticity" to be acted upon. Make use of things as they arise, yet there is no "time" that can be used.
Even if compassion is shown through bitter words, one must not call day night; even with the most skillful means, it remains so.
In the end, one cannot point to the east and call it the west. Such talk might be possible; that would merely be a supernatural feat of conjuring illusions, which is not my concern.
As for those who merely parrot words, they fail to realize their own errors and instead wish to pluck flowers from the sky or grasp the moon in the waves—will they ever attain true mental power?
Each of you should reflect upon this today. Only when you suddenly resolve to leave behind these attachments will you begin.
"Knowing that Old Man Rui-long had no choice but to act, he went to such great lengths to circumvent the matter; would you still accept this?

In the fourth month of the second year of the Tiānchéng era (the Dinghai year), the Master requested a burial site from the Shangfu (Grand Marshal). The Shangfu laughed and said, 'Is the Master truly so?

He then dispatched Lu Rénzhāng to select a site at Xīgùan to build a stūpa. Once the stūpa was completed, the Master went to take leave of the Shangfu, entrusting him with the protection of the Dharma."
He took pity on the people and passed away while sitting upright. He had lived through eighty-seven years and sat in meditation for seventy summers.
By imperial decree, his mountain retreat at Mount Tiantai was renamed "Yinji" (Trace of Concealment).
At Huangbo Mountain was Chan Master Hui, a native of Luoyang. He left home to become a monk in his youth and studied the minor sūtras and śāstras.

Later, upon receiving the bodhisattva precepts, he sighed and said: "The Great Being’s restraint of discipline (śīla-saṃvara) and my own originally received śrāvaka precepts are identical in terms of what is maintained and what constitutes an offense.
However, they differ in the number of articles, in the relationship between the branches and the root, and in their specific intent; moreover, they are subtle and minute."
It is difficult to guard against. Among the practices for gathering virtue, he had never performed even a small portion, let alone that which benefits sentient beings.
Furthermore, as the world is but a bubble and an illusion, how can one be attached to this body and life? He then set aside his lecturing and intended to cast himself into the water to feed the fish.
Just as he was about to act upon this thought, two practitioners of the second dhyāna met him and spoke with him at length, saying that there were many spiritual teachers in the south.
“Master, why do you linger in one corner? You should turn your mind back from here to seek the Way. At that time, the frontier passes were strictly guarded;
the Master said to the guards, “I am not here to enjoy the mountain scenery, but have sworn to seek the ancestral Way. On another day, I shall surely not forget your kindness.

The guards perceived his resolve and did not detain him with harshness, saying instead, “Since you, Master, have forgotten your own body for the sake of the Dharma, we pray that when you return, you will not be stingy [with us].”
Having heard this, the Master expressed his gratitude and departed directly for Shushan. At that time, Master Ren was seated in the Dharma Hall receiving visitors.
The Master first looked toward the assembly and then posed the question: "What is it like when one departs in a single kṣaṇa?
Shushan replied, "It fills the void; how will you go? The Master said, "Filling the void is not as good as not going at all. Shushan then—
"Stop," the Master said. He descended from the hall to consult with the First Seat. The Seat remarked, "Just now I observed the Master’s response to the Abbot;
it was truly extraordinary. The Master replied, "This was merely impulsive; it happened quite by chance. I venture to hope for your compassionate instruction.

The Seat asked, "In a single kṣaṇa, was there any room for deliberation? At these words, the Master attained sudden realization. He prostrated in thanks and withdrew to the tea hall, filled with both sorrow and joy.

The offerings were abundant. Thus it continued for three days. He subsequently resided at Mount Huangbo, where he gathered a multitude and expounded the Dharma. Later, he passed away on that same mountain;
his entire body remains within the stupa today, as if alive.
Chan Master Daojian of Yunju:
Daojian was originally from Fanyang; his clan name has been lost to history. By nature he was pure and refined, quiet and seldom speaking.
Having shaved his head as a youth, he received the full precepts and traveled extensively among various monastic assemblies before visiting Chan Master Ying at Yunju.
He conversed with Daoying for three consecutive days. [Daoying] marveled greatly at him and instructed him to serve the community with diligent austerity.

Consequently, he personally attended to the well and the mortar, managed the firewood and the hearth, and oversaw all temple affairs, yet he did not neglect his scholarly deliberations on antiquity and the present. No one among the assembly realized this;

because of his seniority in ordination (*pravrajyā*), he was appointed as the First Seat (*agrasena*) in the hall. Previously, Gaoshan in Gao’an had been possessed of great spiritual power. Master Ying went there...
Sanfeng had been serving him for some time. When he arrived at Yunju, the deity followed him there as well and took up residence beneath a withered tree;

as the tree flourished, it was called the "Anle Tree Deity" (Peaceful Joy Tree Deity). When it was time for the Master to pass away, the administrative monk asked, "If the Master is about to depart this life, who should succeed him?

He replied, "Jian in the hall. The administrative monk did not intend Jian to be the successor, thinking instead that the Master was merely referring to someone to be selected from among the assembly.
"Who would be fit to preach the Dharma? They all replied, "The second seat [Jian] would be suitable. Shouce then said, "For now, let us pay our respects and first invite Jian.
Jian asked, "How could I dare to accept? Once the request was made, Jian did not decline or refuse. He immediately took up his ritual implements and entered the abbot’s quarters;
he presided over the assembly and expounded the Dharma with complete composure. The administrative monks were greatly discouraged. When the Master learned of this, he fled one night. Anle Tree.
The deity wept aloud. At dawn the next day, the assembly pursued him to Mazhuang (Wheat Village). Repenting their error, they welcomed him back.
From the air, voices called out repeatedly, saying, "The Master is coming! A monk asked, "What is the Master’s house style? He replied, "Attaining mastery wherever one is.
The monk asked, "Is it not true that Vimalakīrti was the Golden Grain Tathāgata? He said, "Yes. The monk asked, "Why then did he attend the assembly of Śākyamuni?"
The junior monk listened to the Dharma and said, “He does not contend with others over self and others.

[The Master] asked, “What is the Bodhisattva Red-Crested King? He replied, “Why ask about this red-headed fellow? He asked, “What is it like when one lies across the body to cover everything? He replied, “Is it still able to cover anything?
He asked, “Why does the snakelet swallow the snake-master? He replied, “What harm is there in principle? He asked, “Regarding the place where all Buddhas cannot speak—”
"Can you, Preceptor, say anything? [The Master] said, "Where do you say I cannot say anything? [The monk] asked, "What should one do when encountering a fierce tiger on the road?
[The Master] said, "A thousand or ten thousand people do not encounter it; why is it that you alone encounter it? [The monk] asked, "What should one do when staying alone on a solitary peak?
[The Master] said, "There are seven empty halls; who taught you to stay alone on a solitary peak? [The monk] asked, "An ancient said: 'If..."
If you wish to take responsibility for this matter, you must simply stand atop the highest mountain peak and walk within the deepest ocean.
What is the meaning of this? He replied: "The high peaks and deep oceans are remote, solitary, and perilous; are they like the soft warmth of your inner chambers? He asked again:
"In the monastic communities, there is much discussion regarding matters of nobility; what is that like? He replied: "It is to make you recognize the Emperor of the Great Tang."
He was not one who merely knew how to write characters; rather, his realization was profound and subtle, and his practice was clearly verified.

In responding to stimuli and engaging with phenomena, he transcended the limits of ordinary capacity, and the world took him as its master. He lived for over eighty years and passed away without illness.
Zhang Chong, the regional commander of Luzhou, erected a stupa for him on the mountain where he resided.
The colophon states: There was a Chan Master Tong’an Pi who, together with the Master, was a direct successor of Master Ying;
they were like brothers born of the same womb. Pi’s successor was Tong’an Zhi, and Zhi’s successor was Liangshan Yuanguan. From Pi to Yuanguan—
All records of his disciples have been lost; there is no transmission remaining. Guàn’s son was Dàyáng Xuán.
A separate record of Yīnggōng is available in the *Sòngchuán*.
The Biography of Master Xianni: Master Xianni was a man of unknown origins. His life and deeds were quite extraordinary. He had no fixed dwelling place;

having received the seal of his mind from Dongshan, he lived among the common people in Minchuan. He did not maintain ritual implements nor observe monastic regulations; throughout both winter and summer, he wore only—
Wearing but a single patchwork robe, he went daily along the riverbank to gather shrimp and clams to fill his belly.
At night, he would sleep amidst the paper offerings at the White Horse Temple on Mount Dong. The local residents called him "Shrimp Master" (Xiānzhe) Chan Master.

When Chan Master Jing of Huayan heard of this, wishing to determine whether he was genuine or not, he first hid himself secretly among the paper offerings. Deep in the night, when the Master returned, Jing seized him and said, "If..."
"What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master replied abruptly, "The wine stand and platter before the deity.
Yan placed his hand firmly upon it and said, "Truly, we share the same root. Later, when Yan went to Chang'an by imperial summons from Emperor Zhuangzong, the Master arrived there first.
Every day he would sing and take selfies, or else feign madness, coming and going through mud and snow without leaving a trace.
His final whereabouts were unknown. Jing emerged from Dongshan; thus it is said they share the same root.

As for the Great Master Weijin, he was the dharma heir of the Great Master Baowen. He was a native of Fuzhou. He had long maintained ascetic practices, never wearing silk or cotton wool, but only crossing through cold and heat in tattered rags;
at that time, he was called a dhūta. Initially, he studied under Xuefeng, where he penetrated deeply into the profound mysteries, and subsequently inquired further about the Dharma.
The lineage of Xuansha was one where the mind-seal was perfectly aligned. One day, he asked the senior monk Jian, "I have heard that you have written a commentary on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*;

is this true? Jian replied, "I dare not say so. The Master said, "How would you comment upon the two Mañjuśrīs [in the sutra]? Jian said, "I beg the Master to examine it for me. The Master then raised his sleeves and departed.
During the Guanghua era of the Tang dynasty, he entered Mount Nanyue and resided at San-sheng-zang. Within the Zang there was a mirror-lamp.
This is one section, composed by the Third Patriarch of the Avataṃsaka, the Great Master Xianshou.

Upon seeing it, the Master suddenly awakened to the gate of the infinitely interpenetrating Indra’s net within the vast Dharma-realm, and the manifestations of the mutual radiance of all Buddhas. He then sighed in admiration, saying:

"This is the marvelous achievement of a former sage. Were it not for the possession of inconceivable wisdom in skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), how could such a work have been created? Thereupon, he composed the Five-Character [Verse].
The verses consist of five chapters; upon reading them, the reader will realize the mutual integration of principle and phenomena.

Later, at Mount Zhongnan, the Master composed the *Baolin zhuan* (Record of the Treasure Grove) in four fascicles, which chronicles the successive lineages of the Chan school from the Zhenyuan era onwards. He also composed the *Juedi song* (Verses on the Ground of Enlightenment) in heptasyllabic meter.
He extensively elucidated the causal origins (*nidāna*) of various teachings and also authored the *Biographies of Eminent Monks of Mount Nanyue*, both of which have been transmitted to the world.
The Biography of National Teacher Gushan (appended from Zhang):

National Teacher Gushan, whose name was Shenyan, was a native of Daliang. His surname was Li. From childhood, he loathed the smell of meat and pungent herbs and delighted in hearing the sound of bells.
When Fan was twelve years old, several streaks of white vapor rose from the walls of the room where he lived. The Master immediately took up his brush and wrote upon the wall:
"White path, change your course swiftly from now on; Cease appearing to manifest as omens of ill omen. I shall surely dispel your heterodox ways and lead you back to the True Vision;
You shall certainly transcend the mundane and enter the realm of the Sages. As soon as he finished writing, the vapor vanished. His age was just reaching the prime of youth.
While he was studying, he fell gravely ill. He suddenly dreamed that a divine being gave him medicine; upon waking, he was immediately cured.

The following year, he again dreamed that a Buddhist monk told him, "The time for you to leave the household life has arrived. He then followed the Chan Master Daogui of Bailu Mountain in Wei Prefecture to receive the tonsure.

Having received full ordination at Mount Song, he said to his fellow students, "The ancient masters have said that after the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal ritual of four proclamations), one's entire being is the embodiment of precept, concentration, and wisdom;
how can this be constrained by mere rules and regulations? Thereupon, he took up his staff and traveled to every Zen monastery, recording only their spoken words.
He remained within the realm of intellectual understanding until he reached the Snowy Range (Xue Ling), where it suddenly became clear and accorded with the truth. One day he visited Xuefeng;

knowing that his karmic conditions were ripe, Xuefeng suddenly rose, seized him, and asked, "What is this? At that moment, the Master attained complete awakening and even forgot the very mind that had realized it.
He did nothing but raise his hand and wave it back and forth. Xuefeng asked, "Are you applying intellectual reasoning? The Master replied, "What reasoning could there be?
Xuefeng, verifying his profound realization, patted him and certified him.

When Xuefeng passed away, the Military Governor of Min established a Chan monastery at Mount Gu at a distance of twenty *li* to the left of the prefectural city, inviting [the Master] to propagate the teachings and the lineage, saying: "Now, for the sake of all..."
O Benevolent One, you have pierced your head and entered the gate of the sages' transformation, yet you shake it off and will not emerge.

This is why I say to you: the teaching cannot reach you; the Patriarch did not come from the West; the Buddhas of the three ages could not chant it; the twelve divisions of the teachings could not carry it;
ordinary beings and sages cannot encompass it; and it cannot be transmitted through past or present. Suddenly, you are this man, yet you have not yet penetrated it.
The news: when he spoke to him in such a manner, the other gave him a slap across the mouth.
Can one still find fault with him? Even so, one must not slap indiscriminately. Gushan usually said: "There is yet another person who does not step through the stone gate;
there must be a phrase for not stepping through the stone gate. What is this phrase for not stepping through the stone gate? Gushan himself remained within the three [barriers].
For over ten years, those who have come from all directions across the five lakes and four seas have gazed upon the mountain peaks and observed the waters;
yet not a single person has been seen to attain clear and penetrating realization. Is there anyone who has attained it even now? Brothers, do not let this remain obscure. Take care.
Thereupon he spoke a verse, showing it to the assembly, saying: "To understand directly is already difficult; to seek through words becomes even more remote.

If one discusses the Buddhas and the Patriarchs, they are, quite unexpectedly, separated by the ends of the earth. The Military Governor of Min held him in high esteem and frequently inquired about the essentials of the Dharma.
Chan Master Baofu Congzhan was a native of Fuzhou. Born into the Chen family, at the age of fifteen he paid his respects to Xuefeng as his preceptor.
At eighteen, he received full ordination at Dazhong Temple in his home prefecture. He traveled through the regions of Wu and Chu before returning to attend upon Xuefeng.
One day, Xuefeng suddenly called out to him, "Do you understand? As the Master was about to step forward, Xuefeng struck him with his staff. The Master—
At that moment, he knew where he belonged. Furthermore, he frequently consulted Master Changqing Ling regarding causes and conditions from both ancient and modern times; Ling deeply approved of him.

In the fourth year of the Zhengming era of the Liang dynasty (the Dingchou year), Wang Gong Qin, the Prefectural Governor of Zhangzhou, having received his reputation for the Way, established Baofu Monastery and invited the Master to reside there.
The Master said: "As for the matter of your travels as a *xiuxing* (monk on pilgrimage), how is it that you do not understand? Go and understand it!"
Do not go about seeking instructions from others. If you have long resided in a monastic community (*saṃghārāma*), you will have some general familiarity with the distances and circumstances;

thus, you may act according to the truth wherever you are. As for those of later learning who do not yet know the proper sequence, this mountain monk does not begrudge his verbal efforts in speaking to you:

matters from across kalpas of dust and time are right here in the present. Do you understand? Question: When one’s speech becomes urgent due to [the intensity of] the discourse, how should one proceed?

The Master said, "Why do you say this? The monk bowed his head and remained silent for a long while. The Master said, "The mechanism that strikes like lightning—your standing there to contemplate it is but a vain labor.
A monk asked, "If one wishes to reach the path of non-arising, one must recognize the original source. What is the original source?

The Master remained silent for a long while, then asked his attendant, "What was the monk just now asking? When the monk repeated his question, the Master shouted at him and drove him out, saying, "I..."
"Do not worry about being deaf. Because the Master was standing with a monk in attendance, he asked, "How can you be so careless?
The monk said, "What is it that constitutes my carelessness? The Master picked up a clod of earth, handed it to the monk, and said, "Throw this out in front of the gate."
A monk threw down [his staff] and said, "Where was my lack of care? The Master said, "I saw you bumping and knocking against things, so I said you were lacking in care.
The Master resided at Baofu for nearly twelve years, with no fewer than seven hundred students. His methods for engaging disciples and benefiting sentient beings cannot be fully recorded here.
In the third year of the Tiānchéng era of the Táng dynasty (the Wŭzǐ year), he manifested a slight illness. A monk entered his quarters.
He went to inquire after his health. The Master said, "I have known you for many years; what skillful means do you have to save me? The monk replied, "I possess many skillful means.
I have heard it said that you, Reverend, do not know how to observe dietary restrictions.

He then addressed the assembly, saying, "For the past ten days, my strength has been exhausted and weak, but there is nothing else; it is simply that the time has arrived. A monk asked, "Since the time has arrived, will the Master depart now?"
"Abiding is it. The Master said, "The Way, the Way. [The monk] said, "How could I dare to act rashly?
The Master said, "To lose one's money and suffer the penalty. Having said this, he passed away.
The commentary states: I ascended Mount Gushan and visited the traces left by the National Teacher. Upon reaching He-shui Rock (Water-Crying Cliff), the scenery was melancholy and desolate.
It is traditionally said that the Master once sat in meditative absorption there; as the mountain stream made a clamorous noise, the Master shouted at it, and the water flowed backward and away.
To this day it remains so; the lofty character of the National Teacher can be contemplated for a thousand years.

The witty sayings of Baofu were like biting frost and a swift gale, sufficient to wither and destroy; yet, a gentleman does not wish to outshine others excessively—would Master Chen have immediately built a city of surrender?
The Biographical Record of Master Dōkan of Rasan:
Master Dōkan of Rasan was a native of the Chen family of Changxi. He left the household life at Mount Kwi and received full ordination upon reaching the required age.

He traveled extensively throughout various regions and once visited Seishō (Shishuang). He asked, "What is it like when one cannot find peace whether staying or departing? Seishō replied, "You must simply exhaust [all conceptualization]."
The Master did not approve. He then went to visit Yantou and asked the same question as before. Yantou said, "He goes and stays according to his own will;

what is the point of managing him? Thereupon, the Master took this to heart. The Military Governor of Min, having tasted the flavor of his Dharma, invited him to reside at Luoshan, where he was titled Chan Master Fabao.
When a monk took leave of Baofu, Baofu asked, "Where are you going? The monk replied, "To pay my respects to Luoshan. Baofu said, "You..."
On the road to Roshan, Baofu went up to the capital in the autumn to have an audience with the Great King. He posed forty questions, the first of which was:
"If a monk suddenly finds that his single phrase does not accord [with yours], do not say 'I did not say it. The monk related this to the Master, who laughed heartily and said:
"Since Old Teacher Chen entered the Fujian region and crossed under the Hongtang Bridge, I have never seen such a thing."
"A hair-tip star has appeared. You and I shall go ask Congzhan about it. Master Chen said, "I have no such questions; I have only a single sword.
Beneath that one sword lies the intent of manifesting a separate body, the path of emerging from oneself. If you do not understand, you must be reduced to dust.
When the monk returned and reported this to Fuyuan, Fuyuan said, "At that time, I too was merely joking with him. It was autumn.
He entered the monastery. The Master specially prepared a tea ceremony and invited Fú to pray for blessings, but Fú did not go.
Instead, he said to a monk, "I previously made some joking remarks; I fear the Abbot might ask about them. When the monk returned and reported this, the Master said, "Tell him:
'A fierce tiger will never eat meat that has already been offered. The monk went again, and Fú then came. As he was about to pass away, he ascended the hall and gathered the assembly.
After a long while, he extended his left hand; the attendants could not fathom the meaning. He then ordered the monks on the eastern side to step back.
Again, he extended his right hand and ordered the monks on the western side to step back. He then said, "To repay the Buddha's kindness, nothing surpasses the circulation of the Great Teaching.
Go now; take care. Having spoken, he smiled gently and passed away.
The commentary states: Among those who attained the Dharma under the gate of Yantou, six people are recorded in the *Chuan Deng Lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp).
Of these, the two Yan and one Xian are the most prominent. While the Head of the Sangha (Sengtong) transmits only Ruiyan Yan, Xuanchuan Yan and Master Xian are not included.
I have therefore set them forth here, so that it may be known from whence the two masters Huanglong and Mingzhao originated.
Huanglong Ji (Huanglong Qi) and Mingzhao Qian transmitted the Dharma on Mount Huanglong.
Chan Master Huiji was the son of the Zhang family of Qinghe. Initially, he visited Yantou and asked, “What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
Yantou said, “Do you know how to make rice cakes? He replied, “I do. Yantou said, “For now, just go make rice cakes.”
He departed and later arrived at Xuánquán. Again he asked, "Do you understand? Xuánquán picked up a stalk of *sòjiǎo* (soapberry) and said, "Understand?
The Master did not understand. Xuánquán set it down and made a gesture of washing clothes. The Master then prostrated and said, "I now know that the Buddha-dharma has no difference. Xuánquán said:
He saw a profound principle. The Master said, "I asked Yantou, 'Do you know how to untangle rice cakes? Untangling rice cakes is merely untangling what is stuck.
When the Master raised up the soapberry lye, that too was untangling what is stuck. Therefore it is said there is no difference."
Quan laughed heartily. The Master then attained realization. During the Tianyou era of the Tang dynasty, he traveled to this mountain to propagate the Dharma.
The regional commander provided his own salary to build a monastery for him. The Emperor granted him purple robes and a formal title. He greatly expanded the seat of the Dharma.

As the Master was about to pass away, a monk asked, "After a hundred years, who will take away your alms-bag? The Master replied, "Take it as you please. The monk asked, "What is inside?"... [text fragment ends]

"What is the matter? The Master said, "Only when the thread frays will you know. [The questioner] asked, "Who attains it? The Master said, "When the swallow returns and the thunder resounds, I shall tell you.

Having finished speaking, he passed away. Previously, there was the Real Man Lü Yán Dōngbīn, a native of Jīngchuān. During the late Tang dynasty, he failed to pass the imperial examinations three times.
He happened upon Zhōnglí Quán by chance in a wine shop in Cháng'ān, who bestowed upon him the art of prolonging life. From then on—
People did not investigate this man further. Once, while traveling at Lushan Guizong, he inscribed these words on the wall of the bell tower:
"One day of pure leisure and self-mastery, The six spirits harmonize, signaling peace and security. Since the treasure resides within the *dantian*, there is no need to seek the Way;

When facing objects with no mind, there is no need to inquire about Chan. Not long after, his path led him to Huanglong Mountain. There he beheld purple clouds forming a canopy and suspected that a person of extraordinary character must dwell there.
He then entered to pay his respects, arriving just as the Master was striking the drum to ascend the hall. Recognizing that this man must be Lü Gong, the Master wished to test him by advancing him;
he raised his voice sternly and said, "Beside the seat is one who would steal the Dharma. Lü stepped forward resolutely and asked, "A world is hidden within a single grain of millet;
mountains and rivers are boiled within half a pint of cauldron—what is the meaning of this? The Master pointed at him and said, "This is a corpse-guarding ghost! Lü...

Lü said, "But what can be done? My bag contains the elixir of longevity and immortality. The Master said, "Even if you have eighty thousand kalpas, in the end you will surely fall into emptiness and oblivion.
Lü was struck with astonishment and flew his sword to threaten him, but it could not enter. He then prostrated himself twice and requested instruction on the ultimate goal.
The Master interrogated him, saying, "I shall not ask about boiling mountains and rivers in a half-measure cauldron; how is it that a single grain of millet conceals the world?"
Jie-lü (Lüyuan) attained sudden realization and spoke in verse, saying: "I have cast away my gourd-bag and smashed my lute;

Now I no longer crave mercury within gold. Since first beholding Huanglong, I have finally realized that all my previous efforts were misplaced. The Master instructed him to provide protection [for his practice].
Chan Master Mingzhao Deqian received the seal of approval from Luoshan; he was not confined to a single corner [of the tradition] and vigorously promoted the profound principles.
The various senior masters feared his quick-wittedness, and among the younger students, few dared to face him.

Once, while visiting Zhaokong, he pointed to a mural on the wall and asked a monk, "Which one is that deity? The monk replied, "It is a Dharma-protecting benevolent deity. The Master said, "During the Huichang suppression..."
"Where have you come from? The monk had no reply. The Master ordered him to ask Attendant Yan. Yan said, "From where did you encounter this calamity during such a long kalpa?
The monk returned and reported this to the Master. The Master said, "Even if Attendant Yan were to gather a thousand followers hereafter, what use would that be?
The monk bowed and requested another word. The Master said, "Where have you gone? Next, [the monk] arrived at...
[Zhaozhou] went to the place of the Elder Tan. Tan said, "In the study of the Way, one must go to where a whole person is, and one must also go to where half a person is.
Zhaozhou then asked, "I do not ask about where a whole person is; what is the place where half a person is? Tan had no reply.
Later, he instructed his junior disciple to ask the Master (Zhaozhou). The Master said, "If you wish to know where half a person is, it is simply..."
This fellow was a "mud-ball jester. The Venerable Qing raised the story of Yangshan planting his spade and asked the Master, "The ancients' intent lay in the place where they folded their hands;
