where did it lie when he planted the spade? The Master called out, "Qing! Qing responded to the call. The Master said, "Did you see Yangshan in a dream?"
Qing said, "Do not offer a formal response, Master; we simply wish to deliberate.
The Master replied, "If you wish to deliberate, there is already the Head Teacher with his fifteen hundred disciples here. He then went to Shuangyan. During a tea service, Shuangyan said:
"I shall ask you a question," he said. "If you can answer it, I will relinquish this monastery for you, Master, to dwell in;
if you cannot answer it, I shall not relinquish it. He then cited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, saying:
"All Buddhas and the Dharma of the Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi of all Buddhas—all issue forth from this sūtra. Now tell me, by whom was this sūtra spoken? The Master [Dongshan] replied: [The Buddha].
[The Master] said: "As for speaking or not speaking, set that aside for now. But tell me, Master, what exactly do you call this sutra?
Yanguan had no reply. The Master said: "All worthy sages are distinguished by means of the dharma of non-action (wuwei)."
"As for this very 'distinction'—is it a fault or not a fault? If it were a fault, then all the worthies and sages would be at fault.
If it is not a fault, then what exactly do you call 'distinction'? Yankuan was speechless. The Master said, "Alas! Xuefeng has spoken to the point. Later, the Master visited Baoning;
they met on the road, and the Master immediately asked, "Brother, you are one of those who walk the Path. He then gave him a nod.
Bitou said, "This thing obstructs me and I cannot penetrate it. May I have it removed for a short while?
Ning said, "How long has it been since you, Master, first arrived here? The Master said, "Alas! You have deceived me; I shall go back now, having already worn out a pair of straw sandals.
Guotai spoke on his behalf, saying, "Not only I, but even all the Buddhas would be at a loss. The Master asked, "Why is that?"
He compared himself to others. When the Master was at Zhiye Monastery in Wuzhou, he occupied the seat of the First Seat. On one occasion, he refused to accept purified water.
The administrator scolded him, saying, "Venerable Elder, you do not understand the distinction between the defiled and the pure. Why do you refuse to accept the purified water?
The Master leaped off his bed, picked up the pitcher of purified water, and said, "Is this defiled or pure? The administrator was left speechless. The Master then smashed it to pieces.
The Master’s junior uncle was at the monastery and was very ill. He sent a letter by messenger to inquire, saying: "I am suffering from this great illness;
right now I am enduring intense pain. I cannot be settled anywhere. Is there anyone who can save me?"
The Master then spoke again: "This Vajra-arrow has been struck into the crown of the head; it has already passed over to the other side.
A monk who had previously been in the Master’s Dharma assembly left to dwell in a hermitage for one year. Later, he came to pay his respects and said: "An ancient said..."
"We have not seen each other for three days; do not look upon me as you did before. The Master then bared his chest and asked, "Tell me, how many eyelashes do I have?
The monk had no reply. The Master then asked, "When did you leave the hermitage? The monk said, "This morning."
The Master said, "When you came, to whom did you entrust this broken-legged cauldron? The monk was again speechless, so the Master shouted at him and sent him out.

The Master resided at Mingzhao Mountain for forty years, and his words and phrases spread throughout the four quarters. As he was about to pass away, he ascended the hall to address the assembly and give his final instructions.
That night, as he stretched out his legs, he asked his attendant, "In the past, when Śākyamuni Tathāgata stretched out..."
His two feet emitted the radiance of a hundred jewels. "Tell me, how much do I emit now? The attendant replied, "At the Crane Forest [Śāla Grove] in the past, it was the Buddha;
today, it is the Master. The Master brushed his eyebrows with his hand and said, "Do not fail me! He then spoke this verse:
"Displaying full majesty amidst a thicket of blades, you all should protect and uphold this well. An iron ox gives birth to a calf within the flames. At that moment—

"Who among you can understand and penetrate my mechanism? Having finished his verse, he sat peacefully and passed away in profound stillness. His stupa and monastery remain there to this day. The commentary states:

It is commonly said that to study the Way of the Immortals one requires the proper bones, and to study the Buddha-way one requires the right conditions. Lü Dongbin was surely one who possessed both the bones and the conditions.
Nevertheless, had it not been for the decisive severing of Huanglong’s skillful means, I fear this fellow would have been difficult to subdue. Mingzhao attained awakening through this.

This is unfathomable. It is like Lord Deng looking down upon grasses and trees and seeing them all scorched; it is what is called "knowing only the total extinction of the Dharma while disregarding the absence of people.
From this, one knows that the lineage of Yantou was solitary and cold, failing to flourish, and could not match the long-lasting and far-reaching influence of the Dharma-stream of Old Man Xianggu.
The Elder of Taiyuan transmitted [the Dharma] to the Elder Fu of Taiyuan.
Initially, while at Guangxiao Temple in Yangzhou, he was lecturing on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. A practitioner of Chan, who was stranded by snow, went there to listen to the lecture.
When the discourse reached the three causes of buddha-nature and the dharma-body of the three virtues, the lecturer spoke extensively on the subtle principles of the dharma-body.
The Chan practitioner laughed in derision. After the Master finished his lecture, he invited the Chan practitioner to drink tea and said, "My own aspirations have always been narrow and inferior;

I rely on the literal text to explain the meaning. Having just been ridiculed by you, I hope you will grant me some instruction. The Chan practitioner replied, "I truly laugh at you, Preceptor, for not recognizing the Dharma-body.
The Master asked, "In such an explanation as yours, what is it that is not correct? The Chan practitioner said, "Please, Preceptor, explain it once more."
“Pervasive. The Master said, “The principle of the Dharmakāya is like the great void: vertically it exhausts the three periods of time; horizontally it spans the ten directions;

it encompasses the eight extremities and includes the two polarities. Responding to conditions and meeting with stimuli, there is nowhere it does not pervade. [The student] said, “I do not say that what you, Master of the Seat (Zhuangzu), have said is incorrect.
However, you have only described the extent and boundaries of the Dharmakāya; you have truly not yet recognized the Dharmakāya itself. The Master said:
Since it was thus, the Zen Master said, "You should speak for me. The lecturer asked, "Do you still believe? The Master replied, "How could I dare not believe?

The Zen Master said, "Lecturer, try suspending your lectures for ten days. Close the door and sit upright; withdraw your mind, collect your thoughts, and let go of all conditions of good and evil at once.
The Master followed these instructions exactly. From the first watch of the night until the fifth watch, he heard the sound of drums and horns.
Suddenly attaining realization, he went to knock on the door. The meditator asked, "Who is it? The Master replied, "It is I.

The meditator rebuked him, saying, "I instructed you to transmit and uphold the Great Teaching and to preach the Dharma in place of the Buddha. Why have you come home drunk and lying in the street last night? The Master said:
"Virtuous Master of Chan," he said, "in the past, while lecturing on the sutras, you were squeezing the nostrils of your biological parents.

Now that you have departed, I dare not do so anymore. The Chan practitioner replied, "Go for now; we shall meet tomorrow. Thereupon, the Master ceased his lectures and traveled extensively throughout all quarters.
His fame resounded throughout the world. He once traveled through Zhejiang and attended a dharma assembly at Mount Jing.
One day, in front of the Great Buddha Hall, a monk asked him, "Have you ever been to Wutai? He replied, "I have. "Did you see Mañjuśrī? He replied, "I did. "Where did you see him?
He replied, "I saw him in front of the Buddha Hall at Mount Jing. Later, when that monk happened to travel to Minchuan, he related this story to Xuefeng. Xuefeng said:

"Why not have him come over the ridge? When the Master heard this, he hurriedly prepared his pack and set out. Upon first arriving at the peak, he stayed at the monastery and, while resting there, shared some tangerines with the monks.
Changqing asked, "Where did you bring these from? The Master replied, "From outside the ridges. Changqing said, "It was no easy matter to travel such a long distance;
how did you manage to carry them here? The Master replied, "Tangerines, tangerines. The next day he ascended the mountain, and Xuefeng heard of it.
The assembly gathered. When the Master arrived at the Dharma Hall, he looked toward Xuefeng and then went down to inspect the administrative affairs.
The next day, he went up again to pay his respects and said, "I offended you, Master, yesterday. Xuefeng said, "Knowing it was such a matter, let it be.
One day, Xuefeng saw the Master and pointed to the sun to show him. The Master shook his hand and walked out. Xuefeng said, "You do not accept me."
"Yes. The Master said, "The Abbot wags his head; I wag my tail. Where is there anything you do not approve of?
Feng said, "In every place, one must conceal it. One day, during the evening assembly, Feng was lying in the central courtyard.
The Master said, "Within the jurisdiction of the five provinces, only this old monk is somewhat superior. Feng then rose and departed. Feng once asked the Master about seeing [the Buddha-nature].
"Is it true that Linji spoke of three phrases? The Master said, "Yes. [Xuefeng] asked, "What is the first phrase?
The Master looked up at him. Xuefeng said, "This is still the second phrase. What is the first phrase? The Master folded his hands and withdrew.
From then on, Xuefeng held him in deep esteem; their understanding was sealed within the teaching hall, and the path of teacher and disciple was in perfect accord. No further...
He was bathing there. One day, Xuansha went up to inquire after Xuefeng, who said, "There is a little mouse here;
it is currently in the bathhouse. Xuansha said, "I shall wait to cross-examine the Master. Having finished speaking, he went to the bathhouse and encountered the Master (Shishuang) pouring water.
Xuansha said, "I have come to see the Senior Monk. The Master said, "We have already met. Xuansha said:
They met during a period of great calamity. The Master said, "Why are you dozing off? The monk then entered the abbot’s quarters.
Baofeng said, "I have already scrutinized him thoroughly. [The monk] asked, "How did you scrutinize him? The monk recounted the previous conversation. Baofeng said, "You have been robbed by a thief!"
Gushan asked the Master, "Before your parents were born, where was your nose?
The Master said, "Brother, you go first. Gushan said, "Now that you are born, tell me, where is it? The Master did not approve. Gushan then asked, "How about this?
The Master said, "Bring me the fan in your hand. Gushan gave him the fan and again questioned him on the previous matter; the Master merely shook it.
Fan did not respond. Mount Shan, unable to fathom him, struck the Master with a single punch. When Gushan went to accept the invitation from the Great King, Xuefeng escorted him to the Dharma Hall.
Upon arriving there, Xuefeng said, "A single holy arrow has shot straight into the innermost city.
The Master said, "He is not yet there. Xuefeng said, "He is a man who has reached the very bottom. The Master said, "If you do not believe me, wait until I go myself."
Having verified this, he pursued him to the middle of the road and asked, "Elder brother, where are you going? Xuanshan said, "To the Ninefold City.
The master said, "What if you suddenly encounter an encirclement by a three-pronged army? Xuanshan said, "He has his own path that reaches through the heavens."
The Master said, "If that is so, then you have left the palace and lost the hall. Fushan said, "Where would one not be called 'Honored One'?
The Master shook his sleeves and turned back. Feng asked, "How was that? The Master said, "A fine divine arrow—it was broken in mid-flight.
He then recounted the previous conversation. Feng then said, "That fellow's words remain. The Master said, "This old, frozen lump still has a sense of local attachment!"
The Master was standing in front of the storehouse when a monk asked, "What is enlightenment that meets the eye?
The Master kicked a puppy, which let out a cry and ran away. The monk had no reply. The Master said, "That little puppy does not deserve more than a single kick.

Later, while Baofu was selecting melons, the Master went to him and said, "If you can say something, I will give you a melon to eat. The Master said, "Hand it over. Baofu passed a slice to him. The Master— [ate it].
Upon receiving [the invitation], he departed immediately. The Master did not appear in the world; those of all quarters referred to him as "The Venerable Fu of Taiyuan.

Later, he returned to Weiyang, where Minister Chen invited him to provide for his needs. One day, the Master said to the Minister, "Tomorrow I shall lecture on the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* once, as a way of repaying your kindness.
When the appointed day arrived, after the vegetarian feast and tea ceremony were concluded, the Master ascended the seat. After a long while, he gestured...
The "Chixia" (One-Finger) version says: "Thus have I heard. He then summoned the Grand Secretary, who responded, "Yes. The Master said, "At one time the Buddha was staying...
and then he passed away.
Dàjìng and Xiǎojìng transmitted [the lineage] to the Venerable Master Jìng of Guoqing Temple. When he first met Master Xuánshā, the latter addressed the assembly, saying:
"All of you, if you can for a lifetime act as if you had lost your parents, I guarantee that you will attain thorough penetration. Master Jìng then took up these words and questioned him.
[The Master] said: "In the teachings it is stated that one must not use the mind of 'that which is known' to fathom the unsurpassed wisdom and vision of the Tathāgata.
How then [should one proceed]? Xuansha replied: "If you say you have thoroughly investigated the mind of 'that which is known' to its very bottom, would you still be able to fathom it?
From this, the Master gained entry through faith. Later, he resided at Tiantai for over thirty years without descending from the mountain, extensively synthesizing the three [vehicles].
In his studies, his conduct was solitary and steadfast. Beyond his practice of meditative stillness, he constantly perused the *Nāga-kośa* (the Buddhist canon).

He was held in high esteem by those both far and near, and was commonly known as the Venerable Dajing. Once, someone asked him: "Disciple, whenever I sit in meditation at night, my thoughts fly about in confusion.

I do not yet understand the method for subduing them; I pray that you will grant me clear instruction. The Master replied: "Take this very mind that flies about in confusion, and investigate that which is flying about."

When one investigates the locus of these thoughts and finds no locus, then where do these fluttering thoughts exist? If one turns back to investigate the investigating mind itself, then where is that very mind capable of investigation?
Furthermore, the wisdom that can illuminate is fundamentally empty, and the objects it perceives are likewise quiescent. This quiescence is not a state of mere extinction.

There is no person who can bring about stillness; there is no illuminator who illuminates. There is no object that is illuminated. When both object and wisdom are utterly still, the mind and its deliberations are at peace.

One does not seek out branches externally, nor does one dwell in meditative concentration internally. When these two paths are both extinguished, the single nature is serene. This is the essential path for returning to the source.
Because the Master perceived the meaning of "illusion" within the teachings, he composed a verse and questioned the assembly of students:
The verse says: If all dharmas of the path exist like illusions, then committing various transgressions and evils should entail no fault.
How is it that the karma one has created is not forgotten, yet one relies on the Buddha’s compassion to be uplifted and guided? At that time, there was an Elder named Xiao Jing who replied:

"An illusory person creates illusory Mount Cakravāḍa; illusory karma can summon illusory objects of treatment. Failing to understand illusion gives rise to various illusory sufferings; [only through] awakening..."
Zhijian (Zhi Ruohan) and Huanchu (Huan Wuweei)—these two senior *sthaviras* both passed away at their original mountain retreats; the ruins of Guoqing Temple remain there to this day.
This concludes the biography of Chan Master Wujie Yan.

Chan Master Yiyen of Wugushan was the son of the Xu family of Wuxing. On the evening before his birth in the third year of the Qianfu era of the Tang dynasty, an extraordinary fragrance filled the room and a crimson light shone as brightly as day.
During the Guangqi era, while accompanying his father on a military assignment in Xin’an, he was pressured into marriage;

however, the Master did not desire it and consequently traveled through various regions. Having attained spiritual resonance with Jingqing, he returned to visit his parents and settled south of the city walls.
He built a separate dwelling to fulfill his master’s wishes. Beside the dwelling was the shrine of Minister Chen, which contained a statue of Chan Master Lin.

When the Master went there to pay his respects, he lost his way. Later, when the Prefect went to perform the sacrificial rites, he saw the Master in meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) among the dense bamboo behind the temple;
ants were gnawing at his robes, and withered leaves covered his thighs. Some said that he was the son of General Xu, who had [disappeared] from himself.
As this samādhi was being entered and exited, Chan Master Nü of Zihu, not yet knowing the master’s attainment, asked, "The concentration in which you dwell is merely that of the Lesser Vehicle.
At that time, the master was just drinking tea; he lifted up his tea bag and said, "Is this great or small?"

Nü was struck with awe. He soon went to visit Chan Master Desheng of Mount Tang in Kuacang. Desheng asked, "What is your surname? Nü replied, "My surname is Xu. Desheng asked, "Who gave you permission [to be here]? Nü said, "There is no distinction.
Desheng recognized him in silence and subsequently granted him the tonsure and ordination. Once, Desheng ordered him to gather peaches; ten days passed without his returning.
Desheng went to search for him and found the master leaning against a rock while picking peaches, absorbed in meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Desheng snapped his fingers to rouse him.
He emerged from it during the Kaiyun era. While wandering at Jianglang Rock, he beheld a stone grotto and said to his disciple Huixing, "I shall enter meditative absorption on this mountain;
you must pile stones to block the entrance and do not worry about me. Huixing followed these instructions. The following year,
When Master Xingyi was about to depart, he opened the shrine to look inside. The Master’s white hair hung down over his shoulders, and his chest was still warm;

he slowly rose from his meditative state of his own accord, with no sign of change in his countenance. Later, when Lord Shen of Wugu, the Governor of Xin’an, heard of Master Fu’s Way, he ordered the monk Shou-rong, a scholar of the Abhidharma, to interrogate him regarding the characteristics of his meditative absorption.
The Master did not debate with him; Shou-rong considered this a slight upon him.
At that time, the people of Xin’an vied with one another to paint portraits of the Master and worship them, all of whom obtained śarīra relics. Consequently, Huirong felt ashamed and submissive;

he prostrated before the image to apologize for his transgressions and also obtained śarīra relics. He sighed, saying, "From this day forward, I shall no longer dare to fathom [the truth] through my shallow understanding.

King Qian Zhongyi was moved by the Master’s appearance in a dream and dispatched an envoy to have a portrait painted. When it arrived, it happened that the King suffered from an eye ailment; as he unfurled the portrait, [he was cured].

The ritual was like a vision seen in a dream; as the śarīra relics rained down, his eye ailment was suddenly cured. Consequently, he was granted the honorary title "Kaimei" (Opening of Enlightenment).

He then composed verses of praise, and thousands of precious vessels and ritual implements were offered. At the beginning of the Duan-gong era, Emperor Taizong, having heard of the Master’s power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), issued an edict to the local prefecture to provide him with special honors for his departure to the capital.
The Master declined the invitation firmly. When the imperial envoys arrived again to convey the decree, the Emperor specifically ordered that he be conveyed by palanquin.

He entered the private palace for an audience; the Emperor ordered him to sit and bestowed tea upon him, inquiring about his meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). His responses were concise and exhaustive, deeply harmonizing with the Emperor’s intent.

He requested leave to return home, but was again summoned for an audience. Having obtained permission to return to the mountains, the carriage tracks were blocked by those seeing him off. In the first year of the Chūn-hua era, he passed away.
His age was one hundred and fifteen; his years since ordination were fifty-seven. At his cremation, a white light ascended to heaven, and his relics were of five colors.
The people of the region fashioned a statue from his bones; to this day, when the local prefectures pray for rain or fine weather, they receive answers as swift as an echo.
Biography of Chan Master Changjue of Pujing Monastery by Li Pu-jing.
Chan Master Changjue of Pujing Monastery was a native of Chenliu. He was born into the Li clan. In his youth, he studied Confucianism, yet he lacked any desire for official rank or emolument.
His mind delighted in mountains and waters, and he devoted himself much to traveling and sightseeing. Upon reaching Guizong on Mount Lu, he happened upon Chan Master Hongzhang.

When Kaifang spoke, [Dongshan] attained realization beneath his words and firmly requested to leave the household life. Not long after, Zhangjiang was about to pass away; he summoned the Master before him and, stroking his head, said:
"You have a karmic affinity with the Great Dharma and will later deliver immeasurable beings. I am merely a man of a single breath."

Unable to fulfill your wishes, he entrusted the matter of your tonsure to his disciples. Chang then passed away. The Master arrived in the second year of the Qiandehua era of the Liang dynasty and received the shaven head ceremony.
The following year, he received the full precepts at the Amṛta Altar of Donglin. He subsequently traveled to Mount Wutai.
Upon arriving at the capital, he stayed alone outside the Qianlijing Gate for two years. There was a neighbor named Mr.

Zhang, a lay follower of pure faith, who invited the Master to stay and provide him with offerings. One night, deep in the dead of the night, his wife and he secretly peered through a crack and saw that the Master’s body completely filled the interior of the bed, while his head and feet both protruded from the outside.
Mr. Zhang was greatly startled; they then ordered their servants to go and look.
He treated him as he had always done. [The donor] developed redoubled faith and respectfully addressed himself as a disciple. He said, "May we live out our lives together in old age.

Would it be acceptable to offer the front portion of my residence to augment the Master’s chamber? The Master joyfully accepted this. In the third year of the Tiānchéng era of the Later Táng dynasty, a large monastery was thus established and granted the name Pǔjìng.
The Master considered that the times were shallow and ignorant, making it difficult for them to bear the ultimate teachings; he feared that if he were to reveal them, it would lead to error.
As a result, slander and resentment arose; it would have been better had he remained silent.
Thereupon, on the third and eighth days of every month, he distributed alms according to his means, and those among the clergy and laity who benefited numbered in the tens of thousands.

He once said to his disciples, "If only the gateway of wisdom remains unobstructed, how could blessings ever be stagnant? One day, Tao Gu, a Court Official for Remuneration, entered the monastery and witnessed the Master's conduct.
Someone asked, "The sutras state that to be free from all marks is itself to be called a Buddha. Yet, before our eyes, things are in a state of chaotic confusion;
how can one be free from them? The Master replied, "Official, what have you seen? Tao was delighted and looked up to him with great respect.

From then on, although princes, dukes, and high officials repeatedly presented recommendations for robes, official rank, and titles of honor, he declined and would not accept them. In the winter of the fourth year of the Kaibao era, he passed away lying on his right side.
Transformation.
The Biography of Chan Master Zhongyun Hui of the Liang Dynasty.
Chan Master Zhongyun Zhihui was born into the Gao family during the Qin dynasty. From his early childhood, he took pleasure in visiting Buddhist temples and delighted in [the Dharma].
His countenance changed as he vowed to leave the household life. At the age of twenty, he received full ordination. He sought the seal of the mind from Chan Master Ren of Baishui.
Because he loved the mountains and waters of Zhongtan, he built a dwelling there and named it the Wenshi Monastery (Warmth Chamber).

He made it his daily practice to provide water and medicine to others. There was a bhikṣu suffering from white leprosy whom the community loathed; the Master brought him back with him and rubbed him day and night.

He washed it for a long time. Suddenly, a divine light and extraordinary fragrance burst forth, and he lost sight of where the monk was. Upon examining the scab of the wound, he found it to be entirely permeated with that wondrous scent.
During the Kaiping era of the Liang dynasty, longing for his former mountain, he returned to Mount Guifeng in Zhongnan. Thereupon, he withdrew into the deep mountains in serene seclusion.

Walking alone upon the rocky crags, he wandered about and looked around. Suddenly, he saw a monastic robe (*māṇava*), a rosary, a copper water flask, and a *tāla*-leaf hat resting against the stone wall;

they crumbled to pieces as soon as he touched them, appearing exactly as if they had been left there for his daily use. He then said in a state of sudden realization, "These are the implements of my former life.
Consequently, he established a temple at that very spot to repay his past causes. Just as he began clearing the weeds, auspicious clouds emerged from the multitude.
Between the peaks, he subsequently named it Chongyun (Double Clouds). Tigers and leopards retreated and departed. There was a dragon pool that was perilous and foul, impossible to approach;
the Master leveled it to create a path, and the dragon likewise departed. Later, Emperor Mingzong of the Later Tang heard of this and sighed in admiration, bestowing upon it the name Changxing.
He served as abbot for over forty years, guiding and introducing later students without weariness even in his old age.
When Wang Yanchao, the Military Commissioner, was still of humble station, he once followed Huī and wished to become a śramaṇa. Huī said, "Your worldly karmic ties are deep;

you shall serve as a protective wall for my lineage. Later, Yanchao indeed governed Yongxing, whereupon he revered his teacher all the more. In the summer of the third year of the Xiande era of the Zhou dynasty.
He went to see Bi Yanchao and entrusted him with the affairs of the mountain gate. It was early autumn and his health was still robust, yet he suddenly spoke this verse:
"I have a single room, built for me by my parents; I have lived within it for eighty years, but lately I perceive its decay.
I had intended to move elsewhere long ago, but such matters involve likes and dislikes. I shall wait until it collapses of its own accord, so that neither side may hinder the other. Thereupon—
He passed away while seated in the full lotus posture. He had lived eighty-four years in the world and sixty-four years since his ordination.
His stupa was erected at his native mountain.

Zhou Dazhang Qinghuo Chongxu succeeded Dazhangshan Qiruan Chan Master. A native of Yongtai in Fuzhou, he possessed a naturally solitary character and was determined to explore the Way of the Patriarchs.
Having entered the chamber of Xuansha, he attained an acute realization of the profound essence. Xuansha remarked, "Your meditation has already transcended the ordinary;
in the future, you will likely not even have a single person to attend to you. From that time on, the Master made no effort to gather disciples nor maintain attendants.
He lived in seclusion on Mount Xiaojie, hollowing out a large, decayed cypress tree to dwell within it, just enough space for his body. Whenever wandering monks arrived, he would...
He responded according to each inquiry. Someone asked, "When birth and death arrive, how can one evade them? The Master said, "When the talisman arrives, it is executed.
The man said, "In that case, one is taken away, constrained by birth and death. The Master said, "A-ye, a-ye. Hearing of the Master’s reputation, Qinghuo Chongxu went to visit him;
he encountered the Master while he was gathering millet. Huo asked, "Where is the Master, the Abbot of the Hermitage? The Master—
The Master asked, "Where have you come from? They replied, "From the foot of the mountain. The Master said, "How did you manage to reach this place? They replied, "What place is this?
The Master gestured with his hand and said, "Go down there and drink some tea. Only then did the two gentlemen realize it was he. The Master then went to the hermitage.
At night, he saw jackals and tigers rushing toward the front of the hut; they naturally became docile and submissive. Suddenly, he had a verse that said: "His conduct is not equal [to others]."
Wandering at leisure, who knows the sentiment of going and staying? A single meal remains unsatisfied; ten thousand households find no joy in living.
If it were not the Way, it would be difficult to subdue; do not strive with empty fists. Where the dragon roars and clouds arise, he lets out two or three idle sighs.
Master, the two masters sought out Mount Dazhang and established a hermitage, inviting the Master to reside there. Sitting alone in both places for fifty-two years, he passed away.
Huàhuō was also a native of Yǒngtài. From his youth, he was intelligent and quick-witted. The National Teacher of Gūshān shaved his head for him.
Initially, Huàhuō visited Dàzhāng; later, he studied under Shuìlóng. One day, Shuìlóng asked him, "Lecturer Huàhuō, which venerable masters have you visited?
Have you attained realization yet? He replied, "I, Huàhuō, frequently visited Dàzhāng and gained a place of conviction. Thereupon, Shuìlóng ascended the hall and assembled the great [assembly].
The assembly called out, "Preceptor Qinghuo, come forth before the assembly to burn incense and speak of your realization; the old monk will provide testimony for you.
The Master then held up the incense and said, "The incense has already been offered. As for realization—I have not realized it. Sleep Dragon was greatly pleased and granted him permission.
A monk asked, "What is it like when one's home is impoverished and suffers a robbery? The Master said, "He cannot empty it to the very bottom. The monk asked, "Why is that?"

[The student] said, "If one does not go to the point where there is nothing left, [what then? [Dongshan] said, "The thief is a member of the family. He is a member of the family; why then has he turned into a 'family thief'?
The Master said, "When there is no response within, one cannot act without. If one is suddenly caught and defeated, where does the credit for the effort belong?

The Master said, "As for the reward, I have never even heard of it. [The student] said, "In that case, one toils but achieves no merit. [Dongshan] said, "The merit is not non-existent; it is simply not yet completed."

[The Master asked: "Where do you dwell? Why do you not dwell [anywhere]? The Master said: "Have you not heard it said: 'Peace and stability are originally established by the generals; yet we do not permit the generals to witness that peace'?

Later, as the Master was about to pass away, he suddenly left the assembly and entered the mountains. He then left behind this verse: "Let the people of the world cease saying the road is difficult to travel;
The path of birds and the sheep’s gut are but a foot apart. Take care, O water by the side of Zhuxi Creek! You..."
"I return to the vast ocean; I return to the mountains. He then went to Guihu to establish a hermitage.

After a short while, he said to his disciples, "After my passing, you shall offer my remains to the insects and ants; do not erect a tomb or stupa. Having spoken these words, he entered Mount Hutou, sat upon a flat rock, and passed away in solemn stillness.
His disciples, following his final instructions, kept the body for seven days, yet no insects or ants came to consume it.
He was subsequently cremated, and his remains were scattered across the forests and fields.

Xu was a native of Fuzhou; he was born into the He clan. From childhood, he remained untainted by meat or wine. He received the tonsure at Gushan, where he attained the Dharma and received a prediction of enlightenment.
At the age of twenty-four, he began teaching the Dharma in Fengcheng, Hongzhou. His reputation for the Way resounded widely, and he was then known as "The Little [Xuefeng]."
Venerable Sirs: During the Zhounian era of the Xiande period, the Prince of Jiangnan invited [Fayan] to reside at Guangmu.

After a long time, he moved to Kaixian on Mount Lu, later residing at Jingde; in both places, he gathered disciples and preached the Dharma. He entered parinirvāṇa in the eighth year of the Kaibao era.
These three masters—Zhang succeeded Xuefeng Xuansha, Huo succeeded Shuilong, and Xu succeeded Gushan—all were the legitimate grandsons of Xuefeng.
Song Dynasty: Biography of Chan Master Yanzhao of Fengxue.
Chan Master Yanzhao of Fengxue was the son of the Liu family of Yuhang. In his youth, he was preeminent and possessed a heroic spirit; there were no books he did not examine.

Nevertheless, he had no intention of engaging in worldly affairs. Initially, after shaving his head, he studied the meaning of the doctrinal teachings (*jiao-yi*), but after a long time, he returned to the school of Chan. He first established his reputation at... [text fragment ends].

With Master Congfú of Jìngqīng, their minds did not meet, like a needle and a mustard seed failing to fit. He then traveled north to the regions of Xiāng and Miǎn, where he encountered the Venerable Shǒukuò, an attendant of Nányuàn.
He secretly investigated Nányuàn’s fundamental tenets and joyfully went to join him. Upon his first meeting, he did not prostrate.
He then asked, "Entering the gate, one must discern the master; I request you, Teacher, to distinguish this for me. The Abbot patted his knee with his left hand; the Master shouted.
The Abbot patted his knee with his right hand; the Master also shouted. The Abbot said, "The single strike on the left has been halted; what about the single strike on the right?
The Master said, "Blind! The Abbot prepared to take up his staff; the Master said, "What are you doing? and snatched the staff away.
[Zhaozhou] struck the Old Monk with his staff and said, "Do not say I did not warn you.
Yunyan leaned on his staff and said, "I have been the abbot for thirty years, yet today I am being prosecuted at my door by this yellow-faced man from Zhejiang.

The Master said, "The Master is much like one who cannot hold an alms bowl and falsely claims he is not hungry. Yunyan said, "Have you come to this place? The Master said, "What kind of talk is that? Yunyan said:
"I would like to ask you something," [Nanyuan] said. The Master replied, "I cannot let this pass. He then prostrated himself. Nanyuan was pleased and offered him a seat, ordering tea.
He then asked, "Who are the people with whom you associate? The Master replied, "In Xiangzhou, I spent the summer retreat together with Attendant Kuò. Nanyuan said:

When he personally met the Master of the House, they first performed the rites of teacher and disciple. He relied upon him for six years before taking his leave and traveling to the Ru River, where he stayed at the abandoned Fengxue Temple.
For seven years he lived as a solitary practitioner, begging for food in the villages by day and burning pine resin for light by night.

Only after that did disciples arrive in great numbers. He opened the Dharma seat as a successor to Nanyuan and became the foremost among all transmitters of the Dharma under the world, namely Master Shanshan Nian.
It was given to Guanghui Zhenya. One day he ascended the hall and said: "If you establish even a single speck of dust, the state and its family will flourish, yet the village elders will frown.
If you do not establish even a single speck of dust, the state and its family will perish, yet the village elders will be at peace.

If you understand this clearly, you have no share in it—it is entirely the old monk. If you do not understand this clearly, the old monk is precisely you, O Kalyāṇamitra. You, Kalyāṇamitra, and the old monk—[are one].
The Monk [Fayan] can awaken the people of the world, and he can blind the people of the world. "Do you wish to recognize the *kalyāṇamitra*? He patted his left knee and said, "It is here.
"Do you wish to recognize this old monk? He patted his right knee and said, "It is here. His eloquence was thus unimpeded.
On the first day of the eighth month in the sixth year of the Kaibao era of the Song dynasty (the *guiyou* year), he ascended the seat and spoke a verse, which continued until the tenth...
On the fifth day, he passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture. He had lived for seventy-eight years and spent fifty-nine summer retreats in meditation.
The commentary states: When Attendant Kuò used three shouts and roughly offended Old Huayan, the Master was serving as the *vinaya-dhara* (Venerable).

He went up to the abbot’s quarters to pay his respects, and Huayan said, "When you came just now, you were not right to twist and manipulate Kuò before the assembly. I, this old monk, must strike him severely."
He gave him a blow and drove him out. The Master said, "It was too late to drive him away. He is a descendant of Linji; his fundamental nature is such.
The Master related this to Guo. Guo said, "Why did you try to stop him? Before I even asked, he already wanted to take my blows so that my words might be put into practice.
Now, however, he has silenced my words. Xue said, "Even so, it has already reached the heavens."
How low [they have fallen]! Master Kuok’s four corners were flat upon the ground, while this Master stands like a sheer cliff ten thousand fathoms high;
the old Huayan was merely a short man watching the performance. This is why the Linji school cannot be scaled, gazed up at, or approached.
The Chan Master who transmitted the lineage of Guizong was named Daoquan. Born into the Liu clan, he was a native of Anfu in Jizhou.
As a youth, he left home to serve Chan Master Si, under whom he received a tonsure and the full precepts (*upasampadā*). Later, he heard of Chan Master Huilun of Changsha; Si [sent him there].

He visited him. At that time, the Ma family was secretly occupying Jingzhou and Chu, which shared a border with Jiankang. Quan, being over twenty years of age, formed a friendship and ventured there despite the dangers.
It happened that the Ma family was extinguished; Liu Yan took possession of the territory, and Wang Kui replaced Liu Yan.
He took charge of the matter. When Sengquan and his companions were seen by Wang Kui, Kui suspected them of being spies; he bound them and intended to throw them into the river.
Sengquan remained composed and showed no fear. Kui was struck by this and asked Daorong: "This practitioner looks upon death as if he were looking at the tip of his own nose.
What kind of person can be so? Daorong replied: "He is surely one who has forgotten his own body for the sake of the Dharma. Having heard of the old monk’s empty reputation, he came here."

He came to resolve [the matter], but Daokui’s interpretation was met with increased reverence. Huizhuan departed with an air of arrogance. He remained at Yanshou for ten years until his death. Huizhuan returned to Mount Lu;
in the first year of the Qiande era, he established a hermitage at the foot of Niu-shou Peak to the southeast. In the fifth year of the Kaibao era...
The Regional Commander Lin Renzhao invited him to reside at Jiufeng Peak and conferred upon him the title of Great Śramaṇa. Shortly thereafter, the kingdom of Jiangnan fell.

During this period, monks were required to undergo examinations on their mastery of the scriptures; however, the Master’s disciples all practiced Chan meditation. Thereupon, he composed a verse and presented it to the Prefectural Governor, saying:
"In comparison, I have forgotten words to merge with the Great Void; Thus, I need not cause the harmonious breath to be partial. Who would have known that the Way and its Virtue are complete?"
It was useless. On this day, because the Monk Gui was skilled in calligraphy, the Prefect of the Province read it and consulted with his subordinates, saying:
"In a sandalwood forest, there must be no other trees; only Master’s single monastery is exempt from examination.

In the ninth year of the Taiping Xingguo era, Zhang Nanjin, the Prefect of Nankang, invited him to reside at Guizong. On the twenty-eighth day of the eleventh month in the second year of the Yongxi era.
At midnight, he took leave of the assembly and passed away.
Faldeng (Fa-deng) was the dharma heir of Gongtai Qin;
his courtesy name was Faldeng. He was a native of Weifu. His eloquence was unimpeded, and he had entered the chamber of the Dharma-eye. Although he understood...
Wu was of extraordinary caliber, yet he remained unknown to others. By nature he was negligent and did not attend to worldly affairs.

Once, while traveling from Qingliang to Yangzhou on a mission, he failed to observe the monastic precepts and did not return for a long time; the entire community spread word of him as a laughingstock. Fayan sent a verse to summon him back.
Upon his return, Fayan ordered him to perform the communal bathing ritual for the assembly. One day, Fayan asked the great assembly: "Beneath the tiger's neck..."

There was a golden bell. "Who can understand this? he asked, but none of those who replied were in accord with the truth. When Fayan saw Qin arrive from outside, he presented the previous statement and questioned him.
Qin said to the assembly, "Why do you not say that the one who ties it is the one who can untie it? Thereupon, everyone changed their perspective.
Fayan said, "This time you lot cannot laugh at him. He appeared in the world, first taking up residence at Shuanglin in Hongzhou, and subsequently moving to Huguo Yuan at Shanglan.
Not long after, the Prince of Li invited him to reside at the Qingliang Monastery, whereupon he said:
This mountain monk originally intended to hide deep within the mountains and valleys to pass my days and spend my life.
However, because there was an unresolved case from the time of the Elder Qingliang, I have come forth to settle it for him. If anyone asks, I shall explain it to them.
At that time, a monk stepped forward and asked a question; Yiqin took up his staff and struck him. The monk said, "What fault have I committed? Yiqin replied, "The Patriarch [did not...]"
[The case was] resolved. The disaster reached his descendants. The National Master asked with composure, "What unresolved koan did the former master have?

Qian replied, "That which is being analyzed right now. The National Master was startled by this. In the sixth month of the seventh year of Kaibao, he manifested illness and addressed the assembly, saying:
I, this old monk, have served as abbot for nearly twelve years. Throughout this time, I have constantly received the support and encouragement of the King;

furthermore, from the lay donors, fellow practitioners, administrators, and junior monks, all have served me with sincere hearts. This remains unspoken and difficult to express. Yet, some have donned hempen robes and carried cloth sashes, which greatly contradicts our Way.
As for my remains, I simply request a grave in the vicinity of National Teacher Dazhizang on the South Mountain.

His tomb remains; his rise and fall are as clear as day, never submerged by the transformations of the world. He further addressed the assembly, saying: "If you simply recognize the mouth [of delusion], there will surely be no fault.
Even if there were faults, they would exist because of you. Take care! On the twenty-fourth day, he sat peacefully and passed away.
Fengxian Shen and Qingliang Zhiming—these two Chan masters were also successors of Yunmen.
When the two masters were traveling together, they heard a monk ask Fayan, “What is form? Fayan held up his whisk, or [another time] he said, “A rooster’s comb.”
"Flower. Or it is said: "A flesh-hugging undershirt. The two men went specifically to seek instruction.
They asked, "We have heard that the Master has three kinds of 'colored speech. Is this true? Fayan said, "Yes. Shen said, "A hawk flies over Silla," and immediately returned to the assembly.
At that time, Lord Yi was in the audience hall and did not approve; he then addressed Fayan, saying, "I shall provide a tea ceremony tomorrow and invite you."

The two men began their dialogue anew. The following day, after tea, Fayen prepared a chest of colorful silks and a sword, and said to Deshen, "If you can provide a correct answer when I question you, I shall reward you with this chest of miscellaneous silks;
if your answer is incorrect, I shall grant you only this sword. Fayen ascended the seat.
Deshen stepped forward again and asked, "Today I have received an imperial decree to engage in dialogue; does the Master permit this?"
"No," he said. "Yes," [the Master] replied. [The Master] continued, "A hawk flies over Silla. He then took up his ceremonial robe and departed, and the assembly dispersed all at once.

At that time, Faden was serving as the *karmadāna* (Venerable of Affairs). He struck the bell to assemble the monks before the Sangha Hall to interrogate Xuanjian. When the assembly had gathered, Faden questioned him.
"I have heard that the two Senior Elders have long resided at Yunmen and possess most extraordinary karmic conditions.
Let us cite one or two cases to discuss them. Deshan said, "An ancient said: 'A white egret descends to the field—a thousand dots of snow;
a yellow oriole perches on a tree—a single branch of blossoms. Venerable Director, how would you discuss this? As Deng hesitated, Deshan struck his sitting mat and returned to the assembly.
Deshen was in agreement with Master Ming. When they reached the Huai River, they saw a man pulling in a net; a fish had escaped through the mesh.
Deshen said, "Brother Ming, how clever! You are just like a true monk. Ming replied, "Even so, it would have been better had you not run right into the net in the first place.
Deshen said, "Brother Ming, you still lack enlightenment. It was not until midnight that Ming finally [realized this].

Postscript: Both masters were eminent at Jinling; they were profound in their devotion to Fengxian and erudite in their mastery of Qingliang, both having been earnestly invited by the rulers of Jiangnan.
Master Lianhua Xiang was the dharma heir of Shen; West Peak Huo was the dharma heir of Ming. Their separate biographies are recorded elsewhere.

Dongshan Bing. The ancient records of Jianfu Temple state that Dongshan Qingbing was a native of Xianyou in Quanzhou. Born into the Li clan, he was young when he took Hongmi of Zhongfeng Monastery as his teacher.
At the age of sixteen, he received full ordination at Taiping Temple in Fuzhou. He first traveled to Mount Heng to visit the ascetic Weijing.
He had not yet even touched the surface [of practice]. Upon arriving at Shaoyang, he paid homage at the ancestral pagoda and then traveled to Yunmen.
Yunmen asked, "Where did you depart from today? He replied, "Huilin. Yunmen raised his staff and said, "The Great Master Huilin departed like this—do you see him?

He replied, "I deeply appreciate this question. Yunmen looked to his left and right and simply smiled. From that time on, the Master entered the room for formal instruction and received his seal of approval.
Wu then went to Jinling. The ruler of the state, Lady Li, invited him to reside at Guangmu Monastery.
Before long, she again commanded him to enter the Chengxin Hall to compile essential sayings from various quarters. After ten years, he was welcomed to reside at Dongshan.
Jianfu Chenggu was a native of Xizhou. His family lineage was unknown. In his youth, he served as a scholar and was renowned for his extensive learning.

Upon reaching maturity, he was selected by his district to attend the Ministry of Rites; however, his arguments did not accord with those of the officials, who grew angry and tore off his ceremonial cap.

He subsequently traveled through mountains and rivers until he arrived at Lianshan in Tanzhou, where he saw Chan Master Jingxuan shaving his hair and followed him as a disciple. Having already paid his respects...
Master Ya of Nanyue was the dharma-heir of Dongshan. His realization was exceptionally high, and he was permitted to enter the inner sanctum [of Dongshan].

Later, while traveling through Mount Lu, he passed by Ou Peak and, finding the quietude of the Hongjue Pagoda Cloister to his liking, sought residence there. His monastic regulations were so rigorous that all who passed by were struck with solemn reverence.

At that time, the monastic community referred to him as the "Ancient Pagoda Master. He first preached the Dharma at Zhishan and became a successor to Yunmen. This was during the beginning of the Jingyou era.
When Lord Wen Zheng Gong Zhongyan was governing Ráo, he invited [Zhaozhou] to reside at Jiàn Fú Temple. Addressing the assembly, he said:

"Now, those who have left the household life do so for the sake of the unconditioned Dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). Within the unconditioned Dharma, there is neither benefit nor merit. Lately, those who have left the household life have become greedily attached to blessings and wisdom, which is entirely contrary to the Way.
If one seeks blessings and wisdom, one must first clarify the mind; yet if one wishes to realize the Way, there is no need for you [to seek blessings and wisdom]."

Regarding the point of applying the mind: for this reason, I have always exhorted everyone not to study the Buddha-dharma, but simply to let the mind rest. Those of sharp faculties will attain liberation at that very moment;
those of dull faculties may take three or five years, or at the longest no more than ten. If you do not awaken, you will depart [from this life] without having realized it.
"The old monk shall cause you to fall into the Hell of the Severed Tongue.

He added: "The Master passed away more than a hundred years ago; upon reading these words, I attained awakening and subsequently succeeded him without hesitation. At that time, the lineage of Yunmen was flourishing, and none dared to voice dissent.
This was because what he had attained was indeed the truth. I do not know why [this was omitted] from the *Chuan Deng Lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp)."
Is it because the master was not recorded? Chan Master Shoushan Nian’s biography records Chan Master Shoushan Xingnian.
A native of Diqiao in Lai Prefecture, he left home at a young age and received full ordination at Nan Chan Temple.
He was a man of simple gravity and refined discernment. He used to recite the *Lotus Sūtra*, so the community called him "Nian Fahua" (The One Who Recites the Lotus).
Later, he served as the guest prefect (*zhikè*) within the assembly at Fengxue. He lived and acted in accordance with the community without engaging in formal inquiry or debate;

nevertheless, he remained ultimately suspicious that there was a subtle, separate transmission outside the teachings that had not been spoken. Fengxue often reflected on the prophecy of Dayang regarding the Dharma-lineage of Linji.

Regarding the saying, "When encountering wind, one stops," he feared that his own body would be the one to receive its consequences. He focused his attention on mindfulness. One day, as he ascended the seat, he said:
"When the World-Honored One looked toward Kāśyapa with his blue-lotus eyes—right at that moment, tell me, what was it?
If one says, "He spoke without speaking," that again becomes a burying of the former sage. Before he had finished speaking, Nian descended from the seat. The attendant stepped forward.
Nian Fahu said, "I have nothing more to say," and departed. Why was this? Xue said, "He has understood. The next day, Nian and Zhen Yuan-tou went together to pay their respects.
Xue asked Zhen, "What is the meaning of 'The World-Honored One speaks what is not spoken'? Zhen replied:
A sparrow cried from the top of a tree. Xue said, "What is the use of performing so much foolish merit? He then asked the Master.
The Master replied, "To move one's countenance is to manifest the ancient path; it does not fall into the trap of silent stillness. Xue said to Zhen, "Look at how he delivers his words.
One day, Xue ascended the seat again and looked out at the assembly; the Master immediately descended. Xue then returned to his quarters. From that time on, his reputation spread.

His reputation was esteemed throughout all quarters. One day, when the Venerable Chuzhao of Baimiao arrived in Ruzhou to propagate the teaching, Master Xue sent his teacher to deliver a message to him.
As soon as they met, [the teacher] held up his sitting cloth and asked: "If you unfold it, what is it? If you do not unfold it, what is it? Zhao replied: "..."
"Look for yourself. The Master then gave a shout. Zhao said, "I have personally attended upon teachers of the Dharma;
I have never dared to act so recklessly. The Master said, "The grass-robbers are utterly defeated. Zhao said, "If I see Fengxue tomorrow, I shall report this to him in detail.
The Master said, "Do as you wish, but do not forget it. The Master then returned home first and reported this to Fengxue.
Xue said, "Today you have captured another bandit. The Master replied, "A skilled hand does not advertise its name.
The next day, Zhao went to see Xue and recounted the previous conversation. Xue said, "Not only yesterday; today I have caught you with the stolen goods.
Later, the Master established the Dharma at Shoushan, where he served as the first patriarch. Those who entered his gate were all refined and experienced masters of the monastic community.
O patch-robed monks! Yet when the world speaks of the preeminent Dharma assemblies, it invariably points to Shoushan. He once said to the assembly, "The Buddha-dharma is not so vast;

it is simply that you yourselves lack sufficient self-confidence. If you could truly have confidence in yourselves, even if a thousand sages were to appear before you, they would be unable to move you."
There is nothing I can do for you. Why is this so? Because in my presence, you have no opening through which to speak.
It is simply because you lack self-confidence and instead run outward in pursuit; therefore, you have arrived here. Even if it were Śākyamuni Buddha himself...
I would give you thirty blows as well. Even so, what principle do beginners and those of later learning rely upon?
Let me ask you all: have you attained such a state yet? After a long silence, he said: "If you attain such a state, only then can it be called 'matters-free'. A monk asked:
"Regarding Linji’s shout and Deshan’s staff, what matter on which side do they clarify? The Master said: "Try [to explain] for me."
"Watch the Way," the Master said. The monk then gave a shout. The Master said, "Blind! The monk shouted again.

The Master said, "You blind fellow! Why do you keep shouting recklessly? The monk bowed; the Master struck him. Thereupon he said, "Venerable seniors, you must not shout recklessly or indiscriminately.

As I have often told you: when one is the guest, one remains the guest from beginning to end; when one is the host, one remains the host from beginning to end. There is no second guest, and there is no [second] host."
"Two masters. If there are two guests and two masters, they are simply two pairs of blind men.
Therefore, if I stand, you must sit; if I sit, you must stand. If I am sitting, I sit together with you; if I am standing, I stand together with you.
Even though it is so, you must still open your eyes before you can succeed. The Master’s Way spread throughout the world, and he moved to Guangjiao Monastery on Baishan Mountain.

The assembly did not exceed forty members. Having grown old at Baoying Temple, on the fourth day of the twelfth month in the third year of the Chunhua era, he remained there with the monks to observe the New Year’s retreat and composed a verse, saying:
"I am now advanced in years, sixty-seven; Old age and illness accompany me as I pass the days."
"Record this year’s events for next year; record today’s date for tomorrow. When that year, month, and day arrive, he ascended the seat and addressed the assembly, saying:
'In the world of white silver is a golden body; sentient and insentient beings share one true reality.'"
"When light and darkness are exhausted, there is no longer anything to illuminate. After midday, the solar orb reveals its entire body. Having spoken these words, he sat down peacefully.
As the sun was about to set, he passed away. Upon cremation, five-colored *śarīra* relics were obtained, which were enshrined in a stupa at Shoushan.

The commentary states: When Dayang was making this prophecy, Guishan questioned him persistently. After a long silence, Dayang said, "To offer this body and mind to every dust-mote world—this is what is called repaying the Buddha’s kindness.
This implies taking over the master's duties, as it were, stepping beyond his station to act as his assistant.
Therefore, there is no doubt that Shoushan was Dayang’s subsequent incarnation. To have one’s legs stretched out while within the space where they are folded—in this, how could Guishan be surprised?
After [Fenyang]’s passing, the lineage was silent for a long time.
Then came the three Chan masters Fenyang Zhao, Yexian Sheng, and Shending Yin, who transmitted the Dharma at the Taizi Monastery in Fenzhou.
Chan Master Zhanshao was born into the Yu clan of Taiyuan; his capacity and insight were profound and far-reaching, and from his youth he possessed the karmic affinity.
He was adorned with great wisdom. Having lost his parents at a young age, he was left in solitary hardship. By nature, he took no pleasure in worldly affairs;

consequently, he shaved his head, received full ordination, and set forth with staff in hand, wandering freely. Wherever he went, he did not linger even briefly to sightsee, saying: "The patriarchs of old practiced *dhūta* (wandering) precisely because their sacred understanding had not yet been fully realized;
they traveled about to seek resolution and discernment, not for the sake of mountain scenery. He thus visited and studied under seventy-one masters.
Yuan Zhishi finally went to Shoushan and asked, "What was the meaning behind Baizhang rolling up his mat? Shanshan said, "The dragon’s sleeve is swept aside, and the entire body is revealed.
Yuan pressed further, "What about your own intention, Master? Shanshan replied, "Where the Elephant King walks, there is no trace of the fox."

Thereupon, he attained great enlightenment. Rising from his prostrations, he said, "The moon in the empty realm of the ten-thousand-year-old azure pool—only after repeatedly searching and grappling with it does one finally come to know it.
Someone asked, "What principle did you perceive that led you to such self-acceptance? He replied, "It is precisely where I have surrendered my body and life.
From then on, he lived in obscurity between the regions of Xiang and Mian; whenever local magistrates sought to establish him at famous monasteries, he was invited there eight times in succession.

"Please," [he said], "lie firm and do not rise. When Shoushan passed away, the monastics and laypeople of the West Road united their hearts to draft a formal petition and dispatched the śramaṇa Qichong to invite the Master to reside at the Taizi Yuan in Fenzhou.
At that time, the Master was in the midst of closing his retreat; Qichong pushed open the door and entered, admonishing him with words of great principle:

"The great matter of the Buddha-dharma outweighs the minor point of retiring in seclusion. Fengxue feared he would fail to respond to the prophecy, and thus he worried for the fundamental tenets of our school."
It is falling into ruin. Fortunately, there was my former teacher. My former teacher has passed away. You are the one with the strength to shoulder the Great Dharma of the Tathāgata;
at such a time as this, how can you wish for peaceful sleep? The Master rose, took Cōng by the hand, and said, "If it were not for you, these words would never have been heard.
He hurriedly prepared his belongings and departed. Upon arrival, he sat in meditation upon a single mat, his feet never crossing the threshold for thirty years. Heaven...
He looked down and said, "Fenyang. He did not dare to call him by name. One day, while ascending the hall, he said to the assembly:
"Under Fenyang’s gate there is a West River Lion crouching at the entrance. Anyone who comes near is immediately bitten to death.
What skillful means is there to enter this gate and see this man? If you can see this man, you are fit to be a teacher to the Buddhas and Patriarchs."
I do not see this person; they are all men who have died standing on the spot. Is there anyone today who can still enter? You must enter quickly to avoid letting your life be in vain.
If you are not a guest of the Dragon Gate, take care not to suffer the "dotting of the forehead. Who, then, is a guest of the Dragon Gate?
[The Master] points them all out at once, raises his staff, and says: "Withdraw quickly! Withdraw quickly! Be careful! [This was spoken in the region of] Bingfen.

It was bitterly cold. After the Master had concluded the night assembly, a strange monk arrived, shaking his mendicant’s staff. He approached the Master and said, "There are six great beings (mahāsattvas) within this assembly;
why do you not preach the Dharma? Having spoken, he ascended into the air and departed.

The Master secretly recorded this in a verse: "The foreign monk with the golden staff’s radiance Sought the Dharma at Fenyang. Six men shall become great vessels; He exhorted me to proclaim it forth. At that time...
Chuyuan Shouzhi was a preeminent leader whose name was renowned throughout the monastic communities. Li Hou, the Governor of Longde Prefecture, had long been acquainted with the Master.

He sent messengers to invite him to Chengtian Temple three times, but the Master did not go. Consequently, the messengers were punished. When they returned once more, they said, "We must have you come with us;
otherwise, we shall face death. The Master laughed and said, "I am old and ill; I have already decided not to leave this monastery."
"Since we are borrowing this for a journey, it is a matter of priority; why must we do so simultaneously? The messenger said, "If you, Master, agree, then the priority is yours to choose.
Zhaorun ordered food to be prepared and began to pack his belongings, saying, "I shall go first. He paused with his chopsticks and passed away.
A servant emerged from the assembly and said, "Wherever the Master goes, I shall follow. He also stood there and passed away.
Chan Master Xing resided at Guangjiao Monastery in Ye County. He was the son of the Jia family of Ji Prefecture.

Having reached the age of twenty, he entered the monastic life and received full ordination at Baoshou Monastery in Yi Prefecture. Later, he traveled to various regions and visited Shoushan. One day, Shoushan held up a bamboo stick and asked, "If you call it a bamboo stick, you fall into the trap of direct confrontation;
if you do not call it a bamboo stick, you turn your back on the truth. What would you call it? The Master snatched [the stick] away.
He threw it onto the ground and asked, "What is this? Shanshan replied, "Blind! At these words, the Master attained sudden enlightenment.
Fushan Yuan was his dharma-son who received the transmission.
Hongxin was born into the Hu clan; he was a native of Xiangshui. Having received the seal of transmission from Mount Shou, he lived in seclusion at the Sengzang Cave on Mount Heng.

A man from Xiangyin came traveling and entered the master’s quarters to see him. The master’s countenance was tranquil and serene; a single alms bowl hung upon the wall, and he showed no distinction between intimacy and distance.
The visitor loved him so much that he forgot to leave. The master said to him, "How can you bear to remain a long-term guest under others? You too desire—"

[He asked,] "Do you reside on the mountain? [The master replied,] "My family shrine is beneath the cauldron of the neighboring temple; it is a place where my ancestors have planted blessings for generations.
It has long lacked a presiding abbot, so we may go together. The Master smiled and said, "Yes. He then loaded his own horse with the Master and returned him home.

Only after ten years was the monastic community finally established. A single dilapidated bed served as the Dharma seat. He delighted in austerity and plainness, beyond compare. The monk Qisong traveled while still young...
The Master sat upon the hall receiving their offerings. Pointing to two small jars beneath the courtyard, he said with wonder, "Come here;
this is the time when the temple first has sauce for food. The next day, as they were about to eat congee, one laborer carried a basket and took various items to place in the monks' alms bowls.
Hui-sung looked up and down at them; some chewed and swallowed immediately, while others left the food as it was, remaining composed. Hui-sung hid his hands in his sleeves.
He went out to observe the hall and saw that all the cakes and biscuits had been crushed. He questioned the elders, who said, "This monastery has never cooked porridge since its founding.
However, if there is a donor requesting a meal offering, Master Wen sequentially directs the monks to attend, instructing them to take along whatever dry leftovers they have."
Collect them in a storage chest, roast them finely, and divide them equally to serve as flour. When the Abbot says, "You have come at just the right time," it is indeed so.
Song was greatly startled by this; he had already seen the lifelong character of Old Yin. His other works are contained in the *Lamp Records*.
The commentary states: The practice of versifying ancient cases (songgu) began with Fenyang. Consider his verse on the "Puba" (Dust from the Hair) koan:

"The attendant, in his initial resolve, yearned for superior conditions; He took leave of his master, intending to go and study Chan. Niaoke knew that his faculties were matured; Blowing upon the hair, he attained peace of mind at once.
Compare this with the verse by Hūseng Jinxiguang. Observe how he expresses himself—truly, he is a master. Indeed.
The True Patriarchs and Masters—every single gesture and every single utterance flow forth from within their very nature; they do not value the piling up of flowers or the layering of brocade at all.
This was transmitted by the two masters Guyin Cong and Guanghui Lian.
The Chan Master’s name was Yunchong. He was the son of the Zhang family of Guangzhou. Initially, he studied under Baizhang Heng but did not find resonance there; he then went to visit Shoushan.
When asked, "When a person arrives at a precious mountain empty-handed, what then?

Shoushan replied, "A torch before every door. At these words, [Yunchong] attained great enlightenment and presented this verse: "I am now twenty-seven years old, Having sought and searched for the Way. Now I have found it— It is right here before my eyes."
"Today morning I joyfully encountered him, yet for now we do not know one another. Later, he resided at Guyin Mountain in Xiangzhou;
those from all quarters called him Guyin Cong. Da guan Ying was his son who carried on the family legacy; he has a separate biography.
Chan Master Yuánliàn was the son of the Chen family in Quanzhou. He had a narrow forehead and a broad brow;
his gaze was steady and profound, such that merely beholding him caused one’s worldly thoughts to vanish. He went to visit Shǒushān, who asked, "Where have you recently come from?

Yuánliàn replied, "From Hànshàng. Shǒushān held up his fist and said, "Is there still this in Hànshàng? Yuánliàn said, "What kind of bowl is this that makes a ringing sound? Shǒushān said, "Blind! Yuánliàn [stood there].
He said, "It is exactly as if one were to strike once and then depart.

Later, he saw [the Master] again and attained great enlightenment under the discourse concerning the torch, saying, "I no longer doubt the tongues of the old monks throughout the world. Subsequently, he appeared in the world at Guanghui Monastery in Ruzhou;
Huayan Long was his foremost successor in the Dharma lineage, and Yang Guishan Dayan also emerged from beneath his seat. There is...
A letter addressed to Li Gong, the Internal Secretary, describing the origins and development of the lineage, states:
The commentary says: "The single torch of Shoushan first burned Guyin and later burned Guanghui; thus these two elders were able to emerge with their radiant flames.
Furthermore, there were two Zhisongs: one resided at Sanjiao and one resided at Tiefo; they too were disciples of Shoushan."
[End of] Volume Six of the *Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks* (Bǔxù gāosēng zhuàn).

[Beginning of] Volume Seven of the *Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks*. [The text] is bright and clear. It has not yet been transmitted. [End of] Volume Six of the *Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks*. [Beginning of] Volume Seven of the *Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks*.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Minghe of Huashan Temple in Wu Commandery during the Ming Dynasty;
the "Chapter on Practicing Dhyāna" was transmitted by Dayang Xuan of the Song Dynasty.
Chan Master Dayang Jingxuan was the son of the Zhang family of Jiangxia. His ancestors were originally from Jinling.
His uncle, who had become a śramaṇa named Zhizong, resided at Chongxiao Temple in Jinling; the Master went to rely upon him. At the age of nineteen, he became a full monk (*bhikṣu*).

Upon hearing the *Nirvāṇa-samantabhadra-bodhi-citta-utpāda* (the *Yuánjué jīng*), he was immediately able to refute and humble his lecturers. The lecturers marveled, saying: "This man is young in years, yet his insight..."
"Master, it is like this. What could my own possessions possibly add to it? Please inform him of this and send me forth to travel.
He first visited Chan Master Guan of Liangshan and asked, "What is the formless Dharma-hall? Shan pointed to the Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva image on the wall and said:
"This is a painting by the scholar Wu. As the Master was about to offer a word in response, Shanshan hurriedly asked, "This has form;

what is that which is formless? Thereupon, the Master realized the essential meaning beneath these words. Rising from his prostration, he remained in attendance. Shanshan said, "Why do you not utter a single phrase?
The Master replied, "I would not decline to speak, but I fear it would merely stain the paper and ink. Shanshan smiled and said, "In the future, this..."

When the inscription for Master Yu-shang was completed, the Master presented a verse to demonstrate his understanding. Master Shan praised it, saying that he could rely on him as the successor to the Dongshan school;

the Master himself also took pride in this, and none among his peers dared to challenge him. At that time, his reputation was widespread. After Master Shan passed away, he left the mountain and went to Dayang, where he visited Chan Master Jian.
Master Jian was delighted and yielded the Dharma seat to him, requesting that he preside over it, while he himself withdrew to live in a side room. All...

This was the year of Pinggengzi (1060). The Master’s spiritual countenance was extraordinary and majestic, possessing a profound dignity. From childhood, he observed the practice of eating only once a day.
Out of respect for the gravity of the Dharma-transmission entrusted to him by his predecessors, he did not step beyond the boundary of his room and did not let his side touch the mat for fifty years.

When Master Yuan of Fushan was among the assembly, he once visited the Master at Dayang; however, because the Master’s seniority in the monastic order was so advanced, [Yuan] had no one to attend to him.
A successor to the Dharma sighed one day and said to Yuan: "The school of Dongshan is like a hanging thread about to snap;
only you can revive it. Yuan replied, "There is Attendant Ping here. The Master pointed to his chest and said, "Ping, this place is not good.
He then pressed his thumb between his fingers and showed him, saying, "He will die here in the future. Thereupon—
He entrusted his leather sandals and cloth robes to Yuan, instructing him to seek out a suitable person for them.

On the sixteenth day of the seventh month in the fifth year of the Tiānshèng era, he ascended the seat to bid farewell to the assembly. Three days later, he composed a verse to send to Minister Wáng Shù.

The verse reads: "My age is eighty-five; I have reached this point through the cultivation of causes. If you ask where I am returning, The mark upon my crown will forever be difficult to behold. Having finished, he cast down his brush and passed away.
Huazhi left a final testament stating, "If my entire body remains unharmed for ten years after burial, a memorial service shall be held at Dayang Mountain and I shall be enshrined in a stupa.
Later, he was indeed killed by Pingshi; Ping was also forced to return to secular life because of this and, wandering without refuge, was eaten by a tiger.
Thus, the Master’s words were proven true. Yuan received the Great Mandate and obtained the Blue Avataṃsaka Sūtra, which he transmitted to Lidi, who succeeded to the Master’s Dharma.
...Thus it is.
Chan Master Ciming Yuan transmitted the Dharma to Chan Master Chuyuan of Shishuang, who was styled Ciming. He was the direct heir of Fenyang. Born into the Li clan of Quanzhou, he was young...
He was a scholar who left the household life at the age of twenty-two. His mother possessed virtuous conduct and sent him to travel abroad. The Master had joined eyebrows and handsome eyes;
he was tall and robust, yet he suddenly disregarded the rules and standards. Wherever he went, he was rebuked by the elder monks as one who had spent too little time in the monastic community.

The Master leaned against a cliff of firewood and laughed, saying, "A dragon or an elephant may trample; it is not something a donkey can endure. He once carried a box of antiques in a bag, slung over his shoulder with a bamboo staff.
While traveling between the regions of Xiang and Mian, he heard of the reputation of Fenyang Wuye and went to visit him, along with Dayu, Guquan, and Langye.
Fenyang looked at them and silently took note of them, yet for two years he did not permit them to enter his room; whenever they saw him, he would invariably scold them.

He scolded him, saying, "Some people slander and revile [the teachings], claiming that all the instructions from various quarters are merely vulgar matters of worldly custom. One night, [Yang] complained, saying, "Since arriving at this Dharma assembly, two summers have passed;
I have received no instruction, but only an increase in mundane, defiled thoughts. Time has slipped away, yet I have not clarified my own fundamental task.
Before he had finished speaking, Yang stared at him intently and rebuked him, saying, "This is a wicked teacher who dares to deceive and sell me out! He was enraged.
He raised his staff to chase him away. As the Master prepared to intervene and rescue him, Yang covered the Master’s mouth.

Thereupon, he attained great enlightenment and said, "Now I know that Linji’s Way transcends ordinary circumstances. He served [Yang] for seven years before taking his leave and following Tang Ming’s Master Song.
Song directed him to meet Yang Dainian; through Dainian, he further met Li Duye. Both gentlemen regretted having met him so late and provided him with lodging in their quarters. Day after day...
In the evening, he questioned Zhizheng, taking him as a Dharma friend. After a long time, he took his leave to return to Hedong to visit Emperor Tang Ming.
Lord Li dispatched two monks to inquire after the Master. At the end of the letter, the Master drew a pair of feet and wrote the names of the visiting monks upon them to send back.
Lord Li composed a verse, saying: "A black brush-stroke extends over a thousand li; The golden coffin reveals a pair of feet. Humans and devas can hardly fathom it— Please take care."
As for the Red-Bearded Barbarian (Chixu Hu): because his mother was elderly, the Master returned south to Junzhou and became the head of the assembly at Dongshan.

At that time, Chan Master Cong resided there. Previously, Fenyang had said to the Master, "I have traveled everywhere visiting the descendants of Yunmen, yet I particularly regret not having seen Cong.
Consequently, the Master stayed with him for three years before traveling to Yangshan. Da Nian then sent a letter to Yi.
In the spring, the Prefect Huang Zongdan sent an envoy to invite the Master to assume the abbacy. The Prefect left Nanxuan vacant to wait for the Master, but the Master did not accept.

He subsequently went specifically to visit the Prefect to express his wish to travel. The Prefect asked for the reason; the Master said, "At first I declined out of courtesy, but now I simply desire to go.

The Prefect greatly admired this. After staying there for three years, he departed to visit his mother. The Prefect presented him with white gold as a gift for his longevity, but the mother threw the gold away.
