[The master] threw it on the ground and scolded him, saying, "You are but a young traveler who has been carrying a cloth bag;

how could you possibly possess such an object now? I hoped you would save me, yet you instead cast me into hell! The Master showed no sign of shame; he calmly gathered the items and departed. He went to visit Master Yin of Shending, whose monastery was at Mount Shou.
Master Yin was a senior disciple of the foremost stature, highly esteemed in his time. Among the monastics, none dared to approach him unless they were of truly exceptional character.

One who entered his gate had resided on the mountain for thirty years; his disciples’ reputations eclipsed those of all other quarters. The Master’s hair was long and uncut, he wore tattered robes, and spoke with a Chu accent.
When someone came to announce their arrival and addressed him as "Dharma-nephew," the entire assembly burst into laughter. Yang Yi sent a youth to inquire, "Whose successor is this elder?
The Master looked up at the roof and said, "I have come directly from Fenyang. Yang Yi then emerged leaning on his staff and, looking back, saw [the Master].
The master stood tall and straight. He asked, "Is there a 'Lion of West River' at Fenzhou? The master pointed behind him and shouted, "The roof is collapsing!
The boy turned and fled. Huileng (Ding) looked back with a startled expression; the master sat on the ground, removed one shoe, and looked at him.
Huileng, old and confused, forgot his question and lost sight of where the master had gone. The master slowly rose, adjusted his robes, and walked away, speaking as he went.

He said, "To see a person in person is not as good as hearing their reputation. He then departed. Zhao Ding sent someone to pursue him, but it was to no avail. Sighing, he remarked, "Fenyang has such a son!
From that time on, the Master’s fame grew weighty within the monastic community. When the seat at Daowu was vacant, the local administration sent an official letter [inviting him].

He wished to have a great master of Chan lead them. Master Ding responded to the summons; his regulations were strict and orderly, and those who were willing to sacrifice their lives for the Dharma gathered there.
The Great Function and Great Activity of the Master are inconceivable.

As the biographer says, "The Master’s mind of unimpeded practice in every matter cannot be fathomed by either ordinary people or sages"—this may indeed be considered a statement made by one who truly knows. Shui-an addressed this to Minister You.
Yanzhi said: "In the past, Dayu, Ciming, Guquan, and others formed a group to visit Fenyang.

The region of Hedong is bitterly cold, and while the rest of the group found it unbearable, only Ciming did not mind it day or night. When he sat through the night and felt drowsy, he would pull out a needle and prick himself."
He sighed, saying: "The ancients regarded the matter of birth and death as so great that they neither ate nor slept. What kind of person am I, that I instead indulge in such wild dissipation?
To live without benefiting the age and die without leaving a name for posterity—this is self-abandonment. When he took his leave to return home, Fenyang sighed and said:

"The various patriarchs, I have never heard of, neglected their studies to take such a burden upon themselves. Moreover, my years are still young and my vigor intact;

"The Master’s conduct was eminent and he treated all people with kindness and benevolence. Even when facing guests, he never once provided them with food different from that of the assembly. At night, he would invariably join the monks..."

He slept in the main hall rather than entering the private chamber. By nature, he delighted in giving; whatever gold, money, silk, or cloth he obtained was invariably exhausted as it passed through his hands.
He was also highly talented in the arts, excelling in poetry and calligraphy with a refined style.

When living in seclusion, he would not speak of worldly affairs, remaining composed and at ease even when visitors arrived in great numbers. Thus, there were none among the virtuous scholars and officials of the time who did not gather around him.

Hearing of his reputation, all turned their aspirations toward him, wishing to associate with him. Initially, at the recommendation of High Gong Ruone, who was a Participant in Government Affairs, he was granted a purple square-cut robe.
Subsequently, at the recommendation of Li Gong Duanyuan, a Regional Commander, he was granted the title of Great Master Yuantong.

In total, he was invited ten times and accepted four of these invitations; on each occasion, he traveled to famous mountains and great monasteries throughout the land where his spiritual influence was just beginning to spread.
He would frequently find pretexts to withdraw in secret; though the provincial and local authorities wished to entreat him to remain, they could not prevail.
He had fifty-five disciples. His collected poems, hymns, and literary works comprise five fascicles.
Furthermore, he compiled a single treatise detailing his life’s trajectory from youth to old age, titled *The Record of Youth and Senility*, by which he sought to manifest himself to the world.
Fǎbǎo, whose secular surname was Wáng, was a native of Xiǎoxī in Suìzhōu. He served under Cóngjiǎn of Xìngshèng Yuàn, where he became a monk and studied the Dharma.
He was seen in all four directions, like [the masters of] Quánshān’s Fǎyán, Huángbò’s Nànyuè, Yúnjū’s Zhìbǎo, and Heshān’s...

He was a man of talent whom the world regarded as a great *kalyāṇamitra*. He questioned everyone he encountered on this matter. In his daily life, he frequently sat in meditation, calculating the divisions of day and night;
he slept only twelve or thirteen hours, always lying on his right side and never removing his robes.

He remained thus until the end of his life. The Master traveled to Luoyang three times. When he first arrived in Luoyang, people did not know him to be a Chan master; when he arrived a second time, they recognized him as such.
He was a practitioner of Chan. On three occasions he arrived, and [the Master] knew that he was a Chan practitioner, yet one who did not practice Chan in vain.

As for his secret applications in responding to the world and his skillful means in observing the capacities of beings, no one can adequately conjecture or deliberate upon them. Among the worthy scholars of Luoyang...

Those who studied under the Master were very numerous; it was not necessarily that they all understood the Master’s Way. They merely loved his lofty conduct and harmonious temperament, his concise speech and exhaustive reasoning.
Grand Master Wen (Wen Pulu Gong) presented a memorial regarding his conduct, and he was granted a purple cassock.
He came to Luoyang three times and frequently resided at Jianjue Monastery. The community joined forces to construct [his quarters] for him, and more than ten of his disciples were all...

He once studied under the Master together with others. There was also a lay devotee who abandoned his family and rushed to serve him. Once the Master resided at Shanjue Temple, those who came to inquire after him increased even more.
Some urged him to distribute his surplus wealth for the benefit of others, to which the Master replied, "I have not yet done so myself."

What leisure has he had to act for others? Having embraced the Way to respond to the world for nearly fifty years, the reason his discourses and essential teachings have not been widely transmitted in the world is likely because he was so humble and self-effacing. Minister Han Wei said:
"When I first met the Master at Heqiao, he never failed to speak [of the Dharma]. I questioned him, yet he could not [speak of it] for several years. I was then serving as..."
In Yingchang, he was welcomed into the official residence as his quarters; yet the Master never spoke of it. Although I wished to question him, I did not know what to ask.
Alas! The Way cannot be realized without hollowing out one’s heart. Having manifested illness, he wrote letters everywhere to bid farewell to those who came and went, and then suddenly passed away.
He was sixty-nine years old; this was in the ninth month of the sixth year of the Yuanfeng era.
Above the Bodhi Monastery at Longmen, where the bones were enshrined, was the Chan Master known as Fayan of Fushan.
His secular name was Fayuan, and he was a native of Zhengpudian. He descended from the Wang clan; he left home to become a monk at the age of nineteen and first visited...
In Fenzhou, he obtained a glimpse of the seal of the patriarchal lineage. He then went to study under Master Xing of Yexian, who was serving as the abbot there alongside Tianyi Huai.
[Xing] was austere and strict; the practitioners of all quarters stood in awe of him. When the Master arrived, it was mid-winter with heavy snow.
Xing scolded and drove him away, even splashing water on him until the robes and boots of the assembly were soaked. They departed in anger, leaving only the Master and Huai behind.
Xia Ruofeng adjusted his robes, spread out his sitting mat, and sat down as before. Xian arrived and scolded him, saying, "Are you still not leaving? Do you expect me to beat you?
The Master stepped forward and asked with deference, "I have traveled several thousand li to come and consult the Abbot to clarify the Great Matter.
How could I leave after being splashed with a ladleful of water? Xian laughed and consequently allowed him to remain. He stayed in his company for several years.
Though he encountered myriad setbacks, the Master remained as one from beginning to end; it is said that "true gold becomes ever brighter the more it is forged in the fierce flames.
The Prefect first entrusted him with the Dharma and his robes. On the day he ascended the hall, he held up the incense and said: "You, Hai, have produced flowers upon a withered tree."
"Separately welcoming the spring colors" refers to Ye County. The Master was discussing the Way with Wang Zhi, the Academician;

he drew a single circle and asked: "One, you may not have a lone steed and a single spear; two, you may not return home in brocade robes; the magpie may not rejoice, and the crow may not suffer calamity.
Speak quickly, speak quickly! Wang was at a loss. The Master said, "I have seen through you. That evening, the Master...
During his annual retreat at Seongnamsan, he expounded the profound mysteries of the Buddhas and Patriarchs and composed the Nine Banners (Kudae) to enlighten his disciples.
His act of preaching while playing chess became so renowned that it was known by every household. The Master’s jade-like bones protruded from his forehead, and his gaze shot outward;
he had the appearance of a prince and was sternly awe-inspiring. He habitually called himself the "Old Man of the Firewood Stone. At the time of his death, he was already over seventy years old.
Lord Wen Zhengfan inscribed his stupa, saying: "Alas, Master Yuan! A hero among the sons of the Śākya. A sweet rain for the groves of Chan; a true dragon for the ocean of Dharma.
His lifespan was limited, but his life of wisdom is infinite. As his bones are buried in the cold crags, he leaves a pure wind to endure for a thousand years."
Throughout his life, the Master valued truth and authenticity. He sternly suppressed superficial eloquence in his pursuit of realization and certification. He once said to Master Zhenguang of Daowu:
"If one's study has not yet reached the Way, yet one flaunts what one has heard and seen, racing about with intellectual insights and using verbal cleverness to triumph over others through debate."
It is like painting a latrine with vermilion and cinnabar; it only serves to increase its stench. The disciple of the Dharma named Daozhen succeeded Da’jue Lia.
He resided at Jingyin Temple, where the Way of the Dharma flourished greatly in the capital. This was during the time when the illustrious sovereigns initiated the three courts.

He frequently entered the palace to preach the Dharma, receiving imperial favor that was both profound and generous. By nature, he was dignified and inclined toward quiet withdrawal, appearing as if he were unable to speak.

He maintained the utmost simplicity in his personal life; for twenty years he did not change his single cotton skirt, which consisted of only five panels—just enough to cover his calves—and he made no pleats, saying, "They are merely a waste.
He had no worldly attachments or preferences. Once, when he had cleared the western wall of his quarters of snow, he commanded Wen [to write] upon it.
When he was about to sweep away his ink bamboo painting, he said to others, "I shall let travelers see it, so that their minds and eyes may feel cool and refreshed;
this gentleman (the bamboo) is surely preaching the Dharma on my behalf. He passed away in the eighth year of the Yuanyou era.
The Biography of Chan Master Fahua Long.
Chan Master Dao Long’s lineage and clan are unknown. Initially, he went to visit Master Shi-men Che and asked him:

"In ancient times it was said that if one simply attains peace and ease wherever one is, one will naturally accord with the tracks of the Buddhas. Although there is this saying, my doubts have not yet been extinguished."
"How is it at such a time? The Gatekeeper said, "If you know [it] exists, you can be at ease wherever you are. It is like a person living in a prefecture or a county;
even if they hear or see thousands of wonders and hundreds of anomalies, they treat them all as ordinary. To be at ease without knowing [it] exists is like a person living in a village;
if there is even a slight sound or sight, they are startled and spread rumors of it. At these words, the Master attained realization.
[Shishuang] bestowed upon him the entirety of the school’s profound principles. When [Fengxue] appeared in the world, he then succeeded Guanghui.
Someone asked, "The Chan Master personally met Shimen; why did he instead succeed Guanghui? The Master said, "When I first met Guanghui, he was just about to shave my head.
He had me bring a stool over and said, 'Dharma-heir, I have a poem about a stool; listen to this poem.'"
He said, "To let go is to attain peace; at that moment, I truly accepted it. He then recounted what he had attained at Shimen.
Huì remarked, "What Shimen showed you is like a feast of a hundred flavors—it simply cannot satisfy one's hunger. Later, there was a stick of incense;
not wishing for two ends or three threads, I burned it away for him. At the beginning of the Zhìhé era, the Master traveled to the capital and stayed as a guest at Jingde Temple.
The temple was located in the city; every day he would tour the metropolis and return home at the second watch. One night, unable to enter, he lay down beneath the gate.

Emperor Renzong dreamed that he arrived at the gate of Jingde Temple and saw a dragon coiled upon the ground. Startled awake, he dispatched an imperial messenger in the middle of the night to investigate.

Thereupon, one monk was fast asleep; having already begun to snore, he only woke when shaken. When asked his name and reported back, the Emperor heard that it was Daolung. He said with joy, "This is an auspicious omen.

The next day, he summoned him to the private palace (biandian) and inquired about the fundamental tenets (zongzhi) of his school. The Master’s responses were detailed and appropriate, and the Emperor was greatly pleased.
An imperial decree was issued for him to be housed in the Shaozhu Yuan of the Great Xiangguo Monastery. From this point on, his spiritual transformation flourished.

Zhen once expounded the Dharma with Master Da-jue Liàn in the Huacheng Hall. His spiritual acuity and eloquence were swift and incisive, and the Emperor was greatly pleased. The imperial guards all shouted "Long live the Emperor! at his presence.
Whether responding with verses or staying overnight within the Forbidden City, the honors and treatment accorded to him were exceptionally generous.

He was granted the title Chan Master Mingwu (Illuminated Enlightenment) by Imperial Decree. Consequently, the Master submitted a memorial requesting that Liàn be appointed in his stead; however, upon reading the petition, the Emperor did not grant his request. There was...
At the gate of Cao’s residence, he constructed a vihāra to invite the Master. The Master named it Huayan Chan Monastery. There was a monk who composed a verse on Master Liaṅ;
the Emperor asked about a Buddhist gāthā, saying: "Having nodes yet not being bamboo, three stars in a crescent palace;

one person dwelling beneath the sun, not the same as the common crowd. The Master said: "The Buddhas speak of the mind in order to destroy the characteristics of the mind. Liaṅ has composed this [verse]."
Verse: A nail driven into space. It says: "A steel nail driven into space; a heap of bones rising from level ground.
Do not take idle scholarly understanding and place it upon the steps of the Buddha. Furthermore, I saw Chan Master Daguan Ying composing a verse in jest, which says:
"He can answer the dialectical sayings of all quarters and compose five-character poems; both are fine arts, yet they are simply slow at seeing the cash. The Master [said]:
He said, "The Buddha-dharma has instead become mere frivolous discourse (*prapañca*). It is not right for those of later generations, lacking discernment, to hastily imitate and study it;
such things cannot be cultivated. There are, however, two general types. Although they are mixed with worldly ways, they are superior to other separate practices.

A monk asked, "Dongshan Baogong criticized Chan Master Wuzu Ji, saying his conduct was 'hidden within the public eye' (*xingzang luoren*). Suspecting that he had arrived at Dongshan, [Baogong] ascended the hall and spoke this verse:"
"Alas! Behold the world’s perverse and deceitful speech; those whose words are pure but whose conduct is turbid are many.
If it were not for Old Man Yama, who could do anything with you? The Master said, "Baocu’s conduct is insolent; he sells his teacher’s name for profit. This must not be tolerated.

Caoshan said, "A true practitioner of the Way does not see the faults of the world. To speak of another’s shortcomings is because one’s own shortcomings already exist within oneself. Baocu was violent.
As for the faults of that master, who is there to examine them? For all śramaṇas and sons of the Śākya, silent stillness is the essential requirement. The *Avataṃsaka-śāstra* says:
"Only silence, only stillness—this is the manner in which the mind creates the Tathāgata. Non-attachment and non-clinging—this is the track for entering the Dharma-realm.
As for Bao Mai at Dongshan and Jiang Chu at Shuangfeng, they have already become objects of ridicule for practitioners of the Way. Master.
He was broad-minded and generous, never boasting of his own virtues. He practiced a mind of universal reverence through true compassion. At the time of his death, he was over eighty years old.
During the height of summer, he sat peacefully for seven days; his hands and feet remained supple and soft. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa to the east of the monastery.
The commentary states: Now, a monk who was snoring in his temple entered the Emperor’s dream;

the Emperor dreamed that he was a dragon and did not find him loathsome, but instead treated him with supreme honor, lodging him within the imperial palace. Were it not for the Master’s Way having permeated the world, how could such a thing have occurred?

The Chan teachings of the capital flourished greatly from this point on. This also demonstrates that Emperor Renzong’s insight was profound and far-reaching; had he encountered a mediocre ruler, the Master—
Would he not have been reduced to mere dust and ashes? I have therefore set him forth for all to see.
Regarding the transmission of Guquan by Daodao and Zongdao:

Guquan was a native of Southern Quan. From his youth, he was intelligent and quick-witted; by nature, he endured filth and grime, and his grandiloquent speech was insolent, which the common folk detested.
He left the household life to become a śramaṇa, yet he cast aside the precepts and acted according to his own whims. He treated fellow monks with contempt;

wherever he went among the monasteries, he would immediately cause them to be dismantled, showing no concern for the springs [of merit]. He traveled to Fenyang, who marveled at him and secretly bestowed upon him a prophetic transmission.
He returned south to wander freely, frequently coming and going through Xiangzhong. Daowu visited Ciming; Daowu had a pond inhabited by a venomous dragon.
When the leaves fell and touched the waves, thunder and rain would inevitably rage for days; those passing by did not dare even to breathe.

Once, as he was returning home with Ciming at dusk during the autumn heat, he seized Ciming’s robe and said, "We should bathe together. Ciming pulled his arm away and went straight on. Thereupon, Quan stripped off his clothes and leapt into the water.
A clap of thunder followed immediately, and a stinging wind blew with the rain as the forest trees shook violently. Ciming crouched amidst the grass.
Yiquan died. After a short while, the weather cleared and brightened. Suddenly, he extended his neck from between the waves and said, "Li. Later, he resided at Lan Zan Rock on Mount Nanyue.
He subsequently moved to Bajiao, and was about to move again to Baozhen. On the wall of Bajiao, he wrote in large characters:
"In this Bajiao Hermitage of mine, I dwell in seclusion amidst the massed clouds. The various extraordinary sights need not be enumerated; First, look at the stunted pines."
Three or four trees; when the cold comes, I burn the withered cypresses. When hungry, I eat large purple yams. Now I abandon them and depart; I know not who will come to dwell here.
Dwelling at Baizhen, I sat on the ground at night beneath Mount Zhurong. A great python coiled around me. I untied my sash from a spring and bound it around my waist.
The next day, as I sought it out with my staff, I found the sash hanging from a pine branch. It was indeed a pine.
She was a female spirit (*yakṣī*). Once, while passing through Hengshan County, she saw a butcher cutting meat and stood by his side, assuming a pitiable expression.
She pointed to the meat and then to her own mouth. The butcher asked, "Are you mute? whereupon she nodded her head. Moved by pity, the butcher cut a large piece of meat and placed it in her bowl.
The woman departed with joy, her gratitude exceeding all expectations. The entire market laughed aloud, yet the woman herself— [The text provided ends abruptly.]
If one carries a large wine gourd on a staff while wandering through the mountains, and people ask what is inside the gourd, he replies, "The elixir of the Great Way.
He then composes a verse: "Who am I to govern you, Heaven? Who am I to govern you, Earth? I have donned this tattered paper robe."

I am solely intent on the art of sleeping; let the golden crow rise in the east and the jade hare fall in the west as they may. What concern have honor and disgrace for me? What relevance has prosperity or decline? With a single staff and a gourd hanging by my side, I roam between the southern and northern mountains. I keep a servant named Tiao Gu, whom I order daily to gather firewood and draw water from the mountain stream. Sometimes I call him to sit with me upon the rocky crags. To him I offer this gift: A staff, a gourd, and a patched robe— These three things are enough to sustain one’s life. The world’s affairs are like a dream; Why trouble oneself with them? If you wish to know the Way, Seek it within your own mind. Do not seek it outside yourself; It is not found in books. If you can understand this, You will see the Buddha-nature. If you cannot understand this, You will remain a common mortal. This is the Dharma-gate of the Unconditioned. May you all attain liberation. May there be peace and happiness. May all beings be well. *Gong'an* (Case) No. 100: The Monk Who Asked about the Buddha-Nature. The Master said: "The Buddha-nature is not something that can be sought through words or concepts. It is like the moon reflected in water—clear and bright, yet without a fixed form. If you try to grasp it, you lose it; if you try to describe it, you miss it. It is only when you let go of all seeking and conceptualization that you may encounter it. *Gong'an* (Case) No. 101: The Monk Who Asked about the Patriarchs. The Master said: "The patriarchs did not transmit anything at all. They simply pointed directly at the human mind, showing people how to see their own nature. Do not look for it in scriptures or in the biographies of the ancients. Look within your own heart. *Gong'an* (Case) No. 102: The Monk Who Asked about the Ultimate Truth. The Master said: "The ultimate truth is beyond words and beyond thought. It is like the vast sky—empty and boundless. If you try to express it, you limit it; if you try to conceive it, you obscure it. Only by ceasing all mental activity can you realize it. *Gong'an* (Case) No. 103: The Monk Who Asked about the Path. The Master said: "There is no path to walk. There is no destination to reach. If you think there is a path, you are already lost. If you think there is a destination, you are already far astray. The true path is right here, right now, beneath your feet. *Gong'an* (Case) No. 104: The Monk Who Asked about Enlightenment. The Master said: "Enlightenment is not something that comes from outside. It is not something that can be attained through effort or practice. It is the very nature of your own mind, always present, always shining. Do not seek it elsewhere. *Gong'an* (Case) No. 105: The Monk Who Asked about Suffering. The Master said: "Suffering arises from attachment. When you are free from attachment, there is no suffering. When you are free from grasping, there is no pain. This is the way to transcend suffering. *Gong'an* (Case) No. 106: The Monk Who Asked about Nirvana. The Master said: "Nirvana is not a place to which one goes. It is not a state to be entered. It is the cessation of all delusion and the realization of the true nature of reality. It is the end of all seeking and the beginning of all peace. *Gong'an* (Case) No. 107: The Monk Who Asked about the Dharma Body. The Master said: "The Dharma body is not a physical body. It is not a form that can be seen. It is the essence of all phenomena, the source of all existence. It is the emptiness that is everywhere, the luminosity that is within. *Gong'an* (Case) No. 108: The Monk Who Asked about the Mind-Ground. The Master said: "The mind-ground is vast and level. It is without high or low, without near or far. It is the ground upon which all things arise and pass away. It is the foundation of all wisdom and compassion. *Gong'an* (Case) No. 109: The Monk Who Asked about the True Self. The Master said: "The true self is not the body, nor is it the mind. It is not the ego, nor is it the personality. It is the pure awareness that is prior to all thoughts and perceptions. It is the witness of all experiences, the observer of all illusions. *Gong'an* (Case) No. 110: The Monk Who Asked about the Ultimate Reality. The Master said: "Ultimate reality is beyond description. It is beyond definition. It is the silence before a word is spoken, the stillness before a thought arises. It is the suchness of all things, the unchanging nature of the universe. *Gong'an* (Case) No. 111: The Monk Who Asked about the Way of the Buddhas. The Master said: "The way of the Buddhas is not a way to be followed. It is not a path to be traveled. It is the spontaneous expression of the enlightened mind. It is the natural flow of compassion and wisdom. *Gong'an* (Case) No. 112: The Monk Who Asked about the Way of the Patriarchs. The Master said: "The way of the patriarchs is not a way to be imitated. It is not a method to be practiced. It is the direct pointing to the mind, the immediate realization of the nature. It is the transmission of the lamp, the light of the Dharma. *Gong'an* (Case) No. 113: The Monk Who Asked about the Way of the Ancestors. The Master said: "The way of the ancestors is not a way to be sought. It is not a goal to be achieved. It is the living presence of the Dharma in every moment. It is the continuity of the lineage, the heart-to-heart transmission. *Gong'an* (Case) No. 114: The Monk Who Asked about the Way of the Masters. The Master said: "The way of the masters is not a way to be studied. It is not a doctrine to be learned. It is the direct experience of the truth, the personal realization of the Way. It is the meeting of minds, the merging of spirits. *Gong'an* (Case) No. 115: The Monk Who Asked about the Way of the Disciples. The Master said: "The way of the disciples is not a way to be followed blindly. It is not a path to be walked alone. It is the practice of the Dharma in daily life, the application of the teachings in action. It is the cultivation of virtue, the development of wisdom. *Gong'an* (Case) No. 116: The Monk Who Asked about the Way of the Laity. The Master said: "The way of the laity is not a way to be separated from the monastic life. It is not a path to be distinct from the spiritual quest. It is the practice of mindfulness in the marketplace, the cultivation of kindness in the world. It is the integration of the sacred and the profane. *Gong'an* (Case) No. 117: The Monk Who Asked about the Way of the World. The Master said: "The way of the world is not a way to be avoided. It is not a realm to be escaped. It is the manifestation of the Dharma in all its forms. It is the play of the Buddha-nature in the mundane. *Gong'an* (Case) No. 118: The Monk Who Asked about the Way of the Mountains. The Master said: "The way of the mountains is not a way to be climbed. It is not a peak to be reached. It is the stillness of the peaks, the depth of the valleys. It is the meditation of the sages, the retreat of the saints. *Gong'an* (Case) No. 119: The Monk Who Asked about the Way of the Rivers. The Master said: "The way of the rivers is not a way to be crossed. It is not a current to be navigated. It is the flow of the Dharma, the movement of the mind. It is the cleansing of the soul, the purification of the spirit. *Gong'an* (Case) No. 120: The Monk Who Asked about the Way of the Forest. The Master said: "The way of the forest is not a way to be entered. It is not a grove to be visited. It is the solitude of the mind, the seclusion of the heart. It is the place of awakening, the site of enlightenment. *Gong'an* (Case) No. 121: The Monk Who Asked about the Way of the City.
He spoke in verse: "I have a mountain boy named Diaogu (Tiao Gu). He does not recite sutras nor pay homage to the patriarchs.

He understands how to split firewood to ward off winter’s cold; His clothes are tattered according to his means, never mended. He knows how to plant vegetables and can grow taro; He travels through thousands and tens of thousands of mountains without fear.
A-he-he! What need is there to seek him out? When an elder arrived to visit, he asked where the hermitage master was."
Ma. Quan said, "Who? He replied, "A wandering monk. Quan asked, "What are you doing here? He replied, "I am coming to pay my respects to the abbot.
Quan said, "It happens that the abbot is not here. He replied, "And what about you? Quan said, "I told you he was not here; why are you asking about you? I shall grab my staff and drive you out!
The next day he came again, and Quan drove him out once more. One day he came yet again; Quan grabbed him by the chest and twisted him, saying, "As for me—"
Tigers and wolves roam within; he wets his bed. The "little devils" come three times or twice—what are they seeking?
[The Master] said, "People say the Hermitage Master personally saw Fenyang come. Yunquan shook out his robes and said, "You say that I saw Fenyang come?"
"How extraordinary! He visited Ciming again and sent him a verse, saying: 'Since we parted, half a year has passed;
I know not with whom you have been discussing Chan. Within the verdant beauty of Mount Xiang, You yourself guide your disciples while I sleep.
Ciming merely smiled. He then instructed Nan Gong to visit Quan again. When Quan spoke with him, he was struck with amazement and said: 'Five...'"
"Is there such a bald-headed practitioner within this prefecture? During the Jiayu era, a man named Qing was executed for spreading demonic incitements.

In the height of summer, while carrying earth along the main thoroughfare, he set down his burden and recited a gāthā: "Today is the sixth day of the sixth month; Guquan has been struck by the heat. It was not...
"To ascend to heaven is to enter hell. Having said this, he smiled and passed away with serene composure, like a cicada shedding its shell.
His body was cremated, and the resulting *śarīra* relics were beyond counting; the people of Ch'en enshrined them in a stupa and established a shrine there.
Zongdao was a man of unknown origins who traveled between Shu and Qi, frequently staying at Touzi. By nature he was fond of wine and was never sober.
The villagers loved and respected him, regularly providing him with fine liquor. One day, while he was in the midst of bathing, he heard that someone was seeking Zongdao;
anticipating they would surely bring a wine jug, he stepped out naked. Upon receiving the wine, he went straight away.

Everyone laughed aloud, yet Zong remained haughty and felt no shame. Once, as he was descending the mountain with his robes discarded, someone met him and asked, "What is the 'house style' of a man of the Way?
He replied, "A *kāṣāya* wrapped around straw sandals. "What is the meaning of this? [The questioner asked. "Barefoot," he said.
When Chen Tuifu of Tongcheng was first heading to the provincial examination hall, he passed by Zong and jokingly asked, "Guan, on this journey..."
"Would you like to become the top graduate? Is it possible? Zong looked at him intently and said, "It is not possible. The man did not understand the meaning of these words and withdrew.
Later, he indeed ranked third in the examination while Yan became the overall winner; only then did he realize the significance of the phrase "not possible.
Zong visited Xuedou, where he lived with unrestrained freedom, appearing as one of the lineage of the *Lotus Sūtra*.
The Biography of Chan Master Fuchang Shanshan.
Weishan was a man of unknown origins who resided at Fuchang Temple in Jingnan. He was a successor of Chan Master Mingjiao Kuan.

By nature, he was reverent and dignified, and he held the Way of the Dharma in profound esteem. When he first took up residence as abbot, there were only some ten or so dilapidated buildings and a handful of weary monks.
The Master burned incense in the morning and lit lamps in the evening; when he ascended the seat to preach the Dharma, it was as if he were facing a thousand-fold assembly.

All that is required for the sustenance of a Zen monastery was prepared in full readiness. When guests arrived, he received them with solemn reverence. It took more than ten years before his disciples finally gathered, reaching a number of about one hundred.
Whenever the Master saw someone approaching, he would invariably examine and test them. There was a monk who called himself Ying Damo; as soon as he entered—
The Abbot held up his sitting mat and said, "When spread out, it pervades the entire Dharma-realm; when not spread out, host and guest are indistinguishable.
Is it when spread out? Or is it when not spread out? The Master said, "You have already finished your meal on level ground.
Ying said, "A clear-eyed venerable elder truly has something to offer. The Master struck him. Ying said, "If you snatch the staff and strike me down, do not say I did not warn you!"
[The monk] did not speak. The Master said, "A fellow staring with eyes wide open inside a coffin. Sit and drink tea.
After the tea was finished, [the monk] came forward and said, "Just now, I easily offended the Master. The Master said, "A double case—shoo him out!
He then asked another monk, "Where have you recently come from? [The monk] replied, "Chengtian. The Master said, "Without traversing the road, bring forth a phrase. The monk gave a shout. The Master—
[The Master] struck him. The monk made a gesture with his sitting mat as if brandishing a staff. The Master laughed and said, "A medicine bag dangling behind a funeral carriage.
He asked again, "How old are you, layman? [The man] replied, "Forty-four. The Master said, "Add one, subtract one—how many is that? The man had no reply.
The Master spoke on his behalf, saying, "I still remember just now. He asked again, "Monk, where have you come from? [The monk] replied, "From Deśanā."

[The Master] said, "By the side of the Wuling Stream. He asked, "Bring me a phrase of the Way. The monk was speechless. The Master then provided his own substitute [answer]: "When the water arrives, the channel is formed.
The Master’s spiritual edge was so sharp that it could not be provoked; those from all quarters feared and submitted to him. His dharma seat revived the style of Yunmen at Nan Chan.
The Master once said, "When Yuai of Cuiyan and I were at Fuchang, I happened to suffer from a cold. I took medicine and came out..."
Huan Yue followed his fellow practitioners in requesting bedding from all of them, but none had any. There were those who possessed paper quilts, yet these were all worn out and few in number.
Huan Yue sighed and said, "Master Shan is truly an artist of the original school."
The Biography of Chan Master Xuedou Xian:
Chan Master Xuedou’s name was Chongxian, with the courtesy name Yinzhi. He was the son of the Li family in Suizhou. From his youth, he was sharp-witted and resolved to transcend the mundane world.

He relied upon the venerable Puan Congshen to leave the household life and receive full ordination. He traveled extensively through lecture halls, mastering the sutras and treatises with effortless ease.
His questions were as swift as a galloping wind; his fellow students held their breath, not daring to respond. Abandoning such pursuits, he returned to Chan.

Traveling from Shu into Chu, he once served as the guest prefect at Dayang. There, while discussing the fundamental tenets of Zhaozhou with a visitor, the guest said, "The Chan Master Fayan once met Jue Tiezi in Jinling.
Jue was an attendant of Zhaozhou and was renowned as a man of clear vision. He then asked, "Zhaozhou..."
"Do you remember the story of the cypress tree? If you do, please do not slander my late teacher. Jue said, "I have no such words.
Fayen clapped his hands and said, "Truly he has come from the lion's den. When Jue Gong said he had no such words, Fayen approved him. Wherein lies the meaning of this?
The Master said, "In the Gate of the School, there is the art of suppression and exaltation; how could there be fixed rules or tracks? At that time, there was a man of ascetic practice named Han.
The elder brother had a somber and haggard appearance; whenever he stood by the Master’s side, he would invariably withdraw with a suppressed smile.

After the guests had departed, the Master reprimanded him, saying, "I was merely conversing with the guests, yet you dared to treat me with such disrespectful laughter. What was it that made you laugh? He replied, "I laughed because I knew your eyes were not yet upright."

He was unclear in his discernment of the Dharma. The Master asked, "Do you have any say? He replied with a verse: "A single rabbit lies across the ancient road; As soon as the blue hawk sees it, he seizes it.
The hunting dogs that follow lack any spiritual nature; They vainly search for it at the old spot where the withered post stood.
The Master secretly marveled at this and took him on as a friend. In his prime, the Master excelled at calligraphy and composed verses on the *Dharmapada*, which he pursued...
He admired Master Xiu of Chanxiu. There was a poem that said: "Beside the red peony, butterflies dance; within the green wutong trees, orioles sing.
At the parting pavilion, one does not pluck the willow branches; how much more so when the spring mountains both see one off and welcome one back.

He once stayed with Master Shi of Xixian, but their spiritual affinities did not harmonize, so he composed a poem on Lion Peak and departed. He took Qi and Yue as companions and together went to visit [the master].
The Fifth Patriarch, Master Jie, was resting before the mountain villa when he sent Yue ahead. Their exchange of words did not accord, and the Master likewise never saw him again.
Consequently, he traveled south to visit Zen Master Zuo of Zhimen. Zuo was the legitimate son of Master Yuan of Xianglin and the grandson of Yunmen;
his insight was lofty, and among scholars, none could fathom his spiritual mechanism. The Master was brilliant and outstanding, and Zhimen held him in high regard.
One day, Xuan asked, "If one does not give rise to a single thought, how can there be transgression? Zhimen called to the Master;
as the Master stepped forward, Zhimen struck him across the mouth with his whisk. As the Master was about to open his mouth, he struck again. The Master attained sudden and complete enlightenment.
He relied upon [the master] for five years and fully attained the Way. Master [Zhaoqing] was on close terms with Prime Minister Zeng Gong;
while they were together at the Huai River, Zeng Gong asked the Master where he was going. The Master replied, "I intend to travel to Qiantang, bypass Xixing, and ascend Mount Tiantai and Yandang.
Zeng Gong said, "Lingyin is a most excellent place in the world. Chan Master Shan is an old friend of mine; I shall recommend you to him in a letter. When the Master arrived at Lingyin...
He remained in seclusion for three years, submerged like a submerged object among the masses. Suddenly, Master Zeng was dispatched as an envoy to Western Zhejiang to seek out the Teacher.
At Lingyin, no one recognized him; at that time, there were over a thousand monks in the hall. The envoy’s officials searched through the bedding and calendars, seeking him by physical description.

When they finally reached Master Zeng, he asked about the letter previously entrusted to him. The Teacher tucked it into his sleeve and said, "Your Excellency’s intent is indeed earnest, yet a wandering monk is not a district magistrate."

Master Zeng laughed heartily. Master Shan regarded this as extraordinary. When the Master entered the world of public teaching, he first resided at Cuifeng in Wujiang and later moved to Xuedou in Mingzhou;

he was personally invited by Master Zeng while the latter was serving as the Governor of Yue. He ascended the hall and said: "The spring mountains layer upon layer of chaotic green; The spring waters shimmer with empty azure.
Within the vast expanse of heaven and earth, I stand alone—gazing toward what infinite horizon? Having spoken, he descended from his seat.
Turning back, he asked his attendant, "Was there anyone who just came to visit the abbot's quarters? The attendant replied, "There was. The Master said, "The heart of a thief is always apprehensive.
For over thirty years, the Master had propagated the teachings of the school, and extraordinary practitioners from throughout the land vied with one another to attend upon him.
In his later years, lamenting that students sought the branches while losing the source, he composed the "Verses on the Daily Diminution of the Way," which says:

"Three parts of one's life have already passed; The single point of the numinous mind remains unpolished. Greedy for life, one rushes about in pursuit of the days; If called back, one does not turn—what can be done?
He also wrote an inscription on a wall to admonish those who followed him in their studies, the gist of which states: "The body is like a moving latrine; profit..."
He was called Ruanzai (Soft Robber). A hundred years are not long; there is no peace within the three realms. One should cherish every moment and seek liberation.
As he read, his nose grew moist with emotion. One day, while walking for meditation, the Master happened to lean his staff against a tree in the forest, surrounded by a circle of monks.
Suddenly he asked, "When the clouds part and the trees wither and their leaves fall, what is it like? Yunmen replied, "The body is exposed to the golden wind.
Did Yunmen answer this monk, or was it an explanation? The Senior Monk Zong stepped forward from the assembly and said, "I will speak once this old man has attained realization.
The Master stared at him intently and said in surprise, "Is this not Han Daba? He replied, "This old man has had a sudden flash of insight."
Thereupon, the drum was struck and the assembly gathered. The Master said, "Great assembly, today the Senior Monk Zong of Xuedou is none other than the Great Yang Han Da-po of old.
Possessing great insight and vision, he has hidden his traces and concealed his brilliance;

now, wishing to propagate the spirit of our school, I pray that he will graciously ascend this seat. Zong then ascended the seat. A monk asked, "Before the precious sword has emerged from its scabbard..."
"How was it? he asked. [The monk] replied, "Its divine light shot toward the Dipper and Ox constellations. He asked again, "How was it after it emerged from the scabbard?

[The monk] replied, "A thousand soldiers are easy to find; a single general is hard to seek. The monk withdrew. Zong then said, "Before the precious sword has emerged from its scabbard, its divine light shoots toward the Dipper and Ox constellations.
A thousand soldiers are easily found; a single general is truly hard to seek. He then descended from his seat. The entire assembly was greatly astonished. This was at Chengtian Monastery.
This was Chan Master Zong. One day, as the Master was wandering through the mountains and surveying the scenery on all sides, he said to his attendant, "When shall we come here again?
The attendant pleaded for a final verse of farewell. The Master replied, "Throughout my life, I have only been troubled by the excess of words.
On the following day, he distributed his staff, sandals, robes, and alms bowl to his disciples and said, "We shall meet again on the seventh day of the seventh month. When that date arrived—

Having washed his hands and rinsed his mouth, he adjusted his robes and passed away with his head toward the north. He had lived seventy-three years in this world and sat in meditation for fifty summer retreats.
His entire body was enshrined in a stupa in the western valley of the monastery. He was posthumously granted the title Chan Master Mingjue.
The commentary states: The Yunmen school found its revival through Xuedou; had it not been for him, it would have surely faded away.
The Master’s bearing was grave and dignified; that he returned a letter from his sleeve to its original owner after three years was alone sufficient to awe all posterity.
The family reputation is vast and far-reaching; descendants continue in an unbroken line.
How could this be mere coincidence? Regarding Master Dongshan Xiaocong:
Chan Master Dongshan Xiaocong was a native of Qujiang in Shaoyou Prefecture. He was born into the Du clan. He beheld the manifestation of Mañjuśrī as a true deity.

When the Master first traveled to Mount Lu, no one recognized him. At that time, the Dharma seat at Yunju was at its peak of prosperity, and the Master served as the head of the lamp-keepers (*dengtou*).
Hearing the monastic community discussing how the Monk Sengqie of Sizhou had recently appeared in Yangzhou, someone posed a question, saying:
"If he is the Great Sage of Sizhou, why did he appear in Yangzhou? The Master said, "A gentleman loves wealth, but he takes it by the right way.
The entire assembly laughed heartily. Later, a monk recounted this to the Hermitian Master Lianhua Xiang, who was greatly startled and said:
"The descendants of Yunmen still remain. Gazing afar toward Yunju, he prostrated himself; thus, the Master’s reputation became weighty within the monastic community.

Subsequently, he relied upon Chan Master Dongshan Quan as his head seat (*śrāmaṇera*). When Quan moved to Qixian, he entrusted the Master to the donors and the assembly, and the assembly followed his lead.
They requested him before the Prefectural Governor, who also granted his request. In the third year of the Dazhong Xiangfu era, the Master entered the world [as a public teacher].
Dongshan ascended the hall and said: "The Patriarch came from the West specifically to sing of this matter.

It is because you, Venerable Ones, do not realize it for yourselves that those who enter through the gate do not possess the family treasure. To mistake the shadow for the head—is this not a great error?
Since the Patriarch came from the West specifically to sing of this matter, why must I further address the assembly with repeated words of 'carefulness'? The Master saw a monk.
Whenever someone came with a question, he would glare at them with wide-open eyes and say, "You do not understand my tiger-slaying art; get out!
One day, while carrying firewood up the mountain himself, a monk met him and asked, "Since you live on the mountain, why are you carrying firewood from the foot?
The Master replied, "I need wood to burn on the mountain as well. He addressed the assembly, saying, "The entire Great Canon of the Teachings is merely this character 'zhi' (之). The Patriarch...

"Coming from the West" is the character for "right. What is the meaning of "right"? After a long silence, he said: "When the weather is clear, repair the roof; while there is leisure, harvest the grain.
Once the royal taxes have been paid, one beats the belly and sings aloud. To the northeast of the mountain, the Master personally planted ten thousand pine trees.
For every single tree he planted, he would sit and recite one scroll of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. He called this practice "planting pines."
"Monk," [Fenyang said], "the ridge is named Vajra Ridge. [The monk] asked, "If the ridge is here, where is the Vajra?
The Master pointed and said, "This single pine tree was planted by this old monk himself. Fenyang once said to Ciming, "I have traveled everywhere to study the descendants of Yunmen;
my only regret is that I have not yet met Cong. You must go see him. Thus, although Ciming—
The formal retreat had already concluded, yet I was still able to behold his countenance and hear his further discourse. One day, the Master felt unwell;
he ascended the hall to bid farewell to the assembly and spoke a verse on "Penetrating the Dharmakāya": "In practicing Chan and studying the Way, do not be muddled.

Ask until you penetrate the Dharmakāya, where the Northern Dipper is hidden. I am now old and decrepit, exceedingly frail; Lacking the strength to engage in discussion with others. He spoke again: "This Dharma seat..."
He instructed that his own relics be enshrined, and upon finishing these words, he passed away. His body was cremated, and śarīra were obtained, which were enshrined in a stūpa on Mount Jingang.
Previously, Xu Gongshi, the Director of the Ministry of Revenue, had been dispatched to govern Nanchang.

While passing through Lotus Peak, he heard of Master Xiang’s reputation and said, "The practitioner Cong is in Jiangxi; let us go seek him out. This monk is a 'human and celestial eye'. Having said this, Xu...
Upon his arrival, he heard that the Master was living in the mountain hermitage style. He composed a poem to send him, containing the lines:
"Sitting through the night upon Cloud-Linked Rock / Planting pines in the spring amidst the rain. He was about to visit him, but the Master had already passed away.
Master Xianggong was a successor of Chan Master Shenshen of Fengxian. His insight was exceptionally high, and his spirit overawed all quarters.
At the end of his life, he ascended the hall and, raising his staff, asked the assembly: "Tell me, when the ancient Buddhas arrived at this point, why did they refuse to stay?
No one in the assembly could respond. He then said himself, "Because on that path, they were unable to gain strength. He added further, "How does one gain strength?"
He departed. Placing his staff crosswise upon his shoulder, he said, "Carrying my *zhuli* staff, I shall not look back at men;
I go straight into a thousand peaks and ten thousand peaks. Having finished speaking, he passed away. Master [Fengxue] and Wenshu Zhen were brothers in their practice.
Cong was the successor of Wenshu, while Xiang was his nephew. Cong’s dharma-disciples were Yunjusi and Mingjiaosong. Xiang succeeded Jiyuan.
Biography of Chan Master Xian of Beichen in the Song Dynasty:
Chan Master Zhixian succeeded Master Ya of Fuyan; he was the fourth-generation descendant of Yunmen. He propagated the Dharma at Beichen in Hengzhou.

On the eve of the New Year, during a small *can* (informal sermon), he said: "The year has ended and the lunar month is exhausted; there is nothing left with which to celebrate the passing of the year with you all, O elders."
The monks cook: they roast a white ox in the open air and boil rice from the fields with vegetable soup.

They burn firewood and sit in a circle around the hearth with the assembly, singing "The Joy of Returning to the Fields. Why is this so? Because it spares one from "relying on another's gate and leaning against another's wall."
This caused the people of the time to call him "Lang" (The Butcher). When he descended from his seat, the Rector called out loudly from behind, "An official has arrived at the county seat!
The Master turned around and asked why; the Rector said, "It is said that you, Reverend, slaughter oxen but do not accept their hides or horns.
The Master laughed and threw his warm cap to the ground; the Rector then picked it up and departed. The Master leaped down from his meditation seat, grabbed him by the chest, and shouted:
He said, "Thief! Thief! Then Na took the cap and covered the Master’s head, saying, "The weather is cold; please return, O Monk. Na then went out. At that time, Fachang was serving as attendant.
The Master looked back at him and asked, "What do you make of this case? Fachang replied, "Recently, paper has been expensive in the city;
one statement covers it all. Fachang’s name was Yiyu; he was a successor of the Master. [This account] is recorded separately. The Master spoke again:
He had a successor named Shaoxian. During the Jixing era, he compiled the *Biographies of Chan Master Shanjian Xian of Kaishan*.

Chan Master Shanjian Xian of Kaishan was a native of Linjiang Commandery. His conduct was pure and austere, and his wisdom and insight were clear and penetrating. [The biography of] Chan Master Huiyuan...
The Master was at Deshan; he went there to rely upon him. One day, Deshan ascended the hall and, looking over the assembly, said, "The lion yawns;
the elephant king looks back. At these words, the Master suddenly had an awakening. He entered the room to present his realization, and Deshan asked, "How do you understand this?
The Master looked back and said, "The donkey in the back garden is eating grass. Deshan approved. From then on, his spiritual eloquence became swift and sharp. Thus it was in Chan.
Linmu was known as "The One Who Roams Across the Sea on the Path of Siam. He also studied under Xuedou Xian, who, admiring his brilliance and elegance, kept him at his seat for several years.
Xuedou intended to recommend him to reside at Jinge Monastery in Mingzhou. Upon hearing this, the Master wrote two verses on the wall and departed, saying:
"It is not that I lack the intent to continue the ancestral lamp; I am ashamed that my Way has not yet reached the level of Neng of Lingnan. At the third watch, the moon..."

Descending from the crags and caverns below, he lingered in silence, longing for the azure peaks. For over thirty years amidst the four seas, he sought teachers and chose friends without a moment’s respite.
This morning, having reached the ground of no-mind, he was instead driven out of the mountains by that very state of no-mind.

Later, he resided at Kaixian and succeeded Chan Master Deshan Yuan as his heir; he subsequently corresponded with Xuedou. As for the old woman before the mountain, she saw [the messenger] in person...
A messenger arrived to inquire, "The Head Seat Xian has taken over a monastery; for whom does he burn incense? The special envoy replied, "For the Venerable Yuan of Deshan.
The old woman then scolded him, saying, "Xuedou shook out his intestines and preached Zen; because of you, he has come to such a state of betraying his own great kindness.
On the day of the opening of the hall, after the head monk had finished striking the gavel, the Master said: "Even if the thousand sages were to appear, they would still only be..."
I prostrate and offer praise to all the ancestral patriarchs of successive generations who have lifted us up when we were unable to rise.

Therefore, from Kāśyapa down to this mountain monk, for over two thousand years, the moon has illumined the lamp of wisdom and the stars have arrayed themselves along the tree of the Way. Humanity and devas are universally enlightened;
both the ordinary and the holy flourish together. But tell me, whose grace and power does this rely upon? It is the Old Barbarian (the Buddha). He simply said: "When the morning star appears..."
I shall attain enlightenment simultaneously with all sentient beings of the great earth. If this is so, then since they are already "great men" (puruṣa), I am likewise so.
What is there that cannot be? It is simply because people are unwilling to accept this that they naturally give rise to despondency;
thus, they push aside one or two who have already emerged as predecessors, each seeking to enlighten the other, merely acting as witnesses for one another.
"Listen! Among the assembly of devas and humans today, is there anyone who has not long wandered?

One who has long roamed the Red Water, who has long dwelt at Mount Jing, who carries treasures in their sleeves and possesses the eye atop the crown of the head—such a patch-robed monk who has trodden the site of awakening wherever he goes?
Please act as a witness for this newly enthroned Elder. Is there anyone? The Master resided at Kaixian for eighteen years before passing away.
At his home mountain, Yunju Yuan was his direct successor; this is recorded separately.
Nanyuan Yan’s lineage:
Master Nanyuan Yan was born into the Zheng family; he was a native of Tong’an in Quanzhou. He entered the monastic order at the age of eleven.
As a youth, at the age of seventeen, he became a full monk (*bhikṣu*). Traveling through various regions, he arrived in Luling and paid his respects to the elder master Huo of Xifeng.
Huo was a descendant of Yunmen. The Master stayed with him for five years and fully mastered his teachings. From then on, his spiritual powers were unfathomable;
the world traditionally held him to be an emanation of Dīpaṃkara Buddha. At the Huarin River, there was a dragon that harmed people. As the Master approached the crossing, he spoke a verse:

He warned them, and the *jiao* spirit withdrew. Before long, sand surged forth to block the opening, and the pool was transformed into an island. At Huangyang Gorge in Meizhou, there was a lack of water;
the Master struck it with his staff, and it gushed forth. The elders took this to be a divine manifestation and gathered to watch, but the Master vanished.
Wherever he went, he encountered droughts or floods; he would write a gāthā and cast it into the waters, and there was nothing that did not accord with his wishes.

When he traveled south to Huangshi Rock, the area was infested with many snakes and tigers, yet the Master stayed there and could command the snakes and tigers to obey him. Whenever the Master instructed others, he invariably used gāthās; at the end of each gāthā, he would necessarily inscribe four characters:
"Presented with the Middle" (Zengzhi yizhong). No one in the world could fathom the meaning of these four characters. Yuan Jing served the Master with reverence as if he were a divine being.

His family painted his portrait and invariably offered sacrifices when eating and drinking. When a monk from a neighboring temple died, the Master—ignorant of the law that such matters should be reported to the authorities—simply cremated him.
When the officials pursued him and he was seated in the courtyard, they questioned him about the circumstances, but he did not answer. They demanded paper, and he composed a verse, saying:
"A wild monk dies beyond the clouds; A wild monk is burned beyond the clouds. These two dharmas are without distinction; The path to Bodhi is not far. The calligraphy [was exquisite].
His calligraphy was rugged and forceful, like the large-scale *da-zhuan* script carved into stone niches. The magistrate was greatly incensed, deeming him both mad and insolent.
Later, while the master was sunning his *saṃghāṭī* robe in the midday heat, he was released from custody; he then wrapped his head with a cotton cloth and wore white garments.

The Master regretted that those who heard his teachings were divided equally between doubt and faith, and so he remained silent for six years. The mountain temple was required to pay a tribute of cloth, which the common people had to provide annually in rotation.

The Master could not bear this. He placed the letter inside his cloth sash and sought to escape. When the official found it, his anger intensified. Although he questioned him further, the Master did not answer.
The official considered him a sorcerer and burned his cloth cap; yet when the fire was extinguished, the cap was even more bright and fresh. Thereupon, he took paper and composed a verse, saying:
"By the power of universal compassion and patience, All are born from my own mind. Bound by the harsh constraints of kings and officials, The Buddha-Dharma cannot flow forth."
He traveled on. Thereafter, he gradually began to speak. Later, he went to Mount Panggu in Nan’gang. Previously, the Venerable Pali from Western India had begun the construction there and prophesied:
"In the future, there shall be a lay bodhisattva who will come to flourish this mountain. The Master resided there for three years and established a monastic community (*saṃghārāma*).
He then returned to Nan’an. At Miancha in Jiangnan, a log was obstructing the path of passing boats; when the Master’s boat passed by, it floated away.
He stroked it and said, "Go, go! Do not cause harm to others. That night, the raft was swept away.
A monk coming from Huizhou said, "In Heyuan there is a great boat stuck in the sand; ten thousand oxen cannot move it.

I wish to obtain it to carry bricks for building a pagoda at Nanhai as a field of merit for all sentient beings. The Master said, "This is an object belonging to the underworld. Nevertheless, I shall give it to you."
"Take this verse," he said. The verse read: "The heavens shed rain, the waters rise; the King of Boats moves through the underworld.

Do not linger long standing upon the sands; receive blessings and take refuge in Bodhi. The monk then chanted the verse as he stood upon the boat, and the vessel began to move. The multitude cheered with joy.

When they reached Wuyang, a great merchant requested to borrow the boat for transport. The monk granted his request. Just as they were untying the mooring ropes, a wind suddenly arose, and the boat was lost.
In that place, there was a śrāmaṇera who lacked the nature of great learning, yet his conduct was diligent and reverent.

His teacher took pity on him and composed a verse for him to recite, thinking that after a long time he would become intelligent. The verse said: "Great wisdom arises from the mind; where in the mind can it be sought?
It accomplishes all meanings; there is neither past nor present. Thereupon, regarding worldly scripts, texts, and languages, he could read them at a single glance and recite them from memory.

Regarding the verses and phrases he had forgotten, he would produce them instantly upon taking up his brush. The Master’s extraordinary deeds were so prominent that his local authorities submitted a formal report to the throne, and an imperial edict praised him.
Prime Minister Wang Qinruo, Grand Councilor Zhang Anren, and all others below them composed poems in his honor;
the Master never looked at them, merely placing them upon the ceiling beams. On the sixth day of the first month of the Yimao year of the Chunhua era, he gathered the assembly and said:
"On this day of my birth, now is precisely the time. Thereupon, he passed away reclining on his right side. He was posthumously titled Chan Master Dingguang Yuanying. The commentary states:

"The spirit of the perfected person gathers within the mind; its manifestation in speech is verified by experience. Jiyin remarked: "The verses and words of this Master are all phrases that accord with the nature (*dharmatā*);
they are not a realm reachable by intellectual knowledge. This is truly so, truly so. As soon as one engages in discursive thought," [the truth is lost].
This is merely the livelihood of the ghostly realm. Since he himself was still shrouded in mist and dew, how could he possibly cause others not to be deluded?
Dongsan Bao and Letan Cheng both transmitted the lineage from Bao.
Bao was a native of Hefei, Luzhou; his surname was Wu. He possessed extraordinary features from birth and entered Puning Monastery at a young age.

Having already harbored a vision that transcended the common herd, he heard that the Fifth Patriarch, Master Jie—a master craftsman of the Chan school—had established the principle of "placing water to test the needle" and that its truth resided in silent realization.
He consequently entered the inner quarters to receive the Dharma transmission. When the Patriarch was ill, he ordered an attendant to go to the storehouse to fetch fresh ginger for decoction.
Bao, who was in charge of the storehouse, rebuked him. The attendant reported this to the Patriarch, who then instructed him to take money back [to pay for the ginger].
He purchased it and gave it to him. Later, he went to Dongshan, where Master Cong recognized his character and treated him with exceptional esteem.
Upon his death, he left a final instruction for [Zhao] to succeed him on the seat. The Prefectural Governor also sent a letter requesting that Zhao recommend someone he knew to preside over Dongshan.
The Patriarch said, "He is like a man who buys raw ginger. Not long after he took up residence, shoes were piled outside his door;

the monastic community became so prosperous that provisions accumulated in great abundance, with a surplus of over a million [coins] at all times. At Mount Huangbo, the supply of gruel and rice was failing, so Bao moved his staff there to take charge of it, and because of him, Huangbo became well-provided for.
Court Official Zu Jun Wuzhe and Provincial Inspector Cheng Jun Shimeng both manifested their love for and delight in the worthy.
As for the name "Shan": after his ancestor had brought the Treasure-Master back to Guizong, Cheng subsequently sent him to Yunju to present the Treasure.

In total, he presided over four famous monasteries during his career. While at Guizong, one day as he was walking out the gate leaning on a staff, he saw a procession coming down the road and asked, "What is this?"
The official said, "The County Magistrate has ordered you to clear the way. Baoyun stood to one side on the left of the road. When the horse reached him, it knelt before him and would not proceed.
Baoyun said, "Even a beast recognizes a man. The Magistrate realized this was Baoyun; he bowed twice and departed.
While staying at Yunju, one night a mountain deity carried him in a sedan chair, circumambulating the monastery with Baoyun inside. Baoyun said, "Lift your father! Lift your mother! Lift [them] up!"
The Abbot went away. Shen Zhi led him directly up to the Abbot’s quarters. Bao was a person of refined discipline; he strictly upheld the precepts.

When he first traveled as a wandering monk (*xingjiao*), he stayed overnight at an inn and was harassed by a courtesan, who shared his bed. Bao sat upright throughout the entire night. At dawn, the courtesan demanded money;
he gave it to her, left the room, and burned the bedding before departing. The courtesan told her parents the truth of what had happened.
He then invited [Huiming] back to his residence to hold a vegetarian feast in thanks, remarking that he was a true son of the Buddha.

However, because Huiming was fond of reputation and concerned with outward appearances, wherever he went he would select famous monks to follow him as his "wings and feathers. When Huairang (Baoshi) received the Dharma from the Fifth Patriarch, the Patriarch, in his later years, left the assembly to visit him.
Huairang, considering Huiming’s conduct and concealment of his status to be subject to public suspicion, did not pay him formal respect and instead spoke a verse to him:
They ridiculed him. Baizhang then went to Dayu. One day, in front of the Sangha Hall, he leaned on his staff and passed away while chatting and laughing.
Although Bao had a great reputation, the monastic community nonetheless held him in low esteem for this. When the Master was at Dongshan, he once personally laid the bricks for his own burial vault.
More than twenty years later, he finally passed away at Guizong. He was seventy-seven years old, with fifty-one years of seniority as a monk.
He passed away. On the eighteenth day, his entire body was enshrined in a stupa; this was in the first year of the Zhìhé era. Yú Xiānggōng Jìng composed an inscription for him, which said:
"That superior man was peerless within the monastic groves. He vigorously propagated the essential tenets of our school and, with a compassionate heart, brought many across to liberation.

When he spoke, he struck the vital point of their faculties, causing them to awaken on their own. Those who encountered him grasped the essentials and proceeded directly upon the path to enlightenment. He came wielding his staff, yet cast aside the raft."
And so he departed. "Miaoyuan" (Wondrous Perfection)—a title bestowed upon the Master by the Emperor—for which humans and devas look up in admiration.
Chan Master Huai Cheng was a man of unknown origins; like Bao, he emerged from the school of the Fifth Patriarch.
He appeared in the world at Letan in Hongzhou, and the various quarters called him Letan Cheng. Huanglong Nan publicly relied upon him for the longest period. However...
The Dharma-way of Yunmen underwent a slight transformation upon reaching our Master; thus, Master Yue of Yunfeng compared it to quicksilver, which flows away when smelted.
Da’jue Lian was his successor; that which is called "the green surpassing the indigo" is detailed elsewhere.
The commentary states: This is Dongshan. He transmitted it to Quan; Quan succeeded Wenshu. After Quan’s death, he transmitted it to Bao; Bao succeeded Wuzu.
To see how the lineage is maintained and the Buddha’s wisdom-life sustained is no small matter. When the ancients spoke of transmission and succession, they meant nothing less than this.
The Master did not allow even a hair’s breadth of private thought to intervene between them. Otherwise, how could masters such as Quan, Cong, Gong, and Lao have lacked their own Dharma heirs?

National Teacher Zhongfeng wrote in a letter to Ding-sou: "The reason the ancients so deeply clarified the lineage of Dharma heirs and direct transmissions was that the source and course of the Great Dharma must not be misrepresented.
In this degenerate age when customs have grown thin, people offer gold to request a whisk."
There have been instances of those who exchanged their monasteries for their heirs; I have often felt deep pain over this matter. Bao was also an outstanding descendant of Yunmen.

It is a pity that his great virtue was obscured by a single blemish. The *Lamp Records* (Denglu) claim that Bao was born in a brothel and had no family name, but this has not been properly investigated.
Biography of Chan Master Zhifeng of the Song Dynasty.
Zhifeng was a native of Yuhang. From birth, he loathed pungent foods, and his skin and body were fragrant and pure. He left the household life at Langzhan Monastery on Mount Dongshan in Lin’an.
He was thoroughly versed in the Three Studies (Tripitaka). Once, he dreamed that he ascended Mount Sumeru and beheld three Buddhas seated in a row.
First Śākyamuni, then Maitreya—both he prostrated at their feet—but as for the third Buddha, he did not recognize him and merely gazed upward.
At that moment, Śākyamuni pointed to him and said, "This is the Buddha Siṃhacandra, the Teacher Maitreya who is currently in the position of succession.
Only then did he prostrate. After waking, he examined the Tripitaka and found it accorded with his dream. Later, while traveling, he met National Teacher Yao in Tianmen.
Daichueqiwu. One day, he entered the Hall of Samantabhadra to sit in meditative repose. Suddenly, a divine being knelt before him. The Master asked, "Who are you?
He replied, "I am a guardian deity of the precepts. The Master said, "I have a long-standing transgression that I have not yet purified;
do you know of it? He replied, "What transgression does the Master have? It is merely a minor fault: whenever you poured out the water from your bowl,"
The master used to pour away the offerings made by donors; this was not appropriate. Having said this, he vanished.

From that time on, the master drank all the water from his bowl after washing it. After doing so for a long period, he consequently developed a spleen ailment, which only began to heal after ten years.

The King of Wuyue, admiring the master’s spiritual influence, summoned him to bestow upon him purple robes and a title, and commanded him to reside at Gongchen Monastery. At the beginning of the Kaibao era, the Zhongyi Wang...
He established the Pumen Monastery and invited the Master to serve as its founding abbot to propagate the essential tenets of the school.

In the fourth year of the Kaibao era, the Master firmly declined the abbacy, wishing instead to dwell in seclusion among the forests and springs. At that time, the general Ling Chao founded a monastery on Mount Wuyun and offered it to the Master as his place for the remainder of his life.
As Wuyun was frequently infested with tigers, the Master would often carry a large fan while begging for money to purchase meat to feed them.
Whenever tigers appeared, they would immediately submit in a state of docility. At dusk, when he returned to the mountain, the tigers would come to meet him; he would mount one and ride it back home.

Consequently, he was known in the world as Chan Master Fuhu (Taming Tigers) and was also called Dashi Heshang (The Great Fan Monk). He passed away in the second year of the Yongxi era at the age of seventy-seven.
His stupa was named Baofeng Changzhao (Precious Peak Constantly Illuminating).
Biography of Chan Master Chengshi of Qixian, Song Dynasty Chan Master Chengshi was a native of Jianning.
He was a dharma heir of Master Heng of Baizhang, who in turn was a dharma heir of Fayan. Thus, the Master was the direct grandson of Fayan.

By nature he was lofty and simple; he disciplined himself with rigorous austerity, and his actions never transgressed the bounds of the Dharma. In his later years, he recited the entire Tripitaka three times.

If one considers reading while seated to be a lack of reverence, then one should recite while standing or study while walking. Master Nanyuan of Huanglong first traveled to seek instruction when he was still young;
he followed [his teacher] for many years, and thus much of what he did throughout his life was modeled after him.
He once said, "The Venerable of Qixian must have descended from among the devas and humans; he is a beacon for the monastic community. Xuedou Xian once [stayed] in Huai...
Shanlai relied upon him, but seeing that the Master received him with little favor, he felt a sense of discord and resentment.

He then composed a poem on Lion Peak and departed, saying: "Perched upon the ground, its soaring form never ceases; How could its claws and fangs ever mingle with the common herd? Heaven ordained it to be born atop a thousand peaks;
Even without the clouds supporting it, it must still raise its head. The Master resided at Xiqian, for his teaching style was steep and rigorous.
Therefore, his assembly was not large. One evening, when the assembly had gathered for the late session, the Master said, "In the morning I did not meet with you all;
tonight I must not remain silent. He then descended from his seat. His manner of cutting through [delusions] was like this.
The postscript states: Master Baizhang Heng’s three-word instructions for ascending the hall were:
“Drink tea,” “Be careful,” and “Rest. These are what are known as Baizhang’s Three Secrets: “Drink tea, be careful, rest. Master Shi’s summary is thus;
he truly possesses his father’s style, leaving not even a drop of its essence behind. From this, one can observe the transmission between master and disciple.
The Source of Receiving [the Precepts].
Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks, Volume Seven;
Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks, Volume Eight.
The Chapter on Practicing Dhyāna, composed by the Śramaṇa Minghe of Huashan Temple in Wu Commandery during the Ming Dynasty;
based on the teachings of Chan Master Xintang of Xingjiao Monastery in Xuancheng during the Song Dynasty.
Chan Master Tantian was the son of the Niu family in Wenzhou. He worked as a silversmith, and upon sharpening a vessel, he attained awakening.

He immediately left the household life to study under Master Langya Huijue, with whom his spiritual dialogue was instantly in accord. When Tiantai Yihuai resided at Xingjiao Monastery, the Master served as the First Seat.
Later, when Tiantai Yihuai accepted an invitation elsewhere and wished to request the Master to succeed him at that monastery, the scholar Diaojingchun was present.
While serving as the governor of Wanling, he feared that outsiders might raise objections.

He then made a vow before Guanyin, saying, "If the Head Seat Tan possesses clear insight into the Way and is fit to serve as abbot, I pray you will manifest a dream to Scholar Diao. That night, Scholar Diao dreamed of an ox standing upon the seat of the Dharma Hall.
The next morning, when Yī took his leave of the prefecture, Diao recounted the dream to him. Yī laughed heartily. Diao asked him why.
Therefore, the Abbot said, "The Head Seat Tan’s surname is Niu (Ox), and he is also of the Ox year. He then had a messenger take his seat and present a formal invitation.

The Master accepted the invitation and ascended the seat. There was a messenger from Xuedou named Shengzong, who stepped forward and asked: "Before the Buddhas appeared in the world, everyone’s nostrils reached the heavens;
after they appeared in the world, why is there no news at all? The Master replied: "Before Mount Jizu, the wind is still."
However, Xingzhou said, "Not yet; speak further. The Master said, "Great snow fills Chang'an. Xingzhou said, "Who understands this meaning? It makes me remember Nanquan.
He then brushed his sleeves and returned to the assembly. The Master said, "Xingzhou has lost today.
He immediately returned to his quarters and sent someone to invite Xingzhou, saying to him, "Just now you were mistaken; you should have given a single turning word for the sake of humans and devas."
