Before the assembly, [Zhaozhou] did not pay obeisance, but instead covered himself with his robe. Yunmen Zong said, "A great man has gold beneath his knees;

how could he be willing to prostrate? You blind old fellow! The Master said, "I have another saying. Zong then proceeded to explain his previous words up to the point where he had said, "Wait until later, and I will speak further.
The Master said, "I have thirty blows for you; I entrust them to you to administer. Thereupon, Xuedou Zong paid obeisance.
Homage.
The Biography of Chan Master Yuán of Yúnfēng Monastery in Nán’ān.

Yuán was a native of Nánxióng. His nature was pure and sincere. In his youth, he traveled to various regions; although he had studied extensively under many masters, he had not yet attained full penetration. Having heard...

Chan Master Nan resided at Jicui Hermitage on Huangbo Mountain. [The author] went there to rely upon him. One day, while sitting in leisurely conversation after the evening board had been lowered, he heard two monks discussing the karmic cause-and-effect story of Baizhang and the wild fox.
One monk said, "Even so, as long as one is not oblivious to cause and effect, one has not yet escaped the body of a wild fox.
The other monk replied immediately, "Precisely because one does not fall into cause and effect, how could one have ever fallen into the state of a wild fox?"
"Is it a fox body? Yuan was struck with awe, finding his words strange; unconsciously, he rose and climbed to the top of the hermitage.
As he crossed the stream, he suddenly attained great enlightenment and beheld Master Nan. He recounted the events to him, but before he had finished, tears flowed down to his chin.

Master Nan ordered him to go to the attendant’s bed and sleep soundly. Suddenly, he arose and composed a verse, saying: "Neither falling nor obscured; for monks and laity alike, there is no taboo. The spirit and bearing of a man!"
Like a king, he vied with others to receive the bag and the cloak; with a single staff, he went wherever he pleased. A wild fox leaped into the ranks of the golden-haired lions.
Master Nan laughed heartily for a long while. Later, he composed a verse on the wind and the banner:
"It is not the wind, nor is it the banner; White clouds still cover the green mountains. In my old age, I have grown utterly powerless; I have stolen a moment from the midst of busyness."
Zi Xian: The Elder Yun’an often personally transcribed these two verses and praised them highly, remarking that their sharpness of wit was no less than that of Master Ying of Shaowu.
Later, he emerged from seclusion to reside at Yunfeng Temple in Dayu, though his final whereabouts remain unknown.
Huangbo Sheng, Zhaojue Bai, and Xinsiang Xian—these three masters transmitted [the lineage] solely through Sheng.
A native of the Luo clan of Tongchuan, he received the Dharma from Master Huanglong Nan. However, even before meeting the Master, he had already attained great enlightenment;
the Master merely served to seal his realization. At that time, the seat at Huangbo had been vacant for a long period, and the Governor of Ruizhou commissioned [Sheng].

Long (Yuanzhao), the Master of the Dharma, had Huanglong beat the drum to assemble the congregation and spoke these words: "Reciting hymns atop the bell tower; planting vegetables beneath the bedframe.
He said, "Whoever can explain this shall dwell at Huangbo. The assembly remained silent. Sheng stepped forward from the crowd and said, "A fierce tiger sits blocking the road.

Huanglong was greatly pleased and consequently appointed him to the post. His reputation for the Way shook the world, and his fame spread throughout the land. He reported this to the Governor of Zizhou.
Fei’u Ren was surnamed Zhi. His father, Qian, had heard the Way from a practitioner on Mount Song who treated life and death as a game;
he lived in white robes yet maintained pure conduct (*brahmacarya*). He once said, "My faculties are dull and I cannot enter the Perfect and Sudden [Teaching].

It would suffice for me if I had a son to continue the life of wisdom. From his youth, Fei’u Ren had heard his father’s instructions; he listened attentively and contemplated them deeply, as if they were long-standing habits. One day, while crossing a stream, he suddenly—

Having attained a realization, he subsequently went to Mount Emei to shave his head. Father and son relied upon one another as they traveled and lectured, mastering the sūtras and śāstras of both the *Xing* (Nature) and *Xiang* (Characteristics) schools.
He then departed for a southern journey, first visiting Master Taiping Jun at Lizhou. Jun declared, "Truly, you are my Dharma heir."
He was entrusted with the great robe for preaching the Dharma. Baizhang bowed and declined, saying, "I have heard that Huangbo’s reputation is great;

I shall go to him. For three years he remained there without receiving formal certification (*inka*). He applied himself to his duties even more diligently. One day, as Sheng was about to raise his head [to speak], Baizhang rebuked him, saying, "You old fellow!
Sheng laughed heartily and accepted this. At the end of the Yuanfeng era, the Prince of Nankang invited Sheng to the capital. Baizhang attended him on the journey. It happened that...

A student of the Imperial Academy submitted a memorial in defense of a *boshi* (doctor of Buddhist studies), in which the name of Cheng was mentioned. By imperial decree, Cheng was granted leave to return to Shu, whereupon his disciples dispersed like stars.
Bai alone followed him, carrying only his headcloth and alms bowl. Upon arrival, he resided at Zhaojue Temple; the grandeur of his Dharma assemblies was like that of Huangbo.
When Cheng was about to pass away in Chengdu, the Military Commissioner asked who should succeed him as the presiding master. The Master replied, "None is better suited than Bai."

The "White Opening" (Bai Kefa) follows the regulations of the South and thoroughly washes away the defects of monastic life. Not transcending the ocean of nature is the bondage of principle and phenomena;
not penetrating the wheel of sound is the bondage of language. This was the address for the formal ascent to the hall (*shàngtáng*).

It was transmitted and recited by practitioners everywhere, who all followed its lead with great enthusiasm. Recorded by Feng Gan, Court Disperser; Duan Xi, Court Consultant; and the recluse Song Fang of Mount Tiantai.
The Tang-dynasty scholar Zu Siyu and others all drew near to him, performing the rites of disciples. At the end of the Yuanyou era, the position of *śāstrī* (abbot) at Baishui Temple was vacant.
Cai Jing, who was then the regional commander of Shu, appointed Bai to the post. Bai was displeased and consequently declined both the appointment and the invitation to Zhaojue Temple;

he returned to his former monastery to preach the Dharma. After a long time, he manifested illness and composed this verse: "The wind is high and the moon is cold; the waters are distant and the sky..."
Chang’s shadow vanished as he stepped out the door; in all four directions, there was a serene stillness. Xian then succeeded him in the Dharma. Xian was the son of the Wang family of Tongchuan.
In his youth, he was successful in the civil service examinations and enjoyed a great reputation. Once, while playing by scooping up mountain stream water, he thought of it again at night.

He saw water, cool and filling the room; yet though he wished to draw it, he could not. Suddenly, the dusty realm of his world vanished of its own accord, and he realized: "The net of my worldly existence has been torn asunder.
He went to rely upon Baizhang for ordination and followed the assembly to inquire and consult. One day, Baizhang asked him: "Standing atop the high, high peak,"...
"Walking on the bottom of the deep sea—how do you understand this? Xian was suddenly enlightened beneath the words and said, "Your heels are nailed down.

Bai raised his whisk, and Xian smiled and departed. He served under Bai for seven years, then traveled south to see Master Wuzu Yan, where he remained in the attendants' quarters for a long time until he thoroughly mastered the depths of the Dharma.
It was only after more than forty years that he returned; at that time, Bai was still [alive].
I am well. [The Master] Jue was succeeded by Changsong. Qian succeeded Baofu Xinsiang. Su Yuanlao, the Grand Music Master, wrote a preface for his recorded sayings, stating:
"Recently, in our land of Shu, the Dharma was considered peerless only in terms of lecture halls and ordination platforms; the loftiness of the Patriarchal Way was not yet known.
It was only late that we obtained Chan Master Zhenjue Sheng, who, coming from Huangbo, propagated the teachings at Chengdu’s Zhaojue Temple."
The first assembly [discussed] the vastness and greatness of the *I Ching*, wherein change and movement circulate through the six voids;

it further traced the subtlety and mystery of the Way, which is formed as a unified whole and existed prior to heaven and earth. Thereupon he said: "My Dharma encompasses and covers heaven and earth, yet this is not considered great;

it dissolves and exhausts empty space, yet this is not considered difficult. It is realized in the present moment and established according to its function. When those of the clergy and laity in the southwest heard this suddenly...

Most of them stared blankly and could not enter [the state]. After a long while, they were each filled with despondency; none failed to lose their joy and shed tears, lamenting that they had encountered [the teaching] too late.
After Master Sheng passed away, Master Shao succeeded him; his Dharma was just like that of Master Sheng (Shao was Juebo).
Yet the number of those he transformed and saved increased even more. After Master Shao passed away, Master Xian succeeded him; his Dharma was just like that of Master Shao.
Furthermore, as the conditions for his practice have become increasingly abundant, he has moved from his former residence at Changsong to now dwell at Baofu.
The number of disciples who take refuge in him is beyond reckoning, and his merit in delivering and uplifting others knows no end. Alas!

This is the separate transmission of Śākyamuni, personally bestowed by Kāśyapa, protected by the patriarchs of the Western Heaven, and inherited by the venerable elders of China. How distant and remote it is! Yet I did not expect that today—
I, Dayu, have personally witnessed this with my own eyes. Nevertheless, as for the Master’s profound phrases and subtle words, I have not yet dared to fathom them;

I shall merely set forth the general outline to enlighten those among our circle who have newly resolved their intent, hoping that we may join hands in a dance and together hasten toward the Master’s gate.
Thus, the worthies of the time sighed over him in this manner. Minghe said:
"Xian emerged from Shu and reached Dongshan; after the longest period of polishing and refinement, he finally attained the profound depths of the source.
When he appeared in the world, he was the only one to offer incense to Jiao. Critics remarked that he obscured the reputation of the Way with his minor skills."
Thus, their sentiments were confused and they distorted the lineage of their masters. The monastic community referred to them as the "Xian-niu-zi" (Ox-headed ones).
It is said that Chan Master Baoben Yuan transmitted the Dharma to Huiyuan.
Huiyuan was the son of the Ni family of Chaozhou; he became a fully ordained monk at the age of nineteen and traveled extensively through various monasteries. Under Huanglong... [text continues].

He attained enlightenment upon hearing a pivotal phrase and returned to the Anji Monastery to report his realization to the principal temple. He was solitary and steadfast in character, possessed of refined elegance, and his deportment was dignified and grave;
he would sit upright throughout the entire day. Among the disciples of National Teacher Nan, Yuan alone was able to fully trace the details of his conduct and private life.
When Yuan first began teaching the Dharma, a letter from his dharma-heir arrived. Master Nan looked at the name and said, "I had momentarily forgotten him."
This monk said to the special envoy, "I do not wish to open the letter yet; you may have him come in person to see me. The envoy returned with his report.
Yuan immediately set out, carrying only his meditation satchel. Upon reaching Yuzhang, he heard that Master Nan had passed away, so he stayed there in sorrowful lamentation.
Just then, the elder Huitang came out of the city to meet him. Speaking with him, Huitang marveled at him and said, "It is my regret that the Old Teacher did not live to see you. Yuan then spoke.
He converted the region of Eastern Wu, and those who returned to him were as numerous as clouds. Once, while returning by boat after begging for food, he encountered bandits.
The boatmen cried out in terror as crossed blades flashed before them. Yuan sat calmly and composedly, saying slowly, "I offer everything I possess as a gift;
you must not harm human life. When the bandits had departed and people arrived at dawn, they thought the Master must have died, yet his complexion was unchanged.
During the turmoil, his spirit remained as usual. Regarding the transitions between life and death, or fortune and calamity, he was able to remain detached and free from entanglements in this way.
Since he began preaching the Dharma, his single mat has been desolate; he sat upright for long periods without lying down, remaining as constant for over thirty years as on a single day.
After his passing, his entire body was enshrined in a stupa on Mount Xian.
The Biography of Chan Master Jingfushun:

Master Shun was a native of Western Sichuan. He possessed far-reaching insight and was diligent and tireless in his efforts. Among the junior monks of the monastic community, all honored him as their mother for his virtue.
He received the Dharma from Old Huanglong. When he first left Sichuan, he traveled together with Yuantong Ne;

later, he also spent a very long time traveling with Da jue Lian. One who praised his portrait said: "He traveled with Ne and dwelt with Lian; he received the Dharma from Nan and became Nan’s eldest son.
Yet his karmic conditions were thin, and all the monasteries where he resided were small temples in remote regions. Students passed by him..."
No one at the gate could recognize him. The Master, too, remained transcendent and self-contented, regarding the world as mere motes of dust passing before his eyes.
He lived for over eighty years and passed away while seated on Mount Xiangcheng; his countenance remained as if alive. Throughout his life, he had been close friends with Pan Yanzhi.
As he was about to die, he sent someone to invite him to bid farewell. When Yanzhi arrived, the Master had already departed. He composed many verses to instruct the multitude.
These are all words of virtue. There is a verse that says: "In summer, everyone waves a fan; In winter, they fill the stove with charcoal.
If one can fully understand this, The ignorance of kalpas will vanish instantly. Furthermore, he composed a verse on Zhaozhou’s interrogation of the old woman:
"Zhaozhou asks the way; The old woman replies, 'Go straight ahead. All say she was 'tested and seen through' by the old man."

"Old man! You have no place to clear your name. He also composed verses on the Three Barriers of Huanglong, saying: "The long river’s clouds disperse and the waters flow vast; Suddenly a wild wind rises and the waves grow high.
Failing to recognize the profound mystery of the fisherman’s house, One needlessly tosses about amidst the wind and billows.
He further said: "A Persian from the South Sea enters the Great Tang; If there is one who discerns jewels, they shall deliberate upon them. Or:
Sometimes it meets with the lowly, sometimes with the noble. As the sun reaches the western peaks, the shadows gradually lengthen.

It is also said: "The Old Monk Huanglong had a saying regarding his 'birth affinity. I, this mountain monk, have inherited his lineage; today I shall raise it up for you. I raise it up for you: the cat."
A biased understanding is like catching a mouse.

This is the biography of Chan Master Huiji of Wujiang, whose successor was Chan Master Zhaoqing. His name was Zhaoqing, his courtesy name was Xianzhi, and he was a son of the Lin family of Quanzhou. When young, he was unrestrained...
Relaxing his efforts and letting his spirit roam, he became a great merchant. For over ten years he traveled back and forth across the sea, accumulating vast wealth.
One day, he gave away all his possessions to his siblings, instructing them to support his parents.

With empty hands, he entered Kaiyuan Temple in Zhangzhou, where he left the household life and received full ordination. His fellow villagers marveled at this. After some time, he said to his companions: "A son of the Buddha should seek..."

The Master sought the Way, seeking liberation from birth and death; otherwise, he would have been like a gourd tethered to one place, a mere earthen figure. He subsequently crossed the mountain passes to visit various spiritual teachers (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Later, he met Master Nán of Huánglóng, who showed him the "Three Barriers" (*sanguān*) koans. At first, he did not understand them at all.

Consequently, he served by the Master’s side for a long time until he fully mastered his Way and succeeded him as his dharma heir. He appeared in the world and presided over three monastic seats (*daochang*), including that at Gāoyóu.
Regarding Qianming, Wujiang Huizhi, and Guangling Jianlong: Huizhi was situated in a remote mountain range where there were hot springs and human tracks were rarely seen;
he delighted in dwelling there. As for Qianming and Jianlong, they were places where he was compelled by lay donors and officials, and though he fled from them, he could not escape;
it was not his preference. The Dharma attained by the Master was vast and great.
He was subtle and refined. Furthermore, there was no branch of learning to which he did not attain mastery.

When preaching the Dharma for others, he would sometimes rely on the sutras and śāstras, sometimes on Laozi and Zhuangzi, sometimes on divination and physiognomy, or sometimes on medical prescriptions;

even regarding all manner of worldly matters, he manifested great skillful means according to their individual capacities. He did not merely adhere to the words and phrases of the ancients. Since the Tang dynasty, the Chan school has been widely prevalent.

In this world, there were only the two schools of Yunmen and Linji. At that time, the descendants of Yunmen occupied great monasteries, standing out prominently throughout the regions of Huai and Zhe.
As for the lineage of Linji, from the Yangtze River northward, there was only this master alone.
Consequently, some disciples of Yunmen did not approve of the Master. Upon hearing this, the Master laughed and said, "This is precisely why I am a son of Linji."

He was a disciple of Sun. In his later years, the Master suffered frequently from illness and resigned from the position of abbot. He resided in Gaoyou, where he joined the assembly of Chuan’an, a dharma successor of Liquan.
On the sixteenth day of the eighth month in the fourth year of the Yuanyou era, he passed away while reciting a gāthā.

Lay patrons from Guangling escorted his remains back to Jianlong Temple, where a stupa was erected for them. Among the scholar-officials, those who observed the rites of disciples were as numerous as dragons.
Sun Jue (Xinlao), a Court Attendant of the Imperial Library, together with Yan Mu (Qiuren), an Associate Magistrate of the Department of State Affairs from Wujiang, and others,
felt that because their service had been long and their spiritual affinity was profound, none could compare to Qin Shaoyou (Guang). At that time, being in the capital,
he composed an inscription for his stupa from afar.
The Biography of Chan Master Longqian.
Longqian was the son of the Zhuo family of Gutian, Fuzhou. His mother dreamed that a foreign monk gave her a bright pearl, which she swallowed and subsequently conceived.
Upon his birth, a white light illuminated the room. From childhood, he would not approach wine or meat. At the age of eleven, he entered the service of Mount Sheng in Jianzhou.
Elder Yuan shaved his head and received full ordination at the age of seventeen. At twenty, he took leave of his teacher to travel afar, meeting various great elders.
Finally, he had his mind certified by Master Huanglong Nan. The Master often sighed, saying, "The Way of the Patriarchs has not fallen to the ground;
it rests in this man. While the Master was alive, students already turned toward him; once the Master had passed away, there were no eminent seniors who could surpass him.
As for his successor: during the Xīníng era, Governor Zhāng Jiàn of Lúlíng invited him to reside at Lóngqìng.
Before a year had passed, Governor Wáng Sháo of Zhōnglíng invited him to reside at Lóngquán. Not long after, he requested to leave due to illness.
The clergy and laity of Lúlíng, because he had abandoned Lóngquán, transported him back by boat and settled him in the West Hall of Lóngqìng, where they served him with even greater devotion.
Du. The Master’s nature was pure and ultimate; he had no personal preferences. His appearance was robust and his speech was sparse.
Wherever he went, he stayed alone, rarely engaging with others. Should anyone approach him, he would simply raise a hand and depart.
Initially, while the Master was at Huangbo, he and Cuiyan Shun both served Nanquan as their father; in their spiritual acuity, they yielded to neither. Shun complained to Nanquan, saying: "Xian..."

[The Master] spoke easily. Furthermore, his words had not yet distinguished between defilement and purity. Master Nán said, "The Dharma is thus. To seek it through worldly sentiment is to create right and wrong; how could that be possible?
On the seventh day of the third month in the fourth year of the Yuánfēng era, he addressed the assembly before entering *nirvāṇa*, reciting this verse:
"The physical form has floated in the world; suddenly the physical form floats toward extinction. Fifty-three years—six, seven, and eight months—at Nányuè Tiān."

At the Terrace, amidst the pines and wind, the mountain streams and snow—cherish this, O connoisseurs. Amidst the red furnace, the *utpala* flower; he passed away while sitting in meditation, his countenance and expression unchanged, his hands and feet supple and soft.
His hair, having been shaved, grew back again. The assembly wished to preserve his entire body as a relic, but the Elder Lian followed his final instructions and performed cremation.
When the wood was exhausted and the fire extinguished, his cross-legged posture remained undispersed. Only after adding oil and more fuel did it finally burn away. On that day...
Clouds rose and winds blew; tiles flew and trees were broken. Wherever the smoke reached—among the grasses, trees, sand, and pebbles—all yielded śarīras, golden in color.
When crushed, they were like fine sand. Commoners gathered them and sold them, without ceasing for several days;
the total amount obtained was nearly several *hu*. Su Ziyou wished to compose a record for this, but he doubted the matter while lying ill with a fever. He then dreamed:
A critic remarked, "What is there to doubt? To doubt is itself a sickness. Thereupon, Su Shi composed several hundred words in a dream;

they were exceedingly elegant and sublime. Upon waking, he continued the composition, and his illness was cured accordingly. The inscription briefly states: "I prostrate before the Honored One of the Three Realms."
Master Xian did not stop at this alone. Out of compassion for the narrow-minded and inferior people of the world, he merely demonstrated these minor points.
How well you understand his words! [This was written by] Ziqi (with Daoying appended).

Ziqi was the son of the Xu family of Quanzhou. He received ordination after passing the scriptural examinations and specialized in the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* and the *Awakening of Faith*. Later, he abandoned them to travel to the Yangtze River.
Huai went to pay his respects to Chan Master Zhen of Cuiyan and asked about the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma. Zhen spat on the ground and said, "Where has this single drop fallen?

The Master rubbed his chest and said, "Today, this student suffers from a pain in the spleen. Zhen laughed heartily. He took leave and went to study under Master Nan at Jicui, from whom he fully attained the Way.
Together they deliberated upon the teachings of the past and present. It happened that there was a heavy snowfall, and Master Nan pointed to it and said:
The Master said, "Can this be used to sweep the floor? The Master said, "It cannot.

[The other] asked, "In that case, when the sky clears and the sun rises, and the clouds disperse and fade away, would they ever exist again? For one who knows their existence, all words and phrases are like splitting bamboo;
though there be a hundred nodes, each shall be severed as the blade meets it. How could there be room for sound or deliberation? One day, Master Nanyuan sent a monk.

He posed three reverse questions regarding the "critical words" (guanyu). The Master replied with a stern voice, "You have long been occupied with matters of the past; what do you know of the affairs of the present?

Nanquan was all the more amazed by this, and thus his fame spread throughout the monastic community. After Nanquan passed away, the Fourth Patriarch, Zen Master Foyan, appointed him to share the teaching seat.
Within the room, he gave a hanging word (a koan): "There is a person with a mouth, yet the Way cannot be spoken; who is this person?

Later, when this was transmitted to Chan Master Donglin Zong, he sighed and said, "The Head Seat Qi is like an iron mountain ten thousand fathoms high; it is ultimately difficult to engage him in the flow of his speech."
Not long after, Kaiyuan was established as a Chan monastery, and the Master was invited to serve as its first patriarch. He was granted the title Great Master Juezhao (Awakening Illumination).

Daoying, whose secular surname was Hu, was a fellow native of the Master’s home district; having heard of the Master’s renown, he succeeded him. Daoying’s realization of the ground was stable and profound.
In preaching the Dharma, there are no set paths; one ascends directly to the highest level. Among those of middling or inferior capacity, few are able to encounter this realization.
He once composed a verse saying: "North, south, east, and west, dwelling amidst perilous crags; In the ancient cliff, the cold cassia tree stands lonely and tall.
No one comes to the place where I walk in meditation; To whom shall I entrust the bright moon and the clear breeze? He also said: "Every time I take up my gourd-bowl and set it askew..."
This causes the world to indulge in groundless suspicions. Only after the autumn wind has swept the gardens bare can one truly believe that the character of the cold pine is not lowly.
Chan Master Huanglong Xin transmitted the ancestral mind.
He was a native of the Wu clan from Shixing in Nanxiong. In his youth, he was a renowned scholar; at the age of nineteen, his eyes—
He was blind, yet his parents permitted him to leave the household life; immediately thereafter, he regained his sight. He then went to rely upon Huìquán at Longshān Temple.
The following year, when the scriptural examinations were held, he alone presented a poem. The examiners marveled at it and subsequently reported that he had passed with distinction.

He subsequently resided at Shòuyè Yuàn, where he did not observe the monastic precepts and encountered various adversities. Consequently, he abandoned that place to visit Yúngfēng Yuègōng, who found him difficult to manage due to his stubborn and independent nature.

He informed [his teacher] of his departure. Feng said, "You must go and rely upon Master Huangbo Nan. He resided at Huangbo for four years; though he knew [the truth] was there, his capacity did not yet manifest.
He again took his leave and went up to Yunfeng, but by the time he arrived, Yunfeng had passed away. Consequently, he stayed at Shishuang, where he had no one to consult for resolution.
Later, while reading the *Chuan Deng Lu*, he reached the passage where a monk asked, "What is the bamboo grove of manifold blessings? (and so forth). At that moment—
Suddenly awakened, he saw his two teachers face-to-face and went back to Huangbo. Just as he was spreading out his sitting mat, Master Nan said, "You have entered my room.
The Master leaped for joy and said to himself, "The Great Matter has always been thus;
why does the Master require people to contemplate the phrase and offer responses, searching with every possible means? Master Nan said, "If I did not cause you to investigate in this manner..."
He soon reached the state of non-mental engagement and, seeing it for himself and affirming it within himself, said, "I shall now bury you.

He went to see Cuiyan Zhen, who was greatly amazed by his conversation with him. He also visited Letan Yue, whose mastery of the profound meanings of the sutras and treatises had reached a divine level.
When he heard that his colleagues in various quarters were laughing at him, considering it as "leaving the heights for the depths," the Master said:
"They guard what they have already attained and block the way forward; I, with my study of the 'Wordless,' am like the hundred rivers flowing toward the sea.

Initially, Master Nan had appointed him to share the teaching seat, and upon Nan’s passing, the Master succeeded him. For twelve years, the Way of the Dharma flourished greatly. Furthermore, his nature was authentic...
Xue Shu did not take pleasure in serving and five times requested leave to depart; only then was he able to resign from his post and live in seclusion. His students grew even more devoted to him.
Xie Jingwen, whose courtesy name was Shizhi, was governing Tanzhou. He sent word to the great Maitreya Monastery to invite Xue, but Xue declined three times and did not go.

Furthermore, he instructed Peng Ruli Qizi, the Vice Commissioner of the Jiangxi Circuit Transport Commission, to inquire about the reasons for his refusal to go to Changsha, expressing a desire to meet with Xie.
The Duke did not wish to take charge of Daowei. Prior to Mazu and Baizhang, there was no office of abbot;
practitioners merely sought one another out in the desolate reaches of empty mountains. Although the office of abbot existed thereafter, kings and ministers honored and venerated them.

"While the Teacher of Gods and Men was still alive, he merely registered his name with the government; if he were an ordinary subject, the five-hundred-strong patrol would have simply been dispatched to summon him.
How could he possibly be treated as such? When Shi Zhi heard this, he did not dare to let the affairs of the monastery interfere, and wished to meet him."
Upon arriving in Changsha, Shi Zhi wished to receive his instruction in the Dharma. Master [Nanyue] raised up its fundamental principles for him; Shi Zhi heard what he had never heard before.

Later, he went once to the capital and soon returned to Mount Lu. It happened that Daqi was stationed at Jiujiang, who asked: "When a person approaches the end of life, is there a definitive judgment?
[Nanyue] replied: "There is. [Daqi] said: "I wish to hear the explanation. [Nanyue] said: "Wait until Daqi dies, and then I shall explain it. Daqi—
This inspired Ziqi to increase his respect, saying, "This matter must be entrusted to the Master alone.

For among the high officials of the four quarters, he would respond from a thousand li away if they were harmonious with him, yet would not go even a few houses' distance if they were not. Nanquan’s dignified countenance and majestic virtue were extremely difficult to approach;
even those long experienced in the monastic forests would break into a sweat upon seeing him. Yet the Master went straight before him with an air of profound composure.

Throughout their entire lives they spoke and laughed together; for forty years, master and disciple remained oblivious to their own status. Many among the scholar-officials were awakened by hearing of their character.

Because his skillful means were boundless and his universal compassion was impartial, those who had not yet seen him might have been arrogant or slanderous, but once they encountered his countenance and received his words, none failed to submit with devotion.
As his years grew advanced, he moved increasingly to mountain huts, retiring deep into the remote recesses to abandon all study.

Furthermore, after more than twenty years [of teaching], he passed away in the winter of the third year of the Yuánfú era. He had lived for seventy-six years and had spent fifty-five summer retreats in meditation.
He was posthumously granted the title Bǎojiào (Treasure Awakening) and was buried to the east of Nángōng’s stupa; these two are known as the "Double Stupas."
The Biography of Chan Master Tianyi Huai.
Huai was a native of the Chen family of Leqing, Wenzhou. His ancestors had made their living as fishermen. His mother dreamed that a star fell onto the roof of her house.

A light illuminated the door as she conceived; when the child was born, there were even more auspicious signs. When the boy was young, his father ordered him to sit at the stern of a boat to string fish.
The Master could not bear it and threw the fish into the river. His father grew angry and beat and reviled him, yet he accepted it with equanimity.

Later, he traveled to the capital and relied upon Jingde Temple. He passed the scriptural examination and received ordination. The Master was slender and emaciated, and his gait was slow and deliberate; when seen from afar among the assembly, he resembled a crane.
While among a flock of chickens, it is said that Fahua encountered his teacher in the marketplace; he patted the teacher’s back and said, “Linji and Deshan have gone.
Initially, he visited Shan of Jinkuan, then Xing of Yexian; with neither did he find accord. He then visited Mingjue at Cuifeng.

While the teacher was in charge of preparing the meals, Fahua went to draw water from a mountain stream, whereupon he broke his carrying pole and attained realization of the essential meaning. Mingjue certified his enlightenment. After Fahua took his leave, there was no news of him for a long time. There was a monk...
A man coming from the north of the Huai River said, "I have come to see the world-transcending Iron Buddha. Master Feng had him recite his words of exhortation, which were as follows:
"It is like a wild goose passing through the vast sky; its shadow sinks into the cold water. The goose has no intention of leaving a trace, and the water has no mind to retain the shadow.
Master Jue was deeply impressed by this, considering it akin to his own realization. He first had him comforted and consoled, and only then did he venture to offer the formal greetings of a disciple.
Throughout the various regions, all were impressed by his refined discernment. From Tiexi to Tiantai, he presided over five successive dharma assemblies.
At every location he reached, he invariably manifested celestial pavilions and preached the Dharma with such dynamic mastery that it was difficult for anyone to encounter or behold him.

When Old Man Shun of Mount Lu questioned this, he later heard of these accounts and sighed, saying, "He is truly a true *kalyāṇamitra*. In his later years, due to illness, he resided at Shanshan in Chizhou.
An. His disciple Zhicai resided at Mount Furi in Hangzhou, where he stayed to attend to the Master’s needs and provide medicinal care.

While Zhicai was away in Suzhou and had not yet returned, the Master urged him to come back. Upon arriving at the gate, the Master had already parted from the assembly. Zhicai asked, "The egg-shaped stupa is now complete; what is the ultimate matter?
The Master raised his fist to show him, then lay down, pushed aside his pillow, and passed away. He had lived for seventy years.
2. He sat in summer retreat forty-six times. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa on Mount Foji. During the Chongning era, he was posthumously granted the title Chan Master Zhenzong.
This concludes the biography of Master An Yan'en.
Faan was the son of the Xu family of Linchuan. In his youth, he took leave of his parents to serve as a disciple under the Elder Muxian of Chengtian Monastery.

At the age of twenty, having recited the sutras and received full ordination, he harbored no intention of maintaining his household or inheriting a begging bowl; instead, he sought out masters to inquire about the Way.
He did not perceive the mountains, rivers, cold, or heat. Initially, he relied upon Xuedou Xian; after Xian passed away, he relied upon Tianyi Huai and received his seal of approval (*kanna*).
He resided at the Dharma seat for several years, and his fellow practitioners all ranked him as supreme. Fayun Xiou was particularly close with him in friendship.
At the age of thirty-seven, he took it upon himself with great resolve to adorn the Buddha-lands. He first resided at Ruyi on Mount Huang.

The monastery had dilapidated buildings and ruined walls that offered no protection from wind and rain. The Master labored to renovate it; before ten years had passed, a magnificent hall was completed, appearing as if a celestial palace had descended to earth.
Monks returned, and it eventually became a great monastic center. Thereupon, the Master took his leave once more and traveled to a certain county in Nanchang, where he restored the Yan'en Monastery.
When he first arrived, there were only a few thatched huts and broken beds without wooden slats; yet the Master dwelt therein with transcendent ease.
The County Magistrate Pei Shizhang wished to consolidate the local gentry to renovate the temple for the Master. The Master said, "The Dharma is fundamentally intended to deliver sentient beings.
To force them to do so when they have not yet awakened the aspiration for enlightenment is called 'merely performing labor,' not 'Buddhist practice. He firmly declined his request."

He also resided there for ten years. In every place where he settled the assembly, it was warm in winter and cool in summer; they rang the bells and struck the fish-hammer for morning gruel, and rang the bells and struck the fish-hammer for the midday meal.
Those who came found rest therein. Throughout his travels, his footprints spanned ten thousand *li*, yet he remained solitary with but a single bowl.

He was tirelessly devoted to engaging with sentient beings, making the benefit of living things his primary concern. As for the convergence or divergence of causes and conditions, he left them all beyond his calculations. This was his dwelling at Yan'en.
Those who beheld him could not bear the sorrow [of his absence]. At that time, Master Fayun Xiou had a following of over a thousand;
he preached the Dharma like clouds and rain, and the world in which he dwelt was so adorned that it seemed as though one might join wings with his brothers and soar to heaven.
He sent a letter to summon the Master; the Master opened the letter and merely smiled.

In the seventh month of the Jiazi year of the Yuanfeng era, he manifested illness and passed away in his quarters at Yanyan Temple. He had lived for sixty-one years and had spent forty-one summer retreats in meditation.
A stupa was constructed on the rear mountain, one hundred paces from the temple, where he was interred. Chan Master Lingyuan Qing said to Huang Shan谷 (Shanwu):
When I first resolved to attain enlightenment, it was truly due to the grace of Master Yan’en. Master An admonished and exhorted me as if he were my parent, teacher, or friend;
in my heart, I considered that for anyone dwelling in the mountains, such is the nature of the Dharma. Later, as I traveled through various regions, I rarely encountered anyone like Master An.
Therefore, his instructions to guide my ears remain unforgotten in my mind. As for Master An’s reputation and the offerings he received, they were indeed not... [in excess].
He was able to vie with the eminent masters of the world; yet, even this did not satisfy Master An’s single smile.
For this reason, Shangu composed an inscription for his stupa.
This concludes the biography of Chan Master Haoyuan of Yuyuan in Jingmen Commandery.
Chenghao was the son of Wang from Danling in Meizhou. He left home to become a monk under the guidance of Daliliyuan.

After receiving full ordination, he traveled to various regions and visited Beita, where he realized the essential point of the mind. During the Yuanfeng era, he led the assembly of monks at Guyin, his reputation towering above all quarters.

Zhang Wujin was serving as an envoy to the Jingzhou Southwest Circuit when he went to visit [the Master]. He asked, "From whom did you receive the Dharma? The Master replied, "From Master Guang of Beita.
Zhang asked, "May I hear how you reached a mutual accord with him? The Master said, "It is precisely because of him that he refused to explain it through to others.
Wujin highly approved of these words and subsequently established the Dharma at Dayang in Yingzhou. At that time...
The abbot of Guyin was privately delighted and said, "My head seat has gone out into the world. He gathered a great assembly of both monastics and laypeople, who were filled with admiration.
The Master ascended the seat and said, "I, Chenghao, have been at Guyin for ten years, yet I have never drunk a single drop of Guyin’s water nor chewed a single grain of Guyin’s rice.
If you do not understand this, come to Dayang and I shall explain it to you for you. He then departed.
Leaning on his staff, he descended from the seat and departed with an air of haughtiness. Thereupon, he entered the monastery first;

later, when the local officials of the prefecture and district saw him, they reprimanded him, asking, "What instructions did you receive, Elder, to enter the monastery ahead of us? The Master replied, "I am a man of the mountain forests; who cares for the formalities of prefectures and districts?
He then dragged his staff away and left. Wujin sent a letter to the Governor of Ying, saying: "Hao is a man of the Way; he does not..."
"You may reproach me for failing in worldly etiquette; you ought to extend formal invitations. The abbot followed his words, and the Master had no choice but to return.
Soon after, he was appointed to Yüan-ch'uan. Addressing the assembly, he said: "Last night, the rain poured down in torrents, knocking over the grape trellis.

The administrators, head monks, attendants, and laborers—those who were leaning, they leaned; those who were propping up, they propped up. Propping and leaning, propping and leaning, until daybreak. It remains as it is."

The ancients were truly pitiable. They claimed that this verse concerns matters above the Dharmakāya, yet as Master Fu Dashi said, "Empty-handed, I hold a hoe," and Dongshan said, "On Mount Wutai, clouds steam the rice"—these only eulogize matters on the side of the Dharmakāya.

However, he was a man of transcendent and unrestrained character, not easily categorized as either ordinary or saintly. He once fashioned a loincloth (*vṛṣaṇāvaraṇa*) and wrote the names of the patriarchs of successive generations upon it before wearing it.
He remarked, "Only Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra are slightly superior," and thus inscribed their names on his sash.
Consequently, the monastic community referred to him as "Hao the Loincloth Man. When a local monk imitated him, the Master saw him and scolded him, saying:

“What reasoning do you possess that you dare to treat this as a mere jest? It will be of no avail once you have vomited blood. Soon thereafter, the Master passed away at Lumen (Deer Gate) exactly as he had said.
When Su Changgong arrived in Jingnan, he heard that the Master’s spiritual edge was unassailable; intending to suppress him, he immediately sought an audience while traveling incognito.
The Master asked, “What is your honorable surname? He replied, “My surname is Cheng (Scale). [The Master remarked,] “That is to say, you are one who weighs all under heaven.”
Lao Di was weighing something when the Master gave a shout and said, "Tell me, how much does it weigh? Lao Di had no reply, whereupon he paid him the highest respect.
At the winter solstice, he addressed the assembly, saying: "As the movement of the sun's shadow shifts, my coarse cloth trousers are a brilliant red.
Do not blame me for not washing them; there is nothing else to replace them. A monk entered the room just as a dog was inside. The Master scolded it, and the dog immediately went out.
The Master said, "The dog understands, but you do not. As he was about to pass away, his disciples gathered around him.
The Master smiled and said, "I am eighty-one years old; when I die of old age, my corpse shall be carried out. Let all you young men exert yourselves together!

Of the three hundred and sixty days of the year... Having finished speaking, he passed away. Among the Master's Dharma heirs was one named Wenqing, who resided at Xingjiao in Linxi. He heard [of the Master’s passing]... Xiù.
Yuantong was residing at Xiqian when Huixiu abandoned his assembly to visit him. Yuanqing’s appearance was so haggard that people did not even open their eyes [to look at him].

Huixiu dispatched a supervisor to oversee the rice harvest at Shiqiao Village. Once the supervisor had departed, those with discernment remarked, "Yuanqing has lived in seclusion at Xiangxiang for over ten years;

he is the dharma heir of Master Huihao. Huixiu then sent someone to offer his apologies and to invite Yuanqing back to the mountain. Yuanqing replied, "I shall wait until the harvesters have finished."
Quin then returned. Xiu marveled at him in his heart and recommended him to the assembly, proposing him as his own successor. He resided at Qixian for twenty years before passing away.
This concludes the Biography of Chan Master Gang of Fuyan.
Cigan was the son of the Du family of Tongchuan. His countenance was stern and cold; he was solitary, rigid, and stood out prominently among his peers.

At that time, the monastic community often referred to him as "Iron Face Cigan. He first led the assembly at Chengtian Temple in Jiangzhou. At that time, Chan Master Foyin Yuan was about to move his residence to Qizhou.
The local governor, having heard of his reputation throughout the region, wished for him to succeed [the master] and summoned him to discuss the matter. Cigan said, "I, your servant, reflect..."
This was not enough; the Master intended to finally appoint him as the host for the community’s rice gruel and meals so that they might together establish a monastic center.
[Foyin] did not dare forget his virtue; however, as for the succession of the Dharma, he already had his own teacher. Foyin was inwardly convinced and had already spoken of this.
Because the matter had been settled, [Wuzu] did not dare change it again, and thus began to teach the Dharma as a disciple of Huanglong. His fame became preeminent in his time.
He lived in constant simplicity, carrying his bundle and leaning on his staff within his square-chamber (fangzhang), making no plans for even a single night.

From the regional governor downward, all held him in faith and reverence. Once, when a new Prefectural Governor had recently taken office, he came to confront him with official business. The Master, moved by the encounter, smiled and composed a verse, which he cast into the courtyard of the prefecture and departed without bowing.
The verse said: "The monastery is a monastery within the Great Song Kingdom; The prefecture is a prefecture within the Great Song Kingdom. Within this prefecture..."

There was a monastery where he could not find lodging; what harm was there in wandering with a single bowl across the Five Lakes? The Prefect sent men to pursue him, but he had already crossed the river.
Later, he resided at Fuyan on Mount Nanyue, where he passed away and was interred in a stupa at his dwelling place.
Zhen Dianxiong (Attendant Shan). Zhen was a native of Fuzhou.

He studied under Ciming and applied himself with rigorous austerity. He habitually pointed at his chest with his finger; thus, those throughout the various quarters called him "Zhen Dianxiong" (True Pointing-at-the-Chest).
He delighted in conversation and possessed a spirit that transcended his peers. Together with Attendant Shan, he sat out the summer retreat at Jin...
Luan was a high-ranking disciple of Ciming and truly prided himself on his realization. Having personally met Ciming, he believed there was no one in the world who could satisfy him.
When Ciming spoke with him, he knew Luan had not yet reached full penetration and laughed at him.

One day, while walking in the mountains, as they engaged in a sharp exchange of debate, Luan picked up a piece of tile and placed it upon a flat rock, saying, "If you can produce a turning word regarding this, I will grant that you have truly seen me."
When Zhen was looking left and right as if seeking a response, Ciming scolded him, saying: "You have been hesitating and halting your faculties;
your consciousness has not yet penetrated. When did you ever even dream of this? Zhen was filled with shame and trepidation, and immediately returned to Shishuang.

When Ciming saw him, he rebuked him, saying: "A true traveler of the Way must know the proper timing. What urgent business brought you here so soon, not long after the summer retreat ended? Zhen wept.
[Daowu] said, "Because my elder brother Shan was possessed by a poisonous mind that ultimately obstructed others, I have come to see the Master.
Mingju asked, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? He replied, "Cloudless, clouds arise upon the ridge; moon present, the moon sets in the heart of the waves.
Mingju glared at him and shouted, "With hair white and teeth falling out, you still hold such a view! How will you ever escape birth and death? This is truly not [it]."
He dared not look up; tears flowed down his cheeks. After a long while, he stepped forward and asked, "I do not know what constitutes the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma.
Ming said, "No clouds arise upon the peaks; the moon descends into the heart of the waves. Upon these words, [Fengxue] attained great enlightenment.

From then on, his intellectual eloquence was swift and incisive, and the monastic communities stood in awe of him. He entered the world to reside at Cuiyan, where he frequently cited the karmic occasion of Luzu’s wall-gazing.

He asked the scholar, "There are few who have attained resonance with this. He himself composed a verse, saying: "Severing the ten thousand peaks and myriad mountains, I urge people to eliminate the difficulties of right and wrong.
In Chiyang, there has been no news lately; The prediction of that year was not for self-examination.
He once said, "The Buddha-dharma throughout the world is like a single boat. My elder brother, Master Kuān of Dàníng, sits at the head, while I occupy the stern."
Among them, Zhen was truly capable of taking the lead; whether he went east or west, it was up to him. The Elder Zhenggong was also a successor of Ciming;

by nature he excelled at lecturing, and many who followed him were devoted to the study of the *Yi* (Book of Changes). One day, when Zhen saw Zhenggong, he tucked up his robes with his hands, exposing both his calves, and walked past slowly.
Zhenggong asked him about this in astonishment, and Zhen said: [...]* *Note: The source text provided ends abruptly after "Zhen said. This translation reflects the available portion.*
"The front porch and the rear eaves are all nothing but tangled vines; I fear they might trip you up. Zheng laughed heartily and said, "True Brother, we are fellow practitioners.
Why must you revile me whenever you see someone? Zheng stared at him intently and said, "How could I ever revile you?
I have kept this mouth of mine prepared solely for reviling Buddhas and Patriarchs. What business is it of yours? His resolute strength was such that he could not be bent.
As he was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he manifested a severe illness and great suffering. He spread straw mats upon the ground and turned over and over, finding no rest.

His attendant, Zhè, wept as he said, "Throughout your life you reviled the Buddhas and scolded the Patriarchs; why now have you come to such a state? Zhēn rebuked him, saying, "Do you still hold such views?
He immediately rose and sat in the full lotus posture, commanding that incense be burned. As the smoke rose, he passed away. Sān returned seven times.

In Min, there was a prophecy concerning Ciming that his "scale-weight would fall into the well. From Fenglin, he moved to Zifú, where he remained unremarkable and left no significant reputation behind.
Consequently, his words and phrases rarely circulated in the world. What a pity!
Chan Master Xuan (Haoyin) of Guizong Monastery in Jiujiang, Song Dynasty.
A native of Hanzhou, he became a monk in his prime and went beyond the gorges to rely upon Master Langya Huijue.
Suddenly, with a single phrase, his many doubts were instantly resolved. Langya approved of him, and before long, he was ordered to share the teaching seat. Layman Gengong of Jingkong...

Wang Gongfu once visited the Master’s gate to inquire about the Way and his character. Later, when the Master was leading the community at Nanzong, Gongfu was serving as the Commandant of Nanchang and subsequently became the Governor of Nan’gang.
Resenting that the Master did not pay him formal obeisance, he subjected the Master to various forms of harassment. The Master then sent a letter to Gongfu, saying:

"My karmic ties in this world still have six years remaining that have not yet been exhausted. Now, having no choice but to endure your oppression, I wish to take rebirth in your family. He looked forward to...

The Master and his disciple illuminated one another, and then he transformed and departed. Gongfu received the letter and was filled with joyful surprise. In the middle of the night, his wife saw the Master enter her bedchamber in a dream.
She cried out in alarm, "This is not the place where the Monk comes from! Gongfu shook her awake and questioned her; she related what she had seen.
He called for a lamp, took the letter, and showed it to her. Consequently, she conceived. When the child was born, they named him Xuānlǎo (Old Man Xuán). At the age of one...
His age was as it had been in former times. By the time he was three years old, Master Baiyun Yuan passed by his home.
Chenggong invited him out to meet him; upon seeing him from afar, he called out, "Teacher and nephew! Yuan asked, "How many years has it been since we parted from the Master?
Pointing his fingers, Chenggong said, "Four years. Yuan asked, "Where did we part? He replied, "At Bailian Zhuang. Yuan asked, "What serves as proof?"
[The monk] said, "Grandfather, Mother, please invite the Master for a meal tomorrow. At that moment, there was the sound of a cart being pushed outside the gate.

Xuedou asked, "What is that sound outside the gate? [The monk] then made the gesture of pushing a cart. Xuedou said, "What about after it has passed? [The monk] replied, "A ditch across level ground."
He passed away peacefully after six cycles of the fruit [of his practice].
Chaoxin, whose secular name was Haiyin, was a native of Gui Prefecture. He was also a successor of Langya and resided at Dinghui Temple in Suzhou.

Having propagated the Way for many years, his reputation was preeminent in his time. At over eighty years of age, he had long been supported by the household of Defense Official Zhu and frequently visited his residence.
One day, Zhu asked, "Master, will you be able to come to your disciple’s home to take rebirth in a future life?
The Master smiled and nodded in assent. Upon returning to the monastery, he fell ill and passed away after several days. On that day, at Zhu’s house—
A daughter was born. At that time, Chan Master Yuanzhao was residing at Rui Guang Temple; hearing of this event, he went to visit her.
Just as she emerged from the month [of birth], she was held out; upon seeing him, she smiled. Yuanzhao called out, "Haiyin, you have made a mistake.
The girl wept several times and then vanished. There are verses on the "Wild Fox" of Baizhang and a poem by the Old Monk, which were widely circulated throughout the monastic community.
Recite: Ying Zhongwen said, "Faith is the enlightened eye of the patriarchs.
The Biography of Master Lin of Yuehuashan (including Yun Da). Master Lin was a native of Duzhu in Qujiang.
His surname was Deng. In his youth, he studied Confucianism and was able to discourse on the grand strategies of the kings and lords.

He studied Buddhism and attained liberation through the recitation of sutras. He was proud of his own poetic talent and traveled between the regions of Jianghuai, where he read extensively and maintained a vast memory;

thus, he was regarded as a "monk of letters. However, he later realized this was not the truth and completely cast aside his former habits. He went to visit Master Bao at Dongshan, who, upon seeing him, recognized that he possessed great potential.
After some time, the Master transmitted the mind-seal to him. Consequently, he returned south and built a hermitage on his former mountain.

This was the White Lotus [Temple]. When students heard its fame, those who came from afar were beyond counting. The Prefect submitted a formal petition on behalf of the multitude requesting that the Master take up the abbacy.
The Master hid within the Great Cave for several months; yet as the crowd’s seeking did not cease, he was eventually found and reluctantly complied with their request.

From then on, whenever officials in court robes or commoners in lay dress passed by the riverbank, there were none who did not moor their boats and visit his chamber. The Master delighted in profound discourse and brought them to a state of sublime realization.
Everyone who encountered him attained realization and returned home. Monastics from the four quarters flocked to his path; under a single word, they reached the essential core of the mind.

Those who became teachers of men numbered in the dozens. In his later years, he avoided clamor and retired to live in the West Hall. Because of this, practitioners from all quarters came to call him "Master Lin of the West Hall.
As Mount Baolin was the site of the Sixth Patriarch’s practice hall, an imperial edict selected him for his renowned virtue, bestowing upon him a distinguished title and command.
He wore [the robes] to dwell in them, and the Official of the Transport Office (Zaotai) proposed his elevation to office; he firmly declined and would not go.

He then built a brick burial vault at his own hermitage, saying, "I shall return my bones to this place. This site was formerly the location where the monk Lang Hong of Yuehuashan propagated the Dharma.
After Lang passed away, the assembly dispersed and the temple subsequently fell into ruin. When the Master [Zhanran] restored it on a grand scale, everyone declared him to be Lang’s reincarnation.

Lord Xiang Yu Jing inscribed his funerary stele, saying: "The nature and characteristics of reality are fundamentally unconditioned; when they encounter physical forms, they are subject to maintenance or decay.
In years to come, this illusory body shall return here; he once said that there is no Buddha, effectively dispelling the notion of a knowing subject. Yun Da was from Yangshuo, Guizhou.
Ren once said: "Life is fundamentally without substance; how can there be a native hometown? Awakening resides within the mind; why indulge in frivolous discourse?
He traveled south to Dongshan, where Master Bao transmitted to him the essentials of the Mahāyāna.
Ultimately, he did not emerge into the world, but remained hidden in the Yellow Dragon Cave on Mount Luofu, attaining realization for himself alone.
The Biography of Master Xinxin of Fuchang.

Xinxin was born into the Xiao clan of Min County, Fuzhou. The Xiao family made their living by fishing. When he was a child, he would follow his father to fish in the river and immediately cast aside whatever they caught.
Furthermore, he was naturally unimpeded in all matters and free from anxiety, resentment, suspicion, or fear; he was ever composed and harmonious.
He spoke thus. His words were perhaps beyond the reach of ordinary human understanding. At the age of twelve, he left home and practiced the dhūta austerities with great severity.
While traveling in the mountains, he encountered a tiger and vowed, "If I am destined to don the robes of the Tathāgata and become an eye for the world, may you not harm me.
The tiger tucked its tail and departed. At the age of twenty-six, having met the requirements for reciting the scriptures, he obtained the monastic robes.
In his ordinary life, he labored together with the common folk, working with their single hands. He studied under many teachers and followed various practices.
Finally, he entered the quarters of Jia Shan Zhen; teacher and disciple were in perfect accord, like a stone cast into water, meeting no resistance.
In his reception of people, the Master did not employ the barriers of surging waves or perilous cliffs to block or distance them;

yet, those who were not karmically compatible could never find the gate through which to enter. At Jia Shan, he served as head of the workmen and the kitchen steward for over ten years, planting cypress and pine trees until they filled the mountains, and turning all uncultivated land—both on water and on dry ground—into fields.
He resided at Chan Chang Temple for twenty-one years, from its very beginning.

He wore garments of grass and ate from the trees; he slept and ate within a few dilapidated rooms. Before long, he lived in a grand hall where he was no longer aware of cold or heat, providing offerings for several hundred people.
The Master adorned these matters with solemnity, never flagging for even a single day. Someone once advised him, saying, "Why trouble your physical body to attend to such worldly affairs?
It would be sufficient to dwell in leisure and cultivate the Way. The Master replied, "All worthy sages emerge from and enter into the world..."
"Death. To accomplish the welfare of boundless sentient beings, if one's practices and vows remain unfulfilled, it cannot be called the fulfillment of bodhi.

What kind of person am I? I shall exert myself all the more for their sake. On the intercalary twelfth month of the third year of Yuanyou, he manifested illness. When asked about the time of day, he replied: [He passed away].
It was noon. He rose from his seat and passed away at the age of fifty-nine. He was buried to the left of Chan Master Shanshi of Fuchang.
He had a *yulu* (recorded sayings), which Huang Shanggu wrote an epilogue for and circulated.
Fashou (with Xiaoshou appended).
Fashou was a native of Longcheng in Qinzhou. He was born into the Xin clan. His mother dreamed that an elderly monk sought lodging, saying, "I am a monk from Maiji Mountain.
Upon waking, she became pregnant. Prior to this, there had been a monk at Maiji Mountain whose name has been forgotten. Every day...
He recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and was on good terms with Master Lu of Yingqian Temple.

Once, wishing to travel abroad under Master Lu, he was about to depart when Lu, seeing that he had grown old, said to him: "In the future, you should seek me out before the Bamboo Mat Slope and below Iron Strong Ridge."

Suddenly, a boy was born there. When Master Lu heard of this, he went to see him. The boy smiled at him once. At the age of three, he wished to follow Lu back home; consequently, he adopted Lu’s surname.

By nineteen, he had mastered the scriptures and become a great monk. His celestial bone-structure was lofty and prominent; amidst the ten thousand monks, he stood out majestically, as if a figure from a painting.
When he lectured on the Great Sūtras, he analyzed every chapter and dissected every phrase, penetrating them directly and transversely with a sharpness of wit that left no room for hesitation.
This was indeed touchable; his reputation resounded throughout the capitals of Jing and Luo. He relied upon the *Guifeng Chao* (The Compendium of Guifeng) to analyze and evaluate various meanings.
However, he harbored a regret: Guifeng studied Chan while paying exclusive respect to Yuan of the Northern Capital’s Huayan school. Yet, he lamented that Yuan was not a lecturer. [He reasoned:
"If the teachings exhaust the Buddha’s intent, then one such as Master Yuan should not disparage the teachings. If Chan is not the Buddha’s intent, then one such as Guifeng should not study Chan."
However, I did not believe that the World-Honored One had privately transmitted the Dharma outside the formal teachings to Mahākāśyapa; thus, I ceased my lectures and traveled south.
Addressing my fellow students, I said: "I shall exhaustively investigate his lair, root out his kindred, and annihilate them, only then having repaid the Buddha's kindness.
Upon first arriving at Huguo Monastery in Suizhou, I read the stele inscription for Chan Master Jingguo and began to harbor doubts.

Yet he remained resentful and dissatisfied. When he eventually went to visit Master Huai at Wúwéi, he saw that the master sat with a stern, austere countenance, his tears falling so as to soak his robes;
[Daoxuan] was somewhat contemptuous of him. Huai then wiped away his tears and asked, "What sutra does the Preceptor lecture upon?

He replied, "The *Avataṃsaka*. He asked again, "What is the fundamental principle of the *Avataṃsaka*? He replied, "The Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is its principle. He asked further, "And what is the principle of the Dharma-realm?"
The Master said, "The mind is the fundamental principle. He asked again, "What is the fundamental principle of the mind? The Master was unable to answer.

Huai said, "A difference of a hair's breadth results in worlds as far apart as heaven and earth. The Master withdrew, overcome with self-reproach and struck with awe; he then respectfully submitted, vowing to remain and receiving the Dharma day and night.
When Master Huai went from Chizhou to Wuzhou, the Master followed him for ten years. He first began to propagate the Dharma at the four borders of Huai.
On the mountain, he possessed nothing beyond his staff and alms bowl, maintaining only the basic requisites. His disciples followed him tirelessly, enduring hunger and cold.
Lamenting that the ancestral Way was failing and the monastic communities were withering away, the Master took it upon himself to revitalize them. He had resided at Qixian for many years;

after the passing of Master Yuan of Jiangshan, Emperor Shu invited the Master with due ceremony to succeed him on the seat. When the Master arrived at the mountain, the Emperor visited him both before and after his arrival.

However, as the Master was occupied with administrative affairs of the monastic community (sōrin), he did not see the King from time to time. The King, taking this to be an act of arrogance toward himself, became estranged and departed.
He went to stay at Changlu in Zhenzhou, where his assembly numbered over a thousand people. When an Elder from Quanpao arrived and ascended the seat, the assembly looked upon him with smiles.
No one came forward to ask a question. Thereupon, the Master stepped forward, bowed, and hurriedly asked, "What is the self of Fa-xiu?
Quan-jiao laughed and said, "Xiu has an iron face; does he not recognize his own self? The Master replied, "Those who are in the midst of the game are often deluded.
Thus, the entire assembly marveled at his resolve to uphold the Dharma. Imperial Princess Jiguo built Fayun Temple and subsequently issued an imperial decree appointing the Master as its abbot.

The founding patriarch [Dongshan Liangjie]. Emperor Shenzong dispatched an imperial messenger to bestow incense and a robe made of ground silk, while also transmitting the Imperial Decree to express the etiquette of the Emperor’s own personal visit.
Day and night, scholars and officials came to inquire about the Way. At that time, Sima Guang (the Duke Wen) was just beginning his tenure as a high official;
fearing that the Dharma of our school was becoming too prevalent, he sought to regulate it. The Master said: "Your Excellency is brilliant and a hero among men; this is not due to—"
The Buddha-dharma cannot be thus; how could it suddenly rely on the power of deluded vows? Lord Wen did not take this to heart. In the eighth month of the fifth year of the Yuanyou era, he lay ill.
An imperial edict summoned a physician from the Hanlin Academy to attend to him. When the physician requested to examine his pulse, the Master looked up at him and said:
"Who are you? I am ill and shall simply die. To seek to live is to regard life as something worth clinging to. He remained composed.

Regarding the dream of birth and death, he made no distinction between the three [realms], casting them all aside. He called for his attendant, changed his robes, sat upright, and passed away while reciting three lines of verse.
He had lived in this world for sixty-four years and spent forty-five summers in seated meditation.

Li Gonglin, whose style name was Bo-shi, was a master at painting horses, rivaling none in his skill; yet the Master rebuked him, saying: "You are a scholar-official who has gained fame through painting. Furthermore—"

Furthermore, when he painted horses, people expected him to produce works of such exquisite skill that they would marvel at them; yet even entering the belly of a horse was enough to cause fear. For this reason, Li Bai Shi (Li Gonglin) ceased painting.
His teacher urged him to paint images of Avalokiteśvara to atone for his transgressions. Huang鲁直 (Huang Tingjian) composed flowery verses, which people vied with one another to disseminate.
The teacher rebuked him, saying, "Would you so willingly apply the subtlety of your brush and ink to such things? Huang Tingjian laughed and said:
"Furthermore, would you have me end up in the belly of a horse? The Master said, "With your seductive words, you have stirred the lustful hearts of people throughout the world.
It is not merely that you will end up in the belly of a horse; I fear you will instead be reborn in the hells.

When Wang Shun Jinjing, the Prince of Huaiyin and General of the Household, visited the Master, the Master was in the midst of entertaining guests. Jinjing waited for him by painting ink bamboo on the western veranda. The Master arrived, but—
When he bowed and looked back, he was displeased; once the Duke of Jin had departed, he immediately smeared it over.

Huaixiu had relied upon Master Huai for the longest time, and both were renowned as those who had "fully experienced" the Way and possessed great reputations; thus, the monastic community referred to him as "Little Xiū," implying that the Master was the "Great Xiū.
Upon hearing the "Three Barriers" (Sanguan) of Chan Master Nán, Little Xiū wished to go see him. The Master said: "I..."
He was no longer in doubt. Xiaoshou then traveled alone, and after some time, he attained realization and became a successor to Master Nan.
Hearing that the Master was residing at Qixian, he sent him a verse, saying: "Seven hundred eminent monks fought upon the field of Dharma; with a single verse from Master Lu, they all surrendered."

"No one cuts off the road to Huangmei; it is only by chance that one passes through the nine rivers so far away. The Master smiled and set the matter aside. Xiaoxiu was the son of the Ying family of Yiyang;
his family had been engaged in the study of Confucianism for generations. He entered the monastic life at Dayue and propagated the Way of Huanglong.
He composed "Verses on the Three Barriers," which were widely circulated throughout the monastic communities.
The Biography of Chan Master Yuanzhao Zongben.
He was the son of the Guan family of Changzhou. By nature, he was simple and lacked artificial refinement; his appearance was robust and substantial, and his speech was free from flowery elaboration.

At the age of nineteen, he took refuge under Chan Master Daosheng of Yong’an at Chengtian Monastery in Suzhou. Wearing tattered robes and with a face covered in grime, he maintained a life of austerity.
Jiudian served as the cook to provide for the assembly. At night, he would enter the room to attend to the Way.

Dao Sheng asked him about his weariness, and he replied, "If one were to abandon even a single dharma, it could not be called the fulfillment of bodhi. Since I truly desire to realize this in my present body, how could I dare speak of weariness?

Dao Sheng secretly marveled at this. After another ten years, he shaved his head and received full ordination. He served with diligence for three years before taking leave of Dao Sheng to travel abroad. At first...
He arrived at Chizhou and paid his respects to Master Huai. Upon hearing the Master’s words, he attained realization; yet none among the assembly were aware of it.
He once served as the attendant, and he was so fond of sleeping that his snoring was loud. Those who heard it grew weary of it and reported it to Master Huai.

Master Huai laughed and said, "This boy is a banner of diligence for my house. You all shall depend upon him in the future; do not speak of this much. The assembly was then astonished. When [Master Huai] passed away...
Master Gong moved his residence to Tiantai in Yue and later to Jianfu in Changzhou; both followed him there. At the beginning of the Zhìpíng era, Master Huái retired to Shòuśèng on Wújiāng.
When Commissioner Lí Fùguī visited Master Huái, they conversed at night, and Lí said, "The Dharma seat of Ruìguāng is vacant;
I wish to have a monk of true realization take charge of it. Master Huái pointed to Fǎběn and said, "None surpasses this man."
He was merely a human being. Once he arrived at Rui Guang, the assembly gathered in great numbers, reaching five hundred people.
Chen Gongxiang, the Governor of Hangzhou, earnestly entreated him, saying: "I borrow the Master for three years to plant blessings for this region; I dare not occupy you for long."
The number of students was twice that at Rui Guang. Subsequently, the people of Suzhou requested him to reside at the two monasteries of Wanshou and Longhua;
more than a thousand people came to welcome him, saying, "We first borrowed our Master for three years, and now nine years have passed; we wish to take him back with us.
The Governor of Hangzhou dispatched a county magistrate with soldiers and guards to protect him, so they were unable to take him away. In the fifth year of the Yuanfeng era, by means of the Way...
The Master entrusted his disciple Shanben with the site and resided at Ruipeng Hermitage. When the people of Suzhou heard of this, they plotted to seize it even more urgently;
fearing that their own strength would not prevail, they did not yet dare to act. At that time, Censor-in-Chief Master Zeng Xiaoxu happened to be in Suzhou;
having once sought the Way from the Master, he visited him at the hermitage and provided a boat at the river crossing. Once the Master had bid him farewell and departed, [Shanben] escorted him.
Upon boarding the boat, he conversed and laughed with them as they traveled back home to comfort the longing of the people of Suzhou.
Thereupon, he returned to Fuzhen Yuan on Mount Qionglung; at that time, he was sixty-three years old.

Not long after, Emperor Shenzong reorganized the sixty-four courtyards of Xiangguo Monastery into eight Chan and two Vinaya schools, issuing an imperial summons for the Master to preside over Hui-lin Monastery. Once arrived, he was summoned for an audience.

At the Yanhe Hall, after the "Mountains Cry" (shanhū) ritual was concluded, the Emperor ascended the hall and granted him a seat. The Master immediately took his place, sitting with his legs crossed in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*).
The attendants looked at one another in astonishment, yet the Master remained composed. The Emperor asked which monastery he had studied at, and he replied, "Chengtian Yong'an. Tea was then served.
He raised his cup and drank deeply, then swirled it about. The Emperor was pleased by his sincerity. Zhiyu said, "The Chan school is just beginning to flourish; you should provide excellent guidance.
After the Emperor withdrew, he watched him with his eyes and said to those around him, "He is a truly blessed and wise monk.

On the first day of the Yuanxiao festival, when the imperial carriage visited the residence of Chancellor Zhishi, none of the assembly came forward to welcome him. The Master, receiving the Emperor’s profound praise, propagated the Buddha-dharma.

Matters. The people of the capital and the four directions placed their great trust in him. When the Shenzong Emperor passed away, the Master was summoned to enter the Funing Hall to preach the Dharma.
Seeing that the Master had been honored and respected by the late Emperor, those around him were overcome with sobbing and could not contain their grief.

In the first year of the Yuanyou era, he requested to return home on account of his old age; the court granted his request and issued an imperial decree allowing him to wander freely as he pleased, and no one was permitted to restrain him wherever he went.
When he was appointed as abbot, he ascended the seat with joy and addressed the assembly, saying: "I am originally a guest without a home; how could I bear to wander at will?

With a favorable wind, I shall add oars and rudders to my boat and sail down to Yangzhou. Once he had departed the capital, carriages and horsemen belonging to kings, dukes, and nobles followed in an unending procession to see him off.
The Master instructed them, saying: "The years and months cannot be toyed with; old age and sickness do not wait for anyone."
"Exert yourselves in cultivation and do not be indolent; this is the true purpose of our meeting. Those who heard this were moved to tears.

In his later years, he resided at Lingyan. His successors who transmitted the Dharma are beyond counting. On the *jiazi* day of the twelfth month in the second year of the Yuánfú era, as he was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he bathed and lay down.
His disciples gathered around him and entreated him, saying: "The Master’s Way has spread throughout the world. Now..."
"One cannot do without a verse for the day. Please, exert yourself and sit upright. The Master stared at him intently and said, "Foolish child!

Even in my ordinary moments, I am too lazy to compose verses. What is the point of making such a special effort today? When I wish to lie down, I simply lie down; I cannot make a special effort to sit up today.
Thereupon, he lay down heavily as if in deep sleep. When his disciple, Tachuan, shook him, the Master had already departed. — Disciple Tachuan’s Record of the Tower (Tachiuan-ta)
He passed away at Lingyan Mountain. He had lived through eighty years of the world and completed fifty-two summer retreats.
*Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks*, Scroll Eight;
*Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks*, Scroll Nine.
The Chapter on Practicing Chan, compiled by the Śramaṇa Minghe of Huashan Temple in Wumen;
the Biography of Chan Master Quan of Huangbo in the Song Dynasty.
