Daquan was the son of the Wang family in Luoyang. From birth, he abstained from pungent foods and meat. His parents sent him to serve his maternal uncle, Master Guang’ai Yan, by whom he received full ordination.

At twenty, he received the precepts and traveled to Pengcheng, subsequently visiting Shouchun. There, he received the teachings of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* and the *Śītalā-vyākhyāna* from Dharma Master Cheng;
what he received from his teacher in the morning, he was able to lecture upon for his disciples by evening. In Pengcheng, there was a recluse...
Master Dong recognized that his teacher was no ordinary man and urged him to travel south to inquire after the Unsurpassed Way.
The Master then abandoned what he had studied and crossed the river; first, he followed Chan Master Ganlu, but saw nothing at all. He subsequently followed Chan Master Xiu of Qixian.
Fengxiu was courageous in instructing others, demonstrating to them the pivotal mechanism of the Way (*dōjī*).

When [his disciples] were bewildered and unable to enter, they felt deep regret and remorse, even to the point of consuming foul food and drinking bitter water to discipline themselves. This continued for seven years. Fengxiu then traveled to Gaoyang to serve Chan Master Zhenjing Wen.
After five years, he attained enlightenment and told Wen: "With a single blow of the mallet, I have penetrated the bottomless treasury; all manner of precious jewels [are now revealed]."
"All these are mine. Wen approved of this. From then on, his speech and verses flowed forth like a gushing spring.

The Governor of Gaoyang invited him to reside at Shitai Qingliang, but he had already moved to Huangbo. By nature, the Master was straightforward, simple, and sincere; he did not adorn himself with external matters.
In the sixth year of the Yuanfeng era, the Master fell gravely ill. He sought medical treatment in the marketplace. At that time, Su Che of Meishan was in exile...
Gao'an. The Master said to him, "You are tranquil and wise; you are fit to study the Way. Furthermore, he said, 'My illness is due to past karma;
it is likely that I shall not rise again. You must keep the Way in mind so that we may meet again at another time; do not forget one another. His illness then slightly improved."
He lived in seclusion in the mountains. In the winter of the following year, as Zhe was about to depart for Jixi, he thought the Master would surely come to bid him farewell;
however, the Master did not emerge from his room due to illness. On the *yichou* day of the twelfth month, he took leave of the assembly, sat in the lotus posture, and passed away.

His body was fragrant and supple. It remained for fifteen days before being cremated, yielding countless lustrous *śarīra*. He was forty-nine years old and had thirty years of ordination. He was subsequently buried.
To the right of the Duanji Pagoda, I, Che, have composed this inscription.
Regarding the Biography of the Elder Huizhi of Shitou:
The Elder Huizhi was a native of the Wu clan in Wuzhou. At the age of fourteen, he took Baocheng of Zhihui Monastery as his teacher.

He underwent the tonsure examination for which he was well-prepared. By nature, he was serene and simple, and he was thoroughly versed in the *Sūtras* and *Śāstras*. The scholars of Eastern Wu revered and served him.
He once said to a guest, "I wish to synthesize the doctrines of the three schools—Tiantai, Xianshou, and Weishi—into a single work to put an end to the disputes over their divergent traces.
At that moment, a Chan practitioner sitting at the end of the row asked, "Who is the patriarch of the Xianshou school?"
Zhì said, "The Venerable Dushun. The Chan practitioner said, "Dushun has a verse on the Dharmakāya which says:

'In Huai Prefecture, an ox eats grain; in Yi Prefecture, a horse’s belly swells. One searches the world for a physician, yet applies moxibustion to the left shoulder of a pig. To what principle does this meaning correspond?
Does it accord with the Tiantai or the Weishi (Vijñaptimātra) schools? Zhì was unable to answer. The Chan practitioner said, "Why do you not travel to seek teachers elsewhere?"
Thereupon, Zhì ceased his lectures and traveled south to Jiānshān, where he encountered Master Yúnnán.
He studied under him for a very long time before departing to travel along the Xiang River. For over twenty years, he resided at Yúnxī on Shítóu; his temperament was serene and refined.
Whenever he encountered guests, he rarely spoke. When an attendant questioned him about this, Zhì said, "Those high officials of the court are full of knowledge and talkative;
I am but a monk who eats his rice gruel. Upon seeing them, my mouth naturally becomes dull. He then composed a verse: "All affairs brought to rest, I entrust myself to the simple and the foolish;
My traces at times allow the wild deer to join me. Without removing my hempen robe, I make my fist a pillow; For many lifetimes, my dreams have remained within the green [mountains]."
Luohan. Someone asked him, "What is the flavor of dwelling in the mountains? He replied, "Dwelling in the mountains, I shut my thatch door alone with no other pursuits.
Three pieces of firewood are roasted in the shape of the Chinese character for 'three' (品); there is no need to wield a brush for literary elegance to be revealed.
In the first year of the Chongning era, at the age of sixty-two, he took up his staff and went to Long’an; no one could stop him. One day, he asked an attendant monk, "The sun..."
When was this? He replied, "It was evening. He then smiled and said, "We have met within a dream; I have already awakened from my sleep.

You need only not bring disgrace upon the monastic community, and that itself will be repaying the Buddha's kindness. Having spoken these words, he passed away peacefully. His remains were collected and enshrined in a stupa beneath Nanyue Lufeng.
Master Fayun Gaofeng succeeded Chan Master Fozhao Gaofeng.
From his youth, he traveled to various regions to study under Master Yuan Tongji, who appointed him as the head of the assembly and charged him with wielding the whisk.

Because his responses were slow and his speech hesitant, the assembly mocked him, leaving him with a flush of embarrassment. The following day, while tea was being served in the Sangha Hall, he saw the tea ladle fall.
He leaped from the ground and attained the Samādhi that Responds to Capabilities. Later, relying on Zhenjing and reading the patriarchal verses, he suddenly attained great enlightenment.
He said to others, "On the twenty-first day of the eleventh month in the third year of the Shaosheng era, I realized the Zen of the square inch within.
He left the world to reside at Guizong, and was subsequently summoned by imperial decree to dwell at Jingyin. Because Fugao had investigated with vigor and reached profound depths, his words...

It was not the proper time. Whenever he addressed the assembly, he would often cite the old monk. In the eighth year of the Xining era, official documents were being submitted at Fengxiang Prefecture;
that very year, Mount Hua collapsed for forty li, burying eighty villages and their inhabitants.
"How will you young people—mere eggplants and gourds—ever know this? Or he would be questioned, saying: "Upon the precious lotus throne, why do you always..."
They were discussing the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Daogao said, "Foolish men! How could there be two Buddha-natures?
Once, while the Master was at Guizong, after his evening devotions were concluded, he was sitting by the hearth in the monks' hall. Suddenly, he saw two monks enter the hall;

one had a thick, bushy beard and hair as white as snow, while the other was a youth, both possessing tall and elegant statures. The Master felt a surge of joy and thought to himself, "Under my seat..."
When the two monks had thus departed from the hall, the Master followed them out of curiosity. He saw them enter the Buddha Hall; he too followed them inside.
The lamp light flickered brightly, and there was still fire in the incense burner. The Master lit incense and prostrated before the Buddha.

The two monks emerged once more, and he continued to follow behind them until they reached the front of the Buddha Hall, where they suddenly vanished. He thought to himself that he had forgotten his incense box.
The Abbot returned to retrieve it and found that the palace gate was locked and barred. He then summoned the temple attendants to open the door and enter.
At that time, he saw that the incense smoke in the burner had not yet dissipated and the casket was upon the jeweled steps; he could not fathom the reason for this.
It was because Gao’s practice of the Way was so sincere that his spiritual resonance reached unimpededly across the unseen realm; truly, there are matters beyond the reach of thought.
Chan Master Dàtōng Běn inherited the lineage from Shànběn.
His clan was Dòng, a descendant of Zhòngshū of the Hàn dynasty. His ancestors originally resided in Zhòngshū Village in Dàkāng;
his grandfather Qí and father Wēn both served as officials in Yǐng, and thus he became a native of Yǐng. His mother had no children, so she prayed to the White-Robed Great Being (Pīpóshā).

He made a vow, saying, "If I have a son, he must serve the Buddha. He immediately adopted a vegetarian diet and soon became pregnant. When the child was born, his skeletal features were exceptionally refined and extraordinary.
At one year of age, he lost his father and was raised by his maternal great-uncle, Jie. Upon reaching adulthood, he became widely learned and maintained a life of pure cultivation.

After his mother passed away, he mourned her with grief exceeding the prescribed rites. Having no intention of pursuing official service, his temperament was firm and unbending; he remained silent and aloof, looking upon high officials with white eyes. [The Emperor] praised him.

In the eighth year of the Yō era, he arrived at Jizō-in in the capital. There, he passed the examination on the sutras and received ordination. He studied the Vinaya and took delight in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
One night, he dreamed of a youth resembling Sudhana as depicted in secular paintings, who joined his palms and led him toward the south. Upon waking, he said:

"The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have bestowed their grace upon me. Do you wish for me to seek out teachers to the south? At that time, Yuanzhao’s reputation was flourishing in the region of Wu. [Yuanwu] went to visit him;
as soon as Yuanzhao saw him, he recognized him as a vessel for the Dharma and took special notice of him. He served him diligently for five years, mastering all the essential points.
In organizing the framework of *tishī* (mindfulness) and refining the wisdom of discernment, his mastery was comprehensive and versatile, surpassing all others.
Regarding his former regulations, none among his contemporaries could surpass him. Relying upon him, Yuanzhao expanded the prestige of their lineage.

In the seventh year of the Yuanfeng era, he traveled extensively through Mount Ju and Mount Taishouyan; subsequently, he emerged from seclusion to reside at Shuanglin in Wuzhou and later moved to Jingci in Qiantang.
Following Yuanzhao’s succession, his Dharma seat became preeminent throughout Jiangzhe, and he was popularly known as "Daben" (the Senior Ben). The Emperor heard of his reputation...
He was granted an imperial edict to reside at Fayun Monastery in the capital, where he was bestowed the title Chan Master Datong. The Master stood with the solitary majesty of a jade pillar;

he never conformed his speech to worldly things nor lent his countenance to flatterers. Although the gates of the monastery were filled with the offerings of princes, dukes, and nobles, he shared both the refined and the coarse provisions equally with the community.
After eight years, he petitioned the court, expressing his wish to retire to the West Lake. His request was granted, and he subsequently returned to the east.

Anlongshan Chongde shut himself away from the world, sweeping his gate closed and forgetting all worldly affairs; thus, those throughout the land who wished to see him could not do so. When the Master presided over the assembly for thirty years, he never once smiled. Yet, when he was in leisure, he would laugh and talk with animated gestures. When asked the reason for this, [he replied: "When I was in the assembly, I was always mindful of the Buddha’s Way. Now that I am at ease, I can let my mind go. He then composed a verse: "When I was in the assembly, I was mindful of the Way; Now that I am at ease, I can let my mind go. In the assembly, I was mindful of the Way; At ease, I can let my mind go. In the assembly, I was mindful of the Way; At ease, I can let my mind go. In the assembly, I was mindful of the Way; At ease, I can let my mind go. He said, "I have been mindful of the Way for thirty years, yet I have never truly understood it. Now, having attained ease, I can finally let my mind go. He then composed another verse: "The mountain is high, the road is steep; The path is narrow, the precipice deep. If you wish to cross, you must tread carefully; If you do not, you will surely fall into the abyss. He said, "This is what I call 'letting the mind go. He further composed a verse: "Leaning on the staff, I wander through the mountains; My heart is free, my body light. The clouds and mist obscure the sky; The spring wind blows across the valley. The birds sing in the trees, And the flowers bloom by the stream. I am alone, yet not lonely; I am joyful, yet not attached. The myriad phenomena are empty and still; The ten directions are vast and open. The moon shines upon the clear lake; The breeze blows through the pine forest. The sound of the flowing water is like music; The fragrance of the blossoms is like incense. I have no teacher, yet I know the Way; I have no disciples, yet I transmit the Dharma. The great function is spontaneously present; The true mind is naturally so. The ancient Buddhas and patriarchs Have all transmitted this single matter. Now I, too, have attained it; How could I not rejoice? He said, "This is what I call 'the joy of letting the mind go.
