He said: "Without dignity and reverence, how can one lead the multitude? In the past, when I was in the monastic forests, I practiced these things out of necessity;
it was not that my nature was inherently so. Whenever I saw images of Buddhas or Bodhisattvas, whether standing or sitting, I did not dare to sit down myself.

Regarding the *īśvarapūsa* (lay devotee) meal, I would not eat anything named after fish or meat. His sincerity and reverent conduct, as well as his guarding of the mind to remain free from transgression, were generally like this."—From the *Da guan*.
On the *jiazi* day of the twelfth month of the third year, he bent three fingers and said to his attendants, "There are only three days remaining.
Shortly thereafter, he passed away. A strange bird circled and cried in the courtyard before departing. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa at Shangfang.
He had lived for seventy-five years and sat in meditation for forty-five summer retreats.
Baon’en (Requital of Kindness) was a native of Liyang in Wei. His clan was Liu, and for generations they had advanced through military service. His family were devoted to the Buddha;
his mother, née Niu, prayed to the Buddha for a son. She dreamed that the Buddha pointed to an arhat and she became pregnant by him. Once born, he possessed extraordinary features. Not yet...

He received the cap of adulthood, presented his strategic plans, and was ranked first in the imperial examinations. Upon being appointed to an office in the Northern Capital, he sighed deeply and said, "How can this suffice for the remainder of my life?

He requested leave from the court, wishing to cast off his official robes and seek the Dharma that transcends the world. When the Emperor questioned him as to his reason, he replied, "My grandfather died in the service of the state;
I wish to repay his profound kindness. Only through the merit of spiritual cultivation can I hope to provide him with posthumous blessings. Emperor Shen-zong sighed in admiration.

It was extraordinary. The Emperor personally inscribed a calligraphic work and bestowed upon him the name Bao’en (his secular name was Qīnxiàn). He went to Fushou Temple in Beidu to tonsure his head and receive full ordination.
Traveling through various regions, he heard of the Way of Chan Master Touzi Qing and went to rely upon him.
Master Qing recognized him as a vessel of the Dharma. One morning at dawn, he entered the inner quarters, and Qing asked, "Is it light yet? The Master replied, "It is light. Qing said, "Light..."

He then rolled up the curtain. The Master followed this instruction, whereupon he attained sudden enlightenment; his mind became clear and transparent. He immediately informed Master Qing of what he had realized.
Qing approved of it and left him in charge of the towels and ewers. This continued for several years until Master Qing passed away. Then, Chancellor Han Gong Zhen [took over].

He served as the Prefect of Henan. He then resided at Shaolin Monastery on Mount Song. Before his seat was even warm, an imperial decree ordered that Da Hongshan Vinaya Monastery in Suizhou be converted into a Chan monastery, and the Master was appointed to reside there.
At that time, the foundations of Da Hongshan were vast, yet it had been overgrown with weeds and abandoned for a long time.

The Master cleared away the thorns, brambles, and weeds to establish shrines for the images; he transformed the place where jackals, wolves, and foxes roamed into a site of bells, fish-shaped chimes, and Buddhist chants. Furthermore—
The Ritual for Meditative Concentration (*Dingchan yi*): A Great New Paradigm. Because of this, the magnificent halls of Dahong Monastery became a grand spectacle.
In the second year of the Chongning era, by imperial decree, he was appointed to reside at Fayun Monastery in the Eastern Capital (Kaifeng) at the request of Zhang Gong, the Prince Consort.

The Master’s aspirations were for leisure and seclusion; after several years, he earnestly requested to return to the forests and marshes. The court, highly reluctant to contravene his request, granted it.

He proceeded directly to Mount Song and subsequently went to Dayang. Coinciding with the vacancy of the abbotship at Dahong, the local governor petitioned the throne to have the Master returned to his former seat.

He firmly declined, but being unable to refuse, he returned to his seat at the meditation hall (*bodhimaṇḍa*). All that he had previously been unable to attend to was now fully accomplished. The Master was diligent in exhorting and encouraging his students;
seekers flocked to him like spokes converging on a hub, numbering nearly five hundred. Having revitalized the school’s tradition, he maintained the precepts with extreme rigor.

Throughout his life, he wore tattered robes and made no effort to adorn himself. Although he was granted a purple cassock and square-cut robe, he ultimately performed the ritual of circumambulation and dared not accept them.

Therefore, those of high rank and authority who wished to bestow upon him a title of honor all ceased to take the matter further. In the first year of the Zhenghe era, he passed away while seated in meditation.
He was interred in the South Pagoda, which had been the site where the Master had previously intended to build a residence for his retirement. He lived to the age of fifty-four.
He spent thirty-two summer retreats in seclusion. Among his disciples who succeeded him in the Dharma and emerged into the world were thirteen people.

His collected records of discourse comprise three fascicles. The *Record of the Cao-Dong Lineage*, the *Text on Receiving the Bodhicitta Precepts*, and the *Ritual for Tonsure and Ordination* are all still in circulation today.
The Chancellor Zhang Wujin was deeply in accord with and had profound faith in the Master; he once inquired about the Three Teachings in a letter.
The Master replied: "In the Western Regions, the schools of non-Buddhist outsiders (tīrthika) follow many paths;
yet, when their ultimate convergence is examined, they do not transcend the four views of existence, non-existence, both existence and non-existence, and neither existence nor non-existence.
Because they do not take this one mind as the Way, the Way does not belong to them; therefore, they are called 'outsiders' (tīrthika). They do not realize that all phenomena are this very mind."

Consequently, the Dharma varies according to one's views; thus, it is called "wrong view" (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). For example, if one says "it exists," existence itself implies non-existence; if one says "it does not exist," non-existence itself implies existence.
When there is existence and non-existence, views of existence arise in competition; when there is neither existence nor non-existence, views of non-existence arise.
The same applies to the views that "it both exists and does not exist" or "it neither exists nor does not exist. Indeed, as long as one cannot free oneself from these various views, then—
One cannot clarify one’s own mind. If one cannot clarify one’s own mind, then one cannot know the True Path. Thus, a sutra says:
"The teachings expressed through words and phrases are falsely discriminated by those of small wisdom; they cannot comprehend their own minds—how then can they know the True Path?
It further says: "To have views is defilement; this is not yet true seeing. To remain far removed from all views—in this way, one truly sees."
The Buddha. Judging by this discourse, the heterodox and the orthodox follow divergent paths; this is precisely because their insights and realizations lead to different conclusions.

Thus, Qingliang [Zongmi] held that the Daoists’ reckoning of the Dao and the Law of Naturalness (*ziran*) as being able to give birth to the myriad things, and the *Yijing*’s assertion that the Great Ultimate (*taiji*) gives birth to the two polarities (*liangyi*), with "one Yin and one Yang" being called the Dao—taking naturalness and the Great Ultimate as the cause and "one Yin and one Yang" as the Dao—could...
To claim that [the self] gives birth to the myriad things is to posit a false cause; to reckon the One as empty non-being (*śūnyatā*) is to posit no cause at all.
Allow me to examine this: the three realms are but mind, and the myriad conditions are of one essence. Because the mind arises, phenomena arise; because the mind ceases, phenomena cease.
Extending this principle broadly, it encompasses all existence yet is not existent; synthesizing and unifying it, it ultimately reaches quiescent extinction and is not...
It is not non-existence, nor is it not non-existence; it is not existence, nor is it not existence. Once these four attachments have vanished, the hundred negations are thereby dispelled.
Natural causality is entirely mere conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). That which is "void" or "real" is but a provisional designation.

As for the claim that the Great Ultimate (*taiji*) and the Yin and Yang can give birth to the myriad things—that they are the eternal non-being and the eternal being—this is called the gateway to all wonders. Yin and Yang...

It is unfathomable; this is what is called the "spirit without fixed form. Although the Sage employs many methods to provide instruction and awakening, since these differ from the single mind, how could they not constitute the four views?
If emptiness and non-being constitute the Way, then the Way is non-being. If spontaneity, the Great Ultimate, and yin-yang constitute the Way, then the Way is being.
To have both constant non-being and constant being is to be both non-being and being. Yin and yang are unfathomable.

Thus, it is neither existent nor non-existent. The former scholars defined "spirit" (shen) as that which wondrously permeates all things; yet, being beyond things, it is not a thing, and as such, it is likewise non-existent.

Therefore, the great masters of India all regarded the view that phenomena exist outside the mind as heterodox, while taking the principle that "the myriad dharmas are but mind" as the orthodox tradition.
This is because when the mind is taken as the fundamental principle, all dogmatic views naturally vanish; though their expressions may differ, their intent is one.

This is not yet sufficient to be considered extraordinary. If there were dharmas external to the mind, then various views would compete to arise; though their words might occasionally coincide, this is not yet sufficient to be considered identical.
The sages of the Confucian school were not unaware of this, but they preserved it without discussion.

The non-Buddhist outsiders of the Western Heavens are all Bodhisattvas of Great Expedient Means who manifest transformations to deliver sentient beings, deliberately generating various views and exhaustively manifesting heterodox paths.

This serves to clarify the Buddha-dharma; this is called the Right Path, and this is called the Sage. It is the fundamental principle whether followed in direct or reverse order, and it cannot be known through discursive thought.
Thus, an ancient said: "In the past, as the True Doctrine had not yet arrived, Confucius merely used it to bind his mind."

Now that we know the principle has a point of convergence, one should no longer cling to provisional teachings. Yet, while knowing that the provisional is provisional does not necessarily constitute a true understanding of the provisional;

it is only by knowing that the provisional is the real that one truly understands the provisional. This is precisely the original intent behind the establishment of teachings and the formulation of words by the Duke of Zhou, Confucius, Laozi, and Zhuangzi;
it is accomplished through the causal conditions of the One Great Matter, marking its beginning and its consummation. Thus, the three teachings are one.

The mind follows the same path yet takes different tracks. In the ultimate principle of the Way, there is fundamentally no speech. Were it not for the Great Being Vimalakīrti, who could have known this?
Transmitted by Guǎngdào.
Xiguang was naturally pure and sincere, having cast off all worldly concerns. During his travels, he visited Master Zhì of Yúngài and asked, "What is the meaning behind Xinghuá striking Kèbīn?
Zhì descended from his meditation seat, extended both hands, and stuck out his tongue to show him.
The Master struck his meditation mat once. Zhi said, "This is merely turned by the force of the wind. He then asked Shishuang Lin. Lin said, "What is your understanding?
The Master likewise struck his meditation mat once. Lin said, "A fine meditation mat, yet one does not know where it lands.
He then asked Zhenjing, and it was the same as before. Zhenjing said, "He strikes, and you strike too. At these words, the Master [attained realization].

He attained great enlightenment and established the Dharma at Jiufeng in Ruizhou. Monks looked up to him with deep reverence. There was a monk named Upādhyāya Jie who was skilled in the arts of medicine;
having returned from his alms-round, he invited the Master to preach the Dharma. Jie came forward and asked: "What is the realm of Jiufeng? The Master replied:
"The flowing waters of the two ravines; the lofty peaks of the nine mountains. Jie further asked: "What is the person within the realm? The Master replied: [The text ends here].

[The Master] said, "The tall are tall by themselves; the short are short by themselves. Jie stepped forward and asked, "I have already received the Master’s instruction regarding the realm of human phenomena (*jin-jing*).
As for the matter of the supreme vehicle (*zong-cheng*) that lies above it, how is it? The Master replied, "Have you even finished eating the staff [of punishment] yet? Jie bowed and withdrew.

The Master turned to his attendant and asked, "For what purpose did Jie ascend the seat just now? The attendant replied, "Jie, the King of Medicine (*Yao-wang*), made the request. The Master said, "Gold..."
"Maoshi Zizi (The Lion Cub of Fur), upon leaving the cave, lets out a roar. But tell me, who is this Golden-Maned Lion Cub?
After a long silence, he said, "It is none other than Jie Yaowang this very morning," and immediately descended from his seat. That evening, he stayed with his fellow disciple Shen at Baofeng.
During the deep night of heavy snow, as he sat by the fire talking with the Master for a long time, Shen secretly sent someone to remove his bedding. When [Jie Yaowang] went to...
He lay there, leaving things as they were without inquiry. In a short while, he fell into a deep sleep; his snoring was like thunder.
Such was his state of forgetting both objects and self. The recluse Li Shang-lao sent him a poem, which said: "You have already passed through the upper gate of Yun-an Temple;

With incense burner and tea bowl, you simply brighten your countenance. Your head has no intention to brush away the lingering snow; From of old, your coarse robe has worn out upon the craggy mountains. Your slender frame stands straight..."
I suspect a blue cliff stands before me; my aspiration for the Way grows as white gulls rest in leisure.

Returning from afar, I turn my head once toward the horizon; I suspect I am amidst the mist and clouds upon a solitary peak. The lofty spirit and transcendent melody of this Master can be imagined and perceived through this.

Miaoxi also once traveled with him and shall describe his general character: he is a forest of wisdom, designated as such by those who follow the Way; his true reputation accords perfectly with his reality.
Foguo Qin also diligently transmitted [the teachings] to Keqin.

Keqin was the son of the Luo family of Chongning in Pengzhou; his ancestors had followed the Confucian tradition for generations. At birth, he possessed the physical marks of a great man, with a head like a rhinoceros horn and a face like the moon. His skeletal features were [extraordinary].
He was extraordinary. Having received books from his teacher, he memorized more than a thousand words daily. Once, while passing by Miaoji Monastery, he saw a Buddhist scripture;
after reading it three times, he felt a sense of profound longing as if he had recovered a long-lost possession, saying, "I am surely a śramaṇa from a past life.

He then left his home to tonsure his hair and follow Wenzhao, mastering the exegesis of the scriptures. He further studied the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* under Minxing. Suddenly, he fell ill and was on the verge of death.
He sighed and said, "The true path to the nirvāṇa of all Buddhas does not reside within words and phrases.

To seek it through sound or perceive it through form is like throwing a rat's excrement into a pot of soup to defile it; I know that such a person will have no means of death. He then departed and went to see Master Shengjue.
At that time, Sheng was shaving his arm and drawing blood. Pointing to it, he said to the Master, "This is a single drop from Caoqi. The Master was startled.

At that time, there were several renowned and highly esteemed masters whose fame had spread far and wide. Carrying a single alms bowl, he traveled on foot out of Shu, intending to go wherever his heart desired.
He first visited Yiqian Hao and Jinxuan Xin; he also met Dayue Zhe, Haitang Xing, and Donglin Zong, all of whom designated him as a vessel of the Dharma.
Yet, it was Haitang alone who held him in particularly high esteem and recognized his exceptional potential.
Finally, he went to see Chan Master Wuzu Yan and displayed his full range of skillful means; however, the Master would not grant him approval.

He then remarked that the Master was merely trying to force others to change their ways, uttering insolent words and departing in a fit of indignation. The Master said, "Wait until you are struck by a bout of high fever."
Just as he was thinking of me, he arrived at Mount Jinshan. He contracted a severe case of chills and was extremely ill; his usual insights provided him no strength.

Recalling the words of the Patriarch, he made a vow to himself, saying, "Once my illness has slightly abated, I shall return to Wuzu. When his illness had healed, he returned to the mountain. The Patriarch saw him and was pleased;
he appointed him to attend him for only half a month when an official from the provincial government came to visit the Patriarch to inquire about the Buddha-dharma.

The general gist is as follows: The Master was eavesdropping from the side when he suddenly attained a realization. He hurried out and saw a rooster fly onto the railing, flapping its wings and crowing;
at that moment, he attained great enlightenment. Tucking incense in his sleeve, he entered the room to communicate what he had realized.

The Patriarch said, "The Great Matter of the Buddhas and Patriarchs is not something that can be achieved by those of inferior capacity or meager roots. Since you have reached this state, I rejoice with you. Thereupon, he announced this to all the elders in the mountains.
Lao said, "My attendant has attained Zen. Once, while he was cutting down a massive tree, the Patriarch tried to stop him firmly, but he would not listen.
The Patriarch rose up in anger, brandishing a staff, yet the Master stood his ground without moving. The Patriarch threw down the staff he held and departed with a smile.
From that time on, he encountered all things without doubt. During the Chongning era, he returned to Shu to visit his parents. The elders there said to one another, "The Way is traveling westward."
At that time, his fellow disciple Fojian Huiqin was also renowned among the assembly; he subsequently distinguished his master from him by calling him "Chuan-qin" (Qin of the River).
Master [Chuan] was invited by Guo Zhizhang of Chengdu to expound the Dharma of the Sixth Patriarch at Zhaojue for eight years. He then departed from the gorges to travel south.
At that time, Zhang Wujin was residing in Jingnan, who considered himself to have personally grasped the ancient Buddha and had rolled up the teachings of all quarters; when he met the Master...

He was suddenly struck with a sense of self-forgetfulness. He remained to dwell at Birywan Hermitage, devoting his heart and mind to the Master. (The *Chuan Deng Lu* states: Zhang resided in Jingnan, considering himself a master of the Way and rarely seeing anyone who could surpass him.

The Master moored his boat to visit him and engaged in an intense discussion on the purport of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. The essential point was: "The realm of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) in the *Avataṃsaka* is the total reality of principle and phenomena; there is not a single provisional dharma therein. Therefore, the one is the myriad, and the myriad is understood as the one. One after another... )

Ten thousand upon ten thousand, vast and boundless; mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction. Unfolding and rolling up with sovereign ease, unimpeded and perfectly interfused. Although this is the ultimate principle, it remains, in the end, merely ripples on a windless sea. At this, the Master unconsciously drew his seat closer.

The Master then asked, "Upon reaching this point, is it the same as or different from the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Official replied, "It is the same. The Master said, "There is no connection. The Official’s expression turned resentful. The Master said, "Have you not seen Yunmen say:

'Mountains, rivers, and the great earth—there is not even a hair’s breadth of affliction'—this is still a turning phrase? Only when one reaches the point where not a single form is seen is it half-raised. Furthermore, one must know there is a time for the full raising of the upward path. Was that not the case with Deshan and Linji? The Official then nodded in agreement. The following day, the Master again brought up the matter.

The Dharma-realm principle and the Dharma-realm. The ultimate principle is exclusively the unimpeded Dharma-realm. The Master asked again, "Can this be called Chan? The Official said, "It is precisely the time to speak of Chan. The Master laughed and said, "Not so. You are still within the measure of the Dharma-realm. As long as the measure of the Dharma-realm has not been extinguished, it is not yet possible to speak of Chan.

Only when one reaches the Dharma-realm of the non-obstruction of phenomena and events does the measure of the Dharma-realm cease; only then is it appropriate to speak of Chan. 'What is the Buddha? A dried-up shit-stick. 'What is the Buddha? Three pounds of flax. This is why Zhenjing’s verse says: 'Phenomena and events are mutually unobstructed.'"

Acting with sovereign mastery, he held a pig’s head in his hand while reciting the pure precepts as he drove [the practitioner] out of the brothel. Before he had even repaid his wine debt, at the crossroads, he untied his sack. The official said, "How magnificent this discourse! How rarely could it be heard! Thereupon, he assumed the posture of a disciple toward the Master.

He resided at Biyan. He subsequently moved to Daolin in Changsha. Deng Zichang, the Grand Guardian and Chief of the Imperial Secretariat, reported the Master’s virtuous conduct to the Emperor, who bestowed upon him purple robes and the title of Master Foguo.
During the Zhenghe era, he was transferred to Yan Kang at Mount Jiangshan. Students from the southeast flocked to him as if returning home until there was no room to accommodate them.
His fame reached the capital, where he was summoned by imperial decree to reside at Tianning Wanshou Monastery and was granted an audience with the Emperor.
He was honored with exceedingly generous favors. At the beginning of the Jianyan era, Chancellor Li Boji petitioned for him to reside at Jinshan.
When Emperor Gaozong arrived in Wiyang, he entered the imperial presence and was granted the title Chan Master Yuanwu. After serving at Yunju for some time, he again took charge of Zhaojue.

On the day of Jiyou in the eighth month of the fifth year of the Shaoxing era, he suffered from a slight illness; he left a verse for the assembly and passed away after casting down his brush. Upon cremation, his tongue and teeth remained intact.
His remains did not decay; his śarīra were of five colors and beyond counting. He spent seventy-three years in the world and fifty-five summer retreats.

His stūpa was erected beside Zhaojue Temple, and he was posthumously titled Chan Master Zhengjue. The Master was pure and free from conditioned action, never entering into the realm of phenomenal signs.

He manifested the gateway of skillful means to uplift those who had not yet attained awakening. Upon hearing his words but once, there was none who was not moved with solemn emotion; some even shed tears.

Thus, during his time at Tianning Temple, princes, dukes, nobles, men of virtue, talent, and wisdom, as well as scholars of literature, came to his quarters daily until the ruts of their carriage wheels filled the space outside his door.
Even the assembly listening to the Dharma in the Vaiśālī hall could not surpass this. He passed away.

The master had five hundred disciples who inherited the Dharma and attained the Eye. More than one hundred of these became leaders throughout the various regions, occupying great monasteries, guiding the assembly, and preaching the Dharma;
they served as models for later students, which may truly be called a flourishing state. Since the Master himself attained the Dharma...
His reputation was widespread. Moving from Yuelu to Jiangshan, his practice became perfected and his virtue complete; he was constantly protected by divine spirits.
When he passed through Mount Jin, the rebel Zhao Wan occupied Zhenjiang with several hundred troops.

As he steered his warships with the wind to cross over, the wind suddenly reversed, and clouds and mist darkened the sky for day and night. Unable to cross, he halted. Upon arriving at Yunju, he continued his journey.
While Daochang was staying at Lu, the rebel Zhang Yu suddenly arrived and plundered everything he possessed; only the Master’s robes and alms bowl remained.
On another occasion, the Master had collected items bestowed by the imperial court and placed them in a chest. While staying in Yizhen, he instructed his disciples to go and inspect them.

They replied, "Yizhen has been ravaged by a great fire for several nights; what is there left to seek? The Master smiled and said, "Go anyway. When they arrived, the official temples and the eaves of the commoners' houses—[were all reduced to ashes].
The site had been reduced to rubble and debris, yet the master’s book-cases remained sealed as if newly purchased.

Once, while staying at Tianting Monastery in Gong’an, the Elder Jue of Tianxiang dreamed of a woman who bowed twice and approached him, saying: "I beg you to grant me the Eastern Hall so that I may preach the Dharma for humans and devas.
Two nights later, the *Biyán Lù* (Blue Cliff Record) commentary arrived; the woman was none other than the Dharma-protecting deity of Biyán. At Anle Mountain...
When Shen took up residence as the abbot of Yunju, all the senior monks moved to other quarters to avoid him. The Master provided a single mat and lived there, rising and reclining as usual.
The Master was fully endowed with both merit and wisdom; his practice and understanding were so liberated that he could have plucked an entire world from the palm of his hand like an *āmala* fruit.
What need is there to speak of this petty matter? Nevertheless, because it has been passed down by the people of the world and praised by them, I have recorded it.
This is a brief account.
Danxia Chun’s lineage was passed to his son, Chun.
He was the son of the Jia family from Zitrong in Jianzhou. He became a novice at Dajian Temple in the county when he was two years old.

17. Having shaved his head and received full ordination, he took the venerable Master Daoning as his teacher. He thoroughly mastered the vehicles of the teachings and was proficient in the arts and learning.
Upon visiting Old Man Fuyong at Dayang, he inquired about the Great Matter. Fuyong, regarding the Master as a vessel of great potential, pointed him out and said:
"The ancients spoke of taking responsibility before the void kalpa and realizing the essence before the Buddha appeared in the world. You need only step back."

He followed his own path; out of ten thousand, he never missed one by even a single step. What need was there for many words? Under the Master’s instruction, he attained great enlightenment. He attended Fuyong for many years.
When Fuyong appointed him as a *lisheng* (a monk established in the community), his learning and dignified demeanor served as a model for the assembly. Fuyong held him in deep esteem and respect.

He considered this to be the solitary tradition of the Dongshan school and felt that this man could be entrusted with its leadership. From then on, his reputation spread throughout the monastic communities.
During the Chongning era, Wang Gongxin Yu, while serving as a judicial official in the capital region, heard of the Master’s fame and virtue and invited him to reside at Danxia Mountain in Nanyang.

His reputation for the Way grew even more prominent. The Master’s preaching was direct and penetrating, awakening those who heard it. Among his disciples were many worthy and sagely men, such as Liao, Wu, and Ru.
Yù was later to become a Teacher of Gods and Humans for all.

However, as the Way had matured while the world grew distant, it was Yù alone who could act as an attendant and assistant, enabling the Master to sing forth with single-minded peace and ensuring that no deficiencies or failures occurred. After a long time, due to illness, he retired to the West Hermitage of Dàchéng in Tángzhōu.
The Governor of Suízhōu, Lord Xiàng, again urged him to take up residence at Bǎoshòu on Hóngshān, but [he] could not.

He responded accordingly and eventually passed away at Baoshou. The Master was by nature solitary and pure; his temperament was harmonious yet his countenance was stern, his heart was compassionate yet his speech was severe.

From childhood he set his resolve, never wavering until old age. Taking the forgetting of artifice as the foundation of his transformation and the departure from consciousness as the core of his realization, he was able to skillfully proclaim the five stages, overwhelming all quarters with his authority.
He may truly be called a great man. His stupa is located at...
South of Hongshan.
Shousui (with Qingxian appended) succeeded [to the lineage].
Shousui was the son of the Zhang family of Pengxi, Suining. From childhood, he abstained from meat and alcohol and had no fondness for play. He served Nanlu.
When Yuan was a youth under Master Qing, he received full ordination at the age of twenty-seven. Traveling south, he first arrived at Yuquan, where he met Chan Master Qin.
Deeply impressed by him, Qin appointed him as his deputy for administrative affairs. After more than a year, he traveled to Dahong to pay his respects to Chan Master En.

As soon as he had spread his sitting mat in the abbot’s quarters, a small insect suddenly flew down onto the floor. He abruptly reached out his hand to brush it away, at which point he attained a sudden and great enlightenment.
Master En approved him and appointed him to oversee the affairs of the monastery. His preaching of the Dharma was fundamentally based on that of Master En.

During the Wuxu year of the Zhenghe era, he was granted the title "Jingci. Furthermore, Lord Yuan Zhe of Suizhou submitted a memorial stating that the Master’s virtue and conduct were worthy of serving as a model for the monastic community.
Shortly thereafter, he moved to Shuinan. In the Dingwei year of the Jingkang era (1127), he retired to the Yanfu Monastery on Mount Guang in De’an.
At that time, the realm was in great chaos and bandits had risen up across the Yangtze and Huai rivers; strict martial measures were enforced everywhere.

Anshou Li Gongji, concerned that the Master’s residence was remote and desolate, ordered him to move his staff into the city, where he established the Huacheng Hermitage for him to dwell in. After the rebels had besieged the city for a long time, they launched attacks repeatedly.

It was not auspicious. He then said, "There is a strange man in the city," and so he led [the others] away. When Chen Gui, the Pacification Commissioner, heard of this, he sighed and said, "Who could this strange man be?
It must be my Master Jingyan. In the year Yimao of the Shaoxing era, the Pacification Commandery ordered him to reside at Dahong.
Students returned from afar, gazing upon the mountain, marking the height of its prosperity at that time. The Master also exhorted his disciples without weariness until the year Ding...

In the third month of the year Mǎo, he manifested illness and passed away. The Master was naturally gentle and serene by temperament, never at odds with others. He observed the precepts with great care;
throughout his life, he did not wear silk or cotton, did not handle wealth or treasures, and did not come near objects of luxury. When scholars and officials offered him gifts, he would decline them.
He gave whatever he obtained as soon as he received it. His compassion extended even to fleas and lice; unable to bear casting them aside on the ground, he tucked them into his robes.
Qingxian was the son of the Wang family from Guang’an in Shu. He recited Master Ba’s *Song of the Twelve Hours* and attained awakening.

He once studied under Foxing and later met Hongzhi, both of whom provided him with inspiration. Yet, regarding the incense offered to manifest his faith before humans and devas, he alone returned it [to its source].
Jingyan was indeed adorned by purity; his practice of the *kai-chui* (the ritual striking of the gong) was steady and profound, and what he attained was uniquely deep.

Xianxing was tranquil and serene; his worldly thoughts were so still that nothing arose within him. He regarded honor, fame, and noble power as equal to the vast void or drifting clouds—suddenly arising and vanishing, not worth a single glance.
At that time, famous scholars and high-ranking officials all forgot their status to associate with him. [He resided at] Jingxi.

As the Grand Master of the Transport Commission, he proceeded in procession through the capital. While on his way, he was summoned by an official decree from the Ministry of Rites to reside at Dahong.
There, he was bestowed the title "Great Master Juezhao Huikong Fozhi Mingwu. At the seat of Dahong, the grace of the Dharma lineage thus manifested the succession of three generations;
his reputation for the Way did not diminish in the least, and one may observe his family tradition therein.
**Jiaque (with Xipu appended)** Jiaque was the son of the Wang family of Qingzhou.

From his youth, he pursued the Confucian studies and gained the recognition of Sima Guang (the Duke Wen). Nevertheless, he devoted himself to noble pursuits and had no interest in fame or official rank.
He shaved his head and followed Master Fuyong Kai as his teacher; his practice was precise and meticulous, leading to profound realization.
He was transcendent. Residing at Puyan Temple on Mount Dasheng in Zhuzhou, he first cleared away the monastic quarters to establish a hall for the great assembly.
He resounded the great sound of the Dharma, and those of both the ordained and the laity from near and far were gathered and transformed by his presence.

From the main hall and its corridors to the courtyards and eaves, he renovated everything anew, such that those who came to visit felt as though they had entered a royal palace; even before seeing the ceremonial insignia, all were moved to profound reverence.
It is like hearing the music of the *xiao* and *shao*: though one may not understand its notes, there is still a sense of joy.

Thus, many who have immersed themselves in the rich flavor of the Way and the bliss of *dhyāna*, thereby extricating themselves through the gateway of *prajñā*, are found among the gentry and scholars. The temple stele states: Jue was a native of Chang’an.

Possessing integrity and conduct, he severed worldly ties and renounced secular life. He served the Great Elder Daokai as his teacher, thoroughly investigating the "Great Matter" until he attained its very bone and marrow. Among the elite...
Upon hearing his words, people felt a sense of transcendence, as if leaving the mundane world behind; among the contemporaries of his time, none surpassed Jue in this regard.

During the Chongning era, an imperial decree summoned him to reside at Jingyin Monastery, where his reputation and influence flourished even further. One day, he addressed the assembly, saying: "The Patriarch came from the West specifically to sing of this matter alone.
Since then, however, people have been unwilling to grasp it fully, instead rushing outward in search of it—like throwing oneself into the waters of a red marsh to look for a pearl."
It is like going to Mount Jing to seek jade, yet failing to realize that what enters through the gate is not the family treasure.

To mistake the shadows for the head—is this not a great error? Only when the teachings of the Zen school are fully realized will one find the essence quiescent and without dependence, such that divergent thoughts do not arise.
Past and present are without interval; the myriad phenomena of the universe are the family style before one’s eyes. The bird-path stretches across the vast void, yet it does not hinder a single step.
The golden rooster heralds the dawn; the vermilion phoenix soars on high. Flowers bloom upon the jade tree;

fruit forms upon the withered branch. Only beneath the Gate of the Great Sun is there autumn every day; before the Hall of the Bright Moon, there is summer at every moment. Do you wish to understand? It is the shadowless tree.
The moon hangs over the cold mountain stream; the ocean tide flows eastward as the Dipper shifts west. Hee-po also attained the Way of Calligraphy.
Initially residing at Mount Shao, he later succeeded to Tian-ning and subsequently moved to Dan-xia.

As he approached his passing, he summoned his administrators and divided his paper bag into four parts: one for each of the resident monks, the novices, and the temple property, and one for the ferryman. Thereafter, he said:
Dana had a public case (gong’an). From the beginning he had toppled it down and now raised it up; today he reveals it universally to all people. But tell me, what is it?
Looking to his left and right, he asked, "Do you understand? They replied, "We do not understand. The Master said, "How magnificent!
A great man who does not understand the final word," and then he lay down to sleep and passed away in the lotus position.
The Biography of Chan Master Xiaonan (with Hai’s Commentary appended).
Xiaonan was a native of the Zhang clan from Tingzhou. He studied under Chan Master Daoyou at Daolin Monastery in Tan, where he received certification of his realization.

Subsequently, he moved to Lohan Monastery and served as the head of the Hall Administration; thereupon, Daoyou assigned him a seat beside him to receive guests. When Daoyou transferred to Yunju, Xiaonan succeeded him as the abbot.
Scholars unanimously turned toward him. According to his lineage, Huanglong was his great-grandfather;

as their names were identical and his reputation for the Way rivaled that of his ancestor, the monastic communities referred to him as "Little Nan" (Xiaonan), out of respect for Huanglong as "Old Nan" (Lao Nan). Hong Juefan remarked:
"When Chan Master Xiaonan’s insight into the Way was clear and bright, yet he was not yet known to the public, he once visited Donglin Zhaojue."
The bell was struck to assemble the multitude, who went out to welcome him at the edge of Qingxi Brook. His disciples were greatly astonished. From that time on, his fame grew ever more renowned.
When he was about to pass into nirvana, he ascended the seat and addressed the assembly, saying:

"Today, the Arhat rides an iron horse backward up Mount Sumeru; he tramples through empty space, leaving no trace behind. Thereupon, he returned to his quarters and passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture. The Master thus transmitted...
He took the Way as his resolve. Having endured seven cycles of cold and heat, he lived for forty-five years.

Although what he harbored within was not fully unfolded, his brilliant reputation was manifest in his own time and has left a legacy for posterity. Yungju may truly be said to have had a worthy son. This is the evaluation of Chan-friend Hai.
He was a fellow disciple who had received the precepts together with his master.

When the master was about to travel abroad, a monk from the same monastery dreamed of two great serpents, one black and one white, each several zhang in length, which coiled three times around the monastery before leaping away.

At dawn, as the master and [his disciple] Ping were departing the assembly to travel to distant lands, the dreamer patted them on the back and entrusted them with these words: "My two sons, take good care of yourselves; in days to come, you shall be the dragon-elephants of the Dharma."
Ping succeeded Guangjian Ying, who resided at Kaixian and was a neighbor to the Master; both were renowned within the monastic community and were called the "Two Dragons of Mount Lu."

Liyen was the successor of Huanglong Nan. Possessing celestial insight, he was highly esteemed by Huanglong. He established the Dharma at Longqing in Luling, where Chan practitioners followed his teachings.
Wherever his sharp mental acuity reached, it was like the Tai'e or Menglao swords—cleaving through rhinoceros hide and piercing through armor without obstruction.

Regarding those who remained as practitioners: at that time, Huanglong’s disciples—such as Donglin Zong, Huichang Xin, Luohan You, and Dongsan Wen—each propagated the teachings in their respective regions.
The Master alone appeared later. When asked, "How did Huanglong regard Yanyuan? Huanglong replied: [He regarded him as his own eyes.]

His perspective on "the self" was likely in profound accord with this. From the year Yimao of the Xining era to the year Xinwei of the Yuanyou era, seventeen years passed during which the Master propagated the Way;
yet those who transmitted his recorded teachings were extremely few, for he himself had painfully excised all that was superfluous and swept away all that was coarse.

It was more than merely like gathering clouds or draining a flood; thus, the breadth of his Dharma-transformation could not even be ranked among the various mountains [of famous monasteries], leading to a situation where in later generations few knew the Master’s name. How lamentable!

Fayi (Chan Head Constable) Fayi, whose style name was Guandao, was the great-grandson of Li Gonghe, the Grand Preceptor and Prince of Xiangyang. His family had resided for generations in Xiangfu, Kaifeng.
When his mother saw an old monk enter her dream, she conceived him; by the time he reached the age of childhood, all manner of...

No matter how they teased him, he paid them no heed. At seventeen, he entered the Imperial Academy as a student, clad in the robes of the *Shi* and *Shu* classics and carrying himself with an air of self-importance.

He followed his father to serve in Huainan, but when his father sought to appoint him to an official post, he refused. He intended to abandon his household affairs and become a disciple of Master Ze at Changlu.
Weng Nan lamented this. His mother said, "This man was a śramaṇa in his previous life; do not thwart his resolve. Before long, Jie passed away.

He paid homage to Master Tongzhao Yuan of Lingyan, received the *śrāmaṇera* and *bhikṣu* ordinations, and remained under his tutelage for ten years without attaining any realization. He redoubled his efforts with even greater austerity and diligence.

At that time, Yuanwu resided at Jiangshan and recognized him as a successor to the great torch of the Dharma. Yuanwu subsequently received an imperial decree to reside at the capital’s Tian... (Tiantong Monastery).
Ning served as the Master’s attendant. During the chaos of the Jingkang era, Wuzu returned to Shu and traveled with great difficulty to visit Master Qing of Caotang at Shushan.
Through a single word, he suddenly realized the Great Dharma. In the seventh year of the Shaoxing era, Liu Ziyu, the Guardian of the Bowen Pavilion and Governor of Quan, [invited him].
He was invited to reside at Yanfu Monastery. When Chancellor Zhang Gongjun governed Fudang, he moved him to Shoushan.
Later, when Minister Liang Rujia was stationed in Siming, he again entreated him to dwell at Xuedou.

Consequently, high officials and scholars alike yearned to behold his presence and vied with one another to invite him, fearing they might be too late. Tian’ai Wannian Monastery was located in a remote valley; its...

He was merely mediocre and dull-witted. The officials submitted a memorial proposing that his title be changed to "Chan" (Zen). They selected a renowned monk whom the masses trusted and followed to serve as the leader.
The Master subsequently moved again to Wannian, and after briefly responding to the call at Changlu, he returned to the Guanyin Monastery in Wannian.
After showing signs of slight illness for ten days, he recited a verse, entered his coffin, and passed away at the age of seventy-five.

Born into a noble family and raised in a magnificent residence, his nature was in harmony with the Way without the need for formal instruction from a teacher. With a single thought, he turned away from the world;
transcending the realm of worldly toil, he reached the shore of awakening and became a great spiritual teacher of the age. Can he not be called a hero?
The Head Seat of the Dharma Hall was a native of Kaifeng and a descendant of Chancellor Xue Ju-zheng.

In the seventh year of the Xuanhua era, he received the tonsure under Hui-shi of Huayan Monastery in Yi-yang, Changsha. He traveled extensively through the monastic communities and delved deeply into the ocean of meaning within the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
From Lake Xiang to Wannian, he went to visit Yun-chao Xue; "Chao-yi" was the master’s alternative name. There, they reached a profound accord.

He was appointed to oversee the drafting of official correspondence. Later, he led the assembly in the practice of repaying kindness. In his quarters, there was only a single low couch; he possessed no other belongings.
One day, he suddenly said to someone, "A month from now, I shall no longer remain here. When the appointed time arrived, he went to the abbot’s quarters to pay his respects.

Just before dawn, he wrote a *Yúfǔ* (Fisherman) lyric upon the door of his room, then sat upon his couch with his legs drawn up and passed away. The lyric reads: "This matter is the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*..."

Ever exposed to existence, where plum blossoms, snow, and moonlight intermingle their radiance—there, a solitary laugh fills the vast void. Through ten thousand ages, the wind carries the words from the ancient teacup;
far and wide, the Milky Way stretches across the heavens. The dream of the butterfly in the *Nanhua* (Zhuangzi) is still fluttering;

who now treads upon the tiger of Fenggan? Now, one has forgotten the path by which they came. At twilight, mountains and rivers stretch to the ends of the earth; I gaze after the wild geese as they fly away.
Pujiao. Two masters transmitted the lineage to Pujiao:

[the first was] Qingyuan, a son of the Bi family. He was exceptionally intelligent from childhood; before reaching the age of twenty, he received full ordination. He went to Nanping to study the Tiantai teachings.
Once, when he was pressed with difficult questions by someone, he became indignant. He changed his attire and traveled to various regions to visit Master Lètán Qián.
As soon as his feet reached the gate, the Master rebuked him; as [Zhì]yǒu prepared to ask a question, the Master brandished his staff and drove him out.

One day, the Master suddenly called for the teacher and, leading him into the hall, said, "I have an ancient kōan that I wish you to deliberate upon. As [Zhì]yǒu was about to offer a word, the Master gave a shout. The teacher—
Dunwu burst into loud laughter. The official stepped down from his meditation seat, took the Master’s hand, and asked, “Do you understand the Buddha-dharma?

The Master gave a shout and pushed him away. The official laughed heartily. Thereupon, the Master’s fame spread in all directions. Later, he returned to his hometown and stayed at Tiantong, where he remained in seclusion behind closed doors for eight years.
When the monastery happened to have its seat vacant, the local officials requested the Master to open the Dharma hall; fearing that he might flee again, they made this appeal.

He dispatched an official ahead to wait for him on the road; [the official] was not permitted to decline the summons. The Master’s preaching of the Dharma was concise and essential. Whenever he saw a monk approaching, he would invariably shout:
"I have already explained it for you before you even took up your staff! He would then ask: "Now tell me, what did I explain?"
It is also said: "Why do you not stop and leave? He took up his staff and pursued him; such was his quick-wittedness.
There was one named Xu, born of the Chen clan of Putian, who also received the Dharma from Master Qian. He lived in seclusion at Nanhu on Mount He, where he cleared fields to provide for himself.

Students gradually arrived, and he guided them according to the occasion. Chen Ju-min, an official of the provincial circuit, heard of his reputation and invited him with due ceremony to Mount Gu at Fuzhou;
subsequently, he resided at Xuefeng, where his recorded sayings from two assemblies were widely circulated at the time.

When the Master engaged with others and responded to circumstances, it was always against his own inclination; he yielded only when compelled by others, as it was not what he desired. Later, he took leave of the assembly and retired to live in seclusion.
I constructed a thatched hut beside Shimen; I composed a song to manifest my resolve, its lyrics being as follows: "I have built a thatched hut by the side of Caixi.

Looking in all four directions, the peaks and ridges are all sheer cliffs. Shimen rises ten thousand fathoms, locking the celestial river; those who come wishing to ascend find no place to set their feet."
What is the cause for dwelling in this hermitage? Neither poetry nor verse, nor even meditation. When hunger comes, I boil bitter greens with their roots;
stacking stones for a bed, I sleep as soon as I am weary. As the sun shines upon the peaks, I wander on and on;
basking in the warmth, I sit alone—how pleasant the mood! Tamed and docile birds do not fly when pursued; monkeys and langurs feel for lice within my robes. At leisure, I lean upon my slender staff.

Six or seven feet tall, he uses his strength to support those in peril as he travels through mountains and walks through wilds. Stripping through clouds and entering the grass, he never declines the effort.
Meeting people, he shatters their "caves of cultivation. Sometimes resting beneath pines, sometimes sitting upon rocks, he listens quietly to the mountain stream as it rinses jade-like sounds.

From deep sources and profound caves, the flow never ceases; every sound plays out the melody of non-arising (*anutpāda*). Whether the *jiao* or *shang* notes mingle with the *yu*, who can discern them? These are the five musical tones.
The six pitch-pipes are merely struck; sometimes, following my inspiration, I ascend a high peak, laughing loudly and singing wildly as heaven and earth seem narrow.
Initially, when Chen Pinjun was in the capital, he visited Master Qian and asked about the venerable elders of his own hometown, inquiring who among them was worthy of his intimacy.
The Duke said, "You may return home; you have seen enough. Upon reaching this point, he went into seclusion with the Master at Shimen, where they delighted in the Way for the rest of their lives.
This concludes the transmission from the Fifth Patriarch.
Biaozi was a native of Huai’an. He had relied upon the Fifth Patriarch, Master Yuan, for the longest time, yet he had not yet attained realization.
At that time, Yuanwu was serving as the seat-partner and receiving disciples; the Master attended him closely. Yuanwu said, “You have long been at the Dharma-seat of the Senior Teacher;

why must you come here to ‘test the water’? If there is anything you have not yet reached, it would be better to bring it up so that I may evaluate it. Thereupon, the Master brought up the story of Deshan’s informal sermon (*xiaocan*).
Wugao called out to him, saying, "I considered myself unworthy to be your teacher; seeing you as you are, I find I have more than enough. He then ordered him to try again.
When [Zhaozhou] reached the point where he could not answer the question for the rest of the night, Wugao suddenly covered the Master’s mouth with his hand and said, "Just look like this.
The Master was overcome with indignation; he rushed out, struck the ground with his sitting cloth (*zuoju*), and cried out, "What kind of causal connection is there in that? Only then...
He instructed him to contemplate a single phrase. Thereupon, his peers vied with one another to exert themselves. Before long, he attained a realization.

He privately informed the Fifth Patriarch, saying, "He has only grasped a single fragment; the Great Dharma is not yet clear to him. If he undergoes further refinement for a short while, he will surely become a vessel of the Dharma.

Not long after, the Fifth Patriarch announced that he wished to ordain monks on his own initiative, truly desiring to spur him toward reaching the distant goal. When the Master heard this, he was deeply [impressed].

There was one who waited for this opportunity. One day, as he ascended the hall, [Fengxue] looked at the Master with his eyes and said, "Do not engage in false conceptualization," and then descended from the seat.
The Master felt indignant and went to join the Dharma community of Langye Qigong. After a long time, Yuanwu went to visit him;

thereupon, under Yuanwu’s words, the Master attained great enlightenment. They then returned together. Just as Wuzu was about to ordain monks, Yuanwu immediately returned to Sichuan after Yan had passed away.
The Prefectural Governor appointed the Master to succeed to the seat. Holding up the incense, he said:
"If it were for the sake of the present Chan Master Qin of Chengdu Zhaojue, at this moment I would have obtained his marrow; why then would I not act for him? He did not see it thus stated:

"The fish exists because of the water; the son is born from the mother. Consequently, monks from all quarters came to him in an unrestrained flood. The Master posted a notice at the door of his attendant, saying:
Dongshan had three statements: "If you can speak them, you shall be admitted to the community. All the patch-robed monks were disheartened by this.
There was one monk who, carrying his sitting mat, went straight to the Master’s quarters and said, "I cannot speak them, but I only wish to be admitted.

The Master was greatly pleased and called for the *vinaya-dhara* (Vina) to arrange a place for him beneath a bright window. The Master marveled at these extraordinary words and wondrous principles, which he propagated throughout all quarters; thus, they were honored everywhere.
He said, "Since my old age, I have regretted that the Dharma lineage has not flourished; there was only Longhua Gao, yet even his reputation for the Way did not flourish.
Some say this is because Master Yuanwu had the merit of nurturing and protecting you, and you suppressed him as a result."
The Head Seat Yuanli (also known as Puyong Zhizang) was a native of Min.
He received his formal training at Jiaoshan. Initially, he went to study under Master Yan at Taiping in Shu.

Whenever he entered the master’s room for instruction, the master would invariably say to him, "Monks of our tradition must clearly distinguish between the black and the white. This continued for two years before...
Faming had already seen [the Master]. He went to the Abbot’s quarters, where Fayan nodded his approval. When Fayan was about to succeed as the Fifth Patriarch, Faling went with him out of courtesy;
however, Fayan ordered him to share the seat, which he refused to do. At that time, Foyan was only seventeen years old and had a doubt he could not resolve.

Faling said, "Li understands it well," and because of this, Foyan went to Li to request instruction. Later, when Foyan appeared in the world, Li was still in good health and heard of the positions Foyan had recommended.
Once it was said: "Brother Yuan’s reputation is not earned in vain. During the Chongning era, Fali returned to Wuzu. Someone asked, "Where did Wuzu move him to?
Fali replied, "Having eyes but no ears; sitting by the fire in the sixth month. [The questioner] asked, "What is the meaning of this?
Fali said, "At home, poverty is still tolerable; on the road, poverty brings one to despair. Again, someone asked about the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*.
A sutra says, "All wholesome dharmas. What, then, are wholesome dharmas? Lixing said, "Above is heaven; below is earth.
In between, those who sit sit, and those who stand stand. What do you call 'wholesome dharmas'? His spiritual acuity was such as this.
He spent his final years at Ruiyan in Siming. He received the full precepts from Puyong of the same hometown, who had reached the level of the Fifth Patriarch.
When the Patriarch brought up the story of the "Soul-Separation of the Bride" to question him, he attained realization. He presented this verse: "The two women merge into one daughter-in-law;
The turning wheel is severed, impossible to reverse. From of old, coming and going leave no trace; Travelers need not ask the path they took. Thereafter...
Whenever a monk came to visit him, he would speak in the Min dialect and recite a vernacular verse: "At the beginning of the letter, I teach my mother to be diligent in her rest;
at the end of the letter, I teach my mother not to doze off. Now tell me, what was said in the middle? When a monk hesitated to respond, he would immediately push him out.
He once served as the keeper of the treasury, and monks from all quarters called him Rong Zhizang (Fusion Wisdom Treasury).
Chan Master Zhenxie Liao transmitted the Dharma to Qingliao, whose style name was Zhenxie.
He was the son of the Yong clan of Anchang in Zuomian, Shu. As a child, he was brought into a temple; upon seeing the Buddha, his countenance was moved with joy.
At the age of eleven, he left home to become a monk under Dao-ren Qingjun of Shengguo. Seven years later, he underwent the ordination examination.

Fahua attained liberation. He ascended the lecture hall to study the sūtras and śāstras, and was able to grasp their essential meaning. Soon thereafter, he abandoned these studies to devote himself to the power of meditation (*dhyāna*).

He traveled with an air of dignified detachment, carrying a staff. Along the way, both monastics and laypeople blocked his path and tried to detain him, but he shook his head and paid them no heed, saying, "Is the timing for the *kūṇa* and *páng* birds something to be treated with such haste?
Leaving the valley, he went directly to see Chan Master Danxia Zhen. Danxia asked, "What is..."
Before the kalpa of emptiness, the Master [Wuxue] was about to offer a word when Xiyuan struck him with his palm. The Master attained sudden enlightenment.

The following day, as Xiyuan ascended the hall before the assembly, he interrogated him regarding his realization; it was like a pearl casting its shadow or an echo responding in a valley—truly penetrating to the very source and bottom.
Later, he traveled to Mount Wutai and then to the capital. Floating down the Bian River, he arrived at Changlu to pay his respects to Zu Zhao.

The Patriarch [Foyan] presided over the assembly, which numbered ten thousand disciples—both "dragons and elephants" among men—and many of them were men of outstanding talent. When the Master arrived, he struck the right chord with a single word, and the Patriarch appointed him as his attendant.

Before long, the Patriarch promoted him to the position of Head Seat (Śrāmaṇera-purohita) and had him share the seat to preach the Dharma. The entire assembly was greatly astonished. This was in the second year of the Xuandehé era.

Zhao retired from the monastery due to illness, leaving the Dharma seat without a presiding master. One night, he dreamed of a person who told him, "The one to succeed you as Master is a monk from Shu.
Upon waking, he wondered, "Is it Foguo? Is it Foyan? Ultimately, the seat remained vacant for two years.

When Imperial Commissioner Chen arrived and intended to appoint a successor, it was the Head Seat [Chun] who was chosen; he accepted the invitation and ascended the seat to perform the cremation rites for Master Chun.
Xiangzhao lamented amidst his illness, saying, "My dream was indeed like this; I sought it from afar. When Xiangzhao passed away, the Master observed the mourning rites with full propriety.
At that time, the tides of the Yangtze River damaged the fields, and the autumn harvest yielded nothing. The community consequently ran out of food. The Master personally went out to beg for alms.
Upon hearing of him, donors arrived like the wind, and provisions piled up like mountains, such that no one knew where they came from. Every day he beat the drum and ascended the hall.
He instructed others without weariness, widely fanning the winds of his school. In the second year of the Jianyan era, he retired from the monastery and departed for Qiantang.

Passing through Meizong, he paid homage at the traces of the Great Being (Avalokiteśvara). Over seven hundred fishing households along the coast, upon hearing of the Master’s arrival, all destroyed their nets and abandoned their livelihoods;
such was his power in transforming sentient beings. The Governor of Tiantai three times invited him to Guoqing Monastery, but he did not accept; instead, he went to Xuefeng.
Having received this imperial decree, he was transferred from Mingzhou’s Yuyang Monastery to both Longxiang and Xingqing Monasteries in Wenzhou.
When he requested leave for retirement, it was not granted. He then moved to Jingshan in Lin’an, where he resided for five years. Upon falling ill, he returned to Changlu.
After Empress Dowager Cining returned from Jin, she established Chongxian Xianxiao Temple at the foot of Gaoting Mountain; by imperial edict, the Master was appointed as its founding abbot.

In the first year [of his reign], he declined the invitation on the grounds of illness. Being unable to decline further, he finally entered the monastery. Traveling while braving the summer heat, his ailment grew even more severe; yet he still ascended the seat to preach the Dharma.
The Empress Dowager came in person, lifting the palace curtains to listen intently. She drew from the imperial treasury to sponsor a great *shuilu* assembly.

Although the Master’s illness did not abate, imperial messengers arrived in rapid succession to inquire after him. The Master responded with composed courtesy, offering his thanks. After a short while, he called for the Head Seat and said:
"I shall now depart. Thereupon, he closed his eyes and passed away while seated in the full lotus posture. The Cining Palace bestowed incense and granted a sacrificial offering.

A site was divined to the west of the temple in the Peach Blossom Grove, where a stupa was erected to inter his remains. Ten thousand people followed him in his funeral procession, their hearts pierced with grief and their tears falling like rain;
all lamented that the ancestral flowers had withered and the Zen grove had fallen into cold desolation. By imperial decree, he was posthumously titled Chan Master Wukong Jingzhao.
The Master’s physical appearance was tall and slender; his eyebrows and eyes were sparse yet elegant. His spirit was serene and profound, and his capacity for discernment was agile and active.

His realization of the Way was such that there was nothing before him and no need for humility toward those behind; he was without exterior and empty within. Thus, when people followed his transformation, they did so without even realizing it themselves. As for Guizhu’an:
initially residing at Nengren Monastery on Mount Yandang, his karmic conditions for the Dharma had not yet ripened. At that time, the Master was at Jiangxin. Specifically...
He crossed the river to welcome [Zhiyi] back to his quarters and performed nine prostrations to entice the people of Wenzhou; consequently, they all turned toward him with harmonious reverence.
Renouncing the great Dharma without being confined by sectarian boundaries, he was truly a preeminent figure in the ancestral domain and an outstanding talent within the forest of monks.
Minghe said: "Zhenxie bowed to Zhuanan; Zhaojue welcomed Luohan. They knew only to propagate the Way, not knowing they were acting for my sake.
The virtue and loyalty of the ancients reached such heights of sincerity that this style has now died out."
The Biography of Fagong (Zidehui):
Fagong styled himself the "Old Man of the Stone Window. He was the son of the Lin family of Fenghua. His mother conceived him after being moved by a dream of a foreign monk entering her chamber.
He shaved his head and received full ordination, studying the Nanshan Vinaya at Huxin Temple. There he heard of the reputation of Hongzhi of Tiantong.

He went to follow [Master] Huì and served him as an elder brother. Day and night he sat in a meditative posture. One day, while sitting in the corridor of the hall, he happened to hear the speech of a monk;
it entered his ears with crystal clarity, and he attained sudden enlightenment. His sweat drenched his entire body.

Hóngzhì questioned him regarding what he had realized and, finding it was not erroneous, appointed him to the position of attendant. Subsequently, he traveled extensively to study under various masters. Upon meeting Xián Wànnián, Wànnián tested him.
When he asked a question, the Master covered his ears and left. Master Caotang Qing did not permit this;
the Master briefly entered the room, went straight up to him, snatched the whisk from his hand, threw it on the floor, and departed. The entire assembly was struck with amazement.

Later, when Huanglong Zhong placed the sounding block and whisk upon the incense table to test his disciples, the Master said to his attendant, "The Master’s way of being so entangled is truly a bother."
"What is the use of this? After a short while, he picked up each one individually and asked, "If you cannot respond when a single opportunity passes, do not say that I did not tell you.
When the attendant reported this to Zhong, he had them removed. Three years later, he returned to Tiantong to take charge of the treasury keys and served as the First Seat (Diyizuo).

He occupied the seat to preach the Dharma; regarding the essential points of the school raised by Hongzhi, the Master would not compromise or conform to them. Hongzhi loved him and stood in awe of him. [The year of his passing was] Shao... (text fragmentary).

In the twenty-third year of the Xingxing era, the seat at Guangxiao Temple was vacant. The Governor of Yue sent a letter to Hongzhi, requesting that a person of true color (ben-se) be appointed to fill the position.
Hongzhi recommended the Master for this duty. At that time, the pagoda of Yingtian Temple had collapsed, and some suggested that he abandon his post there.
The Master said, "If not me, who else would do it? Once the pagoda was completed, he finally moved to Nanren Temple. In the first year of the Longxing era, Minister Zhao took up the governorship.

In the fourth year of the Ming era, he welcomed the Master [Zhaoqing] to repay his debt of gratitude. Among the remains of the devastation by the invaders, he completed all that his predecessors had left unfinished.
The buildings were spacious and magnificent, becoming the preeminent monastery (*aranya*) in the entire city. In the sixth year of the Qiandao era, he retired to Changsheng on Xiaoxi.
The following year, the Prince of Rongyang invited him to reside at Ruiyan, where he expanded the monastic quarters to settle the assembly.

He cleared mountain fields to provide for his own sustenance and constructed a magnificent pavilion to enshrine the Great Being Avalokiteśvara; its architectural splendor was most grand. When Master Fan invited him to move to Xuedou, he complied.
Later, having returned from Jingci, he eventually restored Xuedou to him. He subsequently resided at Ruiyan.
On the eighth day of the eighth month in the eighth year of the Chunxi era, he manifested slight illness and instructed his disciples: "Do not burden me with medicinal tonics."
"I, I shall now depart. Summon Zide with this letter; come to see me as you did in ordinary times.

He entrusted his final affairs to others and wrote letters of parting for the various scholar-officials and those with whom he had long associated. At dawn the following day, he ascended the seat, recited a verse, and passed away.

He was eighty years of age and fifty-nine years since his ordination. By nature the Master was exceptionally eminent; he maintained the Vinaya with great strictness and repeatedly presided over major monasteries.

As for his daily life—whether rising, resting, sleeping, or eating—he invariably shared these things with the community. He did not concern himself with elaborate adornments and had no other personal indulgences.

Steeped in integrity and possessing a resolute backbone, he would not borrow his words or countenance from others. Toward those who possessed the Way, he exerted all his strength to uplift and guide them; yet toward those who were wise yet deranged, he would certainly rebuke them.

When the seat at Jingci Temple in Lin’an was vacant, he was earnestly invited to take it, but he instead sailed across the sea to evade this summons. Prince Wei, a member of the imperial family, composed [a work in his honor].
Muli always paid him the highest respect and wished to visit him in the mountains, but [the Master] declined, saying, "The road is long and perilous; it would only be a waste of effort.
His sternness and severity were generally like this.
Huìhuī, whose courtesy name was Zìdé, was the son of the Zhāng family of Kuàijī. When he was barely twenty years old, he visited Zhēnxiè at Chánglú and attained a slight realization.
Upon returning home, he went to pay his respects to Hónghzhì. Hónghzhì raised the koan: "In light there is darkness; do not meet it with darkness."
In the midst of darkness there was light, yet he did not perceive it through the appearance of light. When questioned about this, his words did not accord with the truth.

At the end of the first watch of the night, he rose from his seat and went before the sacred image of the Buddha to burn incense; at that moment, Hongzhi happened to arrive. Upon suddenly seeing him, he immediately understood the previous dialogue. The following day, he entered the room [for formal instruction].

Zhizhe approved him, granting him the status of a true son within the lineage. In the Ding-si year of the Xiang-ning era, he began teaching the Dharma at Putuo, then moved to Wanshou, followed by Jixiang and Xuedou.
In the third year of the Chun-xi era, he was appointed to Jingci. In the seventh year, he retired back to Xuedou, where he passed away.
Wang Pi, the Duke of Wei who served as Chancellor, once said: "Since attaining realization, I have been like a single stone in deep clouds. Shi Chuang was the Censor of the Empty Gate;
this was considered a famous saying by those in all quarters.
Biography of Chan Master Depeng (with the appended biography of Shouzhang).
Depeng was the son of the Gu family of Yanguan. Initially, he became a disciple of the renowned local monk Shouzhang and served him diligently for several years.

In the eighteenth year of the Xiangxing era, he entered Mount Jing to pay his respects to Chan Master Zhenxie Li. He stayed overnight at the foot of the mountain. That night, Zhenxie dreamed that two moons entered the monastery.
The following morning, he recounted the dream to the assembly. Just as they were speaking, the Master arrived; Zhenxie felt a sense of wonder toward him.

As they engaged in dialogue, their exchange of *ji-feng* (critical spiritual sparks) was so sharp and profound that it was as if the Master had long been engaged in formal inquiry. Thereupon, he entered the inner quarters and devoted himself to intensive investigation day and night. All...
He endured the rigors of four years of winter and summer. One day, while observing a water leak, he used a pestle to clear a bamboo joint; as it made a sound, he attained sudden enlightenment.

Xie approved of this, and the various quarters of the Buddhist world came to call him Master Zhutong (Bamboo Tube). When Xie was summoned by imperial decree to reside at Chongxian Xianxiao Monastery on Gaoting Mountain, the Master attended him there.
After Xie passed away, the Master succeeded him in accordance with the decree to propagate the Dharma. At that time, he was twenty-three years old.
This was his [ordination] year. From then on, he entered the Cining Hall twice—once before and once after—where he ascended the seat to preach the Dharma, greatly pleasing the Emperor’s heart.

The Emperor bestowed upon him Dharma robes and granted him an annual decree to ordain one disciple as an attendant. Because Master [Feng]zhao was elderly and lacked means of support, he requested to resign from his monastic duties to return home for a visit;
this was permitted. Less than two years later, he received an imperial edict to reside at Chongxian Temple. This was the third year of the Qiandao era.
He passed away without illness. His *Dantang Zhutong Yulu* (The Bamboo-Tube Record of Dantang) circulates in the world.

Chang’s secular surname was Wang; he possessed a singular and exceptional natural character. At the age of seven, he underwent the examination on the scriptures and received ordination. His observance of the precepts was pure and refined, and he was skilled in poetry.
He was titled Chan Master Wenhui. He had a collection known as the *Shiyuan Ji*. He once composed a verse for late spring that begins: "The grasses grow deep amidst the misty scenery..."
Heavy. The forest is lush as the evening sun fades. Flowers fall even before they have bloomed; without wind, the cotton絮 drifts on its own.
In the second year of the Shaoxing era, Emperor Gaozong visited Yuanjue Temple and personally inscribed this quatrain with his imperial calligraphy.
