Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks, Volume Ten.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Minghe of Huashan Temple in Wu County during the Ming Dynasty.
Chapter on the Practice of Dhyāna:
Biography of Chan Master Xiatang Yuan of the Song Dynasty.
Huiyuan, styled Xiatang, was the son of the Peng family from Jinliu Town in Meishan. At the age of thirteen, he enrolled at Yaoshi Monastery.

He became a monk and studied the sutras and śāstras. Later, he abandoned them to rely upon Master Lingyan Hui. Having attained a slight awakening, he went to see Yuanwu while the latter was presiding over Zhaojue.

Upon hearing Yuanwu cite the anecdote concerning Layman Pang’s question to Mazu regarding "not being a companion to the myriad dharmas," the Master attained great enlightenment and collapsed among the assembly.
As the assembly supported him, the Master said, "I have awakened from my dream. From that time on...
His spiritual pivot was sharp and piercing; the assembly dubbed him "Iron Tongue Yuan. When Yuanwu passed away, the Master traveled eastward and successively occupied renowned monasteries.
From Huqiu, he received an imperial decree to reside at Chongguang on Gaotingshan. At that time, Emperor Xiaozong was devoted to the school of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

He summoned the Master to have an audience in Xuande Hall, and whenever he entered the Neiguan Hall to see him, he would invariably invite him to sit and offer tea, addressing him by his title rather than his name.
The Emperor’s courtesy toward him was greater than that shown to his other teachers. The Emperor said, "The other day, while asleep, I suddenly heard the sound of a bell and woke up.
I do not know whether the dream and the waking state are different. The Master said, "Dreaming and waking are no different; the awakened mind is unmoving.
The Emperor said, "Since both dreams and illusions are unreal, from where does the sound of the bell arise? The Master said, "It arises from the place where Your Majesty asks. The Emperor said:
"If that is so, then how can one ultimately escape birth and death? The Master said, "If you do not awaken to the Mahāyāna, you will never be able to escape.
He asked, "How does one attain awakening? The Master said, "Polish the nature that is inherently present; through the passage of years and months, you will naturally attain awakening. He asked again.

"After awakening, what is it like? The Master said, "After awakening, one first realizes that all the questions and answers of today were not [the truth]. [The monk] asked, "After realizing that everything is not [the truth], what then?
The Master said, "The naked body is manifest before you; there is no further appearance to be seen. The Head Monk nodded in agreement.
He was granted the title Chan Master Fohai. One day, the Imperial carriage visited his quarters. On the wall of the room hung a portrait of him walking in meditation. The Emperor—

The Emperor pointed and asked the Master, "This is merely ink and water, empty dust; where does the 'Real' reside? The Master joined his palms, stepped forward, and said, "The spring air is mild and warm;

we respectfully wish Your Majesty a myriad blessings. The Emperor laughed heartily and subsequently composed a eulogy for him. The Master’s person became the focal point of the Dharma gate’s expectations;
his extraordinary words and wondrous phrases were disseminated throughout all quarters, and students flocked to him like clouds rushing toward rain or rivers flowing into the sea.
To follow where the Master is found is to return to the correct path; it is as if a Buddha has appeared in the world. In the autumn of the year Yiwu (1175), he addressed the assembly, saying:
"On the first day of the ninth month of the intercalary late autumn in the second year of the Chunxi era: Do not show your head in the midst of the clamor; cast your eye upon the cold ground.
Brightness and darkness do not interfere with one another; each side is divided into its own half. Who would teach you to become a nobleman? Who sells firewood and charcoal to you?"
"The Way cannot be disparaged, nor can it be praised; its essence is like empty space, without shore or limit. Call out to one another, come back!

The first day of the New Year is surely the fifteenth of the first month. This was rumored throughout the capital, yet people remained skeptical. When the appointed time arrived, all the princes, ministers, and high officials gathered there.
The Master ascended the seat to preach the Dharma, then entered his quarters and bolted the door from within. The Master had previously kept a monkey that was quite...
Having become tame and familiar with him, he clothed the monkey and named him "The Monkey Walker. After some time, the crowd peered through a crack in the window;

there was no sound or movement, and they saw only the monkey holding a scroll while attending by the master's side. They hurried inside, but the master had already passed away. The writing on the scroll was his verse of farewell at the end of his life.
The verse says: Breaking the scale-weight, overturning the proclamation; the light of the pivot suddenly emerges, where even a crow cannot fly across.
For seven days his countenance remained unchanged; his entire body was enshrined in a stupa on Mount Wu at the monastery.
The Biography of Chan Master Shouchun (with the appended biography of Zhicai).
Shouchun, whose style name was Fodeng, was the son of the Shi family of Anji. He first visited Chan Master Guangjian Ying, but did not find resonance with him.

He then proceeded to Taiping, where he joined the assembly to seek instruction; however, he made no progress whatsoever. Thereupon, he sealed his bedding and made a vow, saying: "If I do not penetrate [the truth], I shall not [rise from this bed]."
He performed this [prostration]. Thereupon, he remained standing upright day and night, as if he had lost his parents.

After more than seven weeks had passed, Master Fojian ascended the hall and said, "The myriad phenomena of the universe are all sealed by the One Dharma. Upon hearing this, the Master attained sudden enlightenment.
Fojian said, "What a pity! A single bright pearl has been picked up by this madman. He then cited the words regarding Lingyun’s realization of the peach to question him.
He understood it completely, without any lingering doubt or obstruction. Rising from his prostrations, he presented this verse: "All day long I gazed at the sky without raising my head;
Only when the peach blossoms were in full bloom did I lift my eyes. Even if you had a net that could cover the heavens, Once you have penetrated the secure barrier, you may simply rest.
Upon entering the assembly, he spoke with a stern voice: "This time, Seat-Holder Xun will sleep soundly forever. When Yuanwu heard this, he suspected that this was not yet the case.
He said, "I must first examine him before he may be accepted. He sent someone to summon the master and took him along for a mountain excursion.
Upon arriving at a certain pond, he suddenly pushed the master into the water and immediately asked, "What was it like when Niutou had not yet met the Fourth Patriarch?

The master replied instantly, "The pond is deep; the fish gather there. He asked again, "What was it like after he had seen him? He replied, "The tree is high; it beckons the wind. He asked once more, "As for seeing and not seeing..."
When asked, "What is it like at the moment of seeing? he replied, "Stretching out one's legs is within the drawing in of one's legs. Da-wu praised this highly.

The Master occupied the monastic seat four times throughout his life, his reputation and brilliance shining brilliantly. Later, he passed away at Tian-ning. As he was about to die, he said to the layman Shuang-huai Zheng Ji:
"The eighth day of the tenth month is the anniversary of the passing of my late teacher, Fo-jian; I shall arrive there soon. I beg you to return [to him]."
Four days later, while they were south of Mount Zhang, Lord Zheng sent his younger brother, Sengdao, to inquire after him. The Master said, "Your coming is exactly at the right time.
Although I was born of the same lineage as Fojian, I shall not die of the same lineage. He added, "Come early tomorrow and find a small boat for me;
five feet in height will suffice. Three days later, at the crowing of the cock, he sat upright as usual.
The attendant requested a verse. The Master said, "I have never composed one. Having finished speaking, he passed away. At his cremation, his tongue remained unburnt.
Chen Shiyuan, a local resident, enshrined it in a precious casket and kept it in his home. His remains were interred beside Puying Monastery. The Master’s countenance was pure and dignified;
in proclaiming the fundamental tenets of the school, he fully embodied the spirit of his ancestors. On one occasion, he addressed the assembly, saying, "Brothers..."
Whenever he attained a realization, he would invite [disciples] regardless of the time to reveal his insight. Once, during a snowy night, a monk knocked on the door of the abbot’s quarters.
The Master called him in and, with a majestic roar, shouted: "In the middle of the night under heavy snow, why do you come seeking a resolution for your doubts while your deportment is so lacking?
The monk looked down at his robe and satchel. The Master shouted and sent him out. His sharp, rigorous responses were consistently like this.
On which mountain did he reside? During a year of drought, the Prefect requested that the Master perform a prayer for rain. The Master reluctantly consented and ascended the seat;
with eyes wide and glaring at the heavens, he cursed, saying, "Who taught you to force the heavens? At these words, the rain arrived immediately.
People called him "Xun Who Cursed the Heavens."
Zhicai was a native of Shuzhou. Sharing the same surname and having been a fellow disciple under the same master, he too was a monk of lofty conduct.
He resided at Yuelu and later moved to Longya, where for thirty years he led the assembly with austerity and purity, attracting many who sought refuge in him. He passed away at Yunxi.

Yuan Bu-na transmitted the lineage to Jingyuan, who was styled Ciyuan. He was the son of the Zhang family of Nanxi in Yongjia. At the age of eighteen, he relied upon Lingxi to receive full ordination.
Later, he studied the Tiantai teachings, but eventually left them to visit Yuanwu at Zhongfu. There, he heard a monk reciting the words from Dead Heart’s (Sixin) informal sermon.
He said, "Since one is deluded, one must attain awakening; since one has awakened, one must recognize delusion within awakening and awakening within delusion.

Resplendent and magnificent, all who beheld him were uplifted and delighted. As the teachings were thus restored, many commentators praised Master Xiù’s righteousness, and songs of praise arose spontaneously.
Regarding the path of this Dhyāna Master, he was the direct heir and legitimate successor of the Linjì lineage.
During the decline of the Buddhist order, the remaining branches of the various schools had become faint and were on the verge of extinction; yet the Master alone preserved the entire progeny.
Spreading throughout the world for a hundred years, those who resided on this mountain as Chan masters—fathers and sons, brothers and cousins—followed one after another in unbroken succession.
Yet they all gazed upon their ancestors with weary eyes;
as the eaves crumbled and the walls collapsed, they stood before them in awe, yet none would deign to lift a hand to take up a single tile or a single beam.

While others merely provide relief from wind, rain, cold, and heat, Master Xiou is of a different caliber; he alone knows how to honor the foundation of the Teaching by refurbishing the temple buildings, thereby manifesting filial piety toward one who was not his own ancestor.
This is not only a matter of public appreciation for virtue, but is sufficient to extinguish the selfishness of factionalism.
Thus he corrected the frivolous customs of the age. As for those who, having become heirs to others, neglect their own ancestors—how does this compare to the propriety of Master Gong’s conduct?
Minghe said: "After the Master had seen Yuanwu, because his two parents were already advanced in years, he resided at Baoshan."
He attended and supported his parents for several years. While residing at Tiger Hill (Hǔqīu), he recalled the precedent established by Băi Cūnduàn of erecting a Patriarchs’ Hall.

He then remarked, "As one who follows in another's footsteps, how can it be right if I fail to personally carry out their bequeathed instructions? He subsequently had their portraits painted and enshrined there.
These two matters—one recorded in the *Shānzhì* and the other appearing in the *Chuándēng*—demonstrate the Master’s profound depth of filial piety.
While reading Tianyin’s text on the repair of the stupa, I was deeply moved by its contents. How is it that later descendants do not act likewise?
Therefore, I have appended this text to the end of the biography to serve as a warning for the future, and to show that Master Xiu possessed true capacity;
it is a pity, however, that we lack the means to examine his life from beginning to end. What a shame.
Biography of Chan Master Yuyang (Appendix: Shuian). Duan was born into the Qian clan.
He was a descendant of the Kings of Wuyue. His sixth-generation ancestor had governed Kuaiji and consequently settled there. The Master was naturally gifted and extraordinary from birth.
At fourteen, he drove away crows at Dasha Temple; at eighteen, he received the tonsure and the full precepts (*upasampadā*). He then went to rely upon...
Chan Master Jingci Yi heard a monk strike a pillar and say, "Why do you not speak of Chan? At that moment, the Master suddenly attained a slight realization.
He subsequently visited Longmen Yuan, Ganlu Zhuo, and Letan Xiang, all of whom commended him for his exceptional brilliance.
Later, he met Yuanwu at Zhongfu Mountain. One day, Yuanwu asked, "Who knows that the Eye of the True Dharma was extinguished by that blind donkey?"

[The Master] withdrew. [The Master] asked, "Tell me, is it now extinguished or not? [Zhaozhou] replied, "Please, Reverend, keep your mouth shut. Wuzhuo said, "This is still within the realm of ordinary sentiment.

As the Master was about to respond, Wuzhuo struck him. The Master’s lingering attachments were instantly dispelled. He attended Wuzhuo while residing at Tianning Temple, where he was appointed to oversee the secretariat.
Subsequently, he took his place on the teaching seat; his reputation for the Way resounded far and wide. Throughout his career, he repeatedly presided over great monastic centers.

Like Danxia, Huqiu, Wanshou, and Baoning, as well as Xuansha of Min, Shoushan, and Xichan, he was invited by the clergy and laity of Pingjiang to establish a hermitage at Xihua, where he harbored the intention to spend the remainder of his life there.
Suddenly, however, he received an imperial decree appointing him to the abbotship of Lingyin and Cining.
The Empress Dowager requested that he preach the Dharma and bestowed upon him a golden-embroidered robe and a formal title. He petitioned to return to Xihua, but this was not permitted;

instead, an imperial decree was issued appointing him as the *yùwáng* (Prince of Nurturing). When the Master presided over the assembly, his countenance was invariably stern and majestic. He never turned his back on the community regarding sleep or meals, and he exhorted the Way without weariness.

As he was about to pass away, his disciples requested his final instructions. The Master said, "Exhaust this mind and intention; support one another with the Way. Having spoken these words, he passed away.
After the cremation, his eyes, teeth, and tongue remained uncorrupted, and the ground emitted light throughout the entire night.

Those who obtained *śarīra* relics were innumerable, and they continued to appear for over a month without ceasing. Huang Guan Luo Zhaochang, who had regularly sought instruction from the Master, returned from outside and found him alone.
He obtained nothing. His resolve for the Way was earnest and fervent. While he was eating with a guest, as he was chewing, there appeared something like an object;
when he spat it out, it was a *śarīra*, about the size of a bean, with a color like amber. A person fond of such things took it away. He then prostrated himself again at the site of the cremation.
Hearing a sound from the incense casket, he opened it immediately and found what he had obtained as before, though it was slightly redder and glossier. His disciples then received it.
His remains were interred at Xihu on Mount Mao, and he was posthumously titled Chan Master Dawu.
His disciple Shi Yi, whose style name was Shui’an, was one of the masters who received the Dharma from him.

While the other monks under his leadership were intent on maintaining strict discipline, only Shui’an was by nature serene and simple, living with extreme frugality. He stood tall and dignified amidst the crowd, never once deigning to worry about such matters.
The Master did not press him too strenuously. After the Master passed away, Shuian’s Way flourished greatly. He traveled through four prefectures and served as abbot of eight monasteries;

wherever he went, he was cautious and diligent in practicing the Way, making the establishment of the Dharma his primary concern. In the fifth year of the Chunxi era, he retired from Jingci Monastery on West Lake, leaving behind a verse that says:
"For six years I swept and cleaned the imperial capital temple; Now its rubble has been transformed into a palace of Śakra and Brahmā."

Today, his work accomplished, he returns home; from the tip of his staff, a pure breeze rises in all eight directions. Though the officials and commoners block his path and entreat him to stay, he does not stop, finally passing away at Tianning Monastery in Xiuzhou.
The *Dongyang County Gazetteer* states: Shui’an was surnamed Ma. He left home to become a monk at the age of sixteen and received full ordination under Fayan Shanzun as his teacher.
Later, he passed through Qiantang and visited Zhaoqing Temple, where he met a strange man who prophesied of him, saying, "This is a dragon among monks."
Wearing a bamboo hat with snow and flower-patterned shoes, he traveled extensively, visiting various Chan monasteries. In the seventh year of the Qiandao era, he moved from Baolin to Jingci.
On the Buddha-bath day of the ninth year, he entered the Inner Contemplation Hall. He planned to spend his final years at Bao’en in Jiahe.
Before long, he fell ill and wrote a letter to bid farewell to the local officials; he then sat upright and passed away. Upon cremation, five-colored śarīras were obtained.
His teeth remained clenched in a fist without decaying. His verse on departing this world says: "Throughout my life, I used what was necessary;

a dead snake, I have skillfully brought to life. With a single blow of the fist, I shattered empty space; even Buddhas and Patriarchs cannot find a crack to peer through. He has several volumes of recorded sayings.
Prefaced by Grand Director of Education Gao Wenhǔ. Zuozhen was the son of Lin [family] of Xinghua;
his mother was née Chen. She dreamed that a foreign monk bestowed upon her a bright pearl, and she therefore questioned the monk.
"Where have you come from? He replied, "My surname is Huang and my name is Nirvana. While my mother was pregnant with me, she became enlightened;
when I was born, I possessed extraordinary marks. The hair over my entire body is two inches long. Once, I went to Drums Mountain to visit Chan Master Jianchun.

Upon seeing me, he marveled at me, saying, 'This is a golden-haired lion; truly a vessel for the Dharma. Later, while I was out begging for alms for the monks, I arrived at Huangshi, where there was a Zhu..."

As for Xing: one night he dreamed that a yellow Nirvana ascended his gate. At dawn, the Master arrived. Zhu was overjoyed and offered him five hundred strings of cash, bowing to him before seeing him off.
He subsequently went to consult Chan Master Foxin at Dongshan. When Foxin moved to Guqiao, [Xing followed him].
He requested the Master to serve as the Head Seat (Śrāmaṇera-pramukha). The assembly was all astonished and looked at one another, saying, "Master Linji has never before opened his mouth;

even if there were the Buddha-dharma within his breast, how could he possibly proclaim it? That night, the Head Seat held the whisk and responded to questions according to their capacity, his discourse being inexhaustible under every challenge.
From then on, his reputation for Chan spread far and wide. Focin (Fuxin) subsequently vacated the position, and [the Master] succeeded him. He later moved [to other positions].
Quanshi Fashih addressed the assembly, saying: "To seek the ox, one must follow its tracks; in studying the Way, the absence of mind is prized.
When the tracks are found, the ox returns; when there is no mind, the Way is easy to find. He raised his whisk and said: "This is the track. Where is the ox? He further said:
"As for this matter, it is like a person eating rice: when full, they simply stop. If they are not yet full, they will surely continue."
There is the mind that craves the food of thought; yet if one eats too much, there is the affliction of injury to the heart.

When one reaches this point, how can one attain the state of being exactly right? After a long silence, he said: "For now, return to sleep beneath the cliff, and together we shall watch when the moon is bright. These were the words of the Master’s instruction.
Be truly vigilant. Those with shallow faculties and inferior understanding are rarely able to meet [this teaching]. Throughout his life, the Master lived with frugality and austerity;

he exhausted the contents of his purse to construct a stone stūpa for the Seven Buddhas outside the triple gate of Fashi Temple. On the day the work was completed, he immediately ascended the hall to bid farewell to the assembly and departed.
He went into seclusion at Baishuiyan (White Water Rock) on Jialing. Those living near the rock all said: "In the past, there was..."
The Master Dao once said, "Forty years hence, there shall come a flesh-and-blood Bodhisattva to flourish upon this mountain.
It has now been exactly forty years since that prediction; let us all exert our strength to renovate this mountain retreat. The Provincial Commissioner Chuan Zide is devoted to the practice of Chan.
He alone showed exceptional reverence for his teacher, once saying, "Master Fashí is a Buddha of antiquity in the present age;

one must take refuge in him. As he was about to pass away, he spoke this verse: "Birth is fundamentally without birth; death is fundamentally without death. Between the two paths of birth and death, there is ultimately no distinction between self and other.
Upon cremation, the *śarīra* relics were beyond counting, and people vied with one another to obtain them. The remainder were interred at Fashí.
The inscription for his stupa was engraved upon stone, and his *yulu* (recorded sayings) were compiled and circulated. Minghe stated:
"At the end of the Tang dynasty, there was a śramaṇa named Wenju, also known as Niepan. His secular surname was Huang.

He lived in seclusion beneath a high crag on Nang Mountain, sitting in the lotus posture and abstaining from food. When he walked, two tigers followed him; at times he would ride them when going out or returning."
His prophecies were all fulfilled without exception. Some say he was an emanation body of a Pratyekabuddha; thus, his dwelling place is called the Pratyekabuddha Grotto.
The grotto has a small opening from which a strange fragrance occasionally wafts forth. His miraculous traces are so numerous that they cannot be enumerated;
the people of Min are all able to recount them.
Liaocan succeeded Liaocan.
A native of the Luo clan of Quannan, he entered the quarters of Master Qin at Jiangshan and attained great insight and knowledge.

He developed unimpeded eloquence and resided at Jingzhong in Zhangzhou, later moving to Taiping Xingguo. The State Councilor Zong honored him as his teacher; the Master maintained himself with strict adherence to the monastic discipline.
He was beyond reproach. His path of expounding the Dharma was vigorous, swift, clear, and penetrating; he ascended directly to the Supreme Vehicle (*anuttarayāna*).
Whether writing characters or composing poetry, he attained the *samādhi* of playful mastery, yet the Master never once applied conscious effort toward these things.

On the Double Ninth, he ascended the hall for the assembly and said: "The Double Ninth, the day of the new chrysanthemums— A single phrase, luminously manifest throughout antiquity and today. Yang Guang’s camel..."
There is no place to be found. Last night, his footprints were seen in the shade of the pines. The Grand Chancellor, Lord Li, once visited the Master at Qiyun;
his inquiry into the Way was to his satisfaction, and they established a society for the recitation of scriptures. The Master’s disciples compiled his words into a book.
The Layman Deng Su of Binglu wrote a preface, stating: "The Abbot Can of Daping Temple followed Jiangshan [Hui]—how could he ever have obtained a rabbit's horn?"
He dwelt in great peace; fundamentally, he had never established even a needle-point of existence.

Occupying the lion’s throne, he let out the lion’s roar, yet he never once preached so much as a hair’s breadth of Dharma for the sake of the human world. Scholars from the four quarters all touched their foreheads to the ground;
they gathered his residual grace and preserved it as a treasure. Alas! This was merely the dregs of his teaching—how could it be the truth itself? Nevertheless, what else is there beyond these dregs?
This is the truth. To view all as empty at once—whether one says "the head exists" or "the head does not exist"—is acceptable.

Like the thundering sound and profound silence, they are fundamentally simultaneous. If disciples gain awakening through this, then every cough, laugh, movement, and breath is the meaning of the Westward Journey.
If, however, one clings to this to seek a teacher, then the plucking of the flower and the smile are already superfluous.
As for the Dharma: for one who awakens to it, heaven and earth are but a single finger; for one who clings to it, a hair’s breadth becomes a thousand li.
He returned to question his teacher, but the teacher remained utterly silent. Alas! Could the teacher have been merely one who possessed the eyes to read the scriptures?
Zhijian’s Biography:
Zhijian was a native of Quanjiao in Chuzhou. Born into the Wu family, he had already taken delight in Buddhist scriptures since childhood;
he would often take blank paper as sutras and sit in the full lotus posture to recite them, his clear and resonant voice moving all who heard it. His mother once washed a sore on his hand for him.
He asked in jest, "What kind of hand is this? The boy replied, "A Buddha’s hand. His mother looked at him and laughed loudly. Shortly thereafter, both his parents passed away.
He went to rely on Zhenxie of Changlu, where he left home to become a monk and applied himself with such vigor that for several years his side did not even touch the mat.

At that time, Master Daxiu Jue was the head seat (shouzuo) and recognized him as a vessel of the Dharma. He received the full precepts from Master Daofa and entered the lineage of Zheng of Mount Xiang.

He lived in a thatched hut on a mountain situated in a remote and isolated place by the seashore, where many demons and spirits abounded. The Master dwelt there alone, his reflection as his only companion, and though a hundred monsters sought to bewilder him, they could not disturb him.
Since the ground was high and lacked water, he prayed, saying, "I have come here to cultivate the Way; may the deity grant me a spring.

He then dug a small pit with his hoe, and after a short while, water overflowed from it. When his food ran out, he sustained himself on pine and cypress needles to stave off hunger. Thus he practiced.
One night, while sitting in meditation, he heard the rocks behind the hermitage rumbling and crashing like a violent battle.

Rising at dawn to investigate, he saw that a massive boulder had flown down and stood beside the hermitage, blocking its entrance; yet not a single large tree was crushed or torn, and the hermitage alone remained uninjured.
One day, a giant python entered the hermitage, raising its head and glaring fiercely. After several days, it returned and coiled itself around [the hermitage].
The master did not look back and departed. A hundred strange apparitions manifested, yet the master raised his hand and remained unmoved;

gradually, they subsided into stillness. One night, while in deep samādhi, he attained a sudden and complete awakening. His body, mind, and the world became as transparent as lapis lazuli. He thought to himself:
"Before the time of Vipaśyin Buddha (Vīraṇarāja), there was self-realization without a teacher; after the time of Vīraṇarāja, those who have realized it without a teacher are all Buddhas."

The outsider Māra then descended the mountain and saw Yan-shou. He said, "These past days my belly has grown large but there is nothing to eat; this hermitage is small and there is no bed to sleep on.
If you can provide me with food and expand this hermitage, I shall stay; otherwise, I shall depart.

Yan-shou engaged him in a series of questions and answers, but he could not overcome him. Consequently, Yan-shou inquired about the realization he had attained, and the outsider presented a verse. Yan-shou said joyfully, "Master Jian!"
Che also set sail again by sea and met Dayu at Yue-lin. Testing his wit and eloquence, which were unimpeded, Dayu sighed and said, "Even the Buddhas and Patriarchs could do nothing against you.
Thereupon, he went on almsround, carrying two cloth bags and accepting whatever he obtained. He underwent every kind of hardship and toil that others could not endure.
When Cui-shan Zong-bai had grown old, he said to the Master, "To exert oneself for the sake of the assembly is not without its merit..."
Lao said, "You must know that there is one who does not labor. Zong said, "When one cannot be contained within the station of the Honored and Noble, what then?
The Master said, "Meeting him everywhere, yet not being recognized. Zong said, "That is still the guest and host on the road. What is the Host within the Host?
The Master said, "The fire is extinguished by the wind of Bing and Ding. Zong covered the Master’s mouth with his hand. The Master brushed it away.

Xiu followed Zong when he moved to Xuedou, accompanying him and managing all communal affairs. At that time, the Dharma Hall had been newly renovated, and Zong ordered the Master to deliver a general discourse (*pūsè*).
Listening in secret, Zong sighed and said, "I have had ears since birth, yet I have never heard such a thing. Later, the Master served as the incense-bearer for Da-xiu.
Throughout his career, he occupied the seat of enlightenment on six occasions, each time being recommended by princes, dukes, and high officials. In the second year of the Shaohui era, he retired.
His affairs were concluded at the East Hermitage of Xuedou. In the seventh month of the following year, he manifested signs of illness and instructed his disciples, saying, "I am departing.
For my funeral, you must strive for simplicity; do not wear white mourning garments or wail in grief. Having finished speaking, he passed away.

He had lived for eighty-eight years and spent fifty-three summer retreats in the monasteries. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa on the left side of the mountain. The Master was simple and sincere by nature, and his realization of the ground...
He was steady and prudent; his conduct was austere and rigorous, never wavering even unto death. Possessing great eloquence, it was vast and boundless;
when questioned, it flowed forth inexhaustibly. Offerings bestowed upon him accumulated like mountains, yet he spent them all for public purposes.

Consequently, six abandoned temples with arrears totaling several thousand strings of cash were revitalized by him within no more than a month, such that every affair was renewed. As for the room where he slept, it was merely a *zhangshi* (a small study).

He lived in such solitude that his ritual vessels were as empty as hanging bells. Furthermore, moved by his refined sincerity, his prayers for rain during drought and his efforts to relieve the suffering of the sick were answered as surely as an echo.

Whenever sacrificial animals were being slaughtered at a shrine, he would invariably replace them with vegetarian offerings. Some even preserved his hair and beard and obtained *śarīra* relics from them;
these were all unprecedented occurrences in the secular world. The Master did not wish for others to speak of them, considering them to be outside the Way.
The ultimate. That he was able to possess such [attainments] was entirely due to the remnants of his teacher’s influence.
His teacher’s reputation resounded throughout the land, yet his physical traces never once crossed the borders of Siming; thus, he styled himself "Zu'an" (The One Who Stays at Home).
The Biography of Chan Master Fohuiquan of Fanchuan.
A native of the Shi family of Suizhou, he served as the abbot of Jiangshan Temple. Through diligent and arduous management, he brought the monastic community to completion.
He was a spiritual friend to Su Dongpo. When Dongpo’s boat reached Jinling, he was detained by a gale along the riverbank; at that time, the Master...
He was welcomed to the temple. Su Shi asked, "What is the lamp of the ocean of wisdom? The Master replied with a verse: Pointing it out, what is clearly revealed?
Lifting one's head, the hawk has already flown to Silla. From the beginning, this bowl has been most rare;
How many people can truly ask about the lamp? Su Shi was delighted and replied with a poem: "Today at the riverhead, the sky..."
The colors are ominous; thunderclouds arise and the wind is about to blow. Gazing alone toward Mount Zhong, I call out to Master Bao: "That white pagoda amidst the woods is like a solitary crane.
Master Bao’s bones are cold; he is angry that he did not hear me. Yet it is Old Quan who has come to call upon me.

With lightning eyes, tiger teeth, and a tongue like a clap of thunder, he blows away the clouds from a thousand peaks for my sake. Having traveled ten thousand *li* from the south, what business have I here? Let us take one draught.
Caoqi knew the taste of water; had he painted a picture of Mount Jiangshan in later years, he would still have addressed the Master as "Master Quan" and called him "Layman.
When the Master resided at Nanchan in Quzhou, Zhao Qingxian Gong Bian visited him daily, yet the Master never once permitted him to utter a single word.

Later, while serving as the Prefect of Qingzhou, he attained enlightenment while sitting in meditation upon hearing a clap of thunder. As he was about to pass away, he sent a letter to his teacher, saying:

"Had it not been for your constant admonitions and instructions over these years, I certainly would not have gained such strength at this moment. The teacher lamented this with a verse: "In service, you were an auspicious omen for the state;

In retirement, you became a model for the world. The Golden Grain has departed from the human realm; The Jade Tower is now perfected in heaven. Your sword of wisdom is without a single flaw; [The water...]"
The jar is utterly clear; the spring wind flows through the waterway. A solitary moon shines brightly upon the clouds.

In his later years, the Master accepted an imperial decree to reside at Zhaihai Chan Temple in Daxiangguo. He then asked the assembly, "I am departing for Zhaihai and leaving Jiangshan; which course of action is correct? The assembly remained silent.
The Master then took up his brush and wrote this verse: "Whether it is mind or not mind, all is but idle conjecture. To obtain the skin..."
"Having attained the marrow, I discuss it in vain. Farewell, dear fellow practitioners of Zen; outside the gate, a thousand mountains bask in the setting sun.
Having finished writing this, he passed away.
Recorded by Faqing and Fayi.
Faqing was a native of Yanling. He was tall and robust in stature, and his speech was clear and resonant.

Having encountered many venerable elders, he remained silent wherever he went, never flaunting his knowledge or insights. Only when provoked would he speak, such that few people recognized his true character.
Once, at Tianning Temple in Chizhou, he sat with his *saṃghāṭī* draped over his head. It happened that Minister Zeng Kai entered the temple and, seeing him, asked: "Venerable Sir..."
"Where is the Immortal Village? He replied, "Yanzhou. He asked, "Is it the same as this place, or is it different?

The Master pulled his *kāṣāya* down to the ground and, bowing, said, "Gentleman, have you ever been to Yanzhou? He was at a loss for what to say. The Master said, "Wait until you reach Yanzhou, and then I shall tell you.
Subsequently, he traveled to Mount Jing and was invited by Furi to serve as the head of the assembly (*zuoyuan*). The Master...
The Master declined, saying, "This assembly of one thousand seven hundred people are all heroes and sages. How would I dare to walk or stand before them? Fajian did not grant his request.
Fojie said, "If you raise one, you cannot raise two; if you let go of the first, you fall into the second.
What is the meaning of this? The Master said, "The alert are alert; the dazed are dazed. Fojie said: [Note: The provided text ends abruptly with Fojie's statement.]
"How can one serve as the Head Seat (Shouzuo) of Jing Mountain? he asked. Consequently, he was escorted by the assembly back to his quarters.
Later, he established the Dharma at Jiuxian in Longxing and succeeded Master Huiriyaya. As for Master Yaya, he in turn had a successor named Fayin, a native of Pingjiang.

He received full ordination at the age of twenty-four and traveled to various regions until he met Master Yaya at Donglin. There, he was questioned regarding his realization upon seeing the plum blossom (Lingyun).
Regarding the causal connection of Taoyuan: Yaya (Yuanzhao) was shaking his hand and saying, "No, no. Suddenly, Taoyuan had an awakening and presented a verse, saying:
"Peach blossoms bloom upon the crag; from where do the flowers come? As soon as Lingyun saw them, he turned his head and performed the Three Terraces Dance.
Yaya said, "What you have perceived has already reached the subtle; yet you must further spur yourself on to clarify the Great Dharma. Thereupon, Taoyuan received the teaching and resided at Luoshan.
For thirty years, he did not associate with the world; the monastic community honored him as the "Abbot of the Hermitage" (Ānzhǔ).
During the Jiànyán era, when bandits rose up, he followed the current back to the east. The local people built a hermitage to serve him, and those who came to seek the Way followed one after another.

He once said to the assembly, "If you maintain the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) to satiety, you will have no worries about the morning meal or the pursuit of worldly gain. In his later years, he wandered freely and at ease.
He was known as Wǔ Sōngsǎnrén (Five Loose Persons).
Dàoníng’s biography states:
Dàoníng was the son of the Wáng family of Xīxī. In his prime, he became a practitioner of the Way. At Chóngguǒ Temple, he served as the attendant for the ritual bathing. One day, he was about to...

While washing his feet, he happened to recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Upon reaching this passage—"One who is able to give rise to faith and take this as real"—he suddenly forgot all that he had learned.

He then cast his feet into boiling water, whereby his own insight was revealed. Later, he shaved his head at Jiangshan and traveled extensively through the monasteries to consult various renowned masters.
In his later years, he arrived at Bailian, where he heard Zen Master Wuzu Yan’s informal discourse (*xiaocan*) citing:
National Teacher Zhong was an ancient Buddha’s pure pitcher; Zhaozhou’s "The dog has no Buddha-nature" koan is a sudden penetration into the source of the Dharma.
During the Daoguang era, Grand Councilor Xi Zhen of Tanzhou invited him to preside over Kaifu Temple. Monks followed him like a shadow, and his conduct and teaching stood preeminent.

His name and his reality corresponded perfectly. His preaching of the Dharma was without fixed paths; it was concise, essential, and direct, enabling every listener to attain realization for themselves.
He possessed the style of the ancient patriarchs. In the third year of the Zhenghe era, as he was about to pass away, he addressed the assembly, saying: "This body of mine, of purple-gold hue..."
Today it exists; tomorrow it is gone. If you say I have entered nirvana, you are not my disciple.
If you say I have not entered nirvana, you are likewise not my disciple. If you can discern this point, you will know where Kaifu has descended.
If you have not yet reached this realization, Kaifu comes thus: throughout the world there is no one who knows him; he is like the moon in water or flowers in the sky.
"Who is firm, and who is real? Having resided here for five years, it was all like a mere moment. Auspicious clouds have vanished and the spring breeze has arisen;
I have lost Mañjuśrī and met Maitreya. Having finished speaking, he passed away.
Biography of Shouhui (Puna Xiao Chang):
Shouhui was the son of the Chen family of Xinghua. He was a high-ranking disciple of Chan Master Qianfeng Min.

He resided at Yuantong Monastery in Jiangzhou and later moved to Mount Dabao at Daopei in Tan. The Master’s conduct was precise and subtle; he never conflicted with things, and wherever the Wheel of Dharma turned...
He arrived, and the eminent masters (nāgas and elephants) flocked to him in droves. During the Zhenghe era, he entered the inner court three times to preach the Dharma.
Upon hearing this, Emperor Huizong’s countenance brightened with joy, and he bestowed upon him a six-character master title: *Chongxu Miyin Tonghui* (Profound Void, Secret Seal, Penetrating Wisdom).

His influence within the Dharma gate shone brilliantly, reaching the height of its prosperity at that time. Thus, when Chen Yingzhong wrote the preface to Chan Master Min’s *Yulu*, he specifically referred to him as "Chan Master Hui."
The Master was able to perpetuate his learning through his descendants, yet he did not excel in other matters.
There was a man named Bunan who was about to take up residence at Tianning Temple on Mount Tiantai; he took leave of the Master before departing.

The Master said to him, "The Perfect Man responds to the world in subtle harmony with the perfect and eternal. His vast truth shines forth without clashing with things; he activates the numinous mechanism, arising instantaneously."
Transcending worldly affairs, he responded universally to all levels of station; whether in motion or stillness, he remained complete within himself.

Facing him, one could not discern whence he came; following him, one could not fathom whither he went. From what the Master said, the character of this patched-robed monk (Bunatsu) can generally be perceived.
The Master also had a kinsman named Kōjō who attended him for the longest time. In his dealings with others, his face was always filled with a smiling countenance. [The Master] Bunatsu...
Ziyun followed him, and his eyes were always filled with joy. Grand Marshal Liu Qi held him in particular esteem;
in their correspondence, he addressed him as "Chan Master Huankui" (Joyful). At the request of Anfu’s Huo Li, he moved from Sansheng Monastery in Gong’an to reside at Daopei.
The Master’s teaching of the Dharma was rooted in a single source. Those who followed his path were exceedingly numerous. Some say that Puna was the Master’s younger brother;
judging by his words of "lifting the ear," they bear a distinct air of domestic intimacy. On the night of the Mid-Autumn Festival, the Master addressed the assembly, saying:

"This mountain monk has been naturally inept since birth; when he opens his mouth, there is not a single word to be said. Tonight, pointing at space and painting in space, I have made the clear breeze and bright moon laugh until they fall over.
Thereupon, he passed away. For several days, his countenance remained unchanged, solemn and as if alive.

The Biography of Chan Master Bieping Yin (with Huichao appended) Chan Master Bieping, whose name was Baoyin and courtesy name Tanshu, was born as the son of the Li family in Longyou. His ancestors had lived for generations at the foot of Mount Emei.
From his youth, he was exceptionally brilliant and perceptive; however, he took no pleasure in the secular life and thus followed the path of Qingyuan of Deshan Monastery.
The man attained liberation. From the time he was a young child, he had already mastered the Six Classics and the doctrines of the hundred schools.

Upon reaching this stage, he further followed eminent masters such as those of the *Avataṃsaka* and *Śraddhotpāda* traditions to exhaustively investigate their sources and explore their profound mysteries; he would not cease until his realization surpassed that of his fellow students.
At that time, Meditation Master Min, known as Mijin, was preaching the Dharma at the Zhongfeng Monastery. Thereupon, [the man] took up a straw raincoat and went to follow him there.
One day, Miyin raised a koan. A monk asked Yantou, "What is it like when arising and ceasing never cease? Yantou rebuked him, saying, "Who is it that arises and ceases?
At these words, the Master attained a sudden and great enlightenment. From then on, his sharpness was unassailable. Miyin regretted having met him so late.
When Yuanwu returned from the south to Chengdu at Zhaojue, he sent the Master to visit him; consequently, the Master followed the assembly into [the monastery].
In the quarters, Yuanwu raised the question: "How did the various sages of antiquity receive people? The Master raised his fist. Yuanwu said, "This is what I, an old monk, use.
What is it that the various sages of antiquity use? The Master immediately waved his fist.
Yuanwu also raised his fist, and as their fists crossed, they laughed heartily and ceased. Yuanwu sighed in admiration and said, "This man will surely [attain greatness] in the future."
He was like my teacher. He remained at Zhaojue for three years; while Miyin was still at Zhongfeng, he appointed [the Master] as the First Seat of the Hall. The Master declined.
Miyin became greatly enraged, saying, "I have obtained people through the Dharma, yet these people do not transmit it to me.

How can I still preach the Dharma? I wish to abandon the assembly and depart. The assembly was terrified and hurried back to Zhaojue, where they prostrated themselves in rows and earnestly entreated him. Yuan...
Wu also assisted him in his request to begin his practice. His reputation for the Way grew daily, and students vied with one another to seek him out;
even Yuanwu’s seal of transmission could not obscure his brilliance. After some time, he traveled south to visit various great Chan elders, finally knocking at the door of Miaoxi at Mount Jing.
For the Master alone, he swept out a room. This caused everyone in the hall to be greatly astonished. When Miaoxi was exiled to the south, the Master followed him.

He returned to the west and initially resided at Phoenix Mountain in Linqiong. Holding up the incense, he became the dharma heir of Miyin. Once his Way had become widely prevalent, he built the Conghui Hermitage;

it was secluded and profound with its pines and bamboo. On days of leisure, famous scholars and worthies would all gather there. Upon hearing a single word from the Master, they all felt their worldly attachments dissolve.

Should they happen to be separated for even a short while, they would immediately say to one another, "In our hearts, base and stingy thoughts have begun to sprout. Thus, his virtue and character moved them deeply.
People were like this. Shortly thereafter, he descended through the gorges to take up residence at Jinling (Nanjing). Ying’an Hua was then residing at Jiangshan;
he invited the Master to stay in the Shangfang Hall and petitioned the Imperial Commissioner Zhang Tào to recommend him as his successor. Upon hearing this, the Master departed that very day.
It happened that Chancellor Chen Junxiang had arrived in Jinling and invited the Master to reside at Baoning Temple. Soon after, he was transferred to Mount Jing in Jingkou to teach.
This [monastery] draws [devotees] from all directions. Since the time of the military upheavals, although the Golden Mountain Monastery was repeatedly repaired, it could never be fully restored.

It was only now that it began to flourish once more, reaching a state even superior to that of the peaceful era. In former times, those who resided on this mountain rarely remained for more than three years.
The Master sat alone in meditation for fifteen summers. When Wang Huixian, Prince of Wei, governed Siming, he sent an invitation from Xuedou. The Master resided there for four years;
delighting in the mountain forests, he intended to spend the remainder of his life there. However, as his reputation grew even more eminent, he received an imperial decree to reside at Mount Jing.

It was the fifth month of the seventh year of the Chunxi era. In the seventh month, he arrived at the imperial residence. Emperor Shouhuang dispatched an imperial messenger to summon him into the inner palace.
Because of his old age, illness, and a lame foot, the Emperor granted him a palanquin within the Donghua Gate and provided him with a meal in the Guantang Hall.

The Emperor summoned him to Seondeokjeon Hall, where he was granted a seat and received profound inquiries and kind greetings. The Master quoted an ancient master, saying: "If one penetrates seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing;

if one makes use of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing; if one does not fall into seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing. The Emperor was delighted. When the Master finished his discourse, he withdrew.
More than ten days later, the Emperor again ordered him to open the hall at Lingyin Mountain, and an imperial messenger arrived bearing gifts from the Sovereign.

Incense. His kindness and courtesy were most complete. In the second month of the tenth year, the Emperor composed a commentary on the *Nirvāṇa-parivarta* (the *Yuanjue jing*) and dispatched an envoy to deliver it, while also commanding him to write a preface.
As the Master grew older and increasingly weary of the affairs of abbotship, his disciples feared he might travel far and not return;

they therefore built a hermitage to the north of the mountain to await his coming back. When the Guangzong was still in the Eastern Palace, he inscribed the two large characters "Bieping" (Distinct Peak) as a plaque for it.
In the winter of the fifteenth year, he submitted a petition requesting to retire to a separate peak to recuperate from illness, and his request was granted.

The following year, when Guangzong received the internal abdication (the throne), he took the imperial calligraphy previously bestowed upon him, marked it with the Imperial Seal, and presented it to him once again.

In the eleventh month of the winter of the first year of Shaoxi, the Master suddenly went to see the successor to the mountain abbot, Zhice, to bid him farewell. When Zhice asked the date of his departure, the Master replied: "When the water arrives..."
When the canal was completed, he returned and took a sheet of paper upon which he wrote in large characters: "On the night of the seventh day of the twelfth month, at the hour of the rooster's crow.
He passed away exactly as scheduled. His physical remains were brought back to the Dharma Hall of the monastery and remained there for seven days;

his complexion remained radiant and clear, his beard and hair had grown long, and the crown of his head was warm like freshly poured hot water. On the fourteenth day of that month, he was buried on the western ridge of Biéfēng. He was eighty years of age.
He was twelve *lǐ* tall and sixty-four *suǒ* in age. His disciples who attained the Dharma were so numerous that his fingers could not count them one by one.
Among them was Huìchuó, the son of the Lu family of Shānyīn; he declined an official post he was entitled to by virtue of his family lineage and followed his teacher to shave his head.
Having received his prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*), he withdrew into mountain caves and did not emerge for the rest of his life.

After the Master passed away, the Emperor issued an edict to the relevant authorities to determine his posthumous title as "Cibian" (Compassionate Eloquence), his stupa as "Zhiguang" (Wisdom Light), and his hermitage as "Biepeak" (Distinct Peak). He thus received the highest honors from beyond the secular world.

For several decades, the Master had preached the Dharma; wherever he went, his disciples compiled his teachings into a *yulu* (recorded sayings). In his later years, he encountered the Shouhuang Emperor, who bestowed upon him imperial calligraphy.

He consulted on the essentials of the Dharma and submitted all matters in detail to the messengers. These were recorded separately for circulation in the world; they are not fully set down here. Jingquan transmitted [the teachings] to Jingquan.

Jingquan was a native of Zhuji in Yuezhou. His surname was Weng. For generations his family had been farmers; in his youth, he personally engaged in plowing alongside his father and elder brother. All...

Whenever he reached forested ravines or by springs and rocks, he would invariably sit in meditation, forgetting to return. People marveled at this. Having reached the age of twenty, he left the household life;
his teacher bestowed the scriptures upon him, yet he understood almost nothing. Thereupon, he turned his steps toward Mount Jing and visited Miaoxi.

Miaoxi asked, "What are you capable of? He replied, "I am able to sit in meditation. Miaoxi asked again, "What is the purpose of sitting in meditation? He replied, "If you ask what the purpose is, it is simply..."

There was no place for him to set down his bowl, which filled the onlookers with wonder. The Master had grown up in a farming family; he was simple and rustic, without any refined adornments, and his eyes knew nothing of books.
People called him Old Man Mugda. One day, the group gathered to harvest pepper, and the Master joined them.
His peers teased him, saying, "Try composing a verse on picking pepper; how about it? The Master immediately replied at the sound of their words: "Enveloped in mist, bearing dew."
Autumn has arrived. Every grain is a deep crimson, its fragrance pervasive. Its eyes protrude and it opens its mouth to laugh; this time it no longer clings to its old branch.
The assembly was greatly astonished; they truly looked upon him with new eyes. A donor offered Miaoxi a monastic ordination certificate (*sengjie*) and commanded that one person be ordained.
Miaoxi ordered ten attendants to each draw a tally (*zhou*) to determine their respective lots. By chance—
The Master obtained it. The other nine men were dissatisfied and began to reproach one another. When they drew lots again, the Master obtained it once more.
If he had drawn it three times in succession, he would have shaved his head and received the precepts. Later, Zhu’an Guang resided at Lingyin and appointed the Master to oversee the guest quarters;
when Huanyuan Mi presided over Jingci, he invited the Master to share half of his seat. However, the Master’s ambition lay in remaining in seclusion, and he had no desire to respond to the world.
However, his natural talent was perfected from an early age without relying on the instruction of a teacher.

Although he could not recognize a single stroke of a character, the words he uttered and the phrases he spoke were composed as verses and hymns that even veteran masters and long-established scholars could not surpass.

The Minister You Mao, the Count of Baowen Wang Houzhi, and the Chancellor Qian Xiangzu all maintained a relationship of "external friendship" with the Master. He once wrote his own eulogy, which begins: "The Spoon..."

He was not fit to be ranked even among common villagers; there was not a single trace of literary refinement within his breast. He once attempted to fathom the very bones of empty space, yet he won only a reputation for harsh words throughout the Puhuan and Jianghu regions.
For this reason, he styled himself "The Useless One" (Wuyong). Throughout his life, he successively presided over several great monasteries, finally residing at Tiantong in Siming.
In the third year of the Kaixi era, he passed away. His secular age was seventy-one, and his years as a monk were forty-five.
He was interred with his entire body to the west of the temple.

Mi (Mishan) succeeded Hui’an (Huanglong Huinan), and Guang (Foguo Yuan Guang) succeeded Miaoxi (Dongshan Liaopeng). Thus, Mi was the nephew of his teacher’s lineage, yet he did not feel any hesitation in sharing the seat [with him].
In short, when the ancients propagated their teachings and exalted the Way, they made it their primary concern, regardless of personal ties.
He was fastidious regarding outward forms and traces; thus, he is worthy of esteem.
Chan Master Benzhi of Jia Shan was a native of the Guo family of Gao’an, Junzhou. When he was five years old, during a great famine, a distinguished guest passed by his door and saw him.

Qi-gu (his father) left ten thousand coins for his parents and intended to take them away with him. His grandmother, Liu, happened to be returning from a neighboring house; seeing this, she looked at him in anger and said, "On the night you were born, I dreamed that flowers rained from the sky. This was an auspicious omen for our family. I would rather starve to death than give these to others. She pushed the money back to him. Once he had grown up, he visited Bao'en Temple and heard a monk reciting the *Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish*. He heard the passage: "The Buddha told the bhikṣus: 'In the past, there was a king who gave his own flesh to feed a starving tigress. At this, he suddenly realized the meaning of the Dharma. He immediately returned home, took leave of his parents, and went forth as a śramaṇa. He traveled to various places seeking instruction, eventually reaching Mount Lu where he studied under Master Huiyuan. Later, he resided at the Jingye Monastery on Mount Zhong, where he composed the *Commentary on the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* in one fascicle. He also lectured extensively on the *Lotus Sūtra*, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, and the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*. He passed away at the age of sixty-one. Emperor Wu of Liang bestowed upon him the posthumous title "Great Master of the Great Vehicle" (Dasheng Daoshi). His disciples built a stupa for him at the foot of Mount Zhong. Regarding his family background: he wished to become a disciple of the Gate. Liu Shi said with joy, "This is my own aspiration.
At the age of nineteen, he underwent the scriptural examination to become a monk; the following year, he received full ordination (*upasampadā*) and immediately set out to travel.

At that time, the venerable elder Yunju Shun and the practitioner Kaixian Xian were the preeminent masters on Mount Lu. The Master frequented the circles of these two elders for a long time before hearing [the Dharma].
Chan Master Fahua Duan was a profound master of the Dharma cave, his presence commanding the entire monastic community. The Master went to visit him and remained for ten years;
consequently, his reputation spread far and wide. Li Gongduchen, the Governor of Shu Prefecture, invited him to preach the Dharma at Longmen.

On the day he took his leave, Zhiyuan led the assembly to see him off. The Master’s horse bolted and outstripped him; looking back at Zhiyuan, he said, "In the practice of benevolence, one does not yield.
Zhiyuan smiled and said to the great assembly, "At Guoqing, men of talent are esteemed; in a wealthy house, children are arrogant.

Their father and son’s playful engagement in the joy of the Dharma was often like this. Not long after, he left the monastery and returned to Mount Lu. At that time, Prime Minister Zhang Jingguang was serving as a Hanlin Academician.
Scholar Lin was appointed to govern Changsha; he invited [the Master] with due ceremony to reside at Falun Temple on Mount Nanyue. Students vied with one another to take him as their master.
He moved his residence to Nantai, then to Daolin, then to Yunyi, and finally to Shichuang. This lasted for a total of thirteen years.
The Way is grand and manifest. He invited all the renowned dukes and high officials of the time.

Since the Master was already advanced in years, Chen Gongju, the Commissioner of Transport for Hubei, insisted on bringing the Master to Jia Shan. The Master did not decline; with joyful serenity, he took up his staff and departed.
When people asked him about this, the Master said: "To be attached to whether one stays or goes—how could that be the business of the Way? Whether it be Hunan or Hubei, it is truly [the same]."
It was merely a single dream; why then speak of superiority or inferiority, or of avoidance and pursuit?

On the night of the Yuanxuan Festival in the first year of the Daye era, he bathed, changed his robes, and sat upright, passing away at Jia Shan. He had lived seventy-three years and observed the monastic precepts for fifty-two years.
After his cremation, his teeth, bones, and prayer beads remained unburnt. He was buried to the west of Lebu Hermitage. The Master’s nature was straightforward and sincere.
He did not involve himself in worldly affairs. His courage and spirit surpassed those of his contemporaries. He composed verses with a free and unrestrained hand;
he was truly an outstanding figure of the Chan forest at that time.
Juesou Yingchuan. His courtesy name was Yingjin.
He was the son of the Luo family of Tahe in Jizhou. Orphaned at a young age, his mother took pity on him. By nature he was intelligent and quick-witted;

by the time he reached the age of seven, he could recite over a thousand words daily and had mastered the general principles of the *Shi* and *Li* classics. While playing with other children, he would mock them.
When he played with it, his vital energy would emerge from the top of his head. His relatives and old friends loved and respected him, so they had him wear a *fengye* robe and become a scholar;

however, he would immediately fall ill until he was on the verge of death. When his mother permitted him to leave the household life, he recovered at once. He subsequently became the novice monk Donglong.

At the age of eighteen, he underwent an examination of his studies and received ordination. Immediately thereafter, he wished to travel through various regions to observe the Way and repay his parents' labors.
His mother showed a look of distress at his laborious virtue; he therefore built a hut outside her chamber and named it "Diligence" (Jingjin).

The scholar-officials were pleased with his character and composed poems as gifts, praising him to the utmost. When his mother passed away, he observed the three-year period of mourning according to the heart's intent and cultivated pure deeds for her posthumous merit.
He then traveled through the Huai and Hai regions, staying briefly wherever he went. At that time, he was known as "The Man of Clear Vision."

The Venerable Elder visited many masters in succession. Later, he met Yun’an, who told him that the essential karmic conditions for entering the Way were found in Huangbo’s reception of Linji and Yunmen’s reception of Dongshan;

these were the points by which all quarters had been scrutinized and refined. The Elder pointed out his points of doubt and posed questions to him, whereupon he attained a sudden, great awakening, as if the bottom of a bucket had fallen away.
Chan Master Foyin was renowned throughout the monastic community as a Great Master, and his fame was widespread.

He was known for his caution regarding granting permission to others; he alone regarded the Master as a preeminent talent. The Master possessed a spirited air and delighted in displaying his own strengths to stimulate those who studied under him.
For thirty years, he remained steadfast in his integrity without wavering; thus, Foyin called him "Iron Beak. Initially, he established the Dharma at Kaifu Temple in Changsha.
Within ten years, the halls and pavilions were magnificently completed, yet he soon abandoned them and traveled light to Mount Wutai.
Having visited all the sacred sites, he returned south to Mount Liangshan, where the monastics of the world increasingly revered him.

In the Jia-wu year of the Zhenghe era, the clergy and laity of Hengyang welcomed him to reside at Tianning Temple on Huayao Mountain; those who invited him were all prominent officials and nobles of the time.

The Master transmitted the school of the "separate transmission outside the teachings" to those of superior capacity, employing both skillful means (*upāya*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) to transform both the clergy and the laity.

In his old age, he grew even more robust and vigorous. His diligent practice never faltered. He would often prostrate before the Buddha in the middle of the night; whether resting, eating, or drinking, he never allowed himself to turn his back on the community.

The monastic centers trusted his sincerity, and the common people were transformed by his teaching. In the winter of the third year of the Xuande era (1121), he retired from his duties and returned to his hermitage at Liangshan.

In the twelfth month of the following year, he manifested illness and cast off his mortal coil like a cicada shedding its shell. Regarding his exhortations on the Great Matter and the immersion in his enlightened speech:
It is said that three records circulate in the world: the *Baoci*, the *Yanfeng*, and the *Youtai*.
Tudu Ce was the dharma-heir of Zhice;
he was the son of the Chen family of Tiantai and styled himself the Master of the Tudu Rock. He was brilliant, astute, and exceptionally gifted, with a rugged and imposing physical bearing.

Chan possessed a demeanor that transcended the mundane. At the age of sixteen, he shaved his head and studied the sutras and vinaya; his realization of the principles was so penetrating that he far surpassed his contemporaries.
At nineteen, he went to Guoqing Temple to visit Jishiguang, whereupon he attained a sudden and profound awakening.
Jishiguang granted him approval, remarking that even those who had long resided within the monastic community could not surpass him. Wushi of Yuyang and Dayuan of Wanshou were both of his time.
Damingde was unwilling to grant him approval. Dayuan said, "Master Ce may truly be called one who is luxuriant without weeding and straight without support.
Dayuan saw him off as he departed; as they walked, Dayuan patted the Master’s back and said, "The treasure lies near;
this city is not real. The Master nodded his head. He then traveled to Yuzhang to visit Dian-niu, passing through Yunju on the way. Wind and snow blocked the road.
He sat in meditation for forty-two days. At the first stroke of the noon bell, a resonant *keng* sound rang out, and he attained a sudden, great enlightenment.

He stamped the ox with his seal and said: "He stands forth in brilliant transcendence beyond Buddhas and patriarchs; when he leaves this place one day, a single unicorn will suffice. Had Zhenjing been alive, [he would have recognized him].
Upon seeing his son, he also prostrated himself. Dianiu was possessed of sharp and incisive eloquence; none could withstand the edge of his wit.
When the Master discussed matters of antiquity and the present with him, [his words] flowed like a spring and sped like the wind, leaving those who heard them struck with awe and wonder.

Dianiu took up residence in a hermitage below Wuya in Huaixi. Later, when Dayuan moved to Daming Mountain (Daimiao), he invited Dianiu to occupy the first seat. Dianiu once visited the master’s quarters.
He went to inquire after his health. Seeing Dayuan with his head bowed and silent, the Master asked, "Why are you so distressed?
Dayuan replied, "I expected you to have a vast assembly like those of Xuefeng and Yangshan. Yet those who discuss the heavens say that you will have no successors. What do you think of this?
The Master said, "In studying the Way, one only fears having no foundation. If one truly has a foundation, one may preach even before a clay image."
Fahai also rose above all quarters. Dayuan sighed and said, "My son’s capacity and insight surpass those of others;
the 'dark wine' and 'great soup' are flavors that the common stream cannot appreciate. He returned to the East and again shared a seat at Guoqing.

At that time, Ciana Yuanfang was residing at Huguo Temple, who said to the Master, "Now that you have come home, Sanfeng Jinyuan will immediately withdraw his waves and billows. (Recorded from the *Chanzong Zhengmai*).
He resided at Huangyan Puzhai, where he served as the ritual director for the incense offerings. He traveled through Taiping in Yingtai, Xiangfu in Jizhi, Dengci in Yue, and Darenren;
wherever he went, the reputation of the Way flourished. Subsequently, he moved from Huguo Huazang to reside at Mount Jing, by which time the Master was already advanced in years.
He strove diligently to propagate the ancestral path, and his assembly grew to over a thousand members. As he approached the end of his life...
He summoned his disciples to entrust them with his final affairs, saying, "You all should offer me a written memorial. The Master sat upright with his robes adjusted and listened;
when they reached the words "May you enjoy the offering" (*shàng xiǎng*), he raised his eyebrows and smiled. Two days later, he passed away peacefully.
He was seventy-six years of age and had spent sixty summers in meditation. His disciples enshrined his remains in a stupa at the foot of East Ridge. The Master was by nature stern.
Jian’s conduct in both public and private life was solemn and dignified. He particularly disliked superficial associations;

if someone was virtuous, he admired them, but otherwise, even if they were close relatives, he would never have contact with them. His preaching of the Dharma to save sentient beings was luminous and magnificent, stirring the hearts of his contemporaries.

Those who looked toward the Master and sought refuge in him came like surging clouds and rushing waves, hoping to personally receive the sound of his voice as their greatest fortune. Truly, this was the end... [text truncated].
A bridge for the world, such as he was, is not easily found.
Chan Master Fozhao Guang transmitted the Dharma to Deguang.
Deguang was the son of the Peng family of Linjiang; the Pengs were an ancient clan. His mother, Yuan, dreamed that a strange monk entered her chamber, which she found startling.

He conceived while dreaming; once he was born, his grandfather said, "My family has accumulated merit for generations; this child will surely bring glory to our lineage. For this reason, he was given his name.
At the age of nine, encountering the disturbances of bandits, he sought refuge at Muping Temple in Yuan.

There, the Great Master Miaoying Bo Hua, who was skilled in physiognomy, remarked, "This child has a 'subdued rhinoceros' mark extending through the crown of his head; if he leaves the household life, he will surely become a pillar of the Dharma-gate."
Suddenly losing his parents, he returned to his paternal uncle. At the age of twenty-one, he heard someone reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and attained a realization.
He said to his paternal aunt, "I have just heard the recitation of the sutra; my body and mind are filled with joy.

All the myriad affairs of this world are truly like illusions and dreams. I wish to leave the household life. He then distributed his family wealth among his kinsmen and went to Old Master Zu’ān at Gwanghwa Hermitage to receive the tonsure.
Zu’ān took him with him into Fújiǎn and said to the Master, "This journey is to choose for you a teacher upon whom you may rely.
Dōngchán Yuè’ān Gùgōng possesses the eye of a true monk; if you rely on him, at times you will have me as well. Upon meeting Yuè’ān, their spiritual resonance and words were in perfect accord.
At that time, many veteran masters had gathered in Fújiǎn, such as Miàozhàn, Fóxīn, and Yuánjué, whose reputations were highly esteemed within the monastic community.
Lin visited every master without exception, traveling to over fifty *kalyāṇamitra*s. Finally, he met Dahui at Yuyuan Temple.
When Dahui brought up the story of the bamboo stick, Lin was about to respond when a severe blow followed. He attained great enlightenment, and all that he had previously acquired dissolved like ice.
Dahui said, "Now you have finally reached the bottom. He then spoke a verse and transmitted the *uṣṇīṣa* to him.
He followed [the master] to Mount Jiang, where he visited Ying’an. Ying’an praised him incessantly, saying to others, "Brother Guang is a tiger with wings; I must yield to him.

In the Dinghai year of the Qiandao era, he resided at Hongfu in Taizhou and was later transferred to Guangxiao. This was at the invitation of Li Hao, the Vice Minister (Shilang) of the Imperial Household serving as Governor of Tai.
Emperor Xiaozong had long heard of the Master’s reputation, and in the third year of the Chunxi era, he received an imperial decree to reside at Ling[shan].
Yin entered to have an audience in Seondeok Hall. The Emperor asked about the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma, saying, "Are my mind and the Buddha’s mind the same or different?
Yin replied, "Directly beneath [this very moment], there is no second person. The Emperor said, "If that is so, then the Buddha is precisely the mind, and the mind is precisely the Buddha?
Yin replied, "To realize all natures is the mind; to be free from all marks is the Buddha. The Emperor asked again, "Śākyamuni..."

"What have you accomplished during your six years at Mount [Jingshan]? he asked. He replied, "I feared that Your Majesty might have forgotten. The Emperor was pleased and conferred upon him the title of Chan Master Fozhao.

From then on, there was not a single year in which he was not summoned for an audience. Eventually, he was invited to stay in the Inner Contemplation Hall (Nei Guantang), remaining there for five nights before departing.

His imperial favor was extraordinary. In the first year of the Shaoxi era, when Emperor Xiaozong moved to the Chonghua Palace and was addressed as the Taohuang (Venerable August), the appointment of Jingshan...

The Master declined with earnest humility. The Shouhuang Emperor said, "I merely wish to see you frequently; why do you decline? At the beginning of the Qingyuan era, he requested to retire and was granted permission to return to Yuyang.
While the Master was in the Neiguantang (Inner Meditation Hall), the Emperor would occasionally pass by the hall in a small palanquin.
Upon arrival, he would sit together on a narrow seat or walk alongside him, trailing his sleeves, as joyful as they were in their youth. He bestowed upon him gold and jade articles for personal use.

The silk and brocades amounted to over thirty thousand strings of cash. Together with the offerings bestowed by kings, ministers, and elders, he dedicated them all as fields for King Aśoka to support the monastic community.
The court historian Lu You recorded these events in detail. Having built a few thatched huts himself, he called them the "Eastern Hermitage" (Dōngān).

He closed his door to enjoy solitude, seeking repose from the world. In the third month of the Jiatai *guihai* year, he addressed the assembly, saying: "My worldly karmic ties are drawing to a close..."

[His life] came to an end. Before long, he asked those around him, "Is today the day of the full moon? They replied, "Yes. He immediately requested paper to write a final testament for those with whom he had been close.
He gathered the assembly to bid them farewell; all his words were essential points of the Dharma, without a single word concerning other matters.
He requested a bath, changed his robes, and wrote in large characters: "Eighty-three years of sins as vast as the heavens. At the very end—"
With earnest devotion, he explained everything thoroughly and then passed away peacefully. His disciples enshrined his entire body in a stupa behind the hermitage.
He had sixty years of monastic seniority (śrāmaṇeraka) and was posthumously titled Great Chan Master Puhui Zongjue. His stupa was named Yuanjian.
Minghe said: "Among the patriarchs after the Southern Crossing, none surpassed Master Miaoxi in the number of disciples he produced.

Those who ascended the hall to preach the Dharma and were clearly recognized as teachers of gods and men numbered no fewer than several dozen. Yet, with few exceptions, their lineages soon fell silent and faded away.

Only [Zhaozhou] was able to ensure that the lineage of the Way remained long-lasting and its branches and leaves flourished, thereby not disgracing the transmission and entrustment of his master’s school."
There was only the Master alone. Ancient sources praise Miaoxi as one who could greatly awaken others within the lineage of Yuanwu.

I, however, maintain that Miaoxi’s attainment of his teacher was just like Yuanwu’s attainment of Miaoxi. When the *Continued Lamp Record* lists those among the successors of Miaoxi whose realization was vast and great, it names nine individuals, yet the Master is not included therein;
this already reveals a failure of judgment. It goes so far as to say of his disciples—

He was a man of transcendent excellence. Furthermore, he passed away prematurely so that he would not have long opened the Dharma for others, thereby ensuring that his Dharma heirs could spread it widely.
In this regard, was the Master not indeed a man of transcendent excellence who met with an untimely end? Alas! This is what is called "staring with eyes wide open yet failing to see Mount Tai."
Supplementary Biographies of Eminent Monks,
Volume Ten and Volume Eleven.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Minghe of Huashan Temple in Wumen, Ming Dynasty.
Chapter on Practicing Chan:
Biography of Chan Master Jifu Wenben of the Song Dynasty.
Wenben was a native of Jiangzhou. Having attended upon Miaoxi at Yunmen in Jiangxi, he eventually traveled to Xiaxi in Quannan.
At that time, the eminent and talented gathered in full, and many received his seal of approval. The Master privately thought they were abandoning him and wished to depart.
Miaoxi, knowing this, said to him: "You need only focus your mind on investigation.

If you have any realization, I shall recognize it even before you open your mouth. Later, there was someone who heard of the Master entering the room, so he said to the Master: "The original attendant..."
This person has been practicing Chan for many years, yet day after day he can only say, "I do not understand. The Master scolded him, saying, "You little imp!
Before you were even born, I already had your teeth pulled out three times at the Huoshan Temple. This will surely make you understand!"
