From this point on, his resolve became even more keen as he took up the "dog has no Buddha-nature" koan.

One night, when the third watch had arrived, while he was leaning against a pillar in the hall and drifting into a drowsy sleep, the word "no" (wu) involuntarily escaped his lips. Suddenly, he attained sudden enlightenment. Three days later, Miaoxi returned from the prefectural city.
The Master hurried to his quarters; as soon as Miaoxi’s feet had crossed the threshold, before the Master had even uttered a word, Miaoxi said, "The original..."
"Huizi, this time it is truly from beginning to end. He then went to seek out his fellow practitioner, Master Qian, at Jianyang Hermitage.
Qian cited the case of the Immortal of the Five Supernatural Powers as recorded in Baoning’s verse: "For immeasurable kalpas, he has never yet awakened."
"How can one reach the midst of it without moving? "Do not say that the Buddha-dharma is nothing much;
most painful is that single penetration of Gautama. Qian replied, "I love how he reaches the midst without moving.
"Since he does not move, how then did those ancients, having attained it, casually bring it forth? Naturally, they seize upon the person's most sensitive spot. The Master [said].
[The Master] said, "For what reason, then, do you say, 'Most grievous is that one thing of Gautama'?
Qian replied, "Before you were born, I had already three times removed my fangs within the temple of Mount Huo. Thereupon, they looked at each other and laughed heartily.

The benefit of such mutual refinement among friends is like the perfect correspondence between a seal and its impression, leaving no room for discrepancy; when it comes to meeting the mind with a hearty laugh, it can truly be described as such.
Later generations will long for his wind and bearing. While the Master resided at Boshan, he established the institutional framework and propagated the Way of the Dharma.
At that time, Preceptor Xuedang Xing was residing at Jianfu. A monk came from Fuzhou, and Xuedang asked him, "Along your journey, have you seen any fine elder masters?
The monk replied, "Recently I passed through Xinzhou; although I have never had the honor of meeting the Abbot Ben of Boshan, I have heard much of him."
"What a fine elder! Xuedang said. "How could one know he was a fine elder? The monk replied, "The paths leading to the monastery are wide and clear;
the corridors and eaves are well-maintained; incense and lamps never cease in the halls; the bells and drums are distinct at dawn and dusk; the morning and evening gruel and meals are pure and clean;
and when the monks see people, they show them courtesy. By these things, I knew he was a fine elder. Xuedang laughed.
He said, "Master Ben is indeed virtuous. However, you also possess the discerning eye. I shall take these words directly to the Prefect, Lord Wu Fu-peng, and say:
'This monk’s presentation of his argument is somewhat similar to the manner in which Fan Yan-ling recommended Zhang Xi-yan.

Yet your excellence, Excellency, does not fall short of that of Lord Zhang Zhong-ding. This old monk is advanced in years; I beg that Master Ben be requested to act in my stead, so that he may serve as a model for this monastery.'"
This was a momentous occasion. Lord Wu was greatly delighted. That very day, the Master moved to Jianfu Temple and Xuetang Temple, where he succeeded Longmen’s Master Yuan as his dharma heir.
His uncle was Master Xing.

Jiàn-táng Jī inherited the Dharma from Xíng-jī and was known as Jiàn-táng. He was the son of the Yang family of Tāizhōu; his appearance was striking and his talent surpassed that of the Confucian scholars.
At the age of twenty-five, he abandoned his wife and children to study the supramundane Dharma. Later, he met Cǐ-ān, with whom he attained a profound realization. He subsequently entered Fānyáng.
Guanshan lived as a solitary practitioner for seventeen years. Once, during the height of winter, snow and rain fell continuously and his supply of thick gruel was exhausted;
yet the Master appeared as if he neither heard nor saw it. He had this verse: "The earthen stove has no fire, the traveler’s bag is empty;
The snow falls like willow blossoms as the year draws to its end. I gather discarded hemp to patch my tattered robes, Unaware that my body dwells in desolation. He would often say to others:
"I am still not yet settled," he said. "Is dwelling in the mountains truly my affair? One day, while watching a tree being felled and brought to the ground, he suddenly attained great enlightenment.
The obstruction that had long weighed upon his chest dissolved like ice melting away. Not long after, he received an invitation from Yuan Tong in Jiangzhou.
He remarked, "My Way is about to be put into practice," and with joyful serenity, he took up his staff and departed. Ascending the seat to preach the Dharma, he said: "Yuan..."

Tong did not open a pharmacy for living medicine; he sold exclusively the "heads of dead cats. No one knew whose lack of calculation this was, yet those who consumed it were covered in cold sweat from head to toe.
Monastics and laypeople alike were struck with wonder, and his Dharma seat flourished greatly because of this.
He moved from Yuan Tong to Guo Qing, where he retired to Jingxing Rock. There, he became a friend beyond the secular world with the Court Official Wu Fu. The fifth year of the Chunxi era...

In the [X] year, when Jingxing departed for Yijing, Huo Yuanming composed thirteen poems to see him off, expressing his profound sense of longing and hoping that the Master would soon return so they might enjoy retirement together. The Master was clear-sighted, serene, and upright;
whenever a monk made even a slight error, he would shield and protect them to help them perfect their virtue. He often said: "Who among men is without fault? It lies in rectifying it."

This was considered admirable. While residing at Guanshan, he would regularly descend the mountain each day. Hearing the sound of mournful weeping by the roadside, the Master inquired with compassion.

He learned that a family had been stricken by a cold-related illness and had already lost two members; being too poor to afford the means for burial, they were specifically borrowing coffins from the market to bury them.
The local people sighed with deep emotion. Li Chunnian, a Court Gentleman, remarked to the literati: "In our region, there is the Elder Ji."
He was a monk of the Way who, moreover, bestowed compassion upon all things. How could he remain long in Guan Mountain?
Throughout his life, he had found contentment in the Way and did not seek fame or honor. When he accepted the invitation to Yuan Tong, he carried with him nothing but a staff and straw sandals.
As for those who saw him, they were moved by his dignified appearance and enlightened understanding. Lin Shuda, the Prefect of the Nine Rivers, remarked of him:

"This man is a bridge and a ferry across the Buddha-dharma; his conduct truly embodies the standard of the former masters. Thus, on the day of his passing, even the couriers and messengers exerted themselves [in mourning].
Tears fell for him.
Or-an was the dharma heir of Master Ti;
he was styled Or-an and was the son of the Luo family of Taizhou. Initially, he studied under Ci-an Yuan Bunan at Tiantai.
Huguo was once reciting Pang Jushi’s verse on "Selecting the Buddha" when he reached the third line; at that point, Chan’an shouted, and the Master attained great enlightenment.

He subsequently went into hiding deep within the mountains. When Chancellor Qian Xiangxian admired his character and offered him the position of Abbot at Tianfeng, urging him to emerge from seclusion, the Master shook his hand and said, "I do not understand hanging up the head of a goat while selling dog meat. Thereupon, he fled by night.
He departed. At the beginning of the Qiandao era, Xiatang was residing at Guoqing Temple.

Upon seeing the Master’s eulogy for the image of Yuan-tong, he was struck with joy and said, "I did not expect this Chan-an to have such a son. He searched everywhere and found him among the crowds at Jiangxin, where he invited him to serve as the First Seat.
When Xiatang moved to Huqiu, the Master visited him. The clergy and laity of Pingjiang then requested him to reside at Juebao Temple. Jue...
The old name was Lao-shou-an (Old Longevity Hermitage). The Master said, "My late teacher entrusted me with this, saying that one day I would encounter 'Old Longevity' and stop there.

Now it fits as perfectly as a tally. Thereupon, he joyfully accepted the command and entered the monastery. He gave a small assembly discourse (*xiaocan*), saying: "The Way is constant and never changes; affairs have decay and must inevitably transform.
In the past, the various patriarchs of Jiangxi and Nan-yueh each took antiquity as their instruction. Examining what is appropriate..."
No. Uphold the Middle Way and strive to accord with the human heart; take awakening as the standard, so that the ancient style remains serene and has not perished even to this day.

Yet, if we speak from the standpoint of the patch-robed monks, to gain realization before words is to diminish our school’s tradition, and to be clear-cut within a phrase is to bury the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
Nevertheless, when one walks until the water ends and sits watching the clouds arise—by this path...

This was so; both the clergy and the laity rejoiced at what they had never heard before, and those who returned were as numerous as in a marketplace. In the sixth year of the Chunxi era, he moved to Mount Jiao.

As his time to pass away drew near, he manifested a slight ailment and wrote a letter with his own hand, attaching a single inkstone to it as a parting gift for the Prefectural Governor, Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, Zeng.
By midnight, he had finished reciting a gāthā and then departed, at the age of seventy-two. Master Zeng lamented him with this verse: "Lightly fluttering, the single sandal..."
Chasing the western wind, there is not a single thing within the cloth bag. Leaving behind the inkstone, what will it be used for?
This old man has no brush to constrain empty space. I have indeed known those who speak thus. You, Master, bear the Dharma upon your person as your teaching;

you do not rely solely on words. He often said: "The monastic community is preserved by its practitioners; practitioners are preserved by their virtue and conduct. He also said: "To obtain one's own body..."
The glory of this [worldly life] is not equal to attaining fame for a single lifetime;

attaining fame for a single lifetime is not equal to obtaining one virtuous monk-disciple, so that future students have a teacher and the monastic community has a master. Alas! There is nothing in the world as private as this body;
by gaining even one step toward it, one gains one step toward the Way. Thus is the saying: "The Master attained two, and Baosan attained three."
Truly, these words transcend all worldly names and phrases; I vow to recite them for the rest of my life and dare not forget them.
Yuan Kumoku (Yuan Kumu) transmitted the lineage from Zu Yuan.
He was the son of the Lin family of the Seven Min regions. Initially, he visited Xuefeng Ding Fuxin Cai, and they both attained mutual resonance with the fundamental principle. Later...
He visited Miaoxi at the Yangyu Hermitage on the ocean islets. His physical bearing was refined and slender; he would sit upright for the entire day.
Miaoxi designated him as "Yuan the Withered Tree. He attained enlightenment while trimming a lamp, and Miaoxi bestowed upon him a verse.
Among the thirteen people at Yangyu who clarified the Great Matter, the Master was one of them. While residing at the Fuyan Hermitage in Lianjiang, his community grew large, and each day—
There was no time to spare. In the hermitage there was a temple with a great many clay figurines. The Master posted a verse at the shrine to enlighten them, saying:
"A small hut, a small cottage, a small grove—why does the local deity require eight or nine attendants? If you understand, take turns coming to offer incense."
"Otherwise, you will later be ground into a heap of dust. That evening, the deity appeared in a dream to a lay devotee before the mountain, wishing that [the master] would follow his instructions.
When he emerged into the world at Nengren Monastery on Mount Yan, he showed this verse to his disciples: "The withered tree of Mount Yan is true head-seated Chan;
It does not lie within clever or novel phrases. Suddenly reaching it with one's back turned, The great leviathan swallows the moon as waves surge to the heavens."
Ying Zhongwen said: "Among his contemporaries, the Master was most renowned for being dull-witted; yet when he withdrew from the world, even the gods followed him.
That his disciples continued to revere and admire him even more as he responded to conditions was surely because he came from a state of extraordinary prajñā—how could it have been otherwise?"
The Biography of Chan Master Miaofengshan. Chan Master Miaofengshan was the son of the Liu family.
His ancestors had lived in Pengcheng for generations, but later they moved to Wuxing. At the age of thirteen, he shaved his head to become a monk.

His teacher instructed him in the sutras and treatises; however, upon reading them only once, he immediately grasped their general meaning. After some time, he abandoned them. At that time, there was Fozhao...
He traveled to Mount Mao (Maoshan) to study under Master Chàngdào. Upon hearing the dialogue concerning the wind and the banner, he attained realization of the fundamental principle.

Fózào praised him with a verse: "Today I have opened a single thread for you; cutting through nails and severing iron, you shall revive our school. From then on, his eloquence and wisdom surged like a spring.
Yet, he did not consider this sufficient and entered the Lú Mìgāo Peak in Wǔkāng, where he sat in meditation against a cliff wall for ten years, remaining hidden from the world.
His fame became widely renowned, and scholars honored him as Chan Master Miaofeng.
He appeared in the world at various monasteries such as Huìyīn, Hóngfú, and Wànnián in Tāizhōu;

after retiring to Liú Temple on Gāotíng Mountain for over ten years, his disciples urged him incessantly, so he again took charge of Ruìyán in Míng, Wànsòu in Sū, Huázhàng in Cháng, and subsequently arrived at Línghǐn.

Lingyin Temple was situated in close proximity to the imperial palace, where the traffic of carriages and horses gathered in great numbers. Yet the Master would shut his door as if he heard nothing, never engaging in any reception or formal courtesy.
When high officials and nobles encountered him, he would offer them no more than a simple greeting of seasonal inquiry. At that time, Tiantong Monastery had its seat vacant;
Zheng Qingzhi, who held the reins of government, declared that none but the Master was worthy to occupy it, and thus urged him to go. The Master replied, "This old monk is [advanced in years]..."

"He is old! Does he still travel by night without rest? Duke Zheng held him in high esteem. Master Shan was skilled at guiding and assisting those who followed him; he never raised his voice or showed a harsh countenance.
Yet, once instructed, there were none whose minds did not achieve integration and spiritual transformation, leaving them feeling full and having attained realization.
It is traditionally said that while the Master resided at Lingyin, he sat in the abbot’s quarters at night and was carried in and out by four ghosts. This is similar to [the account of] Dongshan.

Matters concerning the "Treasures" (the *ratnas*) are of a similar nature. Among those who have attained the Way, there may occasionally be such instances; however, fearing that they might cause confusion by appearing as anomalies to practitioners, he avoided mentioning them.
This is what Zhongfeng meant when he said that at that time, it was fortunate to have encountered Miaofeng, who was like Master Wang, yet lacked the power to truly integrate his practice.
When he was about to pass away, he bathed his body, sat in the lotus position, and wrote this verse: "Coming was thus; going..."
It was likewise so. Coming and going were as one; like a clear breeze across ten thousand *li*, he then departed.
This is the biography of Master Chianet (Miaokong Zhinan).
His secular surname was Xia, and he was a native of Chongde in Xiu. His mother dreamed of a woman dressed in yellow who placed [an infant] upon her...

[The Master] took [the child] from his basin and handed him over. Consequently, she conceived. When he was born, he was exceptionally brilliant. At the age of four, he attended upon his elder brother, the Venerable Cixiang Daozi.

At fourteen, he received the tonsure. His natural disposition was extraordinary; he pursued the maintenance of incense and lamps and practiced the precepts with such proficiency that he appeared as if already an adult.
After some time, he attained awakening and sighed, saying: "I am cultivating the unsurpassed Way, yet I seek it only in words and phrases."
[He] was in the middle [of the river]. This was the "carving on the boat" [parable]. He immediately abandoned it and departed. He studied Chan at Tianting Monastery in Tongchuan.
One day, while crossing a stream, a written document emerged from the flowing water. He picked it up and examined it; it was the Heart Sutra.
As he read it—"The five aggregates are all empty"—he felt as though there were a sudden resonance with his own mind. He went to Ruiguang Monastery in Gusu to see Master Jingzhao Xin. The Master...

Upon seeing him once, [the Emperor] said with joy, "He is a śramaṇa from a previous life. Not long after, Jingzhao moved to reside at Changlu in Zhenzhou, where his assembly of students coming and going numbered several hundred.
The Master’s learning was perfected and his conduct was honored; he was ranked among the highest disciples.

The people of Huai admired and loved him, saying, "If there is one such as Master Nuo, would it not be fitting for him to preside over a monastic center? He was invited to reside at Tianning Chan Temple and was granted [imperial favor].
The Great Master Miaokong presided over the confluence of rivers and roads in Yizhen and Dangyang, as well as the three regions of Wu, where offerings from donors gathered in great abundance.
He renovated a monastery to such an extent that nearly ten thousand foundation stones were used. At the beginning of the Jianyan era, he resided at Lingyin Monastery.

Empress Dowager Cisheng visited him in person and issued an imperial decree for the Master to ascend the seat and preach the Dharma, bestowing upon him the title Fohai. The following year, the Jurchen invaders captured Qiantang. The Master...

He was captured. The great chieftain untied the Master’s bonds and placed him upon a couch, honoring him with reverence. When it was time for him to depart, ten horsemen were prepared to escort him back.

King Hyeon of Silla (Han Se-jong) submitted a memorial requesting that the Lingyan Temple in Pingjiang be established as a merit-field temple (*gongde-yuan*) to dedicate the blessings of his ancestors, and he commanded the Master to preside over it.
Although the Master had already departed, he was retained once more; in total, he served as abbot five times over a period of twenty-odd years. Finally...
Having received an imperial decree to reside at Mount Jing, in the twenty-seventh year of the Shaoxing era, the Master took his alms bowl and traveled to Huating County in Xiuzhou.
A local man named Zhu Feiqing, having heard of the Master’s reputation, prepared vegetarian offerings and selected an auspicious day, dispatching a letter to invite him.
On the twenty-sixth day of the eleventh month, the Master arrived at his home, sat upon the seat, and preached the Dharma; monks and laypeople alike gathered there. A monk stepped forward.
He prostrated himself and asked about the root of birth and death. Before the Master had finished his reply, he raised his whisk, struck the meditation seat, and passed away with a single blow.
Monastics and laypeople rushed to the scene; the streets were emptied as they climbed over one another to offer praise and pay their respects, as if at the parinirvāṇa of a Buddha.

His disciples prepared a boat to carry him back to the mountains, for he had already issued instructions on his funeral arrangements. Seven days later, when the body was enshrined in the coffin, his entire form remained as if alive. He was then interred.

At Baiyun An in the monastery, he reached the age of eighty and had been a monk for sixty-seven years. The Master’s physical presence was remarkably imposing, and his deportment was upright and silent.
Although he practiced the supramundane Dharma, he devoted himself to building pagodas and temples, performing vegetarian feasts and offerings, and carrying out various Buddhist rites.
Regarding his distribution of gold and silk, he did so once a year; there was no surplus stored within his bags. While he was in Yizhen, the wife of a local man surnamed Wang fell ill and died.
Later, her replacement, a woman surnamed Meng, also fell ill. One day, while her mother-in-law was reciting scriptures in the Buddha hall, she heard the sound of knocking against the wall.
When she asked who it was, the voice replied, "It is Wang. I have a remaining bag containing hairpins, earrings, and other such items; all of these should be returned to Meng."
He said, "You may sell one or two [of your possessions] and invite Master Nǜ of Tiānníng Monastery to preach the Dharma for me, so that I may attain liberation.
Then I shall leave your home; Mèng’s family will likewise be unharmed. That very day, the family members rushed to inform the Master.

When the Master arrived at the Wáng residence, he leaned against a young woman standing by his side. Once the preaching was finished, she leaped for joy and knelt in thanks. Several days later, she appeared in a dream.
He said, "I have already received my subsequent body. When Mengshi’s illness had finally subsided, Master Xu recorded these events as a memorial.
During his time at Lingyan, the prominent local family of the Hu clan hosted a great vegetarian feast (*dàzhāi*). All the senior monks were assembled there.
On the eve of the ceremony, someone dreamed that a person informed him: "Tomorrow morning, one who rides a red horse and wears a yellow-brown robe will arrive; he is a Pratyekabuddha."

At dawn, they searched for him by his physical description, but the Master’s fur robe and horse were as if from a dream. The entire Hu family came out to welcome and prostrate before him, leaving everyone in their seats utterly astonished.
Lingyan Temple was situated on a mountain peak, yet for several centuries the supply of well water had been insufficient. The Master selected a site and oversaw the construction;
he hewed stones and excavated a well, from which emerged clear and sweet spring water. People no longer suffered from the difficulty of drawing water, and it is now known as Fohai (Buddha-Ocean).

Quán said: "The *Sangha* stupa at Tianning Monastery in Yizhen is several hundred feet high, and its great *dharmacakra* storehouse is so magnificent that it stands foremost in the Huai and Hai regions;
both were the work of this Master. When Minister Sun Di passed by, he sighed and remarked: 'Your talent and wisdom are not inferior to those of Daosheng and Jiacai.
Yet, as times are fraught with many troubles, you have hidden yourself within the ranks of the Buddhist clergy—this is truly a pity. Subsequently, he resided there five times."
Lingyan built a chamber to the west of the abbot’s quarters. Sun Deng visited him there, inscribed the name "Five Arrivals" upon it, and left a poem before departing.
After the Master passed away, Sun Deng further composed an inscription for his stupa, expressing his profound grief and longing.

Daoxian’s biography: Daoxian was the son of the You family of Jianzhou. His ancestors had followed the scholarly tradition for generations. From childhood, he was intelligent and wise; whenever he read a book, he would memorize it at once.
Having lost both parents early, he sighed and said, "As a filial son, I have failed to provide them with the nourishment of sweet delicacies; I ought to follow the teachings of the Buddha."
He studied the supramundane Dharma to repay his parents' boundless kindness. He subsequently shaved his head and went to visit Foguo, yet he attained no realization.
Later, he followed Miaoxi as he resided at Quannan; when Miaoxi took charge of Mount Jing, the Master also attended him there.
Before long, Miaoxi sent the Master to Changsha to deliver a letter from Layman Ziyuan, Zhang Gong. The Master reflected that he had practiced Chan for twenty years without making any entry.
At the head of the group, he again performed this practice, becoming utterly despondent and intending not to practice at all.
His friend Zongyuan scolded him, saying, "One cannot practice Chan while on the road; you must not go. I shall go with you. The Master had no choice but to proceed.
On the road, he spoke weeping to Yuan, saying, "In my entire life of practicing Chan, I have found nothing at all that brings me strength. Now..."
Furthermore, as you are traveling along the road in such haste, how can you achieve realization? Yuan told him:
"You need only take whatever you have studied in various quarters, whatever you have realized, and whatever Yuanwu or Miaoxi have explained for you—do not concern yourself with any of it."
"Along the way, there may be matters that can be substituted; I shall substitute for you in all of them. There are only five matters for which I cannot substitute;
these you must attend to yourself. The Master asked, "What are these five matters? I wish to hear their essentials. Yuan said, "Wearing clothes and eating food;
defecating and urinating; carrying a corpse along the road. At these words, the Master realized the meaning and was struck with sudden realization.
He danced with his hands and stamped with his feet. Yuan said, "This time you may finally send a letter; you should proceed. I shall return first.
When the Master saw Lord Zhang, Lord Zhang was overjoyed and presented him with the two characters "Self-Confidence" (Xìn-zì) as a gift. The Master accepted them with a smile.

Upon returning to Mount Ji, Miaoxi saw him and said with joy, "Son of Jianzhou, this time you are truly leaving. Later, he returned to his home village to reside at Kaishan, where his reputation resounded far and wide.
As he was about to pass away, an attendant requested a verse. The Master smiled and said, "The myriad dharmas are fundamentally empty."
The three realms do not exist. Where, then, can death and birth find their resting place? Is it because his forbearance was startling to worldly customs?

His conduct was rigorous yet his spirit was harmonious; he was generous and tolerant in dealing with others. He transformed others through silence, and was thus one of the most eminent figures of the Chan school.

Zongyuan was also a native of Jianzhou. He had relied upon Miaoxi for the longest period and shared the seat to preach the Dharma. When Lord Zhang was the regional commander of the Three Mountains, he [invited him]... [text ends].

The Shuyuan (Numerous Monastery) welcomed him, but he did not accept the invitation. He returned to his native village and built a thatched hut, naming it "Zhongmiao Garden" (Garden of Myriad Wonders).
He gave this instruction: "These few things are just like encountering a man who would kill you; if you do not kill him, he will kill you.
It is unknown how he ended his life.
Biography of Chan Master Yu’an by the Scribe Chuliang.
The scribe’s courtesy name was Suweng. He was the son of the Liu family of Shanyin, Kuaiji. At the age of nine, he received the tonsure as a youth.
At thirteen, he began traveling to various regions; though he had only recently outgrown his robes and hat, passersby marveled at him. Initially, he served under Master Miaoyuan...

Xi was a personal attendant. He had also served as the secretary under Master Wan’an Yan, where he stood out with his brilliant talent and upright bearing. While traveling between these two masters, he received their formal transmissions (*kairitsu*).
Beyond his religious duties, he was capable in literary composition and skilled in calligraphy; thus, he was widely acclaimed by various quarters as an excellent secretary.
Nevertheless, because his discussions were sharp and incisive, leaving no room for compromise, he was not tolerated by those in other circles and remained largely unrecognized there. Yet, he alone...
Among the assembly, he once resided at Faxi Monastery in Xiuzhou, where he lit the incense to designate himself as the dharma heir of Wan’an.

With only a handful of monks and barely enough food for half a bean, he remained there for two years before withdrawing to a hermitage on the coast near Kuaiji. It happened that the Grand Music Master Mr.

You was serving as the governor of Linhai and invited the Master to take charge of the purple robe. However, because the local magistrate did not approve, he abandoned the position and departed. After a long time, he took charge of Jianyan in Kunshan.
At Zifu Temple, he subsequently passed away due to illness on the day of Wuyin in the sixth month of the fourteenth year of the Chunxi era.
His final instruction was that his remains be interred at Zhilin Temple on Mount Lu; this temple had been built by Wan’an and the Master together.
Yuán'ān Zhēncí was the son of the Li family from Tōngzhōu. Initially, he relied upon the Zhengfǎ Monastery in Chéngdū to leave the household life and receive full ordination.

Later, he traveled to various lecture halls to study the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, specifically the chapter on Perfect Enlightenment (*Yuanjue*). Upon reaching the passage: "When the four great elements are each separated, where then will this deluded body be? [he attained realization].

Ultimately they have no substance; in reality, they are identical to illusions and transformations. Thereupon, he attained a realization and composed a verse, saying: "A single bright pearl is here within me;
touch it or move it, and it emits light that shakes the earth. He returned and presented this to his teacher, who then questioned him.
The Master said, "Though there be hundreds, thousands, ten millions, or billions of *kōans*, they do not go beyond this verse.

His teacher considered this insolent and dismissed him. Consequently, he traveled south to Yuantong on Mount Lu. At that time, Wan’an was serving as the West Hall Attendant; when he entered the room for the assembly, he raised the following case:
A monk asked Yunmen, "When one sweeps away the dust and sees the Buddha, what then? Yunmen said, "Even the Buddha is dust. The Master [then spoke].

As soon as the voice was uttered, he gave a shout and pointed his finger at his chest, saying, "Even the Buddha is but a dust mote. He then recited a verse: "Clear away the dust to see the Buddha, yet the Buddha is also but dust.
The question is finished, the answer is finished; turn yourself around right here and now. I urge you to drink one more cup of wine:

Once you pass the Yang Pass to the west, there will be no old friend left behind. He further composed a verse on the Samādhi of Dust-to-Dust (Chen-chen Sanmei): "Rice in the bowl, water in the bucket—distinctly so."
The Jewel-Kunlun sits at the bottom of the deep pool; atop every single speck of dust, Mount Sumeru runs. A clear-eyed Persian laughs and snaps his fingers.
He laughs and snaps his fingers: a pure breeze rises upon the coral branches. Wan’an deeply approved of this.

Having completed his studies, he transmitted the Dharma to others. He was styled Zhaotang. A son of the Xu family from Fenghua, while still a young child, he would sit silently in a corner when playing with a group of other children;
yet upon hearing Buddhist chants, he would leap up, his countenance brightening with joy. His father remarked, "The child is like this."
At fourteen, he was ordained at Dayun Temple; at sixteen, he had mastered several tens of thousands of words of scripture.
Having studied them exhaustively day and night without ceasing, he sighed and said: "The Supreme Vehicle of the Tathāgata is not something to be reached by relying on external supports.
What use is there in attending to mere dregs? He then entered the capital and studied under Master Miaozhan Hui of Xiangguosi for several years.

He exhausted himself in his studies and became a preeminent disciple. He then traveled downstream to Bianzhou, crossed the Huai River, passed through the region of Wu, floated along the Zhe River, ascended Mount Tiantai, and entered Xuefeng.

There he met with various senior masters until his inner and outer understanding were completely transparent and he was free of all doubt. When Miaozhan arrived to take charge of Huangbo, the Master had come from Xuefeng;
his learning was perfected and his conduct was honored, so the assembly recommended him as their leader. The Master’s physical appearance was extraordinary.

Pang was sparing in speech and laughter; he sat upright on a single mat, profound and still like ice in an ancient well. When anyone came to question him, his words surged like clouds and fell like a spring—emerging more and more inexhaustibly.
By nature, he was solitary and aloof, intent on distancing himself from worldly affairs and refusing to engage with people.
When he was about to depart for Xuefeng, Zeng Tian, a Court Consultant (Chao-yi Dafu) who was a close friend of the Master, requested that the Master deliver a letter to the Military Governor of Fu.

When Grand Councilor Zhang Gongshou heard of the Master’s reputation, he suspected that the Master intended for him as his successor; thus, he placed the Master’s robe and bowl in a chest and did not bring them out.

After some time, the seat at Shiquan became vacant. The Councilor said, "The chief disciple of Huangbo is naturally capable. That very day, he sent a letter and dispatched a rider to welcome the Master.

The Master declined, expressing his unwillingness. The messenger returned five times before the Master finally accepted. On another occasion, when the Councilor visited the Master, the Master presented him with the *Tian* (恬) letter and further...
This led to his intention not to depart immediately. The Duke said with joy, "The treasure hidden in a casket remains deeply concealed and is not for sale;
as for me and you, Master, we are both free from shame as host and guest. After three years had passed, he was transferred to take charge of Shengquan Temple.

It happened that Ye Mengde, the Vice President of the Left, came to govern Fuzhou and said, "As for Huangbo, an ancient site of enlightenment, among the famous monks of this age, who could surpass Master Yigong? He then dispatched an envoy to summon him.

He prepared letters and gifts to welcome the Master. Upon reaching the borders of the entire district, both monastics and laypeople rushed out to meet him, shouting with joy and leaping about, their voices resonating through the mountains and valleys.
Indeed, since the Master had emerged from seclusion at Shiquan and presided over three great monasteries for fifteen years, he had expounded the True Vehicle and enlightened his later disciples;
everyone was turning toward the Way and taking the Master as their refuge. Shortly thereafter, as they were about to arrive...
Tongxiang Xie replaced him with various Chan masters, but one night [the Master] abandoned them and departed. He returned to lie down in his former cottage at Xuefeng.
Ye Tinggui, the Governor of Quannan, was a man who delighted in the Way; he invited the Master to Yunmen, and later he moved to Fashi.

When Tinggui returned to his post in the capital, the Master also returned to the Xuefeng Hermitage on West Lake—the very place where Miaozhan had resided—where he closed his door for days on end, such that no one could see him.
When he saw his face, it appeared as though he were about to pass away. Suddenly, he received an imperial decree to reside at Mount Jing; this was the twenty-fourth year of the Shaoxing era.

At Mount Jing, there was not even a single ridge of land available for cultivation, yet the assembly of students numbered in the thousands. When the Master entered and took possession of the abbot’s quarters, he found himself presiding over such a vast community.

Great assemblies for almsgiving were held, and provisions were prepared without being sought. On the mountain was a square-zhang site at Zhiyan (Mushroom Rock), which the Master once pointed out to his disciples, saying, "I shall build a dwelling there to reside.
At first, they did not understand what he meant. In the third month of the following year, he manifested a slight illness and retired to the Moonlight Hall (*Mingyuetang*).
There, he distributed the robes from his chest to provide offerings for the Buddha and meals for the monks. At dawn on the following day—
He took up his brush and wrote a gāthā, then sat in the lotus posture and passed away. He was sixty-four years of age and had fifty years of monastic seniority.
His entire body was enshrined in a stupa at Jiryan, which is precisely what is meant by the phrase "building a house" mentioned in the parable.
Wen'er Chuanwen'er was a native of Changxi, Fuzhou. His surname was Li. At age eleven, he took leave of his parents to enter the monastic life; at sixteen, he became a full monk;

at seventeen, he received the precepts; and at eighteen, he set out on foot to travel to Zen assemblies. He visited Master Guo of Yue'an, but found no entry [into realization] and forgot [his former state].
Whether sleeping or eating, sores covered his entire body; he sat hunched over his knees in a precarious posture.
Every time he heard the sound of the five-watch bell, he would break into a cold sweat and say, "Another day has passed. Later, through an encounter with an object, he attained realization.

He entered the monastery as an attendant for several years, then traveled to Luling where he was urgently requested by the assembly to reside at Qingliang Monastery in Jishui. He subsequently moved to Fushan in Xingguo and [then to] Ningdu.

Taolin. In the twenty-first year of the Xianchun era of the Shaoxing period, when District Magistrate Li Ziyang first arrived, he was stern and aloof, having few associates; yet, he alone shared a spiritual affinity with the Master.
He invited the Master to reside at Ba’en Temple. Ba’en was a renowned monastery, but its buildings had long been in ruin and the Dharma seat had fallen into decline.
The people of Gāng were of meager means and stingy in their charity; yet the Master received them with such sincerity and integrity that they all exerted their full strength.

The halls, structures, and sacred images were renovated one after another until the monastery was fully restored. At this time, Qi Shu besieged the city in rebellion, and both monastics and laypeople fled in the night.

The Master said, "If I leave, the temple will surely be reduced to ruins," and he remained there without moving. After one hundred and twenty days had passed, the rebels repeatedly attempted to harm him by setting fires. The Master—

He granted pardons at random, and thousands of commoners and officials were sheltered and saved by him. After ten years, he cited illness as a pretext to request leave and subsequently moved to Qingyun.
That place was remote yet provided with ample resources; in other times, the local administrators had merely cultivated their own lands for profit. When the Master arrived, however—
He renovated the three gates and planned the construction of the temple buildings; he excelled both in administrative affairs and spiritual practice, becoming even more earnest as he grew older.

One day, while walking with his disciples through the western garden, he pointed to a plot of ground measuring several *zhang* and said, "This place shall remain for my sake. Not long after, he passed away while sitting in meditation. This was indeed the winter of the second year of the Qiandao era.
He reached the age of forty-six and had completed thirty-one summer retreats. His disciples buried him at the site he had indicated.

At this place, the Chancellor Zhou Bida composed an inscription upon the stone, stating that when the Master resided at Ba’en Temple, Miaoxi Gao and the dignitary Zhang Wugou were returning north together.
Daily, scholars and officials went to seek his instruction, yet the Master initially offered no words.
Miaoxi alone said to Wugou, "The realization attained by this man is upright and substantial; it must not be underestimated. I—[the author]—...
Only after hearing these words did I truly come to know my teacher. Thus, regarding those who were dull-witted as being sharp, from that time on I thought all the more to associate with him;

yet, due to the shifting demands of official service, the days we met were few. Last winter, my teacher showed signs of intending to visit me, and I was just about to send him a letter in response when he passed away.
Such was the extent of the admiration and longing he inspired among the virtuous of his time.
From Kuò (Yìyì). Kuò was the son of Lin of Chángxī.

From childhood, he was exceptionally intelligent and did not engage in idle speech or laughter. When groups of children forced him to join in their play, he remained indifferent as if he had not heard them.
He delighted in hearing the supramundane Dharma. At the age of fifteen, he shaved his head and received full ordination.
At that time, there were many men of the Way in Min who all went to follow him and study under him. Upon meeting Foxin Cai, Cai praised him;
he later met Lan’an Xu, for whom he served as an attendant, and subsequently relied upon Dayuan Pu, who was a high-ranking disciple of Miaoxi.

His character was solitary and austere; at first, he encountered difficulties. After a long time, he suddenly attained realization. He served diligently for several years, and Dayuan took him under his wing, considering him to be like himself.
However, he harbored a regret that he had not yet met Miaoxi. Undaunted by the pain of blistered feet from the long journey, he went to see him beneath Huayan Peak (Huiyuanfeng) in Hengzhou.
Miaoxi held him in high esteem and treated him with great respect. After staying for three years, he requested leave to return home. Miaoxi sent him off with a verse, and furthermore...
He wrote to Shu Pu, saying: "Kuo is an excellent monastic; he is one who can be brought to full realization, so that in the future he may serve as a 'grass-seed' for my lineage.

In the Bingzi year of the Xiangshu era, Miaoxi was appointed by imperial decree to reside at Yuyang Monastery, and Kuo again came to rely upon him there. When Miaoxi moved to Jingshan, [Kuo followed].
Puo succeeded him on the seat; the assembly numbered over a thousand. The Master served as the First Seat (Dìyīzuò) under the Preceptor.

When Prime Minister Shen Gong invited him to the world at Mount Lu, Miaoxi’s fame was already preeminent throughout the land, and there were none who did not wish to enter his gate in order to gain prestige.
On the day he opened the hall, he offered a fragrant incense pellet to succeed Dayuan; for this reason, the various quarters held him in even higher esteem. Subsequently—
When the position at Yewang Monastery was vacant, Minister Han invited Miaoxi to recommend someone to take his place; yet there was no one like the Master.

A great assembly of Zen monks gathered, for Yewang was a renowned monastic center within the realm, where three generations of patriarchs had successively propagated the teachings—a source of great praise throughout the monastic community.
The Master, whose talents and character were already highly esteemed, took advantage of his leisure time to undertake construction projects involving earth and timber.
The craftsmanship was in every case of the utmost magnificence. His revenue increased by several thousand *hu*. Donors presented gold and silk in abundance.
He established five centers for the "Longevity Bureau" (*Changsheng Ju*), where all necessities were provided. Monthly, he bestowed gold and silver coins to feed ten thousand monks.
Furthermore, he constructed a golden stupa to enshrine the *śarīra*. These were merely his secondary undertakings. It was the fifteenth year after Emperor Xiaozong ascended the throne.

An imperial edict was issued for the precious stūpa containing the śarīra relics to proceed to the place where the Emperor was residing. The Master attended the journey. Upon arrival, he was ordered to enter the inner palace to enshrine it in the Hall of Contemplation.
The Emperor partook of a simple vegetarian meal and burned incense while gazing upon and venerating the relics, personally beholding their extraordinary excellence.

He subsequently summoned the Master to the Bilin Hall and asked from whence the śarīra had manifested. The Master replied, "They have manifested from the sacred mind of Your Majesty. The Emperor was greatly pleased.
The King personally inscribed the "Hall of Wondrous Victory" and bestowed upon the Master the title of Chan Master Miaozhi (Wondrous Wisdom).

Furthermore, he ordained five monks and granted ten thousand *mǐn* of paper currency; such generous favor had never before been seen. When the Japanese King read the Master’s verses, he declared that he had attained new insights.
He went so far as to abdicate his throne to follow the Way, annually performing the rites of a disciple with profound humility in declining the formal gifts. Moreover—
Excellent timber was sent to construct the Śarīra Hall; its utensils were exquisite and its adornments were beyond compare.

When the Prime Minister, Lord Shi, governed the Seven Min Provinces, he urged Master Gu to return to Mount Drum. Prince Yingyang exerted great effort to dissuade him from going, and Prince Wei went out to station his command there.

Upon seeing his dignified bearing for the first time, he was hailed as a dragon among monks. Hearing further that his intellectual eloquence was sharp and incisive, he felt a profound sense of reverence.
Later in life, the Master used his robes and alms-bag to establish a hermitage on Mount Wushan, naming it "Laughing at the Moon" (Xiàoyuè) as his plan for the end of his days.

He composed a verse which said: "The three peaks withdraw their idle clouds; The vast ocean coldly reflects the autumn moon. In the late spring of the Gengzi year, he shook off his robes [and departed].

He returned to the hermitage and closed his door, no longer associating with the world. Suddenly, manifesting a slight illness, he spoke a verse and passed away at the age of sixty-two, forty-seven years since his ordination.
He was buried in the sleeping quarters of the hermitage. The Master’s family discipline was extremely strict; the assembly of students followed the Master’s words.

The *Chui* (Assembly) was a massive compendium. When Master [Fayan] saw it, he rebuked him, saying, "You lot produce interpretations based merely on the words; you are moving further and further away from the Way. He adamantly refused permission.

Only after his passing did [Zhaoqing] finally manage to carve one or two out of every hundred for publication. Among his more than a hundred disciples, there was one named Yiyi who had attained the Dharma most precisely.
Residing at Kaiyuan in Pingjiang, he was just beginning to proclaim the Way with great renown when he suddenly passed away.
The World: Our School Laments His Passing.
*Tiegu Valley Yunchuan* (Appendix: Master Xuan of Shiqiao).
Chan Master Yiyun was the son of the Huang family of Minqing, Fuzhou. In his youth he entered a private school, and upon reaching the age of maturity, he entered the local district academy.
He was exceptionally gifted and possessed a great reputation. While reading the "Doctrine of the Mean" from the *Analects*, he attained a profound realization.

Later, hearing Chan Master Shantang Chun preach the Dharma, he resolved to leave the household life. He traveled extensively throughout the rivers and lakes until he reached Wu, where he met the Chan master Tie'an Yida.
He served as an attendant, and Tie’an held him in high esteem. At that time, Fozhao was propagating the Way at Lingyin;
the Master went there to rely upon him. When Fozhao moved to Yuyang, the Master followed him. For ten years, he served as the First Seat.
Upon hearing his preaching of the Dharma, Fozhao sighed and said, "This disciple’s proclamations are exactly like those of Master Xuedang Xing; my *bōdài* (the lineage bowl) has found its recipient."
He then departed to reside at Mount Xiangshan. After staying there for five years, he moved to Kuangxiao Temple in Taizhou, and later to Ganlu Temple in Zhenjiang.
At that time, both Wanshou Temple at Huqiu in Pingjiang and others wished to invite him as their abbot. Hearing that Wanshou was somewhat in decline, the Master joyfully accepted the invitation.
Furthermore, Yu Gong Chou, the Commissioner of Transport for Huainan, invited him to Changlu; the Master and Yu Gong...
He possessed a refined character; therefore, he followed [the Emperor’s] summons once again. At that time, as King Ashoka’s seat was vacant, the court appointed the Master to fill it.
Meanwhile, Fozhao resided at Dong’an; father and son frequented one another daily, elucidating the orthodox lineage of Linji.

Students gathered like clouds, but when demonic disturbances arose, the Master immediately left the assembly and retired to Xiangshan, intending to spend the remainder of his life there. However, the imperial decree summoned him once more.

The Master preached the Dharma with such purity and compassion that his enlightened radiance shone brilliantly, causing the capital city to be stirred with awe. One day, leading his assembly, he entered a neighboring district to collect alms.
That evening, a fire broke out at the temple, leaving not a single building intact. When the Master returned, only the triple gate stood towering amidst the ruins of bricks and rubble.
The Master, with an unmoving countenance, said: "Formation and destruction follow one another; how could there be any permanence?
Who knows that today’s destruction will not become a place for the fourfold assembly to cultivate merit? When the Son of Heaven heard this, he drew gold from the inner treasury to bestow upon him.

From high ministers and noble relatives downward, everyone emptied their coffers and transported gold, fearing only to be left behind. Within less than a year, vast halls and deep corridors were completed.

The lofty halls and magnificent pavilions were indeed more grand than they had been on previous days. Thereupon, the Emperor personally took up the brush and calligraphy to bestow upon him the three great characters "Huiji Ge" (Wisdom Sun Pavilion).
In the fifth month of the second year of the Kaixi era, he manifested a slight illness; he composed a verse to bid farewell to the assembly and passed away.
He was fifty-eight years of age and thirty-five years since his ordination. He had resided at the mountain for nineteen years. His disciples enshrined his entire body.
The stupa is located at the northeast corner of the monastery.
Master Shiqiao Xuan was the son of the Xu family of Jiading in Shu.

Having studied under Fozhao and attained the Dharma, he resided at Mount Jing and established the Huacheng Monastery above the Shuangxi River to receive the assembly of traveling monks. The Master gained the recognition of Chancellor Luoguo, and at that time—
He was renowned as a scholar-official; people followed and revered him with one accord, nearly rivaling Tui Gu in their pursuit of excellence, though his karmic fortune was slightly inferior.
When he passed away, he was interred in a stupa behind Huacheng Temple.
Xiaoweng Kān (笑翁堪) was the dharma heir of Miaokan.
His style name was Xiaoweng. He was the son of the Mao family of Cixi. He had a broad forehead and a flat crown; his physical bearing was clear and noble.
He received instruction from Yuan’an Daoqin and was renowned for his extensive memory and vast learning. Later, he devoted himself single-mindedly to investigation and took refuge under Xixian Guan.
He traveled to Mount Jinshan and then to Lingyin Temple to see Songyuan, but in neither case did he find resonance. At that time, Wuyong was residing at Tiantong; he went straight to his quarters.
Wuyong asked, "Are you a wandering monk or a mountain-roaming monk? He replied, "A wandering monk. Wuyong asked, "What is the matter of a wandering monk?
He took up his sitting mat and struck him with it. Wuyong said, "This monk dares to come here and grab a tiger’s whiskers!"
He was appointed to the Hall. One day, while using the "Dog has no Buddha-nature" koan, as soon as [Yongjue] was about to open his mouth, Yongyuan struck him on the mouth with a bamboo staff.
At that sound, Yongjue presented a verse, saying: "The great poison-drum, Thundering through heaven and shaking the earth;

Turn the head, twist the brain— A corpse lies across ten thousand *li*. Yongyuan nodded in approval and appointed him to attend the incense burner. Subsequently, he was ordered to share the seat and emerge into the world, occupying the seat ten times in total.
The various monasteries were all famous sites within the realm. On three occasions he received imperial summons, and was further entreated by eminent dukes and ministers;
it was only after yielding to these pressures that he finally accepted. Although he bore the weighty responsibility of the Chan school, he did not confine himself to its specific doctrines.

Regarding the various teachings on the profundity and shallowness of the Buddha-dharma, there was nothing he did not comprehend through synthesis. As for both mundane and supramundane dharmas, there was none he did not propagate concurrently. He often said: "At..."

When the mind harbors acceptance and rejection, it is because the consciousness and emotions have not been exhausted; when phenomena appear as "this" and "that," it is because the eye of wisdom has not yet become clear.
Formerly, the Tiantai school lacked a Vinaya tradition. While residing at Ba’en Temple, [the Master] deliberated with the Great Minister Qi Gong and merged ten temples into a great monastic center.

He constructed a *śīla-maṇḍala* (precept platform) and commissioned those who bore the burden of studying the *Vinaya* to propagate the laws of what is permitted and prohibited, and what is maintained and transgressed, thereby exhorting and inspiring the new students of the Tiantai school.
He was the first to establish the Nanshan school. Residing at Lingyin, he found that the mountain gate was in close proximity to slaughterhouses and taverns;
deeming it unfitting, he moved his hermitage outside Feilai Peak to separate the clamor from the silence, saying, "One must not allow the foul vapors of the *caṇḍāla* to defile the Three Jewels.
When the Governor-General of Jinghu reported to the throne that the state lacked funds, he petitioned that monks and Daoists be permitted to contribute capital to purchase purple robes.

The Master’s title was [to be] conferred so that he might take charge as abbot. Upon hearing this, he sighed and remarked, "If this were the case, then even the sons of those with a thousand pieces of gold could preside over the Dharma;
my Way would be in peril. He consequently submitted a memorial of protest and sent a letter to the one who held the reins of government, whereupon the proposal was finally shelved.
An imperial edict ordered him to move to Tiantong, but he declined resolutely. He returned east to Cuiyan, where he built a dwelling to maintain the ancestral offerings.

When the seat at Yuyang became vacant, an imperial decree summoned the Master; he declined a second time, but was not permitted to refuse, so he accepted the mandate. Therein he propagated the legacy of Dajue and followed the teachings of Miaoxi.
Everything was orderly and well-arranged. Before long, he received another summons from Tiantong. Grand Councilor Zhao invited him to preside over Jingci Temple, but he declined both offers firmly.

Shortly thereafter, he manifested illness and wrote his final testament. He composed a letter for Zhang Gong, the Prefectural Administrator, and Cao Gong, the Acting Governor of Yongjia, came to inquire after his health.
They conversed at ease regarding their family ties for some time. Then, he wrote a verse, saying: "The mirror of karma hangs high."
At seventy-two years of age, with a single blow he shattered [all attachments]; the Great Way was revealed in its natural ease.
He set down his brush and passed away in serene stillness.

Songyuan Yue transmitted the Dharma to Chongyue; Songyuan was his title. He was the son of the Wu family of Longquan in Chuzhou. From childhood he did not enjoy play; as he grew older, he longed for the monastic life.
Regarding worldly affairs: at twenty-three, he left home, donned the robes of a monk, and swept the pagoda. He first served Master Ling Shi Miaogong;
subsequently, he met Chan Master Dahui Zonggaof at Mount Jing.

After some time, when Dahui ascended the hall and praised Master Ying’an Hua of Jiangshan for his direct and swift character, the Master heard of this and set out before dawn. Upon arriving, he entered the inner chamber for instruction. Before long—
Upon hearing this, Xuefeng withdrew and redoubled his efforts. In the middle of the night, he took up the koan regarding the dog having no Buddha-nature;
suddenly, he attained realization. He went to consult Ying’an, who presented him with the saying: "The World-Honored One has a secret word; Kāśyapa did not conceal it.

The Master replied, "This leaves the Master at a loss. Ying’an let out a sharp shout. From then on, he consulted Ying’an morning and evening. Ying’an was greatly pleased and regarded him as a vessel for the Dharma.
He spoke in verse to encourage him to shave his head, saying, "You shall be a pillar of my Way.

In the second year of the Longxing era, the Master finally received the full precepts at the White Lotus Hermitage on West Lake in Lin’an. From then on, he traveled extensively to the doors of the great masters throughout Jiang-zhe, yet rarely met with their approval.
He then crossed the sea to enter Min, where he visited Master Muguan Yong. Muguan raised the question: "The phrase 'having words' and 'having no words'—like..."
A wisteria vine leans against a tree. The Master says, "Torn asunder. Mukan says, "Lan-yang said, 'What a pile of rotten firewood!

What do you think? The Master says, "Adding a point to an arrow. They exchange such responses several times. Mukan says, "Brother, your utterances do not surpass this old monk's; yet you have not yet reached it.
In the future, when the fly-whisk handle is in your hand, you will be unable to act for others or test them."
"No. The Master said, "For one who acts as a teacher, it is indeed difficult to cause an ordinary person of common ground to leap directly into the realm of the sages.
However, when it comes to testing people, if one strikes them right before their eyes without waiting for them to open their mouths, one already knows their very marrow.
What difficulty could there be? Muguan raised his hand and said, "I have told you clearly: opening the mouth is not a matter of the tongue. Hereafter...
He knew this himself. Over a year later, he met Mian Huikai at Xishan in Quzhou. Whenever Mian asked him something, he would answer immediately.
Mian smiled and said, "Huangyang Chan, you are truly intent on clarifying the Way, to the point of forgetting both sleep and food. Mian subsequently moved to Jiangshan Huazang and then to Jingshan;
Huangyang followed him to both locations. One day, while Mian was entering his room for private instruction, he asked a monk standing nearby, "It is not the mind."
"It is not the Buddha; it is not an object. As the Master attended to him, he attained a sudden and great enlightenment, whereupon he said:

"Only today do I know that what Muan said—'The opening of the mouth does not depend on the tongue'—is indeed so. From then on, his eloquence and discernment were纵横 (unrestrained and pervasive), and his sharpness was unassailable.
When Muan moved to Lingyin, he appointed the Master as the First Seat. Subsequently, the Master went forth into the world at Chengzhao in Pingjiang.
Mimian was his successor. [He served at] Kuangxiao in Jiangyin, Yueyi at Yefu, Jianfu in Raozhou, and Huqiu in Pingjiang—all famous mountains throughout the empire.
Yet Yefu was the most secluded and had been destroyed by fire;

as soon as the Master arrived there, eminent monks from all quarters came to him one after another, and the monastic buildings flourished once more. People said that the Master could cause whatever he resided in to thrive.
Mount San was vast. In the Ding-si year of the Qingyuan era, he received an imperial decree to reside at Lingyin. He remained there for six years;

his Way flourished, those who attained the Dharma were numerous, and his monastic seat became preeminent in its time. Yet, the Master harbored a desire for seclusion and retirement, so he submitted a petition requesting to relinquish his duties as abbot.

The Emperor, perceiving his sincerity, granted his request. He retired to the Dong’an (Eastern Hermitage), where he soon suffered from a slight illness, yet he did not neglect his practice even in that state.
While preaching the Way, he suddenly uttered a phrase to test his disciples, saying: "Why can a person of great power not lift their foot?
When the mouth opens, it is not upon the tongue. He also sent a letter to his various Dharma heirs, entrusting them to uphold the Great Dharma, and wrote this verse:
"Coming, there is no place from which one comes; Going, there is no place to which one goes. In a flash, the mysterious pivot is turned— Buddhas and Patriarchs [are surpassed]."
At a loss for what to do, he sat in the full lotus posture and entered nirvana on the fourth day of the eighth month in the second year of the Jiatai era.
He was seventy-one years of age and had spent forty summers in retreat. His disciples enshrined his entire body in a stupa upon the plain of Beigao Peak.

Yanxi Wenchuan was from the Lin clan of Hougan in Min. His family had been engaged in the study of Confucianism for generations. He possessed sparse eyebrows and prominent eyes, a wide mouth, and full cheeks.
He followed his paternal uncle, Zhilong, at Guangxiao Monastery in Wangling. At eighteen, he received the tonsure and the full precepts. Initially, he visited Tie...

Niuyin Shao was a member of the Muzhu lineage of the Wuji branch; he had followed [his teacher] for a very long time. Hearing that Zhe’eng was preaching the Way at Tiantong, he went to visit him with incense in his sleeve.
When they first met, their spiritual resonance was discordant. Later, when the Master moved to Jingshan, Niuyin followed him there. The Master greeted him with a smile, saying:
"You have come! One night, while sitting beneath the eaves, he heard the watchman strike the gong three times; as he entered his room, his sandals caught and he stumbled.

It was like waking suddenly from a dream. The following morning, he went to the elder’s quarters. When the elder raised the koan of Zhaozhou washing the alms bowl, the Master was about to open his mouth when the elder abruptly stopped him.
At that moment, the doubts of his entire life were instantly dissolved like melting ice. In the year Wuzi of the Shaoding era, Hu [the Governor] of Zhiming...
Master Gong attained realization through Xiao Jingci. He successively resided at eight mountains: Xiangshan, Wanshou, Xuedou, Yewang, Jingci, Lingyin, and Jingwu.
At every location he reached, he reformed abuses, supported what was collapsing, and widely accommodated disciples; his spiritual influence spread extensively. It is said:
"At the crossroads, you have no place to hide behind a stone pillar; with a single cry, 'The Minister comes from across the river.'"

There is no place for you to evade it. For those of us in the lineage of patch-robed monks, whether going out early or returning late, whether stepping forward or following behind, one must be careful.
Should you suddenly strike or bump against it, the staff of Jingci Monastery has another way of handing it over to you. It is also said: "One sheng and three he."
At the tip of the staff, ten thousand waters and a thousand mountains; at the heel of the straw sandals, one receives the meaning before the words are spoken.
In whose hearth is there no smoke? Raising it up, one goes directly; in every place there is water in the well. Do not say you come empty-handed and go empty-handed;
through all these paths, one is never alone. To wash away the dust and awaken the spirit—this may truly be called skillfully expounding the essential teachings. (Jingding 4th year)
He passed away at the age of seventy-five. Although his dharma heirs were numerous, it was only the two masters Yunfeng Gaodi and Hongjian who were able to revitalize the Way of their master.
Zang-sou Chen Gong transmitted the Dharma to Shan Chen.
His style name was Zang-sou; he was the son of the Lü family of Nan’an in Quanzhou. At the age of thirteen, he shaved his head; at sixteen, he began his travels to seek teachers.
Upon reaching Hangzhou, he received full ordination and visited Master Miaofeng Shan at Lingyin Monastery. Entering the master’s room, he attained realization of the essential meaning. Later...
He emerged from his residence at Guangxiao Temple in Liling and ascended to Chengtian Temple. He subsequently moved to Sijixi Yuanjue in Anji, then to Xuefeng in Fuzhou.
Again, by imperial decree, he was transferred to Yuwang in Siming and then to Jingshan in Lin’an. Upon ascending the hall, he said: "Lingyun attained awakening upon seeing peach blossoms;
Xuansha remarked, 'I dare guarantee that you, elder brother, have not yet reached the ultimate. Xiangyan heard the sound of a bamboo being struck..."
Wuqu said, "Yangshan said: 'The Ancestor’s Chan has not yet been understood; among ten or five pairs of Chan practitioners, none can show me a path of acceptance within this one gate.
It is unknown whether Lingyun or Xiangyan were there, but one must know that these two great elders ground their wine in the falling blossoms and borrow it from within the lute and song.
Again, he took his seat in the room and said: "Right here is where one inquires and burns incense."
Xiang came to the old monk’s side. "Do you know where Xuandi is? "Dullard! It is tolerable enough that you yourself are muddled, but do not come here to muddle me.
The Master’s dharma words were free from obstruction; for the most part, they were like this. When his disciples requested a title for a portrait of the Master, he waved his brush and said:
"In Zen there is no awakening; in literacy there is a limit. His eyes are triangular, like those of the people of Yan-shan."
The sorrowful Hu (the Chan master) had a face with a hundred wrinkles, like Zhao Po drinking vinegar; he stood far above all others from the moment he first appeared.
He dared to say, "Rice is made of grain. He was born in the Jiayin year of the Shaoxing era and passed away in the Dingchou year of the Jiaiding era at the age of eighty-three.
He presided over six great monasteries and received many disciples, yet among those who entered his inner chamber and attained the marrow of his teaching, there was only Master Yuansou Duan alone.
Thus it was. After Duan, the dharma lineage continued in an unbroken succession until our Ming dynasty, where there were still those who could rouse themselves to roar as teachers.
From this, one may know that the Master’s Way has a distant source and a long, flowing current.
Rujue: Rujue, whose courtesy name was Jing-sou, was a native of Wuzhou. He was the fifth-generation descendant of Yuanwu and the son of Chidu.
When he first met Chidu, a monk in the meditation hall asked, "What is the Buddha? Chidu instructed Rujue to provide a response. Rujue replied, "Rotting winter nails."
He then presented this verse: "What is the Buddha? A rotten winter melon. Biting into the frost, it penetrates the teeth.
Though its roots have no storage pit, It blooms once every year. Chidu laughed and approved it.

Later, he learned that upon meeting Emperor Muling, an imperial decree was issued during the Duanping era for him to ascend from Yewang Monastery to take residence at Jingshan. When he first opened the hall for formal preaching, he composed this [verse].
The inscription was used to admonish the multitude: "This illusory body is like a dream-house; its forms and colors are empty. The past limit is infinite; how can the future limit be reached?
Emerging here and perishing there, ascending and sinking until one is utterly exhausted, one cannot escape the three wheels of existence. When will there be rest?
Clinging greedily to the world, causes and conditions form a solid substance. From birth to old age, there is nothing at all gained. Fundamental ignorance is thus perpetuated."
Deluded! Time is precious; every moment is unpredictable. If this life passes in vain, the next will be blocked. To go from delusion to further delusion is entirely due to the six thieves.
Wandering through the six realms and crawling through the three worlds—seek an enlightened teacher early and personally attend upon one of high virtue.
Resolve the nature of body and mind, and clear away the thorns. Let the world float and sink as it may; how can you be pressured by external conditions? Investigate and exhaustively study the Dharma.

As for principle, take awakening as the standard. When both mind and objects are discarded, there is nothing to record and nothing to remember. The six sense-faculties become tranquil; whether walking or standing, one remains silent.

When the single mind does not arise, the myriad dharmas all cease. Addressing the assembly at the commencement of the summer retreat, he said: "In this school of mine, the true command is fully upheld.
It is like a sudden gale and torrential rain, surging forward without obstruction; it is like a spark from flint or a flash of lightning, which cannot be overtaken by pursuit. He raised [his hand]...
The mind is itself the source of delusion; as soon as you lift your eyes, you have already missed it. This is not a dharma of the present moment; do not give rise to various thoughts.

Even if you were to cultivate the three types of practice simultaneously and strive for realization within a fixed period, you would be at the first or third stage—struggling by the thousands and tens of thousands, becoming increasingly frantic.
Little do you realize that before the skull is even formed, the Eye is already clear; one must first understand the single sound of the "clapping of hands" (*tāla*). All is finished.

This is indeed so. Nevertheless, among those who have realized it through direct personal experience, there is not one in ten thousand; those who have misunderstood it are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Although the Master’s realization is lofty and clear, not yielding to the ancients, his fortune and karmic conditions are perhaps slightly inferior.
Some say that the Master’s spiritual power is even more vast than that of Yuanwu; this too is likely the result of insufficient reflection.
The Biography of Chan Master Wuzhun Shanfu:

Shanfu was the son of the Yong clan of Zizhong. At the age of nine, he entered the monastic order under Daoqin at Mount Yinping. Upon merely glancing over the scriptures and books, he could recite them from memory.
In the winter of the fifth year of the Shaoxi era, he received full ordination (*upasampadā*). The following year, he spent the summer retreat in Chengdu, where he encountered an elder monk.
The one named Yao requested further instruction on the method of *zazen*. Yao asked, "What is this 'zen' (*dhyāna*), and who is this 'sitter'?
Fan received these words and investigated them day and night. One day, while on his way to the latrine, he brought up the previous dialogue and attained realization. He then departed from Shu.
Fayan visited Foguo Zhao at the Yuwang Monastery. Zhao asked him where he was from, and Fayan replied, "A man from Jianzhou.
Zhao said, "Have you brought your sword with you? At these words, Fayan let out a shout. Zhao laughed and said, "This black-headed fellow is acting recklessly.

Because Fayan had grown his hair long and did not shave it, Foguo Zhao often addressed him as "Black-Headed Fellow" while in his quarters. After some time, Fayan wished to visit the Tiantai and Yantaishan mountains and invited Zhao along.
Sekishigetsu (石溪月) went along with him. Upon arriving at Suiryōan (瑞巖), Yunō (雲巢), who was presiding over the abbacy, invited him to serve as a guest lecturer (*funza*).

One night, he suddenly dreamed of a person in magnificent robes and cap who presented him with a bundle of thatch grass. The following day, a special messenger from Seiryō-ji (清凉寺) in Mingzhou arrived.

The Master accepted the invitation to enter the monastery. Upon seeing the shrine set up for the monastery deity (Galanashin), he found that its surname, clothing, and headgear were no different from what he had seen in his dream.
He ascended the hall and, thereupon, offered incense for Pō’ān, thereby demonstrating the intensity of his devotion to the Dharma and the depth of his realization of the ultimate meaning.

Subsequently, he succeeded [to the lineage] at Jiaoshan and Xuedou; by imperial decree, he was transferred to Yuyang, where he resided at Mount Jing for the longest period. Although he twice suffered the calamity of fire, [the temple remained].

He soon returned to his former abode, where the Dharma assembly flourished once more. Emperor Lizong once summoned the Master to enter the Ciming Hall, where he ascended the seat to preach the Dharma.
The Emperor personally attended to listen and was greatly pleased, bestowing upon him the title of Chan Master Fojian, along with a golden-edged *saṃghāṭī* robe.
In the autumn of the Wushen year of the Chunyou era, he built a dwelling by the Moonlight Pond and inscribed it "Retiring from Plow Work" (*Tuigeng*). He then requested retirement from the court.
Just as his chronic illness had flared up, on the first day of the third month he ascended the hall to bid farewell to the assembly.
By the fifteenth day, he was arranging his final affairs and personally drafting his testament and some ten letters; his speech and laughter remained as they were during ordinary times.
When his disciples requested a parting verse, he took up his brush and wrote rapidly: "When coming, empty and bare; when departing, likewise naked. What more do you wish to ask?"
Truly so. At Tiantai there is a stone bridge; [the Master] moved his head toward it and passed away.
Chan Master Shitian Xun transmitted the Dharma to Xun, who was styled Shitian.
He was the son of Peng Menglou; from birth he was intelligent and precocious. When he was three or four years old, he saw...
The monk was immediately delighted. At the age of sixteen, he left the household life under Zhimíng at Fǎbǎo Yúan on Shílóng Mountain in Dānléng.
At twenty-two, he shaved his head and received full ordination. Traveling to Shīshuāng, he paid homage at the stupa of Lèiqiān and composed a verse, saying:

"A single thought of compassionate countenance is fundamentally never separated; why need one suddenly act with such wilful contrariness? To level the high and conform to the low, his compassionate heart is most earnest."

This vexed Leigong, leaving him busy all night long. Because of this, Xun became greatly renowned. Having heard of the spiritual reputation of Chan Master Xian of Po’an at Qionglong in Wumen, he went there to rely upon him.
Upon their first meeting, [the Master] knew that Xun was a vessel for the Dharma.

In the meditation hall, when the Master raised the story of the World-Honored One holding up a flower and Kāśyapa smiling, Xun said: "A parched brick strikes and freezes through to the bottom; red eyes collide with fire."

Chaitou. P’an broke through his doubts and marveled at him. Because Chaitou constantly raised such doubts regarding the words and silences of daily life, Xun resolved to follow him, relying on him for guidance whenever the opportunity arose.
He and Wuzhun Fan encouraged one another daily. Later, he met Songyuan Yue, Kentang Chong, and Dun’an Yan;
all of them remarked that because he had come from the forge of a master, he was naturally different.
He first resided at Gaofeng in Suzhou, then moved to Fengqiao. When the seat at Zhongshan became vacant, he was appointed to fill it.
At the beginning of the Baoping era, he moved to Jingci; in the second year of the Duanping era, he moved to Lingyin. On the full moon of the third month in the Jiachen year of the Chunyou era—

He said to his disciples: "If you only obtain the root, do not worry about the branches. What do you call the root? What do you call the branches? 'The pine and cypress remain green for a thousand years, yet they do not suit the tastes of the age; the peony blooms red for a single day, and the young gentlemen of the city all fall into intoxication. When I, this mountain monk, speak thus, if there be anyone who does not agree, he is my fellow student. A disciple painted his likeness and requested a eulogy. Thereupon [he wrote]: * *The pine and cypress remain green for a thousand years,* *Yet they do not suit the tastes of the age;* *The peony blooms red for a single day,* *And the young gentlemen of the city all fall into intoxication.* When I, this mountain monk, speak thus, if there be anyone who does not agree, he is my fellow student. He said, "The final phrase has been entrusted to Chushan. The assembly marveled at this. The next day, he manifested illness and passed away.
Chijue Chong (癡絕沖) transmitted the Way; he styled himself Chijue. He was the son of Xun of the Changjiang clan in Wuxin; his mother was Lady Guo. She once dreamed of a mountain.
Beneath a papaya tree, its fruit hung in clusters. Upon taking and eating one, a diviner declared, "A man of extraordinary talent shall be born here. Shortly thereafter, a child was born;
he was tall in the upper body and short in the lower, possessing a natural endowment that surpassed others. When he grew up, he failed in his attempts at the jinshi examinations.
He subsequently received ordination at Miaoying Monastery in Zizhou and traveled to Chengdu, where he studied the sutras and śāstras with great renown during the Shaoxi era.
In the *rénzǐ* year, he traveled out of the gorges and wandered through the regions of Jing and Chu. At that time, Songyuan was propagating the Way at Jianfu in Raozhou;

[Dahui] went directly to his hermitage, but as it happened to be a year of famine, he was not accepted. He then met Master Caoyuan Sheng, who was serving as the Head Seat at Yunju and had recently assumed the abbacy of Miaoguo.

The Master [Caoyuan] granted him entry into the inner chamber and appointed him to attend to the incense burner, administering severe blows with his old fists and heavy staff without sparing him. By this time, [Dahui’s] entire life...
