His insight was utterly without trace. Nevertheless, he always felt a sense of deficiency because he had not yet met Songyuan.
When Songyuan moved to Lingyin Monastery, the Master said, "I still have these two hands of a destitute man; I must go to the various quarters to scratch where it itches. Upon arriving in Hangzhou...
Songyuan’s gate was lofty and steep; for eight months he could not enter. Each time he hesitated, wishing to speak, Songyuan repeatedly rebuked him and would not allow him to draw near.
One day, someone informed Songyuan [of his presence], and Songyuan said, "I have already opened the eight gates for you;

it is simply that you have missed the mark right before my face. Upon hearing these words, the Master lost both his mouth and ears, and only then did he realize he had been serving as a mere attendant.

During his time at Yuan, his playful jests and angry rebukes were nothing other than skillful means of admonition. Subsequently, after Caoyuan had passed into stillness, he traveled to the gates of various elders for over twenty years.
He then emerged into the world at Guangxiao Temple in Xiuzhou and Jangshan in Jinling.
At Mount Gushan and Xuefeng in Fuzhou, during the Wuxu year of the Jiaxi era, an imperial decree was issued for him to reside at Mount Taibai.

As the abbots of both Yung-wang Monasteries had not yet been found, the Emperor, because of the Master’s arrival, compelled him to concurrently hold those positions. The Master traveled back and forth between the two mountains, and scholars from all quarters followed him as if returning home.
His reputation reached the capital, and by imperial edict, he was transferred to Lingyin Monastery. [The Emperor] then recalled him with deep remembrance...
Mimian Songyuan was formerly a traveling companion [of Wuzhun Shifan]. Just as he was contemplating how to revitalize the ancestral style, demonic obstacles arose beyond his expectations;
these were difficult to resolve through mere words. He suddenly resolved to retire to his old mountain and departed in haste, beating the drums [to announce his departure].

Although Lord Jiezhai Zhao, the Governor of Jingzhao, sent a letter earnestly urging him back and issued an official decree (tangti) appointing him to the Tiger Hill Monastery, [Songyuan remained firm].
When Master Sheng was invited by Lord Xu Zhai to rise from his seclusion at Jiangshan, neither could turn his mind. In the spring of the Wushen year, the assembly at Yuyang concluded;
among the eminent elders, who were as sparse as morning stars, only the Master remained as a venerable patriarch of the monastic community.

The public petitioned the court for his appointment, and the people waited day and night for him to emerge, yet he firmly declined and would not relent. Furthermore, there were those who wished to entice him to serve as...

When he first arrived at Fahua, he earnestly entreated [the authorities] three times, yet they would not grant his request to leave. However, imperial edicts commanding him to reside at Mount Jing continued to arrive. The Master said, "I have already given my word;

it is truly impossible to disobey the sovereign's command. How could I possibly evade my duty? Consequently, in the ninth month he arrived at Fahua, and after a month had passed, he ascended Mount Shuangjing.
The response from both humans and spirits was such that the sound of joyous acclaim was like thunder. When the Master preached the Dharma, it was direct and simple.
Brilliant and clear; he did not fall into conventional molds. He once said: "Throughout the entire universe, there is not so much as a single thread’s breadth of space.
Yet you people, slinging your staffs over your shoulders, wander the four continents on pilgrimage. I have been nowhere I have not reached, and there is nothing I do not know. But tell me:
what Dharma was the Master Śīlabhadra at Nālandā Monastery in India preaching today? Furthermore:

He said: "There is one person who, in a single thought-moment, attains sudden realization and enters the ranks of the Buddhas; there is another person who, for kalpas on end, remains an icchantika, having no wish to become a Buddha.
Now tell me, which of these two deserves to receive the offerings of devas and humans? After a long silence, he said: "The butterfly pierces the fragrant path, its two brows damp with dew;
the bee plunders the withered flower, its two thighs thick with nectar. His poetic intent reached such lofty heights. Shortly thereafter, he fell ill.
From winter through spring, although his physical form had grown emaciated, when he ascended the hall to give formal teachings, his clarity and vigor were as they had always been.
Suddenly, he wrote a record for his funerary niche and composed some ten letters, stating: "The anniversary of Wuzu’s passing falls on the eighteenth;

I shall depart on the fifteenth, so I will not be able to prepare incense or perform offerings. The attendant monks were startled by these words and urgently requested his final verse. The Master [responded]:
He laughed and said, "The final phrase cannot be deliberated upon; it requires only that a person directly take it up.
He passed away silently after a short while. He was eighty-two years old. The Master was sincere and without artifice, consistent in both outward appearance and inner character.

He was patient with others while maintaining strictness in his own conduct; he was adept at engaging with the world while leading the assembly with solemnity. He resided on the mountain for thirty years, and wherever he went, he inspired [others].
He took it as his personal mission to propagate the ancestral style and regarded it as his own concern that the Dharma had not yet found its successor.

In his daily life, he was simple, serene, and profoundly silent, appearing as if unable to speak. Yet, when seated in the hall to deliberate with and examine the monks, his spiritual sharpness—once triggered—was like the rushing of thunder and the flashing of lightning;
it caused the sea to surge and the rivers to overturn, leaving everyone utterly bewildered and ignorant of where to find a foothold. He vowed never to treat them lightly in word or expression.

Jiaren was deeply esteemed by those who came to study under him. In his later years, he had no other interests; he devoted much attention to the art of calligraphy and attained the *samādhi* of small-character script (*xiaokai*).

His style was often dignified and solemn, reflecting his character. Monastics and laypeople alike turned to him with reverence, seeking his Dharma words, verses, and eulogies without a day’s interval.
Despite bitter cold or intense heat, he never grew weary of wielding his brush. Many scholar-officials delighted in following him.
He traveled extensively and was especially esteemed by renowned scholars and high-ranking officials, such that his teachings and reputation spread abroad.
There were those who traveled across the vast ocean to inquire about the Dharma, bearing letters and gifts; his virtue and character moved people to such an extent.
While he was at Tiantong and Yuyang, he received an imperial decree to open the hall at Lingyin, whereupon he packed his belongings and prepared to depart for his journey.
However, a person from a neighboring peak who harbored malice toward him intended to incite a group of unruly elements to obstruct his path.
When those on his left and right heard of this, they reported it to the Master. The Master said, "I have always treated others with sincerity;

what could they possibly do to me? He remained entirely unmoved. Consequently, that man ultimately desisted without being able to carry out his plot. [He visited] Shuangjing, Lengquan, Taibai, and Xuefeng.

Mount Feng is a premier monastery within the realm. Those who harbor the desire for rapid advancement, clutching their secret depths and boasting of their support, climb the steps through clever artifice;
such efforts may even reach the divine. But the Master was not thus: clad in coarse hemp and plain cloth until the end of his life, he was never moved by power or profit.
Thus, his advancement did not depend on introductions, and his withdrawal was always characterized by a constant serenity. He was truly a pillar of the Dharma-gate.
He was a pillar and beam for his time and a standard for later scholars.

Jing Meng, whose personal name was Cheng, was a native of Pingyang in Wenzhou of the Shao clan. His lineage was very large, and many of its members were distinguished as Confucian scholars; he studied under Master Yingda.

Kaishuang was naturally open and spirited. From his youth, he took joy in hearing the sounds of bells and sutras. At the age of thirteen, he followed the Great Master Weifan of Huian to don the saṃghāṭī robe.

He studied the teachings and contemplations of the Tiantai school with great clarity and diligence. However, he felt that the study of names and characteristics (nāmālambana) was insufficient for realizing the Great Matter.
He departed to travel to Guoqing Temple and further visited Master Fozhi of Yuyang. When the Master asked him about his native place, he replied, "Yong..."
Jia said, "Do you still recognize Master Yongjia? Before he could answer, [Dongshan] slapped his cheek and left. This happened a second time, leaving him dazed as if in a stupor;
for months on end, he was unsettled in both sleep and food. While practicing the Way, he suddenly heard the sound of a bell and attained enlightenment.

He immediately went into the master’s room. The Master again posed the previous question. The teacher replied, "On this day, I humbly wish that the Honored Master’s health and daily activities are well."

"Ten thousand blessings! Ask me about the matter that transcends [the ordinary]. When the Master attempted to answer, he was driven away. On the following day, he went up again just as the official was about to pose a question;
the Master raised his voice and said, "Old man, today you have met with defeat! With a single strike of his staff, he departed. The official laughed and said, "How brilliant!"
On his way back to his hometown to visit his mother, Longxiang Xinwen heard of him and, upon seeing him, regarded him with deep appreciation. He asked, "Words do not unfold the reality;
speech does not meet the occasion. Those who rely on words perish; those who linger in phrases are deluded. Try to deliver a message from the place where verbal expression falls short.
The Master drew a circle with his left hand. Xinwen struck the left side with his whisk. The Master drew another circle.
With his right hand, he struck it once; then he drew two lines across the center with both hands held out in offering.
Yunmen struck him. With the whisk, he drew two lines across the center. The Master bowed and stood up. Yunmen laughed loudly and said, "For thirty years I have been selecting seedlings;

today this seedling has encountered the *vatsanābha* (aconite). He then had him attend upon him, fully revealing the depths of his realization. Soon after, he returned to Deer Park, as if returning to his own hermitage.
Xian, Xue’an Jin, Yi’an Jian, Quan’an Cun, and Jungu Da were all eminent figures under the guidance of Huan’an Chun;
yet the Master alone stood out as a prodigy at a young age. Xinwen named his hermitage after the Master’s style name and composed an inscription for it.
The reputation of this attendant has grown ever more eminent. Furthermore, he once visited Master Zhi of Xian-ning in Lin’an.

Master Zhi’s teaching style was as steep as a cliff, such that students kept their distance; yet he alone said to the Master, "If the inherited traditions and remaining splendor of your ancestors have not fallen into ruin..."

"It still rests upon your person; I shall wait with bated breath to behold it. Initially he resided at Zhimen and later moved to Ruiyan, both appointments being secured through the recommendation of the Duke of Shishui, Wei Hao.

While Duke Wei was in Yongjia, he maintained a relationship of "square friendship" (a non-monastic bond) with Xinwen. After retiring from the相位 (prime ministership), he lived as a country recluse and dreamed of him as if they were still together in life.
Beside him was a monk named Jingmeng, whose appearance was ancient yet whose spirit was pure; they conversed and laughed for a long time.
Upon waking, Jue went to visit Tiantong Pu and asked, "The name of this monk is quite extraordinary; is there such a person? Pu replied, "He is currently the first seat (shouzuo) in the hall.
Jue summoned him and found that he was as if seeing him again in a dream. When they discussed the supramundane Dharma, his responses were as clear and resonant as echoes.
When Jue inquired about his teacher, it was Xingwen. Pu was greatly impressed by him, subsequently promoted his reputation, and had him reside at Zimen. And so it continued...
When the seat at Ruiyan was vacant, the Master was again summoned to fill it. He was solitary and aloof, transcending the mundane;

though physically frail and unable to bear the weight of his own robes, he was stern and severe, impossible to approach or fathom. Once he sat upon the site of enlightenment, those whom he struck with his mallet or brushed with his whisk were like dragons and elephants being trampled—his path became illustrious.
As for Zhimen and Ruiyan, both had survived the remnants of ruin; people considered them irredeemable.

The restoration was undertaken; the Master planned it with composure, and before long, the work was completed. The structure was renovated with such splendor that its magnificence even surpassed its former state.

Possessing great talent and wisdom, he never revealed even a fraction of his abilities in ordinary circumstances; yet when the occasion arose, they were manifested, leaving all who witnessed them to sigh in admiration.
From this, one can know the depth of his hidden cultivation.
The Biography of Chan Master Duanqiao Lun.
He was the son of the Xu family of Huangyan in Tiantai; his mother was Liu. She conceived him after dreaming of the moon.

At the age of eighteen, he received the tonsure at Guangci Monastery in Yongjia. There, he met Guyuan Dao at Ruiyan, where he heard the saying "three pounds of flax" and gave rise to a state of doubt.

He traveled extensively throughout all directions, yet his spiritual capacity and words failed to accord with the truth. He thought to himself, "My mouth is stammering and my ears are deaf; how can I possibly fathom this?

It would be better to focus on practical cultivation, making the daily recitation of sutras my primary task. While reading the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* at the Cloud Dwelling Mountain Hall (Yunju Shantang), he reached the passage:
"Even mosquitoes, insects, and ants have no speech, yet they are able to accomplish their tasks. At that moment, he attained sudden enlightenment and said, "Zhao..."
The story of the Cypress Tree at Mount Zhou is indeed extremely direct and straightforward; yet, he did not explain it to others, but went straight to Xuedou to see Chan Master Wuzhun Fayan.
Wuzhun interrogated him, and although he offered thirty turns of responses in succession, none were in accord. He pleaded earnestly, saying, "Is there no expedient means?
Fayan answered him with a verse by Zhenjing. [Zhaozhou] stood transfixed for a long while. Hearing the sound of the wooden board, he attained realization.
Sweat broke out from his body, and he was thereby finally liberated; he was no longer obstructed.

Following the precedent of Yǎowáng and Shuāngjìng, where all followed their teacher and were permitted to share the teaching seat, he subsequently emerged in the world at Zhīyuán, moved to Ruìyán and Guóqīng, and finally preached the Dharma at Jìngcí.

His style was direct and complete in its standards; those with superior faculties and keen insight could grasp it, while those of inferior capacity could not approach it. At times, he would ascend [the seat]...

The Hall Master raised up the case of Chan Master Daguan Ying, who addressed the assembly, saying: "The Seven Buddhas are the subjects of one's nature; the myriad dharmas are the slaves of one's mind. Now tell me, where is the master?
He then gave a shout himself and said, "From the Seven Buddhas downward, they all come forth. He then responded himself, saying, "Each attends to their own duties.
To call the Seven Buddhas "subjects of one's nature" and to point to the myriad dharmas as "slaves of one's mind"—this is Daguan.
To claim for oneself that there is a path leading out of this world, and to respond with one’s own shouts and assents—these are merely matters pertaining to slaves.
When has the master ever dreamed of such things? Do you wish to see him in the midst of the great assembly? [He] brandishes the whisk once and says: "At dawn, a spring breeze stirs;
throughout the gardens, flowers bloom all at once. Such is the general outline of his exalted awakening. As he was about to pass away...
He entered the room with the assembly. When the session concluded, he took up his brush and composed a poem bidding farewell to the various mountains and the Duke of Wei.
The Duke sent him medicine, which he did not accept. The Duke then sent someone to ask, "Master, you were born at Tiantai; why have you died at Jingci?

He replied, "The sun rises in the east and sets in the west at night. Thereupon, he passed away in a state of profound stillness. Some say that when he first visited Wufan, Wufan asked him, "From where have you come?"
[The Master] called out, "Come! He replied, "Tiantai. [The Master] asked, "Do you still see the Stone Bridge? He replied, "I have already kicked it through with a single step.
From that time on, the monastic community referred to the Master as Master Duanqiao Lun (Lun of the Severed Bridge).

Daosheng’s lineage was Daosheng. He was the son of the Wu family of Jian’an. At birth, he had a fleshy protuberance shaped like a ring upon his left breast; it only began to disappear once he entered the monastic life.
By nature, he was intelligent and wise. At nineteen, he shaved his head and donned the robes of a monk, possessing a vast aspiration to travel and study. His father passed away early.

He was renowned for his filial piety toward his mother. After his mother passed away, he traveled to Changle and visited Master Fozhi Gong. Upon entering the master’s quarters, he attained sudden enlightenment at the moment the words were spoken.
From then on, his spiritual acumen and sharp wit were so swift that no one dared to challenge him. When Fozhi moved to Lingyin Monastery, the Master served as the Head Seat (Shouzuo).
He subsequently returned to his hometown and built a hermitage at the foot of Mount Dawang, naming it "Cold Rock" (Han Yan). Not long after, the Governor of Quanzhou invited him.

Because it was a renowned monastery, scholars gathered there like clouds. [The Master] followed the practice of calculating the number of mouths to be fed, whereupon he brushed off his robes and returned home.
He composed the "Song of Laziness" to manifest his resolve. When Li Dunlao governed Fujian, he inquired among the various mountains for an outstanding successor to Fozhi;

everyone pointed to the Master. Consequently, he took up residence at Zhiti Mountain. When Deng Chengcai governed Yuzhang, noting that the Master’s aspirations lay in the mountain forests, he... [text ends].

When Quan Chengtian invited [Zhaozhou] Huanglong, his successor was unaware of the Master’s reputation. When the Master wished to depart, he happened upon Zhang Anguo, the Governor of Tan, who invited him to Shishuang;
the Master declined both offers twice. While traveling through Xishan, Shen Chiyao was transferred from the position of Transport Commissioner to become the Governor of Min.
He submitted a formal petition for the Master’s resignation from his post, exerting every effort to entreat him to remain, and thus established him at Letan Temple. The temple had recently been...

The temple was burned down. When the Master arrived, offerings poured in from all directions, and the buildings were restored to a brilliant splendor. Because of his advanced age, he earnestly requested to return to Jian’an.
Shortly thereafter, Prime Minister Shi Fu summoned him to preside over Gushan. The Master maintained himself according to the Dharma and oversaw the assembly with rigorous discipline.
Seeing the decline of the Dharma gate and the competitive scramble among novice monks, he was filled with sorrow. He once said to others: "The monasteries are desolate and cold."
The character of the age was languid and decadent; this matter was like the joints of a horsewhip, gradually becoming more pointed as it went along.
He resided in six great monasteries, all of which he accepted only because he was urged, pressed, and compelled by high-ranking officials and scholars.

Yet, he proclaimed the Dharma, led others in practice, and restored what had fallen into ruin, with his efforts renewing themselves day by day and month by month. Ultimately, he never pursued matters that were not his own primary aspiration. Such was the Master.
Chengwei, who had taken it upon himself to uphold the Buddha-dharma, one day after the summer retreat suddenly asked his attendant monk, "What date is today?

The attendant replied, "The sixteenth. He asked again, "What is the day-stem and branch? The attendant replied, "Xinmao. Chengwei then entered his room and passed away while seated. He was sixty-nine years old.
His body remained for three days with a countenance as if alive; he was buried at the foot of Mount Xianglu.
Zhìdēng (智燈) transmitted the lamp of wisdom to Zhìdēng (智燈). A native of Jīnhuá in Wùzhōu, his style name was Zǔyìn (祖印). He received the Dharma from Dàowú Fǎzhēn (道吾法真).

By nature he was refined and quick-witted, possessing great moral capacity; both monastics and laypeople flocked to him. He entered the world at the age of only twenty-one, yet he established the school and planted the Way.
Zhi lived in seclusion, conducting himself as a venerable elder. He preached the Dharma for thirty years, and his followers gathered like clouds.
He retired to Dengjue Temple, where he passed away while seated. There is one volume of his recorded sayings (*yulu*), which Zou Zhengyan Hao prefaced, saying: "I was once in Zhongtao."
Once, while discussing the famous monks of the world with Master Litaoyuan, Master Y渊 said to me: "The Master Zu (Nanyue Huairang) whom I encountered was a man of the Way.
Early on, through karmic conditions, he became a guide for the world; later, he retired to Dengjue Temple in the capital.
To behold his countenance was like seeing a tree at the end of autumn; to listen to his expositions was like hearing the tide at midnight."

At first, I privately thought that he had never departed from my own school; yet in the end, he was like a single reed in the great ocean—looking around in trepidation, one could see neither shore nor boundary.
Several years later, I again encountered Master Yuan in the capital.

When I asked about what he called the "Patriarchal Seal" (Zuyin) and intended to seek it out, he said, "He entered into nirvana long ago. He then presented to me two volumes of the recorded sayings (*yulu*) he had compiled.
He showed it to me. Only then did I come to understand the words my teacher had spoken regarding his profound and extraordinary nature—that which could still be expressed in words.

As for the names of the patriarchs and their seals of transmission, they are not listed in the *Chuan deng lu* (Records of the Transmission of the Lamp), nor are their life stories recorded in the biographies. Fortunately, there remain only a few lines of authentic words that have reached our ears.
Thus, Zhengyan knew Yan by virtue of Master Yuan’s self-knowledge; together with Zuyin, they gave rise to a vital spirit that endures for a thousand ages.
Alas! How many ancient worthies have been lost to obscurity!
The Biography of the Venerable Huìyuán:
The Venerable Huìyuán was a native of the Yú clan of Suānzǎo in Kāifēng. His family had followed the profession of farming for generations. He left the household life at Jiànfú Temple;

by nature he was blunt and simple, yet he was diligent and never slackened in his efforts. Having received full ordination, he traveled abroad and heard that the Way of Chan was flourishing greatly in the south. Thereupon, he went there.
At Donglin Monastery in Jiangzhou, the monastic community held him in contempt. One day, he asked his companions, "What is Chan?

They mocked him, saying, "To go ask 'the one who can sing'—that is merely a cicada. Yuan did not understand their meaning, so he turned his back to a wall and meditated deeply until he was reduced to a mere skeleton.
Several months later, while walking through the palace courtyard, he suddenly tripped and fell, at which point he attained clear realization.
Upon attaining enlightenment, he said to the practitioner Xingyi, "I am unaccustomed to using brush and inkstone. I wish to compose a verse; you must write it for me upon the wall.
The practitioner smiled and consented. The verse says: "This one encounter, this one encounter— Even ten thousand taels of gold would be worth it.
A straw hat upon the head, a bundle at the waist; The clear breeze and bright moon are carried upon the staff. That very day, he departed.
When Chan Master Zong of Donglin saw this verse, he was greatly astonished and said, "If a monastic's investigation of the Way is such as this, it is beyond praise.
He ordered someone to track his whereabouts, but in the end, no one knew where he had gone."
Xuzhou (whose courtesy name was Chuan Pudu) was the son of the Shi family of Jiangdu in Wei-yang. Although he grew up studying secular texts, he had no intention whatsoever of remaining in the world.
His mother, recognizing his resolve, sent him to the Tianning Monastery in the prefecture to enter the monastic life. There, he spoke with General Bi.
The master marveled at him greatly, saying, "This boy is short and sturdy, yet his voice resonates like a bell. In days to come, he will be a formidable talon among the ranks of the Dharma.
He brought the boy back to Wulin and had him pay respects to Zu Xin of Dongtang Monastery, who became his preceptor.
After serving him for five years, he resolved to travel to visit various masters. He first met Tieniu Yin at Lingyin Monastery, and subsequently traveled through Jiangxi, Jiangdong, and Henan.
He traveled extensively throughout the north. At that time, Wugaitong was preaching at Jianfu Monastery in Raozhou. The Master resolved to seek him out and pay his respects;
when Tong later moved to Foyan and Huazang, the Master accompanied him there as well. During one session of entering the room for instruction, Tong asked:
"Who is it that does not take the myriad dharmas as a companion? The Master replied: "An iron Kunlun under a golden incense burner. Tong said: "I had thought this..."
The Dwarf. His insights and understanding were limited to this alone. The Master bowed deeply and paid his respects, saying, "I thank the Abbot for providing this testimony.
Tiantong Huirang Guang, Daci Shiyuan Lian, and Huqiu Shishi Di all recognized his extraordinary potential upon first meeting him and retained him to assist with monastic affairs.
At the beginning of the Chunyou era, Zhao Xinan, the Governor of the Imperial Secretariat, invited him to Banzhan in Jinling.
He went forth into the world, serving successively at Jinsan (Golden Mountain), Lüyuan (Deer Park) in Tán, Shūshān, and Chéngtiān in Sū.

During the Jiǎding era, Jia Tàifú memorialized for his appointment as Abbot of Zhōngtiānzhūk; subsequently, he requested imperial edict for his promotion to Línghyìn. This was in the Dīnchū year of the Zhìyuán era.
He was appointed to reside at Mount Jing. His teaching of the Dharma was direct, straightforward, and concise. He bore the burden of the Dharma-gate with tireless vigor even in his old age.
He once said: "The myriad dharmas are the radiance of the mind; all conditions are but the awakening of one's nature. Fundamentally, there is neither delusion nor enlightenment;
people simply need to realize this today. He also said: "Since there is neither delusion nor enlightenment, what has anyone realized? No one could grasp his underlying intent. His...
While residing at Mount Jing, he encountered the aftermath of a fire. Resolving to restore the monastery, his efforts were just beginning to take shape when he suddenly fell ill.
He asked for a brush and wrote in large characters: "Eighty-two years; I have boarded the bottomless boat and, having capsized it, I return. The bright moon fills the sky. Thereupon, he passed away.
The Biography of Chan Master Tianqi:
Master Tianqi Rairen was a native of Zhongling in Nanchang. His father was Jiangtang and his mother was Lady Xu.

While traveling with his father on business to Yingzhou, the Master reached the age of nearly twenty when he suddenly resolved to seek the Way. He proceeded to Jingmenshou to study under the Venerable Wushuo Neng.

He left the household life and was instructed to contemplate how the myriad dharmas return to the One. Later, at the place of Buddha Zhao, he encountered the head seat Dao Yi, who exhorted him with bitter words and pressed him relentlessly day and night.
One day, while listening by chance to people conversing in the corridor, Dao Yi struck him immediately. The Master said:
"I have never been drowsy," the Master said. Daoyi remarked, "If you have never been drowsy, where have you been listening?
Furthermore, while two monks were cutting and measuring a skirt, the Master glanced at them with his eyes. Daoyi immediately struck him, saying, "What about those eyes of yours?
If you cannot keep your focus on the *huatou*, how can you attain realization? From then on, his practice became even more earnest; yet for five years, he could not get the "cotton" onto his body.
For two years he had no inner robes; throughout both winter and summer, he wore a single tattered *pāṃśukūla* (cast-off rag robe) that was so threadbare it was barely wearable.
He traveled to consult various elder Chan masters for the sake of definitive discernment. From Master Jing Donghui, he heard the account of Dahui’s affliction with carbuncles.
Subsequently, he visited Zhongzhu Chushan and Xuefeng, each of whom had realized persons among their disciples. Finally, he arrived at Gaofeng Temple in Nanjing, where he met Master Baofeng Xuan.

Only then did he have a sudden flash of realization. He remained there to spend the winter, but before long, he took his leave. Feng bestowed upon him a Dharma robe and a hair-whisk, and spoke this verse:

"At Jishan, the staff and shout were like a light touch; From now on, the hand-eye for killing and giving life shall be intimate. Holy understanding and ordinary sentiment are both cut off at their root;
A fresh branch of the *dharma-puṣpa* flower still blooms. When the Master appeared in the world and opened the hall, he gained many disciples. There is a saying:
The *Qingjue ji* (Collection on Solitude and Severance) was recorded and circulated in the world.
The words in the *Qingjue ji* that reveal the truth are urgent and incisive, never losing the essential character of the "tongs and hammers" [of Chan pedagogy].

While the *Songgu* (Verses on Ancient Cases) are secondary, as for the *Lianfang jiyuan* (Linked Fragrance: Records of Occasions), the name of each person is followed by a single verse, upon which the Master appends [his own verse].
Question: People provide a single answer that, when expanded, becomes a voluminous scroll. Those at the highest level do not transcend the mold and framework of Wan-song of Qingzhou;
those at the lower level have already entered the realm of scholastic learning and naturally feel their own efforts are meaningless.

When you, Master, first traveled on foot as a pilgrim, you encountered a monk on the road who said you were too fond of composing verses and hymns. That was one occasion; when things enter the basket, they are vegetables—how can one possibly do both?
Collected. The editor lost his eyesight, resulting in the obscuring of the brilliance of this complete gem. How regrettable!
Xutang’s *Foolish Record of Wisdom and Folly*:
Xutang is the pen name of [a monk] from Siming. Having received full ordination, he traveled to study under Master Yunnan Yan, attaining realization upon hearing his words.

His intent was such that throughout his life he traversed ten monasteries, and his transformative teachings spread like the wind. At the end of the Shaoxun era, he was summoned by imperial decree to reside at Mount Jing.
In his quarters, he established three turning phrases to test practitioners; few were able to encounter his spiritual mechanism. He asked:

"For one whose own eye is not yet clear, why do they take empty space and wear it as trousers? He asked again: "One draws lines on the ground to make a prison; why is it that one cannot penetrate through this?"
However, he said: "Entering the sea to count the grains of sand at its bottom—why then do you stand with your feet raised upon the point of a needle?
He further said: "The empty hall has no doors or gates; it does not allow people to draw near, nor does it cast them into the land of nothingness.
It simply requires that all of you become like iron, entering the earth and transforming together with the soil, only then can you break forth. As for the operation [of this], how is it so?"
"Regarding those who introduce excrement: I can do nothing for them. One day, Master Songyuan raised up [the case of] Linji’s passing and addressed the assembly, saying:
"Among the elder brothers who have long practiced and walk upon the true path, there are those who simply cannot apply the 'black bean' method.
The Way of Linji is about to vanish and become unheard of—how tragic! [The Master] commented: "The Great Elder of Vulture Peak seems to be leaning on a staff while riding a horse."
Although he was free from the hardship of lying stiff in death, he could not avoid the censure of bystanders.

Previously, when the Master was at Jingci Monastery, his exchanges during the day of his entry into the monastery had been cut short when an imperial messenger arrived at the gate to deliver an edict. The Emperor asked: "Why did Zhaozhou travel on pilgrimage for eighty years?
Why did Xu Tang dwell in the mountains for eighty years? The Master immediately cited the story of Zhaozhou’s pilgrimage to Linji and offered this verse: [Verse omitted as per instructions]
Zhaozhou first set out on his pilgrimage at eighty; at eighty, he returned to reside at Mount Xu Tang.

Possessing a distinct capacity that expanded upon the Buddhas and Patriarchs, he moved the imperial countenance within the nine-layered capital. When the Emperor requested a verse for his return, Zhaozhou submitted one, which greatly pleased His Majesty.

He was specially granted five hundred *shí* of rice and one hundred rolls of silk. Zhaozhou subsequently opened the hall to settle the assembly, and later passed away. His stupa was erected below Zhiling and named Tian.

However, previously, the King of Goryeo had invited the Master to preach the Dharma in that country. After eight years, he returned to the mountain, followed by a thousand disciples who had questioned him on the Dharma.
During the Jiajing era of our Ming dynasty, Goryeo still sent his dharma heirs here to sweep the pagoda;
thus, the path of the Dharma in that country was exceedingly flourishing.
Supplementary Biographies of Eminent Monks,
Volume Eleven and Volume Twelve.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Minghe of Huashan Temple in Wumen, Ming Dynasty.
Chapter on the Practice of Dhyāna:
The Biography of Chan Master Fuguang Daowu.
Daowu’s secular surname was Kou; he was a native of Lanzhou in Shaanxi. He was born with teeth. At the age of sixteen, he sought to leave the household life.
His parents would not permit it, so he fasted for several days until they finally allowed him to shave his head. Two years later, while returning from Lintao, he stayed overnight at Wanzi Dian.
During the night, he was awakened by a dream of a Buddhist monk; just then, he heard the neighing of horses and attained sudden, great enlightenment.
Upon returning home, he was overcome with joy and sang in verse: "Jian ye la! Jian ye la! Pervading all of empty space, There is but one. He then went to inform [his parents].
His mother said, "I picked up an object. She searched through her bags and pouches but could not find it, so she asked, "What kind of object was it?
The Master replied, "Since beginningless time, I have never seen an object that can be fully grasped. His mother did not understand.

Later, when he wished to travel to various regions, a fellow villager who was seeing him off requested a verse. [The Master wrote: "When water flows, it must reach the sea; when a crane emerges, it is white."
Regarding the phrase "the words at the head of the clouds": Upon reaching Mount Xiong’er, he indeed met Master Baibun Hai.
Previously, when people asked Hai why he did not select a dharma heir, Hai had also composed a verse containing the lines: "The orchids and lilies flourish, emerging uniquely from Western Qin.
When the Master arrived, at night he heard a voice in the air saying, "Tomorrow, go to receive Guest Minister Guo. At dawn, Hai called for the monks to set out.
He ordered [the disciple] to carry incense and flowers to receive his disciples from Guansi. This temple was built by Tang’s Guo Ziyi; now, Qu himself has come to serve as its abbot.
Once they arrived, their words were in perfect accord, and he immediately entrusted him with his robes and alms bowl. Previously, there had been a bandit who robbed and killed people near the temple.
When the victim came to report the emergency, the Master called out to the assembly to seize him, saying, "You are the thief! He subsequently discovered the bandit's den.
At Xue, a band of rebels requested his life. The Master showed them the essential words [of the Dharma] and released them. For several decades thereafter, no one picked up lost items along the roads.
Because of this, people further believed that the Master’s previous incarnation was the Prince of Fenyang.

In the twenty-fourth year of the Dading era, after Baiyun had passed away, the Master opened the hall to appear in the world; first at Puzhao in Zhengzhou, and subsequently at Zhuge Hermitage in Sanxiang.
At that time, he wore white robes, rode an ox, and played the transverse flute as he wandered along the Luo River; no one could fathom him. He once said to people:
"If you say I am an ordinary person, I am heading toward the rank of the sages. If you say I am a sage, I am heading toward the rank of the ordinary.
If you say I am neither sage nor ordinary, I have just begun to find a place for my practice atop the crown of Vairocana. (Tahe 5)
In that year, he entered the summer retreat at Dashi Temple in Lintao and began lecturing on the *Nirvāṇa-samantabhadra-bodhicitta-uttaratantra-sūtra* (The Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment).

Ascending the seat, he said, "This lecture will only reach halfway through. On the evening of the twelfth day of the fifth month, after the evening session, he finished his morning ablutions the following day.
He called to his attendant, saying, "I am ill; go and seek medicine. Before the attendant had even reached the gate, the Master had already passed away while reclining.
Above the abbot’s quarters, five-colored clouds appeared like a precious canopy, within which were three red lights resembling suns.
He was fifty-five years of age and had thirty-nine years of seniority as a monk.
Zhengyan. Regarding the lineage of the two masters, Zhengyan and Liaochi:
Zhengyan was a native of Changshe in Xu Prefecture. His surname was Wang. At the age of nine, he entered the service of Elder Jingliang of Zifu Monastery.

He served as an attendant to his teacher for ten years before taking leave to travel and study at the academies. At that time, Master Hao, the Chief Monk Registrar (*Senglù*), resided in Nanjing and was lecturing on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*.

[Fahai] went to visit him to resolve doubts regarding the nature and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of phenomena; his penetration of principle was profound and ultimate, leaving Master Hao so captivated that he appointed him to lecture in his stead.
His reputation rose significantly, and as the lecture seat came to rely heavily upon him, he eventually changed his course and settled there.
Chan [Master] sat in quiet meditation at Longtan on Mount Song. He then built a thatched hut at Ziyun Peak in Ruizhou, yet he had not yet attained any realization.
Hearing that Chan Master Cizhao was propagating the Way at Xiangshan, he went there to join him. Cizhao cited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, saying:
"The Tathāgata is the meaning of the suchness of all dharmas. How do you understand this? Thereupon, he suddenly attained a realization and said: "All conditions..."
"Though it perishes, its nature is not extinguished; like clouds dispersing across the vast sky, the heavens are bright with the moon.

When he presented this to Cizhao, Cizhao did not immediately agree. He then went to the capital to see Guanghui, who appointed him as the head of the secretariat. After a long time, he finally became settled in his position.
He subsequently emerged from seclusion to reside at Mount Yangtian, moved to Yian Temple in Yidu, and later to Puzhao Temple in Zhengzhou, and [Hennan]...

Fayun resided at Tiantan and Longquan in Zhe; these were all places where he established his transformative influence. Wherever he went, the sound of the Dharma flowed far and wide, reaching all like an echo.

In upholding the fundamental tenets, he cast off all conventional molds; he was like a hawk soaring into the vast sky or a steed galloping across the open plains—so swift and unrestrained that it is difficult for others to catch sight of or follow.
He composed one hundred verses each on "Eulogies on Ancient Cases" and "Excerpts on Ancient Cases. Regarding the *Vajra*...

His *Jingzhengdao ge* (Song of Verifying the Path) exists; his *Zhujintai* (Commentary on the Golden Terrace) exists; and his *Luzhenxin* (Record of the True Mind) exists—all of which circulate in the world.
Furthermore, he was able to employ his surplus energy in "playful" fashion to honor and adorn monasteries, achieving results that can be examined.
Moreover, he differed from those who practice Chan by remaining withered and silent, casting all worldly affairs aside, or who grow old fishing at the banks of the Yingbin. By [doing so],...
In the year of Yisi of the Dading era, he entered nirvana.
Liaochi was a native of Fushu in Baixu; his surname was Pan. At the age of sixteen, he underwent the scriptural examination and received ordination.

He specialized in the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, exhausting its profound mysteries and penetrating its depths. He traveled to study under various spiritual mentors, until finally, through the words of Guanghui, he attained realization. He subsequently returned to Xi Creek, west of Luzha Water.

Above all these, he wore coarse hemp garments and maintained a vegetarian diet, eradicating worldly traces and severing all attachments for over ten years. He established the Zhulin (Bamboo Grove) Monastery for the sake of various nobles and powerful patrons;
disciples gathered like clouds, and when his alms bowl was spread out and seats were arranged, their number reached five thousand.

In the nineteenth year of the Datong era, he passed away peacefully on his right side without illness at the age of fifty-one. After his cremation, the śarīra relics were found in five colors in countless quantities, and a stupa was erected.
Thus it was. The Elder of Zhongxu in Huyang inscribed this epitaph: "The Master came in response to conditions; while all things were yet unformed, he acted with skill.
When conditions ended and he departed, he remained entirely unentangled by birth and death. He played amidst illusions, severing the deluded attachments of coming and going."
Sublime and without abiding—this is the command of the Master that is put into practice. Alas! This is the inscription for him.
Master Qingliang Xianggong, whose style name was Xixi, was born into the Wang family of Yishui. Initially, he left home to become a son of the Buddha and served the Venerable Zu Zhao.
This man obtained monastic robes through his mastery of the sutras; he then read freely both Buddhist and secular texts for ten years, investigating and observing much therein.

Hearing that the Venerable Xuming Heng resided at Puzhao Temple and was highly esteemed for his reputation in the Way at that time, he completely abandoned all that he had previously studied to study under him.
Xuming knew he was no ordinary man and joyfully accepted him.
Ten years later, he was invested with the seal and entered the world to reside at Dajue in Zhengzhou, Shaolin on Mount Song, Puzhao in Yizhou, and finally at Qingliang.

The Master was diligent in receiving and examining those who came to him. Whenever there were those who sought his counsel and resolution, he would investigate their questions and provide instruction, emptying out his granaries and storehouses until no further room remained.
Thus, although he had retired from public office and declined active affairs, students drew closer to him than ever.

He was kind-hearted and meticulous in his dealings with others, yet he harbored an excessive intolerance for evil. If anyone acted contrary to reason, he would invariably enumerate their faults in detail, becoming visibly indignant.
His spirit could not be concealed. When he was at leisure, he would tell his students: "The Way of Chan is subtle; unless one is single-minded and tranquil, it is absolutely impossible to enter it.
Worldly learning and intellectual understanding merely waste one's days and efforts. Yet, when composing poetry himself, as well as in his speech and actions, he expressed everything through them;
even for the briefest moments of eating or resting, he could not forget [the Chan state]. This was Yuan Yishan Hao-wen.
He traveled with his teacher to Lanruo Peak. Along the way, they discussed matters concerning the recent disturbances and the evasion of bandits.

The teacher remarked, "In general, one who enters the world must be able to transcend life and death before they can achieve anything of significance. Although life and death are momentous affairs, one must regard them as merely turning over one's hand.
Thus, whether halting in a pit or flowing along with the current, there is nothing that is not possible; this, however, must stem from the power of stillness."

He came from within; moment by moment, he did not set his mind upon external objects, and so he would naturally mature of himself. At that time, shortly after a light snowfall, the road was steep and the stones were slippery.
The Master was already old, and his strength could no longer support him. His foot slipped once, and he fell, breaking a limb. His companions cried out in alarm.

No one could save him, and he fell straight down for several dozen feet before coming to rest, barely stopped by a large tree. Yishan asked him in alarm, but the Master’s expression remained composed;
he said slowly, "I have studied Chan for forty years, yet my heels have been subjected to an examination by Shitou.
Those who heard this all laughed heartily, and they together marveled at his words regarding the "maturity of his state," which were indeed the matters of his daily life and not mere falsehoods.

He passed away at the age of sixty-four. His collected writings consist of three volumes titled *Guile*, *Tuixiu*, and *Qingliang*, along with one volume of recorded sayings, all of which have been transmitted throughout the various quarters.
Yuanxing (圓性) transmitted the Yuanxing lineage. He was the son of the Hou clan of Huairou in Shunzhou. From his grandfather upward, all had lived in obscurity without complaint.

His father was Qi, and his mother was Lady Du. She conceived after dreaming that a strange monk bestowed upon her a divine pearl; when she gave birth, the room was filled with light. During his childhood...
He abstained from meat and blood, and his deportment was upright and solemn. At the age of nine, he requested permission from his parents, wishing to become a monk; they granted him their consent.
He took Master Zhen of Fengfu Temple in the capital as his teacher. At fifteen, he received the full precepts and studied the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and the *Awakening of Faith*.
Whenever someone questioned him, he answered like an echo; his meanings were refined and his essential points subtle, all transcending the realm of ordinary thought.

After some time, he sighed and said: "This Dharma cannot be understood through discursive reasoning or conceptual discrimination. Does the fruit [of realization] truly reside in words? At the beginning of the Tiande era, Chan Master Furi entered Bianzhou.
The Master [Fayan] took incense in his sleeve and went to visit him. Furi silently recognized his capacity and applied the probe of the needle.

The Master further disciplined himself through ascetic practice, and within forty days, he attained a sudden realization. Foji (Buddha-sun) approved of him. When Foji accepted an invitation to Liaoyang, the Master accompanied him as an attendant.
Upon arriving at Hui’an, [Foji] appointed him to ordain monks and instructed him on the most essential points; the entire assembly was filled with reverence and submission.
Later, by imperial decree from the Empress, he resided at Gongde Monastery in Hanzhou. Not long after, he departed and crossed the Great [River].
The river flows through Qi and Lu. At that time, Master Zhao resided at Yuefeng Peak. He was about to visit him.

That evening, while sitting in his room, Zhao saw a great deity dressed in magnificent robes standing before him. The deity said, "The Great Being Guanghui is coming; you should prepare lodgings to await him.
At dawn the next day, Zhao prepared the assembly and waited expectantly for his meal. Then the Master arrived. The assembly was greatly astonished. Zhao [remained] vacant...

The Emperor’s heart was filled with profound reverence, and he informed him of what he had seen. The Master merely smiled. Traveling along the Bian River to Luo, he reached the region west of the Pass;
wherever he went, the senior masters and scholars of long standing all bowed before him. At the beginning of the Tiande era, he received an imperial decree to preside over Zhulin Monastery.
The following year, he moved to Hui’an. Empress Ming-su dispatched an imperial messenger to present him with a *moluona* robe, along with gold, silk, and various other items to support him.
As the expenses for the opening of the hall accumulated over time, the former assembly at Zhulin, never ceasing to think of him as their "Dharma-milk," all said, "He is our teacher.
How could Hui'an detain him? Using skillful means, they sent him back. At that time, Hailing held the keys to the monastery;

he had long admired the Master’s spiritual influence and was granted the title "Guanghui Tongli" (Broad Wisdom and Penetrating Principle), as well as purple robes, a sandalwood jeweled stupa, and an image of the Great Being. In the end...
The deity of Fuyue Peak spoke these words to him: "During the Dading period, you shall move to Tanzhe.

When you intend to undertake a major reconstruction, some may say that because the temple has long been abandoned, its scale is so vast that it will be difficult to complete; they may ask that you reduce it somewhat.
The Master replied, "My plan is already settled; I only fear a lack of sincerity. Within ten years, Tanzhe was completed, surpassing its former state.

When the construction first began, as they were carving into the mountain, a massive boulder collapsed and fell with a roar like thunder. The multitude was terrified and fled to avoid it, but the Master remained calm and paid it no heed.
When the rock reached the Master, it came to a halt, not more than several feet away; it was as if some divine power had warded it off.
When he was at Zhulin Monastery, the monastery was actually very distant from the residence granted by the Emperor, which was as grand as a palace.

Although it had been converted into a Buddhist temple, its tiered gates still remained. The Master remarked that such a place was not fit for a monastic residence and ordered that they be demolished immediately.

He obtained one million old bricks to pave the foundation of the abbot’s quarters (*fangzhang*). Furthermore, using the remaining materials, he renovated the former foundations into a lay residence for the secular community.
His undertakings were such that they would endure for all time; he exhausted his resources, not sparing even his robes or bowl.

Governing himself and managing his affairs, he committed to the canonical scriptures everything that could be practiced for a long duration to benefit future generations, so that it might be transmitted to posterity.
Such was the singular dedication of his resolve. In the sixth month of the fifteenth year of the Daye era, he passed away at Tanzhe, at the age of seventy.
2. His monastic seniority was fifty-seven years.

Minghe said: "This biography was taken from the inscriptions on the stone of the pagoda. The inscription was composed by Yang Bangji, the Imperial Commissioner for the Yongding Era of the Jin dynasty.
It states that Foguo came from Western Sichuan to Bianjing and transmitted the seal of the mind to Furi; Furi [transmitted it to...]"
Guanghui was the seventeenth generation descendant of Nanyue. Thus, it is beyond doubt that Furi was Miaoxi.
However, later it states that the Master attended Furi when he traveled to Liaoyang, and further mentions that he frequently accompanied Furi into the imperial palace to preach the Dharma.
When examining the dates and locations, this again seems inconsistent with Miaoxi. I am utterly bewildered as to who Furi actually was.
If this were indeed a marvelous occurrence, why is it not recorded in the *Nianpu* (Chronological Biography) or the *Chuandeng lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp)?

The *Nianpu* merely states that the Jurchens were acting with arrogance and seized several dozen Chan masters; the Master was selected as the foremost among them. The chieftain of the captors was impressed by him and did not yield him up.

By this, the entire assembly was spared. As for his practice being that of one who attained realization without a teacher, as Yang had stated—did those who later compiled the genealogical records merely wish to conceal this?
Or is it that the "Furi" (Sun of the Buddha) was not Miaoxi? Is there perhaps another Furi distinct from the lineage of Foguo?
Since Yang Wending had a basis for his claim, there must certainly have been one person to correspond to it. Generally speaking...

From beginning to end, Miaoxi was like the bright sun in a clear blue sky, leaving no room for concealment or evasion. I have recorded this to await the critical examination and verification of those of lofty intelligence.
Transmitted by Xiangliao.

He was known as Xiangliao. He was the son of the Song family from Yizhou. At birth, he possessed auspicious omens. In his childhood, he always gazed straight ahead when walking and sat in the full lotus posture when seated.

One day, hearing his grandfather reciting a poetic fu, he reached the line: "If Qin Shi Huang and Han Wudi did not die, where would they have returned? He immediately asked, "Where do those who die return?
His grandfather marveled at this and said to his father, "This child is no ordinary person of the mundane world; you should let him leave home."
He left his home and followed a teacher to shave his head. He traveled to lecture halls and became proficient in the *Avataṃsaka*, *Complete Enlightenment* (*Yuánjué*), and other sutras.
His intellectual faculties were sharp and quick, and his expositions were precise and authoritative; he was highly revered by his fellow students.

While reading the *Complete Enlightenment Sutra*, upon reaching the passage, "The scriptural teachings are like a finger pointing at the moon," he was suddenly struck with doubt and said, "Since the sutra is merely the finger pointing, where is the moon? I shall go and ask about this."
He traveled to various regions to seek out learned masters. Packing his belongings in a cloth bag, he went to see Master Yue of Qing’an, and also visited Master Ding of Xiānpíng.

He then journeyed to Mianzhou to pay his respects to Master Yòu of Dàmíng, yet found no resonance with them all. Master Yòu said, "Your karmic affinity does not lie here. Master Chāo of Chóngfú in Yìzhōu is your teacher; he will surely reveal its profound mysteries for you.

He immediately went to visit Master Chāo. Upon meeting him, the Master— (Note: The provided text ends abruptly at "公一" [Master... one], leaving the sentence incomplete. The translation reflects the available portion.)
He held the position of head of the community; though his administrative duties were numerous, he devoted himself all the more to intensive study until even sleep and food were entirely neglected.
One day, while a lay practitioner was requesting instruction from Master Chao regarding the "One Finger" koan of Master Juzhi, the Master stood at the edge of the seat and suddenly asked:
"Master Juzhi’s 'one-finger Zen' was inexhaustible in its utility; I wonder, Master, how much Zen do you possess? Master Chao—
He gave a shout. The Master, having received the essential meaning beneath that shout, felt his body and mind liberated into emptiness, as if dwelling amidst a precious moon within lapis lazuli.
Overjoyed and invigorated beyond measure, he presented this verse: "Having pierced through the floating clouds, the moonlight is cold;

By chance, it suddenly ceases and the skull dries up. Light permeates my entire being beyond the realm of Wei-yin; Universally responding to all capacities, I act as a great condition. The Duke snapped his fingers in approval.

He was appointed as its abbot. Not long after, the former abbot retired due to old age, and the Master was commissioned to fill his position. He moved to Songlin, then to Hui’an, and later transferred to Tanzhe.
Subsequently, he took charge of Zhulin. By nature, the Master was fond of quiet retirement; although he repeatedly occupied great monasteries, it was always out of necessity.
At both Songlin and Tanzhe, he even abandoned the assembly and fled. When people sought him out and surrounded him, they found him there.

He departed. The Master was ultimately unable to maintain his own independence. He often lamented that the ancients could conceal their persons without leaving a trace, whereas he could not do so, which he considered a hindrance to his progress on the Path.
Furthermore, his innate nature was upright and pure; he was compassionate and never acted in opposition to others.

Throughout his life, he never once gave rise to even the slightest anger. Even when encountering abuse or disparagement, his countenance remained unchanged. Wherever he went, he simply relied on conditions with a sense of contentment.

He did not concern himself with worldly adornments, for these are not the essentials of the Way. Regarding those practices that benefit one’s life, nature, body, and mind, he would neither engage in them himself nor encourage others to do so.
These matters are all manifest and can be spoken of; as for his hidden virtues and secret deeds, they are likely beyond human comprehension.
In the third year of the Taihe era, he sat upright in meditation, recited a verse, and passed away at the age of [blank].

He was seventy years old and had been a monk for sixty-two years. When his body was cremated, hundreds of thousands of butterflies emerged from the blazing flames and transformed into five-colored auspicious clouds appearing in the sky.
His teeth remained unbroken; they were placed with the remaining bones and interred at Longquan Ancient Temple.
The Biography of Fayaun.
Fayaun was the son of the Hou family in Yanzhou. In his youth, he served Ming, the Head Seat of Ziyang, as his teacher.

During the Dading era, he received the monastic robes for his proficiency in reciting the scriptures. He devoted himself to the study of Buddhist doctrine and principles; his faculties were exceptionally sharp, and few among his fellow students could equal him.

Wherever he traveled, he visited and inquired of various masters, gaining profound insight into their deep and secret teachings. He received the seal of transmission from both Master Shansheng of Mount Ming and Master Lingyan Cai.
Subsequently, he led a community and presided over Mount Gao, where he elucidated the subtle and profound mysteries of the Dharma.

During a time when the world was peaceful and the regulations of the Chan monasteries had not yet declined, his reputation for the Way was widespread, and he was highly esteemed by all quarters. He later moved to Puzhao Monastery in Yanzhou.
The younger brother of Duke Xuan, Xuanshu, immersed himself in the inner teachings of the *Śāstra* (Nèi Chéng). He engaged with the Master in a fellowship of Dharma-joy and refinement.

When the Master ascended the seat, Xuanshu would don his court robes and prostrate; yet, though the Dharma was revered and the personage honored, and the wise and eminent were inclined to bow before him, the Master remained silent and self-contained.

He did not employ written characters or speech to startle the common world for the sake of establishing a sectarian gate, nor did he strive to expand or renovate the monastery’s facilities while serving as its abbot.
Scholars were numerous and their activities as frequent as swarms of bees; yet, until now, there had been none who received the manifest empowerment. Such was his reluctance to grant it lightly.
Among the Master’s disciples was one named Master Bian, who inherited the Dharma from Master Heng at Xuming Pavilion.

This pavilion stood directly above [the site] and was not toppled by thunder, clouds, wind, or rain. During the aftermath of the Dragon-Rising suppression and destruction, several dilapidated buildings remained.

The rafters were exposed, and the remaining monks, numbering only three or four, sustained themselves by tending the garden. They refused to lightly frequent the doors of the powerful and influential of the day.
Someone once presented them with a poem that said: "The Way is vast, so one should remain lofty and upright; Zen is withered, yet it endures solitude.

A single thatch of reeds covers the head; three strips of bamboo bind the belly. One can imagine their refined character and see how their solitary loftiness and self-reliance must have had a profound source.
From my teacher. Later, returning from the south to Bian, I composed this mournful narrative: "In Bian, I shaved my head and served my teacher for five or six years.

It was only then that I fled the war to the south. By the time I returned, my teacher had been deceased for some time. My teacher was born at the beginning of the Zhenglong era and passed away at the end of the Xingding era;
he was over sixty years old. Yet, because of the chaos following the loss of the capital, the times were in decay, and as for my teacher—"

His life’s deeds cannot be verified. As for the dates of his death and burial, these too remain unknown; this is simply because these events occurred before the relocation of the capital south of the Bian River.
Yuan Haowen relied upon this [limited record] to compose the inscription for the Master’s stupa.
Yigwang (Daohai), whose secular surname was Fan, was a native of Wenyang.
The Fan clan was an ancient and distinguished lineage. From his childhood, the Master had an intense fondness for reading Buddhist scriptures.
At the age of twenty, he completed his tonsure and took Venerable Wei of the Jietanyuan Monastery on Mount Song as his preceptor.
He received full ordination there. He resolved to travel west to Danxia to inquire about the Dharma with Chan Master Zhi. In a single glance, their minds met like a needle and its eye.
Master Zhi wished to manifest the formal transmission to him, but the Master (Wuye) learned of this and fled. He once said to others:
Wisdom is generated from meditative concentration; it necessarily takes the Vinaya as its dwelling place. To depart from the mundane and attain the sacred, one must take Samādhi as the path.
If one’s learning has not been broad and one’s practice has not been refined, how could one reach such a state?

Therefore, with single-minded devotion, he practiced with precision, never becoming complacent in his knowledge or views. He passed through Fangcheng and reached Baquan Mountain, where he was surrounded by virtuous men.

He thatched a hut to enshrine [the image] and called it the "Ancient Buddha Hall. After residing there for several years, it eventually became a great monastic center—this is the present-day Pujisi (Puji Temple).
The Master entered deeply into meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) while taking the Pure Land as his primary practice. He wore the *Avataṃsaka* and *Nirvāṇa* sūtras upon his head;
he would circumambulate the Buddha exactly five hundred times and prostrate himself exactly five hundred times, reciting the Buddha’s name for a fixed number of days each day.
Ten thousand recitations. At night, he would sit upright and solemnly; he took this as his constant practice. He continued in this manner for twenty years, becoming even more earnest as he grew old.
When others requested that he open the hall for the assembly to expound the Unsurpassed Vehicle (*anuttarayāna*), the Master smiled but did not answer.

Subsequently, due to old age, he retired to the White Lotus Hall and entrusted the affairs of the monastery to Daohai. Daohai was a man of tranquil retirement and supreme conduct; he attended upon [Master] Zhang.
Master De Yuan was quite capable of providing clarifying insights. The Master used skillful means to engage him, making it impossible for him to decline.

Consequently, Hai ascended the seat and preached the Dharma for the fourfold assembly; those from near and far turned toward him in devotion. The Master rejoiced that he had found a worthy successor to whom he could entrust the teachings.

In the second year of the Dà'ān era, he recited three gāthās and passed away while seated. Hai attended to the funeral arrangements with all his heart. On the day of the burial, fifty thousand people came to see him off.
The mournful resonance vibrated with intensity. The Master maintained the purity of his precepts; whether one was noble or lowly, old or young, he treated everyone with equal compassion.

The deeds of his lifelong practice were so numerous that they could not all be recorded. The Master’s reputation for the Way was so exalted and venerable that the people of Zheng during the Liang dynasty revered him as if a Buddha had appeared in the world.
When he returned to the ordination platform, he visited and attended to his uncle, the Duke Wei, while the Duke was still in good health. The Master served him with devoted care.
Kekun attended to every matter, no matter how great or small, personally managing them all without any difference from when he was a śrāmaṇera.
This single practice alone is something difficult for others to achieve; that Hai was able to submit to his teacher was truly because the teacher had moved him.

The Biography of the Great Being Haeyun. He was a native of Ningyuan in Langu, Shanxi. His surname was Song, a descendant of the lineage of Duke Wei. He was born in the *Renxu* year of the Taihe era of the Jin dynasty.
His character was grand and imposing; even in his childhood, he possessed divine insight. At the age of seven, his father taught him the Classic of Filial Piety.
In the "Chapter on Opening the School and Clarifying the Meaning," it says: "What is the school that is opened? What is the meaning that is clarified?

The father was struck with wonder and knew he was no longer a man of worldly toil; he took him to see Master Yan of Fuji. Yan wished to examine his spiritual capacity and gave him the "Song of the Thatched Cottage," which includes the lines:
"Whether it be broken or unbroken, the Master is fundamentally present. The Master asked, "Where is the Master? Yan replied, "Where?"

The Master asked, "As for that which is apart from both the broken and the unbroken, what do you call it? He replied, "This is the guest. The Master asked, "And the host? Yan remained silent and contemplative.
Thereafter, he went to pay his respects to Master Jō of Chūgan-ji and took him as his teacher. At age eleven, he received the full precepts (upasampadā) through the imperial decree of Emperor Enna.

A senior monk named Wōgen asked him, "Now that you have received the great precepts, for what reason do you still act like a novice monk? The Master replied, "It is because the Sangha is small; therefore, the precepts [remain so]."
This was said to emphasize the greatness [of the matter]. The Master asked, "Venerable Elder, are you old or young? The Elder replied, "My body is old.

Before he had finished speaking, the Master shouted loudly, "Cease creating such conceptual distinctions! One day, as the Elder was instructing a monk to leave, the Master struck him once on the back.
Waiting for him to turn his head, the Master held up one finger to point at him. The monk, following the instruction, struck the Master on the back; the Master then immediately held up one finger.
Zuo found this most extraordinary. When the Master was twelve years old, Zhong went to listen as he questioned his teacher.
The teacher instructed him, saying: "What you desire is merely words and language; from now on, cease all of them. Let your body and mind become like withered wood or dead ashes.

When the present moment reaches its ultimate limit and your practice is fully matured, you will awaken to the reality. After one great death, there shall be no lingering breath remaining. Upon reaching that state—
At that moment, with a sudden flash of self-acceptance, one finally meets me. The Master received these instructions reverently. One day, Zhongguan was assisting him;
Zhongguan said, "Master Faden says, 'Look at how busy his affairs are! Tell me, by whose power does he do this?
How do you understand this? The Master gave Zhongguan’s hand a tug. Zhongguan said, "You wild fox spirit! The Master said, "Yes, yes."
When the Master was thirteen years old, Emperor Chenghiz was campaigning throughout the world. The Master was at Ningyuan;
at the moment the city fell, he was ordered from among the crowd to tie his hair in a topknot. The Master replied, "If I follow the state protocol, I shall lose my monastic appearance.
He thus remained as he was. When the Master was eighteen, the Yuan troops recaptured Lan City, and the fourfold assembly fled in search of refuge.
The assembly dispersed. The Master remained alone, attending to Zhongguan, who said, "My years are as ripe as the setting sun, while you are still in the prime of your life.
Now, for both jade and stone to be consumed by fire together—what benefit is there? You may depart. The Master wept and said, "Cause and effect do not err;
death and life are matters of destiny. How could I abandon my teacher in search of deliverance? Even if I were to escape, it would not be the way of a filial son."
[The Master] was indeed mindful. Observing that the Master was sincere and resolute, he instructed him, saying: "In the future, you shall have a great karmic connection in the northern deserts;
I shall cross north with you. The next day, the city surrendered. When the Generalissimo Shi Tianze saw the Master’s dignified bearing, he asked, "Who are you?
He replied, "I am a śramaṇa. Shi asked, "Do you eat meat? He asked, "What kind of meat? Shi replied, "Human [meat]."
[The official] asked about meat. The Master said, "Humans are not beasts. Even tigers and leopards do not eat one another, much less humans.
[The official] said, "Under the edge of weapons today, can one avoid injury? The Master said, "One must certainly rely on external protection. Shi was greatly pleased.

Furthermore, the Commander Li Qijie asked, "Since you have become a monk, are you a follower of Chan or of the Teachings (Dharma)? The Master said, "Chan and the Teachings are both the work of monks."
...the wings and feathers [of the state]. Just as a country employs people, it must necessarily rely on both civil and military talents combined.
Li said, "If that is so, where must one dwell? The Master said, "One dwells in neither. Li asked, "What kind of person are you?
The Master replied, "I am a Buddhist teacher. He added, "My teacher is also here. The two gentlemen saw that the Master was young and felt no fear; they responded—

He found him extraordinary. He immediately went to visit Zhigong of the Middle Way (Zhongguan). Upon hearing his instructions, which were most earnest and profound, he was filled with great joy and said, "A father such as this must surely have a son such as this.
Together they paid homage to Zhigong as their teacher, and they formed with the master a bond as firm as metal and stone.

Thereupon, the King bestowed great honors upon him, inviting him to reside at Hyangchwan-yon in Heungan-sa, and appointed him as the State Preceptor (Junggwon) and Great Zen Master (Dae Seonsa) Jijeong.
The Master was a man of profound stillness and brilliant insight. All his needs were provided by the government.
When Junggwon passed away, the Master went out to beg for food and tended the stupa. One night, he heard a voice in the air calling the Master’s name. The Master looked up...

However, he experienced a realization. He then moved his residence to the Sanfeng Dao-yuan (Three Peaks Monastery). Again asking others for advice, they told him, "The Great Matter is about to be accomplished;

go now. Do not linger here. At dawn, he took up his staff and traveled toward Yan. Passing through Songpu, he encountered rain and stayed overnight beneath a cliff. There, while striking a fire, he attained great enlightenment.
He touched his own face and said, "Only today do I know that my eyebrows are arched and my nose is straight. He believed that the Way pervades the world.
The Old Master did not sleep and spoke thus. Previously, when Zhiguan was about to pass away, the Master asked him, "Upon whom should I rely to resolve this great matter?
Zhiguan replied, "Wait until you are eighty. After the Master entered Yan, he arrived at Daqingshou Monastery.
He then reflected on these words and went directly to visit the Elder Zhonghe, Master Zhang.
One night prior to this, Zhonghe had dreamed that a strange monk, leaning on a staff, walked straight to the abbot’s quarters and sat upon the lion throne.
The next day, when the Master arrived, Zhonghe smiled and said, "This man is the one I dreamed of last night. The Master asked, "I have come without coming; how will you receive me?"
Zhonghe saw him and said, "In this practice, you must practice truly; in this awakening, you must awaken truly. Do not go wandering off into the wilds.

The Master said, "Because of striking the fire and seeing the sparks scatter, I have come to know that my eyebrows are horizontal and my nose is upright. Zhonghe said, "It is different here with me. The Master asked, "How so?
Zhonghe said, "The teeth are a single piece of bone; the ears are two pieces of skin. The Master said, "I thought there was something else. Zhonghe [laughed].

[The Master] said, "Wrong! The Teacher shouted, "The grass-robbers are utterly defeated! Huo, go rest. The next day, Huo again raised the case concerning Linji’s two head monks simultaneously shouting.
The Teacher held up his fist and gave a single clap; at that moment, the meditation hall shook.

Consequently, he received the seal of approval from Zhonghe. Throughout his career, he sat upon great Dharma seats many times, all under the patronage of Grand Masters, kings, and various high officials.
In my master’s quarters, I once used the "Four Statements on Non-reliance" to test students, but not one was able to respond with eloquence.
One day, I encountered several monks in the corridor; I questioned them one after another, but none were in accord with the truth, and they were all struck. Finally, I questioned the last monk.
"Where are you going? The monk said, "I am going to seek out the Master. The Master said, "Why seek him out? The monk said, "I intend to give him a thorough beating.
The Master said, "With what will you strike him? The monk looked around and said, "I will not bring a staff.
The Master struck him four times in succession and said, "You empty-headed fellow! The assembly all fled. The Master called out, "Venerable ones! and the assembly turned their heads.
The Master said, "What is it? In the first month of the Dingyou year, he was conferred the title of State-Protecting Bodhisattva of the Pre-Celestial (Xiantian).
In the winter of the Jihai year, he was appointed to preside over Daekyungsa Temple. In the Renyin year, King Hurbirel invited the Master to his military encampment.

He questioned [the Master] on the general meaning of the Buddha-dharma. The King was greatly delighted and received from the Master the precepts of the bodhicitta. Thereupon, he submitted this memorial:

"The Dharma of our Śākya clan is discussed in the 'Chapter on the Correct Discourse of Royal Law' within the deliberations of the imperial court; its principles are indeed manifest, being neither difficult nor easy.
Yet, I fear that the Sovereign may not be able to implement it in its entirety. Furthermore, it would be appropriate to seek out the great sages and eminent scholars of the empire."
He questioned [the Master] regarding matters of governance, chaos, prosperity, and decline throughout antiquity and the present, and he heard much that was instructive.

The King was greatly delighted and bestowed upon him a pearl-embroidered robe and a seamless great robe of gold brocade. He honored him with the rites due to a teacher. As the Master was about to depart, the King asked, "After you have gone, how shall the Buddha-dharma be upheld?
The Master replied, "Faith is difficult to engender and roots of goodness are difficult to produce; now that they have been produced, you must strive to maintain them."
One must protect and maintain this with single-minded devotion and without forgetfulness. Do not perceive any faults in the Triple Gem.

Constantly mindful that the common people are not at peace, provide them with kind governance, administer rewards and punishments with clarity, exercise authority without partiality, employ the worthy, and accept counsel.

At all times, always practice skillful means; all of this is the Buddha-dharma. After the Master had departed, there was a young man of ill repute who spoke slanderously against the Dharma. The King investigated him and was about to—

He added this to his petition. The special envoy reported it to the Master. The Master replied with a message, saying: "When a bright mirror stands upon its stand, beauty and ugliness appear of their own accord.
