When the divine blade is held in the palm, rewards and punishments are impartial. If right mindfulness is present before you, the external demons of false views may be slain;
yet a sovereign should always take benevolence and forbearance as his heart. The King revered him all the more, and soon thereafter he was commissioned to lead [the army].
The Emperor bestowed ten thousand taels of white silver, whereupon a great assembly was established at Houtian Temple to pray for the blessing of the nation.

When Emperor Mengke ascended the throne, his favor toward the Master was most profound and generous. On the *bing-xia-chen* day, Emperor Xuweilie presented him with a golden staff and a *kāṣāya* robe embroidered with gold threads, requesting words of Dharma for his instruction.
In the seventh month, the Master gathered the elder monks and recorded his remaining possessions.
He appointed someone to manage his affairs for the future. In the summer of the Ding-si year, having finished reciting a verse, the Master said, "You all have been somewhat noisy; I wish to rest.
The attendant monk hurriedly summoned the administrators, but the Master had already passed away peacefully and auspiciously.
His worldly age was fifty-six. After his cremation, countless *śarīra* relics were obtained. King Hubilei erected a stupa for him at Daqingshou Monastery.
Beside the temple, he was posthumously titled the Great Master Foji Yuanming (Buddha-Sun Perfectly Bright). Tracing back to Linji, he was the sixteenth generation.
Yuan Zhengyin (Original True Cause) transmitted [the Dharma] to Zhengyin (True Cause).
He was a native of Jinpu, Renhe County, Hangzhou, and belonged to the Yu clan. He was born in the sixth year of the Jiading era of the Song dynasty; at birth, his skin was purple.
His flesh was of a pure, jade-like quality, shaped like a lotus flower cradling his feet. Beneath his chin was a black mole from which several hairs grew, each over an inch long.

In his childhood, he could foreknow events before they occurred; there were matters he understood naturally without study. At the age of fifteen, he took up the life of a man and was already adept at warding off calamities, with immediate efficacy.
He followed his paternal uncle, Shouchang, and left the household life at Shusheng Monastery, where he practiced asceticism and studied with such diligence that his side never touched the mat.

He remained in his seat for three years, always finding joy in what he heard and saw. When he intended to go out on a journey to seek instruction, Chan Master Xiweng Kan—whose reputation for the Way was shaking the entire monastic community—was at Yuyang, and the Master went there to pay his respects.
At first, the Master Yang refused him, ordering him to sit beneath the meditation platform for a month.
One night, hearing the sound of a thunderclap, he suddenly broke into a sweat all over his body; he felt a sense of exhilaration as if he had shed his old skin.
Clapping his hands, he laughed loudly and said, "So it is, so it is. He entered at once to see the old man, who consented and had him attend upon him as an attendant.

Consequently, he styled himself "Thunderclap" (Pili). Initially, he presided over Xiangfu Temple on Mount Huang in Huizhou. He was a descendant of the various grandsons of the Prince of Xiushou during the Song dynasty.
He was highly esteemed by Cao [Xun]. He was invited to establish a *jinglan* (monastery) on the waters of the Zhe River, and was also requested to take up residence at Baoning Temple in Jiankang;

in both cases, he declined. Shortly thereafter, due to the death of his father, he returned to Jinpu, where he brought his mother into the temple to provide filial care until she reached the end of her natural life.
The Master enjoyed the deepest recognition from Emperor Muling, who bestowed upon him the title of a Preceptor and purple robes. From the imperial princes and members of the royal kinship down to...

Even those in the villages and alleys who believed in the good took refuge [in him], regarding him as a true son of the Buddha. After Hangzhou had returned to the Yuan dynasty, the livelihoods of the people were not yet settled;
the Master provided gruel for the hungry, numbering a thousand per day. On the anniversary of the Buddha’s birth each year, he likewise did so.

He established an unobstructed assembly (*amogha-pūjā*) to universally provide for the posthumous merit of his ancestors. Emperor Shizu (Emperor Taizong) subsequently sought out eminent figures from Jiangnan. The Censor-in-Chief, Mr.

Cui, reported that the Elder of Shusheng Temple in Hangzhou possessed extraordinary virtue; though an invitation was sent, he could not be brought there. The Emperor issued a decree to his attendants to compel him to come to the capital.
Upon being summoned for an audience, he preached the Dharma to the Emperor’s satisfaction. He was subsequently appointed to the Jixian Academy and received exceptionally generous rewards.
Five years later, he announced his retirement and returned to the mountains.

The Emperor conferred upon him the title of Chan Master Yuanming Tongying and issued an edict for the high officials and eminent scholars of the capital to prepare a ceremonial send-off at the main gate of the city to honor his departure. While the Master was in the capital, [he had been treated with such great respect].

In the autumn of the Dinghai year, the floods were severe and the suffering of the starving people was even worse than the previous year. The elders of Hangzhou looked on with longing hope that the Master would return, yet they had not yet been granted their request.
They sent a swift letter urging his disciples to contribute all the funds from their robes and alms bowls to provide sustenance during this time of hardship.
Those whom he saved and brought back to life were exceedingly numerous. Having returned to the mountain, he addressed his disciples, saying:

"I am old, and the maintenance and repairs of the monastic community are in a state of neglect. To empty my purse and exhaust my granary is not what I begrudge; I intend to gather craftsmen and calculate the expenses. You should all work together to plan for this immediately.
The assembly joyfully agreed to listen, and each exerted their utmost effort. Within a few years, the monastery was transformed and resplendent.

However, before long, he manifested illness. He exhorted his disciples with the Way, saying, "I shall depart in twenty-seven days. When the appointed time arrived, he sat upright and passed away in stillness.
His entire body was enshrined in a stupa in the rear garden. His worldly age was eighty-five, and his monastic seniority was sixty-one.
The Biography of Chan Master Yuansou Duan:
Duan’s courtesy name was Yuansou. He belonged to the He clan of Linhai, a family that had been Confucian scholars for generations.

At the age of eleven, he received the tonsure from his paternal uncle, the Venerable Maoshang, at Huacheng Monastery in Yuhang. His temperament and insight were profound and far-reaching; he was filled with a resolute determination to pursue the Way for himself.

Ren renounced worldly life and studied under the elder Chan Master Zang-sou at Mount Jing, where he attained the essential meaning of the Dharma. Subsequently, he served as the Secretary (Ji-shi) to Master Lin of Shi-lin at Jing-ci Monastery.
In the *Gengzi* year of the Dade era, he took up residence at Zi-fu Monastery in Lake District;

his reputation spread throughout the capital, and by imperial decree, he was bestowed the title "Chan Master Hui-wen Zheng-bian. Later, Minister Zhang of the Secretariat for Military Affairs recommended him to reside at Zhong-tian-zhi Monastery.
He subsequently moved to Lingyin Temple. By imperial decree, he was summoned to Mount Jinshan to preside over a Water and Land (Shuilu) vegetarian feast and was commanded to preach the Dharma.

Upon concluding the ceremony, he entered the capital for an audience with the Emperor; his responses were to the Emperor's satisfaction, and he was granted the honorary title "Buddha-Sun Universally Illuminating" (Furi Puzhao).

He returned south and immediately retired, dwelling in a hermitage west of Liangzhu. In the year Renxu of the Zhizhi era, the leaders of the three schools and the fourfold assembly collectively petitioned the Xingxuanzheng Yuan.
He requested that the Master be appointed to the abbotship of Mount Jing; furthermore, he submitted a memorial to the throne requesting an imperial edict to provide protection.

By this time, the Master had received the gift of the gold-embroidered robe three times, which others considered a great honor, yet the Master remained indifferent toward it. He presided over the seat of Mount Jing for thirty years.

He did not step beyond his threshold; his Way was exalted and his virtue profound, such that he was looked up to by all quarters. He occasionally composed poetry and prose, which were pure, transcendent, and elegant in the ancient style.
The elder Lin Shitian resided on Mount Wu, keeping his door closed and refusing visitors;

yet the Master held him in particular esteem and admiration. He once presented the Master with a poem containing the lines: "Able to chant Tianbao verses without abandoning Lingnan Chan. Thus, Shitian truly knew the Master.
If even a poem is known to be held in high esteem, how much more so one who knows the Master as a man of the Way? Formerly, when Xianhu Yan resided at Mount Jing, the Master served as his First Seat.
Every time Yan ascended the Dharma seat, he would cite the account of Emperor Duzong being besieged by the northern troops.
He commanded a Daoist priest to perform a great *zhai* ritual and submit petitions to the celestial court to inquire about matters of great importance to the state.

Master Gao prostrated himself before the petition tablets, yet for a long time no response was received. When the ceremony concluded, he asked for the reason. Master Gao said, "I am currently determining the forty-eighth generation abbot of Mount Jing;
the gates of heaven have not yet opened, which is why the response has been delayed. Yuanjian cited this to show that the office of abbot is no trivial matter. To—
Regarding the forty-eighth generation of abbots, the celestial court had already predetermined him for that position. When the Master heard this, he was somewhat displeased.

When it came time for the Master to succeed to the seat, it coincided exactly with that succession. In the *Xinsi* year of the Zhizheng era, he passed away and was interred in his entirety at Jizhao Monastery.
He was eighty-eight years old.
Chan Master Huiji Xi’s lineage was transmitted by Yuanxi.

His courtesy name was Huiji; he was the son of the Tang family of Yuzhang. His family had followed the Confucian profession for generations. [He studied under] Master Ming of Mount Xishan’s Mingjue Monastery.
The Master was the younger cousin of his paternal uncle. He gathered the youth of his clan to instruct them in the secular classics.
The Master and his elder brother, Yuan-ling, both studied for the jinshi examinations. Once Yuan-ling had passed the examinations, the Master subsequently followed Minggong in shaving his head.

Intending to travel as a wandering monk, his mother secretly prepared silver to provide for his journey. The Master said that wealth is sufficient to ruin one’s will and skillfully declined it; he did not take any with him.
Yiqian traveled on foot and heard that Master Wuchu Guan was propagating the teachings at Yujı. He went there to rely upon him;
from their first conversation, [Wuchu] was struck by his extraordinary nature and kept him in his service. After some time, he visited Dongsou Ying at Nanping, who appointed him as the recorder.

During the Zhìyuán era, the Imperial Commissioner Yang Lianzhenjia, acting on imperial decree, went to retrieve the śarīra relics from Yuyang Temple and personally approached the Master to request a commemorative record.
Regarding the beginning and end of Śāri’s life: he was invited to join [the assembly], but the Master, being young, did not wish to go. Shanyan said, "I have an elderly mother;

whether she survives the war is unknown. He subsequently returned to Jiangxi. Yuanling had previously died while serving as a regional commander at Linjiang, rising up with Wen Tianxiang to fight the enemy.
Only his mother remained in the hall, and the Master served her with such filial piety that it became renowned throughout Yuanzhen.
In his second year, he first entered the world at Baizhang, where he resided for twelve years until the Dharma assembly flourished.
At the beginning of the Dade era, in response to an invitation from Jingci Monastery, the day he entered the temple, officials of the Provincial Administration prostrated themselves to welcome him.

The Master expounded upon the essential tenets of the school, and eminent monks from all quarters gathered like spokes converging on a hub. On the day the retreat began, he ascended the hall for the assembly and made the gesture of tying a cloth bag with his hands.
Nanshan said: "Today, I have finished tying the mouth of the cloth bag. You all, each and every one, must dwell within it with body and mind settled in the wisdom of equality.
Should there suddenly be someone who breaks through the azure void and knocks down Mount Sumeru, do not say that the knot was not tied securely.
After a long silence, he said: "A net spread across the heavens in hundreds of thousands of layers—this is preaching the Dharma with total freedom."
Such were the conventions of his school. After residing there for seven years, he moved to Mount Jing. Shortly thereafter, he took up his staff and returned to Nanping.

When the disciples of Baizhang and Dayang heard that the Master had retired from public life, they vied with one another to welcome him back. Unable to refuse their entreaties, the Master eventually returned to Mount Yang.
Three years later, he passed away at the age of eighty-two. He was buried beneath Golden Cock Rock (Jinji Shi). His disciples...
As for Hang, he enshrined the stūpas of his fingernails and hair at Jingci’s Xiyin. The Master succeeded Wuchu; Chuchu succeeded Beijian;
and Jian was the son of Fozhao. Since the source of this Dharma lineage has such origins, the sense of reverence toward the Master after his passing is all the more profound among those who study.
The Biography of Chan Master Shuisheng.
Shuisheng’s courtesy name was Zhuyuan, and he styled himself the Elder Wuzhu. He was the son of the Fan family from Leping in Raoyang.

At the age of seventeen, he relied upon Master Chang at Luoshan Yuan; although Chang sent him to study under Confucian scholars, the Master constantly practiced *dhyāna* concentration and engaged in needlework and sewing.
Blood flowed from his nose as he was copying the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. [The master] once rebuked him, saying, "Can the study of Confucianism oppose birth and death?
He then fled from Du and went to pay his respects to Master Zhong of Yueting at Jiangshan Mountain. There, he sat upright in a single room, contemplating his three hundred and sixty bones and joints.
The eighty-four thousand pores, as well as the mountains, rivers, and the great earth, were all subsumed within a single thought-moment.

His initial awakening underwent transformation, followed by a state of profound stillness. His two pupils merged into one; though tears flowed from the corners of his eyes, he was not even aware of their sting.
After three or four days, when he saw forms and heard sounds, he remained unshaken despite being gradually shaken and jostled. He then made this vow: "In this life, I am unable..."
"You shall become a Buddha, but you must first enter the Avīci Hell. Those who looked on at the side were so struck with awe that they could not help but gasp in astonishment.

Shortly thereafter, he passed through Mount Kuanglu and stayed at Donglin. Once again, he declared resolutely, "Tonight, I shall surely die upon this rush-mat. Thereupon, he straightened his robes and sat in the full lotus position.
Exerting the power of diligence, when the night reached its deepest and most perilous hour, he cast aside his life and leaped forward in a single bound, unaware of his surroundings.
It was as if he had emerged from a thicket of thorns; the ground beneath his feet suddenly leveled and opened up, while the pale moon in the autumn sky shone alone with exquisite clarity.
Looking back at himself, his body was profound and translucent, with nothing remaining but a single thought that did not fade. Upon returning to the hermitage...

The mountain—its entirety suddenly manifests all at once. While casually reading the words of Miaoxi (Huihong) stating that "awakening the mind and seeing one's nature is not the business of a śramaṇa," I again harbored doubts.
Five years later, I met Master Guzhou Ji at Jiangshan; though we spoke, there was no accord between us.
He went again to Wúwéi and saw Wúnéng Jiàogōng. He recounted Jì’s words to question him, and Wúnéng said, "It is because you do not understand.
The Master suddenly had a great realization; he completely cast off all subtle and wondrous intellectual understandings and reviewed everything he had previously awakened to.
"All of these were merely within a dream; they have no power," [the Master] said, as he patted his back and recorded this, saying: "In the future, you shall greatly propagate my school.
The Master took his leave and traveled east to Mount Tiantong in Mingzhou. Subsequently, he returned to rest at Fuliang.
Having retired to Nan'ao, a member of the local Liu family donated mountain land to construct a *aranya* (monastery) for the Master to dwell in; the site was situated beneath the Five Peaks.
Originally there were five dragon pools; upon hearing that the Master had arrived, they all vanished, shifting away amidst wind and thunder.

In the Jisi year of the Tianli era, an official was dispatched to invite the Master to preside over Miaoguo Temple on West Lake. The Master extensively propagated the fundamental tenets of the school, causing a profound impact throughout the four quarters.
The disciples gathered as one; there were even those who had come from as far as ten thousand *li*.

At that time, the imperial decree for the dispatch of monks was already in effect, so the Master withdrew and returned to his former seclusion at Nanchao. Nevertheless, those who looked up to him with admiration became ever more numerous.

The Prince of Xuangrang of the Imperial Clan repeatedly dispatched envoys to invite the Master, but the Master firmly declined on account of his old age and illness. The *Lianfangshi* (Censor-in-Chief) of Huaixi, Duke Wang Lun, [also sent an envoy].

The Censor-in-Chief Chang Gongdao was particularly devoted to him in his admiration. The Academician of the Jixian Academy, Fu Gongli, and Master Wuyuan, Wu Guncun, maintained a very close extramural friendship with the Master.
Master Wuyuan even expressed a sigh that he had only heard of the Way late in life.
The Master often addressed his disciples, saying: "All those who have shaved their heads and donned the dyed robes ought to penetrate the essence of all Buddhas."
The Heart School consists of the correspondence between practice and realization. By means of the state of correct awakening, one’s numinous awareness illuminates itself.

As the years pass and months deepen, one comes to possess great fearlessness; like a lotus flower reflected in water, it remains undispersed even when touched by ten thousand waves and a thousand ripples.

Only then is one no longer deluded by the demons of birth-and-death or the aggregates. This Master was one who throughout his life truly realized and awakened to this truth; therefore, he also used these words to instruct others.
He was a man of such stature. His master’s conduct was severe and transcendent, possessing the spirit of standing like a wall ten thousand fathoms high.
Guangxin Zhufanyuan once remarked: "Zhu Yuan of Fanyang and Duanya of Wuzhong—these men were like solitary peaks and overhanging cliffs;

they could be gazed up at from afar, but could not be climbed. This was considered a truthful assessment. In the fourth month of the summer of the Dinghai year of the Zhizheng era, he summoned the fourfold assembly.
He exhorted them with strict discipline. Taking paper upon his knees, he wrote a verse and passed away while sitting upright.

On the night before his burial, there was a light like a bolt of silk descending from the horizon, illuminating everything and interlacing in a continuous stream. Before long, it spread across the summits of the five peaks and then converged back into the stupa.
This continued for three nights before ceasing. The residents of Chao, numbering in the tens of thousands over several dozen *li*, gathered to witness it in astonishment.
He was a man of exceptional character. His worldly lifespan was seventy-two years, and his monastic seniority (*saṃgha-rakṣā*) was fifty-three years.
One, Master Rūgong, recorded this based on the transmission from Master Dàgōng of Bényuán.
He was a native of Fúmiǎn. When the Yuan troops descended upon Jiangnan, the Master was young and was captured by marauding soldiers. They brought him to Lín...
He was abandoned and departed. A wealthy man of the Hu clan took him in and raised him, enjoining him to study with the children of his household at a local village school.

Whenever there was a lecture on the scriptures, he would focus his mind and listen with profound stillness; he silently grasped the teachings without forgetting anything. Master Hu watched him and was delighted.
When the boy had grown up, Hu sent him to the Wuxiang Temple in the district to become a monk, where he studied under Master Gaofeng of Yunfeng.

The Duke [resided] at Mount Jing; there he received the imperial decree. The Master was strict and rigorous in his observance of the precepts; his dharma robes and ritual implements never left his person. He first took up residence at Wanshou Temple in Zhejiang.
Later, a prominent member of the Huang family, who deeply revered the Master’s spiritual conduct, regularly provided him with *iṣvāsa* (vegetarian) meals.
One day, he invited the Master to his home, where his offerings became even more diligent. Thereupon, he opened his private treasury and showed the gold he had stored away.
The jade was brilliantly radiant. The Master wished to move his heart with it, but the man looked at him and smiled.
The Master said to those around him, "That Huang family showed me treasures from their treasury, wishing to entice me to die and become their son.
They do not realize that I regard these things as mere dung and soil. How many have fallen into this trap in antiquity? It is not only for the sake of their sons; it is for their—"
It is said that oxen and horses possess horns; I personally consider this to be the case with the Huang clan.

At the beginning of the Tianli era, Master Xiaoyin of Central India received an imperial decree to open the great Longxiang Monastery, and consequently recommended three individuals from Zhongtian to serve as its successive abbots.
The Emperor personally inscribed the master’s name, and the Xuanzheng Yuan issued an official decree to formally invite him. At the time of his passing, there were many miraculous signs. Shanda (字:
Benyuan), a native of the Chai family of Xianju, traveled as a pilgrim in his youth with Master Jin’an Xin.
Possessing lofty aspirations, his insight surpassed that of all quarters. He visited Xueyan at Dayang, where he joined the assembly without seeking formal instruction. Later, he ascended...
He entered the chamber of Yunfeng at Shuangjing. After a long time, he received the seal of approval. The Master’s character was transcendent;
in his self-discipline and conduct, he became even more earnest as he grew old. Baoning, Jingci, and Jingshan were all great centers of the Way within the realm.

The Master visited them in succession, bringing order to the monastic communities and leading the assemblies with such success that his achievements are well worth recording. His private quarters remained simple and austere.
Outside the round cushion, there was not a single thing; at night, he would sit alone by a solitary candle, burning incense until dawn, making this his constant practice.
Furthermore, his physical constitution differed from that of others: in severe cold he wore fine linen, and in great heat he wore silk and wool.
With his remaining resources, he established the Dayuan Monastery on a mountain halfway along the eastern road as a small retreat for his fellow practitioners to eat and rest.
At the place where he rested, one day he gathered the assembly; having finished recounting the matters of his lifelong travels, he passed away suddenly and silently.
Both masters emerged from the school of Yunfeng and both possessed extraordinary character; they were truly brothers in the Way.
The Biography of Chan Master Hengchuan Gong:
Gong’s courtesy name was Zipu. He was the son of Lin Chushi of Yongjia, who married the daughter of Kang Gong Pizu, an official of the Court of Imperial Clan Affairs, and raised three sons;
the Master was the youngest. He was born in the Renwu year of the Song Jiading era (1222). When the Chushi [his father] saw the Master as an infant...
Gu was solitary and strict in his purity, abstaining from meat; he was difficult to sustain within the ways of the mundane world.
His younger uncle, who had become a Chan monk named Zhengze, took him as a novice at the age of fifteen. After receiving the precepts, Gu immediately set out on a pilgrimage.
Initially, he followed Shitian at Lingyin; when Chijue arrived there, Gu remained with him. However, he ultimately found no entry due to lingering doubts and obstacles. Upon hearing of Tianmu...
Chan Master Liri’s assembly at Taibai was very large. [Zhao] went there to cast off his doubts; Zhao examined him to see if he could receive the transmission.

He raised the examples of "the bamboo shoots of Nanshan" and "the cuttlefish of the Eastern Sea. As the Master prepared to respond, Zhao struck him with his palm. Thereupon, the Master suddenly attained realization and remained as an attendant.
At Guoqing, Duango, Mingyan, Jin, Kenke, and Qiu Zangzhu all recognized the Master's worth. When Duango moved to Jingci, he appointed the Master as...
The first seat-holder, Qiao, once remarked, "The first seat-holder possesses both practice and realization; he is fit to serve as a model for high ministers.

Thereupon, he appointed the Master to lead Lingyan Chan Temple on Mount Yan, where the Master preached the Dharma as a successor to Tianmu. The Master was distressed by the corruption of the ancestral teachings and the distortion of ancient echoes.
He was stifled by the constraints of what was permissible and impermissible, yet he did not hesitate to distinguish between right and wrong.

In his expositions and praises, he was invariably as lofty and prominent as a towering cliff, striving for originality to outshine the ancients; he never yielded to the common preferences of the vulgar or avoided what they disliked. His eloquence was so powerful and self-assured as this.
Yet, when conversing with others, he would whisper with a quivering mouth, stammering and not daring to speak out; to the observer, he appeared to be a person of humble and docile character.

He gathered his followers with sincerity, employing no methods of bit, bridle, or forceful restraint. Sometimes they would argue face-to-face or resist him with insolence, and those listening by the side were all filled with indignation;
yet the Master never punished them, instead gathering them in and polishing them further, so that they did not take his opposition as a cause for resentment.

At first, people found him lacking in authority, but after a long time, they came to cherish him. He was subsequently appointed to the position of Abbot at Nengren Temple during the disturbances of the Bingzi year.
He then returned to his quarters for tending the cattle and, feigning illness, remained confined to bed, refusing all visitors.

In the twentieth year of the Yuan era, an imperial decree was suddenly issued appointing the Master as the abbot of Guangli Chan Temple at Mount Yuwang. The Master stared in astonishment, claiming it was not for him; after months of hesitant refusal, he finally accepted.
It was likely that there were memorial petitions submitted to the Emperor that were not disclosed; the same applied to his relocation to Nengren Temple.

Since the public selection of monks had fallen into disuse, positions were sought through personal influence; yet the Master always arrived of his own accord, which contemporary opinion esteemed as an honor. Having thus established the lineage and occupied the ancestral seat, the Master...
He suppressed the studies of his time; as the years passed and he matured, he gained the admiration and faith of others.

At a time when the Dharma was in decline and many great teachers had passed away, students had nowhere else to turn and thus all gathered around him. Consequently, in his later years, his reputation for both learning and character resounded far and wide, shaking the entire world.
Yet, the Master never relied upon or clung to such fame and praise, nor did he treat minor matters with negligence or contempt, even regarding things as humble as tiles, kilns, wood, or plants.

Regarding the broths, pickles, pungent and salty flavors, and even the fragments of food, he was one upon whom the multitude relied; he surely exhausted his thought and effort, such that there were always traces of his work to be observed and recounted.
After six years, he retired. In the year prior to his retirement, he built a hut by the side of Zangxue Temple, calling it "This Hut.
As he approached death, he said, "I shall depart tomorrow morning. He returned to his seat, wrote a parting message for the assembly, and passed away.

He was sixty-eight years old, in the third month of the twenty-sixth year of the Zhizhi era. His character was simple; outwardly he had few adornments, while inwardly he was composed and free from distraction.

He was able to maintain a steady composure, remaining unchanged in the face of anger, joy, resentment, or affection. In his later years, he resided at Nengren and Yuyang Monasteries, where his Way shone even more brightly.
Fearing that his teachings might not be transmitted, the Master diligently exhorted others through lectures, never tiring of his post, and refusing the company of those who sought leisure.

[The Master’s] mind was such that even when pressed by circumstances, he would respond with joy; he avoided and discarded [worldly things] as if they were mere hairs or chaff, and he harbored not even a hair’s breadth of resentment toward those who advanced or retreated against him.
The disciple [received] the final instructions and interred the Master’s entire body in a stupa.

The Master himself had previously composed a stupa inscription and words of parting for the assembly, which, along with his recorded teachings, were compiled into a catalogue. Shi Yuanzhi of Gao’an wrote a preface and circulated them.
The Biography of Chan Master Zhuxianlin Chuanfalin. His alternative name was Liaohan.
He was the son of the Huang family from Ninghai, Taizhou. He left home to become a monk under Master Tong Tairu.
Upon contemplating the words of Muzhou, he attained realization. He visited Yuansou at Zhongzhu, where he thoroughly penetrated the depths of his own being. Dongyi was at Jingci Temple.
He invited [Zhao] to share half his seat; their discourse was so profound and awe-inspiring that it evoked the style of the great masters of antiquity.

Zhuyuan, while at Fushan, encountered the Master’s words of exhortation and praised them incessantly, subsequently extolling him with a verse that said: "Among a multitude of five hundred, he dwells as the foremost."
Regarding the phrase "one of wondrous understanding, fit to be a teacher of devas and humans," he resided in the Meng Hall for nine years without stepping outside the door.
Provincial Governor Tuohan invited him to preside over Wansu Temple, after which he moved to Zhongzhu. In the fourth year of the Zhiyuan era, he took charge of Lingyin Temple;

Emperor Shun bestowed upon him a golden-embroidered Dharma robe. At that time, Jizhao was at Mount Jing; father and son were simultaneously propagating the Way, and the people of Mount Wu all praised them.
Considering this a great honor, the Xingyuan Court sent gifts to offer him a seat at their assembly. The Master firmly declined; however, the messengers returned repeatedly without ceasing.
The Master then withdrew to Mount Kuaiji. When the Xingyuan Court realized he could not be compelled, they instead requested that he take charge of Lingyin Monastery.
Not long after, he retired to Liaohan Hermitage. In the spring of the fifteenth year of the Zhizheng era, he was stricken with illness and gathered his disciples to address them.
He recounted the details of his life from beginning to end and further admonished them, saying: "The decline of the Buddha-dharma has never been more severe than it is today.

You should each exert yourselves; my karmic ties to this world have ended here. He wrote a verse, which said: "Seventy-two years, driving stakes into empty space; the final phrase—unspeakable, unspeakable. Suddenly, he passed away.
His remains were kept in the funeral chamber for ten days, during which time his countenance did not change. He was then interred in full.
The stupa stands to the west of Songyuan’s [Songyuan Xiancheng] stupa. Before the stupa is an ancient cassia tree; when spring arrives, it blooms, its fragrant scent filling the road.
Those who see it marvel at the wonder. Huang Jinqing, the Attendant Lecturer and Scholar, witnessed this event himself and recorded it within the inscription for the stupa.

Yiguan Chuan Zhengquan, whose courtesy name was Yiguan, was the son of the Fang family of Fanyang. Initially, he studied under Huiji; his discourse was already transcendent and beyond the mundane, and Huiji nodded in approval, granting him a seat by the bright window.
From then on, various masters of Chan and the doctrinal schools vied to invite him with letters, wishing to have him emerge [from seclusion].

The Undersecretary [Liu] Kui did not follow him. At that time, Yuanxiao Duan was preaching the Dharma at Mount Jing; people revered him as the contemporary Miaoxi (Wuzu Fayan). Kui then went to follow him.
As soon as he entered the gate, the Master let out a fierce shout like the crash of thunder. All his attachments and fetters were instantly cast off, and he immediately prostrated himself.
The Master asked, "What have you truly seen? After several rounds of question and answer, all of which satisfied the Master's mind, [Kui’s realization was confirmed].
Looking to his left and right, he said, "This man is one of those in the stage of Prajñā. He was subsequently enrolled as a disciple and returned to serve in the office of the attendant;

later, he was promoted to the position of Record Keeper. Afterwards, he emerged from seclusion at Chongyin Monastery in Jinling. The Imperial Preceptor, recognizing his worth, conferred upon him the title "Buddha-Sun Universal Illumination" (Furi Puzhao).
The *New Gazetteer of Mount Jing* states that [Zhi] Kui saw this in the biography of Song Lian, yet it does not actually appear in Song’s collected works.

Furthermore, regarding the title of Imperial Preceptor bestowed upon him, it was the same as that given to Yuqi Chushi; Chushi was also a dharma successor of Yuansou, whose lineage filled the land under the Yuan dynasty.
There is no doubt that [the entry for] Kui exists [somewhere], but I do not know upon what source the new gazetteer relies. For now...
Recorded for reference. Regarding the transmission from Miaoyuan to Miaoyuan:

He was the son of the Chen family of Xiangshan in Yuezhou. Having received the full precepts and observed the directions [of the Dharma], he attained realization upon encountering the right conditions. He saw the stream of monks...
Chasing after external objects and abandoning the Way, his distress was manifest on his countenance. He said, "I cannot endure the toil of worldly dust;

how can my mind be restrained? I wish to practice humble tasks to subdue it. He resided at Tianning Temple in his home province. During a great famine, he went barefoot from door to door begging for alms to support the community.
His master, Xutang Yugong, refused to bow before the Prime Minister Wu Qian. Wu Qian became enraged and imprisoned him.

The abbot treated him with contempt and humiliation, yet the Master served him with the utmost reverence. Whenever he had doubts, he would inquire, and the abbot would provide explanations according to his questions.

After a long time, he attained a state of total clarity. One day, while at the empty hall, the abbot snapped his fingers and said, "Yuanhu! You have now reached the Great Peace. Later, when Xutang resided at Mount Jing, his years were already advanced;

he appointed the Master as the head of the assembly. Disciples stood like a forest beneath the administrative quarters, and as the Master analyzed the subtle and elucidated the wondrous for them, he gained great mastery over Xutang.
At the Xutang Monastery, Xutang said, "Could you not emerge once more to benefit others? He then vigorously supported Master Pingjiang Jianyan, never neglecting either internal or external affairs.
He was nominated for the positions of Gushan and Guoqing, but declined both; he did, however, accept the position at the Shuilu Monastery in Quanzhou.

As his reputation grew as eminent as a sacrificial offering, people’s faith and admiration for him increased all the more. He said with a somber expression, "I would rather not remain here for long. Taking up his staff, he prepared to return home.

Those who knew him further discussed the matter of settling at Shuiding (Water-Determined). They said, "Master Yuan’s conduct is firm and his reputation lofty; if we entreat him with sufficient effort, he will certainly not decline.

Using someone with whom he had a prior connection to convey their intent, they succeeded in persuading him. He came with joy, and the fame of his Way grew even more widespread. Some, however, [said]: [Note: The provided text ends abruptly. The translation reflects the portion available.]
A question was raised regarding the similarities and differences between Confucianism and Buddhism. The Master said: "Both are alike in being moved by external things;

it is the Han Confucians who have erred, and from that point on, differences arose. Confucianism takes the cultivation of others as its study, while Buddhism takes the cultivation of the mind as its study.

Although their outward manifestations differ in whether they cultivate others or the mind, their underlying Way has never been different. When people became excessively extravagant, the Master admonished them, saying: 'Regarding emolument...'"
If one diminishes [worldly attachments], blessings will increase; why not simply be cautious? Clad in plain robes and iron-like garments, he sat like a corpse all day long.
Yet his speech was penetrating and swift, rushing like lightning across a deep ravine, impossible to restrain. When he slightly withdrew and composed himself, in an instant he would be at his desk.
Zen practitioners looked up to him, and scholars took him as their model. He was refined in poetry, yet refused to display it outwardly. His former residence was in Yue...

At Yunzheng, as he was about to pass away, he expressed his wish to be released from the waters of meditative concentration so that he might return [to the world]. He further instructed that no stupa be built for him and that he not be cremated, but allowed to decay naturally.
His disciples could not bear this and ultimately buried him. This was in the eighteenth year of the Zhiyuan era. He was seventy-five years of age at the time of his death.
The Biography of Chan Master Tie-shan Qiong:

Chan Master Qiong was born with an innate awareness of the Buddha-dharma. At eighteen, he took leave of his parents to serve the Buddha; at twenty-two, he shaved his head and donned the monastic robes.
He traveled to Shi-shuang to study under Master Xiang-an, where he practiced the contemplation of the "white at the tip of the nose. His body and mind became pure. Suddenly—
There was a monk who came from Xueyan to inquire about the character and style of Chan Master Daqin. That very day, he set off with his satchel slung over his shoulder.

Xueyan instructed him to single-mindedly uphold the "Mu" (No) koan. The master practiced accordingly; on the fourth night, sweat flowed from his entire body, and a sense of clarity and refreshment was beyond description.
Later, upon meeting Master Miaogong of Gaofeng, he finally attained a state where his practice became continuous and solid. Subsequently, he visited Mount Meng. There, the Master asked:

"To what stage of Zen practice have you reached? This is the point where the work is finished. Unable to answer, he entered the room several times to offer his insights, yet each time it was said that something was still lacking.

One day, seeing the *Sixin Ming* (Inscription on Faith in Mind) by the Third Patriarch, which states, "Returning to the root, one attains the essential; following illumination, one loses the source," he suddenly attained realization.
He presented this to Master Shanshan, who said, "Another layer has been peeled away. For the most part, this matter is like peeling the layers of a pearl."
It is as if the more one peels away, the more it becomes clear and pure. To peel it once surpasses the effort of many lifetimes.
Nevertheless, my phrasing was still merely lacking something. One day, while in meditative absorption, I suddenly encountered the character "lacking" (quàn).

My body and mind were suddenly enlightened, penetrating to the very bone and marrow, like accumulated snow suddenly clearing under a bright sun. Unable to restrain my joy, I leaped down from the meditation seat and seized him.
Mount Yun said, "What am I lacking? Yun struck him three times with his palm. The Master bowed.

Yun said, "It is fortunate that after many years you have finally reached this point; today you have at last completed it. Later, while residing at Tienshan on Mount Nanyue, he burned incense for Xueyan, saying:
"The Master did not fail me; it was truly I who failed the Master. It was because I left the Master too early that I have only today come to see the Master's true functioning.
For the Master to leave the mundane world and act for the sake of others is no small matter; though he dwelt in a grass hut on a solitary peak, his influence pervaded the entire world.
Thus, the Way of the Dharma did not flourish [as it might]. Some say that the Master’s conduct of the Way was 'unprovoked,' as the Master Zhongfeng Ben of Silla once remarked."
The three trainings of precept, concentration, and wisdom act as a vast net spread across the heavens;

cast once into the east, amidst the whale-waves of ten thousand *li*, it causes both the monastic and lay communities of the Kingdom of Goryeo to boil with agitation from top to bottom, rushing back and forth.

Regarding Master Doo-gwang, the master who ordained him: there is a separate portrait of the teacher that has been handed down, showing him with short hair reaching his forehead, looking back with a towering air.
Yet his beard was shorn and his complexion was as wan as a vegetable. He has a work titled *Pǔshuō* (A General Discourse), the phrasing and meaning of which are incisive and poignant;
he is truly a banner of light for the final age. Standing alone like a wall, his singular style does not fall behind that of the ancients.

Jingri transmitted the Dharma to Jingri, who was styled Dongyan. He lived as a layman in Duchang, Nankang, and belonged to the Liao clan. From childhood, he abstained from meat; he sustained himself on vegetables and fruit.
At fifteen, he requested permission from his parents to shave his head at Xianglin on Mount Lu. He possessed a broad back and a tall stature, and his physical appearance was magnificent.
Yao traveled to Yangshan and Shichuang to seek the Way, and subsequently entered Zhejiang to visit Chijue. After two summer retreats there, he found no resonance with him.

He then went to Mount Jing to see Wuzhun, who highly approved of him. Later, he visited Xiyuan Hui at Tiantong; Hui was a great disciple of Wuzhun, and his instructions were entirely based on those of Wuzhun.
His critical insights were so swift and sharp that one could not perceive him either welcoming or resisting; his influence ceased like the subsiding of a wind.
Shuixi’s mind became clear and settled; he subsequently entered into a profound harmony with the Master’s intent and finally submitted to his guidance. The Master appointed him to guard the library.

Later, when Wumen Can was inaugurated as the abbot, Shuixi was invited to serve as the First Seat. Can was also one who emerged as a preeminent Chan master; through this, Shuixi’s reputation grew even more prominent.
During the Jingding era of the Song dynasty, the Regional Commander of Jiangdong, Wang Lixin—who was extremely discerning in his endorsements—recommended him to preside over the Yuan Tong Monastery.
He succeeded to the abbacy of Donglin. In the *Renchen* year of the Zhizhi era (1292), he was transferred to Yuyang. Not long after, he retired to live in seclusion at Xuedou.

In the *Gengzi* year of the Dade era (1300), by general consensus, he was appointed as the abbot of Tiantong. The Master’s conduct was lofty, pure, and complete; his speech was gentle and his demeanor harmonious, such that the assembly was increasingly able to draw close to him.

He accepted his disciples to enable them to clarify their nature and restore its original state. He did not indulge in flowery rhetoric, but instead untied the entanglements of their delusions. Thus he dwelt there...

In this world, even if one performs no active deeds, those far and near will look up to and admire them; blessings follow such a person without being sought. Yet, among these, his merit regarding Tiantong was most prominent.
Having resided at Donglin for a long time, he inspired the common people and the masses, who vied with one another to paint his likeness as an act of devotion.

Consequently, when he established Tiantong, the people of Mount Lu offered their wealth to assist him in great abundance. He was born in the year of Xinsi, the fourteenth year of the Jiading era of the Song dynasty.
In the first year of the Daye era, the wu-shen year, at the age of eighty-eight and with seventy-one years since his ordination, he was about to manifest his passing.
He exhorted his disciples and wrote verses in rhythmic meter to show them, saying: "Heaven is the canopy and earth is the casket;
what need have I for stupas or hermitages? Let my bones turn to ash within the mountains and rivers; once my words are spoken, do not engrave them. Two days later, he bathed.
He passed away sitting upright. Upon his transformation, his tooth roots remained undecayed and were enshrined at Qingfengwu on the western cliff.
