The Chapter on Practicing Dhyāna, composed by the Śramaṇa Minghe of Huashan Monastery in Wujun during the Ming Dynasty;
the original was transmitted by Zhimei.
Zhimei (To-Mei). Shihu was his style name. He was the son of the Bi family of Jinling. From birth, he was exceptionally brilliant and refined, possessing no desire for worldly affairs.
He entered the monastic life at Chongmu Monastery; during the Xianchun era of the Song dynasty, he received ordination and ascended to the rank of full precept-holder.

Disregarding worldly conventions, he applied himself with keen resolve to visiting great masters. Yujian Ying, Yunfeng Gao, and Yuepo Ming were all eminent patriarchs within the realm, and he studied under them all.

He occupied the seat of the foremost disciple. Day after day, he engaged in debate and refinement with many eminent practitioners amidst the whistling of the celestial winds and the cold pipes of nature, vowing to continue until his original resolve was fully realized.
Finally, he met Master Wuwen Chuan at Jingci Monastery. Master Chuan practiced the ancient Way with vigor, preserving its formal traditions;
there, dragons and elephants galloped side by side and the monastic groves flourished. The Master devoted himself wholeheartedly to him.

He thoroughly investigated the origins and depths [of the teachings]. In the Dinghai year of the Zhizhi era (1267), the Metropolitan Commander issued a formal document to summon the Master to preside over the Shuangta Temple in Wu.

He offered incense as a tribute to Wuwen, thereby acknowledging his own spiritual lineage. Not long after, he was transferred to Santasi Temple in Jiahe. At that time, Santasi had been in ruin for a long period;

while the Master provided instruction in his leisure time, he was dedicated to restoring what was dilapidated and repairing what was broken, with the resolve to plant the withered and raise up the fallen.
He newly constructed the Yangmeng Hall to accommodate future eminent guests; as the construction of timber and earthworks flourished, the inner and outer structures became magnificent.
Since the temple’s assets had long been depleted, he acquired over five hundred mu of fertile land to enrich the monastic provisions.

He established a "Longevity Treasury" to collect monthly interest, using the proceeds for the community to perform incense-offering rites on the first and fifteenth days of the month to pray for the Emperor, and to provide funds for the carving and restoration of one thousand volumes of the Tripitaka.

Regarding the sacred images of the Buddha and the missing records of the temple, these were fully restored by the Master. He built a residence on the eastern side of the monastery and inscribed its plaque with the name "Huànxiū" (Cultivation of Illusion), as if intending to spend the remainder of his life there.
However, having received an imperial decree, he was appointed to reside at Lingyan in Pingjiang, and subsequently moved to Yongfu in Poyang, and then to Yuyang in Siming.
In the year Xīn-wèi of the Zhìshùn era, he was again summoned from Jingci in Hangzhou. Wherever he went...
He was diligent and tireless in propagating the Way, taking its establishment as his personal responsibility without the slightest laxity.

One day, he summoned his disciples to instruct them on his final affairs and entrusted them to Huànxiū, further directing that those who were truly worthy of the name of a "Fourth Dhyāna" practitioner should be placed in that position. He sat in silence until noon the following day, when he passed away peacefully.

He was seventy-four years of age. Commentators remarked that the Master’s conduct was rigorous yet simple, and his deportment in both public and private life was upright and composed. Thus it was said...
From beginning to end, there is no inconsistency; it is indeed a truthful record.
Zu Ming’s Biography:
Zu Ming, styled Guding, was the son of Ying Shi of Fenghua. From childhood he was exceptionally intelligent and did not consume meat. As he grew older, he studied...

He was well-versed in the texts of the hundred schools of thought, yet he took particular delight in the Buddhist scriptures. At the age of eighteen, weary of dwelling in the mundane world, he followed Master Xigong of Jinge to study the supramundane Dharma.
At twenty-five, he received ordination and the full precepts. He then traveled through various regions, first relying on Master Tanxi of Zhuxi and serving as his secretary.
He subsequently journeyed to Fujian and Zhejiang, visiting many teachers for inquiry, yet found none with whom he reached accord. At that time, during the Yuan...
The Elder was at Lingyin; the Master went there to pay his respects. Upon hearing a single word from him, he immediately became free of all doubt and obstruction.

After some time, he reached the innermost depths of the Elder’s teaching, and his reputation for virtue soon spread far and wide. Those with whom he associated were all men of refined renown, such that their coming and going weighed heavily upon the monastic community.
Yet the Master remained increasingly humble and self-effacing. When someone arrived to welcome him with a carriage and attendants, he would simply decline them.
He completely rejected all [such offerings], accepting only a staff and sandals.

In the first year of the Yuansheng era of Emperor Shundi, when the Master was fifty-four years old, he first departed from Mount Jing and took up residence at Longjiao in Changguo. Students did not mind the perilous journey and vied with one another to seek admission beneath his seat.
Eight years later, he moved to Putuo. The Eastern Zhejiang Regional Commander-in-Chief, Duke Wanhaerdou, possessed great—

He resounded throughout the seas. When the Master arrived, [the ruler] treated him with the utmost reverence. Japanese merchant vessels, having repeatedly received imperial mandates, brought abundant gold and silk to pay their respects;

however, the Master always declined and withdrew from them. Not long after, he moved to Central India (Zhong Tianzhu). In the seventh year of the Zhengting era, he returned to preside over Mount Jing.
While the Master was at Central India, there was a youth surnamed Qiu who followed him, carrying his traveling bag and sunshade, and stayed overnight at his lodging.
At Chengtian Temple in Suzhou, he saw a precious cauldron in the sky, with celestial deities guarding it on all sides, as if announcing:
"The Heavenly Emperor has returned this cauldron to Mount Jing. The next morning, he went to verify the matter with the temple monks.
They said, "This must mean that Master Guding is to be reinstated at Mount Jing. Consequently, he accompanied them there to seek employment.
Shortly thereafter, the imperial decree for Mount Jing arrived; those who heard it marveled at it.
Because of the flourishing of the Master’s Dharma seat, the court conferred upon him the title Chan Master Huixing Wenmin Hongxue Pujie. In the eleventh year, the rebellion of Ying Hao broke out.

The Master established Miaoming Hermitage on the banks of the Fangsheng Pond (Pond for Releasing Living Beings), saying, "I shall grow old here. In the seventeenth year, Hangzhou was again struck by military conflict.
The Master retired to live in a hermitage. After several more months, the Miao tribesmen set fire to and plundered Mount Jing.

The Chancellor, Daśī Tīmūr, invited the Master to enter Yunju Hermitage. In his leisure time, he would visit the Master to inquire about the Way, his requests for instruction becoming increasingly earnest.

One day, while the Master was requested to look over the scriptures, he merely sat in silence. The official asked, "Why does the Elder not look at the scriptures? The Master replied, "I am merely counting the lines."
"Is Master Mo reading the sutras? The official had no reply. The Master turned the sutra and said, "I, this old monk, am reading the sutras; I am going to read the sutras.
The official covered the sutra with his hand and said, "Please explain it to me. The Master asked, "Who were Yi Yin and the Duke of Zhou?

Thereupon, the official attained realization. Shortly thereafter, he manifested a slight illness. He changed his robes, sat upright, and sent a letter to the Chancellor, entrusting him with the protection of the Dharma.
Regarding the intent of the Buddha-dharma, he suddenly pointed and said to his disciples, "Avalokiteśvara’s golden platform has arrived;
the merit I have cultivated throughout my life has borne fruit. He then wrote a verse in large characters: "Life and death are pure and true; The great void is pure and full.
In seventy-nine years, The cradle's rope has snapped. Having finished writing, he cast aside his brush and passed away. His body remained for seven days, his countenance unchanged.

The funeral rites were conducted according to the prescribed protocol for high officials of the provincial and prefectural governments. A sacrificial table was set out along the road, and the cremation took place.

His tongue, his rosary, and other remains remained unburnt; five-colored lights appeared, and countless *śarīra* relics were obtained. Stupas were erected at Mount Jing, Longjiao, Putuo, and Qingshan.
Four volumes of his recorded sayings (*yulu*) and several volumes of his external collections have been transmitted to the world. The Master’s temperament was straightforward and expansive.
He was simple and did not adorn himself with external trappings. In his dwelling and daily usage, he maintained a life of pure austerity and detachment.
From the time he rose in the morning to wash his face and bathe, he never employed servants for such tasks. From his youth until old age, he never rested even for a moment.

He cultivated the practice of purity by performing one thousand prostrations before the Avalokiteśvara image every day; yet, regarding the Great Dharma, he penetrated its profound mysteries and provided direct, incisive instruction with great vigor.
His responses were versatile and his adaptability was inexhaustible. Although his pedagogical approach was rigorous and formidable, he never failed to temper it with leniency;

according to the innate capacities of his disciples, he primarily guided and nurtured them through compassion until they reached full maturity. As for literature, this was the hereditary vocation of the Master’s family.
Among his contemporaries were Yuan Wenching Gong Yue of the village, Hu Changru of Jinhua, Huang Gong Ming, and Yu Wenjing Gong Ji of Shu County.
Changsha’s Master Ouyang Xuan praised and admired him; those who have seen his writings can all verify this.
(The Bodhisattva Fuguang, appended) Xian-du (First Vision), style name Wujian, surnamed Ye, was of a prominent lineage from Xianju in Tiantai. He was born during the Song dynasty’s Xian... [year].
Chun was of refined character and exceptional intelligence. From childhood, he abstained from meat and strong flavors and delighted in reading; whatever he saw once, he could recite by heart.

His parents had long hoped that he would establish a family through the study of Confucian learning. It happened that the śramaṇa Dongzhou Shan encountered him and recognized his potential, saying, "This is a vessel of the Dharma;
he should not be detained in the countryside. His parents consented, and he followed the Venerable Hou of Gutian to receive the tonsure and enter the monastic order. Immediately—
He traveled extensively to seek instruction, visiting Master Zangshi Chen at Tianfeng and Master Fangshan Bao at Xian’an on Ruiyan.
Although he attained a degree of realization through his interactions with these two masters, he had not yet reached the ultimate state. Consequently, he built a hermitage atop Mount Huading.
He applied himself with diligent austerity. One day, while engaged in manual labor, he experienced a sudden awakening; his lifelong stagnation was instantly dissolved like ice.

He then went to the western hermitage to present his realization. The Master [Zhaoqing] confirmed it for him with a verse. He took his leave and returned to Huading Peak, which the Master could not retain him from staying.
Huading Peak is high, cold, secluded, and remote; no one else can dwell there for long, yet the Master remained seated there for forty years.
His feet never once crossed the threshold of his quarters. Within his study, he constructed the Śāla Pavilion to instruct and guide students.
Dream Hall Master E’s preface states: "During the Zhiyuan and Dade eras, Chan Master Wujian Du propagated the Way of Master Baoshan Bao in the southeast.
Consequently, the elite and talented of the realm, those of lofty integrity and noble companionship, as well as the heroic and eminent..."
Those of eminent caliber, hearing his reputation, felt their spirits soar; beholding his traces, they submitted their hearts.

Without exception, they bound their satchels upon their shoulders and wrapped their feet in straw mats, enduring hunger and thirst, braving cold and heat, their forms crowding together like shadows following one another, hastening to his presence.

As for the Meditation Master, he would exhale warm breath upon them and instruct them, yet subsequently scold and rebuke them; he would rely upon them and treat them with haughtiness, yet subsequently comfort and show compassion toward them. Thus they flew [to him].
Above, I snare him with my fletched arrows; below, I ensnare him with my nets. I care only for his capture;
why should I worry about the toil of shooting or setting traps? When metal is forged, the vessel is formed; when wood is carved, the material is realized.

Thus, it is fitting that he should cast aside glory and splendor to savor the simple and plain, abandon cleverness to return to the pure and unadorned, and submit with effortless grace. This is the way of the disciple.

There was no contradiction among these accounts. On the fifteenth day of the fifth month of the first year of the Yuanyuan era (corresponding to the wuxiu year), he sent a letter to his fellow practitioners, recited a verse, and passed away while sitting in the lotus posture.
Upon cremation, white milk flowed forth like a stream, and the *śarīra* relics accumulated and formed five colors.
He was interred in the western section of the monastery; he was posthumously titled Zhenguang (True Enlightenment), and his stupa was named Jiguang (Tranquil Light).

His disciples compiled his dharma discourses, verses on sudden enlightenment, and other writings into a single volume. Huang Min of Jinhua wrote the preface, which was then carved into printing blocks and circulated.

The Master’s conduct was exceptionally sublime, soaring like the clouds above the heavens as he looked down upon the mundane world; thus, all who entered his gate were practitioners who took life and death with earnest sincerity.

Apart from the direct lineage, there was one known as Layman Pang, who was also an extraordinary man. He possessed a spirit that rivaled that of Shitou and traveled extensively to visit venerable masters.
Upon hearing the words of his teacher, he attained complete realization. He remained at Mount Huading, accompanying [his master] like a shadow, never departing for elsewhere.
At the age of seventy-three, he passed away without illness. Originally a master craftsman, he reached the pinnacle of skill in sculpture; thus people called him "Layman Pang."
Chan Master Tianmu Duanya Liaoyi was a native of Deqing.
His secular surname was Yang, and his mother’s surname was Zhang. He was born in the year of Guihai during the Jingding era of the Song dynasty (1263).

He did not begin to speak until he was six years old; even then, he could only recite the *Lotus Sūtra* with his mother and remained utterly ignorant of worldly affairs. His physical appearance was serene and dignified.
However, his resolve was such that he seemed to be waiting for something. At the age of seventeen, a monk encountered him and recited the words from Peak Master’s discourse on ascending the hall.
The Master started up in alarm and stood upright, saying to the monk, "Can you lead me to see him? His mother prepared his travel gear and sent him off.
On the way, he met Peak Master at the Death Barrier of Lion Rock on Mount Tianmu and served as an attendant to his side as a novice.
He commanded that the myriad dharmas be returned to the One, asking, "To what does the One return? For this reason, he was named Congyi (Following the One).

On another day, while in his room, he raised the story of the ox passing through the window lattice. As the Master was about to open his mouth, Feng struck him with a heavy blow of his staff; the Master fell unconsciously down a cliff.
His fellow student Mingtong felt his way up the creepers and climbed the steps to rescue him, finding him already halfway down the mountain and free from suffering.
Yantong said, "My karmic conditions do not lie here; I am going to Jiangxi to see Master Qin. Yantong replied, "You have incurred the old man's staff!
He then returned to the West Chan Hermitage on Mount Huan and made a vow: "If I do not realize the truth within seven days, I shall certainly depart.
He remained upright and firm as a wall, forgetting both sleep and food. At night, he would climb trees and stand out in the open air until dawn.

At dawn, before he had even reached the appointed place, he attained a sudden and great enlightenment. He rushed to Siguan and called out, "Old Monk! Today you shall not deceive me! He presented this verse:
"The mountains and rivers of the great earth are a single expanse of snow; As soon as the sun rises, they leave no trace.
From now on I have no doubts regarding the Buddhas and Patriarchs; There is neither north, south, east, nor west. The next day, Feng ascended the hall.
He said: "My all-encompassing net has been used to strike phoenixes and capture dragons, yet I have never encountered so much as a shrimp or a crab.
Today, a tiny gnat has flown right into it. Thirty years from now, I shall go to the solitary peak at the very summit and let out a great shout!"

From then on, he rebuked and exhorted his fellow students with no lack of severity, saying, "If there is a single person throughout the entire earth who has awakened to the truth and returned to the source, I know them all.
Feng (Fengxue) marveled at his brilliance and quick wit, while those who had long been in the assembly felt ashamed;

some were even so anxious that their lives seemed like a thread hanging by a thread. He subsequently returned to Deqing, where his mother sold her hairpins and earrings to enable him to enter Wukang Shangbo together with him.
He lived in a thatched hut on the mountain. People saw him mingling with the mundane world and could not fathom his intent.
Feng summoned him to return to the mountain and said, "There are many people on the Way; you are merely muddying the waters. The Master replied, "Two eyes facing two eyes.

Feng then shaved his head for him and conferred the full precepts, changing his name to Liaoyi. In the year of Yiwu (1295), the Yuan Zhen era, Feng passed away, and the Master likewise concealed himself in obscurity. Or...
You lived in the Chan-lin Monastery, occupying the lower quarters. He was solitary, austere, and stern, never condescending to others in word or expression.

At times he would jest, laugh, scold, or revile, using coarse words and foul language that others could not endure; at other times, without being requested, he would provide guidance according to their capacities, his voice like a rolling thunder.
Consequently, princes, dukes, and nobles vied with one another to welcome and serve him, and offerings poured in so profusely that he regarded them all with utter indifference.
In the third year of the Taiping Xingguo era, he returned to his ancestral mountain. A great assembly of scholars gathered, and he addressed them, saying:

"Setting aside the paths of speech and silence, movement and stillness, bring forth a single phrase. He further asked: "When this one breath does not return, where will you establish yourself and find your life?"

The respondents all failed to accord with his intent. Master Guan accepted the invitation to take his seat out of a sense of duty, yielding to the expectations of the assembly as much as possible, for he had no choice in the matter.

During the Zhishun era, Emperor Renzong, having heard of the Master’s spiritual practice, issued an edict through the Xuanzheng Yuan to send an official bearing incense into the mountains to inquire after him and commanded the relevant authorities to provide protection.
In the second year of the Yuantong era, he was granted the title “Buddha-Wisdom, Perfectly Enlightened, Rightly Awakened, Universally Saving.”

The Chan Master had passed away before the imperial edict reached the mountain. On the day prior, he summoned the assembly and said, "You must all be diligent in mind of our ancestral tradition and propagate the Great Dharma.
Remember to repay the Buddha's kindness and do not give rise to indolence.

At dawn, as the assembly heard the sound of distant thunder in the sky, the Master had already assumed the full lotus posture and passed into nirvana. His secular age was seventy-two, and his years of monastic seniority were forty.
9. His entire body was enshrined behind Lion Rock.
National Preceptor Chungbong Puyeon’s lineage successor was Master Mingben.
His secular surname was Sun, and he was a native of Qiantang. When his mother was pregnant with him, she dreamed of the Wayman Wumen (Wumenguan).

He was born into the family of Jideng Longqi. From birth, the Master possessed a natural disposition that was not inclined toward play; instead, he delighted in chanting Buddhist hymns and sat in the lotus posture.
While still wearing his topknot, he read the *Lunyu* and *Mengzi*, but ceased his studies upon the death of his mother.

At the age of fifteen, he immediately set fire to his arm to uphold the precepts, vowing to seek the state of emptiness and stillness. After some time, while reading the *Chuan Deng Lu*, he encountered points of doubt; his resolve was set on seeking resolution, and so...
He ascended the barrier of death and met Master Miao. Miao’s hair was long and unshorn; his robes were tattered and never changed.
He was solitary, austere, and stern, never once opening his mouth to smile, nor did he ever shave the heads of his disciples. Yet, as soon as he saw the Master alone, he was filled with joy.

He wished to have his hair shaved, for he already recognized that [the Master] was a vessel of great capacity. After some time, as he recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, he felt as though he had attained a sudden awakening.
The Master remarked to himself, "My faculty of discernment is broad and penetrating; there is no meaning or principle I do not comprehend," yet he added, "This is not my true nature.

He subsequently underwent tonsure and served at the "Gate of Death" (the Master’s quarters). Then, he entered Mount Tianmu, which is the highest and coldest among all the mountains to the southeast, and lived on alms...

The timber for the granary was so heavy that it could not be moved there by mere manual labor. The Master applied himself to physical labor by day and devoted himself to meditative concentration by night;
for ten years, his ribs did not even touch his mat. Later, under Miaoyan, he attained a profound resonance with the essential teachings.

Because he so perfectly emulated [his predecessor], Miaoyan wrote a verse and entrusted it to him. The Master further concealed his own excellence and never presumed to assume the role of a teacher. Nevertheless...

When jade is in the mountains and pearls are in the abyss, their radiance and vapor cannot be concealed; how much more so when one examines them through consultation and resolution, and values them through recorded instructions?
During the Zhizhen era of the Yuan Dynasty, Qu Tingyuan of Songjiang donated land to establish a temple on Lotus Peak, naming it Dajue Zhengdeng Chan Temple.
When Miaojing was about to pass away, he entrusted the temple to the Master. The Master declined. The Master, whenever...
That is to say: his dwelling is necessarily the unsurpassed Great Way; by its power, he can enlighten humans and devas.
His long-accumulated roots of merit provide the power to gather and shelter a community of disciples. His brilliant wisdom and adaptability provide the power to respond to and manage all affairs.
Therefore, in all matters of maintaining the Dharma, the Way constitutes its essence (*tattva*), while conditions and wisdom constitute its function (*vṛtti*).
It may still be tolerable if the essence exists but the function is deficient; in such a case, the transformative authority will not be universal and ritual protocols will not be complete.

However, if the essence is absent and one relies solely upon the function, then even if one leads a community and the community follows, or if one regulates affairs and those affairs appear appropriate, it is not worth mentioning.
How much more so for one who, lacking all three [of these], yet presumes to occupy the position of its director—could such a person not stand in awe of cause and effect?
When the five mountains were devoid of abbots, high ministers and officials repeatedly sent letters and gifts to request his presence; the Master declined them all with great resolve.
He even retreated to remote crags and solitary islands, dwelling among the grasses and sleeping upon the waves, concealing his traces to avoid the world. Yet, throughout the four...

Now, as for those who study [the Dharma]: to the north they exhaust the limits of the Dragon Desert (Lungmo); to the south they cross the Six Zhao; to the west they connect with Śrīvijaya (Shendu); and to the east they reach the Bo-sang trees.
Wrapping their provisions and treading upon corpses, they travel ten thousand *li* in haste, yet those who flock to the Master like spokes converging at a hub hardly let a day pass without arriving.

The monk Xuanjian of Nanzhao was long proficient in the teachings and contemplations (*jiaoguan*); his eloquence was vast and his brilliance outstanding. He said: "I have heard that the Great Tang possesses the Chan School. May [the Master]..."

"I shall examine whether this is correct; if it is, I will follow his teachings. Should it prove otherwise, I will revise its fundamental tenets and cause them to conform to the methods of doctrinal study and contemplation.
Having come from his country, as soon as he heard the Master’s words, he immediately realized his former errors and thoroughly fathomed the source and depth of the teaching.

He was just planning to return home to propagate the Way when he passed away in Zhongwu. His disciples painted the Master’s portrait and brought it back to their country; the portrait has since appeared there.
Divine light illuminated the heavens. Nanzhao subsequently honored Chan, enshrining him as the first patriarch of the Chan school.

On the third day of the spring in the third year of Zhizhi, the trees on the mountain withered like grain; his senior disciples marveled at this anomaly. On the *jiazi* day of the eighth month in autumn, the Master entered nirvana.
His entire body was enshrined in a stupa on the western ridge of the mountain. One day before his passing, he sent word to take leave of his mother.
He protected [the monastery] and its affiliated properties, each of which was transcribed by the Master’s own hand. On that day, a white rainbow pierced the mountain.

The Master’s worldly age was sixty-one, and his monastic seniority (*śrāmaṇerī*) was thirty-seven. Wherever the Master went, the fourfold assembly looked up to him with longing; they offered incense, tea, gold, and silk, and through their prostrations and offerings, these places were all transformed into jeweled monasteries.
Yet the Master wore but a single robe and used but a single bamboo bowl, never once casting a glance at such things. People marveled at this...

In the heat of summer, when his flesh was plump and his pores were moist with sweat, he would wear a garment of *ge* (hemp) cloth to ward off the oppressive heat; yet the Master never once let it touch his body.

Other matters may be inferred from this. Although he repeatedly declined invitations to famous mountains, preferring instead to roam freely among forests, hills, rivers, and seas, he would untie his straw sandals, cast off his robes and hat, and settle in thatched huts wherever he went.
All of these were designated as "Illusory Dwelling" (*huànzhù*), where he sat upon meditation cushions and used the wooden board for zazen, practicing throughout the day.
The night assembly: the regulations and statutes are orderly and meticulously arranged; the ceremonial protocols are solemn and rigorous, as if presiding over a thousand people.

As for the vigorous exhortations and the raising of the Dharma, the application of the kōan is swift and dazzling; those who encounter it lose heart, and those who hear it find their resolve dissolved.
I have always maintained that this teaching transmits the Buddha-mind school, holding up the direct pointing alone, and abhors any so-called subtle or esoteric transmission. It abhors...

What is called speech relies upon understanding. Therefore, regarding the teachings, whenever one wishes to remedy its defects or treat its maladies, one must lead by example and serve as a teacher to all things.
Whether in matters great or small, high or low, slow or urgent, first or last, one must not reject anything nor neglect anything in receiving others.
Although people may see this as arising from compassionate vows, they do not realize that it is rooted entirely in sincerity and nothing else.

This was merely empty talk. Among the high officials and scholars of the age, such as Master Xu Junwei, Master Zheng Pengnan, and Master Zhao Zuna, they already knew to revere him upon first hearing of his Way;
yet when they personally attended to his words and countenance, there were none who did not admire him throughout their lives.
Even the Chancellor of Jiangzhe, Duke Tuo-huan, who was renowned for his gravity and severity, read the Master’s writings.
Adjusting his robes, he prostrated himself in expectation. The King of Jin of Goryeo, as a kinsman of noble blood, traveled ten thousand *li* to offer incense and pay his respects.
Rising, he said to those around him: "I have observed many people, yet none possesses such supreme merit and virtue as this Master.

Having received the Master’s instruction, I was moved to tears and inspired. If the Master applies himself personally to the pursuit of the Way, how could there be even a hair’s breadth of worldly intent?"
How remarkable! Yet its name is manifest though not proclaimed, and its Way is believed though not spoken.

Were it not for the sound corresponding to the practice of the precepts, truly bringing about a lasting and ever-increasing benefit, clearly revealed and never obscured—how could this have been achieved?
The Biography of Chan Master Shiwu Qinggong.
Qinggong, whose style name was Shiwu, was a native of Changshu, Suzhou. His secular surname was Wen, and his mother was Lady Liu. At the time of his birth, there were extraordinary lights.
Upon reaching adulthood, he relied upon the monk Yongwei at Chongfu Temple to leave the household life. At twenty, he shaved his head; three years later, he received full ordination.
He went to Tianmu to see Master Gaofeng. Gaofeng asked, "For what purpose have you come? The Master replied, "I wish to seek the Great Dharma.
Gaofeng said, "Is the Great Dharma so easily sought? You must first burn incense with your finger. The Master said, "Today I have personally met the Master.
Gaofeng silently regarded him with esteem and bestowed upon him the phrase, "The myriad dharmas return to one. For three years, he gained nothing at all.
He took his leave and departed. Feng said, "There is a blind donkey in Wenzhou, and Ji’an in Huai. You should go see them. He then went to see Ji’an.

Ji’an asked, "Where have you come from? The Master replied, "From Tianmu. Ji’an asked, "What instructions did he give you? The Master said, "All dharmas return to the One. Ji’an asked, "How do you understand this?
The Master was speechless. Ji’an said, "This is a dead word. What kind of feverish delirium is this?"
The Master said, "Why do you act like this? The teacher bowed and requested instruction. The Hermit said, "Where there is a Buddha, do not dwell;
where there is no Buddha, pass by quickly. The teacher asked, "What is the meaning of this? His answer did not accord with the truth. The Hermit said, "This, too, is a dead word."

The Master was unaware that sweat was pouring down his back. Later, when he entered the room, Xuansha questioned him again regarding their previous conversation. The Master replied, "When one mounts a horse, one sees the road.
Xuansha rebuked him, saying, "Having been here for six years, you still hold such a view! The Master left in a fit of indignation. On the road, he suddenly looked up and saw a pavilion;
at that moment, he attained a sudden realization. Returning, he said to Xuansha, "Where there is a Buddha, one must not dwell."
“This is a dead word. To run swiftly past where there is no Buddha—this is a dead word. Today I have understood the living word. The Hermit asked, “How do you understand it?
The Master said, “On the Qingming festival, when the rain has just cleared, the yellow oriole sings clearly upon the branch.
The Hermit nodded his head. After a long while, the Master took his leave. As the Hermit saw him out the gate, he instructed him, saying, “It is already...”

Later, he shared a meditation cell with him. Shortly thereafter, the Hermitage moved to Daochang on Lake Dao, where the Master went to visit him again. The Hermitage appointed him to keep the treasury keys.
The Hermitage often said to the assembly, "This man is a golden-scaled fish that has passed through the net in the ocean of the Dharma. The entire community watched him with bated breath.
Later, he entered Xiawu Mountain and established a hermitage named Tianhu, where he personally gathered firewood and vegetables, composing poetry as he found inspiration within himself.

He harbored the resolve to remain there for the rest of his life. Subsequently, when the seat at Fuyuan on Mount Danghu became vacant, they earnestly entreated him to take it, but the Master lay firm in his refusal and would not rise.

Someone urged him, saying, "A śramaṇa ought to regard the propagation of the Dharma as his primary responsibility. To dwell in seclusion and cultivate oneself alone—how can that be considered sufficient?
Thereupon, he changed his mind and set out. The eminent disciples followed him like dragons and elephants; they gathered like surging clouds and rushing waves, each fearing only to be left behind.
Before long, he returned to Tianhu. During the Zhizheng era, the imperial court heard of the Master’s reputation and sent down incense and ceremonial silk to honor him.
Empress Qide bestowed upon him a gold-embroidered *kaṣāya* robe, which people considered a great honor; yet the Master remained as indifferent as ever.

On the twenty-first day of the seventh month in the autumn of the Renchen year of the Zhizheng era, he manifested a slight illness. At midnight, he took leave of the assembly. His disciples asked after his health.
Regarding his final affairs, he took up his brush and wrote: "The green mountains do not accommodate stinking corpses;
once dead, what need is there to dig into the earth to bury them? I, too, lack the fire of samādhi; I am but a pile of firewood that has outshone the past and cut off the future.

Having cast down his brush, he passed away. His cremation yielded relics of five colors, brilliant and countless. His disciples collected his sacred remains and, together with the relics from the hermitage, enshrined them in a stupa.

The origin of Tianhu (Heaven Lake) demonstrates that he did not forget the words spoken in the same meditation cell. His secular age was eighty-one, and his monastic seniority (*śrāmaṇeraka*) was fifty-four.
Among his disciples, Yu Taigu was a man from Goryeo. The Master spoke a verse to certify him, which contained the line: "A golden-scaled fish goes straight up the hook.
Later, [Taigu] returned home, where the King honored him and appointed him as National Preceptor (*Guk-sa*). The King frequently extolled the Master’s virtue.

Filled with profound longing, upon the Master’s passing, he reported the matter to the imperial court. A decree was issued bestowing the posthumous title "Chan Master Foci Huizhao" (Buddha-Love Wisdom-Illumination).
An official letter was sent to Jiangzhe, requesting Master Pingshan Lin of Jingci Monastery to travel to Tianhu to collect half of the Master’s relics.

These were escorted back to the country, where a stupa was erected for their enshrinement and veneration. The Master’s recorded discourses from the Dharma hall, mountain dwelling verses, and hymns were compiled into a volume that remains widely circulated today.
Wenshu was styled Wenzhu; his courtesy name was Wuzu.
A native of Cixi in Ming, he maintained personal purity from childhood and would recite the classics with a low, rhythmic chant.

Whenever he encountered [a text], he would immediately master it through recitation. Having grown up, he studied the Five Classics under a teacher and extensively surveyed the works of the philosophers, historians, and the hundred schools of thought.
Upon reading Buddhist scriptures, his mind suddenly merged with their essence and his spirit attained realization; it was as if he had practiced them for a long time.

That very day, he informed his parents, expressing his wish to leave the household life to transcend birth and death. He shaved his head under Master Mu at Dongxi and received the precepts from Master Daoyong. He subsequently traveled and studied under various masters.
Upon reaching Mount Jing, Master Yuansou Duan praised him highly, regarding him as a vessel of the Way.

Later, he visited Hai Dongyu at Jingci Temple, where he was likewise recognized for his potential. However, as he had attained neither understanding nor realization, he eventually took up his staff and entered Tiantong.

He met the Chan Master Qiji at Guai Stone. Their conversation reached a state of perfect accord. Qiji, wishing to rely on him to expand his lineage, immediately ordered him to enter the inner quarters to serve as a scribe.
Subsequently, Zhiping Shi presided over this mountain and also managed the treasury keys; thus he became a dharma companion among the monks of various mountains.
Consequently, his reputation spread far and wide, and all wished to welcome him with prostrations to proclaim and expound the Great Dharma.

At that time, the seat of the Equal Compassion (Dengci) Dharma Assembly at Fengyue Mountain was vacant; by imperial decree of the Xingzheng Yuan, the Master was appointed to preside over it. Shortly thereafter, he was transferred to Husheng at Damei.

Both monasteries were in a state of decay, and the regulations and models of the monastic community were largely neglected. Upon the Master’s arrival, he issued strict injunctions, and everyone [conformed].

Regarding the Vinaya: when he preached the Dharma for the assembly, he cast aside conventional molds and stripped away the branches and leaves, causing his listeners to attain a sudden, clear understanding free from doubt.

Monastics of renowned virtue flocked to him like grass bending in the wind. The Master’s fame spread even further, and the Imperial Preceptor conferred upon him the title "Jue-zhi Yuan-ming" (Awakened Wisdom Perfectly Illuminating).
He retired to live out his final years at Fuchang Temple. To the left of the temple, he opened a small pavilion and inscribed its plaque with the characters:

Shu Xiao was a man of renowned virtue throughout the lakes and seas. Eminent figures such as Duan Jiangyue, Jiang Shangyin, and Mengtang all welcomed him into their midst to provide offerings and support.
Among the scholarly gentry, there were also those who frequently visited him to become companions beyond the mundane world;
notably, Liu Daochuan, Huang Jinqing, Wei Taipu, and Li Jihe were especially considered his true intimates. He was nearly seventy years of age.

Feeling increasingly weary of worldly distractions, he retired to Huashu Lake. When the white lotuses were in full bloom and the moonlight was exquisitely beautiful, he sat cross-legged in a small boat, drifting upon the waters;
his serene and transcendent appearance was such that even Subhūti could have been depicted as a painting.

He always rose early to perform prostrations and recite scriptures, never flagging even in the midst of bitter cold or sweltering heat. He was extremely solemn when presiding over the assembly, yet when receiving guests and friends, he was...
It was truly so. His joyful countenance and eyes were visible; he clapped his hands and laughed as they conversed, the flow of their talk never ceasing.
When someone asked why this was so, the Master said, "To bring disciples to maturity, one must not fail to maintain solemnity. But when a guest comes with joy, it is otherwise.

Master Yū of Sanshan Wenhǎi traveled the four quarters carrying but a single alms bowl, yet he always regarded the arrival or departure of such a person as a matter of great importance. However, [the Master] alone...
He followed his master while traveling upon the lake; filled with reverence and deep affection, he remained for so long that he forgot to leave.

It was likely because as one’s experience of the world increases, one’s worldly attachments grow ever more淡薄 (thin and distant). He then sought out deep mountains and dense forests, departing resolutely for a long journey, causing those who met him to cast down their canes and stand rooted to the spot, wishing to behold his dignified bearing.
In the ninth month of the second year of Huangqing, he manifested illness and passed away.
The Japanese National Teacher Mu’ō transmitted the Dharma to Chihatsu, who changed his name to Sosho and took the style name Mu’ō. His surname was Minamoto, and he was a native of Settsu Province.

He was a ninth-generation descendant of Emperor Uda. Having left home at the age of nine, he could immediately memorize any book upon a single reading. Upon reaching adulthood, he painted the nine transformations of a corpse.
While sitting alone in contemplation, he was moved by a profound resolve to seek the Way.

One night, he dreamed that he traveled to the two monasteries of Shushan and Shitou in China, where a monk with a long, bushy beard presented him with an image of Bodhidharma, saying, "Serve this well.
Upon waking, he sighed and said, "Only through Chan meditation can one clearly illuminate my original mind. He then changed his name to Shushi and went to pay his respects.
He met Master Wuyin Fan, but they did not reach a deep accord. Later, he sought guidance from Master Fohui Ri at Gaofeng;
there, upon hearing a word, he attained realization. One evening, while sitting for a long time, he happened to lean against the wall, and his body suddenly collapsed.

He attained a sudden and great enlightenment. The obstruction that had weighed upon his chest throughout his life was dissolved like ice melting and snow thawing. His mind’s eye shone brilliantly like the moon;
the profound mysteries of the Buddhas and Patriarchs were all at once shattered through illumination.

Peakong instructed him to protect and uphold [the Dharma], and presented him with a letter in his own hand from Master Yuanwu Keqin, sealing it as a token of the intent behind the transmission and entrustment of the lineage. The Master’s will was set upon the mountain mists.
Kōsha. Leaving the world was not his original wish, yet he declined all invitations with firm resolve.
Ryūzan-an on Mount Katsuragi in Kōshū, Kyūkō-an on Mount Gūdai, as well as Hakusen-an, Taikō-an, and Tōzai-naion, were all places where the Master sought seclusion.
When those who admired him pursued him incessantly, he even fled to a coastal island to avoid them. He lived for fifty... years.
11. Later, the sovereign, Emperor Go-Daigo, forcibly invited the Master to enter Nanzen-ji. Upon his arrival, the Emperor led him to a seat.
The Master stated his intention to retire. The Emperor replied, "My mind has no other purpose than to inquire after the Way morning and evening.

When the Empress Dowager passed away, he again compelled the Master to enter Nanzen-ji and requested that he proclaim the Great Precepts (Upasampadā). He treated the Master with even greater reverence than he had shown his younger brother, bestowing upon him—
Regarding the title of National Preceptor (Guoshi): after the King passed away, the Heavenly King of Taicang again received the precepts from the Master, vowing to become his disciple.

While the teachings were being proclaimed, two stars descended into the courtyard, their radiance like that of the midday sun. The two royal consorts requested that the Master receive the five precepts at Xian-dong.
The court deliberated upon the Master’s profound virtue and reputation, and once again compelled him to enter Tianlong Monastery, where they conferred upon him [the title].

He was titled Zhengjue Xinzhong Pujì (Universal Salvation of the Mind-Source of Right Enlightenment). He left behind a handwritten letter, a portion of which reads: "My Way has vibrated through three reigns; my fame has flown across the four seas.
I presided over the seat of Tianlong, turning the Wheel of Dharma twice more. Wielding the authority of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, I repeatedly crushed the fortresses of Māra.
The nation regarded this as its glory. Later, he passed away in the Inner Court of Tuṣita Heaven. His worldly age was seventy-nine, and his monastic seniority was sixty. His younger brother—
The disciple enshrined the entire-body stupa behind the monastery. Those who escorted it, numbering over twenty thousand monastics and laypeople, were all overcome with inconsolable grief.
They divided the nails and hair the Master had trimmed during his lifetime and buried them at Yunju; from within the hair, śarīras grew in clusters.
The Master’s appearance was lofty and radiant, and his wisdom and learning were profound and deep; wherever he resided, it was as if a Buddha had appeared in the world.
He offered incense and flowers, fearing even the slightest delay; thus, the administrator, Monk En, relied upon him. He once said to others:
"I followed my predecessor and listened to the National Teacher’s extensive discourses on the Buddha-dharma, through which I attained a fair understanding of the True Vehicle (*satyayāna*).

Consequently, I have been able to regard life and death as one and remain undaunted when facing critical matters. Yet my predecessor ultimately died for his loyalty; I, too, know that I must devote my body to serve my sovereign."

This is entirely due to the power of the National Preceptor’s transformative guidance. Thus, the Master’s Way not only thoroughly elucidates the study of the mind, but is truly sufficient to enhance the gravity of worldly instruction.
Furthermore, his aspirations were loftily sublime; he regarded honor, profit, fame, and sustenance as if they were non-existent, desiring only to dwell among the forests and springs.
Although he repeatedly presided over great monasteries, these were all undertaken only because he was compelled by royal decree.
The world calls him a great spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*); who other than a teacher could be worthy of this title?
Wenxuan of the Song dynasty said: "After the Southern Song moved its capital south of the Yangtze, it was from Master Kyōkō Yōsei that the lineage of Bodhidharma was first transmitted to Japan.
Subsequently, Master Mugaku Genkō, following the teachings of Master Fukan Hōgen..."
His son traveled east by sea vessel and greatly propagated his school. Gao Feng compiled and inherited it;
the Master is a descendant of Gao Feng, having received the transmission from the master Songyin Mao.
Songyin, Chan Master Maoyan, styled Shian, was the son of Zheng of the Fuhua clan in Ming. From childhood, he delighted in sitting in meditation.

At the age of sixteen, he entered the monastic order under Xiyan at Chuanfa Temple. When his master assigned him menial tasks such as managing grain and salt, the Master sighed and said, "I have left home to seek the Way;
if I am merely bound by such trivialities, how is this different from those who behave like dogs or flies? Thereupon, he secretly practiced the Great [Way].
To the west of the Yangtze River, he met Master Nanjian Quan. The Master focused his mindfulness day and night without interruption for even a moment.
One night, as the moonlight shone through the pines, he was walking along the eaves when he heard the sound of a spring and felt a sudden resonance. He immediately went to inform Master Quan.
Master Quan said, "The ordinary teachings provided here are insufficient to trigger your great potential and great function. Why not go to see Master Moling of Gulin?
The Master immediately set out, carrying his staff and traveling bag. Upon his arrival, Gulin asked, "What do you intend to do by coming here?
The Master replied, "Precisely because the matter of birth and death is so great, I have come specifically to seek liberation. Gulin said, "You are clear."
He realized that the four great elements and the five aggregates are the root of birth and death. "For what reason have I entered this leather bag?
The Master was about to offer a reply when Lin struck him with his staff; the Master suddenly attained a profound realization. From then on, his spiritual eloquence became peerless.

He moved with effortless mastery in all directions. Lin Shen esteemed him highly and appointed him to the first seat. In the *Renwu* year of the *Zheng* era (1362), the Xuanzheng Yuan commissioned him to lead Qingliang Monastery at Ruiyun;
disciples flocked there from all quarters, and their exchanges of spiritual insight were as swift as a hawk swooping down upon a fleeing rabbit.

Whenever he blinked his eyes, he would immediately lose [his realization]. A śramaṇa arrived and questioned him; before the questioning was finished, the master clapped his hands on the ground and laughed.
The śramaṇa said, "Why trouble yourself to bring out this stagnant merchandise? The master gave a sharp shout. The śramaṇa attained awakening and departed.
He resided at Qingliang for fifteen years; at that time, he withdrew into the Eastern Hall, never venturing beyond the mountains, where layers of dust accumulated.

The assembly was full. Yuan Mingliang Gong, a Dharma nephew of the Master, invited him back to Cixuan at Tiantong. One day, the Master manifested a slight illness. His attendants requested that he write a verse.
The Master raised his hand and pointed to his heart, saying, "Within this of mine, all is vast and empty; what need is there for a verse?
He sat upright leaning against a small table, clenched his right hand into a fist, and rested his forehead upon it, passing away. His worldly age was eighty.

Fifteen: At seventy years of age, the funeral bier was drawn forth for the *dhyāpita* (cremation) rite. Just as the fire was about to be lit, there suddenly appeared a substance drifting through the clear sky;
it resembled snow yet was not snow, falling in fine, shimmering, and profuse clusters, circling above the fierce flames until the fire was extinguished, at which point it ceased.

This was what is known as "celestial flowers" (*devapuṣpa*). After the cremation, the *śarīra* (relics), resembling pearls and beads, were quite numerous. The Preface by Wenxian of the Song Dynasty states:
Liao have heard that according to the records of the classics, when enlightened monks manifest their passing, there are frequently auspicious signs such as celestial flowers.

Some may argue that within the realm of the Mahāyāna, coming and going leave no trace; why then resort to miraculous anomalies? Yet they fail to realize that the prevailing customs of the age have become diluted and corrupt.
People harbor weariness and indolence; if there is no means to stir their gaze and attention, how can one manifest true awakening and open the way for correct faith?
Manifesting subtle expedient means is, in truth, identical in principle to the reality of all phenomena, as was the case with the Master.
It is said that he indeed did not fall short of the ancients.
Regarding the biography of Master Zhu Yuan-yuan:
his courtesy name was Zhu Yuan, his secular surname was Ouyang, and he was a native of Nankang. On the night of his birth, a Buddhist monk appeared in a dream to his father.
After his mother had fully observed the precepts, she went to visit Master Linggong of Xugu. The Master questioned her with the story of Longtan extinguishing the paper torch.
The Master replied, "A scorched stone can break through layers of ice. The Master asked, "What is done after it is broken?

She responded, "One must explore it to know. The Master pressed her, "What is it that you know? Just as she was thinking of how to answer his words, the Master suddenly raised his staff and struck her.

The Master was struck with awe and understood in silence. From this point on, his wisdom opened and his consciousness became integrated; he was unimpeded both internally and externally, and people turned to him in devotion.
Throughout his life, he presided over five major monasteries, all of which had been invited by envoys dispatched by regional governors and high ministers.

Though his rank was exalted, he did not consider it an honor; though his virtue was profound, he maintained it with humility. While residing at the monastic centers, he expanded the quarters and dwellings.
[The biography] is incomplete. He presided over Mount Jing. At Lingyin, he buried the remains of those killed by the chaotic soldiers;
although the pavilions and halls were all reduced to ashes, only the dwelling of the Master remained, as if a deity were protecting it.

On the sixth month of the twenty-first year of the Zhizheng era of the Yuan dynasty, he passed away at the age of seventy-three. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa on Mount Jing, while his disciples buried [other remains] elsewhere.
His fingernails and hair were left at the site of enlightenment, where the *śarīra* relics remain clustered among them.
Tóngjiāng Dàgōng (Great Master of the Tóng River) was styled Dàshào;
he was the son of the Rǔ family. His ancestors had long resided in Tóngjiāng in Yán, and thus he took this as his title. The Master’s spiritual countenance was solitary and transcendent.
Jie did not delight in dwelling amidst the dust and grime of the world; as soon as he was touched by worldly vapors, he feared only that they might defile him.

After receiving full ordination, he went up to Mount Shuangjing to pay his respects to Master Ling Gong of Dabian. Master Ling’s reputation for the Way resounded throughout the southeast, and upon meeting the Master, he was greatly pleased and transmitted the seal of mind to him.
The Master withdrew and reflected to himself: "Is the Great Dharma of the Tathāgata merely this? He then took his leave immediately.
He departed and traveled through various monastic assemblies. When the venerable elders spoke to him, it was no different from his time at Mount Jing;
he sighed deeply and said, "From this day forward, I know that the Dharma has no diverse flavors. He then returned to see Master Gong, who appointed him to attend upon him as a personal attendant.
The Master exerted himself even more vigorously; for several years his ribs did not touch the mat.

Morning and evening he sought instruction, so that regarding the realization of doubts and the discernment of delusions, there was not even a hair’s breadth of regret. He subsequently attained mastery and fearlessness. Having thus clarified the Dharma of the mind, he...
Furthermore, one must not fail to master both mundane and supramundane wisdom. Every night, he would spread his mat upon the ground and, before an image of the Buddha, read from a long-burning lamp.
He read the entire Great Canon three times, thoroughly penetrating its essential meanings in each instance.
Yet the Master’s resolve was still not satisfied; he also selected and savored the works of the Confucianists as well as those of Laozi and others. From then on—
This was the study of both the internal and external [teachings]. He was beyond reproach in either. Having transcended the world, he sat upon the site of enlightenment three times;
disciples gathered beneath his seat until there was not even room for them to sit. He could rectify his own countenance to awaken others, such that the malice of those who saw him would dissolve.

When anyone sought textual passages, he would take up his brush and write at once. He had mastered the sūtras and śāstras, yet he took the primary meaning (*paramārtha*) as his ultimate refuge. Occasionally...
He indulged in the art of calligraphy and composed poems; his style was serene, harmonious, concise, and profound, bearing the lingering influence of the Táng dynasty.
As for his various constructions, whether laying stone or transporting bricks, he personally undertook the labor to lead the assembly.

His hands never grasped gold or silk, entrusting all matters entirely to those who understood the law of cause and effect. When some criticized him for this, he would say: "I know only how to uphold the Dharma. Once...
Suffering from dysentery, he could not bear to use toilet paper for wiping clean; instead, he plucked bean leaves to use in their stead.
Throughout his life, he did not keep any superfluous possessions; the cotton robe he wore was sometimes not changed for over ten years. He passed away at the age of seventy-four.
The *vinaya-dhara* opened the deceased’s casket, intending to proceed with the traditional ritual of distributing the robes (*cīvara*). There was nothing there but a single set of paper bedding;

he laughed aloud and departed. Such austerity is something that ordinary people cannot endure; were it not for one whose insight is correct and whose power is vast, how could such a state be easily attained?
The Biography of Chan Master Qianyan Chang.

His courtesy name was Wuming, and he was also known as Qianyan. He was the son of the Dong family in Xiaoshan, Yue. At the age of seven, he could recite from memory any scripture or book upon merely glancing over it.
Whether entering or leaving, his every step followed the proper measure, appearing as if he were an adult. As he grew older, he began to study the Confucian classics under a teacher.
The Master was studying the *Lotus Sūtra* and, pointing to a passage, asked for its meaning; the Master was unable to answer.

Later, while receiving full ordination at Lingzhi Temple, he attended a vegetarian feast for the monastic community hosted by the Chancellor at his residence. The Master entered with the assembly, where the Venerable Zhongfeng Ben was seated.

Upon seeing the Master, the Venerable called out to him and asked, "How do you spend your daily life? The Master replied, "I do nothing but recite the Buddha's name. The Venerable asked, "Where is the Buddha now?"
Just as the Master was about to deliberate on the matter, the Duke shouted at him with a stern voice. The Master then prostrated himself and requested instruction.
The Duke bestowed upon him the word "Wu" (無). Thereupon, he entered retreat at Lingyin Mountain. Subsequently, he followed the conditions of the world for nearly ten years.
Once, he sighed deeply and said, "The aspirations of my life have filled the heavens and the earth; how can I now become a vinegar gnat in a jar?
He immediately returned to Mount Lingyin and sat in meditation so upright that his ribs did not touch the mat for three years.

Later, while traveling to Wangting, he attained realization upon hearing the cry of a sparrow. He hurried to see Master Ben, but the Master again rebuked him. The Master returned home in indignation. At night...

As he was about to retire for the night, a mouse suddenly turned around and ate from the cat’s bowl. It fell to the ground with a sound, whereupon he attained great enlightenment as if shedding his skin like a cicada. Amidst defilement, he floated within the profound mystery; from the heavens above to the earth below, all became clear and bright at once. He put on his robes and waited for dawn, then went again to consult Master Gong. Gong asked, "Why did you say in Gan Prefecture that there were none? He replied, "The mouse ate the cat’s food. Gong said, "Now you have truly seen it. He then bowed and departed. Later, when he returned to the capital, he stayed at the temple of the Chan Master Xingfu. One day, while sitting in meditation, he heard a dog barking outside the wall. Suddenly, he attained great enlightenment. He composed a verse: "A dog barks outside the wall / The Chan master is enlightened / The whole world is one body / Where can the mind be sought? He then went to see Master Xingfu and presented this verse. The Master said, "You have indeed attained it. He then took leave and traveled to Mount Tiantai, where he resided in seclusion. He later visited the Chan Master Changsha Jingcen, who asked him, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Mount Tiantai. Changsha asked, "What dharma did you hear there? The Master said, "Not yet. The attendant replied, "The rice bowl has been broken. The Master asked, "What was done after it broke? He replied, "It was crushed into small square bricks.
The Master then smiled slightly and instructed him to protect and maintain them, saying, "When the time arrives, the principle will manifest of itself.

Having received this entrustment, the Master withdrew to the eastern hermitage of Tianlong Mountain, where he delighted in the flavor of Chan, remaining aloof from external entanglements. There were two snakes there.

For several days he circled around the Master’s seat. The Master preached the precepts of taking refuge to him; the snake raised its head and bowed up and down, making gestures of prostration before departing.
From then on, his reputation and influence grew daily. Xiangyin Fang was the abbot of Zhongzhu and earnestly recommended his revival in the monastic world.

The Chancellor Tuohan also dispatched an envoy to urge the Master to assume a monastic position, but he refused both times. Not long after, the various mountain monasteries vied with one another to entreat the Master to accept their invitations.
Fadu was not tolerated by his contemporaries. Carrying his staff and alms bowl, he crossed the Tāng River and traveled eastward until he reached Fúlóng Mountain in Wūshāng.
He made a vow, saying, "If there is water on this mountain, I shall dwell here. Suddenly, a spring gushed forth from the mountain, appearing the color of white milk.
The Master then took up residence beneath a great tree; it was the tenth month of winter in the Dingmǎo year of the Tàidìng era. After a long time, the local villagers gathered in harmony.
Nevertheless, the local gentry, the two Lou families, established the original cause for it and constructed a great monastery based on its former name.
With its multi-storied pavilions and towering halls, its grand gates and wide avenues, it radiated its brilliance across the forests and valleys.
From within—Qi, Lu, Yan, Zhao, Qin, Long, Min, and Shu—to without—Japan, the Three Han, the Eight Fan, Luo Dian, Jiaozhi, and Liuqiu—all came to run toward it and prostrate themselves in worship.

I pay my respects. Regarding those who have consulted on resolving their studies of the Way, there were those whose yearning for the Path was so intense that they severed their own arms before their masters to manifest their resolve.

To this, the Imperial Court thrice dispatched high-ranking ministers, bestowing upon them famous incense as a mark of honor and praise. Among the powerful vassal states along the Yangtze and Huai rivers, such as those of the Prince of Xuangrang...

Consequently, an edict was issued to grant protection to his teachings. As for Prince Zhennan, he personally inscribed the temple plaque, bestowed upon him the *saṃghāṭī* robe, and conferred a monastic title.

The Imperial Preceptor (Dishi) also issued a decree twice to ensure that powerful families would not encroach upon or oppress him, and further granted him the title of Great Chan Master (*Dachanshi*).
Furthermore, the Zai Zheng Yuan petitioned the Eastern Court, ordering court officials to compose a monastic title for him.
He also bestowed upon him a dharma robe of gold-threaded brocade. The Master had sparse eyebrows and prominent eyes, full cheeks and a beautiful beard;

his talent and insight were brilliant and inspired, such that he could compose a thousand gāthās in an instant, encompassing immeasurable subtle meanings. Those who obtained even a single word of his cherished and protected it with the utmost care.
Commentators remarked that the Master’s practice was grounded in reality and his eloquence was swift and sharp, perhaps not inferior to that of Zhijue (Zhiyi).
It is said that in the Dingyou year of the Zhizheng era, when the Master was seventy-four years old, he manifested a slight illness. He gathered the assembly and wrote a verse, saying:
"Throughout my life I have been talkative; today I am exposed. One phrase roars through heaven—the Eye of the True Dharma is extinguished. Thereupon, he laid down his brush and passed away.

The disciples used a ceramic casket with a lid to enshrine the master’s entire body and interred it at Chongseong-am Hermitage. Song Wenxuan composed an inscription for it, the preface of which states:
"When I, Lian, first went to Fulong Mountain to see the Master, his speech thundered like a rushing torrent.

At that time, I was still full of pride and somewhat wished to humble him; we engaged in debate for several thousand words, but without reaching a mutual understanding, I withdrew. After two years had passed..."
The following year, he went again to visit him. The Master asked, "I have heard that you have read through the entire Tripitaka;
is this true? Lian replied, "It is so. The Master asked, "Is it read by the ears, or is it observed with the eyes? Lian said, "It is indeed observed with the eyes.
The Master asked, "As for that which enables the eyes to observe, whom do you call it? Lian raised his eyebrows toward him. Thereupon, they looked at each other and laughed. From that time forward...
I recognize that the Master’s Way transcends both existence and non-existence; it is truly beyond the scope of ordinary human intellect to fathom.

Consequently, we have maintained a relationship as external friends for over thirty years. As for the letters exchanged between us regarding the exaltation and elucidation of the ultimate truth, those preserved within my bookshelves—
The ink was still wet. Although he was entangled in worldly phenomena and unable to achieve realization, his mutual understanding was most profound.
As for this inscription—who else would be more suitable than I, Lian? Such is the way these renowned worthies pursue their longing for him.
Wuyong Guishou (字: Wuyong; 別號:
Shui'an) was the son of the Zhen family of Wuzhou. His family’s occupation was farming and wood-gathering.

Every time he was sent to deliver food offerings among the fields, Master Zhi took no pleasure in it. There was a young boy from the same village who followed the Master to study the Odes and the Books.

Having shaved his head, he went to Master Yuansou Duan of Mount Jing, whose teaching style was strict and severe. Because the Master had not yet clarified his own realization, he went there to seek resolution.
Yuansou asked, "Where have you recently departed from? He replied, "Jingci. Yuansou said, "What brings you here?
He replied, "I have long admired the Master’s spiritual influence; I have come specifically to pay my respects. Yuansou asked, "When Zhaozhou met Nanquan, what did he do? He replied, "He bowed."
His head touched the heavens and his feet trod the earth. An old man asked, "What is it like after seeing [the Buddha]? He replied, "When hungry, I eat; when sleepy, I sleep.
The old man said, "Where did you learn this empty talk? He replied, "Today I have personally seen the Master. The old man nodded in approval and appointed him to the position of attendant.
Later, he was promoted to the post of keeper of the storehouse. After some time, he left the monastery to become the abbot of Mount Lu in Cixi and Dongshan in Yue Province.
Shan was a gate to the wisdom of Siming. At the beginning of the Hongwu era, he was summoned due to his possession of the Way.

Together with Yi Zhong of Jingwu and Rizhang of Upper Zhu, he went to the capital and was lodged at Tianjie Monastery. He entered the inner court several times, and his responses were in accord with the imperial will.

He remained there for three years. Emperor Shizu granted him permission to return to Zhimen, where he built a hermitage to the east of the temple and inscribed it "Haoyin" (Ocean Seal), intending to spend his final days there.

Shortly thereafter, the seat at Mount Jing was vacant, and the Emperor compelled the Master to fill that position. He preached the Dharma, saying: "If you raise one, you must not raise two; to let pass one move is to fall into the second.
When the ancients spoke thus, they were truly like those who embrace their own stolen goods while crying out for innocence. To the east...
Mountains are not like this. To raise both is not permitted; to raise one is to let pass a single point and fall into the seventh stage.
At this juncture, you must know that there is a path leading upward before you can succeed. "What is the path leading upward? After a long silence, he said:
"Do not plant exotic green grass upon the cold crags; sitting amidst white clouds is altogether not sublime.

Formerly residing at Mount Xiangyuan, he began the construction of a Buddha hall but passed away before its completion. The Master completed it through his own efforts. The expenses were provided by Ge Derun of Gusu.
One day, he suddenly fell ill and his condition became critical. His attendant requested a verse, to which the Master rebuked him, saying: "My worldly lifespan is still—"
There was a period of three years. Subsequently, it turned out exactly as predicted. On the day of his passing, he clapped his hands and said, "A-he-he!
O assembly, look at this! He then entered final stillness. He was eighty-four years old. His entire body was interred on the right ridge of Jizhao.
The Biography of Chan Master Chu-shih Qi (Fànqí).
"Chu-shih" was his courtesy name; his childhood name was Tányào. He was a native of Xiàngshān in Míngzhōu and belonged to the Zhū clan. His father was Gǎo and his mother was Zhāng.
Zhāng dreamed that the sun fell into her bosom when the Master was born. While the Master was still in his swaddling clothes, a divine monk appeared...
He stroked [the boy’s] head and said, "This is the Sun of the Buddha. In the future, will he not be able to illuminate the dark alleys? Consequently, people named him Tanyao (Dawn Radiance).
At the age of seven, his spiritual nature was exceptionally sharp; whenever he read a book, he immediately grasped its great meaning.
When someone asked what kind of words he preferred, he replied at once, "The gentleman is guided by righteousness. As for composing verses or imitating calligraphy, he surpassed them all.

Surpassing his peers, he was hailed as a prodigy by those both near and far. At the age of nine, he renounced secular life to enter Yongzuo Monastery, where he received the scriptures from Master Nengong Mu.
Subsequently, he followed Master Jingong Xun at Chong’en Monastery in Lake County; Master Xun was his paternal great-uncle.
Duke Zhao Wei recognized the Master’s potential and purchased a monastic certificate for him, whereby he was tonsured and became a śramaṇa. Thereafter...

He traveled to Zhaokong Temple in Hangzhou to receive full ordination; he was already sixteen years of age. He inquired about the Master’s relocation to Daochang Monastery and served as his attendant.

Not long after, the Master appointed him to oversee the library. While reading the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, he reached the passage: "When conditions see through the cause of illumination, darkness becomes a place where seeing does not exist.
At this, he had a sudden realization. Subsequently, he perused a multitude of texts without relying on a teacher’s instruction. His literary [skill]...
The phrases were self-evident; yet, being stuck on names and forms, he had not yet been able to cast off his entanglements.

Hearing that Master Yuansou Du was propagating the Way at Shuangjing, the Master went there to inquire, saying: "When speech issues forth, it is not sound; before form, there is no object—what is the meaning of this?
Yuansou used the Master’s own words to interrogate him. Just as the Master was deliberating how to respond, Yuansou shouted at him and sent him out. From that point on...
These many doubts congested his chest like boulders filling it. It happened that Emperor Yingzong issued an edict to grind gold into paste for the purpose of copying the Great Canon (Tripitaka).
The authorities, noting that the Master was skilled in calligraphy, selected him to go to the capital of Yan. One night, he heard the drums striking at the West City Tower.
Sweat poured from him like rain. Striking the table, he laughed and said, "Today, the nostrils of Mount Jing have fallen into my hands.
He then composed a verse containing the lines: "Picking up a single speck of snow from a red furnace / Is indeed the ice of the Yellow River in the sixth month.
He then turned southward and returned once more to Shuangjing. Upon seeing the Master’s countenance full and radiant, Yuansou remarked, "The secret transmission of the West..."
I believe Master Xi has attained it; he was immediately appointed to the first seat. Furthermore, [Zhao Mengfu] remarked, "The Great Dharma of Miaoxi is entirely present in you, Master.
Whenever anyone came to seek instruction or inquiry, he frequently had the Master resolve their doubts.

During the Yuan Taiding era, the Xuanzheng Yuan (Bureau of Buddhist and Tibetan Affairs) became well-acquainted with the Master’s reputation and commissioned him to take up residence at Fuzhen Monastery in Haiyan. Subsequently, he was promoted to head Yongzuo Monastery. At Yongzuo...
At the site where the Master received the scriptures, he constructed a Great Treasure Pavilion and cast the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa in bronze.
Within it were enshrined images of Vairocana, Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, and the Thousand-Handed and Thousand-Eyed Avalokiteśvara.
He further constructed a seven-storied stūpa, over two hundred and forty feet in height. When the work was nearly complete, the structure became unbalanced and was on the verge of collapsing.
The Master prayed for it, and that night there was a great wind and rain. The local residents heard spirits conversing with one another, saying: "The Tiantai Stūpa is leaning."

He hurried there to rescue it. At dawn, the stupa was exactly as it had been before. He moved [the image] to Baoguo Temple in Hangzhou, then to Benjue Temple in Jiaxing, where he further constructed the Wanfo Pavilion.
Its nine bays were vast, magnificent, and grand, appearing like a celestial palace descended from heaven to the human world.
The Imperial Preceptor, admiring his religious practice, conferred upon him the title Chan Master Furi Puzhao Hui bian. Buddha...
This remarkably coincided with the words of a divine monk from days past, which those who understood the matter found extraordinary. At that time, the abbacy of Baoen Guangxiao was vacant;
everyone agreed that Baoen was a preeminent monastery in the entire prefecture and that none but the Master could occupy it.

The Master reluctantly complied with the public request and went there, but he soon withdrew to seclusion at Yongzuo, where he built a western study as his plan for the remainder of his life. In the year of Jia-mao (the tenth year of the Zhizheng era), the state...
Now, Master Qiāng presided over the affairs of the monastery. At that time, the stupa had been destroyed by war; the Master rebuilt it.

Jǐnghuán cast a precious urn and placed it upon its summit, which moved the heavens to manifest the auspicious signs of celestial flowers and extraordinary fragrances. The Master appointed Jǐnghuán as his successor and returned to live in retirement at the Western Chamber.
In the first year of the Hongwǔ era of our Ming Dynasty, an imperial edict summoned ten great *bùtú* from Jiangnan.
Other individuals held a great Dharma assembly at Jiangshan Chansi Temple, and the Master was indeed included among their ranks;

he ascended the seat to preach the Dharma, thereby inspiring the listening of humans, devas, dragons, and ghosts. His Majesty was greatly pleased. In the spring of the second year, it was repeated as before;
a banquet was hosted below Wenlou, and the Master personally received the Emperor’s inquiries. Upon his return, the inner treasury bestowed white gold as a gift. In the third year—

In the autumn, the Sovereign, considering that the nature and circumstances of spirits and ghosts are subtle and difficult to fathom, felt that the canonical scriptures must contain clear and profound instructions.
He therefore inquired of those among the monks who were masters of the Tripiṭaka. The Emperor appointed Master Mengtang E and Master Xingzhong Ren to serve together at Dajianjue Temple.
The Ministry of Rites was ordered to provide them with provisions. Subsequently, they cited scriptural evidence...
The sutras and treatises had been completed as books, and he was about to enter the capital to present them at court. Suddenly, the Master manifested a slight illness.

After four days had passed, he urged his attendants to prepare a bath and change his robes. He then requested a brush and wrote a verse, saying: "True nature is perfectly luminous; fundamentally, it is without birth or extinction.
A wooden horse neighs in the night; the sun rises in the west. Having finished writing, he said to Mengtang, "Brother Master, I am about to depart. Mengtang replied:
"Where are you going, my son? The Master replied, "To the West. Mengtang asked, "If there is a Buddha in the West, is there no Buddha in the East?
The Master let out a single, stern shout and then passed away peacefully. At that time, cremation was prohibited by law;

the Ministry of Rites reported this to the Emperor, who specially decreed that he be permitted to follow his own religious tradition. After the cremation, his teeth, jaw, tongue, and prayer beads remained entirely unburnt, and *śarīra* relics were produced.

The remains were stitched together; the relics were piled up like pearls. His disciples took the bones and those parts that remained uncorrupted back to Haiyan, where they constructed a stupa at Tianning Yongzuo Chan Temple and interred them there.
His worldly age was seventy-five, and his monastic seniority was sixty-three.
His skillful application in preaching the Dharma is seen in the records of his six assemblies of discourse, while his playful mastery of calligraphy is seen in [the surviving works].
