Regarding his works on the Three Sages of Tiantai and Huiyuan, as well as those on Yongming Yanshou, Tao Qian, and Lin Bu, he composed separate poems on the Pure Land and verses on Maitreya’s Rebirth Above.
His *Three Collections from the West*—comprising the *Northward Journey*, the *Phoenix Mountain*, and the *West Chamber*—total several volumes in all, all of which have been transmitted to the world.
As for the Master’s character: though his physical stature was short and small, his spiritual countenance was refined and lucid. He upheld the True Dharma with great vigor.

It spread out vast and expansive, as if one could never know its limits. In every place he visited, both monastics and laypeople looked up to him with devotion, like waters returning to their valleys.
In the space of a single finger-snap, palaces and soaring pavilions would emerge, their peaks piercing the clouds; yet he was never seen to perform any deliberate action.

The gentleman says: Master [Daoyi] moved with ease in both vertical and horizontal directions; he responded to things without leaving a trace. Like mountains and rivers from which clouds emerge, or like thunder coiled and lightning flashing, his divine power withdrew and was gathered in, becoming silent and soundless.
Consequently, those within—of Yan, Qi, Qin, and Chu—and those without—in Japan and Goryeo—consulted him regarding the essentials of the mind and hastened to his seat.
Having obtained even a single word from the Master, they would adorn it in a scroll and preserve it as a treasure, as if it were more than enough.
A curved jade璧 (bi). The Master may truly be called one who brings no shame to the descendants of Miaoxi.
The lineage of Chan Master Xingyuan Ming of Lingyin Temple was transmitted from Huiming.
His courtesy name was Xingyuan, and his alternative style name was Huan Yin. He was the son of the Huangyan Xiang family in Taizhou; his mother was surnamed Chen. At seven...
The Master suffered from carbuncles for a year and was on the verge of death; he was placed upon his bed, and suddenly he was no longer there. After some time, he was found.
When asked how this had happened, he said, "Recently, while asleep, four youths carried me here. Those who understood this knew that the Master was protected by celestial deities.
Having grown up, he was dissatisfied with remaining in secular life and went to rely upon Master Baoguan of Dongshan, the Duke of Lu, in Wenzhou, to renounce the world.
He visited Master Zhuyundao at Mount Zituo in Xianju to inquire about the essentials of the mind, yet he did not achieve significant realization.
He then went to study under Yuansou of Jing Mountain, who asked, "Does it come from the eastern ridge or the western ridge? [Zhong] pointed to his straw sandals and replied, "These cost three coins."
[The Master] said, "I have bought it with money. The Old Man said, "Not yet; speak further. The Master said, "I am only like this; what about you, Reverend?
The Old Man said, "Out of consideration for your long journey, I grant you thirty blows. At these words, the Master realized its essential meaning.
After some time, he exhausted his own depths and served as the keeper of the treasury. Not long after, he emerged into the world at Wufeng in Ye, and later moved to Jinge. — Hong.

In the fifth year of the Wǔ period, he accompanied Lè Jìtán to the capital at the imperial command. Jìtán received an edict to reside at Tiānjiè Monastery and invited the Master to occupy the first seat.
There, the Master grasped the essential principles and upheld the core teachings, establishing a model for the monastic community.

Shortly thereafter, he was appointed to Jinshān. In the eleventh year, he ascended to the abbacy of Línyǐn. Students gathered there in great numbers, and the Way of the school flourished once more. When the Master first arrived—
The planning for the Great Hero Hall (Daeungjeon) was completed in a mere year; it stands majestic, rising like a mountain. Once, while in his room, he gave this instruction:
"The Lotus Peak has been eaten away by mayflies by half, yet why does it not know? He also said:

"Setting aside for a moment the Cold Spring Pavilion swallowing the Ravine Thunder Pavilion, as for the Southern High Peak and the Northern High Peak contending for their foreheads—where do they rank?"

His spiritual capacity was such that few could harmonize with it. He resided at Lingyin for ten years, through both winter and summer. Before long, the temple was consumed by fire until not a single thing remained.
He was arrested, and some advised him to make an early plan for himself; the Master paid no heed. With a serene countenance, he went to the authorities.
Before his interrogation had even begun, he recited a verse beneath the corridor and passed away while sitting upright. He was sixty-nine years old.
Biography of Chan Master Tianjing Jing:
Jing, whose courtesy name was Tianjing and alternative style name Puyin, was a native of Kuaiji in Yue. His father was Ni Ji, and his mother was of the Yan clan.
The Master first left home as a youth and received the precepts from Vinaya Master Ru of Zhaoqing. He was dignified and possessed far-reaching ambitions.
When Lord Han Zhuangjie Gong Xing taught him to compose prose, as soon as he spread the paper and took up the brush, his thoughts flowed forth in an inexhaustible stream that could not be restrained.
The Lord deeply admired and praised him. Subsequently, he followed Dharma Master Tian'an Ji to study the Tiantai teachings, mastering them all completely. Tiantai...
The various elders of the school vied with one another to invite him with letters, wishing for him to enter their gates as a disciple. The Master did not comply.

When Master Yuansou Duan was preaching the Dharma at Shuangjing, people revered him as the contemporary Miaoxi. The Master went to follow him; upon entering the gate, Yuansou let out a piercing shout.
The Master felt as if he had heard the roar of thunder, and all his attachments and fetters were completely cast off. He immediately prostrated himself in homage and asked again.
The Master replied with three or four turns of phrase, all of which satisfied the old man’s wishes. He was subsequently adopted as a son and appointed to oversee the secretariat.

After some time, he traveled to Jianye (Nanjing) to pay his respects to the Venerable Quanwu Yin at Dà Lóngxiáng Temple. Quanwu’s monastic style was lofty and rigorous, and he did not easily grant approval;
yet upon seeing the Master, he praised him most highly. Subsequently, he went to Línchuān to visit Yú Wénjìng Gōng Jí. Master Yú, in particular—

He was thus honored. After staying for ninety days, he returned. Others, such as Huang Wenxian Gong Qin, Menggu Zhongjie Gong Taibuhua, and Hanlin Xueshi Wei Gong Su, likewise addressed him as their teacher in identical terms, no differently than they had with Duke Yu.

His fame and conduct were proclaimed by the Xuanzheng Yuan. In the sixteenth year of the Zhi Zheng era of the Yuan dynasty, he was requested to take charge of the world at Changqing Temple in Kuaiji, and subsequently ascended to Tianyi Wanshou Chan Temple.
Those from all quarters who sought the Way heard of his reputation and came to him in submission.

Because the Master’s physical strength had declined, he grew weary of receiving guests and welcoming visitors; he therefore constructed a secluded hermitage where he retired to live out his final years. This is the Hutuo [Monastery] in Shanyin.
Furthermore, when our Great Ancestor ascended the dragon throne, the Master was selected for the Dharma assembly at Zhongshan Mountain.
Together with Dongming Mugong and Bifeng Jingong, he was specially summoned into the inner court, where they conversed at ease on the Way; having been granted a meal, they retired.
Thereafter, he took his leave to return to Hetang Monastery, intending to remain there for the rest of his life. Before long, the abbacy of Lingyin became vacant;

various monasteries presented formal letters and offerings to invite the Master to preside over it. Reluctantly, the Master accepted the invitation. Less than a year had passed when the disaster of Chongde occurred.

When the Master entered the monastery, barely a full ten days had elapsed, when the senior officials of the left and right wings of the temple remarked that the administration of the monastery was indeed...
The affairs were numerous and lacking in management; the administration was handled by the temple’s administrative monk-officials. The Master said, "Why do you not select a suitable person?

The assembly all replied, "There is one named Xian who is renowned for his many talents. In the past, he managed the estates of Chongde Temple and was able to clear away the wasteland to provide food for the fourfold assembly.
If he were promoted on account of his merit, who would say it was not right? The Master agreed. Previously, this had been heard of by the veteran monks, who had already admired Xian.
In order to secure the profits of the temple lands, he led a group of unprincipled bhikṣus to request that the former abbot replace him.

When it came time for Xian to be selected, the former abbot became greatly afraid that his own misconduct would be exposed; he fled to Chongde County and reported Xian’s transgressions. The magistrate and vice-magistrate of the county dismissed the matter and did not investigate it.
Just then, Jian arrived and submitted the case to the Ministry of Justice. After the Ministry of Justice had conducted its interrogation and established the facts, they [reported] to the Master...

He served as the abbot of the monastery. Having failed in his oversight and examination, the law dictates that he should be held liable by association. An official warrant was issued to arrest him. Someone said to the Master, "This was an event from three years ago;
moreover, you truly did not know of it and were unaware of the report. It would be appropriate for you to plead your own case."
The Master smiled and said, "Can one escape fixed karma? Upon arriving at the ministry, the official in charge asked him, "Are you aware of the transgressions for which you have been brought here?

He replied, "I am aware. The official said, "Since you are aware, you must write down a confession of your offenses and submit it. The Master immediately took up his brush and wrote exactly as the official had instructed.
When the Minister and the Secretaries read it, they were greatly astonished and all remarked, "This Master is a man of renowned virtue in the present age."

"It is only right that this should have happened; we must examine the matter thoroughly to ascertain the truth. The Master had no differing words to offer. Consequently, both were demoted to Shaanxi to become commoners.
Yuanwen was deeply remorseful and said through tears, "I am but a blade of grass or a shrub; how could I have intended to bring such harm upon the virtue of my Master?
Had I known it would come to this, I would rather die ten thousand deaths than do so. The Master paid him no heed. When they reached Baoying, he said:
An attendant said, "My four limbs feel somewhat different from usual; my retribution-body is likely nearing its end. That night they stayed at Ningguo Temple.
The abbot of the temple was an old acquaintance of the Master. They met with great joy. The Master’s younger sister’s husband, Chen Yian, was also there.
While serving as an official, he was transferred to Fengyang. As his route passed through the temple, the Master said with joy, "My remains now have a place to rest.
That evening, they shared a meal, and he spoke at length about the circumstances of his exile; yet he showed no sign of exhaustion.
The following morning, he suddenly sat upright with palms joined, repeatedly chanting the name of Amitābha Buddha, and then passed away peacefully. This was in the eleventh year of the Hongwu era.
It was the nineteenth day of the first month of that year. Yian and others performed the enshrinement of the remains in a sarcophagus to await the arrival of the Master’s younger paternal uncle.
Dao, his heart pierced with grief, dispatched his dharma-grandson Fanyì to carry the relics back to Baoying.
Within the bones, śarīras were clustered like pearls. When the local magistrate and the gentry came to view them, they all sighed in admiration.
He departed. His disciples prepared a grave beside the ancestral mound at Hetang and interred him there. He was sixty-seven years old and had been a monk for fifty-three years.
There were two volumes of recorded discourses from his three assemblies, and his collected poems and writings were titled *Pugwan-jip* (The Collected Works of Pukwon).
The Master’s appearance was imposing and dignified, and his disposition was as warm as spring. As for the worldly arts of traps, snares, and deceptive maneuvers, he did not know what they were.
By nature, he esteemed integrity and righteousness. Master Duangiang (En) formed a friendship with him that transcended age;

when Duangiang passed away, the Master published his collected poems and further requested Master Yu to compose an inscription for his stupa. He presided over three famous mountains, raising funds to restore dilapidated structures and achieving significant accomplishments.
In expounding the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and elucidating the insights of former sages, the Buddhist community has always relied upon him. [He has benefited] hundreds and thousands.
Among men, not one or two have ever seen [this]. In the end, he was exiled to death despite being innocent.
If we do not attribute this to fixed karma (*niyata-karma*), whom else can we blame?
The Biography of Master Tan’uo of Mengtang.
His courtesy name was Wumeng; he styled himself You’an. He was the son of Wang Shēn of Cixi, who passed the jinshi examination under the Song dynasty.
His father, Wang Lu, served under the Yuan. His mother was Lady Zhou. When the Master was six years old, his father passed away, and the lady [instructed him].
From his time at the local schools, Master You’s spirit and bearing were lofty; he possessed the ambition of one who can travel a thousand li in a single day. There was no book he did not explore.

He studied literature under Hu Changru, and his refined thoughts burst forth in abundance, flowing freely in all directions—forward, backward, upward, or downward—exactly as his mind desired to express.

His reputation suddenly surpassed that of all the veteran scholars. Soon thereafter, moved by certain realizations, he sighed and said, "Toiling over books and refining rhetoric—this is merely a worldly phenomenon.
Why not seek the Dharma that transcends the world? He then took leave of his wife and went to Changlu to pay homage to Master Xueting Chuan.
At twenty-three years of age, he shaved his head and became a monk. After receiving full ordination, he set his mind upon spiritual cultivation.
Regarding the teachings, he eventually set them aside to devote himself entirely to Chan meditation. When Xueting moved to Lingyin Monastery, the Master went to serve him there.

After Xueting passed away, Master Yuansou Duan came to succeed him. Yuansou’s standards were strict and severe; no one who was not a scholar of long-standing study dared to even step through his door.
The Master went straight forward to seek instruction, showing no fear whatsoever. As their spiritual sparks clashed, [the Master’s] sentiments...
He thought the path was cut off; yet after one turn, and continuing through the sixth and seventh, his speech became increasingly clear and forceful. Yuansou joyfully nodded in approval.
At the beginning of the Yuanyou era, an imperial decree was issued to establish a great Water-Land Assembly at Mount Jinshan. Eminent monks, worthy scholars, and high officials all gathered there.
The Master assisted Yuansou in expounding the essentials of the Dharma and engaging in debate with the assembly; his insights were brilliant and inspired, such that none could surpass him.

He did not recommend [himself for] honor. When the Prince of Zhennan heard of this, he invited him to Guangling, where he accorded him the utmost respect and hospitality. Only after many years did he dispatch Chongji.

In the fifth year of the Zhiyuan era, the military governor of Zhejiang East, together with the officials and magistrates of the prefectures and counties, requested that the Master take charge of the world at Baosheng in Qingyuan.
He was subsequently transferred to Kaishou in Cixi, and thrice appointed to Guoqing. Wherever the Master went, all...
Taking it as his own responsibility to shoulder the Great Dharma, he tempered his disciples with a diligence that seemed never to suffice, and many among them attained awakening.
At Reiryū-ji, he changed the succession from the administrative system (jia-yi-bing) to a Zen monastery;

the Master was its founding patriarch, and because of him, the temple’s prestige increased until it ranked alongside the most famous monasteries. Once, when a typhoon arose over the sea, torrential rain poured down like a cascade.

The multi-storied buildings and long corridors all collapsed, and the master’s quarters were likewise buried under the ruins. People thought the master must have been ground to powder; they hurriedly removed the debris to search for him.
There, a massive beam lay propped across his meditation seat, and the master sat upright beneath it as if protected by some divine power.

Throughout his life, the master occupied four monastic seats; whether departing or remaining, he followed the conditions of his destiny without the slightest hesitation or attachment. Not long after...
He retired from public life. The monastic community admired his lofty reputation and virtue, and they frequently opened rooms for him to dwell in.

The Master instructed his disciples, saying: "I and you all must investigate the school of Emptiness (*śūnyatā*). You should cast aside concern for your physical bodies and forget both sleep and food, so as to eliminate the habitual tendencies accumulated over kalpas;
only then will the ground of your mind become luminous. From that time on, he took but one meal per day and sat in meditative concentration throughout the night.
He reached the age of eighty-nine. In the second year of the Hongwu era, he was summoned by those on the Way and lodged at Tianjie Temple.
After his audience with the Emperor, His Majesty took pity on his advanced age and released him to return to the mountains. Four years later, he passed away without illness.
His final words were: "The three realms are like empty flowers; they are like smoke swept away by the wind. The six sense-objects are illusory shadows."

Like pouring hot water on snow, from antiquity to the present, only this single nature remains. My illusory body shall now enter extinction; after my passing, it will be cremated and the bones reduced to dust.
Do not build a stupa to burden future generations. The Master’s physique was well-proportioned and his forehead broad;
he stood tall like a crane amidst a flock of chickens. His literary inspiration gushed forth like a spring; whenever anyone brought scrolls seeking poetry or prose, [he would grant them].

The manuscripts accumulated like bundles of bamboo shoots. When the weather was bright and fine, he would leisurely take his seat and wield his brush with rapid strokes until everything was finished in an instant.

Whether long or short, refined or coarse, there was nothing that did not conform to the standard. Master Yuan Wenqing once pointed to the teacher and said to others, "This man is one among the Arhats.
Observing his compositions, they increasingly approach those of the ancient masters since the crossing of the Yangtze."
The worthy ones of old followed in the footsteps of Su and Li, boasting of a style that was bold, spirited, and direct.

They led one another until this became the prevailing custom, and this chronic malpractice persisted for nearly two hundred years. I did not expect that a withered scholar from the mountain forests would be able to exert himself to such an extent.
Zhang Gongzhu, a Hanlin Academician, remarked: "Master E’s appearance is grand and dignified; his observance of the precepts is strict and pure; his writing..."
His chapters are concise yet archaic; he is the sole venerable elder today in the ocean of Chan. His being esteemed by the gentry is of this nature.
Throughout his life, the Master’s writings were abundant, yet he never preserved any drafts. In his later years, he revised the *Lidai Gao-seng Zhuan* (Biographies of Eminent Monks Through the Ages);
his penmanship was vigorous and powerful, and those who recognized his talent remarked that he had attained the mastery of Sima Qian, the Grand Historian. Even the King of Japan...
Though dwelling in the remote lands of the Eastern Barbarians, he also admired the Way of the Master and repeatedly sent petitions to welcome him there. The Master resolutely refused to go.
The King and his attendants plotted to abduct him and bring him back. However, Wan'erdu, the Commissioner for the Propagation of Comfort in Zhejiang, hid him, and he thus escaped.

From that time forward, whenever he encountered a calligraphic work by the Master’s hand, he would invariably purchase it at great expense to take with him, marveling at how it could emit extraordinary light.
Such was the esteem in which he was held abroad.
Leji Lezhuanzongle was a native of Linhai in Taizhou.
His courtesy name was Jitan, and his alternative style name was Quanshi. At the age of eight, he followed Xuyao Yin to study Buddhism;
at fourteen, he tonsured his hair; and at twenty, he received full ordination. In the fourth year of the Hongwu era, he resided at Mount Jing. [Emperor] Taizu...
The Emperor Gaozong summoned a Buddhist monk of realized virtue from Jiangnan. The Master responded to the call and was pleased by his words;
he was ordered to reside at Tianjie Temple. The Emperor established a grand memorial Dharma assembly at Taiping Xingguo Temple on Mount Jiangshan.

There, the Master stayed in the fasting quarters for one month, abstaining from meat and strong flavors. Wearing a leather cap and holding a jade scepter, he ascended the hall to face the Great Hero (Śākyamuni Buddha) and performed [the rites].
He performed three prostrations as an offering. An imperial decree was issued to assemble the spirits of the deceased and lead them into the hall to pay homage to the Three Buddhas.

He commanded the Master to ascend the seat and preach the Dharma. The Emperor visited him in person, bestowing meals upon him without fail on any given day, and composed poems for him each time, addressing him as "Old Man Le.

In the winter of the tenth year, he decreed that the Master should provide annotated commentaries on the *Heart Sūtra*, the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, and the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, and compose hymns of praise.
The Buddhist Musical Score. In the year Ding-si, having returned to court from an imperial mission to the Western Regions, he was appointed Right Street Overseer of the Sangha (Youjie Shanshi).

Consequently, the Emperor ordered him to grow out his hair, intending to appoint him to a Confucian office. The Master obeyed the command, and when his hair had grown long, the Emperor summoned him to grant him official rank.

The Master declined a second time, seeking exemption on the grounds that he wished to remain within the Buddhist community for the rest of his life. The Emperor praised this with admiration and granted his request, bestowing upon him the title "Exempted Official" (Mianguan) to honor his resolve.
Biography. Daoyan of Xiangcheng possessed extraordinary aspirations. He would sway his knees and chant aloud with such lofty air that he seemed oblivious to those around him.
His master would often rebuke him with a stern expression, saying, "Is this the speech of a son of the Śākya? The scholar Song Gong Lian once praised the Master’s portrait, saying:
"The son of Xiaoyin and the grandson of Huiji; endowed with great merit and virtue, he was sufficient to shoulder the Buddha-dharma and realize great wisdom."

His wisdom was sufficient to subdue the armies of Māra. In the snap of a finger, he awakened to the four shouts and two mysteries; he unified a thousand sutras and ten thousand treatises within a single gate.
His "upward" barrier was like a drum smeared with poison—striking it meant certain death. His mechanism of killing and giving life was like a diamond sword—contacting it caused one to flee.
He repeatedly presided over famous mountains, and his teachings were received far and near. By imperial decree, he was promoted to the capital monastery, and his fame overflowed.
A member of the court nobility, you received the prophecy long ago at the assembly on Vulture Peak; today, you have been selected for the knowledge of the Sovereign of Ten Thousand Chariots.

As the Milky Way shines and turns, the Imperial Edict has bestowed its harmonious verses upon this complete volume. With such abundant favor, the Jade Voice summoned you for an audience in the Purple Palace.
Standing firm like a central pillar in midstream, you turn the Wheel of Dharma throughout the great earth; you are truly a Chan master of the ten directions.
He was a leader among the monastic community and one who shared the same path and rank as the ancient worthies.

Later, during the persecution of the followers of Hu Weiyong, he was arrested along with his teacher and reduced to the status of a common monk (*sanseng*) to perform manual labor at the construction of a temple. Xu investigated the matter and realized he had been wronged, so he was released and restored to his former position as Right Supervisor of the Sangha (*you shanshi*).
Not long after, he was granted leave to return to Mount Chafeng due to old age; while crossing the river, he passed away at Jiangpu.
Shifosi. The Master was profoundly versed in both ancient and modern learning; whatever scripture he glanced over, he could immediately recite from memory.

He was skilled at composing literary works, and his *Quanshi ji* (Collected Works of Quan Shi) circulated throughout the world. Among the eminent monks of the early Ming dynasty, the Master was renowned alongside Fuxianxin;
yet while Fuxianxin was unrestrained and unconventional, the Master was prudent and meticulous, and thus the harm he suffered was notably lighter. Alas! This too was fortunate.
The Biography of Chan Master Gufeng Deming. His style name was Gufeng.
He was the son of Zhu Shi of Changguo, Ming. His father was named Youcheng, and his mother was Huang Shi.
His father was friends with the monk Jie of Putuo Mountain; having heard the sound of a rooster, Jie entered the Way. Whenever he preached the Dharma, he would invariably flap his wings.
He was named Chijiao. Long after Jie had passed away, his mother dreamed that Jie came to stay with her as a guest. Upon waking, she became pregnant and gave birth after fourteen months.
He did not enjoy playing or frolicking; instead, he frequently sat upright in the *paryaṅka* (lotus) posture. At the age of seventeen, he became a full monk (*bhikṣu*).
Moved by a profound resolve to seek the Way, he first visited Master Zhuxi Tan at Tiantong, and subsequently met Master Huiji Xi at...
Jingci and the two elders nodded in approval, yet the Master did not consider himself satisfied. From then on, he redoubled his self-exertion, vowing that realization was his ultimate goal.
Upon arriving at Shuanglin, he met Master Mingji Jun; in the mere instant they first beheld one another, their voices harmonized like the duet of the *xun* and *chi* pipes.
He ordered the keeper of the treasury to assemble the Japanese envoys and welcomed Mingjue as National Preceptor (Guoshi).

The Master escorted them to the seashore, at which time Master Zhutian Lin also arrived from Xuedou; seeing that the Master’s countenance was extraordinary, he invited him back to his mountain retreat.

He was seated in the foremost position. From that time on, his many doubts were suddenly dispelled. Furthermore, he invited Master Zhongfang Lun to establish a hermitage in the Peach Blossom Gully, where they exhorted and inspired one another.
In their leisure, they would read the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, remaining within the threshold of their door for five years.
His reputation grew daily, leading Zhu Tian to exclaim: "The Eye and Lamp of the human and heavenly realms remains resplendent as if still present."

He served as an official in the Administration Commission for Buddhist and Tibetan Affairs (Xingxuan Yuan) and was invited to reside at Dongchan Monastery in Songjiang, where he burned incense to succeed Zhutian, never forgetting what he had realized.
He moved again to Baoning Monastery in Jiqing, where he sat for fifteen summer retreats. He refined those who came to study him with the utmost skillful means;
when he had the capacity to spare, he restored ruined sites and repaired what was damaged, leaving no detail, great or small, neglected. Thus his reputation for excellence became even more prominent.
At that time, he was known as Jian-shen; there were none who did not wish to associate with the Master. He moved three times, eventually residing at Daochang on Lake [Tiantai].
After two years had passed, the seat of Jingci Monastery became vacant. The Chancellor of the Provincial Administration, Prince Kangli, earnestly invited the Master to preside over it.

During the final years of the Yuan dynasty, military turmoil raged and state affairs could no longer be sustained. By the time the Sagely Dynasty (the Ming) had begun, the Master was already advanced in years.

He returned to the Zhulin Hermitage at the site of his former practice. One day, manifesting a slight illness, he instructed his disciples not to allow the fourfold assembly to wear hempen garments or wail.
He requested a brush and wrote a verse, after which he passed away at the age of seventy-nine. Upon cremation, his cranial bone remained unbroken.
The śarīra relics emerged from amidst the ashes and were enshrined in a stupa on the eastern ridge. The scholar Song Jingliao composed an inscription for it.
Great Master Ji’ān Liang, whose courtesy name was Yongzhen, took Ji’ān as his style name. He was the son of the Fan family of Wuxian County, Suzhou, and a descendant of the Duke Wenzheng.
He was a tenth-generation descendant. At the age of fifteen, he received the tonsure and full ordination at Yingfu Monastery.

At that time, Xiaoyin resided at Longxiang in Jiqing, where the path of the Dharma was being vigorously propagated. The Master went to visit him; during their exchange of questions and answers, both the staff and the shout were employed.
His ordinary sentiments were suddenly cast away. Later, when Xiaoyin cited a saying to interrogate him, the Master’s words became even more vehement.
Xiaoyin smiled and said, "You have attained it indeed, but what of the second meaning? The Master did not slacken, becoming increasingly devout. After a long time, he finally attained realization.
Clouds vanish into the sky and rivers flow on; there is no lingering obstruction. Xiaoyin said, "Now you know that I did not deceive you.

He was of a talent for transcending the world, having served at Shousheng in Yue and Tianzhang in Yue before moving to Zhongtianzhu in Hangzhou. At that time, the realm was in great chaos and the fires of war followed one after another.
All the monasteries of the two mountains, north and south, were reduced to blazing flames. Lingyin, which had long been renowned as a place of supreme excellence—
The site was filled with cool smoke and white grass, appearing desolate amidst the evening light; passersby could not help but sigh at the sight.

When the Duke of Kanglei served as the Imperial Preceptor (Chengxiang) of the Zhejiang Provincial Administration, he carefully selected renowned monks capable of restoring ruined sites, concluding that Master Mo was the most suitable candidate.
He earnestly requested that he reside there. Once the Master arrived, he cleared away the thorny thickets and thatched together a hut to provide lodging for scholars from all quarters.
Although it was a time of decline, his instructions to the assembly were even more fervent and urgent. His words were as follows:
"The single school of Bodhidharma is nearly exhausted and crumbling away. You must exert yourselves as if your hair were on fire. Yet, among hundreds and thousands...
The Dharma-gate and its immeasurable, wondrous meanings can be fully understood within the tip of a single hair. If you understand this transformation, the great earth may become gold;
you should accept it without hesitation, otherwise you will incur the shame of eating the food of others in vain.
Time flows like lightning; regarding the supreme matter, you must all urgently cultivate yourselves. Among those who study through inquiry, many rely on these words.

As for his entry [into nirvana]: when his conditions for transformation were exhausted, he personally drafted a list of his clothing and assets, which he deposited in the public treasury and distributed among his friends.

Looking at those around him, he said, "At the hour of the snake (10 a.m. tomorrow, I shall pass away. When the time arrived, he bathed, sat upright, and entered stillness. The Master was by nature straightforward and simple.

Although he confronted others' faults face-to-face, there was nothing remaining in his breast. In his dealings with others, regardless of their seniority or juniority, he met everyone with singular sincerity.
When composing verses, he never premeditated; yet the words that issued forth were complete and perfect, as if they had been previously drafted.

In expounding the Great Dharma, he did not strive for ornamental embellishment, yet the intent of the West’s transmission was naturally clarified. Furthermore, he [expounded] the contemplative gates of the Pure Land.
When he was on a sea voyage, he practiced both [Buddhism and Confucianism] concurrently, never for a moment becoming lax. His realization was truly outstanding.
This is the biography of Chan Master Nanshi Wenxiu.
Chan Master Nanshi Wenxiu cultivated both Confucianism and Buddhism; his mastery of both the school (zong) and the teachings (shuo) was exquisite. He possessed transcendent talent and harbored...
Possessing a magnificent and sublime spirit, he traveled to Lingyan to meet Master Zhongren, just as Ciming had met Huanglong.
Later, when the Master entered the world, he offered a fragrant incense cake (bānxiāng) to succeed him, never forgetting his origins.

He first resided at Pumen in Suzhou, then at Lingyan, and thirdly moved to become the abbot of Wanshou. Not long after, he retired to the banks of the Wusong River, where he spent his days with the mountains.
The old man of Ono delighted in speaking meaningless words and had largely forgotten the ways of the human world.

Upon the accession of our enlightened and sagacious Son of Heaven, an edict was issued to all Confucians, Buddhists, and Daoists throughout the realm who were profoundly versed in literary meaning, charging them with the compilation of the Great Canon.
The Monk responded to this summons and rose to the task; he remained in the capital for three years until the writing was completed. At that time, it coincided with the state’s undertaking of...
At the Great Repayment-of-Gratitude Assembly (Bao'en Dazhaihui), the Abbot was invited to participate. Before long, the abbot of Hangzhou was absent from the service.

The Monastic Registrar, Master Ri, declared that none other than National Teacher Nan-shi could suffice for the role. Thereupon, the Master joyfully accepted and set out. Nan-zhou Pu-qia sent him a poem which said:
"In robes of black as water, he hastens to the Jade Capital; His beloved son has come to visit, and his two eyes shine bright. How could there..."
His writings pursue the legacy of Li Bai and Du Fu; I dare say his transmission has reached the heights of Tai and Heng. Under the green lamp and night rain, there is a pact by the cold window;
amidst yellow leaves and autumn wind, there lies the sentiment for one’s native land. It is said that Master Sheng can still gather stones; let my small boat be moored early at the city of Helu.

In the eleventh year of the Hongwu era, during a moment of leisure from the myriad affairs of state, His Majesty took pity upon us, his disciples who follow the Buddha, observing that few among us were able to master the scriptural teachings or deeply investigate the study of Chan.
He graciously issued an imperial decree ordering us to practice the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra*, the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, and the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*.
We were to lecture on these texts by day and practice seated meditation by night, with the aim of attaining thorough understanding.
The Master then spoke seven verses in praise. The first verse begins: "The Sage Emperor personally received the prophecy of Vulture Peak;

Holding the golden wheel in hand, he governs the ten thousand regions. He issues an edict to exhort the monastic community to study and practice; The monasteries suddenly awaken to a brilliant radiance. The final verse concludes:
"To exhaustively master the scriptures and participate in Zen meditation— This is a great karmic affinity, not a minor one. How fortunate to have encountered it!"
If Your Majesty can pay close attention, why should we, your followers, not apply even greater effort?

There are his *Recorded Sayings* (yulu) from Pumen, Lingyan, and Jingshan, as well as one volume of eulogies for Buddhas and Patriarchs, which circulate in the world. His final years have not yet been investigated.
The Biography of Chan Master Jin Baian.
His name was Jin, with the style name Xibai. He was the son of the Yao family of Wu Commandery. At the age of seven, his intelligence and insight were extraordinary.
One day he asked his mother, "I am troubled by the impermanence and flux of worldly phenomena; may I seek the Dharma that transcends the world? His mother replied:
"Leaving home is extremely difficult. You are still young; how can you possibly endure it? He replied, "My heart delights in this; for me, there is no suffering.
His mother pleaded with him incessantly, but knowing that his resolve could not be shaken, she allowed him to follow Master Daoyuan Yan of Baoji Monastery in Wu County.
Later, he met Master Guding Ming at Mount Jing, where he attained a profound realization of the Way. His reputation shone brilliantly.

He emerged from among the monastic communities. In the *dingyou* year of the Zhèng period, he took up residence at Ruiguang Monastery in Suzhou. At that time, Tianning Temple in Jiaxing suffered a fire;
both the prefectural governor and his deputy, deeming no one but the Master fit to restore it, prepared ceremonial gifts and dispatched envoys to earnestly invite him.
Once the Master arrived, before long, he appeared as if the Tuṣita Heaven Palace had descended into the human world. Those who passed by... [could not help but be moved].

He failed to pay homage to, venerate, or praise the Imperial Preceptor, the Great Treasure Dharma King (Dishi Dabaofawang). Regarding the conduct of his worthy teacher, he bestowed upon him a formal title.
The Master had lost his father in childhood; with only his mother remaining, he departed from the city by one *she* and built the Gūyún Hermitage to provide for her support.
When others criticized this, the Master explained to them, saying: "Do you not see the venerable elder Biānpú? Why do you speak thus?"
This was made easy by the Master. In the first year of the Hongwu era, an imperial edict was issued appointing the Master as the abbot of Dajianjie Monastery.
During his leisure from the myriad affairs of state, the Emperor frequently summoned him into the inner court; his responses were often to the Emperor’s satisfaction.

For the Master was profoundly versed in the scriptures of the Western Heavens (India) as well as the various texts of the Eastern Lu (Confucianism). When he engaged in discussion with scholars of high rank, his words flowed forth like falling jade shavings. Thus, all...

He delighted in associating with them. In the fourth year, he commissioned Master Tongchi to preside over the Dharma assembly at Mount Zhongshan; all its ritual protocols and regulations were such that they could be transmitted for posterity.
Soon thereafter, as his mother had reached an advanced age, he appointed Master Le of Mount Jing as his successor and returned once more to his mountain hermitage.
In the winter of the fifth year, an imperial edict was issued to reconvene the assembly as it had been in the fourth year.

The Emperor’s carriage arrived in person, and by imperial decree, the Master was commissioned to expound upon the primary truth (*paramārtha-satya*). From the dukes and marquises down to the common officials, all gathered around to listen;

there were none who did not find joy and submission. One day, he suddenly said to his disciples: "I have a karmic debt from a former life that remains unsettled; I must surely repay it. You all should not [be concerned]."
The world encountered him; before long, he manifested a slight illness. He declined medical treatment and the consumption of medicine or food, passing away in accordance with natural destiny.

Upon his cremation, the śarīra relics were beyond counting; those who witnessed it vied with one another to take them away. The Master’s spiritual appearance was noble and majestic, and his wisdom and eloquence were versatile and profound.

Taking the teachings and the monastic discipline as his personal responsibility, he did not accumulate private wealth. Whenever he received offerings of property, he would immediately distribute them to provide for the poor.
He was truly a great figure of the Dharma-gate.
The Biography of Chan Master Jueyuan Tantan:
Tantan, whose courtesy name was Jueyuan, was a native of Tiantai. He resided at Faguosi Temple in Yue. At that time, there was Guangzhi Xiaoyin Yun...
Master Gong was preaching the Dharma in Central India. When the Master (Wuxue) arrived there, he explained at length his earnest quest for the Way.
Guangzhi rebuked him, saying: "That which enters from the outside is certainly not one's own family treasure. The Way resides within oneself; how could it be sought from another?
The Master withdrew and sat alone in a room in profound stillness. After a long time, he had made no progress. One day, Guangzhi raised the story of Baizhang’s Wild Fox. The Master—
Dawo said, "The Buddha-dharma has fallen into my hands. Guangzhi asked, "What principle have you seen that you dare to speak such great words?
The Master spread out both hands and said, "Not worth a single coin. Guangzhi nodded in agreement.

In the year Bingshen, when the Imperial Army had pacified Jianye, the Master went to pay his respects at the imperial camp gate. The Emperor, seeing that the Master’s countenance and bearing were extraordinary, once sighed and said, "This..."
He was a monk of great merit. He was appointed as the abbot of Jiangshan Taiping Xingguo Chan Temple.

At a time when the year was one of famine, the Master transformed his food offerings into sustenance to provide for them; thus, none among the assembly lacked anything. Many of the people from the fields below the mountain wished to enroll in the military registers.

Fearing that the temple’s fields would fall into ruin and neglect, the Master petitioned the Emperor and had them returned [to the temple]. Furthermore, the timber forests of the mountain were being cut down by woodcutters.

The Master again presented a memorial to the Emperor. The Emperor bestowed a single sword upon the Master, decreeing: "Whoever dares to fell timber from these mountains shall be executed. Thus, the mountain trees were preserved.
In the following year, the year Dingyou, Longxiang was renamed Tianjie. By imperial edict, the Master was appointed to preside over it.
Whenever a grand memorial service (guǎngjiàn fǎhuì) was held, the Master invariably ascended the seat to proclaim the essentials of the Dharma. The Emperor personally led his ministers to attend.

The Emperor’s grace was most generous and abundant. Disciples from near and far, hearing of his reputation, flocked to him; the hall and banquet area became so crowded there was nowhere left to accommodate them.

Previously, the monks’ hall, the quarters, and the storehouse had been temporarily used by the authorities to store military equipment, which remained there for a long time without being returned. When the Emperor saw this, he [took action].

He was urgently commanded to emerge from seclusion. In the first year of the Hongwu era, the Shanshi Yuan (Bureau for the Propagation of Buddhism) was established, with a rank equivalent to the second grade of the imperial attendants.

The Master was specially invested as the Great Chan Master Yanfan Shanshi Liguo Chongjiao, appointed as the abbot of the Great Tianjie Temple, and charged with presiding over the Buddhist affairs of all mountains.
An imperial edict was issued, granting him the privilege of wearing a purple square-cut robe. Those scholars of the Confucian tradition regarded the followers of Śākyamuni as...
"The world's parasites must be eradicated. The Emperor showed this memorial to the Master. The Master said, "Confucius regarded the Buddha as a sage of the West.
From this, we know that a true Confucian need not reject Buddhism; one who rejects Buddhism is certainly not a true Confucian."

The Emperor likewise declined to grant his permission, considering that the Buddha’s teachings already provided auxiliary support for the King’s governance. In the summer of the gengxu year, he was commissioned as an envoy to the Western Regions.
In the autumn of the xinhai year, he arrived at the kingdom of Śrīkṣetra. There he proclaimed the majesty and virtue of the Son of Heaven;

the King of that land was exceedingly delighted and lodged him at Fo-shan Temple, treating him with the etiquette due to a teacher. One day, he called his attendants and said, "I shall not be able to return to my mission."
He sat upright in the full lotus posture. At midnight, he asked, "Is the sun about to rise? He replied, "It has not yet.

After a while, he asked again, and this continued three or four times. Finally, he said, "The sun has risen," and passed away with serene composure. That day was the Bingzi day. Five days later, his countenance remained as if alive.
The King paid him profound reverence and admiration; he carved fragrant wood for a coffin and gathered incense to serve as fuel, then constructed an altar.
He was then cremated. The Master had a broad forehead and full cheeks; his head was flat and his ears large. His face was the color of red jade, and his ears were as white as white jade or snow.
His eyes shone with a brilliant luster that seemed to pierce others. When students beheld him, they were struck with awe even without his exerting any stern authority.
Yet, when one approached him, he was radiantly warm like the spring. When encountering practitioners of Chan, he responded according to their capacity, never striving for artifice or cleverness.
Those who heard him naturally attained realization and insight. Although his rank was exalted and his reputation profound, he always conducted himself as if he were a man of humble means;

he never harbored even a hair’s breadth of self-conceit. He was a man of few words and smiles, expressing joy and anger with natural sincerity; he could not alter his countenance based on whether someone was noble or lowly.
Nevertheless, he assisted and supported the religious teachings without daring to forget them for a single moment, even amidst the vast halls and fine carpets of the imperial court. From...
He was summoned for an audience with the Emperor. Relying on the scriptures and upholding the treatises, he always exhausted his accumulated learning in his responses.
The restoration of Songyuan Monastery and the exemption from private rents were both petitions submitted by this Master.
Yiyuan Ninggong transmitted [the lineage] to Yongning.
"Yiyuan" was his courtesy name; he styled himself the "Vanity Child" (Xuhuanzi). He was the son of the Zhu family from Tongzhou in Huaidong. The Zhu family was an ancient clan of officials.
At six years of age, he entered the local school and was able to comprehend the great principles of the classics. At nine, he left secular life and relied upon his kinsmen.
The venerable Yinmu resided at Lihesi Temple. Prince Tong of Henan, marveling at his youth, recognized his potential and entrusted him to the monastic authorities.

He was granted a certificate of ordination and became a śramaṇa. From then on, he traveled about like a wandering cloud, visiting various elder meditation masters, yet found no point of resonance with them.

At Mount Jiaozishan, he practiced meditative concentration with great diligence; whenever he fell into slight drowsiness, he would carry sand on his head or transport bricks, and hang wooden boards [over himself].
He sat in meditation in the open air for five years. He then went to Mount Taihu in Huaixi to seek realization from Master Wuyong Kuan.

The master’s gate was strictly austere; as soon as the teacher entered the doorway, the master shouted at him with a harsh voice and drove him out. The teacher performed his prostrations outside the door.
He stood with his palms joined. After a long while, [the Master] granted him entry. Upon entering, he was asked, "Where are you from? The Master replied, "Tongzhou.
[The Master] asked, "How has the rise and fall of the Huai and Hai regions been of late? He replied, "The waters overflow the sun, submerging everything; not a single drop remains.

[The Master] said, "It does not stay in the troughs or channels. The Master said, "Please, Master, speak for me. The official then became dazed. The Master withdrew to his meditation hall and did not sleep the entire night. One...
In the morning, he heard Master Gong cite the Yunmen saying, "A single thought does not arise. Before the sound had even faded, he attained realization. Master Gong commanded him to recite a verse.
When the verse was finished, he let out a thunderous shout. Master Gong asked, "What was that shout for? He replied, "Before the mountain of melons, he swallows the flat yoke."

"Having seized the pure wind, I have stripped it of its skin. The Master was so startled that sweat broke out over his entire body. He said, "Only today do I understand the Master’s application [of the Dharma]. He served him for three years.
Consequently, he presented the Master with a portrait of himself inscribed by the Venerable Duānyá Yì, upon which he had personally written a single flower.

He conferred it upon the Master, saying: "Your karmic affinity lies in Zhejiang; when you meet a dragon, there you shall dwell. When you encounter a pond, there you shall reside. During the Yányòu era, he departed for...
Guangde lived in seclusion within a great cave, thatching it with reeds. Not long after, the Dragon Pond at Yixing invited the Master to establish a Chan residence there.
As his name coincided with a prophetic record, the Master joyfully accepted the invitation. He constructed several dozen rooms and named them the Yuguan Xinghua Hermitage.
At the summit of the mountain was a dragon pond; whenever the dragon emerged and caused great floods, the local people suffered greatly. The Master...

He summoned the dragon and received the Three Refuges precepts; thereafter, the dragon did not emerge again. After the Master had lived there for some time, he grew weary of it as being not yet sufficiently secluded and profound.

He chose a remote precipice to build a dwelling. Reaching a place where the cliffs stood sheer like a plane, he carved wood to create a walkway, using hooks, rings, and chains to suspend the planks in mid-air.
For two years, his feet did not cross the threshold of the door. The Master took such reclusion as his practice.
His heart was constrained by circumstances beyond his control, and he reluctantly made one departure. Shortly thereafter, he returned to Longchi due to illness.
In the *Renwu* year of the Zhizheng era, the Jiangnan Branch of the Xuanzheng Yuan appointed the Master to preside over Dahuazang Temple. The Master recommended Longmen Ying to take his place.
The following year, he was again ordered to fill the post at Tiantong; the Master firmly declined on account of his illness. Song Wenxuan remarked that the Master had attained the Dharma...

Thereafter, he remained steadfastly committed to the welfare of the common people as his primary concern. When he presided over major monasteries, he repeatedly retired to Dragon Pond (Longchi) for cultivation.

Although Tiantong was indeed ranked among the Five Mountains, he would shake his head and refuse it. His lofty character and rigorous integrity were like those of the auspicious qilin and majestic phoenix—visible from afar but impossible to approach.
How truly virtuous he was! In the year Wuzi of the Zhizheng era, an imperial decree arrived summoning him to enter the capital and preach.
He preached the Dharma in the Longguang Hall, and the Emperor was delighted. He bestowed upon him a golden-embroidered dharma robe, a jade ring, and a master title.
Shortly thereafter, by imperial decree, he traveled to Mount Wutai carrying incense, where he experienced the auspicious omen of five-colored radiant light. Upon taking his leave, he returned south;

while en route to Yangzhou, Prince Zhennan led his consorts and attendants to invite the Master into the palace, where they received the full precepts from him. The Prince then dispatched his Minister of the Household to escort him back to Long.
In the sixth month of summer in the *jiyou* year of the Great Ming Hongwu era, Master Chi fell slightly ill.
He instructed his disciples to prepare paper for inner and outer robes, saying, "I am about to depart. When someone offered him medicinal decoctions, he waved them away.
Moving his reliquary shrine from Xinghua Hermitage to his residence on a remote peak, at dawn the Master rose, bathed, and donned the paper robes. He then requested a brush and wrote:
The verse says: "For seventy-eight years he guarded his simplicity; it was a clear case of failure. A clay ox turns over at the bottom of the sea;
snow flies in the midsummer sky. Having finished writing this, he lay on his side and passed away. Upon cremation, five-colored light appeared.
His teeth, jaw, tongue, and the rosary he held remained unburnt. The śarīra were beyond counting, and the smoke reached Zhonglin, where they also accumulated.
His remains were piled up as people vied with one another to break off branches to take them. After sifting through the ashes and soil, those who obtained relics were numerous.

His disciples divided the remaining bones and those that had not decayed, constructing stupas at five locations. The Master’s appearance was majestic and imposing; he stood over seven feet tall. His voice was resonant and loud.
In his dealings with others, he did not allow his mind to be swayed by their status, whether they were noble or humble. Wherever he went...
There was no one toward whom he did not show inclination. Among those he treated with the highest courtesy were Dörjö, the Right Chancellor of the Secretariat;
Biébùhuá, the Left Chancellor of the Jiangzhe Provincial Administration Commission; Qáo Wénmǐn Gōng Mèngfǔ; and Fēng Zhìzhèn, the Palace Attendant.
When the four classes of people came to offer incense, silk, robes, and footwear, their shoulders brushed against one another and their sleeves met; there were no idle days.

The Master accepted these offerings and immediately distributed them to others, never harboring even a hair’s breadth of stinginess. As for his own lifestyle, he wore coarse cloth robes and ate simple food, yet he appeared to have an abundance.
Whenever he composed literary verses, he did so without deliberate effort; as he took up the paper and set the brush to ink, the profound meaning flowed forth naturally.
He manifested himself [in the world]. There are four volumes of his recorded sayings (*yulu*) in circulation.
Regarding Yue Zhi, the biography of Master Chongyu states:
Yue Zhi’s courtesy name was Yue Zhi; he was the son of the Chen family of Piling. His mother conceived him after dreaming that a monk with a long white beard entered her chamber.

From birth, his constitution was frail; nine out of ten days he was afflicted by illness. Because of a dream, his parents hoped to seek the spiritual protection of the Śākya clan to cure him, so they ordained him as a *śrāmaṇera*.
Soon thereafter, he received full ordination and became a *bhikṣu*. From dawn until dusk, he devoted himself solely to the practice of contemplating the mind.
He met Master Yuansou Duan and Master Fohui Yi, from whom he sharpened his resolve even further. Although [surrounded by] golden walls and iron...
The wall must be torn down before he will stop. The two gentlemen also expected the Master to establish himself, and thus their exhortations were most earnest.

The Master, however, was in haste to seek realization; he traveled again to Zhongtianzhu Mountain to attend upon Master Guangzhi Xin, remaining in his service for over ten years until he fully mastered his Way.
When Zhang Gong Qiyuan, the Censor-in-Chief, asked Guangzhi, "In selecting a Buddha..."
"Among the monks in this assembly, are there any who do not oppose the Prajñāpāramitā?

Guangzhi replied, "As for the strict observance of the precepts and the consistency between one's words and deeds, there is only Master Chongyu. Since he received ordination, his side has not touched the bedding for thirty years.
Lord Zhang deeply praised and marveled at this; from that day forth, the Master’s reputation and influence began to flourish.
In the Zen forest, when Nanzen began his career in the world, both monastics and laypeople followed him with great enthusiasm. One day, he ordered plasterers to whitewash the walls.
Within the wall, there was a protrusion as if something were embedded; upon prying it open, they discovered an image of Prince Siddhārtha, carved from a Buddha’s tooth.
The Master summoned artisans to gild it with gold, but the gold split apart, and śarīras surged forth from within.
A small, exquisitely carved incense hall was constructed to enshrine it; this too was brought about by the spiritual sincerity of Master Daofa. Soon after, he moved to Yuantong in Jiuyang.
At the beginning of the Song dynasty, the divine monk Daoji (De Gong) was about to pass away.
He had a tower constructed of piled green stones and said to his disciples, "If this tower turns red, I shall return. Subsequently, Master Yuanji Min arrived to preside over the monastery.
During his dharma assemblies, the fruit on his stupa turned red, which people found extraordinary; they called him the "Ancient Buddha.
When he was nearing death, it happened again, and he left a prophecy containing an omen that after three hundred years, Buddhist affairs would flourish greatly.

On the evening the Master entered the monastery, the assembly of monks dreamed that the public official arrived, and his stupa shone with a brilliant light for an entire month. People marveled at this even more, saying that from—
Master Min reached the number of three hundred disciples; that he was able to move others was certainly not in vain.

Following the destruction caused by a disaster, the Master undertook a great reconstruction of the temple’s timber and earthworks, miraculously manifesting a celestial palace. The Duke of Rong, Huinichi, [supported this endeavor].
A high-ranking minister of the court was appointed as the Commander-in-Chief of Jiangxi, where he observed the rites due to a younger brother.

Furthermore, when our Great Founder (Taizu) promoted the Buddhist teachings and established the Saisei-in (Office for the Propagation of Buddhism), he commanded that a great monk (daifutō) preside over it; subsequently, the Master’s name was reported to the throne from all quarters.
He was transferred to Guangli Chan Temple at Mount Ayuwang. Shortly thereafter, he received an imperial decree to join the Dharma assembly at Zhongshan, where the Master took the lead.
Summoned to the private chamber, the Emperor inquired about the essential meaning of the Buddha-dharma; the Master presented his response in verse, which the Emperor read with great delight.

Consequently, the Emperor commanded the Master to inscribe the plaque for Tianjie Temple and granted him a meal in the presence of the throne. During this time, the Master would sometimes doze while seated.
His nasal breathing was faintly audible. A neighbor sitting nearby pulled at his robe to alert him. The Emperor sighed and remarked, "This old man has no artifice in his heart;

he is truly a good spiritual friend. The Master’s appearance was imposing and dignified. In his daily life, he wore coarse clothing and ate simple, unrefined food—all arising spontaneously from his natural disposition without any forced effort.
Whenever he wished to strike the drum to retire, he was detained by the assembly.
Zhi was born in the *jiachen* year of the Dade era; his place of death is unknown. His recorded sayings from three assemblies each exist and circulate in the world.

Jinbifeng transmitted [the dharma] to Baojin, who was styled Bifeng. He was the son of the Shi family of Yongshou in Qianzhou. Many auspicious and miraculous signs attended his birth. At the age of six, he relied upon Yun...

Ji Wen-gong became his disciple. Having shaved his head and received full ordination, he traveled among the lecture halls, exhausting himself in the study of the *Dharmalakṣaṇa* and *Tattvasiddhi* schools.
His fourfold eloquence flew like a galloping horse, and all who heard him listened with awe. Later, he sighed and said, "The texts of the Tripiṭaka are like a finger pointing at the moon.
He then abandoned his studies to practice Chan, entering the Jin-yun Mountains in Shu to visit Master Zhen Ruhuai. The Master revealed to him the essentials of the Way.

The Master gave rise to a profound state of spiritual inquiry (*sīmānta-citta*), to the point that he neglected both sleep and food. He entered Mount Emei and vowed never again to consume grain, subsisting daily on gathered pine and cypress needles.
For three years, his side did not touch his mat; from then on, he remained in meditative absorption (*samādhi*), sometimes not arising for many months.
Once, while sitting in meditation beneath a great tree, the waters of a mountain stream surged across the path. People thought the Master had drowned;
however, after seven days the water receded, and they hurried to look for him. The Master was sitting in *dhyāna* as usual, with only his robes dampened.
One day, hearing the sound of wood being felled, sweat poured from his entire body like rain. He laughed and said, "Miaoxi has attained eighteen great awakenings and countless minor awakenings."
"How could you have deceived me? Regarding matters prior to birth, it is only today that I have come to know their true nature. He hurried to seek verification from the Master.
They debated back and forth with great vigor, even to the point of dragging the meditation seat over and overturning it before departing. The Master said:
"This is indeed so. The next day, they examined it again. When the appointed time arrived, the Master drew a circle on the ground.
The Master brushed it away with his sleeve. The Master drew another circle. The Master added a stroke across the center and brushed that away as well.
The Master drew it once more as before. The Master added another stroke to form a cross and brushed that away too. The Master looked at the Master.
The Master did not speak. He then drew [the figures] as before. The Master added four corners to the cross, forming the *svastika* (卍) symbol, and then wiped it away again.
The Official then drew the portraits of thirty members in total. The Master answered each one in detail. The Official said, "Only now do you realize that the Buddha-dharma is so vast and supreme.
Among those who have studied and practiced for over a hundred years, how could there not be those who have attained realization?"
"How many people are there capable of clarifying the great function of the spiritual capacity? Master Wuyong said, 'From among your disciples, three tigers and one panther shall emerge.
Are you not that panther? However, your karmic conditions lie in the north, where you shall greatly propagate my Way.

This was likely what Master Wuyong, the master of the public [the Emperor], said. Previously, while the Master was in meditative concentration, he saw a mountain that was exceedingly beautiful, with multi-storied pavilions and magnificent towers.
The pavilion was resplendent with gold and lapis lazuli. Within it walked the Buddhas and fifty-two Bodhisattvas.
A master who had been summoned there said, "This is Mount Wutai, the Secret Demon Rock (Bimora). It was here that you practiced the Way in your previous life; your sacred remains still linger."
"Why have you forgotten this? Upon waking, he then traveled to Mount Wutai.

On the road, he encountered a woman with disheveled hair, wearing tattered garments of five colors and walking barefoot at a slow pace, followed by a black mastiff. The Master asked her, "Where are you going? She replied:
He entered the mountains. Someone asked, "What will you do there? He replied, "I shall do nothing at all. After a long while, he vanished.
His companions knocked for him, but none of them could see him. Some said that he was an emanation of Mañjuśrī. The Master then established Lingjiu Hermitage on the mountain.
Hearing of this from all quarters, people came from as far as a thousand *li*, carrying provisions and offerings, arriving in great crowds every day.
The Master stored all of this to provide food for the traveling monks, many of whom numbered over a thousand. Even during years of great famine, he did not refuse them.
In the winter of the *wuzi* year of the Zhizheng era, the Emperor Shundi dispatched an envoy to summon him to the capital of Yan, where he was honored with most gracious consolations.
The Indian monk Zhikong had long resided in Yan; it was widely rumored that he possessed the power of precognition and was said to be three hundred years old.
People revered him as if he were a deity. When the Master went to visit him, [Dao]kong stared blankly at him and did not respond.

Upon his departure, [Dao]kong sighed and said, "This man is truly one who possesses the Way. That evening, there was a great snowfall, and a crimson light rose from the Master’s chamber, reaching up to touch the Milky Way.

The Emperor was struck with wonder and admiration; he bestowed upon him a *kāṣāya* robe of golden pattern and sent him back. The following year, he summoned him again for an audience and commanded him to establish [a monastery].

Whenever he performed rain-prayers at the altar, they were invariably answered. He was bestowed with the title Jizhao Yuanming (Tranquil Illumination Perfect Clarity). One portion of the imperial gifts was granted to relieve those suffering from hunger and deprivation.
By imperial decree, he was appointed as the abbot of Haiyin Chan Temple; however, the Master declined the honor with great earnestness.
From the Chancellor downward, even to the ranks of martial officers and fierce generals, there were none who did not take him as their refuge. Subsequently, he again petitioned to return home.
In the year Wushen of the Hongwu era, our Great Ancestor ascended the throne at Jianye. The following year, Jiyou, the capital of Yan was pacified.
Another year later, in Gengxu, an imperial edict summoned the Master to Nanjing. He was received by the Emperor in the Fengtian Hall, who said, "I have long heard of the Master’s reputation;
because the Central Plains are bitterly cold, I have specifically invited the Master to reside in the south. Thereupon—
He remained at Daitianjie Monastery. At that time, he was summoned to the palace, where the Emperor questioned him regarding the Buddha-dharma and the nature of ghosts and spirits;

his responses were in accord with the Imperial will. Furthermore, on the first day of the tenth month of the winter of the second year, the Xinhai year, the Sovereign intended to establish a Universal Salvation Buddhist Assembly at Mount Zhong.
He commanded ten monks of high conduct to preside over the proceedings, and the Master was among them. The Emperor bestowed upon him the *ipubo* (vegetarian feast).
The meal was prepared at Chongxi Temple. The Imperial Carriage arrived in person, and it was not until some time later that the Emperor returned.

In the first month of the following spring, the year of Renzi (1252), after the full moon, all the śramaṇas had assembled. The Sovereign, wearing his *pibian* (deer-skin) ceremonial robe, personally performed the rite of making offerings to the Buddha.

When night was nearly half spent, he commanded the Master to bestow *mātṛkā-hu* (maṇḍala-offerings) and dharma-food at the Guanyuan of Yuanwu. Upon the completion of these rites, [the Emperor departed].
He was bestowed with abundant favors and gifts. In the fifth month of summer, he sold all his clothing and utensils to fund seven days of Buddhist rites.
He then manifested a slight illness. When the Emperor learned of this, he personally took up brush and ink to bestow a twelve-line poem upon him, containing such words as:

"The profound gate is fully realized; you have already attained Perfect Enlightenment. The celestial light shone brilliantly, and everyone considered it an honor. At that time, his illness had already...
He was unable to go to the Imperial Palace to offer his apologies. On the fourth day of the sixth month, he bathed and changed his robes, bidding farewell to the fourfold assembly.

Sitting upright with his robes adjusted, his eyes were about to close. His disciples requested, saying, "Master, if you pass away without leaving a single word, how shall you manifest yourself to future generations?
The Master replied, "The Three Piṭaka Dharma-treasures are themselves but old paper."
"What does my speech intend to accomplish? With these words, he departed in serene stillness. His worldly lifespan was sixty-five years; his monastic seniority (*saṃgha-rakṣā*) was fifty-nine years.

Three days later, his reliquary casket was respectfully enshrined for cremation at Mount Jūbǎo. The entire city came out to see him off; incense and ceremonial cloths were piled up like hills and mounds.
Fearing they might not be among those privileged to hold the ropes of the bier, some remained outdoors overnight to await the procession. When the fire was extinguished, [relics] were obtained.
The five-colored śarīra, his teeth, tongue, and rosary all remained uncorrupted. People scrambled for them in a chaotic rush until the ashes and soil were exhausted.

The Master’s physical presence was majestic and imposing; he was dignified, grave, and seldom spoke or smiled. Possessing both merit and wisdom in equal measure, he transformed all whom he encountered.

Thus, while he resided in the mountains, those who came to clasp his feet and prostrate themselves before him stood shoulder to shoulder. When he went forth to receive offerings, they carried incense and flowers.
Those who welcomed him by playing *brahman* music were found everywhere in this manner; it was as if a living Buddha had appeared.

His deeds were many and worthy of being recorded, yet his disciples have dispersed in all directions, making it impossible to assemble them into a single account. This brief summary of the general outline is thus.
The Master had a disciple named Zhìtōng, a native of Yān. He was exceptionally brilliant and gifted; initially, he served as a Quanzhen Daoist, but he realized that [his path] was not the truth.

He subsequently shaved his head and, having heard the profound essentials from his teacher, retired to Mount Dacheng. During the Yongle era, he was summoned to the capital by imperial decree and resided at the Great Tianjie Monastery.
Later, he also passed away while sitting upright in meditation. By nature he was upright and prudent, possessing a spiritual insight that bore the style of his father.
Biography of Chan Master Fuzhong Huixin.

Huixin, courtesy name Fuzhong, surnamed Jiang, was a native of Fenghua in Ming. Initially, he followed Master Quan of Banyan at Yanqing Temple to study the principles of the doctrinal teachings (*jiao*), gaining a great reputation for his learning.
After some time, he sighed and said: "The categories of the teachings are so numerous that they are as vast as the ocean."
"Counting sands is merely to weary oneself; what benefit is there? Therefore, change your course and exert yourself in Chan.

When he went to seek instruction from various renowned masters and offered his insights, they were mostly like a square peg in a round hole—utterly incompatible. Overcome by frustration and indignation, he traveled to Mount Tiantong in Mingzhou, where Master Zhuxi Tan was serving as abbot.
Upon meeting him, Zhuxi recognized that he was a vessel for the Dharma, yet he treated him with a stern countenance and would not grant him an interview.

They exchanged a single word, and the Master’s doubts burned even more intensely. From that time on, he remained in attendance, unable to leave, until he attained a state of sudden, expansive enlightenment.
During the Tianli era, he resided at Mount Potalaka and later moved to Dàlóngxiáng Jíqìng Temple. Lóngxiáng was the former residence of Emperor Wénzōng of the Yuán dynasty;
once he ascended the throne, he established a Buddhist monastery on that site, the magnificence of its architecture ranking foremost in the world. Not long after...
It was nearly destroyed by fire. Master Tánfāng, Duke Zhōng, renovated it; however, his work remained unfinished when he passed away.
The Master then drew from his private resources—his robes and alms bowl—to complete what had been left unbuilt. In less than a day, the work was finished.

Although he presided over a great monastery with renowned virtue, he did not emulate others by ostentatiously decorating his carriages or maintaining a grand retinue to boast of himself. From beginning to end, he remained solitary with but a single bowl. Thus it was. At that time...

The imperial administration was in great chaos and the regions were beset by the turmoil of warhorses. The affairs of the temple grew increasingly difficult and dire day by day, yet the Master remained composed and unconcerned, paying them no heed.
One morning, as he rose, he sought a bath with fragrant water; having changed his robes and sat in the lotus position, he said to those around him:
"I am about to depart. You all should take up the Dharma as your own responsibility and strive with diligent progress; this will suffice. Having finished speaking, he closed his eyes.
The attendant shook him and called out, "Master, you are indeed leaving, but why not leave behind a few words to show us?
The Master rebuked him and closed his eyes again. As the attendant continued to call out without ceasing, the Master took up a brush and wrote: "Ping" (Level).
In his life, he possessed a rebellious spirit. For seventy-eight years, he had let his traces leak forth; this morning, with a single release of the hand, he departed.

Like a flake of snow against a ten-thousand-li clear sky, he finished writing and passed into stillness. It was on a certain day in the eighth month of the Dingyou year. He was cremated before Mount Jubaoshan.
His *śarīra* relics were as large as beans and as small as sesame seeds, brilliant in five colors; even where the smoke reached, they lay in profusion.
He was born and placed in a precious vase, from which light radiated outward. By nature, his master was serene and humble; joy overflowed from his countenance.

Throughout his life, he never offended others with displays of sound or color. If anyone committed an offense against him, he would merely nod his head in response. Nevertheless, he was extremely diligent in his cultivation;
from his youth until his old age, he silently recited the *Lotus Sūtra* one volume daily, even when the summer heat was like molten gold or the winter cold could snap glue.

There was not a single day when [the fragrance] was absent. On many occasions, he perceived the scent of lotus flowers; it filled the entire courtyard with such an extraordinary richness that it could never be compared to anything of this world.

When the troops of the Great Ming arrived at Jinling, the monks dispersed like wind and rain, yet the Master alone sat in *paryaṅka* (full lotus) posture, his gaze not turning toward the four quarters.
Though armed men stood before him in great numbers, there was none who did not cast down their staffs and prostrate themselves. His Majesty once...
The Emperor visited the temple and listened to the Master’s preaching of the Dharma. Admiring the Master’s pure and sincere conduct and words, he specially renamed Longxiang Temple “Great Tianjie.
On the day before the Master’s passing, the Emperor was leading troops and was stationed on a sandbar at Jiangyin when he fell asleep during the day.
The Master came to see him wearing a brownish-brown Zen robe. When the Emperor later heard of the Master’s passing, he found that the Master’s robes were exactly as they had been in his dream;
he was greatly pleased. He issued an imperial decree from the Inner Treasury for silk and coinage to assist with the funeral rites and ordered that the date for the burial be divined.

On the evening of the bier’s departure, the Emperor personally presented offerings and escorted it outside the capital gates. The Master has a recorded collection of his teachings known as the *Wuhui Yulu* (Recorded Sayings of Five Assemblies).
*Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks*, Volume XIV;
*Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks*, Volume XV.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Minghe of Huashan Temple in Wumen.
Chapter on the Practice of Chan;
A Biography of the Venerable Qingyuan Wei of the Ming Dynasty.
Huaiwei, whose courtesy name was Qingyuan, later styled himself Zhuanan. He was the son of the Wei family of Nanchang and was the nephew of Quanzhu by secular kinship, as well as his dharma heir.
At birth, he exhibited many extraordinary signs. In both reciting the classics and composing literary works, he required no formal instruction from a teacher;
his understanding and realization improved daily. Quanzhu took great delight in him and urgently invited him to join his assembly. Within a few years, his...
Xue Da advanced further and attained complete enlightenment one day. He exhorted his disciples, but none among the assembly could respond.
The Master stepped forward and spoke at length, like a magnificent hawk crossing the autumn sky, with no hesitation in his gaze. Quanwu rebuked him, and the assembly was struck with astonishment.
The Master’s spirit was not diminished in the least. After such challenges had been exchanged two or three times, Quanwu smiled gently and said, "You may enter."
"I am your master. Quanwu was on the verge of death; he called out to him and told him, "I have occupied this seat of the patriarch for over forty years.
