Though the number of people I have encountered has not been small, those capable of propagating the Way of Dahui so that it does not fall into decline are none other than you and Zongle.
You must exert yourselves! After Quanwu passed away, the Master wandered freely as a carefree traveler. Lord Yu Wenjing...
Ou-yang Wen-gong Hsüan highly esteemed the Master’s literary style and conduct. Everyone said, "He does no discredit to his maternal uncle.
The Master’s moral character was manifested in his writings; those who did not yet know him were initially drawn to him by his literary talent.

The Master smiled and said, "The Buddha-dharma and worldly dharmas do not contradict one another; therefore, I have applied my remaining energy to them so as to bring them to brilliance and refinement."
This is the nature of religion. If one uses such things to boast, how can they know me?

When the Master appeared in the world, he sat upon the seat of enlightenment four times, seeking people for the sake of the Dharma without the slightest retreat. While residing at Jingci, he entered the Imperial Court; this was the assembly on Mount Zhong.
Famous and virtuous monks gathered from all quarters. Once the Master arrived in the capital, he retired to reside at Liangzhu in Qiantang.

Those who came to seek the Way followed one after another, no less than when he was residing on the mountain. On the fourth day of the twelfth month in the eighth year of the Hongwu era, he appeared as if slightly distressed;
he summoned his disciples to entrust them with his final affairs and passed away with a serene countenance. He was fifty-nine years of age. His body was cremated.

The Master had three disciples. He followed the teachings of his master’s instructions and compiled records of four assemblies. He possessed a collection of poetry and prose, was skilled in both cursive and clerical calligraphy, and was also adept at playing the zither.
His fellow practitioners criticized him, saying that these pursuits were of no benefit, but the Master laughed and said, "This is not what you understand;

this, too, is where Prajñā resides. The Master was short in stature, yet his spiritual presence was transcendent and clear. To the end of his life, he maintained the recitation of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*.
Throughout his life, he never spent a day in vain, remaining steadfast in the Way without wavering. At the end of the Yuan Zhi Zheng era, he sought refuge on Mount Kuanglu.
When fierce soldiers came to demand gold and silk, the Master glared at them and rebuked them, saying, "How could a Buddhist monk possess such things?
The soldiers grew enraged, drew their swords, and intended to kill him. The Master extended his neck toward the blades; the soldiers sighed in admiration and departed. His noble deeds were numerous.

This case may be used as an illustration for others. While the Master was residing at Jingci Temple propagating the Dharma, there was an elderly woman named Chen who had previously dreamed that a divine monk appeared at her door.
When the Master arrived, she prostrated herself in worship and requested to become a nun. The Master expounded the Great Dharma to guide her;
she suddenly attained profound realization. Before the Master had even walked a hundred paces, the woman took her leave of her family and sat down [in meditation].
He departed and left. Were it not for the Master’s transformative teachings having entered deeply into people, how could such a thing have been possible? Alas! It was indeed an extraordinary matter.

Regarding the Biography of Dàqiān Huìzhào: His courtesy name was Dàqiān; he was the son of the Mǎ family of Yǒngjiā. From childhood, he was exceptionally gifted and precocious. He once heard someone reciting and practicing...

In the Sūtra it is said: "Join your palms and listen attentively. The Elder Liang was ordained as his disciple; he received the precepts on the Tianning platform and cast off all worldly entanglements like a cicada shedding its skin.
With great vigor, he sought to investigate the Great Matter. He first visited Master Huiji Xi at Jingci Temple.

One day, while reading the *Yuanjing yulu*, upon reaching the passage concerning the Head-dhūta Rock and the Peak of Throwing the Brush, he attained an intuitive realization through silent contemplation, and sweat poured from him until it soaked his robes.
Bai carried his belongings in a cloth bag and traveled to Jianyan in Suzhou to visit Master Haigong of Dongyu.

As they engaged in repeated and rigorous dialectical examination, the Master was like Yiliao tossing a ball, leaping and dancing through the air. Dongyu highly praised him and subsequently retained him to attend upon him.
The Master thought that although he had mastered the mind-dharma, he could not propagate the orthodox teaching without consulting the *Sūtra-piṭaka*.

He captivated the ears of men and gods alike. He was then appointed as the Keeper of the Library (Zangshi). Later, when [the abbot] moved from Dongyu to Jingci, the Master sat on the seat beside him, serving as a model for the fourfold assembly.
In the Wuchen year of the Tianli era, he entered the world at Mingqing in Leqing. Ascending the seat, he addressed the assembly, saying:

"If you wish to attain the Buddha-dharma, do not harbor conceptual understanding before you. Knowing and interpreting bind one to Chan; relying on the teachings is likewise unavoidable. Both are obstacles. How could this be compared [to the true path]?"
When not a single thing is established, how can one be at ease in daily life? Thus, Deshan’s staff and Linji’s shout were both employed out of sheer necessity.
Those who heard them spoke with joy and departed. In the year Yiwu of the Zhengtong era (1355), he moved to Bodai in Siming;
subsequently, the Xuanzheng Yuan appointed him as the abbot of Yuyang. Lamenting that the Great Dharma was declining, the Master applied himself with tireless diligence.
He exhorted and assisted [his disciples] without withholding any effort. He once imparted three "gateless" sayings (*wumen*) to test his students.
The first asked: "A fierce tiger in the mountains takes flesh as its life; for what reason does it not eat its own cubs? The second asked: "Space has no front or back."
For what reason do there exist the south, north, east, and west? The third [question] is:

[If you have] drunk as much as the four great oceans of milk and the like, and your accumulated bones are like Mount Vipula, who were your original parents? This third gate is the most formidable and urgent.
Regrettably, there was no one who could grasp his essential teaching. After nine years, he retired to Miaoxi. He built a dwelling by a spring and named it Meng’an (Dream Hut);
consequently, he styled himself the Dream World Elder. He remained in seclusion behind closed doors, alone; though layers of dust accumulated on his mats, he paid them no heed.
One day, he summoned his disciples and said, "I am about to return to the West. He entrusted his final affairs to the abbot, Yu Gong, with whom he had made an appointment.
He bathed, changed his robes, and wrote a verse; then, with a serene countenance, he passed away. This was in the tenth month of the *guichou* year of the Hongwu era.

He was eighty-five years of age and seventy years since his ordination. Upon cremation, his teeth, eyes, and prayer beads remained unburnt, and five-colored *śarīra* were produced in countless quantities.
The Master presided over three monastic seats and authored several volumes of recorded sayings (*yulu*). His wisdom was profound and deep, and his spiritual faculties were sharp and penetrating.

Tanmai sat in meditative concentration by day and concurrently cultivated pure practices by night. Through long-term accumulation and diligent effort, he reached a state where the three time periods were not clung to;
his discernment was profoundly still, beyond the reach of words or deliberation. Furthermore, his clothing and provisions were frugal, even less than those of ordinary monks.
Although he did not conform to the fluctuations of worldly customs, virtuous scholars and officials recognized his sincerity and knew that he did not engage in affectation.
He adorned himself with virtue and devoted his heart to providing external protection for the Dharma. In his dealings with disciples, he was always sincere and straightforward.
Even when others offended him through their actions, his voice and countenance remained unchanged. His speech was plain and unadorned, yet its underlying meaning transcended the literal words.

Alas! By the end of the Song dynasty, the Chan school had fallen into decay; it had become stagnant and constricted, lacking the means to rouse itself toward brilliance and clarity so as to lead directly onto the path of enlightenment.
At such a time, Master Huang of Hengchuan secretly received the Dharma-seal of Tianmu.

Wielding the *māra-subduing* mace and raising the banner of true correctness, those who entered his hall and his inner chamber felt as though they had received the entrustment of Vulture Peak. Thus was he known in the Buddha-dharma.

For the sake of restoration, there was one named Shilin among the fellow disciples of Hengchuan; he rose up with great vigor, standing preeminent like the horns of a bull, and together they turned the wheel of transformation.
Thus, the Way that came from the West flourished greatly at this time. The Master was indeed a great-grandson of Shilin;
therefore, it is no wonder that at the moment of his birth and death, such radiance and magnificence were manifest. How could it have been otherwise?
In Japan, De-shi first transmitted the Dharma. His courtesy name was Wu-chu.
He was the son of Shen of Shinshū in Eastern Japan. From childhood, he was exceptionally intelligent and did not enjoy playing;

whenever he encountered groups of children at play, he would invariably hide away and withdraw. Upon seeing monks, his countenance would brighten with joy. He followed [the master] to Tianning Monastery in the prefecture.
There was a great bhikṣu named Yigong. Having shaved his head to become a śrāmaṇera, he reached adulthood and traveled to various monasteries in the mountain city.

Once he had received full ordination, he sat and explored a multitude of texts, mastering their general principles. Thereafter, he sighed and said: "In the past, there was the venerable elder Jue'a in my hometown;

his wisdom and understanding were refined and peerless, and he was well-versed in both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. One day, he abandoned what he had studied and boarded a merchant vessel to reach the Central Land, where he visited Lingyin."
Master Yuan attained the Dharma and returned to the East, where the people looked up to him with reverence and honored him as a patriarch of Chan.

As a late-born student of the final age, how could I dare to aspire to follow his transcendent chariot and even hope to catch its trailing dust? Nevertheless, how could I remain stubbornly confined to a single corner?
Yet, in the end, there was no news of him. Consequently, he petitioned the King and obtained permission to accompany a national envoy named Xuanwenxi.

Wenxi traveled to the Imperial Court to present tribute and was quartered at Tianjie Temple. After some time, having received the imperial decree to return to his own country, Wenxi departed, and the Master accompanied him with several companions.
He wished to remain in China to travel and seek the Dharma. [The Emperor] granted his request. He first visited Master Le Qianshi, with whom his words and spirit were in perfect accord;
he was appointed as the Inner Record Keeper. Not long after, Master Le was to depart for the Western Regions, leaving the Master without a patron to rely upon.

Hearing that the mountains and rivers of the ancient capital of Youdu were magnificent, he thought there must surely be extraordinary people dwelling there. He invited a friend to travel and explore, and when they arrived—
His travels had nearly covered every corner of the land. Eventually, he came to rest at Qingshou Temple, as if awaiting something.

In the following year, the Renxu year of the Hongwu era (1382), Master Duan’an Yan arrived to take charge of the temple affairs. He regarded the Master as a spiritual nephew and invited him to his quarters, where they together stimulated and refined the fundamental tenets of the Linji school.
Their minds were in perfect harmony. In the twenty-third year, the Gengwu year (1390), the Master announced his departure.

Neither monastics nor laypeople could stop him from leaving; he thus traveled west, crossing the Zigzag Path (Zhandao) to pay homage at Mount Emei. At that time, Prince Xian of Shu was ruling in Chengdu;
delighted by the Master’s arrival from afar, he invited him to consult on the essentials of Chan. The Prince treated him with diligent courtesy and generosity.

In the year Bingzi, he received an imperial decree to take up residence at Woeiwei Monastery in Daisui, where he offered the incense of his first prostration as the successor to Quanshi, thereby continuing the lineage.

He traveled there, and his reputation for the Way grew ever more eminent. Monastics flocked to him in such numbers that his quarters could no longer accommodate them. He resided there for seven years, and his Dharma assembly nearly reached its full splendor.

At the beginning of the Yongle era, Du’an, having been promoted from Left Supervisor of the Sacred Edicts (Zuoshanshi) to the rank of Junior Master of the Crown Prince (Taizi Shaoshi), dressed in ceremonial robes and cap and sent a letter to invite the Master, noting that he was far away in Western Sichuan.
Once the Master arrived, Du’an welcomed him back to his residence, where they spent their mornings and evenings together.
He discussed the Way. In the spring of the sixth year, he accepted an invitation to preside over the seat at Dongpingsuo. After residing there for two years, he resigned from his duties.

In the tenth year, the Renchen year, he intended to establish a quiet chamber as a plan for his retirement. He encountered Emperor Taizong, who issued a special decree appointing him to take charge of Longquan Temple.
The Master reverently received this imperial mandate and, with diligent effort day and night, prioritized the restoration and reconstruction of the temple.

He applied himself diligently to these tasks. Whenever the buildings were decayed or dilapidated, he felled fine timber to replace them; when the steps and thresholds were crumbling, he purchased sturdy bricks to restore them.
The richness of the vermilion and whitewash, and the freshness of the plastering, surpassed what had been there before.

Previously, Prince Xian and Master Bei had purchased the funds for the mountain site; the Master did not claim ownership for himself, but instead commissioned artisans to apply lacquered cloth as a protective layer.
He fashioned earthen statues modeled after the Three Holy Ones of the West, adorning them with gold, pearls, and vibrant colors, capturing every subtle detail with exquisite skill.

Furthermore, he once used tens of thousands of strings of cash obtained from the offerings of high officials and wealthy households—specifically their clothing and articles of luxury—to commission three statues of the Thousand-Armed Avalokiteśvara.
He entrusted these to those of pure faith to venerate and serve. In his daily life, he was especially fond of providing relief to the needy.

He took pity on the poor and destitute; he was frugal in his own maintenance but generous in his treatment of others. Consequently, though he sat at the site of enlightenment, his satchel held no surplus savings.
A paper quilt and a clay bowl were all he carried with him. These were merely the Master’s skillful means (*upāya*) of conforming to conditions to guide sentient beings.
As for him, who held high the ancestral seal to examine and discern those yet to come, his total embodiment of great function transcends all words.
Among those who appeared as eminent as elephants, none could easily fathom his subtle, superior faculties and sharp spiritual acuity.

Later, he sat upright and composed a verse, then passed away in the Vajra Chamber at Taichu. His body was cremated, and over a hundred śarīras were obtained—lustrous, round, and pure—which were enshrined in a stupa.
This occurred in the ninth month of the fourth year of the Xuande era.
The Biography of Chan Master Feihuan.
His style name was Wuya, and Feihuan was his monastic appellation. He was the son of the Wu family from Fushih Village in Xian’an.
When he was first conceived, his father dreamed that Elder Mingguo arrived at their gate in a sedan chair; on the night of his birth, the same occurred again. Consequently, he was named Yuanseng.
His faith and inclination were firm and resolute. When he first learned to read, he recited one scroll of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* every day.

Due to his father’s past karmic connections, he was sent to Mount Wushi to become a monk under Master Yugong of Jiefeng. Upon first entering the gate, Yugong asked, "Where have you come from? The Master replied, "Empty space has neither front nor back.
Yugong then pointed to the temple bell and instructed him to compose a verse on it. He immediately composed this gāthā: "Hundred..."
It rolls forth from within the smelting furnace. Empty space has never been defiled by dust. Now it hangs upon the human head;
when struck, its great resonance pervades the nine realms. At the age of twelve, Xuefeng recognized his great potential and immediately ordered him to shave his hair and reside beneath his seat.

He personally performed all manual labor without slackening. Over time, his accumulated stagnations were completely dissolved; he wielded his blade with such ease that even the tough sinews yielded to him. Wherever he turned, there was nothing he could not master.

Being without hindrance, he was subsequently granted official recognition. In the first year of the Dinghai cycle of the Yongle era, when Emperor Taizong Wenhuangdi visited Changling, a court official remarked that the Master was an expert in the study of geomancy (dili).
He was summoned and presented himself before the Emperor; his responses met with the Sovereign’s approval, and he was greatly honored with banquets and gifts.
He was immediately appointed as a Wuguan Lingtai Lang of the Qian Tian Jian and bestowed with the robes of the seventh rank, being commissioned to...
He was appointed to oversee these affairs. When the work was completed, the Master earnestly requested to return to the status of a monk;

he was subsequently promoted to Right Director of Propagation (You Chanjiao) in the Office of Monastic Records and resided at Bifeng Temple in Nanjing. Before long, he was commissioned to serve as the abbot of Linggu Temple, where his imperial favor grew even more profound.
On the twenty-eighth day of the intercalary first month of the Gengzi year, he passed away. At that time, the Imperial Court was just...

A great *zhāizǎi* (vegetarian fast) was being held at Linggu Monastery, and the ritual officials oversaw the proceedings with great solemnity. The Master alone appeared unconcerned. His disciples, finding this strange, questioned him.
The Master smiled and said, "I have a matter of my own that is extremely urgent; I have no leisure for anything else.
Thereupon, he bathed, changed his robes, and spread out his sitting mat upon the platform. Two monks brought paper before him, and he took up his brush to write a verse: [The verse follows.]
Life and death drift on, severed from worldly ties; By grace, may we forever enjoy years of peace and stability. This time, casting off my hand, I return to the void;

The snow has cleared and the clouds dissolved—the moon is perfectly full. He set down his brush and passed away. His colleagues reported this to the authorities, who issued an edict for his coffin to remain in the Abbot’s quarters.
On the thirteenth day, another official was dispatched to present a memorial sacrifice. His countenance remained as if alive. On the evening of the cremation:
Auspicious clouds spread everywhere, and śarīra relics filled [the world]. When the Master preached the Dharma, his words were simple yet incisive;

those who followed him to take refuge were like water flowing downward, beyond restraint. He presided over major monasteries, generally succeeding in restoring what had fallen into ruin and reviving what was abandoned.
When it came to the triggering of karmic sparks in debate, he often eclipsed his contemporaries. His fame reached far and wide, and he was truly a giant among the patriarchs of the Chan school.
Muji (Wuzhi) Shou Gong’s lineage may be transmitted.
His courtesy name was Muji; he was also known as Xiu’an. He was a son of the Li family of Linhai in Taizhou. He began with the Exoteric Teachings and later turned to Chan.

I personally met the Honorable Master Duguming. He was the legitimate grandson of the retired master Fulaohan of Huyan. Throughout his life, he occupied the seat of the Dharma four times, all within the jurisdiction of Tiantai.
Monks from various regions, wishing to rely upon him for their own prestige, vied with one another to invite him to preach;
yet the Master remained indifferent as if he had not heard them, constructing the Xiuan-an hermitage in the western valley where he daily cultivated the Pure Land dharma-gate of the *nienfo* samādhi.
Furthermore, he said: "This is precisely the power of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*). How can one forcibly distinguish between sameness and difference?
In the sixth year of the Hongwu era of our dynasty, the Master was summoned by order of the Prefectural Marquis from Tiantong Temple in Hangzhou. The Master readily accepted the invitation.
When he reached the banks of the Qiantang River, the veteran monks of Jingci Temple consulted together, saying: "This is a great *kalyāṇamitra* (spiritual friend); how could we..."

This was a failure. He led his followers to intercept him on the road and took possession of the position. Although the Master repeatedly tried to turn them back, they would not listen; his countenance became dejected and unhappy.
At that time, the year was one of famine, and those seeking instruction gathered like clouds. Just as he was distressed by the lack of provisions, donors arrived one after another.
After two years, he retired and returned to rest at the Bamboo Courtyard. Suddenly manifesting a slight illness, he sat upright facing west and summoned [his disciples].
Those around him said to him, "I am about to pass away. When someone requested a verse, he replied, "My school is fundamentally without words or explanations.

He then joined his palms and repeatedly recited the Buddha’s name until his voice gradually faded into silence. He had lived in this world for sixty-nine years and maintained the monastic precepts for fifty years.
The body remained in the shrine for seven days, its countenance unchanged. Upon cremation, his teeth and jawbone were found to be like strung pearls, unbroken;
and śarīra relics, brilliant in color like gold, silver, and crystal, filled the ground. A stupa was erected to enshrine them.

The Master’s appearance was majestic and imposing, and his insight was exceptionally profound. Regarding honor, profit, and sustenance, he regarded them as if they were nothing at all. He emerged to preside exclusively over the Dharma seat.

All were driven by circumstances beyond their control. At that time, the Imperial Court established the Shanshi Yuan (Office for the Propagation of Buddhism) to preside over all Buddhist affairs throughout the realm.
Some urged the Master to seek an official edict to take charge of a famous mountain monastery, but the Master smiled and did not answer.
Nevertheless, wherever he presided, he did not neglect his duties out of a desire for quiet retirement; he invariably reformed corrupt practices and renewed regulations, ensuring that...
It may be bequeathed for all eternity. His discourse at the five assemblies was often delivered extemporaneously without prior deliberation;
yet, when he encountered objects in daily life, his insights were invariably beyond the reach of ordinary people. He cautioned his disciples not to show these teachings to others.

As for his honoring the worthy, his esteem for virtue, and his practice of extending himself to others, these surpassed what common men could achieve. Truly, he was a great banner of the Dharma in this degenerate age.
Biography of Master De-yin Ren:

Pu-ren, whose courtesy name was De-yin, was the son of the Zhao family of Lanxi. The Zhao clan was a lineage of renowned officials and scholars. From his youth, the Master possessed a mind inclined toward transcending the mundane world.

He read extensively across all branches of literature and studied under Master Liangran Yi of Zhi-ye Mountain. Their exchange of wits was sharp and incisive; he was truly worthy of the name "Ren" (Benevolence).
He never declined requests, and his reputation resounded far and wide, rising from amidst the monastic groves. From Master Hui of Dongyang, he received the office of *shangshi* (chief librarian);
from Master Yue of Nanchu, Master Ding of Guding, and Master Yin of Yuejiang, he shared the seat to preach the Dharma. There was none among them with whom he did not consult and inquire;

they engaged in mutual debate and interrogation every single day. He investigated the karmic conditions (*jīyuán*) of the Chan school, encompassing everything from the vastness of the *sahasra-lokadhātu* to the minute detail of a single hair-tip.
Among those who, following their vigorous exhortation of the True Dharma, also applied themselves to literary composition, none were more intimate than Master Jueyin Cheng and Master Xiaoyin Yun.
In the year Yiwu of the Zhi Zheng era of the Yuan dynasty, an official of the Ministry summoned the Master to take charge of Xifeng in Jinhua.
At that time, the world was in great turmoil; the Master, realizing that his duties could no longer be fulfilled, beat the drum and retired. When...
The Imperial Preceptor gathered his followers at Wuzhou. When the Emperor visited Zhizhe, he observed that the mountains and rivers were profound and beautiful, yet the Dharma seat remained vacant.

He issued a special decree for the Master to take charge of it, but the Master would not accept. To Nanhua in Shaozhou, though it was no less than three thousand li away, he sent the command of the Prefectural Governor, but the Master did not comply.
At Zhongzhi in Hangzhou, the invitation was as earnest as that for Nanhua, even more so; yet the Master’s kindness [remained steadfast].
However, as he was about to depart, the Prefect Zhong [Name], regretting his departure, asked the Master in a relaxed manner, "In the Buddha-dharma, are there degrees of importance?

The Master replied, "No. The Prefect continued, "If there is no distinction of importance in the Buddha-dharma, how can there be any hierarchy of honor or status within the ranks of the masters? The Master smiled and ceased speaking.

After some time, he arose to take up the post at Jingci Monastery; the sound of his fame resounded far and wide, and he devoted himself to restoring what was ruined and reviving what had fallen into decline.
He was appointed, and thus his duties as a librarian began. There arose a false accusation that a monk from Jijeongsa Temple had purchased famous paintings and brought them back.

The case was referred to the Ministry of Punishment (Hyeongcho). The Ministry, considering that Master [Hyegwan] had formerly presided over Jijeongsa, deemed him the appropriate person to determine its authenticity or falsehood, and summoned him for interrogation.

He was about to report these matters [to his disciples] when he suddenly manifested a slight illness in his lodgings in the capital. Counting on his fingers, he said, "The eighth day of the eighth month is most auspicious;

I shall pass away. When that time arrived, he adjusted his robes, sat upright, and entered nirvāṇa. He had lived in the world for sixty-four years and maintained the monastic precepts for fifty years.
The Master’s character and guidance were solitary and austere; he took no pleasure in associating with those of discordant nature. His learning and conduct were...

Whenever a scholar arrived, he would immediately treat them with the respect due to a guest or a teacher. Even if he lacked even a "dan-shi" (ten pecks) of grain in store, he would invariably allow them to stay for a long time without ever growing weary.
Thus, those in official robes admired his magnanimity and delighted in frequenting him. He was skilled in discourse, never tiring all day long; his speech flowed like jade beads strung together.

His discourse was continuous and most worthy of being heard. He was especially adept at drawing in those who followed him, guiding them according to their individual capacities and ensuring they reached completion.
Three collections of his recorded sayings (*yulu*) and one hundred poems on mountain dwelling have been transmitted to the world.
Baekun Dogyo transmitted the Prajñāpāramitā teachings.
His style name was Baekun. He was the son of the Wu family of Nyeoui. At the age of fifteen, he felt a profound resolve to transcend the mundane world.
His parents sternly refused his request, but the Master did not consume fire-prepared food for several days, as if he were about to extinguish his very nature. His parents...
Having no other recourse, he was sent back to Chanzhi Temple to pay respects to Master Jia Kongzhong. There he shaved his head and received full ordination.

He then retreated to Lengqia Hermitage beside the temple to practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) deeply. Every time he sat in the lotus posture, he would remain awake until dawn; he continued in this manner for several years.
Later, he sighed and said, "The vastness of the six directions is such as this; can it be right to remain inertly confined in a single room? Thereupon, he set out on a journey. Seven...
In Min, he traveled extensively across various mountains, yet none accorded with his aspirations. He then returned to Zhejiang, where he met Master Zhi of Lingshi at Jingci Monastery.
He subsequently ascended Mount Tianmu to study under Master Yi of Duanya; his debating prowess was so sharp that no one dared to challenge him.
At that time, Master Wujian Dugong was expounding the Dharma on Mount Huading in Tiantai, greatly revitalizing the lineage of Yuanwu. The Master went there to pay his respects.

Upon seeing him once, [Zhaozhou] felt his heart was laid bare. He served him diligently for several years until he had fully revealed the depths of his treasury. Before departing, [Yunmen] instructed him, saying:
"In the past, Nan Yue left home at fifteen and received the prediction of the Great Mirror (Dajian Huineng). Later he met Mazu, who transmitted the Dharma of the Mind to him."
"The needle and the mustard seed meet; how could it depend on many words? Do not wag your three-inch tongue to deceive others.
You must have true insight and embody it in your conduct; only then will you be repaying the Buddha’s profound kindness. The Master bowed in submission and did not dare forget these words.
He traveled again to Changsha to see Master Wufang Pu, and then to Yunju to see Master Xiaoyinda Da; with both, he shared no differing words.
Subsequently, he returned to Folin, where he and the two masters Duzhong Tan and Chengshan Qin exhorted one another with such diligence that they feared losing even a moment of progress.
Later, at the request of Zhang Gongyi, the Imperial Censor-in-Chief, he emerged from seclusion to lead the community at Pucheng Monastery in Longquan.
Cí had a following of eight hundred people. He moved to Mount Mao and later to Mount Wufeng; his attendants remained constant, as at the beginning.

In the first year of the Ruyi era (the founding of the Ming dynasty), he secluded himself on the peak of Mount Chanzhi. In the Jīyǒu year of the Hongwu era, an imperial edict was issued to summon renowned monks from all under heaven to propagate the Great Dharma;

the Master was among those invited. Initially, he declined with all his might, but a garrison commander compelled him to go. Just as the Master arrived, the matter coincided with the imperial assembly.

The martial restrictions were lifted, and he returned to Hangzhou. The people of Hangzhou welcomed the Master and established him at Hupao. He later entered Huading Mountain, where, before long, he manifested a slight illness.

With a resolute spirit, he set his mind on returning home, but the fourfold assembly earnestly entreated him to remain. The Master said, "Leaves fall and return to their root; this is my wish. He then returned to Folin.
On the fifth day, he suddenly bathed, changed his robes, and asked for a brush to write a verse, which began: "There is no world to..."
[He] declined. "There are many things that can be distinguished. In the vast void of space, why must one drive in a stake? He then threw down his brush and passed away.
His age was sixty-seven; his years since ordination were fifty-two. Upon cremation, five-colored śarīras were obtained. A stūpa was erected to the west of the monastery.

The Master was serene and quiet, speaking little; his functional responses were unfathomable. When presiding over the assembly, he possessed neither the air of urgent supervision nor a stern or severe countenance, relying instead solely on the truth.
He introduced himself to others, and wherever he went, all people revered and admired him as if they were seeing an ancient virtuous master.

Some offered incense and flowers in worship, while others painted his portrait to honor him; these instances were beyond counting. When meeting guests, he never showed a weary expression nor used prolix speech;

if there was something to be asked, he would speak, but if not, he would sit in serene stillness all day long. Regarding the verses he composed, he did not permit others to record them; therefore, none remain today.
Regarding the biography:
The Biography of Master Yugu of Jiepeak.
His style name was Jiepeak. He was a son of the Yu clan from Xian’an in Quzhou. Initially, he followed Master Guyue Song to provide ritual services.
After serving as a sweeper, he became a full monk and paid his respects to Master Guya Chun and Master Shimen Gang.

Weeping and sobbing with grief, he prayed for instruction on the essential points for seeking the source and applying effort. The two masters joyfully spoke to him, and the Master received their words with deep reverence.
He could no longer distinguish between light and darkness; he sat motionless like a withered tree. At that time, he was twenty-five years old.

He traveled west across the surging waves of the Yangtze River to visit various great masters, such as Master Puna Yong, Master Duanya Yi, and Master Zhongfeng Ben. He questioned each of them one by one, but their responses did not accord with his own understanding.
His mind became confused and distressed, so he eventually settled at Mount Nanping, where for three years he did not venture beyond its borders.

At the threshold of his room, he heard that Master Cheng of Zhiyan was propagating the Way at Daci Mountain. He went there immediately to pay his respects. Zhiyan showed him the words of Nanquan regarding the "Three Is Not.

Upon hearing this, the Master’s doubts increased further, and he returned to Nanying. Like one whose breath had ceased, whether walking, sitting, sleeping, or eating, he did not conform to ordinary sensory awareness.
One night, as he heard a monk in the neighboring seat chanting the *Zhengdao Ge* (Song of Realizing the Way), he reached the verse: "Not removing..."
His deluded thoughts ceased their pursuit of truth; suddenly, as if shedding a heavy burden, his vision opened up with penetrating clarity.

Seeing not a single object remaining as an obstruction, he was so overcome with joy that he could not contain himself. He ran swiftly to see Zhiyan, who at that time was traveling in Gusu. Zhiyan proceeded to Tianchi.
He sought certification from Master Xing of Yuweng and returned once more to Zhiyan. Zhiyan shouted, “Where did you see gods or ghosts? The Master said, “Today I have caught the thief.
Zhiyan asked, “Where is the thief? The Master then gave a shout. Zhiyan held up his bamboo whisk and commanded the Master to identify it by name.
The Master then overturned the meditation seat. Zhiyan said, “You wish to come and pull the tiger’s whiskers!”

"Yes," the Master replied and performed a prostration. Yunyan struck him three times and instructed him, saying, "Guard and uphold this well yourself. In days to come, preach the Dharma to deliver sentient beings and continue the Buddha’s life of wisdom.
In the second year of the Zhishun era, he returned to Xian’an and resided at Mount Wushi. There, Cheng dwelt in the seclusion of his thoughts.

For sixteen years, his shadow did not leave the mountain. His reputation and spiritual radiance grew daily, and practitioners of both the monastic and lay orders flocked to his seat, numbering constantly at two to three thousand, until there was no room to accommodate them.
Subsequently, he moved to Xinglong Temple on Shixi in Guangde;

the flourishing of those who turned toward his teachings was no less than during his time at Wushi. The assembly at Wushi felt like children who had lost their mother, exerting themselves [to bring him back].
He welcomed him back. Upon reaching the borders of the commandery, he established four new Buddhist monasteries, namely Guwang, Longyan, Baogai, and Purun;

in each, he invited the Master to open the mountain and serve as the founding patriarch. The Master arose to respond to these calls, and there were none who did not feel deep admiration and exert themselves with vigor.
In the third year of the Hongwu era of our dynasty, the commandery governor and military commander convened a great assembly for the Water and Land rites.

Everyone said, "If it were not for the Master, there would be no one sufficient to rescue those mired in obscurity. The Master pressed on and set out on his journey. Upon completing his mission and returning, he manifested a slight illness.
He summoned his disciples and exhorted them to enter the Way with diligent application. He wrote a verse, cast aside his brush, and passed away.
Seven days later, his entire body was enshrined in the Ciyun Pagoda Cloister at Wushan. His age was seventy, and his years of ordination were fifty. He had attained the Dharma...
He had more than ten disciples, among whom Master Wuya Yong was the most prominent. The Master’s reputation for the Way eclipsed all four quarters;
not only did seekers flock to his Zen grove, but high officials and great scholars—including Gao Gong Nalin, Grand Marshal of State; Huang Gong Dezhao, Minister of War;
Lao Lao, Left Vice President of the Zhejiang Provincial Administration Commission; and Buyan Bu, Vice Commissioner of the Jiangdong Surveillance Commission—also came to him.

They offer flowers; some present incense in caskets to pay their respects, while others dispatch letters to inquire after the Way. Some even come in person to seek audience and receive the profound essentials directly.
They treasure even a single phrase or a solitary word from him more than the finest gold of the South. Thus, the Master’s dispensation may be called vast indeed.
Had he been invited to take his seat upon a famous mountain, the benefits bestowed would surely have been even more extensive. That it now stops at this alone—those with discernment [regret].
He was constantly saddened by this.
Regarding the Biography of Chan Master Wanfeng Wei:
At that time, Wei’s courtesy name was Wanfeng. He was the son of the Jin family of Leqing, Wenzhou. From birth, his room was filled with light; his mother, fearing [the omen], desired to...

Her parents did not raise her. Her paternal aunt took her in and nurtured her. While still in her swaddling clothes, whenever she saw a monk, she would invariably smile and make gestures of joining her palms in reverence.

At the age of eleven, she attained a realization while reading the *Lotus Sūtra*. She went to Hangzhou to receive full ordination and visited the Chan master Zhiyan at Hupao, where he assigned her to investigate Nanquan’s “Three Nots.
She was bewildered and found no way in. She then traveled to Mount Dapeng in Mingzhou and set up her dwelling there.
At An Temple, at the ancient site of the Buddha’s Footprint, he applied himself with such diligence that he forgot even to sleep or eat.

One day, hearing the Abbot, Vinaya Master Zong, cite the story of Muzhou kicking over the water pitcher at Guishan, he suddenly attained great enlightenment. He spoke a verse: "Top-heavy and upside-down is Old Nanquan;
He has burdened my practice for half a year. If one could personally realize it right now, How could he not strike me with a fist to the chest?"
He went to Tuhpao to present his realization. He then returned to Huading to pay his respects to Wu Jian and seek definitive instruction.

Wu Jian deeply approved of him and instructed him, saying, "Your years are still young; go and dwell in the mountains. Daowei returned to Dapeng and lived there alone for ten years, enduring the cycles of winter and summer.
At that time, Chan Master Qianyan Chang was residing at Fulong Mountain, where his reputation for the Way was widely renowned. Daowei took up his bundle and went to visit him; they met face-to-face.
He was like an old acquaintance; his wisdom and eloquence were as swift as a galloping wind, like a celestial horse racing through the void, impossible to restrain.

Yun’gan also exhausted the subtleties of his training, and knowing that [Weyun] had already reached full penetration, he looked toward Chief Seat Zhao and said, "Master Weyun possesses quite the air of a true monk.
Please trouble yourself to escort him back to the hall. He was subsequently appointed as the First Seat. One day, when Yun’gan ascended the hall, he raised the koan: "No wind..."

"The lotus leaves are moving; there must surely be a fish passing through. Before he had finished speaking, Wey rose from the assembly, let out a thunderous shout, and strode off with his sleeves brushed aside.
Yankang showed him a verse which contained the line: "There was one shout, and the waters of the West River flowed backward. Subsequently, Wey took his leave of Yankang.
He resided in seclusion at Mount Song for another decade. During this time, [the Master] personally wrote three invitations to him from various locations on the mountain.

Thus, his affection and high expectations were profound. When [the Master] finally arrived, he was made to share the seat and preach the Dharma; subsequently, he was entrusted with the dharma robe and instructed, saying:

"You are destined for the region west of Zhejiang; you should go there to guide and transform others. My Way shall have a place to rest. Following this command, Daowei entered Wu, where he established three monasteries.
He eventually passed away at Mount Dengwei in Xuamuzhong. There, he cleared away the thick undergrowth and constructed a hermitage to dwell in.
After some time, the fourfold assembly turned toward him in devotion, so he built a great monastery named Sheng'en. Those who flocked to it increased day by day.

On one day, the crowd reached a point where there was no room to accommodate them. Wei expounded the Dharma according to their capacities, ensuring that every person was satisfied. Consequently, people’s admiration and faith in him increased.
On the twenty-ninth day of the first month in the fourteenth year of the Hongwu era, he passed away while sitting in meditation.

He had lived seventy-nine years and maintained sixty years of monastic seniority (*bhikṣu-vaḥ*). His coffin remained open for thirteen days; his limbs were warm and supple, and his body was fragrant and pure, as if he were still alive.
At that time, his disciples enshrined his entire body and buried it on a western ridge of the hermitage. The Master’s appearance was ancient and his spirit was pure;

his beard and mustache were sparse and bright, and he eschewed ornamentation. Qianyan praised him for his unadulterated simplicity and natural integrity, noting that he possessed the air of an ancient sage.

For more than thirty years he had discussed the Way, and among the people of Wu, regardless of age, all knew to revere and admire him; some even painted his portrait to worship it throughout his life.

He had never studied books; rather, he attained realization through profound personal awakening. Whether manifesting in speech or silence, he was always able to strip away all superficiality and abide solely in the reality.
When his disciples requested that he leave behind recorded teachings (fayu), Wei said: "The Buddhas and Patriarchs of the past..."
Of all that he spoke, every sentence flowed toward the ultimate source and every word revealed the Truth. [The disciples] were unwilling to listen to even a brief portion, let alone my words;
they reduced everything to ashes. His disciples, however, secretly recorded a small portion of it to transmit.

A few days before Wei’s passing, the great assembly gathered together, and some asked whether they had attained the Dharma and could be his successors. He showed them this verse, saying: "Compassion is without thought."
The flowers have bloomed and the fruit has ripened; the grounds of his practice are now clearly manifest. The "Entrustment of the Jewel of Wisdom" is a record of the training of Wunian.

Among them, Master Xue received the robe and dharma publicly; he later appeared in the world [as a teacher]. *Huakai guoshu* (Flowers Bloom and Fruit Ripens), *Yindi fengming* (The Grounds of Practice Are Clearly Manifest), and *Huibao chizhu* (Entrustment of the Jewel of Wisdom) concern the four masters: Cui Fenghua, Rongguo Lin, Baozang, and Xue Gong. Among these, Master Xue was the one who openly received the robe and dharma and subsequently appeared in the world.
The flourishing of his guidance is no less than that of Wei; moreover, having been recognized by Emperor Taizu Gao, he was graced with imperial edicts as brilliant as the Milky Way swirling above.
Thus, the source of the Dharma lineage remains unbroken, and Wei has truly found the right person to whom to entrust it.

De-xing Chuan was the son of the Fang family of Wuyi. From his youth, he possessed a志向 (aspiration) that transcended the mundane. He relied upon Master Qianyan Chang as his disciple and attended him for fifteen years.
He was humble and modest, appearing as if ignorant of the subtle workings of the mind; yet whenever he heard the essentials of the Dharma, he would always comprehend them silently within his heart.
Tong once sighed deeply and said, "The sun and moon pass like leaping pellets; human life is like spring frost or morning dew.

To remain long at ease in this state—am I not merely a frog in a well? Thereupon, he traveled on foot through the regions of Wu and Yue, visiting great venerable masters to seek profound investigation.
Yuan'ou Zhenru, Xianxu Xiaoyin, and Zhongtan Tanfang all marveled at him and held him in high expectation.
He consented. Furthermore, he saw a stubborn stone at Shixi (Stone Creek). Yuantian asked where it had come from; the stone replied, "From Fulong (Subdued Dragon).
He asked what its name was; it replied, "Deqing (Virtuous Fragrance). He asked, "Does it have a style-name? It replied, "No. Yuantian said, "Have you not heard?
'This is a humble chamber, yet my virtue alone makes it fragrant. Its style-name may well be 'Orchid Chamber' (Lanshi). The Master joyfully prostrated himself and said, "Thank you."
When the Abbot was about to bestow upon him a formal name, [Feng]xiang shook out his robes and walked straight out. [The Abbot] said, "What a fine monk! To go away just like that!

He then returned to Fulong, where he relied on Master Chang to complete his studies for nearly twelve years. As he was about to depart, Chang instructed him, saying, "You are a man of the level ground of reality, entrusted with a great matter.
I place my hopes in you; you must protect yourself well. In the *wuchen* year of the Zhizheng era, he took up his staff and departed.

Passing through Jinhua, he arrived at the west of the city and stayed there. In that place was a spring called Zhunzi (The Gentleman’s) Spring, which had been the retreat of Liu Qiao of the Song dynasty.
The ridges and peaks encircled one another, and the forested groves were deep and lush. He intended to build a thatched hut to dwell there; his host was Cao Renqing.
He immediately cut [the land] to offer it. Monastics and laypeople alike turned toward him with reverence; offerings of gold and grain arrived without being sought.
Within a few years, he had completed a vihāra whose architectural layout was identical to that of a great monastic complex. He inscribed its name as "Qingyin" (Pure Seclusion).

Although there was not even an acre of income per year, the requirements for all offerings were more than sufficiently provided. Monastics from all quarters came to visit his virtue, regarding the place as their own home. At this time—
When Śūra was absent, the assembly deliberated and concluded that none but the Master was suitable to fill his place. They vied with one another in urging him to accept, but he would not comply.
Consequently, they reported the matter to the local government, which compelled him to take up the post. This was the year *Xinchou* of the current dynasty.

The people of Wuyuan, their longing for him unable to cease, said, "What has our Master Śūra to do there? and so they went together to welcome him back. The following year, he returned once more to Qingyin.
Ten years later, in the winter of the Renzi year of the Hongwu era, he finally passed away. The Master’s conduct was sincere and honest; he did not engage in artificial ornamentation.
Whenever he encountered students, he never spoke a single word to instruct them; for the most part, he taught by means of his own person.
When Su Gongzhong returned from Nanjing, he frequently heard the Master’s name among the gentry and officials, and thus went to pay him a visit. He invited [the Master] to—
He sat in the room for some time, yet there was not a single word regarding his daily activities or external affairs. [The visitor] requested, saying:

"I have heard that when you, Master, receive guests, your speech flows like a hanging torrent, delivering thousands of words in a mere instant. You are a great disciple of the Master; why then do you remain so silent? Are you withholding words to bait me?
Or is it that your adherence to virtue differs from his, such that your performance of Buddhist services is also different? The Master replied: "In the past..."
"My teacher," [Suzong] said, "has never failed to speak, yet has never spoken. Now I have never failed to speak, yet have never spoken.
The Dao has neither concealment nor manifestation; how could there be speech or silence? Su deeply admired these words, regarding them as the utterances of one who possesses the Dao.
The Biography of Chan Master Fashou.
It is unknown where Chan Master Fashou was from; he is mentioned in the "Record of the Prajñā Chan Monastery" composed by Zou Ji of the Left Spring Palace.

One may form an impression of this man through that account, for he was a man of great virtue at the time; it is a pity that there is no means to examine his life from beginning to end. The record states:
On Mount Tianwang in Jiangning, there is a Buddhist shrine called Prajñā. It is located ninety li south of the city of the capital.

The mountain’s topography resembles a lotus flower, with two streams encircling it like a protective arch. Its peaks and ridges are exquisite and beautiful; its springs are clear and its trees are lush.
It is a fit place for an araṇya (hermitage). During the Yuan Dynasty, during the era of the Great Virtuous Ones, Chan Master Fashou resided here for meditation.
The Master received the Dharma from Chan Master Qianyan Chang; his observance of the precepts was solitary and lofty.

He once served as the First Seat at Shengshou Monastery in Wuzhou, where his Way spread to all quarters and Chan practitioners gathered like clouds. In the Jiamu year of the Zhizheng era, the Great Emperor Taizu crossed [the river].

Jiang heard of the Master’s reputation and entered the mountains on a single horse. Their conversation was mutually harmonious, and he subsequently dispatched the Generalissimo Miao to provide offerings for a long time.
Later, when the Master traveled to Mount Lu, no one knew his whereabouts, and the temple grounds gradually became overgrown with weeds.

In the twentieth year of the Hongwu era, the year of Dingmao, His Majesty remembered these events and issued an imperial edict to Huang Ligong, Right Vice Minister of the Ministry of Works, to select one...

A monk who had been practicing the Way rebuilt the old site from the ground up. The Emperor, having heard of this, sent a decree saying: "I crossed the river and once visited Chan Master Fashou; that monk possessed true insight.
You have established this hermitage precisely upon the lotus seed-vessel. He bestowed the name "Bore Chan Monastery" (Prajñā Chan Monastery) upon it.
Li Gong then recommended the monk Shao Yi, who was summoned for an audience, received his instructions, and departed. News of this reached far and near.
Whomever the mind turned toward, all rejoiced in it. They contributed wealth and provided assistance, and before long, a monastic center was established—this is the present-day Bānruò Monastery.
Mínghé said: "In the records of the lineage of Qiānyán, only Wànfēng Wèi and Sōngyǐn are prominently mentioned. How can this be?"
I know there is yet another who is truly eminent. One such as this eminent man is like a divine dragon at the boundary between manifestation and concealment;
he cannot be bound or tethered. He was able to allow my Holy Ancestor to behold him but once, without it being possible to see him again.

Yet the Ancestor’s profound remembrance of that person and his unforgetting of that place is truly sufficient to transmit and uphold the Way of the Teacher, destined to transcend the flourishing era and ascend further.
The True Man of the Celestial Realm was indeed one whom the Holy Ancestor recognized as possessing true insight.
Thus, I cannot entirely dispel my doubts regarding what is seen in the records and maps;
yet, concerning that which is not seen in those records and maps, my reflections and deep sighs of admiration extend far beyond the case of Master Xiou alone.
The Biography of Chan Master Laiben from Xizhu. "Xizhu" was his title.
He was born into the Pei clan of Chongren in Fuzhou. At the age of seven, he left secular life;
at thirteen, he visited Master Ning of Yifeng, who transmitted to him the methods of Chan meditation. He once remained in single-minded concentration for seven days. Once, while listening to...
A man was reading the *Sutra of Purity* when he suddenly attained realization. He composed a verse, saying: "For many years I wandered abroad, losing my true soul;
Today we meet, yet how different! Beside me stands a golden-haired stone lion; Turning its head, it swallows the Iron Kunlun.
Like Yifeng, Feng employed his own authentic tongs and hammers, piercing him with painful prodding. He showed him a verse, saying: "Lush green mountains, layer upon layer..."
The rain falls in a misty haze; the golden mane of the lion cannot be parted. I myself know that the time has not yet come;
ten times I draw my bow, nine times it is in vain. When Xiangfeng entered nirvana, the Master met him within samādhi and composed dozens of turning phrases.
He then smashed a water bowl, emerged from his meditation, and wept with deep sighs of lamentation. Thereupon, he went to Mount Jinshan and saw Cizhou.

Only then did Master Ji attain definitive resolution and subsequently inherit the lineage. Master Zhou, because he dwelt deep within mountain caves, instructed the master to attend to him with complete devotion.

Later, when the Prince of Ning heard that the master’s realization had surpassed all others, he invited him three times with due ceremony. The master did not go, desiring instead to remain in profound seclusion.
Fearing that he might ultimately lose the master, the Prince of Ning sent a letter to inquire about the essentials of the Way; the master then applied skillful means in response.

He spoke to him, revealing [the name]. Fan received it with faith and accepted it, honoring and making manifest the eight-character master’s title. From this time forth, his reputation for the Way spread throughout the world.
He then traveled to Xiuyang and Lichuan, where he stayed in the Shouchang Chan Monastery; students gathered there one after another.

He subsequently entered Shan Pass in Min, where those who flocked to him increased even more. This was because, although the sound of thunder may be distant, those who hear it are naturally struck with awe. Even so...

Desire and suffering obscure and bury one’s traces; they cannot be found. When the multitude arrived, there was no space to accommodate them. The administrator undertook the construction of buildings and earthworks;
as soon as the work was finished, the Master burned incense, sat in the lotus posture, and requested a brush to write this verse:

"This old beggar—when will his teaching ever end? Tumbling and toppling, he lets himself drift with the current. Whether one is a sage or an ordinary person, people do not understand. Hah! Come, come!"
"Come and go; go, go! The sea is profound and the sky is clear; the wind is pure and the moon is bright. Having cast aside his brush, he passed away in serene stillness.
He had lived in the world for sixty-eight years and observed the monastic precepts for fifty-five years. This was on the eighth day of the tenth month in the *Ren-yin* year of the Yongle era.

Ru Jiao’s biography: Ru Jiao, whose style name was Xingtian, was the son of Zhou of Siming. At the age of seven, he suffered from intestinal abscesses; the physician sought to treat him by skinning a live toad.
Upon seeing this, the Master was struck with alarm and said, "All things and I share the same destiny; how can one harm another? He snatched the toad away and released it. His father... [text ends]
His mother marveled at this and said, "He must surely be of the Buddha-seed. She then ordained him, taking Master Zheng’an as his teacher and having him shave his head.
He followed Master Zheng’an into the capital to attend upon Chan Master Jian of Tong’an at Tianjie Monastery.

There he served as the keeper of the library and thoroughly studied the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, reading and lecturing on it day and night without ceasing. From overexertion, he contracted a coughing disease that brought up blood. When Master Tong’an passed away, [he remained in mourning].
While serving as an attendant to Master Zheng’an at Raoye Jingde Temple, the Master’s old ailment intensified.
Desiring to return to Tianjie Temple to recuperate, Zheng’an said, “I am currently relying on you for assistance. If you leave, I shall be left alone here, which will be of no benefit.

Consequently, they withdrew from their positions together and returned. Once his illness had subsided, hearing that Master Guzhu Jun was residing in Fanchang, he traveled there carrying incense in a casket. Gu...
Zhuoming participated in the "Mu" (No-Character) koan retreat at Tiantai Monastery and subsequently returned there, vowing never to leave the mountains and observing a thousand-day silence.

In the Dinghai year of the Yongle era, Guzhuo arrived at Tiantai Monastery by imperial decree; Zhuoming remained to dwell out his final years in the mountains, where he was fortunate enough to have the Master’s personal guidance.
One night, while the world was still and he pushed back the curtain to look at the moon, he suddenly attained awakening. He sighed and said, "So this is how it is!
The following day, he went to see Guzhu. Upon entering the gate, he did not perform a bow; instead, he let out a thunderous shout. Guzhu said, "Jiao, you monk!"
"Today, cold ashes have burst into beans. Is this not like a poor man finding treasure? The Master said, "If it were treasure, it would not be obtained;
if it is obtained, it is not treasure. The monk asked, "On what basis do you say this? The Master immediately stepped forward to pay his respects, then withdrew to stand with his hands folded.
Guzhu asked, "Before your parents were born, what was there ultimately? The Master remained silent and motionless for a long while. Guzhu—
The Master said, "Give me back that phrase above. Before the words had even ceased, the teacher covered his head with the sleeves of his robe and hurried out.
He presented a verse, saying: "At midnight, pushing back the curtain, the moon is a single curve; Gently treading upon the gate above, There is no need to seek it elsewhere from others;
Just like this, with a joyful and smiling countenance. Gu-zhuo read it and, stroking the teacher’s back with his palm, said, "This is precisely..."
This man was one who maintained silence. A gāthā was composed to support him. Xǐ subsequently returned to serve at Zhèng’ān. Shortly thereafter, Zhèng’ān passed away.
He then drifted away across the mountains, arriving at Xīkēng where he built a hermitage and dwelt there. For twenty years he did not venture beyond the mountain.
He sat in the "death-gate" (sitting meditation) for a thousand days. In the *Renzi* year of the Xuāndé era, he was invited by Wúlín to preside over Hǔpǎo Monastery. He did not...
He assented. While dwelling in seclusion at Zutang, he was again earnestly entreated to come forth; having no choice, he emerged once and took his seat upon the lion throne to proclaim the Dharma.
Disciples gathered like clouds. As he approached the end, he addressed his disciples, saying: "Literary works and the Buddha-dharma are but colors in the void;
fame, profit, body, and mind are smoke upon the willow. Only birth and death are the truly great matters; prepare diligently and do not delay. He asked again: "Death..."
"Since you have already been born into this great world, how will you resolve it? When the assembly could not answer, he said slowly, "I have no leisure now to speak for you;
listen instead to the sound of the pines and the mountain stream. Having spoken, he passed away at the age of seventy.
His disciples enshrined his entire body in a stupa on a ridge to the left of the hermitage. The Master was of imposing stature, possessed a refined and extraordinary character, and a vast capacity.
He was magnanimous and broad-minded. His observance of the precepts was simple yet strict and rigorous; he would never speak of the faults of others.

When his disciples transgressed, he would show them only a stern countenance, waiting for them to reform themselves. If anyone committed an offense, he remained composed and did not engage in dispute with them. Furthermore, he was well-versed in secular classics.
The verses he composed at leisure during his daily life were none other than the ancestral intent, displayed to people with brilliant and majestic clarity;
even the venerable elders of recent antiquity find it difficult to equal him.
The Biography of Chan Master Xiangyan Cheng.

Juecheng was a native of Wuzhou in the region behind the mountains. At the age of ten, he abstained from meat and pungent flavors. He received the tonsure under Master Tianhui of Yunzhong and severed all worldly affairs with deep resolve.
He read through the Tripitaka over the course of five years; only after this period had passed did he take up the "Mu" (No) koan for contemplation.

He attained realization, and his reputation for the Way rose to prominence. Great ministers and renowned officials recommended him together for the position of abbot at Xiangyan Monastery in Nanyang, where he was widely venerated by the people.
After more than a year, he abandoned that post and traveled west to Sichuan and south through Jiangnan.

He received full ordination (*mahā-śīla*) at the Ordination Platform in Hangzhou, then returned to Mount Taigang to visit Master Yuexi. He subsequently entered Touzi Mountain to pay respects to Chushan Qi.
The Chan Master subsequently received a seal of approval. Shortly thereafter, he departed and cultivated his stillness on the southern mountains of Gushi.
As many years passed, he traveled again to Mount Wutai to pay homage to Mañjuśrī and request auspicious signs; he obtained what he had prayed for and attained a profound, secret realization.
Upon returning to Xiangyang, he met Qingning, the head seat of Tianjie Monastery, who invited him to reside at Gaoguo Temple. Behind the temple was the Rain Flower Terrace (Huayuantai).
At the place where Master Yun Guang of the Liang Dynasty preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* and the heavens rained flowers, the Master [Dao]xia succeeded to his illustrious footsteps.

He was skilled in exhortation and guidance; he lived in mountain seclusion for over ten years, never setting foot in a city or town, yet those who heard of his reputation were moved to follow his transformation.

His *Yaoshi Ke-yi Yu-hua Ji* (The Ritual Manual of the Medicine Master and the Collection on the Rain of Flowers) circulates in the world. On the ninth day of the eighth month of the Gui-si year of the Chenghua era, he sat upright upon a mat...
However, his transformation was brief. The assembly all wept bitterly. He then slowly opened his eyes and said, "There is no need for this," and once again closed his eyes and passed away.
(The *Wunian zhuan* is appended here.)
Wunian Xuegong was the son of the Chen family of De’an. He entered the monastic life at the age of nine and took Master Wuji as his teacher.
Traveling east to Gusu, he met Chan Master Wanfeng Wei; under a single shout, he attained realization of the essential meaning. Wanfeng then presented him with his dharma robe.
He composed verses to see him off as he returned to Baolin Monastery. His reputation for the Way resounded far and wide, and people from near and afar unanimously revered him.
Baolin was situated at a strategic crossroads on the route to Sihui; when the imperial army campaigned against Chen Youliang, the monastery was destroyed and the monastics were all dispersed.

Only Xue remained alone to guard it amidst desolate ruins overgrown with brambles, spending several years there in solitary reflection. It was during the reign of our Sacred Ancestor that the usurpers were finally suppressed and pacified.
Having brought the four seas under his dominion, he laid down the sword and exalted culture, thereby causing my Teaching to flourish once more.

Thereupon, those of good faith gathered like clouds, following the transformation of the wind. Within three or four years, the precious groves were adorned with gold and azure tiles, reflecting one another like the celestial palace of Nirmāṇarati.
In the fifteenth year of the Hongwu era, Empress Xiaoci ascended to heaven, and the Prince of Chu established [the temple].

A great assembly gathered a thousand monks at Hongshan, and Xue was among them. When the King saw him, he marveled at his extraordinary character and consequently invited him to stay in the royal guest quarters.
He then established Jiufeng Temple for him to reside in. Xue possessed the physical marks of merit and virtue and practiced acts of compassion; upon seeing him, people’s malice would vanish.
Thus, there were those who transformed others through non-speaking. They were able to initiate great conditions and uplift the great monasteries;

all responded to a single call, and the ease with which they accomplished this was like picking up something from the ground. When the current ruler recommended him to the court, the Holy Ancestor summoned him to the private hall and ordered him to sit.

His responses accorded with the Emperor’s will, and he was treated with profound courtesy and generosity. The Emperor wished to retain him to preside over a monastery in the capital, but he firmly declined.

He did not accept [the gifts]. [The Emperor] bestowed generous rewards and dispatched an eunuch to escort him back. In the twenty-ninth year, he again dispatched an eunuch bearing one scroll of the *Imperial Composition:
Poems on Missing the Monks* and one vessel each of pine nuts and ginseng to the mountain, offering words of consolation that were most profound.
The Imperial Edict stated: "The monk Wunian of former times was refined in his observance of the precepts like the bright moon, and steady in his concentration and wisdom like a towering mountain.

Having come for a brief visit, I have long harbored a deep longing for him. This longing not ceasing, I have dispatched an official to see him and have specially provided pine nuts as an offering, while also presenting this poem to express my appreciation (as follows).
Furthermore, I bestow upon the monk Wunian a poem regarding his ordination at the age of nine; his learning is complete."
He chanted in harmony with the musical cadences as presented above. When the Emperor read this, he was greatly pleased;
from that time on, he placed deep faith in our Way and considerably reduced punishments and relaxed the laws. He passed away in the fourth year of the Yongle era at the age of eighty-one.
His entire body was enshrined in a stupa on the southern slope of Lion Rock on Mount Jiufeng.
The monk Jue shaved his head and practiced with diligent refinement. He once drew blood to transcribe eighty-one fascicles of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
He was skilled in versification; his collected works, titled the *Hanhong Draft*, remain extant. He maintained a very close friendship with the Palace Secretary of the Crown Prince, Gui Yanliang.
One day, while Yanliang was attending the Wenhua Hall, the Emperor asked him, "With whom do you associate when you are in your hometown? Yanliang replied, "I have a monk named Jue."
Xingyuan once traveled with [the Emperor], who composed a poem to present to him. Upon hearing the poem recited, the Emperor praised it as excellent and immediately bestowed a verse in response.
He then ordered Xu Ying, the Vice Director of the Directorate of Works, to transcribe it and sent it as a gift to Yijue.
The Son of Heaven received the knowledge of non-thought (amnyom) and paid homage to the Prince; this was the height of prosperity for a single age, entirely moved by his actual practice.

As for the One Awakened (I-gak), he was esteemed because of his weightiness like the cinnamon tree. Yet, there was indeed a reason why the One Awakened was held in such high regard by the cinnamon tree:
Confucians honor the conduct of scholars, while monks prize virtue and achievement. Our Holy Ancestor revered virtue and admired [the One Awakened].
The mind of the Way is identical in both the mundane and supramundane realms; it deeply captures the intent of the entrustment at Vulture Peak.
As for the single section concerning the titles of masters, how chaotic it was during the Song and Yuan dynasties! By our present dynasty, all traces of this have been swept away;
thus, the protection of the Dharma and the honoring of the Sangha by successive emperors has either equaled or surpassed that of former ages. It is only...
The Holy Patriarch said: "To embody the Way and attain the Mean.
Chu-shan Qi was the successor of [Feng]xue Baiqi.
His courtesy name was Chu-shan; he was the son of Lei of Tang'an. From birth he was extraordinary, being careful in his movements and gestures, and sparing in speech and smiles.
At the age of nine, he left home to become a monk and studied Chan under Master Xuánjí. Later, he received certification from Chan Master Wújì of Dōngpǔ.
In the sixth year of the Zhèngtǒng era, he visited Dōngpǔ again. Wújì asked, "Where have you been staying for these past few years?
He replied, "The place where I dwell is vast and open, without fixed location. Wújì asked, "What have you attained? He replied, "Originally there was nothing lost; what is there to attain?"
Dongshan said, "Is it not all that has been learned? Huangbo replied, "If not a single dharma exists, from where could learning come?
Dongshan asked, "Have you fallen into emptiness? Huangbo replied, "I am not even 'I'; who falls and what is empty?

Dongshan said, "To inherit the family estate, one must be a son who can break up the house. At evening, Dongshan summoned him back and questioned him, saying, "Regarding the stages of your previous realizations..."
"Tell me," [Zhaozhou] said. The Master replied in full detail. Pu said, "Bring back to me the meaning of 'no word'. The Master answered in verse:
"This monk’s question is a matter of much complication; How could Old Zhao ever have been involved in thought? A single word spoken from the mouth reveals it all."
[Zhaozhou] said, "This turns out to be in vain, causing people to doubt. Baopu asked, "What is that place where you have no doubt?
Zhaozhou replied, "Green mountains and blue waters; swallows chirping and orioles singing; everything is distinct and clear—what more could there be to doubt? Baopu said, "Not yet; speak further.
Zhaozhou said, "The head touches the void, the feet tread upon solid ground. Baopu then called his disciples, had the bell struck to assemble the community, and took up his *kaṣāya* and whisk.
The Master bestowed [the Dharma] upon his disciples. His deportment was solemn and dignified; even when dwelling in leisure, he was as if facing a pure assembly.

Possessing the discerning eye that selects the Dharma, he examined his students with such precision that he failed not once in a hundred trials. Among his dozens of disciples, only Bao Shan Jin entered deeply into the inner sanctum.
Reading the Master’s recorded sayings, he found them direct, concise, and clear—no inferior to those of the ancients.
Guting Chuan (with the appended biography of Jinglun):
Shanjian. His secular surname was Ding. In the year of Jiawu of the Yongle era, he was born in the southern suburb of Dianshan City.
On that night, an extraordinary red light and a wondrous fragrance filled his room. At the age of ten, he entered Wuhua Temple and took the Venerable Zong as his teacher, changing his name to Shan.

Xian, at nineteen, attended upon the Chan master Boyan. From then on, he practiced seated meditation without ceasing. Boyan marveled at him and encouraged him to maintain the recitation of the name of Avalokiteśvara.
In the second year of the Xuande era, Provincial Inspector Zhang Gongshanxiang said to the various senior monks:
"This boy is no ordinary mortal; after his thirtieth year, he shall inherit the patriarchal seal. You virtuous ones should regard him with care.

In the *gengxu* year, he traveled to Jinling to pay his respects to Master Wuyin Daoheshang. The master showed him the koan "The myriad dharmas return to one," which he investigated diligently for several years.
One day, while reading the *Niyuan jing*, he reached the passage on how both body and mind are illusory; at that moment, he attained sudden liberation, saying: "Apart from this body and mind..."
"Who is it that undergoes this illusion? The objects before one's eyes are not retained by the self; from death to birth, how can they ever cease?

His monastic seniority was forty-nine years. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa at the North Gate to the west of the city.
The two masters Changrun and Shanzhen transmitted the lineage from Changrun.
His courtesy name was Dajian; his style name was Huanxiu. He was the son of the Huang family of Jinxian in Jiangxi. Having lost both parents in childhood, he followed...
His father went abroad on a journey, so he entered Mount Funiu to leave the household life. He studied the method of gathering the mind, but it remained floating and unstable, yielding no results.

He vowed to travel everywhere to seek instruction. He traveled south to visit Master Wansong Lin at Mount Jing, where his understanding was transformed. He then proceeded to the capital to listen to the lectures of the two Dharma Masters Song and Xiu on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
Upon reaching the passage concerning "perfect and clear knowing," he suddenly attained a realization. He subsequently visited Master Liangfang Lian, and finally...
He entered Shaolin to attend upon the master Xiao Shan Shu-gong. Their words and spiritual resonance were in perfect accord, like a lid fitting its box.
Through his diligent pursuit of advancement, he became increasingly refined and courageous. One day, he presented a verse by Dongshan on "Crossing the Water" to request further instruction.
The Master questioned him, saying: "If it is not that, then who exactly is he? At these words, the Master was suddenly enlightened. He replied with a verse: "If you wish..."
"I recognize this person; they have a true message. Formless, they fill the void; with form, they leave no trace.

They have served as teachers to Buddhas and patriarchs, and have often acted as the standard for heaven and earth. A pure breeze arises from a whisk made of tortoise hair; a bright moon emerges from the tip of a staff made of hare horns.
The Duke charged him to provide protection, and before long, the master took his leave. The Duke bestowed upon him a verse, entrusting him with Mount Shaoshi.

The Master declined, saying he was too preoccupied with his duties to do so. When the Abbot passed away, the great assembly went to the capital gate to welcome the Master; though he declined three times, he could not refuse and finally accepted.
Among the one hundred and seven disciples under him, there were none who had not heard what they had never heard before or attained what they had never attained before.

All said that the precious mirror had shone forth once more, and that the former Head Monk’s entrustment had found its rightful recipient. He once traveled to Mount Wutai and lectured on the *Lotus Sūtra* at Shouming Monastery.

At the temple, the assembly saw white light encircling the seat. By chance, while passing by a small shrine, they encountered a group of śramaṇas who bowed in prostration and addressed him as the Patriarch, saying:
"Yesterday we dreamed that the deity of the monastery was sweeping the gate, saying, 'In the morning, the Patriarch will pass by here. Today, you have arrived just as predicted."
The Master smiled and said, "The Patriarch passed away long ago. The Master occupied the position of Hall Head for a long time;
he was preeminent and possessed the style of the ancients. Grand Marshal Wang Gongwen remarked that the Master was tall and robust, with a dignified and solemn demeanor.
His resonance was like that of a great bell; his universal salvation was like a broad raft. He steadied the surging currents as firmly as a mountain standing tall;
he manifested transformations according to the capacities of beings, like a pearl rolling across a tray.

As for his realization of the path of the Pratyekabuddha, he awakened the multitude of deluded ones with tireless diligence, taking the Way upon himself. (And so forth). Truly, these are no empty words. Written in the fourth month of the year Wanyili Badyou (1605).
