He passed away into *nirvāṇa*. Lu Shusheng, the Grand Minister of the Court of Ceremonies, composed an inscription for his stele to eulogize his virtues.
Shanzhen, whose courtesy name was Shixiang, was a native of Nanchang. His surname was Xiong. He studied under Huanxiu, yet he did not fully exhaust the depths of Huanxiu’s teachings.
Others suspected that he fell short of Huanxiu, while some considered him to have surpassed him. In his youth, he pursued the Confucian classics but found no peace within them.

Whenever he asked people which of the Three Teachings was most honored, they would invariably respond that it was Buddhism. Consequently, he abandoned Confucianism and went to Mount Lu to pay his respects to Master Zhantang and receive the tonsure.
With a refined aspiration for travel and study, he first journeyed to Wuyi in Min to listen to Chan Master Mo’an’s lectures on *gong'an*.
For an entire month, he failed to gain any insight; instead, he relied on his own preconceptions to look down upon other practitioners. Later, he came to regret this.

He traveled to Xingguo in Chu province, where a monastery had been established. He restored its pure regulations and settled there with the assembly. The local governor, Lord Ren, served him with the utmost reverence.
His reputation for the Way flourished, yet before even a year had passed, he departed and entered Shaolin to pay his respects to Master Xiu.
When his karmic conditions for spiritual exchange were not yet ripe, he said, "For now, I shall act as a simple monk who prepares long rows of gruel and rice.

Nevertheless, he remarked, "This old man is truly my teacher. Consequently, wherever he traveled thereafter, he referred to it all as Shaolin. From that time on, his travels extended even further, as he journeyed throughout the regions of Wu, Chu, Dian, and Shu;
he paid homage at the stupa of Nanhua and sought out the robe at Jizu Mountain, while visiting Tiantai Yunmen and Mount Emei.
"Snow! It is merely something between my staff and me. When he reached Ganzhou, his illness flared up and his life hung by a thread. He sat upright and did not sleep.

His disciple Mingkong came forward and said, "Master, you once lectured on the method of contemplation as if pointing at the palm of your hand. Why now, facing such a crisis, do you dig a well when you are already thirsty?

I request that you relax your efforts and focus solely on recovering from your illness. The Master nodded in agreement. Once his health was restored, he instructed his disciples, saying: "Father and son go up the mountain together."
Each must strive for themselves. Because he entered Mount Ding to dwell in solitude, he used ginger leaves as clothing and wild vegetables as food.
One snowy night, while carrying firewood, he suddenly attained realization. He remained there for three years before entering Yunwu Mountain in Zhongnan, where he resided at Jiushiping.
People said that this plateau had not been opened for a long time; previously, six or seven men had entered the plateau to gather timber and died there.
When he encountered a tiger, his teacher paid it no mind; he merely felt his way through the creepers, cut away the thorns, and sat out in the open for seven days and nights.

He gradually cleared a path across the plateau and constructed a small room, naming it "The Mountain Cottage of Moonlight through the Creepers" (Luoyue Shanfang), where he practiced meditation. Although he went without food for ten days, he remained composed and self-possessed.
At that time, Master Xiu had already passed away; upon hearing the news, he prepared a seat for him, prostrated himself, and wept, sighing: "The former..."
The Master said, "A single chair is a pity. Someone asked, "Does the Master have no lingering thoughts? The Master replied, "How could there be room for such thoughts here?
I am bound by my ties to the ancestral temple, not by those of men. Not long after, he entered Qin, traveling to Mount Taibai and Mount Ling.
He was about to go to Mount Hua when he lectured on the *Daode jing* and the *Nanhua jing* (Zhuangzi) for the sake of the scholar-officials, who invited him back to Han.

He traveled south and lectured on the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*. He subsequently entered Qujiang County in Shu to reside in seclusion at Mount Hanwang, where he immediately established a monastic community (*saṃghārāma*).

He had already given lectures at Xuefeng and Ningqiang; not long after, his disciples requested that he return to Mount Hanwang. There, in the fifth month of the Wuxu year of the Wanli era, he manifested parinirvāṇa.
Among his bequeathed teachings were the *Yueli lun* (Treatise on the Will for Joy), the *Yixing sanmei shuo* (Discourse on the Samādhi of One Practice), and the *Jing*... [text fragment].
His prophecies regarding the land were fulfilled. His "Night Talks in Mountain Lodgings," as well as various poems and gāthās, have been transmitted to the world.
The Venerable Zibai said: "Master Zhen’s conduct was lofty and pure, and his spirit accorded with my own aspirations. It is a pity that I did not enjoy refined companionship with him;
we met but once at Mount Emei before he passed away. I once offered him a gāthā, hoping to continue our karmic connection for future lives, yet now—"
Enough. Let the gentlemen of the world try reading the various chapters on his "Recorded Intentions" (*Lèzhì*); then they may conceive of him and see him clearly.
This was mentioned because when the Master resided at Wòyúntái on Mount Éméi, Master Dá had once visited him there. Thus it is recorded.
Chan Master Guyu transmitted the lineage to Jingcheng.

Jingcheng was the son of the Zhang family from Xihe in Yanjing. At the time of his birth, two monks happened to arrive at the gate; his father was delighted and immediately invited them to bestow a name upon him.
The monks said, "This child is extraordinary; he should be named Qingzheng. Not long after, both his parents passed away in succession.

The Master resolved to leave the household life. Upon reaching Shuangchengzi, he encountered a monk on the road and requested ordination. When the monk inquired about his background, it was revealed that he was a newly ordained monk.
He subsequently underwent the tonsure at Jinheshi Temple. His preceptor ordered him to study the scriptural teachings, but the Master was not pleased with this.
His preceptor then showed him the Dharma-gate of Buddha-recitation (*nien-fo*). Before a full year had passed, his preceptor died. He then happened to meet Master Shan of Wutai.

His name was changed to Jingcheng. He immediately went to the ancient Huayan monastery to undergo rigorous training, pressing himself day and night until his lingering doubts were suddenly dispelled, as if he had cast off a heavy burden.
He sought certification from the elder Guang’en Yuexi; after Yuexi spoke several words, the Master broke into a sweat and could not respond.
Consequently, Yuexi directed him to investigate the "Mu" (No) koan. After a long time, he received the seal of approval and was granted a whisk and a hand-scroll.
He traveled south to the Ji River, where his boat capsized and he lost everything; he escaped death by clinging to a floating log.

Reflecting that what he had gained was still not to his satisfaction, he made a vow, saying, "If I do not attain great enlightenment upon this journey, may I be like the river. From then on, his practice became even more earnest.
He entered Shu and dwelt alone on Mount Feixue for three years, keeping only his own shadow as company. One day, while preparing a meal, he finally attained realization.
I departed. Upon waking, raw rice had formed a white mold on my bowl. While in stillness, I occasionally heard the sounds of people a hundred li away.

After sitting in meditation for a long time, my feet became afflicted by cold and dampness; suddenly unable to rise, I was fortunately carried by someone to the back mountain, where I began to recover through regulating my breath.
One day, while sitting on a wooden platform in a state of profound stillness, I suddenly heard the sound of a firecracker, and my mind was instantly cleared of all obscurations.
From that time on, he was able, at all times, to attain a state of profound clarity and wondrous insight. He then requested a seal of certification from the Venerable Fa-jian of Yuanjue.
He subsequently visited the Elder Yungu of Guangfu. Upon seeing him, the Elder remarked that he appeared utterly solitary and aloof, and asked:
"You look like a dead man. Let me ask you: when a person who has undergone the 'great death' returns to life, what is it like?"
The Master said, "Eyebrows lie across the eyes; nostrils hang down from large heads. He was asked again, "What is the meaning of the word 'wu'?
The Master said, "When the wind blows, the grass bends; when the water reaches it, the channel is formed. He was asked again, "The great earth sinks flat, and empty space shatters to pieces."

"Where do you intend to settle yourself and establish your livelihood? The Master replied, "The clouds disperse and the mountain peaks are revealed; the sun rises and the heavens and sea turn azure. Guvalley (Gu) approved of this.
In the first year of the Tiānshùn era, he returned to Qingliáng, where his reputation spread far and wide. A regional prince invited him to the inner palace to inquire about the Way.
He was moved by a radiant light that illuminated both the interior and exterior of the hall, and the Prince was greatly pleased. Consequently, he established a monastery at Huáyán Valley.

The plaque above his gate read "Pujie" (Universal Salvation). He received the Dharma from his master and propagated it therein; his *Qingliang Yulu* (Recorded Sayings of Qingliang) circulated throughout the world.
He once composed a poem on mountain dwelling that says: "Poor and content beneath the forest trees, my thoughts wander at ease; On my bamboo cot I lie across, with a stone for a pillow.
My life beyond the ordinary is sufficient as it happens, For in my breast there is nothing sought. He also said: "I dwell by myself amidst the red cliffs and green waters."

Beside him, there was no distinction between honor and disgrace, nor between leisure and haste. This old monk did not understand the principle of returning to the source; he remained for a time as the mountains turned green and the leaves turned yellow again.
He subsequently passed away while seated in his own monastery.
The Biography of Chan Master Huíshí of Shítóu. Huí was a native of Hézhou in Dōngchuān.
His family had been stone masons for generations. Although he was illiterate, his aspirations were directed toward the school of Emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

He became a monk at Jìngdé Temple, where he was meticulous in observing the precepts and careful in his speech. He requested that someone orally transmit the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* to him. Every day, he would take stones from a cliff, with his own hands...

Without laying down his hammer and chisel, he continued reciting the sutras without ceasing. Chan Master Jing of the Southern Hall saw this and took pity on him, instructing him to stop reciting and instead focus his mind entirely on the kōan concerning Zhaozhou’s examination of the old woman.
The Master kept this thought in mind at every moment. After some time, as he was chiseling a stone that was somewhat hard, he struck it with all his might;
suddenly, he caught sight of a flash of light and attained great enlightenment. He spoke a verse, saying: "Having exhausted [all effort]..."
Kungfu. Utterly without a trace. The sparks fly apart; it was originally right here. Nantang Kezhi was a stonecutter and attained enlightenment through stone;
the various quarters called him "Stonehead Monk. He had a verse that said: "Stonehead Monk."
Unable to chew it through, he shattered the void and revealed a trace of his realization. Subsequently, he returned to Mount Diaoyu and established the Huguo Chan Monastery.
There, he opened wide the furnace of his teaching, and those who were transformed by him were numerous. He composed the "Song of the Thatched Hut" to admonish the world; its final lines read:
The old monk does not know how to calculate the cycles of the sexagenary calendar; he knows the autumn of the world when a single leaf falls.

Later, he himself paved twenty-four stone slabs to form a shrine-casket. He entered it, closed the door, and passed away. There was also Chan Master Hui, a native of Wuzhou and a successor of Master Chen of Yuyang.
He resided at Xiyuan on Nanjian. He newly implemented the system of land demarcation (*jingjie*) and cleared away the tea plants.

He planted pine and cypress trees in his garden. When people complained about this to the authorities, they pursued him with great severity. Baizhang Huai returned and said, "Wait a moment; I am going.

He immediately shaved his head and bathed, then ascended the hall to take leave of the assembly, saying: "The summons of the imperial envoys does not pause for a moment; how can it compare to the clarity of long-standing affairs?
Previously there was a song of non-arising; today, fortunately, its melody is complete. With these words, he closed his eyes and passed away.
Thus it was transformed. The officials subsequently laid the matter to rest.
Chan Master Wujingdeng (Inexhaustible Lamp) transmitted the ancestral lamp;
"Wujing" was his courtesy name. His clan was the Wang, and he was a native of Siming. His father, Haoqian, had once transcribed the Avataṃsaka Sūtra.

In the sutras, it is said that five-colored śarīra relics appear at the tip of the writing brush. When the Master was still young, he sighed and said, "How can the manifestations of Prajñā reach such a state?
He immediately sought to leave the household life and relied upon Master Dongbai Ming of Tianning Monastery in the prefecture.

He received the precepts from Vinaya Master Kuai of Kaiyuan Monastery. Subsequently, Master Rixiu Yong arrived to succeed Master Ming in expounding the Dharma, and appointed him to oversee the monastic administration.
Sizangyue was ascending the hall one day when Master [Zhaozhou] came out and asked, "The matter of birth and death is great, and impermanence is swift.
I beg you to grant me some instruction. Yue said, "Throughout the twelve periods of the day, investigate this closely and secretly. When you suddenly strike upon it, come back and ask again.
Master Zhaozhou raised his voice and said, "Impermanence is swift; the matter of birth and death is great. Before he had finished speaking, Yue gave a shout.
The Master immediately prostrated himself. Xixi asked, "What principle have you seen that you prostrate yourself so?

The Master replied, "To open one's mouth is already an error. Xixi understood this. He served him diligently for several years, after which he departed to visit other renowned masters in order to verify his realization.
At that time, Master Zhongfeng Ben was at Mount Tiantai; Master Fangshan Yao resided at Jingci Monastery; and Master Wujiandu lived on Mount Huading. [He visited] Dou...
Master [Zhaozhou] debated with Princess Jingxing of Yanfang; when he questioned her about the "seal," she was no different from Rikyu.
Having attained the Way, the Master thought to remain hidden and preserve it, so he entered Yunfeng on Mount Tiantai and bound grass to make a hut, where he sat in meditation.
Tigers, wolves, snakes, and wild boars frequented his doorway, but the Master subdued them.
He could not be harmed. He lived with his disciples practicing asceticism to provide for themselves. In winter he wore a single fur robe; in summer, a single hempen garment.
Morning and evening, he ate but a single bowl of rice. For more than fifty years, he never let his shadow leave the mountains. Many people were transformed by him.
When someone offered him land as a gift of almsgiving, the Master declined, saying: "The former Buddhas took begging for food as their primary task. How could I possibly use [land]?"
This was the case. However, by nature he was exceptionally filial and conscientious. He welcomed his mother, Lady Tong, to live with him in the mountains. She passed away at the age of ninety-four.

The community, considering this an act unbecoming of a śramaṇa, urged him to desist. The Master said, "The World-Honored One himself ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to preach the sutras for his mother.
What person am I that I would dare forget my own origins? In the spring of the Jihou year of the Hongwu era, he manifested a slight illness.
On the eighth day of the second month, when the night was nearly half over, he looked to his left and right and said, "Is it getting light? They replied, "Not yet.
Someone asked, "At such a moment as this, what would you do, Master? The Master broke into a smile and said, "In the past, when a virtuous elder was sitting in illness..."
Someone asked, "Is there anyone who is not ill? An ancient worthy replied, "There is. He was asked again, "What is it that is not ill?
The ancient worthy replied, "Father, Father. The Master raised this point for a long while and then said, "Can such a thing as this be called being ill?
The assembly remained silent. The Master said, "The physical body has never existed; seek realization early on. The attendant held [the staff].

Regarding the verse for requesting paper, the Master said, "If there is no verse, shall I not be permitted to die? He then wrote: "Birth and death, coming and going, Are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha.
Having toppled the five Sumerus, All is vast and open, without front or back. He threw down his brush, sat upright, and passed away.
His age was seventy-eight; his years since ordination were fifty-seven. When his body was cremated, a wondrous fragrance permeated the air. The śarīra relics obtained... [were numerous].

[The number of those who followed him] is beyond calculation. The pagoda was erected on the left plain of the peak. Lin Jun Xingzong, the Garrison Commander of Weihun, had once studied under the Master.

The Master exhorted him with loyalty and filial piety, and he was ultimately able to serve his country with diligent labor and become a prominent figure of his time. Fearing that the Master’s conduct might not be fully known within the monastic community, he requested the Grand Historian Song Jinglian to compose a text to proclaim the Master’s deeds. Its summary states: ... [text continues] ... The Master’s life was one of constant diligence; he never grew weary of his studies. He would often sit for hours in meditation, his mind focused and unwavering. His disciples numbered over a thousand, yet he treated them all with equal compassion, never showing favoritism.

He was particularly strict regarding the precepts, ensuring that even minor infractions were addressed with firm correction. He taught that the Way is not found in empty words, but in the earnest practice of virtue. He passed away at the age of seventy-two. His remains were interred at the aforementioned site. His legacy endures as a beacon for future generations.
Alas! A master such as Chan Master [Xuanzang] may truly be called one who is able to preserve the Way without wavering. In ancient times, many members of the *saṃgha* took refuge in mountain caves;
they befriended the mist and clouds and kept company with springs and rocks, to the point that not a single step was taken in contact with the secular world.
Their cultivation of the inner self was pure, and their intent toward external affairs was severed. As social customs and teachings gradually declined, students began—
Failing to establish themselves in independence, the thoughts of fame, profit, and gain daily encroach upon their hearts.
They pursue and petition everyone without exception, thereby incurring the derision of those with discernment—how lamentable this is!
The Zen Master, carrying but a single bowl, exhorted his disciples toward the secluded marshes; yet though donors gathered there in great numbers, he revived the declining [tradition].
Abolishing multi-storied pavilions and magnificent halls, they appear before one with a mere snap of the fingers; yet one has never seen them as being conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).

To strike the *huángzhōng* bell amidst the clamor of earthen cauldrons, and to cause the spiritual phoenix to soar amidst the chaotic flight of common birds—can this not be called the Chan Master’s achievement in correcting abuses? Is it not so?
Huìtáng Yuán inherited the Dharma from Yuán.
His style name was Huìtáng. He was surnamed Chén and was a native of Línhǎi in Tái. His father’s name was [blank], who made his living through the study of the Odes and the Documents.
People called him the Stone Spring Hermit (*Shiquan Chushi*). His mother was of the [Surname] clan; he was born after she had experienced a wondrous dream.

The Master’s bearing and character were extraordinary, and he possessed a serene air of transcendence from the mundane world. Initially, he became a disciple of Master Guan at Baixue Temple in Siming.

At the age of seventeen, he shaved his head and received full ordination, thereafter devoting himself to the practice of seated meditation (*chan*). He then traveled to Tiantai to pay his respects to Master Yong of Tianning.
Upon seeing Master Yong once, [the Master] immediately bestowed praise upon him. When Yong was transferred to Jingci Monastery, the Master followed him there.

He consulted with him regarding the essentials of the mind and its realization, and day by day his manifold thoughts gradually subsided, as he aimed to reach the state of non-thought. At that time, the Layman’s years were advanced.

The Master, wishing to fulfill the rites of audience and visitation, returned to the Monastery. On his way, he passed through Ninghai; the sun had already set, and a mournful wind howled through the forest thickets.
The Master hurried anxiously, seeking a place to rest and lodge, but in the end, none could be found.
After traveling three *li* by night, he encountered the host of an inn—a single dilapidated room that could not even shield one from the wind and rain. The Master... [remained there].

He could not sleep that evening. At dawn, he pointed toward the heavens and swore an oath, saying: "If I am unable to build a hermitage to provide lodging for those who pass by in the morning, may I be as guilty as the sun itself.
Within the marketplace stood an ancient temple with wondrous features; its two corridors were desolate, with not a single object remaining.

The Master went back and forth to inspect it. Delighted, he said, "This is sufficient to fulfill my aspirations. He informed the presiding monk and borrowed the western wing to clear away the weeds and filth.
He prepared beds and tables and provided quilts and mattresses; even down to the kitchen and latrines, everything was made orderly and clean.
Scholars from Wu, Chu, Min, and Zhe flocked there, shoulder to shoulder and sleeve to sleeve, arriving as if returning home, all of whom found rest.
They departed, their fatigue relieved and their needs satisfied. The expenses were entirely covered by the strategic planning of the military expedition.

Previously, to the east of the county, there was Taoyuan Bridge spanning the Guangdu River, upon which stood the Yuantong Pavilion; after many years, it was on the verge of collapsing. A local resident, Li Simin, [took action].

He demolished the old structure and rebuilt it anew. He invited the Master to serve as the presiding abbot, who then moved his residence to that location. As before, he received guests with great hospitality. Yet the Master still felt this was insufficient;
he lived frugally in dress and austerity in diet, constructing a magnificent *Avataṃsaka* Pavilion where virtuous men gathered monthly to recite the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
To the south of the bridge, he further erected an Amitābha Pavilion, wherein he depicted the sixteen contemplations of the Pure Land. Those who beheld them...

Observing the signs and initiating his practice, he awakened the true cause for rebirth in Sukhāvatī. His gallery-like walkways traversed the void, and his vermilion roof tiles shone brilliantly in the sun, appearing as solemn as the celestial palaces of devas and humans.
When this matter was reported to the court, the Master was granted a golden-bordered *kāṣāya* robe and bestowed with the title "Buddha-mind Universal Salvation" (*Buk-sim Poje*).
Furthermore, the name of Bogeun Temple was conferred upon him as a mark of imperial favor. Having received these mandates, the Master then...
He reflected: "The Emperor’s grace is vast and generous; yet, beholding this dusty abode cluttered with worldly affairs, I find no way to honor the vision of pure clarity and grandeur.

Therefore, I have selected a site five li north of the county seat, near the southern bank of the Great Bridge. Here, where the forest groves are lush and verdant, forming a sacred ground of spiritual power, I have newly established a precinct for Bao'en Monastery.
Morning and evening, I shall lead my disciples to offer prayers for blessings and to repay [the Emperor's] kindness."

This became his primary endeavor. Consequently, between the two levels [of the pagoda], the bells and fish-shaped chimes responded to one another as if they belonged to neighboring houses on opposite sides of a courtyard.

Toward the end of the Yuan dynasty, political chaos erupted and military forces mobilized upon the seas; the beacon fires blazed across the heavens, and the three pavilions along with the temple were all reduced to fields of lush weeds.
The Master was deeply pained at heart and took it upon himself to restore them, traveling through villages and hamlets with his alms bowl to solicit donations.
In the central region, he established assemblies for the transmission of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* according to each locale, expounding upon cause and effect.

Butchers and wine-sellers changed their vocations because of this, and thus donors gathered from all four quarters. The Master further had the two embankments along the river at Taoyuan paved entirely with stone.
He constructed a magnificent three-bay pavilion and commissioned artisans to sculpt images of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and celestial deities.
Not long after the work was completed, the Master grew weary of the world. One morning, he rose early as usual and, without any illness, requested a bath and changed his robes.
He exhorted his disciples to regard the realization of one's nature as the most urgent matter, saying, "I shall pass away tomorrow. When the appointed time arrived, he called for a brush and wrote:

Verse: He passed away peacefully and in accordance with the Way. On the [blank] day of the third month in the year Wushen of the Hongwu era of our Imperial Court, he was fifty-nine years of age and forty-two years since his ordination (*bhikṣu-vaṣa*).
His remains were kept in the sarcophagus for seven days, during which his countenance remained as if alive. Upon cremation, countless *śarīra* relics were obtained.
His disciples erected a stupa to enshrine them on the northwestern side of the monastery. Song Jinglan composed the inscription for it. From...
This was requested by the student Fang Xiaoyu.
Regarding Xueting:

the person known as Xueting [was named] Geng, styled Meixue Yiren (The Recluse of Plum and Snow). He was a native of Renhe in Hangzhou. His father’s surname was Gui, and his given name was Zheng. His mother... [text fragment].

The Xu family had three brothers; the Master was the youngest. He was born in the *bingzi* year of the Jingtai era. Upon losing his teeth, he lost his father and contracted smallpox and wind-ailments.

His two eyes became short-sighted and sensitive to light, and though he suffered from these ailments without recovery, he was moved in a dream by a golden deity who instructed him to leave the household life.

His mother and elder brother did not permit it. At the age of fifteen, although he admired the Way and sought a teacher, he could not obtain the "correct eye. In the *guizhi* year of the Chenghua era...
Having heard that the Elder Xiuxiu resided at Xianling Temple in the prefectural city of Sichuan, he went there to visit him.

Upon their first meeting, they reached a profound accord, and he began to shave his head and receive the "No-Word" (Wuzu) kōan. He studied it day and night, yet he remained stuck in a state of profound stillness.
The Head Seat urged him to study the teachings, so he read the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. Upon reaching the passage, "Upon a single hair-tip, a jeweled royal land appears," he encountered a doubt. Part II.
Having already stayed at Qianming Temple in Jiangyin, I suddenly beheld the Wanfo Ge (Ten Thousand Buddhas Pavilion), its golden and azure splendor towering before my eyes.

There, I happened upon the phrase "a world appearing on the tip of a hair," through which I first realized that our illusory sojourn between heaven and earth is like a dream or a journey. Another year passed;
while composing a poem on the yellow oriole, a fellow poet remarked, "The technique of this line has not yet been fully mastered; its true intent lies beyond the words."

The path was thus opened; the weeds that had choked it were suddenly cleared away. He spoke impulsively: "With deep feeling and self-assurance, I cherish the spring light; it flies into the gardens, a realm of brocade and embroidery.
I remember how it startled me from my dream at the small window—a courtyard full of red apricot blossoms, bathed in the slanting sun.

Later, upon hearing the temple bell on New Year’s Eve, he attained great enlightenment, saying: "The perfect resonance is not heard by the mind; the great chiliocosm is illuminated as one. I have brushed past it all."

The ultimate barrier: there is no longer any room for the mysterious or the marvelous. In the year Yimao, the Elder Xiuxiu accepted an invitation to Jingci Monastery in Hunan, and the Master once again attached himself to him, investigating his teachings day after day until he received his seal of approval.

He authored works including *Qingyi Jingjin* (Exhortations for Further Inquiry), *Niangu Sònggu* (Verses on Ancient Cases), *Yi Hanshan* (Imitations of Hanshan), and *He Yongming Shiji* (Harmonies with Yongming’s Verses), totaling twenty fascicles, titled the *Huanji Ji* (Collection of Illusory Entrustment). Indeed—

Illusion is the trace of the provisional; the provisional is the trace of illusion. When illusion arises, the provisional perishes; when the provisional is complete, it is entirely illusion. As illusion pursues the provisional, the provisional is entirely illusion.

Like flowers appearing to a cataract-afflicted eye, the mountains, rivers, and the great earth are but such flowers; when the cataract does not arise, the void is the true reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*).
That illusion and the provisional are truly a child’s play—these are the Master’s own words.
The Biography of Chan Master Chengtian Chengdao:
His courtesy name was Jiufeng, and his alternative style name was Xuexuan. He resided in Yunzhou in northern Jiyi and left the household life to receive full ordination.
The three men formed a bond of friendship and traveled by cloud to Qingzhou in Shandong.

Within a layman’s kiln, they applied themselves with bitter diligence to their investigation and inquiry, not touching their mats for more than three years, through both winter and summer. One day, a man suddenly appeared from outside;
his appearance was most ancient. He said to the Master, "You three have studied so ardently; in days to come, you shall surely become Dharma masters."
He spoke of the door, beams, and rafters; having finished speaking, he suddenly vanished. Thereupon, the Master redoubled his diligent austerity.
After some time, hearing that Master Qiu Jiangjie of Jinan was greatly propagating the tenets of the Caodong school, he went to see him. Jiangjie asked where he had come from, and the Master replied:
Qingzhou said, "Have you brought the Qingzhou cotton robe with you? The Master replied, "I have already presented it to the Master.
Qingzhou asked, "What is the matter beneath the robe? The Master said, "Within the peach pit of a thousand years, there is still the original kernel.
Jie approved of this, saying, "This is what you have possessed from the beginning; guard and maintain it well. In the future, you shall propagate my Way and cherish my legacy. He then passed away.
He did not live to see it. Later, he appeared in the world and resided at Dazeshan in Laizhou. Every time he preached the Dharma, there were over a thousand listeners.
In the *Renxu* year of the Hongwu era, an imperial edict was issued to establish the Office of Monks (*Sengsi*) throughout the realm to select those of renowned virtue to occupy its positions;

the Master was the first to be chosen for this selection and was appointed as the Metropolitan Director (*Dugang*) of Qingzhou. When the Great Emperor heard of his worthiness, he summoned him to serve as a Recorder in the Bureau of Sangha Affairs (*Senglü*).

The Right Minister (Siyou) lectured on the sutras and ordered an examination of the monks throughout the empire; [the Master] was deemed to have met the Imperial wishes and was granted a golden-embroidered robe (*jinlan yi*).
He was then commanded to serve as the abbot of Tianjie Temple, but he declined with earnest humility. The Emperor did not grant his request and bestowed a poem upon him to retain him.

When Emperor Taizong Wenhuang succeeded to the throne, he ordered the Master to deliver an imperial proclamation to Japan; before departing, the Emperor presented him with a golden alms bowl, a mendicant’s staff, and other items. This having been done—
Upon his arrival, he proclaimed the imperial grace and majesty of the court and expounded the fundamental tenets of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.

From the King downward, there were none who did not bow in submission and turn toward the transformation [of the Dharma]. The following year, when the Master returned, the people of the country presented tribute and offered their thanks;
the Emperor was exceedingly pleased and promoted the Master to the rank of Left Shanshi. Furthermore, he led the monks of the entire realm to Mount Zhongshan to perform a great [Buddhist rite].
The assembly convened, and the Master preached the Dharma according to the Imperial Decree. Those who listened numbered in the tens of thousands. On that day, auspicious omens appeared.

When the Emperor heard of this, he was delighted and composed three stanzas of a poem on "Responsive Resonance" (*Ganying*) which he bestowed upon the Master. He further granted him gold and silk repeatedly.

A Great Vairocana Hall was constructed behind the temple. When the Emperor went on his northern hunt, the Master entered the capital several times for audience, receiving very generous gifts and rewards from Emperor Renzong.

While [the Emperor] was still in the position of Crown Prince, there was one who resented the Master’s favor and slandered him with fabricated words. When the Emperor ascended the throne, he subsequently banished the Master to Hainan.

Upon Emperor Xuanzong succeeding to the succession, he first dispatched an official to summon the Master back to the capital, and issued an edict to the Left Chief Preceptor of the Ministry of Rites stating that the Master must have a private audience upon arrival.
When the Master arrived, he entered for an audience in the private hall; the Emperor comforted and rewarded him most generously, bestowing upon him rolls of brocade.
He presented several rolls [of silk] and a draft for ten thousand strings of cash. Furthermore, he was appointed to oversee the affairs of the Office of the Registrar of Monks (Senglusi).

Not long after, he submitted a memorial requesting to return to the Western Hermitage of Tianjie Temple in Nanjing to spend his final years there. The Emperor granted this request, bestowing upon him white silver, paper currency, and a gilded Buddha statue.

He issued an edict to the Ministry of War to provide an official post station and a boat, and commanded an imperial eunuch to escort him. After more than three years, in the tenth month of the Xinhai year—
On the eighth day of the second month, he passed away while sitting upright with slight illness. During the cremation, countless *śarīra* (relics) were recovered from the ashes.
The Emperor dispatched an official to offer a memorial sacrifice and grant an inscription for his stupa. The Master stood seven feet tall; he had a broad forehead and full cheeks.
He rose loftily above the common crowd. Serving four successive reigns for over fifty years, he presided over three meditation halls and delivered the Dharma on four occasions.
His recorded sayings (yulu) circulate in the world.
The Biography of State Preceptor Cheongyeon:
As for State Preceptor Cheongyeon, it is unknown where he was from. He restored Yongnyungsa Temple in Namgyeong and exhorted himself with austere purity.
He personally undertook manual labor, never feeling weary or fatigued regardless of cold or heat. The Son of Heaven praised his diligence and conferred upon him the rank of Left Jang.

Yi purified the temple with the ritual offerings of a *shizhu*. Although he occupied a position of honor and prosperity, his austere discipline remained steadfast. His single chamber was desolate and still;
morning and evening, he recited the names of the Buddhas and performed prostrations, seeking swift transcendence.

Suddenly, the image of the Bodhisattva he worshipped emitted white light, swirling like fine silk threads and circling within the room until night, appearing as bright as a held-up candle. Furthermore, in a dream, the Bodhisattva said to him: "You..."
"Pray with a sincere and earnest heart; you should visit me immediately. To realize the mind is the supreme goal. The Master received his prostration and accepted him.
He then withdrew into seclusion at Hongji Temple and took up the "Mu" (No) koan. With mind and thought in constant alignment, he did not let his side touch the mat for three years.

Suddenly, when no single thought arose, the boundaries of the three periods of time were severed. After three days had passed, at night he saw the great trichiliocosm, its light like that of lapis lazuli.
Liyu heard the distant crowing of a cock and rose. He spoke a verse, saying: "Ow! Ow! The golden rooster announces the break of dawn;
Were it not for its sound, how could one know? The three thousand worlds are all as white as snow; A mud-snake at the bottom of the well dances the *zhazi*.
On another day, he presented this verse to Master Xiang of Shanshi Gulin. The Master shouted, "Talkative fellow! The next day, he specifically [bestowed] [the Dharma] upon the Master.

Ascending the hall, as soon as [the attendant] raised his whisk, the Master seized it from him. From that time on, he attained unimpeded spiritual capacity (*anāvaraṇa-vijñapti*), and no one dared to encounter the edge of his brilliance.
Furthermore, he said: "The auspiciousness or misfortune of people is invariably met with a corresponding response. He maintained an extremely simple and frugal lifestyle;
whenever offerings of gold or silk were presented, he regarded them with indifference and gave them all to the former abbot for public use. The assembly must be single-minded and earnest.
People only fear falling short. Regarding all matters that do not benefit the Dharma-gate, he does not entertain even a hair’s breadth of thought.
Thus, the great achievement of establishing Yongning was as easily attained as if he were picking something up. This truly arose from his own spiritual practice;
it was not a mere coincidence resulting from karmic retribution.
Zhengkong Chuan was a native of Quannan. At the age of six, he fell into a well but did not die; he subsequently entered the monastic order.

Upon reaching adulthood, he traveled through Guanzhong and Luoyang and visited Zhongnan and Mount Heng, where he met his teacher and gradually attained realization. In the Jiwu year of the Jiajing era, he entered Mount Luofu to rest.
He resided at Yongfu Temple, relying on alms for his sustenance. A monk there would sew and patch his robes for him. It was the height of late spring, and the temple was crowded with visitors;
yet Ku remained silent, sitting with his bowl empty. Sometimes people would drop coins into it while he sat in meditation beneath a tree or by a Buddhist lamp.
Once he had entered meditative absorption (*samādhi*), he would join the assembly in their daily chores, such that no one knew of his practice. Gong of Longtang was reading a book.
In the temple, he saw that his complexion was radiant and his skin clear, with a singular, transcendent spiritual light. He questioned him urgently and thus learned that he was profound in Chan.
Longtang asked, "Exerting yourself so diligently, can you not feel weariness? Huikong replied, "The rice is not yet cooked; how could I refuse to carry this stone on my waist?
For now, I am merely a practitioner at Huangmei. Longtang said, "If that is so, you shall one day become the Sixth Patriarch."
Yeshi asked, "If it is already accomplished, why wait for another day? I shall accomplish myself; why must I rely on the Sixth Patriarch?

On the day of the Buddha’s Bathing Ceremony, the monks of the temple prepared a high seat and invited Yeshi to preach the Dharma. He did not decline, but ascended the seat directly to expound upon the profound meaning.
His voice was clear and resonant, and hundreds of listeners were so captivated that there was not one who did not praise his excellence. Longtang asked him about this in astonishment.

He replied, "It was merely a coincidence. His success was also due to past causes. Shortly thereafter, he went to Wuyang as a minor counselor. Lord Xu welcomed him to his residence and requested the Dharma.
He passed through Guangxiao Temple and moved to Mount Guanyin. By the time he returned, his followers numbered in the thousands daily.
The earth shook for a moment, and everyone said, "This is the second coming of Caoxi. One day, during a vegetarian feast, he instructed his disciples to prepare a wooden shrine.
When the shrine was completed, he took leave of the assembly and entered it to sit. The crowd was struck with awe and grief; they vied with one another to hold scrolls and request a verse.

Hearing this, Longtang hurried to the scene and, upon arriving, the Master emerged from the shrine. He conversed with him warmly as if they were old friends. Afterward, he entered again and ordered the shrine to be closed. When they looked inside, he had already passed away.
Go! All you donors, reflect upon this. A shrine was established on Mount Guanyin to offer incense and lamps.
Chan Master Jiwang succeeded [his predecessor];
his style name was Gufeng. He was a monk of Jianfu Temple. In the seventeenth year of the Jiajing era, he went to the capital to receive the precepts. His grandmother...
After his stepmother died, both before and after her passing, he lived in a grass hut at her grave for six years. He passed away at the age of seventy-nine.
During that period, he remained in seclusion behind closed doors on four occasions, totaling more than thirty years. The Grand Historian Li Shaozhuang presented him with a poem which says:

"The incense smoke forms clouds of its own accord; the shadow of the curtain is long and idle by day. One can thus imagine the loftiness and tranquility of his character. A monk once asked about Master Nie’s religious name (dharma-name).
"What is it? he asked. "An ancient peak," the monk replied. He asked again, "What is the scenery of the ancient peak? The monk answered, "Heaven and earth never grow old;
alone, it can endure through all time. The monk then asked for his dharma name. "Jiwàn (Continuing Ten Thousand)," he said. "Why not 'Continuing One'?

The monk replied, "'Ten thousand' is precisely 'one'; 'one' is precisely 'ten thousand. Observing his responses and discerning faculties, he did not seem at all like one who was withered and lifeless.
The one who sat [in attendance] said: "Niet" was likely his surname.

According to the *Mǎnxián zhuàn*, Mǎnxián was originally from Xīngzǐ in Jīāngxī; his family name was Qián. From childhood, he was exceptionally intelligent and gifted, and he once received full ordination.

Later, he visited various masters and attained realization. However, because the conditions for his time were not yet favorable, he was unable to propagate the teachings or assist in the transformation of others;
thus, those in all quarters lamented this. The one under whom he shaved his head was Dayuan; the one from whom he entered the inner chamber was Da'an;
and those with whom he studied together and mutually verified his realization were Yuexin and Rongtian. Yet, as for those elders...
Regarding his travels: he first stayed at Huangyan on Mount Lu, where he served as the abbot of Pujie on Lotus Peak. He subsequently visited various renowned monasteries throughout Baixia and Wulin;
whether on solitary peaks or in bustling markets, there was nowhere he did not experience and refine himself. Ultimately, he spent his final years at Zhangjiaqiao in Xiuzhou.
Having left home at an early age, the Master already knew of the matters that transcend the ordinary. Initially, when the topic of "water by the rock" was raised...
"Ling! The phrase 'the fragrance of the wind amidst the flowers' suddenly flashed before me. After a long while, amidst a feverish illness, I broke through the bottom of the bucket;
sweat flowed from my entire body. From that point on, I cast away all established structures and moved with unimpeded freedom. Once, I bound bundles of straw over my head as a roof."

He lived upon grass and wore garments of woven reeds; for many years he endured extreme hardship, dwelling amidst the wind and snow. People held his conduct in high esteem, yet he never boasted of his cultivation by manifesting signs of attainment.
He performed meritorious deeds and Buddhist services with tireless diligence. Furthermore, he occasionally gave rise to sharp, incisive insights, casting aside both conceptual thought and language.
To him, the world-system was like a bubble, and sages were as fleeting as a flash of lightning. People looked up to him as their spiritual lineage. And yet—

In the end, he never allowed his emotions to run wild, remaining perfectly harmonious even amidst the constraints of worldly affairs. He was relaxed without drifting into laxity; he acted without contrivance.
At the age of sixty-five, in the Wanyli era year of Wuxu (1618), he passed away at Zhangjiaqiao. Zhou Haimen composed an inscription for his stupa, which says: [The inscription follows.]
The Biography of Chan Master Wuming.
His name was Huijing, and he was styled Wuming. He was the son of the Pei family of Chongren in Fuzhou. His physical appearance was ancient and dignified, and by nature he was serene and detached.
He had no particular inclinations. At nine years of age, he entered a local school; suddenly, he appeared as if indifferent to the world of men.

At seventeen, he abandoned his brush and inkstone, and with a sigh of resolve, he set his mind on seeking the Way. By chance, he entered the house of a lay practitioner (*upāsaka*) and saw a copy of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* on a desk.
Upon reading it, he finished the entire scroll at once, rejoicing as if he had recovered a long-lost possession. From that moment, he renounced meat and wine, determined to leave the household life.
He entered the household of Master Zhong of Lian Shan and served him for three years. Whatever instructions he heard, he followed them without deviation, as if he were a fool.
Later, while reading the *Chuan Deng Lu*, he came across a monk asking Xingshan, "What is the Way? to which Xingshan replied, "A magnificent mountain. The Master was at a loss.
A sense of doubt arose suddenly within him. Later, while practicing in seclusion at Mount Emei, he attained enlightenment while pushing a boulder.
Only then did he shave his head and receive full ordination. He resided on the mountain for twenty-four years; this was at Baofang, a former monastery of Chan Master Songbao of the same prefecture.
The Master occupied it in the year Jiawu of the Wanli era, when he was forty-seven years old. A monk asked the Master: "Long..."
"An old man living here; whom have you ever met? The Master said, "I have never traveled as a wandering monk. The monk said, "Master, how can one slight the world by means of a single corner?
The Master appreciated these words and consequently abandoned the temple to travel through various regions. His footsteps reached everywhere from the north to the south.
The Venerable Zibo held him in deep esteem, and among the great elders of the Dharma at that time, there were none who did not recommend him in their mutual exchanges.
Yù. Finally, he met the Venerable Wǔtái Ruìfēng, through whom he realized the ultimate depths of the Dharma.

He then began teaching at Shòuchāng, where monastics arrived like deer. Shòuchāng was originally founded by Lái Gōng; the Master shared the same hometown and surname as Lái, and people said that the Master was the latter’s reincarnation.
During his tenure at Shòuchāng, the Master did not seek external support nor did he solicit donations.

Master An Daoxin’s life story: Having reached the age of seventy, he still mingled with the ranks of laborers. Whenever leading the assembly to clear fields, he would always go out first and return last;
for forty years, it was as if it were but a single day. The annual yield could support three hundred people. Thus, throughout his life, the Buddha-dharma never departed from the side of his hoe.
Although he did not cultivate his outward appearance, his demeanor was upright and solemn, like the severity of frost or the warmth of the sun.
He possessed a majestic presence without anger. He never once granted permission to anyone with a casual or light-minded attitude; thus, those throughout the realm held his character in high esteem.
There was not a single word of his that could be used as a pretext for criticism. Such was his extreme prudence and secrecy.

In the twelfth month of the Ding-si year, the Master returned from the fields and said to the assembly: "From this day forth, I shall no longer lay stones. He then wrote a farewell letter to be sent far and near.
His fellow practitioners exhorted him to strike at his own true nature through earnest practice. On the seventeenth day of the first month of the following year, he sat upright and passed away.
Upon cremation, his heart, crown bone, and teeth remained unburnt; they were enshrined in a stupa built at his home temple.
He was born in the Wushen year of the Jiajing era; his secular age was seventy-one, and his years as a monk were fifty-some. Hanshan Deqing said:
The Master’s lofty integrity and solitary style were truly sufficient to stir the customs of this degenerate age. As for his power of diligence and forbearance, one must seek it among the ancients.
Although his shadow never left the mountains, his reputation reached far and wide; was this not like a dragon appearing while remaining still in its lair?
"One who is profoundly silent yet possesses the voice of thunder.
This refers to the *Yungu Heshi Chuanfa Hui*.
"Yungu" is his style name. He was the son of Huai of Jia-shan. At twenty, he received full ordination and practiced the Tiantai school's *Xiǎo*... [text fragment].

Regarding *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, he went to Tianning Monastery in the prefecture to inquire about his practice with Master Fazhou Ji. The Master said, "In the study of the Way, awakening the mind is paramount.
The essentials of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* do not depart from the body, the mind, and the breath; how can one achieve liberation otherwise?"
"What you have cultivated flows toward the Lesser Vehicle (hīnayāna). He then showed him the essential points of the teaching. The Master investigated them with great diligence.
One day, while receiving food, he finished eating without realizing it; his bowl suddenly fell to the ground, and he was struck by a sudden awakening, as if waking from a dream.

The Master granted him formal certification (kṣānti). Thereafter, he remained concealed within the monastic community, sinking into lowly menial tasks. While reading the *Tanjin ji*, he encountered the works of Mingjiao.

The Elder Dharma-protector had deeply cultivated his practice and established his vows; [the Master] wished to emulate him even slightly. He received the teachings upon the crown of his head and recited them with devotion, remaining awake until the end of the night.
Upon entering the capital, he stayed beneath the Vairocana Hall at Tianjie Monastery, where he practiced the Way with refined diligence.

He once entered meditative absorption for several days without rising, such that no one knew of it for three years. Furthermore, appreciating the secluded seclusion of Xixia, he built a hermitage on Qianfo Ridge.

Later, he first came to the recognition and patronage of Lord Lu Wutai. At that time, Qixia Temple had been abandoned for a long period. Lord Lu, pledging his vow to restore it, invited the Master to serve as its abbot.
The Master, however, recommended Master Shan of Mount Song to accept the appointment. He then moved to the deepest part of the mountain and said:

The heavens opened at Tiankai Rock, and he sat in solitary contemplation as before. At that time, many officials and lay practitioners, having been guided by Master Lu Gong, came to the rock to seek instruction and requested an audience with the Master.

Upon their arrival, the Master would inquire after their daily affairs—regardless of whether they were noble or humble, monastic or lay—and without a word of greeting regarding their well-being, he would immediately have them spread a rush mat upon the floor and sit upright.
He would then lead them in profound introspection, continuing until the end of the day.
At night he would not utter a single word. Upon parting, he would invariably exhort them, saying, "Human life is impermanent; do not let your days pass in vain.
When they met again, he would inevitably ask how they had applied themselves since their last meeting. Consequently, those who were frivolous were at a loss for what to say;

even if they wished to see him, they did not dare to approach him. Because his compassion was ever more earnest and his counsel ever more profound, although he made no formal displays of religious instruction, those who saw him—
Those who merely gazed upon the mountain cliffs felt a shudder of awe as if struck by cold. Yet the Master embraced them all with an equal mind.

In his dealings with others, he always spoke with gentle words and a low voice, maintaining a single flavor of equanimity; he never once displayed a harsh word or a stern countenance. Consequently, the number of scholar-officials who took refuge in him increased day by day.

Furthermore, because they were unable to enter the mountains and wished to seek an audience, the Master—whose heart was set on converting and guiding them—would also go out to see them. This continued for years.

Whenever he traveled through the city, he invariably stayed at Huiguang Temple. Each time he arrived, the lay followers of both genders would gather around him as if circumambulating a flower-adorned throne.
Yet the Master regarded them all as illusory transformations, never harboring even a single thought of discrimination.
Thus, those who drew near to him were like infants by the side of a compassionate mother. When he left the city, he often went to Pude Temple, where the monk Yue was as emaciated as a crane.

He truly brought forth this teaching. Lamenting that the path of Chan had fallen silent, in the winter of the Bingyin year of the Jiajing era, he gathered fifty-three people and established a period of seated meditation at Tianjie Monastery.
When a student asked about the direct and immediate point of application for the mind, the Master said:
To look up without turning back is already a deviation; if you attempt to deliberate upon it, when in kalpas will you ever awaken? It is further said:

An ancient master taught that "all day long one eats rice, yet does not chew a single grain; all day long one travels on the road, yet does not tread upon the earth; all day long one wears clothes, yet does not hang even a thread of silk.
Only by applying the mind in this way can there be a slight degree of resonance with the truth. A government official asked: "What is the Patriarch?"
The Master said, "Where there is water, it contains the moon; where there is no mountain, it does not bear clouds. [The monk] asked, "Is there nothing more extraordinary?

The Master said, "One must not mistake a tortoise for a turtle. The Master’s heart was deeply committed to protecting the Dharma. He did not slight those who were beginners, nor did he treat with contempt those who had violated the precepts.
Even when monks were undisciplined, he did not abandon them; rather, he guided them with patience and tact toward goodness. If anyone should interfere with the Dharma, he would act accordingly.
As for "Records": When the Master heard of [such matters], he would go to provide aid without waiting to be asked; he was invariably earnest in attending to the matter, saying:
"The Buddha-dharma is entrusted to kings and ministers as its external protectors. It lies solely in your honoring the Buddha’s mind. To insult the Sangha is to insult the Buddha.
Those who heard this could not help but change their countenances; they would surely attain liberation before they ceased their efforts. Yet, in the end, no one among them truly listened to him.

The listeners, moreover, never considered such extensive instruction to be a burden; over time, they all came to realize that it arose from the compassion of non-conditioned love (*asaṃskṛta-maitrī*).
When Master Yuan Lianfan had not yet passed the civil service examinations, he visited the Master in the mountains and sat facing him for three days and nights without closing his eyes.
The Master asked, "Sir, why do you have no deluded thoughts? The man replied, "I have calculated my destiny and find that there is no lot for me regarding official rank or progeny;
therefore, I rest my mind and entrust myself to fate, free from other delusive thoughts. The Master said, "I had intended to regard you as a hero, yet you are merely an ordinary person.
The sages say: 'Destiny is created by oneself; fortune is sought by oneself. How could the forces of creation and transformation possibly constrain one?"
"Is it a human being? Thereupon, [the Master] gave him detailed instruction on the principles of reforming one's faults, accumulating virtue, and establishing one’s destiny through the mind alone.

The official followed these teachings and practiced them, eventually passing the jinshi examination. He had a son, the Venerable Hanshi, who, while still a novice, served his teacher with extreme diligence.
One day he asked, "The commentators say that my lifespan will not be long; what should I do? The Master replied, "Longevity and early death are merely matters of birth and death."
The Dharma. Zen practice is the method for realizing the end of birth and death. If not a single thought arises, then ghosts and spirits cannot peer through it;

how could the forces of creation and transformation possibly constrain it? The only concern is that one’s eye of the Way is not yet clear. As Master Han was about to travel north, the Master instructed him, saying:
"When the ancients went on pilgrimage, they did so solely to clarify the matter of their own person. You must reflect upon what this will mean for you in the future."
Since you have met your parents, teachers, and friends, take care not to waste the money spent on your straw sandals. Such was his excellence in guiding and assisting humanity.
In the year of Renshen, the Minister of Personnel of Jiahe, Lord Wu Moquan; the Minister of Justice, Lord Zheng Danquan;
the Director of the Court of the Imperial Stud, Lord Lu Wutai; and his younger brother Yuntai, together welcomed the Master back to his native mountains. All...
The Duke would frequently enter the room to inquire about the Way; every time he saw the Master, he would invariably light incense to seek further instruction, observing the etiquette of a disciple.
Together with Lord Lu of Pingquan and Lord Xu of Sian, the Master Zibo visited the Master to inquire about the essential principles of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.

The Master expounded upon the subtle mystery of the perfect interfusion of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), and they all marveled at such an unprecedented teaching. This was during a time when the path of Chan in Jiangnan was still in its nascent stage.
He traveled through many places where people were talkative, yet from beginning to end, there was not a single person who could find fault with him; thus, the Master’s conduct may be known.

After the Master had lived in his hometown for three years, those who had been transformed by his influence numbered in the millions. One night, the people of the four surrounding villages saw fire emanating from the Master’s hermitage.
When they went to look at dawn, the Master had already passed away in tranquility. This was during the Wanyili era, in the year Yihai (1615).
It was the first month of the year. His worldly age was seventy-five, and his years of monastic seniority were over fifty. He was buried to the right of Dayun Temple.
*Supplementary Biographies of Eminent Monks*, Volume 16;
*Supplementary Biographies of Eminent Monks*, Volume 17.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Minghe of Huashan Monastery, Wumen;
Section on the Clarification of the Vinaya:
Biographies of Vinaya Master Liu and Vinaya Master Yuanjue of the Song Dynasty.
As for Vinaya Master Liu, he was one who upheld the Vinaya and practiced asceticism. At Dajue Temple in Kaixian County, Shu, there stands a weathered stele commemorating Vinaya Master Liu.
Of that which remains of the inscription before it has completely peeled away, it can still be transcribed into words. The Master’s name was Faben.
A native of Linjiang Township, from his youth he was spiritually brilliant and exceptionally gifted. His parents had no son other than the Master. Furthermore—

They cherished him deeply. When he was only seven years old, his conduct was like that of an adult. One day, he suddenly said to his parents, "I have long dwelt in the dusty world, yet worldly attachments have not been severed.
Now I wish to renounce the secular life to become a monk; I pray that my parents will not worry about me.

His parents tried to stop him with great difficulty, even weeping as they did so. The Master then ceased taking grain and refused to eat. His parents were terrified and, for the time being, [yielded].

He followed his advice and subsequently shaved his hair. He entered the mountains to live in seclusion, never returning to his family home. He diligently practiced asceticism, never ceasing day or night.
By the age of fifteen, there was no scripture among the Tripitaka—Sūtra, Vinaya, or Abhidharma—that he had not mastered. People from near and far all came to gaze upon and pay homage to him.

He always treated others with generosity and maintained a relationship of spiritual friendship with his teacher. From time to time, he would approach the teacher to request instruction. At the age of ninety-nine, one day he addressed the assembly:
He said, "The conditions of my karma are nearly exhausted; I shall return to the West. You all should exert yourselves and pass away while sitting upright.

The Vinaya Master Yuanjue Deming resided at Nengren Temple in Jinling. He encountered Emperor Taizong, who summoned him for an audience and bestowed upon him purple robes, a portrait of the Emperor, and images of Arhats to take back with him.
His reputation for the Vinaya resounded throughout the region south of the Yangtze River, and seekers of the Dharma flocked to him.

He returned home after gazing [upon them]. When Emperor Zhenzong ascended the throne, he again presented him with poetic verses, which included the lines: "Diligently expounding the Vinaya, you have mastered the true wind;
among the sons of Śākya, your Southern Chan path is rarely equaled. The spiritual conduct of these two masters must have been preeminent in their time, yet it has ultimately been lost to tradition;
we can only recover their names from fragments of inscriptions and broken carvings, and cannot speak further of their deeds.
This is detailed. What a pity!
The Biography of Liaoxing:

Liaoxing was a native of Wanchuan Township in Pingyang. A son of the Song family, he renounced worldly life and received full ordination in his childhood. Later, he traveled extensively to seek instruction from various masters.
In various directions, there were those who heard that Master Xun of Jingxi strictly observed the precepts and devoted himself to diligent practice, manifesting many extraordinary traces.
Whenever he chanted the sutras, tigers would crouch beneath his desk to listen; at times, monkeys would offer fruit and birds would present flowers.

When the local officials were constructing the Chuiyang Dam, they used oxen for the sacrificial rites. One such ox, carrying a blade in its mouth, bolted toward the Master’s location. As the pursuers arrived one after another, the Master untied his *kāṣāya*.
He entrusted him with the task, saying, "Simply dismantle the embankment and set it apart; the foundations may be made firm, but do not use oxen. Later, this proved to be exactly so.
When the ox was let loose in the mountains, the temple steward was about to build a stupa. The Master said to the ox, "Can you help me knead the clay?
The ox lowered its head and accepted the labor. Seven days after the stupa was completed, the ox died. The Master said, "The ox has already been reborn in a good realm."
In the first year of the Tianxi era, the Master passed away while seated. His verse read: "I do not wish to be born in heaven or a pure land;
I only clarify that the mind-ground is fundamentally perfect and eternal. The wondrous nature of Vairocana neither comes nor goes; it illuminates past and present, pervading the ten directions.
Seven days later, his eyes remained brilliant and clear as if he were still alive.
Liao: Faju (with Yukuī appended). Regarding Faju, his clan and native place are not clearly known.

Like a fragrant orchid sprouting in a secluded thicket, his pearl-like brilliance was hidden in its luster; no one recognized his potential, save for Vinaya Master Feirul of Zijin Temple in Jingxi, who marveled at him and took him as a novice.
He thoroughly investigated the study of the Vinaya and maintained the precepts with meticulous care regarding both prohibitions and transgressions.
His nature was attained spontaneously; it was not the result of artificial cultivation. Although his conduct remained within the Vinaya, his aspirations were set upon the joy of dhyāna.

For over ten years, he sought out masters to seek guidance and resolution. He sat upright with a sense of solemnity, his intensity as great as that of one whose head is on fire. It seemed as though there were a moment of illumination.

During the Qingning era, he was summoned to collate and verify the commentaries and manuscripts of various schools. Some who were envious of him plotted to replace him, but the Master earnestly sought to retire, desiring to cease all competition for gain.
Contemporary opinion praised this highly, and his reputation spread far and wide. He was subsequently granted a purple robe and a formal title.

After a long time, he returned to live in seclusion on Mount Mian Shan, and those from both near and far held him up as a model of pure conduct. During the Xianyou era, the Emperor [bestowed] gold upon him...

The affairs of the monastic community on the island were numerous and complex; one required a person of both talent and virtue to manage them. When the records of these matters were compiled, everyone agreed that no one but the Master would suffice.
An urgent summons was issued, and although he wished to decline, he could not do so. At that time, as the ordination platform was first being established, people gathered like clouds.

The Master served as the Great Preceptor (Dàhéshàng) and presided solemnly over the myriad assembly. Even those from remote frontiers and isolated regions braved dangers and risked their lives to come.

Having come from ten thousand *li*, I hoped to behold your compassionate countenance once more and receive your oral teachings; it was as if I had returned with the acquisition of a supreme treasure, as though some divine being had spoken to me to bring this about.
The Khitan Ruler thirstily longed for a single audience and treated you with the etiquette due to a teacher.

From the Empress Dowager and consorts down to all others, they all performed the reverence of prostrating at your feet. By special imperial decree, you were granted the rank of Chonglu Da-fu (Grand Master of Venerable Stipend) and appointed as Acting Minister of Works (*Sikong*). And...
He was conferred the title of "Great Master of Precepts" (Chuanjie Dashi) and honored with a poem containing the lines: "The pine atop the summit of Peak of Practice reaches a thousand feet;

the precepts are as pure as the single orb of the heavenly moon. Such was the esteem in which he was held. Later, he repeatedly accepted invitations to major monasteries, making the propagation of the precepts his sole concern.
Wherever he went, men and women filled the roads; they all abandoned their market stalls and ceased their plowing, forgetting both hunger and thirst.
Successive requests for audiences and worship left no leisure; it was just as if he were being enticed by profit and desire.

Calculating the total from beginning to end, those who received the precepts and called themselves disciples reached over five million, and the number of monks fed was equal to this. Beyond these, there were those who gave out of hearing his name or through acts of spontaneous devotion.

He calculated that even the grasses and trees could not exhaust the extent of his merit. Thus he applied himself with tireless diligence, as if he had never achieved enough, ever fearing that he might fall short.
In his wisdom, he labored until he was stricken with illness; though he rarely partook of food or drink, his vigor never faltered.

He instructed the assembly of students, speaking repeatedly and earnestly of the necessity of observing the precepts. On the fourth day of the third month of the first year of the Dàkāng era, he passed away peacefully amidst the community.
His secular age was fifty-five, and his monastic seniority (śrāmaṇeraka) was thirty-nine. When the news of his death was reported, the Liao Emperor expressed deep sorrow and lamentation.
He ordered the Grand Taster (Taichangqing) Yang Wenqiao to oversee the funeral arrangements. The seven classes of followers wailed in grief as if they had lost their parents.
After the cremation, his sacred relics were collected and enshrined in a stupa to the right of the abbot’s quarters. Someone offered this elegy in his honor:

"Leaving the Jimen Gate to gaze toward the west, I behold the craggy peaks and mountain ridges. Among these myriad hills, high and low, why is it that only this one is called 'Saddleback'? It was not...
Beneath it lies that which was once inhabited by others; the divine lamps flare with brilliance, and the ancient jade is free from flaw.

Transmitting the Buddha’s precepts, they awaken the deaf and the blind; upholding the Vajra, they terrify demons and heretics. The gate of deliverance is opened wide, and those far and near rush toward it like clouds.
Manifesting the virtue of the dragon, he came to attend at the imperial gate. With a single roar, the lion, the celestial steed, leaves its fodder.
Above and below communicate in perfect trust, like a bird breaking open its egg. The Dharma-sound is proclaimed by day, and the Imperial verses are chanted by night.
Alas, the Master’s virtue is inexhaustible; his longing heart remains suspended through the ages. When the Master passed away, the one who succeeded to his Way was named Yukuī. Yukuī...

It was unknown where he was from. He maintained his virtue and strictly observed the precepts, possessing the demeanor of a true master. The Liao ruler praised him and continued to confer upon him the title of Dharma Master for Transmitting Precepts (Chuanjie Dashi).
He was granted the rank of Chonglu Daifu Jianjiao Taishou and appointed as the Superintendent of Tianqing Temple.

Furthermore, he was presented with the Emperor’s own composition, the *Bodhicitta-śīla-sūtra*, and ordered to open a ordination platform (*kai jitan*) to administer the precepts exactly as the Master had done during his lifetime. He reached the age of seventy.
He transformed others through his influence. Kuīxìng was humble and yielding; in all matters, he did not wish to surpass others. He exhorted people to fulfill compassion and cease killing.

Fishermen burned their nets and changed their vocations, numbering several dozen households. He petitioned the throne to abolish hunting grounds and established charitable granaries in several locations to prepare for years of famine.
While the *Poṣadha* ceremony was being recited, there was one who had been eating fish; a radiant glow appeared upon the meat, and the man, struck with fear, began to consume only vegetarian food.
Once, he passed by the Black Raft Wilderness (*Kālakaṭa-araṇya*), where a youth was herding cattle. When the cattle saw him, they approached and knelt to welcome him.

The owner immediately offered both the cattle and the youth to him. In his middle years, he also participated in monastic affairs. When the monks came to the wilderness on business, [he would] first...
He used kind words to guide and encourage them, so that in the end there were no lawsuits. The men thanked him and he gave them a string of prayer beads.
During a year of famine, he once went to Zijin Temple to distribute gruel to the hungry. Someone told him that they lacked water for cooking;

he probed the ground with his staff and, digging about a foot deep, found a spring of sweet water. When the task was finished and he took enough for himself, the monk Kui departed, and the water followed him as well.
This is merely a general outline of his traces. Regarding such a master as this, one need not seek exhaustive detail. **Jin Wumen and Wuzhu:
Biographies of the Two Great Masters of Precepts.** Wumen was the son of the Sun clan from Linhuang.
From childhood, he was intelligent and quick-witted. At fourteen, he donned the robes for sweeping stupas and served the Buddha. At that time, Master Puxian...
The virtuous Master, having been summoned for an audience because of his Way and finding him extraordinary, enrolled him as a disciple. He took him into the capital.

[The youth] was grave in appearance and humble in speech; in performing tasks such as sweeping and responding to others, he was exceptionally proficient. Princes, dukes, and high officials came to recognize and appreciate him.
When receiving the scriptures from his master, while others could only complete a single great volume after ten days, he could finish it in a single day.

When Bi passed away, Min followed his dharma-elder Yujing to study, mastering the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*. When he analyzed the meanings before the assembly, his eloquence flowed like a spring;

among the learned scholars and eminent masters of long standing, there were none who did not sigh in admiration, deeming him unattainable. Yet Min never once used this as a basis for self-aggrandizement.
As people from near and far vied to entreat him to preach the Dharma, he would leave without regard for them. He then went to visit Master Cei Tongli.

Furthermore, he saw Master Jizhao Geng, from whom he secretly received instruction and guidance; his benefit was profound. For another ten years, he set aside his intellectual cleverness and withdrew from worldly activities.
Only then did he emerge into the world, delighting in meditation (*dhyāna*) himself and using the precepts (*śīla*) to guide others.

Puxian was the first patriarch of the Precept Platform School. Puxian transmitted it to Kui; after Kui passed away, it was transmitted to Min, who became the third patriarch. [The Emperor] bestowed [the title] upon him.
His purple robes and monastic title were those of one whose disciples did not fall short of his ancestors or fathers;

furthermore, he attained the realization of the *zhū* (the smallest unit of weight) and transmitted it on, so that the lineage continued without interruption and the seat of the Vinaya was increasingly honored. He entered nirvana in the first year of the Huangtong era at the age of eighty-five.

He was sixty-five years old at death. His innate talent was profound and substantial; he did not engage in artificial refinement. He guarded the precepts like a precious pearl, never transgressing even in the most minute details.

Furthermore, he esteemed the worthy and devoted himself to giving, remaining untiring until his old age. He presided over twenty-two great monasteries (*māhā-vihāra*). Those who received the precepts from him numbered five million.
Beyond his practice of tranquility and concentration, his daily recitations and ritual observances all followed fixed quotas. Some may harbor doubts regarding this...
When [the Master] remarked, "The Way is manifold," Min smiled and said, "The eighty thousand dharma-gates are all functions of my own mind; what 'manifoldness' could there be?

After he had passed away, his body was cremated; the smoke coalesced into clouds, with five colors reflecting one another. His *śarīra* were like small pearls, appearing suddenly as one and then suddenly as many.
Some were even worth double or tenfold their weight; people scrambled for them and treasured them. How extraordinary! This too was a manifestation of the radiance of the precepts.
Wu Zhu (Wu-zhu) was styled Ziping; he was the son of He [Shi] of Linhuang. His father, Chun, was the Regional Commander of the Baixin Army and possessed a distinguished reputation.
Chun had five sons, and Zhu was the third. While she was pregnant, his mother abstained from meat; after he was born, she did not eat past midday.

At seven years of age, he studied the *Shi* and *Shu* classics; his intelligence surpassed that of others. At fifteen, he earnestly sought to leave the household life, but his parents would not permit it.

He subsequently ceased eating. Someone then exhorted his parents, saying: "Though official success is a fine thing in the human world, it may happen that one's virtue does not match their station, or that blessings do not accrue to the people.
To greedily crave wealth and honor for the duration of a horse's blink is to deviate from the Truth."

Losing one's true nature—what benefit does this bring to body and mind? Following his own aspiration, he paid respects to the Great Preceptor of the Baixu Taiwei, who transmitted the precepts, and served as his disciple.
