He received full ordination and mastered the various sutras and treatises; his refined understanding and subtle meanings surpassed those of veteran masters and long-standing scholars.
Later, he met Chan Master Fojue at Wangu Shanshan in Longquan. From that time on, there was no distinction between the school of practice and the school of doctrine.
Aid (Āi). He traveled to the regions of Pinglu, Zhuo, and Yi, where he established more than twenty lecture series on the *Awakening of Faith* (*Jué*) and the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* (*Léngyán*).

People flocked to receive his Dharma teachings as if the Buddha were still in the world. During the Huangtong era, he was appointed as the Right Street Monastic Registrar (*Sēnglù*) of the Central Capital and granted the title of Great Master Wénwù.
Shortly thereafter, he requested retirement and returned to Anshan, where he undertook major construction projects to complete the unfinished work of his predecessors. At...
In the northwest corner of the Hall, a Nirvana Hall was constructed, where he declared, "I shall cast off my skin here. He entered nirvana in the second year of the Jīngliàng-zhēnyuán era.
His precepts were transmitted to Yuǎn Gǒng. Zhū’s life was marked by many extraordinary occurrences; once, while staying at a village temple, a sudden flood broke out.
All the other buildings were completely destroyed, yet his meditation hall alone remained standing firm. When he ascended the altar to recite the precepts, five-colored clouds appeared in the sky;

within the clouds, countless lotus flowers were arrayed. A subtle light shone from his seat, which vanished when one drew near. He applied himself particularly to the doctrine of Consciousness-Only (Vijñaptimātra) and frequently made vows to be reborn in the Pure Land, saying:
"The Compassionate Honored One is in his final birth before Buddhahood; I wish to follow him and investigate the subtle depths [of reality]."
The Dharma-relics were merely [a few]. After the cremation, the śarīra remained filling a handful; the assembly of disciples constructed a stūpa to enshrine them.
Regarding the Biography of Dharma Master Guang’en of the Jia Clan:
he was a son of the Jia family from Mingshui in Shunde Road. In the early years of the Yuan dynasty, he shaved his head and became a monk at Kaiyuan Temple.
The monk’s master was also a man of great learning who trained him with considerable severity. The Master possessed a nature that surpassed others;

he was so deeply absorbed in his studies that he did not notice even the slightest change in facial expression or tone of voice. He applied himself with tireless diligence, fearing only that he might fail to grasp his teacher's mind.

Upon receiving full ordination and becoming a *bhikṣu*, he struck his staff and traveled afar to visit renowned mountains and veteran masters, practicing with such fierce vigor that those he left behind were moved by his departure.
His thoughts were focused on this. Furthermore, his observance of the precepts was strict and meticulous; he spoke little and was cautious in his movements.

His three karmas were solemn and disciplined, remaining as constant throughout the six periods of the day as during a single period. The Great Generalissimo of the Armies, Lu Tongzhen, who was a lay believer inclined toward the Buddha-vehicle, constructed a Pure Land temple.

He invited the Master to reside there. People, regardless of their status—whether noble or humble, near or far—vied with one another to offer donations. The golden and azure decorations shone brilliantly, appearing as if created by heaven or surged forth from the earth.
Because the Master’s reputation for the Way was long established, those who sought refuge in him gathered in great numbers; thus, they arrived without waiting for any summons.

Through diligent effort, he achieved success. One day, Yuanshuai requested to hear the teaching on the Pure Land. The Master said, "The essence of the mind is inherently pure; it is defiled by various activities.
If these activities can be unified, this is called 'attaining the essence. The essence is the pure mind; there is nothing else apart from the mind.
When the land is pure, the mind is pure; their principle is non-dual. Tongwen sighed in admiration and said, "These may truly be called essential words that are free of prolixity."
The memorial was presented to the court. He was bestowed the title of Great Bodhisattva Hugu Xingli Dashi Jia Fazong.
Guangjiao Lishi’s dharma-heir was Famen.
Famen was the son of the Yan clan of Shaanxi and a descendant of King Zhuang of Chu; he took the posthumous title as his surname and changed it to Yan to avoid the taboo name of the Han dynasty.
He was a successor to Master Zhuang. At the age of seven, he served Master Cande Hui. At fifteen, he shaved his head and donned the dyed robes; at twenty, he received full ordination.

He traveled for a long time among the regions of Bian, Ru, He, and Luo, where he studied the *Lotus Sūtra*, the *Prajñāpāramitā*, *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, *Hetuvidyā*, and the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* under the Venerable Master Wen.
Because Master Wen perceived that the Master’s responsibility was grave and the path ahead was long, he entrusted him with the mission of propagating and transmitting these teachings.

Out of devotion to the Buddha, he burned his flesh and set fire to his fingers to manifest his sincere resolve. Furthermore, he drew blood to transcribe the sutras and dwelt on Mount Tai, never crossing its threshold for six years.
He read the five thousand scrolls of the Tripitaka three times, whereby his spiritual practice and realization advanced greatly.

When the Imperial Preceptor heard the Master preach the Dharma, he turned to his disciples and said, "Who would have thought that such a person exists in the land of Han? Not long after, [the Master passed away].
Huī sent him a letter, exhorting him to benefit all equally and not forget his native land. The Master then raised his staff and traveled west.

Upon his arrival, the elders cried out in joy, saying, "The people of our village have found a teacher from whom we may receive instruction. Subsequently, by the command of the Prince of Anxi, he resided at Yishan Temple to the south of the city.
This was the site where the divine monk Dushun had manifested his presence during the early Tang dynasty. His Way was great.

Upon hearing of this, the Son of Heaven issued a summons. He was decreed to reside at Jiaojisi in Dayuan, where he was granted the rank of Ronglu Daifu and appointed as Grand Minister of Works (Dasi-tu).
He was subsequently transferred to Puqing Lanya, where he was further conferred the title of Kaifuyitongsan Si and Grand Minister of Works with a first-grade silver seal.

He was granted the *Kṣudrakavastu* (Jièběn) in golden script by the Emperor of the Liao dynasty. Princes, dukes, and high ministers all looked up to his lofty character, regarding him as a brilliant star or a phoenix;

there were none who did not follow him as their teacher and receive his instruction. In the third month of the fourth year of the Yanyou era, he passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture. This was reported to the throne.

The Emperor was deeply moved by compassion and granted several ten thousand strings of currency for his funeral. He issued an edict for a high minister to oversee the funeral rites, while the relevant authorities provided ceremonial guards, banners, and canopies to escort him.
His secular age was fifty-eight, and his monastic seniority (śrāmaṇera-vassa) was forty-three.
The Biography of Qingliang Xinming (with the inclusion of Yinbao).
Xinming, whose courtesy name was Zhenjue, was the son of the Gao family of Qingliang Tuan on Mount Wutai. He received the tonsure under the elder Zhenghong of the local Qingliang Temple.
At the age of fourteen, he became renowned for his lecturing; at twenty-four, he received full ordination. He composed various treatises.

He widely promoted the *Jiezhang* (Chapter on Precepts) and further authored commentaries (*chao*) on the *Ullambana Sūtra* and other texts. His elucidation of the meanings was so precise and brilliant that they were widely recited by his contemporaries.

Furthermore, he strictly disciplined himself in the gates of practice, reciting the precepts and reading the sūtras without the slightest negligence. When the Emperor summoned him for an audience, the Emperor’s heart was deeply impressed by him;
he was granted the title of Great Master Xingguo and appointed to the office of *Sengtong* (Patriarchal Overseer). He accepted these honors with reluctance, as it was not what he desired.
Later, he followed the Venerable Haiyun of Qingshou to inquire about the essentials for resolving his mind; he attained considerable awakening.

Nevertheless, he did not abandon his practice because of the understanding he had gained, but instead redoubled his self-exhortation and diligence until the radiance of his precepts was unsurpassed at the time.

From the imperial nobility down to the commoners and citizens, those who received the Bodhisattva precepts from him were exceedingly numerous, and his transformative influence spread throughout the region.

In the first month of winter, at the age of sixty-nine, he passed away into *nirvāṇa*. He obtained countless *śarīra* relics. An inscription commemorating his virtuous deeds survives at Zhengjue Temple.
In Yuci, there was one named Yinbao, who was likewise a monk of strict discipline. Although many from all quarters invited him to serve as abbot, he did not accept. Seven.
At the age of ten, he passed away while sitting in meditation. When his body was cremated, a golden light pierced through the fierce flames, and śarīra relics fell like rain;
his eyes and tongue remained unburnt. Later, someone saw him at Yellow Reed Ridge riding a white donkey.
The Biography of Vinaya Master Huiwen.
Huiwen was a native of Yanwu in Guide. In his year of driving away the crows (at age seven), he relied upon the venerable elder Gang as a young attendant.
At twenty, he received the Bodhisattva precepts from the Great Virtuous One, Master Wen. He subsequently succeeded Master En as the presiding master of the Dharma altar. Thereafter...

His virtuous conduct flourished daily and his realization became increasingly manifest; those who followed him grew ever more numerous. According to the Buddha’s regulations, all who are bhikṣus must, though their great principles remain unimpaired, be meticulous in their minor practices.
They must not set eyes upon what is contrary to the Dharma, nor eat at improper times. In their dwelling and every movement, they must act with restraint.
All these have their established rules, intended to restrain negligence and prevent the dissipation of virtue. The Master guarded them with strict care;

he rose at the crowing of the cock and sat waiting for the break of dawn. He remained diligent throughout the entire day, mindful of nothing but the Buddha, even when traveling on the road or staying overnight.
He carried his three robes and one alms bowl with him at all times. His disciplined conduct was exceedingly lofty, yet he was free from artificiality or affectation;
his integrity was firm, yet he left no trace of eccentricity or over-exertion. Consequently, none who spoke of him failed to believe him, and none who witnessed his actions failed to revere him.
Throughout the region between the two rivers, in the ancient cities of the Three Supervisors, those who followed his transformation numbered in the tens of thousands. Monastics and laypeople alike—

Those who came seeking the Dharma of the precepts followed one after another along the roads; upon receiving even a single word of instruction, there was none whose heart was not filled with joy and gratitude.
He preached the Dharma for over several decades and ascended the dais to confer the precepts on more than forty occasions.
Great ministers received him with the etiquette due to a teacher. In the third year of Zhishun, he passed away at the age of seventy-three.
Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks,
Volume Seventeen and Volume Eighteen,
compiled by the Śramaṇa Minghe of Huashan Temple in Wumen.
The Section on Protecting the Dharma:
Biography of Wei Lin of the Song Dynasty (including Tian Shi).
Wei Lin was the son of Shen [Shen] of Wukang, a descendant of Yue. He was fond of learning and skilled in poetry. During the Xining era, Dongpo...

While serving as an attendant in Hangzhou, he requested to reside at Mount Jing. Subsequently, he ascended the Dharma seat of Master Huiyuan, under whom the monastic community flourished and the hearts of the multitude turned toward him in devotion.
After some time, weary of the bustle, he withdrew to quietude at Tóngshān in the district, where he built a hermitage named Wúwèi (Fearless) and styled himself the "Great Being Wúwèi.
At the beginning of the Jiàngguó era of the Jiànzhōng reign, when Sūndāo returned from Dānlǐ to Bīlíng, he informed [the Master] of his illness.

When the Master went to visit and console him, Su Dongpo replied with a poem. Previously, when the Master was residing at Tongsan, there was a pine tree in the monastery with a trunk thick enough to encircle a man’s arms.
The magistrate of the county intended to take it to build an official residence. When the Master learned of this, he ordered the bark to be stripped away and inscribed a poem upon it, saying:
"The Magistrate takes you away to serve as a pillar or beam, No longer will your clear shade protect the green moss. I only fear that when the night grows deep, your light..."

Beneath the moon, he mistakenly caused a crane to fly a thousand li away. When the Magistrate arrived and read his poem, he desisted. In the first year of the Xuande era, the Master was already advanced in years;
as the imperial court then held the Daoist religion in high esteem, an edict was issued requiring monks to become "De-si" (Virtuous Men) and wear crowns.

The Master alone would not accept this command. The County dispatched an envoy to exhort him, whereupon the Master immediately assembled his disciples, recited a gāthā, sat cross-legged, and passed away. The assembly...
Two jars were used to cover his body, and he was buried behind the mountain.
As for Tian Shi, he was a monk from Shisong Temple on the west side of the Water in Hougan County, Fuzhou. For ten years, he planted three pine trees upon a rock.
He personally inscribed a stone, saying: "One is to provide a name and substance for the temple gate; two are for the mountain forests."
It serves as a landmark; thirdly, it provides shade for travelers. A poem inscribed there says: "Like a reclining canopy, it covers the rocky crags;
Through the cold of the year, it stands proud against frost and snow. Its deep roots coil around *fuling* fungi; For a thousand ages, it has been satiated by wind and moon.
The temple was originally named Shisōng (Stone Pine) and later named Shisōng (Stone Cypress) for this reason. One can thus imagine the "Heavenly Stone" as well.
The Biography of Huiming of Ba’en Monastery in Hangzhou:

Huiming was the son of the Jiang family. He left home to become a monk at a young age and became thoroughly proficient in the three studies. Later, he traveled to Linchuan to pay his respects to Fayan.
Suddenly, he attained a profound realization. He returned to the waters of Ningbo and lived as a hermit at Mount Damei.

Although the study of Chan was flourishing within the territories of Wu and Yue, the orthodox lineage of Xuansha had been excluded from its inner sanctum. The Master wished to rectify and guide it; one day, a Chan practitioner arrived at his hut.
The Master asked him, "Where have you recently departed from? He replied, "Chengdu. The Master said, "Upādhyāya, having left Chengdu..."
Upon arriving at this mountain, he remarked, "In Chengdu there were few *shangzuo* (senior monks), whereas here there are many *shangzuo*. 'Many' implies that there are phenomena outside the mind;
'few' implies that the mind and its phenomena are not all-encompassing. When he finished explaining his reasoning, he remained silent, and the Zen guests were unable to respond.
Later, he moved to Bai Sha Hermitage on Mount Tiantai. There was a practitioner named Yanming who prided himself on his sharp eloquence; he came to visit the Master, who asked him:
[The Master] asked, "Have there been any among the former virtuous ones who attained enlightenment? He replied, "There have.

[The Master] said, "When one person awakens and returns to the source, the empty space of the ten directions shall all vanish away. Pointing his finger, he said, "Right now, Mount Tiantai stands majestic;
how can it be known that it has vanished away? Ming opened his eyes wide and stared straight at him before fleeing. Later, the King Zhongyi of Qian invited him to inquire about the Dharma.
The Emperor appointed him to the Chongzi Yuan (Court of Honored Rank). There, he extensively expounded upon the fundamental tenets of Xuansha Fayen.

Consequently, those from other schools who had studied in a superficial manner all submitted in silent reverence. One day, during a great Dharma assembly convened by King Zhongyi for the various mountains, the Master asked the elder patriarchs:
"The inscription for the pagoda of Xuefeng states: 'That which exists through conditions undergoes formation and decay from beginning to end. It is not...'"
"That which exists by way of conditions endures and remains firm throughout kalpas. Let us set aside for now the questions of its firmness and its destruction.
Where is Xuefeng right now? The old master was unable to answer. The King greatly praised him and appointed him as the Chan Master Yuantong Puzhao.
The Biography of Chan Master Zongze of Changlu.
Zongze was the son of the Sun family of Xiangyang. His father died early, and his mother took him back to her own family’s home to raise him.

Upon reaching adulthood, he studied Confucian learning; his character and resolve were lofty and far-reaching, and his scholarship was vast and profound. At the age of twenty-nine, he suddenly exclaimed, “I shall leave the household life.”
Having returned home, he proceeded to Changlu in Zhenzhou to tonsure under Xiu Ciyun and study the Supreme Vehicle.
Before long, Xiu passed away and Fu succeeded him; the Master received the essential instructions from Fu and subsequently became his dharma heir, inheriting the seat of Changlu.

For three successive generations, the father and son of the Faku lineage transmitted and propagated the teaching one after another, so that the Way of Yunmen resounded mightily throughout the regions between the Yangtze and Huai rivers, until there was almost no other sound heard there.
The Master ascended the hall and said: "Though gold dust is precious, if it falls into the eye, it becomes a cataract.
Once the gold dust is removed, where is the eye? He took up his staff and asked, "Do you see? He struck the incense table and asked, "Do you hear?"
Leaning on his staff, he said: "If the eyes and ears are unobstructed, one is sufficient wherever one is; the sounds of water and the colors of mountains flow on of their own accord.
His instruction was thus clear and penetrating. By nature filial, the Master built a separate small room beside the abbot’s quarters and settled his mother within it.
He urged his mother to shave her head and maintain the recitation of the name of Amitābha Buddha. He composed a "Treatise on Encouraging Filial Piety" himself, exhausting every nuance of his grief.
Kěn. Although the Master inherited and transmitted the sudden teachings of the Southern School, he in truth took refuge in the Pure Land.

He moved the two Great Beings, Samantabhadra and Samantamati, so that they appeared in his dreams seeking admission to his society; thus, his sincerity may be known. When his mother was approaching death, she indeed passed away auspiciously while reciting the Buddha’s name.
Throughout several decades from beginning to end, he gathered and transformed others through the single gate of An-yang (Peaceful Nurturing). [The assembly of] monastics...
Bai followed his transformation and maintained right mindfulness at the moment of death; those who were like his mother must surely number in the hundreds.

The Master maintained diligent effort to rectify the Way, attaining his innate nature through a single-minded resolve. Since words cannot reach far enough, he often entrusted his heart’s intent to brush and ink.
Regarding the exhortation to make offerings, he said: "If one lacks a limited mind, one will receive inexhaustible blessings."

Regarding his exhortation to practice seated meditation, he said: "Do not deliberate upon any good or evil whatsoever. When a thought arises, be immediately aware of it; once you are aware of it, it is lost.

After a long time, forgetting all conditions, one naturally becomes a single whole. He further said: "When the Way is high, demonic obstacles are rampant; there are myriad ways of opposition and compliance."
If one can simply maintain right mindfulness before oneself, nothing at all can obstruct it. Regarding his warnings against idle talk, he said:
"Since it deviates from meritorious karma, it is of no benefit to the mind of the Way. Such idle chatter as this harms true virtue. Regarding his warnings against nihilism, he said:
The coarse interpreter of the Dharma lacks the eye of doctrinal penetration; the vain Chan practitioner does not value the gate of practice.

This is the fault of partiality. It is further said: "When both the school and the teachings are mastered, one is like the bright sun shining across the realm of space; mind and body are both tranquil."

It is like a beryl gem containing the light of the precious moon; one might say it is like mugwort growing amidst hemp, straightening itself without support, or like the myriad rivers flowing into the sea, collectively called the Celestial Pond.
Its words and meaning reach their ultimate point; by tasting a single morsel, one can know the whole cauldron.
I have not yet ascertained its conclusion.
Biography of Zongchi (with Juqie and his son Zhao). As for Zongchi:
he was the great-great-grandson of Linji in the eleventh generation and the direct successor of Chan Master Letan Zhun.
He resided at Mount Dongshan, where he established himself through the practice of the Way and became widely venerated by his contemporaries for his unimpeded wisdom.
This mind constitutes the matter of the adornment of merit. Hong Juefan’s *Record of the Ciguan Pavilion* states:

"The Master’s facial features were stern and cold; his heroic spirit transcended the common crowd. He took it as his personal responsibility to uphold the Dharma-way of Yun'an. His preaching of the Dharma possessed eloquence and wisdom;

his protection of the Teachings was characterized by effective action. He disparaged monastic communities that contended over their lineages like ditches and boundaries, or argued about right and wrong based on mere words."

It is not so. The various quarters are in a state of chaotic turmoil, burning fiercely and showing no sign of ceasing; they call themselves "those who run the Way," yet in reality they run after fame and seek profit.
They engage in petty trade and peddling without limit, while the True Teaching grows faint. I wished to abandon them but could not bear it; I wished to guide them but they would not follow.
Thereupon, I built a hall to the east of Fangzhang and named it "The Compassionate Ferry" (Cihang), and I also gave myself a new title.
He called it "Compassionate Awakening" (Cijue), yet he still felt this was insufficient. He constructed a pavilion at the main gate and named it "Compassionate Contemplation" (Ciguan).
A monk from Shu named Ju Jie contributed one million five hundred thousand units of long-measure currency to help complete it. Throughout his life, Jie had maintained extremely frugal habits;
the offerings he received from donors were accumulated bit by bit until they reached the height of several inches. His forty years' worth of savings he gave away all at once.
He bestowed [the land] upon him. Others considered this difficult; however, the monk Zizhao of the Southern Jin possessed genuine practice and innate wisdom.

He was like a man who, with a confident hand, carves both square and round shapes, all of which fall precisely within the lines and measurements. When Cijue appointed him to oversee the affairs of the monastery, there were no matters—whether great or small—that he did not attend to.

They discussed and settled the plans with ease. Jiaozhi managed the construction, overseeing the work with unwavering diligence. With faces soiled and hands cracked by the cold, they did not shrink from the frost and snow.
They felled timber from the mountains and transported earth and gravel, working alongside their servants and laborers.
After half a year, it was completed. Exhausting his wealth for this act of charity, Cijue’s aspiration was finally fulfilled. Both master and disciple were thus devoted to the tradition.
There is nothing to be ashamed of. How virtuous he was!
The Record of the Dharma Master Baojue Daofa by Yongdao.

Yongdao was the son of Mao of Shunchang. Having left the household life, he took the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and the *Śata-dharmaka-śāstra* as his primary doctrines. Furthermore, he received [instruction from] the West...
Tian received the *dhāraṇī* and Tripiṭaka esoteric teachings, as well as the transmission of the Perfect and Sudden Precepts from Master Yuánzhào; he mastered the essentials of them all.
During the Zhènghé era, he was granted purple robes and appointed as the head of Xiāngjì Monastery in the Left Street, receiving the honorary title of Dàshī Bǎojié.

At the beginning of the Xuānhuá era, Lín Língsù, who deluded the Emperor with heterodox ways, issued an edict to change the name of monks to "Virtuous Men" (*déshì*) and require them to wear caps and gowns. Tian—
Those below followed him, none daring to lag behind. Only Master [Dao]xuan remained resolute and defiant in the face of the imperial decree, submitting a memorial that stated:

"From antiquity, the Buddha-dharma has never failed to wax and wane in tandem with the fortunes of the state. When Emperor Taiwu of the Wei dynasty and Cui Hao suppressed the Buddha-dharma, within three or four years, Cui Hao’s entire clan was exterminated.
When Emperor Wen of the Sui greatly promoted it, and when Emperor Wu of the Zhou and Wei Yuansong suppressed the Buddha-dharma, within five..."

Six years later, Yuansong was demoted and died. Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty greatly promoted [the Dharma]. During the Tang dynasty, under Emperor Wuzong, Zhao Guizhen and Li Deyu suppressed the Buddha-dharma;
yet within less than a year, Guizhen was executed and Deyu was exiled to die. Emperor Xuanzong greatly promoted it once more.

In our own nation, the founding Emperors Taizu and Taizong, along with their successive sagacious successors, translated scriptures, examined monks, and greatly promoted the Buddha-dharma—this is the established constitutional precedent.
These matters are fully recorded; they may be upheld for ten thousand generations. Your Majesty, how can you bear to carry out such a world-shocking act upon the sudden advice of a treacherous man?

Your Majesty, do you not reflect upon Emperor Taiwu being assassinated by the hands of eunuchs, Emperor Wu of Zhou becoming a prisoner in an iron dungeon, and Emperor Wu of Tang receiving the retribution of having his life-span shortened and his throne usurped? These are all former warnings.
"Your Majesty should consider this: why do you tread upon the calamities of wicked rulers and violate the laws of your ancestors?

When this memorial was submitted, the Emperor was greatly incensed and ordered Cai Jing to be branded and exiled to Daozhou. Cai Jing then spoke to the Emperor with composure, saying, "The Buddhist images throughout the empire were not made by the monks themselves;
they were all made by sons for their fathers and by subjects for their sovereigns, in order to pray for blessings."
"It was merely for the sake of repaying his kindness. Now, to disparage him so greatly is precisely what will stir the hearts of the people; I fear it is not in the interest of the state.
The Emperor’s mind turned slightly from this. Before long, Ling and Su’s affair collapsed; they were sent back home and executed on the road. [The Emperor] restored the teachings once more.

The Master was transferred to a nearby prefecture, where he soon received an imperial decree allowing him to return home. By imperial order, he was stationed at Zhaoxian Chan Monastery and granted the name Fadao (Way of the Dharma) to honor his protection of the Teaching.
When the Master was exiled to Daozhou, the prefectural governor and his subordinates all previously dreamed of a Buddha image entering the city wearing a cangue.

Soon thereafter, the Master arrived; they all treated him with kindness. At that time, many among the military and the common people were ill; the Master consecrated water with mantras for them to drink.

There was no one who did not recover. As those seeking his help increased, he established a pond within the military camp and performed incantations there for them. Once the Master had returned, the Daoist felt as though he had lost a parent.

When the two Emperors were taken north on their hunt and Emperor Kang ascended the throne, Zong Ze, the Guardian of the Eastern Capital, received imperial authorization to appoint the Master as the Abbot of Tianqing Temple in the Left Ward and to confer upon him the rank of Xuanjiao Lang (Proclaiming Teaching Official) as an aide to the Commander-in-Chief.

He planned military affairs, administered the law for the state, and protected the troops. When the army marched toward the Huai and Ying rivers, he exhorted the local gentry to provide grain to assist the state;
the army relied upon this to survive. Later, he followed the imperial entourage by imperial decree and participated in deliberations on matters of state.

The Emperor wished to invest him with the ceremonial crown and robes, but the Master declined resolutely. By imperial edict, he was granted the title Great Master Yuantong Faji. One day, the Emperor spoke to him at ease:
The Master said, "The Retired Emperor was deluded by sorcerers and destroyed my monastic robes and appearance. Your Majesty has now removed these tattoos for me.
The Master replied, "I cannot bear to destroy the ink applied by the Retired Emperor. The Emperor laughed and said, "This monk remains stubborn to the very end."
He was then commanded to reside at Taiping Chan Temple on Mount Lu. According to established custom, monks were seated to the left and followers of heterodox paths to the right;

however, since the Chongguan era, this ancient regulation had been altered. The Master could not tolerate this and went to the imperial court to debate the matter, ultimately succeeding in having the arrangement rectified.

In the fifth year of the Shaoxing era, a great drought occurred, and an imperial edict summoned the Master to the palace to pray for rain. He established an altar and performed the ritual, using four golden vases, each filled with...

Taking fresh carp, he sprinkled water and offered silent prayers, dispatching four swift messengers to cast them into the river. Before they had even returned, the rain had already fallen in abundance.

The Emperor was greatly pleased and bestowed upon him a golden bowl. Because the state treasury lacked funds, the Emperor issued an edict for monks and Daoists throughout the realm to pay "clear-and-leisure" taxes.

The Master sent a letter to the provincial ministries, arguing vehemently against this measure; it violated the great principles of governance and obstructed wholesome transformation. Although his words—
He did not practice [meditation]. His influence also diminished somewhat. In the autumn of the seventeenth year of the Shaoxing era, he recited a gāthā and passed away while sitting upright.
After his cremation, countless śarīras were found. He was interred in a stupa at Jiuli Song on Mount Jiushan.
The Biography of Chan Master Fading.
His courtesy name was Chuanzhao. He was the son of the Wang family in Huayang, Chengdu. From his youth, he was already able to discourse on matters of integrity and principle.

He was skilled in calligraphy and painting. Transcending the common crowd, he remained unbound by worldly conditions. At the age of twenty-three, he tonsured himself at Chengtian Monastery and received full ordination (*upasampadā*).
He immediately began lecturing on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, and even the venerable elders humbled themselves before him.

His master, Dharma Master Yuanming, abandoned his lectures and departed for Sichuan; the Master attended him on his travels. Upon reaching Gongzhou, the master passed away, and [the disciple] escorted his remains back for burial.
He departed from Chengdu and took leave of the stupa. Traveling down the Jing River and across the mountains of Huai, he reached the Han and Mian rivers in the north.

He visited various masters everywhere, staying for only a short time at each; when their words did not accord with his own insight, he would strike his staff and depart immediately. Ascending Mount Dahong, he paid his respects to Master Kai, whereupon he took him as his spiritual mentor and settled there.

Receiving the master’s countenance and receiving his teachings, they deliberated upon matters of the past and present. [Kai’s] responses were subtle and profound; in the exercise of his virtue, he never shrank from taking the lead.

At the beginning of the Daguan era, Master Kai responded to the imperial summons and traveled west. In the third year, because he refused to accept the official decree and title of "Master," he was dressed in scholar’s robes and exiled to Zizhou.
The Master followed him on foot, his feet blistered with the journey. The monastics and laypeople of Zizhou held his righteousness in high esteem.
Governor Li Guo vacated the Taiping Xingguo Chan Monastery to provide a dwelling for him. Thereupon, the tradition of the Dongshan school flourished once again.
In the first year of the Zhenghe era, Master Kai was released from his confinement and fled eastward to the seashore, traveling over a thousand *li*.
He settled amidst Lake Tai, where he wore clothes of grass and drank from mountain streams, as if intending to remain there for the rest of his life.

The Master (Zhaozhou) still went to follow him, but Kai gestured dismissively with his hand and said, "The path to Yunyan is cut off; the responsibility rests upon your own person. Go now. The Master understood his meaning, bowed twice, and returned. (7)
In his later years, he resigned from his duties at the Institute for the Exegesis of Scriptures and returned west to the capital, where his reputation reached the Emperor.

Shortly thereafter, an imperial decree was issued appointing him as the abbot of Zhenghe Chan Temple at Lumen in Xiangyang. After declining the honor and retiring, the Master was invited to dine in the hall of the Chancellor’s residence.

An official brought a document forward and informed him, "Donglin Temple in Jiangzhou is to be converted into a Daoist observatory, in accordance with the request of the Daoist practitioners. The Master rose from his seat and said, "Mount Lu is the crown of..."

This world is a realm of desolation, and Donglin is its most excellent spot. For ages it has served as a monastic residence; like white gulls upon a spring lake, it was naturally suited for such a purpose.
Now that those wearing yellow caps occupy its midst, is this not a calamitous turn of fate for this secluded sanctuary?

The Chancellor greatly agreed with this view, and the preservation of Donglin was due to the Master’s efforts. Upon arriving at Hanshang, the regional commander exhorted the various mountains to provide gold and silk.

He went to the capital to perform a "Thousand-Preacher Feast" (Qian Dao Zhai). The Master smiled and said, "Since my childhood, I have served the Buddha with single-minded devotion; I would rather die than waver.
Unless one is a madman who has lost their mind, why would they suddenly use the offerings of the ten directions to curry favor with Daoist masters for a thousand *li*?

The regional commander was ashamed by these words and desisted. Nevertheless, when the monastic communities throughout the land heard of this, they marveled at his resolve. Lumen was situated along the Han River. [The text here is truncated.]

The cliffs were a thousand feet high. The temple had long suffered from a lack of water. The Master sat beneath a rocky crag and thought to himself, "I wish to establish a monastic community here to plant blessings for the Imperial Court;
yet the springs cannot suffice for the multitude. Does the spirit of the mountain not know this?
With his staff, the Master prodded the roots of the grass, and suddenly many springs gushed forth. The entire assembly was greatly amazed, and the people of the mountains looked upon him with awe.

He was called Master Denggong Quan. Initially, the Master relied upon Chan Master Ling of Jia Shan. Master Ling’s Way was solitary and his transformation [of others] was such that no one remained as his successor.

Only the monk Weixian had grasped his essential meaning; he lived in seclusion at Mount Nanyue. The Master sent a letter to Changsha, and a messenger went to welcome him out, where he resided at Longan Chan Monastery.
Those who heard of this were moved by his integrity and esteemed his conduct. Formerly, there was Chan Master Huiding...

Zizhao transformed the Vinaya school into Chan. He passed away before his pioneering work was half-finished. Ants nested and bees swarmed there, leaving behind old hives and mounds; ten parts remained as seven.
The Master renovated them all anew, with long corridors and vast halls supported by ten thousand stone pillars rising from the cliffs.

Beneath his staff and whisk, five thousand disciples gathered, and within ten years, the school’s influence flourished greatly. To the common people, he appeared merely as one who moved about with a slow, shuffling gait.

He played with ease, yet was unaware of his own ultimate rigidity, severity, and intensity. He placed firm faith in what he had learned; even before imperial majesty or noble power, he did not dare to act contrary to righteousness.
By nature, he delighted in giving, regardless of whether he possessed much or little; he emptied his granaries and overturned his storehouses to rush to the aid of those in urgent distress.
In the spring of the second year of Jingkang, when the Jin people invaded once more and the two palaces were besieged, Master [Wang] was struck with terror and alarm.
He spoke, dismissing his disciples and closing his door to face the wall alone. A disciple said, "Matters of the court and the military—how do they concern a man dwelling in the forest?
Why does the Master alone harbor such deep anxiety? The Master gazed at him intently and said slowly, "A river’s moisture extends nine li, yet it gradually wets only three hundred paces.
When a tree falls from a height of a thousand fathoms, it tramples down only a single inch of grass. How could there be..."
The Central Plains had fallen, yet could those who dwell beneath the forest trees find peace and leisure?

On the night of the thirteenth day of the fifth month, sitting serenely at midnight, he exhorted his disciples that all matters concerning the Great Matter of the School (the Dharma-gate) must take precedence over private affairs. He then passed away in stillness.

Upon examining what he had accumulated, there was nothing beyond his ritual implements—merely a few scrolls of calligraphy and painting. He had lived through fifty-three years of the world, sitting [in meditation]...
In the summer of the thirtieth year, the whole body [of the master] was enshrined in a pagoda at Hyedŏng-t’a to the east of the Sankyōkei villa.
Wansong Lao Ren (The Elder Wansong). (Appendix: Ch’ŏnŭn). Haengsu’s style name was Wansong.
He was a native of Hae-nŭi. His clan was the Chae family. From childhood he was extraordinary; he possessed a transcendent disposition for renouncing the world.
Zhì repeatedly petitioned his parents to seek ordination as a monk. Although his parents initially resisted, they realized that in the end he could not be dissuaded by worldly ties.
Consequently, they escorted him to Jingtu Monastery in Xingzhou, where he paid homage to Master Yūnyún as his preceptor and received the tonsure.

After receiving full ordination, he resolved to apply himself with determination to the investigation of the Way. He then took up his travel bag and traveled to Yan, resting at Tanzha Monastery and visiting Qingshou Monastery before calling upon Master Shèng.
The old man remained silent. The old master said, "To study this Way is like smelting gold: if the dross is not completely removed, the pure essence will not manifest.
Looking at you, there is something substantial between your brows; this thing cannot be laid down unless you undergo one more thorough freezing."
"You shall see for yourself later; there is no need for this old monk to say more. The Master then redoubled his diligent and fierce efforts until he forgot both sleep and food.
Later, he went to Cizhou to study under Master Man of Yunyan. Thereupon, he attained great enlightenment beneath the master’s words, exclaiming: "To think it was so close!
Only now do I realize that Shengmo’s way of guiding people was driven by such profound compassion and that he had descended so deeply into the weeds. He remained with Xueyan for two years.
Having exhausted the depths of his realization, he entrusted his *saṃghāṭī* robe to him, exhorting him to propagate the Great Dharma.

From that time on, the people of the two rivers and the three provinces all drank in the Master’s fame; the Dharma gate became prominent and relied upon him as its weighty authority. During the Mingchang era, Emperor Zhangzong invited him into the inner court to preach the Dharma.
The Emperor personally presented him with a brocade *kaṣāya*, which he wore under his arm as he ascended the seat. From the Empresses and consorts downward...

All received the Dharma from the Master and prostrated themselves at his feet; each bestowed their cherished treasures upon him. He established a Universal Salvation Assembly (*pudu-hui*), and within a few days, auspicious signs appeared one after another.
His reputation spread far and wide. In the first year of the Cheng’an era, he was specially summoned by imperial decree to reside at Xiying Temple on Mount Yang.
This temple had previously been founded by King Sejong, who enshrined the Venerable Xuanming Yi as its founding patriarch. The Venerable Yi was formerly of the Jin...

The National Preceptor Daichan bestowed fields upon the monastic community to support them; while this represented the height of prosperity for the time, the sound of the Dharma had not yet been widely propagated.

Yet, as soon as the Master ascended the seat and proclaimed it once, ten thousand fingers were turned toward his teaching. Thus, from a lineage of Dongshan that had long been solitary, cold, and neglected, the Master suddenly caused it to rise again.
His merit in propping up the collapsing and continuing the severed line was no less than that of Qing Huayan. Subsequently, he moved to Bao...

He presided over the Jiwansu Monastery and later moved his seat to Bogeun, where he resided at these great monasteries in succession; his spiritual influence never waned. In his later years, he retired to Chongyongam Hermitage.
Amidst the leisure found in the secluded woods, he provided commentaries on Hongzhi’s *One Hundred Odes*, and further composed the *Jeongiknok* (Record of Seeking Instruction).
Following in the footsteps of the *Biyanyuan*, he polished away the accumulated grime from the *Baomingjing*. His work was of great benefit to the Chan school, and students flocked to him.

As for his current lineage of transmission: Master [Chengguan] was naturally gifted with sharp faculties; among the teachings of the hundred schools, there was nothing in which he was not profoundly versed.
He read through the Tripitaka three times, mastering it from beginning to end. Even masters senior in their experience of scriptural exegesis did not dare to deceive him with superficiality.
The layman Li Bingshan composed a treatise to propagate his school, of which people said: "Even if Mātr̥ceṭa and Zao Bo were to appear again, they could add nothing to this."
Nevertheless, those who daily visited the Master and received his instruction were numerous; thus, the Master’s contribution to the establishment of the Dharma was vast.
Later, he passed away without illness at the age of eighty-one.

Línquán Lǎorén Cónglún was a disciple of the Master. He resided at Bào'ēn Monastery in Dàdū and authored two works titled *Kōnggǔ Chuánshēng* (The Sound Transmitted through the Empty Valley) and *Xūtáng Xítīng* (Listening Practice in the Empty Hall), which provide commentaries on the "Eulogies on Ancient Cases" by the two masters Tóuzǐ Qīng and Dànxiá Chún.
In his own preface, he states: "By means of speech that is without speech, I speak of that which is spoken;
I cause that which is unheard to be heard, so that one hears what is truly heard. Commentators say that Master Lun had no intentional desire for words;
rather, wherever the Way resides, one cannot help but speak of it.
The Biography of Chan Master Gaoyun of Yunfeng, who transmitted the Dharma to Miaogao.

His courtesy name was Yunfeng. He was a native of Changxi in Fuzhou. His family had been engaged in the study of Confucianism for generations. His mother dreamed that she received an infant sitting in the heart of a lotus flower, holding it in her hands;
upon waking, she gave birth to the Master. Consequently, he was named Mengchi (Dream-Pool). His spirit and countenance were exceptionally refined and clear, and he was fond of books.
He applied himself diligently to his studies and was particularly devoted to the Buddhist scriptures (*neidian*).
He was so earnest in his pursuit of the Way that his parents, due to a dream, did not thwart his resolve and allowed him to receive full ordination from Master Yunmeng Zegong.

With a keen mind for seeking the Way, he first consulted Chijue Chong, who said, "This boy’s speech is fluent and well-ordered; he is a *hulian* (a vessel of jade) of our school. Subsequently, he visited Wuzhun Fan.

Fan was still attached to his position as a steward. When the Master proposed that he take up a service position, Fan sighed and said, "Seeking personal comfort ruins one's reputation," and he departed.
He went to see Yuxi at the Yuyang Monastery and served as the keeper of the storehouse keys. One day, Yuxi raised a simile: "It is like a cow passing through a window frame;
its head, horns, and four hooves all pass through, but why is it that the tail cannot pass? At these words, the Master had a sudden realization and replied, "The whale swallows the sea water."
When [the weeds] were exhausted, coral branches were revealed. Xi approved of this, and he subsequently resided at Dalu in Nanxing, becoming the direct successor of Yanxi.
He later moved to Baonan, Jiangyin, Quanzhong, Zhechuan, and Heshan; monks from all quarters flocked to him, and the three halls were all filled to capacity.

In the early years of the reign, he was summoned by imperial decree to Mount Jiang. In the year Yihai of the Deyou era, the temple was beset by military forces. Among the soldiers were those who coerced the Master for gold.
The Master said, "This place has only a temple and monks; there is no gold to give you. A soldier happened to brandish a blade at the Master’s neck and rubbed it against him.
The Master said, "If you wish to kill me, then kill me. My head is not a whetstone for your blade. The soldier was moved by these words and cast away his weapon.

He departed. The temple remained unharmed. In the *jiachen* year of the Zhizhi era (1280), he moved to Mount Jing. The mountain had suffered from a fire, and only one-tenth of its structures remained.

The Master exerted all his strength in reconstruction until it nearly regained its former splendor. In the first month of the following year, *jichou* (1289), it was again consumed by fire and reduced to ashes in an instant.
The monastics were greatly alarmed, but the Master sighed and said: "In my past lives, I have owed this mountain a debt; I shall now repay it."
He was grieved, thinking only that people did not understand that even a dog possesses Buddha-nature. The assembly was struck with awe; they then exerted all their strength to rebuild it once more.

It was completed in the tenth month of the Renchen year, consisting of a thousand pillars and costing one million units of labor. Although the Master oversaw the construction of the buildings, he chanted the Way morning and night.
Monks in cloud-like robes flocked to him, their staffs and alms bowls standing in orderly rows, yet he remained as if doing nothing at all. Hardly ten—
Within a single year, he established two magnificent monasteries as if drawing them from his own bosom; his achievement was truly grand.

At that time, the followers of the Teaching (Dharma) were肆意 (肆毁) destroying the Chan school, and the Emperor was about to believe their claims. The various elder Chan masters shrank back in silence. Hearing this, the Master sighed and said, "This is a momentous matter for our school.
I must struggle for it even at the cost of my life. He then gathered one or two colleagues and hurried to the capital. An imperial decree was issued: "Da..."
He convened a formal debate in the imperial court on both the Chan and doctrinal (Teaching) gates. The Emperor asked, "What is the fundamental principle of Chan?

The Master replied, "Pure wisdom is wondrously perfect; its essence is fundamentally empty and quiescent. It cannot be reached by seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing, nor by thought, deliberation, or discrimination. The Emperor questioned him repeatedly.

The Master traced back to the source and followed the current; following the words to meet the underlying principle, he composed a response of over two thousand words that flowed like a cascading spring or the resonance of wind through bamboo flutes.

The Emperor was greatly pleased. From then on, the imperial envoys no longer spoke of Chan to the Master’s disciples, yet the sovereign of the age came to place deep faith in Chan—this was entirely due to the Master’s power to turn heaven. Taking his leave of the throne, he returned south in the year of Gui...
On the seventeenth day of the sixth month, he passed away after composing a verse. He had lived seventy-five years in the world and held fifty-nine years of seniority in the monastic order.
His stupa was enshrined at Juding Monastery to the west of the temple.

Zhiwen’s lineage was passed to Zhiwen. His courtesy name was Qiyu, and his style name was Quan-yi. He was born into the Hao family of Xingzhou. From childhood, he was exceptionally intelligent and discerning.
At the age of six, he met Master Jizhao, who said, "Will you become a follower of the Śākya? The Master [Zhiwen] granted him his heart's desire in his mind. It happened that Jizhao was avoiding...
During the period of turmoil, he went into seclusion in Liaoxi and received the tonsure from Bian’an Nü, a disciple of Faliào.

Later, when Master Wuhuan Fugong opened the Dharma at Wanshou Monastery, he presided over the assembly with great severity; yet the Master did not take offense and went there with ten other monks to assist him.
Subsequently, he served as an attendant to Wansong. Because his talent and spirit surpassed those of others, he was somewhat ill-treated by the community; nevertheless, he possessed a vast memory.
He was widely learned, having perused the teachings of all one hundred schools without exception. He was also skilled in cursive script (*cāosū*), preserving the legacy of the "Madman" Su (Su Shi).
Upon hearing any of Wansong’s verses, hymns, or Dharma discourses but once, he immediately comprehended them and thereby attained the Dharma.

When the Master once had him respond on his behalf, his debating prowess was invincible. Liu Wen-zhen, the State Protector, was but one year senior to the Master; they were close friends since their youth.
Furthermore, Jian Shi was deemed fit for great employment. When Emperor Shizu summoned him for an audience and conversed with him, he was greatly pleased and intended to grant him an official post.

Jian Shi declined, saying, "The circulation of the Buddha-dharma throughout the world is the aspiration of a monk; wealth and status are not what I hope for. The Emperor comforted him and sent him on his way.

Upon the Emperor's return from his campaign in Yunnan, Wen Zheng spoke on his behalf, and the Emperor bestowed upon him the title of *Boguo Puan Dacianshi* (Great Chan Master of Universal Peace in the Buddha-land).
He was entrusted with the general administration of monastic affairs across all regions and was granted an official seal. The Master was resolute in his determination to protect the Teachings;

whenever monastic fields or residences were encroached upon by the wealthy or members of other sects, he exerted all his strength to restore them. He dispatched couriers in all directions, traveling extensively throughout his domain, never ceasing until his objectives were achieved.
Even when others urged him to rest for a while, he never slackened. Toward the end of Emperor Xianzong’s reign, the monks...
The Daoist practitioners each used fallacious arguments to undermine one another. The Emperor ordered that the disputants be assembled at Helin to adjudicate between the true and the false.
The Master debated them alongside various masters from Shaolin; the Daoists' arguments collapsed. From then on, the Buddhist teachings flourished greatly, and the monastic community relied upon him.

The Master subsequently returned his seal of office and resigned. Although he was granted gold annually, it was invariably exhausted as soon as it passed through his hands. He remained indifferent toward the flavors of the world.
Thus it was. He passed away at Tiangong Temple in Huanzhou during the Dingmao year of the Zhizhi era (1327).

Although it was the height of summer, his physical form remained as if alive, and a wondrous fragrance permeated the air. After he had lain for three days, he was cremated; yet his heart, tongue, teeth, and bones remained uncorrupted.
People excavated the ground several feet deep and recovered numerous śarīras. His secular age was fifty-one, and his years of monastic seniority were forty.
Nianchang (Appendix: Jue’an). Nianchang’s style name was Meiwu.
He was the son of Huang of Huating; his mother was Yang. She dreamed of a monk with eyebrows as thick as a brush and hair white as snow, who called himself the Great Elder and requested lodging.
Consequently, she became pregnant. On the twelfth day of the third month of the Renwu year of the Zhizhi era (1342), he was born.

At night, a divine light illuminated the chamber, and a rare fragrance permeated the air, lingering for more than a day before dispersing. As he grew older, he delighted in burning incense while sitting alone;

his physical bearing was exceptionally refined and extraordinary. At the age of twelve, he earnestly sought to leave the household life. His parents, who cherished him dearly, attempted to dissuade him by engaging him in worldly affairs.
In the end, none could thwart his resolve, and he finally abandoned [his former life]. In the year of Yizhen (1295), the Jianghuai Provincial Headquarters granted him a certificate of ordination.

He shaved his head and received full precepts, thereafter traveling extensively through the great monasteries of Jiang and Zhejiang, where he thoroughly investigated the various scriptures under the tutelage of veteran masters and men of eminent virtue.
He treated ritual propriety as a net for catching dragons, yet he always manifested humility and did not accept [the honors].

In the year Dàwùshēn (1288), when the Venerable Fǎzhì Huìméijī moved from Bǎizhàng in Jiangxī to Jìngcí in Hángzhōu, the Master went there to seek instruction; upon hearing the Master’s words, he attained a realization.
He was appointed to serve as the head of the secretariat (zhishi). He served diligently for seven years. In the year Yimao of the Renyong era, Fozhi moved to Mount Jing.

The Master then assumed the position of the Head of the Monastic Order (biaoshuai). The following year, the imperial court dispatched officials to oversee the Buddhist teachings; through this selection process, he was appointed to reside at Xiangfu Temple in Jiaxing.
In the year Kaihai of the Zhizhi era, he traveled to the capital by imperial post, where he was able to admire the splendors of the three capitals and behold the sites of Yan and Jin.
He visited ancient ruins and entered Mount Wutai to pay homage to Mañjuśrī. Moving between the golden gates of the imperial court, he engaged in the study and discussion of the foundational classics.
Both Minister Hong Gong of Yunlu and Master Yinguo of Biefeng, as well as everyone from the Imperial Preceptor downward, held him in high esteem and affection.

Upon returning from the capital, he presided over the Dharma seat at Wanshou Monastery in Gusu. The Master was profoundly versed in the inner meanings of the scriptures and broadly learned in the various secular texts; he then took up the Buddha...

I have examined the beginning and end of the Patriarch’s life in this world, the source and flow of the transmission of the Dharma, as well as how successive rulers and sovereigns have honored it and how kings, ministers, generals, and officials have protected it.
Having reconciled differences and verified errors to establish the correct version, I have applied my heart toward its wide propagation and preservation.

Wielding a pen of supreme impartiality, he compiled these materials into a book titled *The Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs Throughout the Successive Dynasties* (*Fozu lidai tongzai*), consisting of twenty-two fascicles.
The Duke of Daoyuan from the Hanlin Academy composed a preface for its beginning, lamenting that the history of the monastic community had no successor and had been lost to posterity.
[The author] criticized Zhìpán for his lack of method in recording historical events; indeed, he was deeply inspired by the Master’s words.

The Venerable Bǎozhōu remarked that this account by the Master clarifies principles and verifies facts, drawing from the scriptures and examining the transmissions of the Five Houses, thereby providing a significant contribution to the teachings of the sages.
Thereupon, [the author] gathered materials from internal and external classics at the Pújué Studio and compiled them into a volume, titled it *Jī* (Investigation).
The ancient [version] is abbreviated; it has circulated in the world alongside the [present] master’s [text], each detailed or concise version being appropriate for its purpose.
Baozhou, whose name was Ju’an, was the son of the Wu family of Wuxing. He received the tonsure and full ordination from Chan Master Duguming.
He studied together with his teacher Huiji. Later, he established the Dharma at Nanzen-ji in Songjiang and lectured on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.

When he reached the section on the "Sevenfold Investigation of the Mind," water suddenly surged from a pure pitcher and poured onto his chest. The audience was struck with amazement, but the Master laughed and said, "This is merely a coincidence."
**Biography of Master Daiman Zhuang (Jing’an)** Master Daiman Zhuang was a native of Taizhou.
He served as the abbot of Mount Jing. Students gathered around him like clouds. His preaching, which responded to the capacities of his listeners, was as swift as a crashing thunderclap.
Although there exists a *Recorded Sayings* (*yulu*) of Daiman, it has been lost and no longer circulates; the historical records merely preserve his replies.

The *Ruyi bian* (A Single Volume on Confucianism) contains profound and far-reaching insights; its language is grand and unrestrained. It resounds mightily—truly, he was a great figure of the Chan school.
When someone asked about the distinction between the internal [Buddhist] and external [Confucian] traditions, he replied:

"In the past, the Song Confucian Master Huìwēng said that the so-called 'working on the mind' taught by Buddhists is fundamentally incorrect. Master Chéngzi said: 'The learning of the Buddhists [is based on] being reverent and straightforward...'"
Internally, it may indeed exist; however, to square external conduct with righteousness has never been achieved.

Thus, those who are rigid and stubborn fall into aridity, while those who are expansive and unconfined lapse into license. This is why Buddhism is considered narrow. Our Confucianism is not so; it simply follows one's nature.
This principle was fully articulated by the Sage in the *I Ching*. What, then, is the point of the two elders' discourse?
The Master said: "Not so. The teachings differ in being internal or external; thus, there is a distinction between shallow and profound realization of principle.
To seek within, one finds the mind-nature (citta-svabhāva); to seek without, one finds intellectual understanding (vidyā). Therefore, when the mind is penetrated, the myriad dharmas are all fused;
when one clings to forms, one is naturally obscured before one's own eyes. Alas! The error of seeking externally is most extreme indeed."

The current malady of Confucian learning is such that those who are superficial and flowery naturally take literary composition as their task, while even those who are sincere and substantial do no more than take textual exegesis as their primary principle;

in reality, they are all ignorant of the study of the mind. The true Confucians of the Song dynasty deeply understood this ailment and further realized that the work of cultivating one's own mind possesses a fundamental basis.
Thus, they ought to have taught the priority of the root over the branches in order to reject [the former].
It may be granted that [the criticism of] language and characters is incorrect. Yet, you further claim that the practice of the mind is not correct;
how can this not be a self-contradiction? If the foundation itself is not correct, how can it be said to surpass the Confucians?

This demonstrates an inability to exhaustively fathom the principles of Mind-Learning (Xinxue), leading one to become deeply deluded regarding our Buddhist Way and unable to reach a definitive resolution. Observe him...

The words of Mr. Chuan are likewise so. Since you already lament that my Way has "an internal but no external," if one can indeed take the Way as the root, what need is there to worry about the branches once the root is attained?
Your subsequent remarks regarding "withered desolation" and "licentiousness" again lament the narrowness of my Way;
this shows you have not yet perceived its greatness. You further state that the Buddha possesses the principle of awakening, which serves to be reverent and rectify the inner self.
To say again that it is ultimately not so is merely a statement of self-contradictory confusion; how could such a person truly understand this principle?
As for the doctrine of "following one's nature," it likewise does not transcend the work of cultivation within my own mind; one must certainly seek its verification in the *I Ching*.
The *I Ching* is the subtle principle within the mind. Former Confucian scholars did not clarify the substance of the original mind;

consequently, they failed to understand from whence innate knowledge (*liang zhi*) and innate capacity (*liang neng*) arise. They asserted that consciousness exists only after the presence of vital energy (*qi*), thereby tracing the source of nature and destiny (*xing ming*) back to *qi*.

They further traced nature (*xing*) to being the principle within *qi*, and defined the Way (*dao*) as nature following that principle. Therefore, they proceeded according to each matter and each object...
To clarify the principle: one must realize that the forms and vital energies of heaven, earth, people, and things all arise from within the awakened nature (*juexing*).

My fundamental mind, wondrously luminous and universally illuminating, is already present even before thoughts have been aroused. If one attains this realization, it is precisely the meaning of "abiding in the center" (*zhong*).
If one loses this, it cannot be maintained even slightly within; one merely pursues external phenomena and things.

To conclude: to claim that "principle" (yi) lies beyond the world—how could this possibly be so? Those who seek verification in the *I Ching* find that its descriptions of the "Supremely Divine" and the "Supremely Sage" all point to a realm that is unfathomable and unknowable.
Thus, it is said that "without haste, one arrives swiftly; without walking, one reaches the destination.

Furthermore, since these states take "no-thought," "non-action," and "no-stimulation" as their fundamental basis of resonance and penetration, what the *I Ching* verifies is certainly not something external.
The ground of ultimate awakening cannot be reached through study or intellectual understanding. Awakening is termed "internal," while understanding is termed "external";
this is why internal teachings and external teachings differ. Confucianists apply their efforts exclusively to the external;

regarding all that lies beyond the reach of knowledge and understanding, they do not further investigate. Consequently, they do not know the Way of "sincerely upholding the Mean" (*yunzhi juezhong*) or the principle of Heaven (*tianli*).
In places where these [teachings] circulate, they all remain within the realm where discursive thought does not arise and where material desires are utterly exhausted;

yet, even if one’s practice is dedicated, one will ultimately fail to enter the domain of the Sage. This is because they suspect that the traces of the Buddha’s teaching constitute a lack of filial piety and a lack of loyalty to the sovereign.
Consequently, he failed to exhaustively investigate their doctrines, thereby failing to clarify the Way of the Sage Confucius and instead committing the fault of slandering the Buddha.
How lamentable! As the Master was about to pass away, he suddenly said, "Difficult, difficult! A beautiful maiden of sixteen ascends a high mountain; even an old monk cannot support her.
Having spoken these words, he passed into stillness.
Jing’an Zhuang Gong was also a native of Tāi. From childhood, his wisdom was extraordinary. Having shaved his head to take the precepts under Guǎngcí, he held the world and its dust in light regard.
He traveled extensively to consult various masters until he attained realization. During the Yōnglè era, he resided at Jìngshān and was commissioned by imperial decree to edit the Great Canon.

He stayed at Tiānjiè Monastery for three years, during which time figures such as Yáo Guǎngxiào submitted joint petitions to recommend him as abbot; however, he firmly declined and returned to Jìngshān. His...
His noble words and virtuous deeds are a pity not fully transmitted. Aiman once remarked: "Jingan formerly presided over two monasteries in the region of Yue.
Having come to Longhe, Quanshi Weng appointed him to two seats; he then retired to a single room, maintaining himself with such integrity that he is truly worthy of admiration.
One day, he passed away with a smile, and his stupa was erected atop the small pond at Shuiling."
Tianquan Yuan Gong succeeded to Zu Yuan.
His courtesy name was Tianquan, and Yu’an was his style name. He was the son of Yang of Luling and possessed extraordinary qualities from birth.
In the Guiwei year of the Yongle era, he received full ordination at Qingyuan Mountain. He traveled to Jinling to pay his respects to Master Huanju Jie, from whom he received much inspiration;
he was designated as one of his "入室" (入室) disciples, a title the Master once proclaimed before the assembly.

The teacher did not become complacent with minor attainments, but instead burned incense on his arm and pursued the Way with such devotion that he neglected both sleep and food for five years, only then achieving a subtle awakening, like parting the clouds to see the sky.
Moving through the void like a mist, he encountered no obstruction. He then shook his monk’s staff to travel in all directions, making prostrations at every ancestral stupa.

Wherever he went, the monastic communities revered him with awe; his reputation became prominent, rising above his contemporaries. In the year of Renyin, he returned to Tianjie Temple. There, he drew blood to transcribe the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
At the beginning of the Xuande era, he resided on the mountain and expounded the teachings. Duke Yueshan, admiring his conduct, invited him to occupy the seat of honor.
Duan served as a leader among the "dragon elephants" (eminent monks). Shortly thereafter, he was appointed by the Sengluosi (Bureau of Monastic Records) to reside at Xuefeng.

Before long, the seat at Tiantong became vacant, and the Master was transferred there to occupy it. He restored all that had fallen into ruin, and his teachings flourished extensively. In the year Jia-yin, he was summoned to the capital.

The Emperor appointed him as the Left Chief Preceptor (Zuò Juéyì). At that time, the construction of Dà Gōngdé Temple was completed, and as the abbot was difficult to find, the Emperor appointed the Master to hold that office concurrently.

When the monastic community heard this, they all joyfully followed him, gathering like clouds to spread their alms bowls. The Emperor was pleased and granted over four hundred *qǐng* of land to provide for them.
The Master reflected that the names of the three traditions—Chan, Lecture, and Teaching—must be correctly established, and he submitted a memorial to that effect.
The three great temples—Dagongde, Dacien, and Dalongsan—were established for this purpose. Consequently, the disciples of the three schools each had a place to which they could turn for refuge;
as they transmitted the Way and received instruction, the fundamental order of the teachings finally ceased to be disordered.

Furthermore, because many temples throughout the empire had fallen into ruin due to the narrowness of the student body, the number of those permitted to receive ordination was increased by one-fifth beyond the standard quota. I.
At that time, those receiving ordination gathered like rivers converging or clouds piling up; his disciples flourished in great numbers, and many ruined monasteries were restored through him.

He was promoted to the rank of Right Shanshi (Right Supervisor of the World). He distributed the items bestowed by His Majesty and constructed a great monastery on Fengxiang Mountain in Jiangning, which was granted the imperial plaque name "Puning Chan Monastery.
When the Wanshan Jietan (Ordination Platform for Myriad Good Deeds) was completed, he was appointed as the Patriarch for the Transmission of Precepts.
The Master said: "When scholars throughout the world hear of the Master's precepts, they all know what to uphold, and their conduct does not deviate from the Way.
To the left of the temple, the road was blocked by the northern mountains; the ditches were filled with mud and mire, causing hardship for those who traveled back and forth.

The Master, together with the Grand Chamberlain Xingan, reclaimed three hundred mu of land and constructed the Anhe Bridge by paving it with stone. He built a hermitage beside the bridge and commissioned monks to guard it, so as to provide passage for the masses."
Consequently, those who encountered him in the cold did not suffer from the crossing [of rivers], and in the heat, they were provided with tea and drink;

thus, people returned their virtue to him. The Master’s spirit and bearing were vast and profound, and his conduct was pure and white. He was like a deep, still pool or a vast, overflowing ocean; among all worldly conditions, there was not one that could move his mind.
When he offered prayers for the state, he was profoundly sincere and exhausted every measure of his devotion. For his younger brothers...
When he preached the Dharma, he would earnestly expound its essential meaning. He was indeed loyal in serving his superiors and diligent in attending to his subordinates;
for a time, people revered and looked up to him as if he were Mount Tai or the Northern Dipper. The disciples he ordained numbered in the tens of thousands.

Those who succeeded in promoting the religious affairs, as well as those who presided over famous mountains and great monasteries, further numbered several dozen. He was born in the Jisi year of the Hongwu era.

On the fourth day of the second month, he passed away on the seventh day of the third month of the Jisi year of the Zhengtong era. He was sixty-one years of age, with forty-seven years of monastic seniority (*śramaṇa-varṣa*).
At the time of his death, he bathed, changed his robes, and sat upright. He requested a brush and wrote this verse:
"Observing the world for sixty-one years, One is three, and three is one. This perfect circle shatters the traces of coming and going; The bright sun is empty."
A thunderous crash resounded from the sky. Having finished writing, he closed his eyes and passed away. A marvelous fragrance filled the room for several days.
When the Retired Emperor heard of this, he dispatched the Eunuch Wu Bi to bestow upon him white incense, perfumed silks, and ten thousand strings of paper currency.

He also sent Lin Pi, Director of the Ministry of Rites, to present a sacrificial offering. Among the high officials and ministers of the court, there was none who did not offer their own funeral rites. His body was cremated at...

On the western mountains of the capital city, more than ten thousand people, from the noble and the humble, including the elderly and infirm, escorted [the remains] and obtained a handful of śarīra relics.

These were enshrined in the Gongde Monastery. As for the sacred bones, it was reported that they were returned to Puning Monastery in the Southern Capital, where a great stūpa was constructed to house them.
Zhendli’s Biography.
Zhendli, whose courtesy name was Hengqu and alternative style name Yijiang, was the son of the Liu family of Jiangyou. His lineage descended from Yu Xi of Zhongshan during the Tang dynasty.
His father was Fuduan and his mother was Lady Tang. At the time of his birth, he was accompanied by auspicious omens, including celestial fragrances and *zhicao* mushrooms.

Shui was born in the intercalary seventh month of the Xinyou year of the Hongzhi era. As soon as he was weaned, he ceased consuming pungent or savory foods and joined his palms in prayer to the Buddha.
At the age of ten or so, the Yao and Dong bandits committed widespread plunder among the populace; mother and son were separated, and the Master was taken captive.

After a long time, he managed to escape and entered the service of the Regional Commander, Lord Li, as an attendant. He served with such sincerity and diligence that Lord Li came to hold him in high esteem. When Lord Li...

The Duke entered the capital, taking him along with him. On their way, they passed by Pengli and beheld the splendors of Mount Kuanglu and Tianchi. Thereupon, [the boy] wished to leave the household life;
he knelt before the horse and requested permission. Lord Li was a man of long-standing virtue; he marveled at his resolve and granted him leave to serve as his own teacher.

He immediately went to Guanghua Temple and paid respects to Master Wang at the ancestral hall to become his preceptor. Having shaved his head and received the full precepts, he gradually came to understand the profound teachings.

Xuán traveled among various seats of learning, thoroughly mastering the principles of the Perfect and Sudden Teachings. These teachings entered his ears and resonated with his heart, earning him great recognition from his teachers and friends.
Wherever he went, people turned to him in devotion. Whether preaching the Buddha-dharma or composing poetry, the Master traveled everywhere like one ringing a bell, enlightening and guiding many.
At that time, a disaster struck the Zhaoti Monastery in the capital; the lamp flames flickered and nearly extinguished. The Master was deeply moved by compassion and exerted himself to...
Through his strenuous efforts, the matter was quelled before it could spread like a flood; thus, the Master’s contribution was preeminent.

Diligent in making the propagation of the teachings and the protection of the Dharma his primary concern, an examination of his life reveals that he did not limit himself to this single instance or singular deed alone.
In the year of the Ding-si cycle, one day he suddenly dreamed that on the northern bank of the water pond in Xianfang, there stood the old foundations of the Tang dynasty Dharma Master Fuli.
He saw a monk holding a document in his hand, who handed it to him and said, "Master, you possess the power; you should establish yourself in this place.
He then followed the monk, treading upon a depression in the earth and stepping onto a level terrace, where he beheld a lake. Stone cliffs stood like lions and arched like elephants;

the sunlight and mountain colors were so brilliant they dazzled the eyes. Suddenly, he was startled awake. Thereupon, he went with his guest to trace the site and found the abandoned land, as if it were a dream.
The patronage gathered like clouds and fell like rain; in less than a few years, it was completed. The golden and azure hues shone upon one another, resembling the celestial palace of Nirmāṇarati.
As the Master sat upon his seat, he uttered the melodies of the kalaviṅka bird; people flocked to his door to receive the transformation of the nectar of the Dharma.
The Buddhist teachings in the capital were said to have reached a "Restoration" through him. The Master’s bearing was pure and far-reaching; he possessed [the following] verse:
It is said: "Between the trees the breeze is perfectly gentle; at the edge of the clouds the sun is just slow. Commentators remarked that these words possessed the spirit of Chan.
In the Renwu year of the Wanli era, he passed away while seated in meditation. He was interred in a pagoda at the Double Huai Trees on West Mountain.
Mang Huishou transmitted [the Dharma] to Huiding.
His courtesy name was Wujin, and his pen-name was Nanquan. He was the son of the Shao family of Luan’an. He possessed a striking and imposing appearance, with eyes like flashes of lightning.

By nature he was unconventional and took no pleasure in mundane affairs. After shaving his head, he attained realization while investigating the fundamental matter of his own nature, and subsequently traveled to Mount Tai.

He paid homage to the Great Being (Mahāsattva) and subsequently made a vow to provide meals for one hundred and eight thousand monks over a period of one thousand days. He fulfilled his vow; from the stalks of vegetables to the grains of rice, he personally attended to every detail.
