People marveled at his sincerity and devotion. The Master’s physical strength and skill surpassed those of ordinary men; he could perform the manual labor of dozens of people at once.

Furthermore, his speech was plain and straightforward, devoid of ornamentation; for this reason, people vied with one another to call him "Mang the Head. His reputation resounded throughout the monastic community.
Wherever he went, people blocked his path and detained him. He replied, "I do not dwell where it is easy; I do not change my dwelling place.

Disregarding their attempts to stop him, he proceeded until he reached the Ridge of the Old Road, where he built a thatched hut and gathered a community to live there. At that time, bandits were swarming halfway up the mountain, marking out their territory with lines drawn on the ground.
The place was known as the Great King’s Ditch of the North and South. No soldiers or officials dared to arrest anyone there;

travelers shrank back from it in fear, warning one another that unless they gathered in hundreds and sounded gongs while bearing weapons, no one could advance. When the Master arrived, the bandits were intimidated by his reputation, yet they kept watch over him most closely.
One day, when the Master went out, the hermitage was destroyed. Upon his return, three or four remaining monks held onto him and wept, saying, "We pray you will move elsewhere."
Anan tried to avoid him, but the Master exclaimed, "It cannot be! Life and death are matters of destiny; what can these bandits do? He then went to destroy them.
As he spoke, the bandits arrived in great numbers. The Master had no weapons in hand, so he smashed a water jar and struck at the bandits, but it hit nothing.
Knowing the Master had no weapons, the bandits dared to approach him. A spear pierced the Master’s left side; the Master caught the spear in his hand and kicked it away.

The bandits threw him to the ground and stabbed him. Startled, they retreated. As he entered his room to examine the wound, he found it was about three inches deep; fat and intestines had both protruded.
Enduring the pain, he bound himself securely, took up his spear, and went out the door, shouting in a fierce voice, "I was just about to capture and exterminate you lot!
Have you come here to deliver your own death? The bandits were terrified and did not dare advance, but they seized scattered stones and struck the Master from a distance; one hit him on the forehead.

At Lóngquán Pass, there was a military commander named Zheng who was on friendly terms with the Master. Suspecting that the Master had been the ringleader of the bandits, he secretly sent soldiers to protect him.
When the soldiers arrived, the bandits had already dispersed; they searched the entire mountain for the Master but could not find him.
By dawn, they saw a bloodied man lying stiffly in a deep ravine. Upon examining him closely, they realized it was the Master. Zheng wailed aloud, "Heaven! How can you take away such a hero?"
The man was a strong youth. They carried him back home; feeling his chest, they found it still warm. Rejoicing, he said, "This man will not die; his heart-orifices are merely clouded by blood.

He extracted the teeth and poured medicinal wine upon them. After a long time, the man revived. Once he had recovered through treatment, he took leave of Zheng and departed, resolutely intending to strike down the rebels.
Some objected to this, but the Master said: "A great man who wishes to eliminate cruelty and establish the Buddha-dharma..."
"How could I dare refuse nine deaths? He gathered fifty-two like-minded companions, all of whom were heroic and reckless of their lives.
The various frontier generals were already well-acquainted with the Master's reputation; upon this, he visited them all to borrow weapons and recruit provisions for grain.

He submitted petitions to the provincial and regional headquarters, vowing that with a single strike they would utterly exterminate [the rebels]. All were heartened and granted him their support. The bandit leader, along with over a hundred of his followers, [approached] the Master...
He knew the names and residences of all [the rebels] and suddenly confronted them with his troops. Within a few days, there was none who did not surrender and face execution;

their stronghold was thus emptied. At that time, the Master was twenty-eight years old. From then on, he established a monastic community (*saṃghārāma*), providing gruel and rice for the traveling monks from the ten directions.
He took the recitation of various flowers as his fixed daily practice, while concurrently performing all manner of Buddhist rites or cultivating the Pure Land practices.
He sometimes practiced meditative contemplation and sometimes read the scriptures of the Tripiṭaka, doing so for over fifty years as if it were but a single day.

He practiced divination for others regarding auspicious and inauspicious matters; he wrote on paper with such rapidity that his calligraphy was forceful and vigorous, yet initially unintelligible.
Later, his manifestations were frequently verified. Whenever someone who had observed the fast prepared raw fish for offering, he would eat it all at once;

then, standing by the water’s edge, he would vomit it out, which transformed into small fish that swam away in a school. A sea traveler, caught in a storm and on the verge of drowning, saw the monk handling a rope to pull the ship to safety.
When the traveler reached the capital, Zhiyan said to him, "If it were not for me, how could you have survived? The traveler still remembered him.
Mao was a true helmsman. He passed away later, and Emperor Renzong fashioned a clay image of his true body and enshrined it within the temple, inscribing it with the title "Chan Master Xianhua.
The two masters Qingsong and Quanliao succeeded him.
Qingsong was a native of Fuzhou. Initially, he visited Fayan, who pointed to the falling rain and said to him, "Every drop falls into the eyes of the Venerable.

At first, Qingsong did not understand this; later, while reading the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, he fully realized its meaning. Consequently, he entered the mountains seeking a place to establish a hermitage.

Upon reaching Siming, he climbed to a high vantage point and looked out in all directions; he threw down a stone, and at the spot where the stone came to rest, he decided that this was where he would stay.

He stayed there and subsequently built a hermitage to dwell in. Later, when King Qian Zhongyi heard of his reputation, he summoned him to preside over Lingyin Monastery and bestowed upon him the title Chan Master Liaowu.
"Mahāprajñāpāramitā is neither grasping nor abandoning; if people do not understand this, it is like wind and cold amidst falling snow"—this was how the Master preached the Dharma.
One day, while the King was reading the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, he learned that there was a mountain called Zhiti in China. For...
The abode of the Bodhisattva Tianguan (Devamukuṭa) was such that when the elders of all the mountains were assembled for a great gathering and questioned about it, none could know its location.
Only Master Dao knew the reason for this in great detail. The King said, "It cannot be followed unless you go there yourself. He then dispatched men to travel together with him.
Reaching the seacoast, he sought out the traces of the sacred realm. Entering deep into the mountains, he traveled for three days when the sound of a bell was heard.
A white monkey led him forward, and the Master prostrated himself with a sincere heart. He beheld a great monastery within a secluded forest; its plaque bore golden characters inscribed:

"The Realm of the Great Avataṃsaka of the Ancient Buddha. Upon entering the temple, the halls and pavilions rose majestically, and the assembly numbered in the tens of thousands, including a thousand bodhisattvas.
The body sat solemnly atop it; a wondrous fragrance pervaded the air, and its radiance dazzled the eyes. The Master silently contemplated with sincere devotion, rejoicing throughout the night.
At dawn, [the figure] was still there amidst the thickets; what he had seen was a manifested buddha-field. The Master returned and reported this to the King.
He immediately established a temple at that very spot, just as his teacher had seen. He cast a thousand images wearing celestial crowns and set out by sea toward the mountains.
When they reached midstream, a great hurricane arose; the ship became so heavy it was on the verge of sinking, and the crew looked at one another with no strategy left.
They then submerged half of the images in the water, and once they had crossed over, those half-sunken images had already arrived at their destination ahead of them. Such was the marvel.
Quanyue Liao was a native of Yongjia. While traveling to Jingzhou, he entered Tianzhu Mountain, where he encountered a strange monk.

The monk said to Liao, "Your karmic affinity lies in eastern Zhejiang; you shall dwell upon a famous mountain there. In your home province, there is a sacred site (dōcháng) of the Venerable Nāgārjuna which is about to flourish.
You should strive to bring it to fruition yourself. Liao questioned him as to the location, and the monk replied: [The text continues with the description of the site.]
The land was named after its flowers, and the mountains were named after their birds; within them lay a dragon pool, the place where the Venerable One used to rest.

Having resolved to return home, he traveled everywhere until he reached the seashore, where he beheld the clarity and profundity of the mountains and waters. Taking a liking to it, he questioned the local people, who replied, "This is Fuyong Village;
this is Mount Yandang. At this, Miaole attained a sudden realization in his heart. He then entered the mountains and built a thatched hut at the site of the essential assembly.
It is said that he lived in the Furong Hermitage, which is the present-day Nengren Temple. The inscription on Mount Yan was actually composed by Liaofa;
this man was unrestrained and unconventional, and was at times referred to as "Liao the Wanderer."
The Biography of Master Shazhi (with Dao Song appended).
Master Shazhi, whose name was Zhiyan, resided at Jing’an Temple in Huating. On the fifteenth day of the seventh month, the villages and towns held an offering for the Ullambana Festival.
The monks of the temple had almost all gone to attend these invitations, leaving only Zhiyan remaining at the temple. At that time, a man from Sici Village arrived.
He summoned the monks, but there were no monks to be summoned. He wished to take Huaiyan along, and Huaiyan said, "Simply return and prepare the provisions;
I shall follow you. They traveled by small boat and saw some shrimp catchers. Huaiyan bought one peck from them and asked for water to eat it; he ate it all without leaving any behind.
He said to the fisherman, "I will return your payment when we finish our meal," and he repeatedly cautioned the boatman not to reveal their destination. Upon reaching the village, the boat—

The son could not bear this. When the host family heard of it, they treated him with contempt and disdain; they did not invite him to the seat of honor, but provided only a single meal on the bare ground without a sitting mat to humiliate him.
The Master accepted this with joyful composure. Upon returning, he saw the fisherman and said, "Why such loquacity?
Today’s offering lacked money—what was to be done? The fisherman replied, "If there was no money, simply return my shrimp. The Master said, "That is easy. He then asked for water.

He drank [some water], and as it came out, he spat up live shrimp; he returned them to the owner in a full peck-measure. People considered this a marvel and consequently called him the "Shrimp Master" (Xiàzǐ Héshàng).
Yǎn displayed many such extraordinary traces, and those living along the seacoast were all able to recount them.

When his time of passing drew near, he gathered reeds and made more than ten thousand ropes, hanging them from the corridors and eaves, and said to the people, "I am creating karmic conditions for you. Thereupon, he sat and passed away. The people...

They vied with one another to offer money, until the suspended ropes were completely full. With this, they constructed a Buddha pavilion within the monastery; to this day, the temple is known as the Shrimp Son (Xiāzǐ) Dharma-assembly site.
As for Dàosōng, his surname was Wú, and he was a native of Lèqīng in Wēnzhōu. He received his training at Dōngān and lived a life of unrestrained freedom. People...
Huishong was like a peak atop a mountain. Once, two water-buffaloes happened to be fighting on the road; no one dared to approach them.

Huishong went straight forward, grasped both their horns, and called out their names to admonish them. The buffaloes understood and departed. Once, there was a man who wished to invite Huishong to a meal for the monks.
He secretly wrote the master’s name and burned it in the courtyard. The following morning, Huishong arrived; everyone thought he had come of his own accord. The host then spoke [of the incident].
At first, he was treated with suspicion, but later he also passed away while sitting in meditation.
Wumen (無門) transmitted the Dharma to Hui-kai (慧開).
Wumen’s courtesy name was Wumen; he was a native of Liangzhu in Hangzhou. His secular surname was Liang, and his mother was of the Song clan. He paid homage at the Tianlong Temple.

The Master [Zhaozhou] served as the *upādhyāya* (preceptor) for his studies. Hearing that Master Yue-lin Guan had begun teaching the Dharma at Wanshou Monastery, he went there with Shi-shuang Yin to pay their respects.
Yue-lin assigned him the "Mu" (No) koan. For six years, he made no progress whatsoever. He then exerted himself with self-reproach and vowed:
"If I fall back into sleep, may my body rot away. Whenever he reached a point of extreme exhaustion, he would walk along the corridors.
Dao touched the pillar with his head. One day, while standing beside the Dharma seat, he suddenly heard the sound of the meal drum and attained realization.
He composed a verse, saying: "A clear blue sky and a bright sun, A single clap of thunder— The eyes of all living beings on the great earth open wide.

The myriad phenomena and the entire universe bow their heads together; Mount Sumeru leaps and dances through the three stages. He entered the room to communicate what he had attained. Lin (Linji) rebuked him, saying: "What..."
He was able to see spirits and ghosts. The Master then shouted; Lin also shouted. The Master shouted again. From that time on, their spiritual resonance and dialogue were perfectly harmonized.

During the Jiading period, he emerged from seclusion to reside at Baoguo Temple in Anji, then moved to Longxing Tianning, Huanglong Cuiyan, Kaiyuan and Lingyan in Suzhou, Jiaoshan in Zhenjiang, and Baoning in Jinling. During the Chunyou period, he returned to his hometown and stayed at Xixi...
In the deep, shaded forests of Hubei, he lived there in joy. There was a stone that ascended from the foot of the mountain in a zigzag fashion;
it was smooth and polished, yet its surface remained unjoined like a grindstone. When the Master sat beneath it, a spring suddenly gushed forth; its color was deep azure and its taste sweet.
It was as clear and limpid as a deep abyss. Those who spoke said that when the Master moved from Huanglong to this mountain, the dragon followed the Master’s staff back home;
thus, they named the rocky site Huanglong Cave and the peak Huanglong Peak.
Whenever summer rains first clear, there is a creature winding upon the pines, its vapor billowing and yellow—this is the Yellow Dragon. At such times...

Within the borders there was a great drought. The Grand Guardian Meng Gong, Chancellor Wu Qian, and Chancellor Zheng Qingzhi memorialized that Master Shidao’s practice had caused springs to gush forth spontaneously and dragons to appear at will;
he would surely be able to save the withered people from their plight. By imperial decree, he was summoned to Wende Hall to perform the Dharma.
When the Master ascended the seat, he said nothing, remaining only in silent meditation. Rain fell in great torrents at the appropriate time, reaching far and near.
The Emperor was greatly pleased and asked, "By what means did you achieve this? The Master replied, "Tranquil and unmoving, yet responding and penetrating all.

The Emperor rejoiced and conferred upon him the title of Chan Master Fuyan. He bestowed upon him a *kāṣāya* robe woven with golden threads and issued an imperial edict to enshrine him at Huanglong as the Marquis Lingji.
Furthermore, he established the Huguo Renwang Temple at the foot of Huanglong Peak and granted three thousand official fields from Pingjiang for its support.

Emperor Wǔ commanded the Master to open the mountain. The Master’s physical stature was short and small; when he went to respond to the summons, he pointed at the sun for the officials to observe, and only then did he cross the threshold.
He ascended the hall by stepping upon heavy stone slabs placed at the tiers of the seating area. Many court officials laughed to themselves.

The Master vowed to propagate the teachings of the Dharma, saying only that he regretted his physical form was not majestic. At the summit of Mount Dòng, there was a single peak of jade, carved and thrust upward.

The heavenly [image] is as translucent as lard, standing over two *zhang* in height. He then commanded artisans to fashion an image of himself about one *zhang* tall, with floating clouds concealing its feet and a halo of radiant flames rising luxuriantly behind it.
A dragon’s head was carved to coil around it, encircling it toward the void; on the left is a cavity through which one may enter by stooping, with a table placed before it.
All these were carved in accordance with the natural contours of the rock, appearing as if they had miraculously surged forth from the earth, upon which he ascended.
As for those who sat in mid-air, I privately offered this prayer: "May they behold this in their future lives.
On the evening of the Master’s passing, a woman of the Sun family in Qiantang dreamed that a monk holding a lantern, who called himself the Wayman Kaishan, came to stay with her.
The following day, she gave birth to a son who later became a great Chan Master—none other than Zhongfeng Ben. The Master’s Dharma heir was Jianhe of Yongjia.
Furthermore, Gaofeng said to Shiwu, "There is a blind donkey in Wenzhou. This is indeed so. He was also a great master who did not let the family reputation fall;
this is recorded in the biographies of Master Zhaokong and Master Xuanzang.
Yuanzhao was the son of Pan [surname] of Jinghai in Tongzhou; his mother was Lady Zhu.

His paternal uncle, Miaoguan of Liheshi in the same district, took him to leave the household life and served him as a teacher of Yoga. At the age of six or seven, he was already able to compose poetry, reciting it extemporaneously without ever having been seen to study from books.
Once he had become a monk, he became fond of wine and meat, and there was no day that he did not get drunk.

He ate his fill and called out or whistled with wild abandon; he vomited and left things in utter disarray, which the monks of the temple detested. Later, he suddenly manifested divine wonders that no one could fathom.

Once, he went to the river to wash a wine jar, turned it upside down, and made a formal petition from within it; the jar felt as soft as flour. At other times, when he was heavily intoxicated and passing through the marketplace, he would chant:
"The wheat waves are greener than the water waves; the pear blossoms are whiter than the plum blossoms. He would continue to recite this verse without ceasing.
There was a man who sold clean snails. The Master asked him, "Drunkard Monk, you are good at two lines, but you cannot manage the rhyme.

The Master suddenly gestured with his hand toward the man’s neck and said, "It would be well to escort this drunken monk back to the temple, so he may once more view the river moon while returning home.
In the hall, there was a clay Buddha that had not yet been gilded. The abbot intended to solicit donations for it, but the Master said, "There is no need to solicit; I shall do it myself."
"The next day, I shall offer gold to the Buddha, but I do not wish for anyone to see me. The assembly looked at one another and laughed.

The following day, before dawn had broken and while his hangover from the previous night was still severe, he suddenly rose, pushed open the door, and entered the hall. Climbing onto the throne, he placed his feet upon the Buddha’s shoulders and pressed his hands against the Buddha’s head;
he then pulled back the neck and spat into it, until the substance flowed down in a stream. When the hall master saw this, he was struck with panic.
He informed the temple master, who gathered the assembly to open the hall doors. The Master sighed, saying, "Why have you come so early?

He then descended from the platform and cursed, "Thief! Thief! From that time on, he never returned to the temple again. Upon inspection, wherever his spittle had fallen, it all turned into pure gold.
It stopped at the Buddha’s chest, and the assembly first realized that the Master was a sage.

Later, he met Chan Master Jingshan Zhe’ung Yan, who, recognizing the Master’s sharp and keen faculties and wishing to rouse him to great heights, would not allow him to enter the hall for formal study; instead, as soon as the Master saw him, the Master shouted and was driven out.
Furthermore, the Master was asked: "Why does the Great Sage of Sizhou appear in Yangzhou? The Master replied: "Today..."
Furthermore, while he was in Hangzhou, he encountered [Weng], who again shouted at him. After a long time, [Tianyi] attained great enlightenment; snapping his fingers once, he said, "Hūṃ!

Hūṃ! and then entered the room. He served as the Secretary for Records. After Weng passed away, the Master succeeded him on the seat. At that time, it was a period following a famine, and outstanding debts were piled up like mountains.

The Sanghārāma was old and dilapidated; before long, however, its towers and pavilions rose high toward the heavens, and monks in cloud-like robes arrived in succession, no fewer than during the Master’s prime.
Since crossing the river to the south, the Master had abandoned his former ways;

having truly been refined by various elder Chan masters, he had withdrawn his brilliant radiance and become so prudent and circumspect in his conduct that he seemed like a different person from his former self, as if separated from him by another age. His poem on He-shi Rock reads: "Hao..."

When his head first arrived, he welcomed it and sat in meditation before the master. The mountain spirits shifted the location for him, bringing together ten million followers. One must know that the power to transform heaven through the propagation of the Dharma is evident simply by observing the moment when such sincerity split the rock. This was merely a way of manifesting himself by relying on antiquity. He then composed a verse: “Having received the transmission of the Buddha’s seal, I have fulfilled my vow to propagate the Dharma. Later, during the Zhenyuan era, the monk Daoyuan of Mount Tiantai visited the site and saw that the stupa had collapsed. He rebuilt it, and the mountain spirit again manifested a miraculous response, causing the stupa to rise spontaneously.
