"Please dig a small cave for me at Dongjian. This way, even in life and death, I shall not forget my intention to serve my teacher.
Dongjian was the place where the Master was buried.
Xuanzang was a native of Yongjia and served as a monk at Jiafu Monastery; he drank wine, ate meat, and daily played with children.

The people of the city called him "Zangdian. Whenever he saw someone, he would seek out wine; glaring with bared fists, he assumed the posture of Vajrapāṇi, causing those who saw him to fall over in laughter.
Although he was drunk at night, he would invariably rise at the fourth watch to recite the Lotus Sūtra. At dawn, he would return to the taverns once more.
While intoxicated, he would urinate and defecate until his clothes were soaked, yet he never washed them, and there was never any foul odor. One day, he suddenly took leave of everyone.
The various wine-drinkers set a date and passed away while sitting in meditation.
As for the two eccentric masters—Ji-dian (attached is Ma-nao-dian)—Ji-dian’s name was Daoji, and Ming-dian’s name was [Ming]. These two masters manifested their traces at the same time, yet each...
The two were known as Ji Dian and Ming Dian. Both were deranged due to their natural disposition, and thus people called them "Ji the Madman" and "Ming the Madman.

Ji Dian’s madness was the more extreme; he drank wine and ate meat, mingled with the common folk of the marketplace, delighted in performing somersaults, and went about naked without wearing trousers, exposing his body to vulgar gaze.
People mocked him, but he regarded them with equanimity. He entered the monastic life at Lingyin Temple, where none of the monks failed to spit upon him or revile him.

He was driven out to reside at Jingci Temple, where he recited sutras for others. When funeral rites were performed, he would obtain wine and food; he would attend such occasions without even being summoned. He composed a poem saying:

"What need is there for forest scenery more beautiful than that of Xiao and Xiang? I only wish that West Lake might turn into wine, So that I may lie down in it with my whole body. At the western shore...
By the lakeside, whenever a wave came, he would swallow it in a single gulp. He settled people's disputes and saved them from death, all of which he performed amidst jesting and laughter.
His movements were as swift as spirits appearing and ghosts vanishing; no one could fathom him. At the age of seventy-three, he manifested his passing.

As for Mingdian: he was eccentric and wild, his clothes failing to cover his body. In the midst of heavy snow, he walked bare-chested and barefoot, fiddling with iron nails in his hands and picking up shards of tile to place in his sleeves.
When people spoke to him with sincere words, he would respond with sharp, witty repartee;
if they insulted him, he would retort with mad ravings. When he entered the marketplace, groups of children vied to pull at his sleeves to find coins. Or...
They gave him one or two coins, or sometimes nothing at all; they shouted, chattered, and laughed, crowding the thoroughfares until they were blocked.
Some people would give him food, regardless of whether they were far away or nearby, or whether they knew him or not, all arriving at dawn. Sometimes he accepted the offerings, sometimes he did not;
some even reached into their sleeves, took out money, placed it on the low table, and departed without a word of thanks. At that time, the Japanese (Wa-nu) saw this and were filled with admiration.
Baizhuang said: "Once, while at sea, I lost my way due to a storm. Fortunately, I encountered this monk and was spared from death. Furthermore, he was skilled in poetry.

Whenever I brought him a stalk of calamus to request a verse, he would speak extemporaneously: 'Not a single speck of dust or mud beneath its roots; By nature, it loves the seclusion and purity of springs and rocks.
Had it not harbored resentment for the Xiang River at that time, How could every leaf now bear a teardrop? He was truly no different from Ji Dian."
They were acquaintances who happened to meet at Zhujing. [The other] looked at him and exclaimed, "Eh! Jidian then presented him with a poem:

"Before the green bamboo hat, heaven and earth are vast; Beneath the blue grass-cloth robe, water and clouds are wide. Without speaking or saying a word, what do you know? Simply do not deceive your own human heart.
Both "crazies" lived during the Southern Song dynasty.
After the fall of the Song dynasty, there was another eccentric monk from Maṇi Temple who drank heavily and lived a reckless life. He frequently uttered words of indignation toward the world;
he was skilled at painting grapevines with gnarled, dragon-like tendrils and would write poems and prose upon them, imbuing them with profound meaning.
When General Yang offered him fine wine, he would never touch his lips to it; whenever he saw the general, he would invariably curse him, calling him a "grave-robbing thief."

Tonghui (通慧) was a transmitter of the *zhuantong* (transmission of wisdom). A native of Bian, his secular surname was Zhang and his lay name was Wen. Having shaved his head, he was enrolled at Baiyun Temple.

The abbot ordered him to manage the latrines. In the latrine there was a washbasin; whenever someone bought fresh fish, they would pour it into the basin. Tonghui, provoked to anger, accidentally struck it, causing it to fall to the ground and kill the person.
Fearing [persecution], he fled to Zongchi Monastery in Huazhou. After some time, he became the elder of the monastery; his virtuous conduct was renowned.
Suddenly he said, "A case from thirty years ago must be settled today. When the assembly asked him why, he replied, "I shall see for myself at noon."
He then sat cross-legged to await [the visitor]. At that time, Zhang Weigong Xu was leading troops to Guanzhong.
A soldier carrying a bow and arrows entered the Dharma Hall and stared wide-eyed at Huì, intending to shoot him. Huì smiled and said, "I have been waiting for you, old monk.

The soldier replied, "The moment I saw you, I wished to harm you; I did not know what our enmity was. Huì explained the reason to him, and the soldier attained awakening, saying, "Karma of grievance against grievance..."
"When will our mutual retribution end? Being bound to one another through kalpa after kalpa—how could this be by mere chance? It would be better to resolve it together with the Master.
At that moment, he looked at the Master as if standing on the spot and heading toward the Western Heaven; the Master had already passed away. Huì then requested a brush and wrote a verse, saying:
"For thirty years I have wandered about, Producing such a form as this. Who would have known that meeting today Would bring this matter to an end?"
At that time, there were demonic obstacles. Upon finishing the transcription, he passed away peacefully.
As for the two masters Decong and Faning:
Master Decong was a native of Zhangtan in Gusu, born into the Yang clan. He first entered Jingguang Monastery in Hangzhou and received full ordination there.
At Bāntiān Temple, he traveled through various regions and received the Mind-Seal of Great Peace. During the Xingguo era, he built a thatched hut on the eastern peak of Mount Yushan in Huating;
two tigers served as his guardians, named Daqing and Xiaoqing, who followed and attended him wherever he went.
Later, a practitioner of meditation came to visit him. Seeing a volume hanging from a beam, he asked about it. [The Master] said, "This is a Buddhist scripture.

When asked if he had ever read it, the Master replied, "It is like a person looking at a family letter; once one knows its contents, why read it again? He once said, "The ancients valued practice. What more need I say?
Regarding other questions, he remained silent and did not respond. Subsequently, he resided at Chaoguo Temple. Qingsi.
A venerable monk from Zishang arrived bearing an image of Guanyin. The Master had foreseen this in advance and said, "Within three days, a master of the house shall arrive.
When the time came, it was indeed so. In the seventh month of the first year of the Tianxi era (1017), he passed away while sitting in the lotus posture.
For a month, his countenance remained as if alive. He was buried on Mount Shefeng, later to be moved to Nanling.
As for Dharma Master Ning, he previously resided at Jingju Monastery on Mount Maqí in Yizhou; people called him Chan Master Maqí.
One day, while traveling by sea, they arrived at Qinglong. There, Lady Gao, the mother of Zhang Gun, dreamed that a celestial deity announced, "An ancient Buddha has arrived.
The following day, she waited as she had seen in her dream, and the Master arrived just then. She welcomed him and invited him to stay at the garden of the Qian family.

That night, there was light upon the ground; when they dug there, they found a stone tablet which read: "Beneath the Fude Bridge of the Great Tang Chan Temple. They also discovered a *Vajra* [statue].

An image of the Buddha was established there, and a temple was built to honor it. Later, the Right Vice-Minister Zhu E invited the Master to preside over Zhaokong Temple on Mount She, where he passed away.
His stupa was erected to the east of the abbot’s quarters. The Master succeeded Xuedou Ming; Ming succeeded Changlu He;
and He succeeded Fayun Ben, who was a descendant of Yunmen.

Sengqie: Sengqie’s surname was Wu and his given name was Wenyu. A native of Xin’feng during the early Song dynasty, he resided at Mingjue Monastery in the county. His deportment was unconventional and unrestrained;
people regarded him as a madman. He once inscribed upon pine and cypress trees: “The Son of Heaven of the Zhao house, the King of the Zhao house.”

It was said that the Zhao clan was about to flourish, as luxuriant as pine and cypress trees. An old man of the local Zeng family, having no heirs, recognized that Saṃgha possessed something extraordinary and prepared a meal to honor him.
Before he could summon him, dawn broke and he pushed open the door to enter; the Zeng family’s provisions were most abundant.

The Saṃgha said, "You ought to repay this with pearls. Later, he indeed obtained two sons; the one named Sūn Dé was a student of the Buddha who traveled from Tíng to Nán'ān to pay his respects to Chan Master Dìngyīng.
He asked, "There is someone in Yúzhōu who pays homage to me; why is that? Sūn did not understand and said:
Sengqia was my Dharma son. When his grandson was about to depart, the Master took a fan and gave it to him, saying, "Give this to Sengqia.
When the boat reached the vicinity of the town, Sengqia waited for him and asked, "Where is my master’s fan? The grandson handed the fan over; he could not deceive him.
One evening at dusk, he went to the temple, closed the door, sat in the lotus position, and passed away. This occurred in the Jihai year of the Xiangfu era.
The sixth month of the year Wuyou.
Regarding the monk Dongsong:
nothing is known of his origins. His mental agility and transformations were unfathomable; when conversing with others, his responses were like echoes. People...
He was skeptical. Later, there was nothing that did not come true. When General Yue Wumu passed by leading his troops, he asked the monk, "From where does this sound of trickling water come?

The monk promptly replied, "I have joined bamboo poles to draw forth clear spring water. Yue said, "It is always like this in spring and summer. The monk replied, "In autumn and winter, it is likewise natural.
Yue marveled at him in his heart. Previously, the monk had been growing taro; he had built walls of sun-dried bricks and plastered them over [the plants] so as not to let [them be seen].

The people knew this. When Lü Yue passed by and requested that he be granted provisions to reward his three armies, the monk dug up taro from between the walls and made a soup, providing it until almost everyone was served.
Lü Yue was even more amazed by him. Later, when serving him noodles, the monk placed the sauce at the bottom of the bowl; he waited for Yue to ask for it before giving it to him.
He said, "The fine food is stirred with sauce. His words were deeply cryptic; Yue could not understand them, so he wrote a poem on the wall and departed.
Later, when Yue met his downfall, he finally regretted not having followed the monk from Dongsong’s advice.
Qin Hui, believing the monk had indeed instructed Yue, sent Li Ji to kill him. The monk, having foreseen this, wrote a poem that read: "In haste, pack up my tattered *kāṣāya*..."

Sa. Let the bell-towers, drum-terraces, and pavilions be of no concern to you. With sleeves sweeping through white clouds, you return to the ancient cave; with staff bearing the bright moon, you reach the ends of the earth.
Piteous are the cranes in their new nests atop the pines; they still remember the flowers once planted by the hedge.

It would be well to take your dog and cat along with you, lest they wander off and fall into the hands of some rustic family. [He] placed a scroll of a Buddha image on the western bridge of the hermitage, and furthermore—
He inscribed on the wall: "Li Ji comes from the east; I flee toward the west. Were it not for the great power of the Buddha, I would have nearly made a fool of myself.
Thereupon, he fled into the mountains. Less than a mile or two from his hermitage, Li Ji saw the poem and still wished to pursue him.
Upon unfolding the Buddhist image, he first saw [the monk] as one, then suddenly as ten, and soon as a thousand. Li Ji stood speechless, not knowing what to do.
He returned after offering praises. Later, he passed away while seated in seclusion at the bridge where the Buddha image had been placed; thus, it became known as the Bridge of the Thousand Buddhas.
Zhaobo, whose biography has been transmitted, was a man of unknown origin who lived beneath the pagoda at Chongjiao Temple in Taizhou. During his summer retreat, he would sit facing the sun.

In winter, he would lie down amidst the snow. Sometimes he would take up paper and write with rapid strokes; at first his words seemed like the ravings of a madman, yet in the end, none failed to come true.
On the first day of the New Year in the Jihai year of the Xuanhua era, he suddenly took a large scroll and gave it to a passing scholar, sealing it very tightly.
Thereafter, he walked through the market weeping. What was written within began by comparing himself to the rampant invaders, and subsequently dealt with the fall of Liao.
This continued until the time of Emperor Gaozong’s southward migration. When one examines the dates and times, they fit together like the two halves of a tally.

One day, he suddenly took leave of the temple monks and departed. When someone asked where he was going, he replied: "Neither to Mount Tiantai, nor to Mount Wutai; neither going east, nor coming west. Along the way, he chanted and recited scriptures.
After several days, he sat cross-legged beneath a pagoda and appeared to have died. When the assembly wished to carry him back into the temple, he suddenly leaped up.
He ran wildly, climbing the mountain behind the monastery; he scaled its heights like a monkey or a wildcat.
The crowd followed him immediately, seeing dozens of figures leaping and bounding among the treetops, with no one knowing where they had gone.
The Biography of Bodhisattva Heiqi Guang (Black-Lacquered Light).
His clan and lineage are not detailed. He manifested his traces at Jinggou Village in Jimo County, Laizhou.
He received ordination through the examination of scriptures at Chongfu Temple in the prefecture. The Master took recitation as his practice; within his recitation, he focused solely on...

He specialized in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, contemplating it in his mind and expounding it with his mouth; there was nothing he did that was not in accordance with its truth. People of the time praised him, calling him "The Illuminator of the Lotus Sutra.
Wherever he went, he benefited sentient beings and extracted them from suffering, and none failed to receive salvation. People looked up to him as they would to a sovereign jewel or a medicinal tree.

Whenever he traveled among the prefectures, towns, and villages, if he encountered a pregnant woman on the verge of childbirth at a moment of peril whose outcome was unpredictable, the Master would enter her home.

If one preaches the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs" chapter or the "Peaceful Conduct" chapter, one will immediately recover from illness and be lifted up, like picking something from the house of a childless family.
If one preaches the "Universal Gate" chapter or the "Exhortation of Samantabhadra" chapter, whatever one seeks shall be fulfilled, and one will furthermore possess the marks of virtuous wisdom.
Furthermore, if a wooden raft for travelers is wrecked by wind and waves, and they run for help...
The Master instructed him to recite the name of Avalokiteśvara with utmost sincerity and urgency; consequently, he reached his destination safely amidst smooth waters.

Instances such as this were not limited to one. Wherever people turned their hearts toward him, there was no response that did not follow like a shadow follows a form or an echo follows a sound, and they revered him as if he were a divine spirit.
Later, during a great drought, prayers and supplications went unanswered, leaving the people in a state of anxious despair and helplessness. The Master then commanded the assembly...
He gathered firewood to construct a platform and said, "I shall sacrifice my body to bring rain for you all. The assembly knelt and prostrated themselves, wailing in grief.
The Master immediately ascended the platform; fire issued from the crown of his head, suddenly blazing up. In the space of a finger-snap, the rain arrived and poured down heavily.

It ceased after three days, yet the flames remained within the rain without being extinguished. After as many days as there were fingers on his hands, when the sky cleared and he looked upon it, he saw the Master’s true form.
His body sat upright amidst the ashes, yet it suffered not the slightest damage; it was black and radiant—how extraordinary!
The officials reported this to the court, who bestowed upon him the title "Bodhisattva Black-Lacquered Radiance. An edict was then issued to lacquer his body, and he was escorted back to the capital.

At Daci Temple, he was enshrined so that he might be venerated forever. One who offered praise for him said: "He opens the gate of universal salvation and responds to the capacities of sentient beings. One.

Just as the moon’s light reaches every body of water, the clouds of the Awakened One bring sweet rain to the great earth. His impartial compassion, free from partiality, evenly moistens those who suffer and are weary.
He raises the banner of diligence; fire becomes cool and ice becomes warm. The void proclaims his praise, and the myriad phenomena listen to his teaching.
Yinsu transmitted the seal to Yinsu.
His style name was Puan. He was the son of the Yu family of Yichun in Yuanzhou.

When he was six years old, he dreamed of a monk who pointed at his heart and said, "In the future, you shall realize it yourself. Upon waking, he showed his chest to his mother; she saw a small mark upon his heart.

It was crimson and translucent, about the size of a cherry seed. Not long after, he left the household life under Master Xian of Shoulongyuan at the age of twenty-seven, shaving his head and receiving full ordination.
The Master possessed a majestic appearance and a mind of clever wisdom; Xian recognized his potential and encouraged him to study the *Lotus Sūtra*.

The Master said, "I have often heard that the fundamental principle of all Buddhas must consist in awakening and realization. What benefit is there in counting characters and following the lines of texts?
He then took his leave of his teacher and traveled to Lake Xiang. There, he visited Master Zhong of Muguan at Daming Mountain and asked, "All phenomena return to the One;
where does the One return? Master Zhong held up his whisk, and the Master attained realization. He subsequently returned to his home monastery, which had a neighbor...

Regarding the Master Cihua of the Temple: the assembly requested him to serve as abbot, yet he never remained in that position. He used a coarse quilt for bedding and paper for clothing, and partook of gruel twice daily.

Aside from his meditative stillness, he devoted himself solely to reading the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and its commentaries. Suddenly, he attained great enlightenment; sweat poured from his entire body, and with joy he said, "I have now personally realized the realm of the *Avataṃsaka*.
He composed a verse, saying: "It cannot be formed into a ball, nor can it be dispersed; why need one go to Mount Nanyue?"
Furthermore, at Tiantai, the gates of the six sense-faculties were unoccupied, which provoked a foreign monk to come all this way on purpose.

Thereafter, he gave rise to words and phrases that awakened both the hidden and the manifest; there were instances where things occurred spontaneously, without being sought. One day, a monk suddenly arrived through the snow.
The Master looked at him and said with joy, "This is my uninvited friend. He invited him to sit in silence together and they questioned one another.
He replied, "Sometimes with a laugh, sometimes with a shout. The monk said, "The Master is one who has returned; before long, you shall greatly propagate our Teaching.

He then pointed to the snow, wrote a verse, and departed. From that time on, those who looked toward him with admiration became numerous. The Master preached the Dharma according to the needs of the occasion or wrote verses for them.
To those who were ill, he would break off grass to serve as medicine; upon taking it, they were immediately cured. There were also those afflicted by pestilence whose tracks were visible.
To those who did not come to visit him, he bestowed verses upon them, and all attained perfection.

As for his prayers for rain or fine weather, the felling of monstrous trees, and the destruction of licentious shrines, his spiritual responses were manifold. Consequently, he renovated Buddhist temples. Someone asked the Master, "What practice have you cultivated to attain this?
The Master made a single stroke in the air and said, "Do you understand? The man replied, "I do not. The Master said, "Stop, stop; there is no need."
He spoke thus. As he was about to pass away, he wrote a verse upon the wall and gathered the assembly to instruct them, saying: "The Buddhas do not appear in the world, nor is there any nirvana.

Those who enter my room will surely be able to achieve profound resonance with the mystery. Guard and uphold this well; let it not be lost or regressed. He requested a bath, sat in the full lotus posture, and passed away.
This was in the seventh month of the fifth year of the Qiandao era. His worldly age was fifty-five, and his years as a monk were two.
18. Tà Quánshēn (The Whole-Body Stūpa).
From Deng to Chuan.
Deng was the son of the Zhou family of Huái'ān, Fúzhōu. His mother dreamed that Śāṇakavāsa wished to become her son. [He was born] after fourteen months.
He was born with exceptional brilliance from his youth; he was able to master the classics and compose literary works, excelling in calligraphy, particularly in the cursive and clerical scripts.

He abandoned Confucianism for Buddhism, shaving his head and dyeing his robes, and styled himself Puan (Lotus Hermitage). His eloquence was like the wind; every day he gathered monastics to discuss the profound meanings of the Dharma and received Confucian scholars to discourse on the Classics and histories.
When he first arrived at Shimen, Chen Pinjun Yi and Cai Langzhong Shu heard of his reputation and invited him to join them.
He replied, "I wish to build a bridge at the mouth of the sea to ferry sentient beings across; I have not had the leisure to dwell here.

After several years, he reached the sea and the bridge was completed. Upon his return, he learned that Yao had already passed away, so he settled at Shimen. There, he would occasionally speak of people's fortunes and misfortunes.

His deeds were largely in accordance with destiny. The local Confucian scholar Chen Wenhū saw him before he had reached the age of twenty. The Master said to him, "At the age of twenty-nine, you shall be selected for recommendation;
at forty-two, you shall suddenly cease to speak. Subsequently, everything occurred exactly as he had foretold. Whenever he composed poetry or prose, he did not engage in prolonged reflection;
he would simply take up his brush and complete the work instantly. His style was bold and unrestrained. [He was a contemporary of] Chen Xixuan and Lin Aixuan.

The brother of Liu Zhuozuo both "scratched their eyes" (took note) upon meeting him. In his later years, he returned to reside in Qingyuan Village to the west of the county seat. Magistrate Lu wished to test his talent;
one night, he sent someone to deliver a stone with calamus roots and demanded a poem immediately. The Master took up his brush and replied:
"The sound of knocking at the gate, *pò pò*, at midnight, The wind disturbs the vast sky as the moon is about to set. The nine-layered [palace]..."

Outside, the sound of thunder roared; ten-thousand-acre waves surged with clouds of ominous hue. The Earth Deity lost sight of Mount Dongting; the pufferfish hut was transformed into a pavilion on Mount Penglai.
What deep intent did Master Lu harbor in entrusting me? The seventy-two peaks have now added five more to the Five Sacred Mountains.
On the day of his passing into stillness, his body was cremated; the rising smoke and the crumbling remains were all transformed into *śarīra*. His disciples...
A stupa was erected at the Linyang Monastery.
Relying upon the monks Chuan and Hui, [the boy] remained silent and seldom smiled when he was five or six years old; he abstained from meat. Before long, his parents passed away one after the other.
Hui-tou entered the Lohan Monastery and served as a monk under the Elder Konggu. While reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, he attained awakening.

At the age of twenty, he took leave of the Elder to travel abroad for nearly twenty years. At the beginning of the Kaibao era, he came to Duidiyan Rock, where he cleared away stones and swept the earth.
There he dwelt, reciting the sūtra daily while sitting upright on a rush mat, remaining awake throughout the night until he finally attained penetration and clarity.
Whenever he spoke of fortune or misfortune, his words were immediately verified. A local man named Youyan was about to depart on a journey when Hui said, "May you have a safe return;

may you have a safe return. Upon his return home, however, his wife had fallen ill with a disease for which there was no cure. Although she was still healthy when he arrived, she suddenly fell ill that night and passed away.

There was also a man who had lost his ox; after searching for several days without success, he went to consult Hui. Hui said, "It is at the foot of a certain mountain in such-and-such a village. Go and search there. When he searched, he found it.
Guo Dejian was once seen clutching his chest in pain. Hui said to him, "Are you suffering from heart pain? If you grind a rock from a bee’s nest and drink the water, you will be cured immediately.
Shortly thereafter, it proved to be so. At the age of ninety-odd years, as he was about to enter nirvana, he wrote a verse upon his desk, saying:
"Birth is understood, death is understood; At ninety-three years, how much has been worn away! Now I shatter the great void— One!"
A full moon wheel appeared, clear and bright. He passed away while seated in meditation more than ten days prior, but it was only then that the local people learned of it.

They carried him out and buried him; his complexion remained as if he were alive. A fragrant scent wafted intensely from the tattered robe upon his body, leading people to say, "This is Master Lai’s Buddha.

They enshrined him in an image for worship. When drought struck, prayers offered before the image were answered immediately. Because he was born at Mount Laishan in Guihua, people called him "Lai Seng" (The Monk Lai).
Jin Fachong: Master Fachong was a person of unknown origin who resided on Mount Wutai. His spiritual anomalies were unfathomable.

During the Dading era, the Daoist priest Xiao Shouzhen submitted a memorial requesting that he compete in feats of strength against a śramaṇa. The Jin ruler granted permission, and the Master responded to the summons.
He entered the capital and stayed at Haotian Temple. The next day, they were tested in the palace courtyard.
Xiao was able to drink a *dou* of wine without showing any sign of intoxication, and he said to Chong, "Can a śramaṇa drink? If you cannot, you shall rank below me.
The Master replied, "I could drink ten *hu* at a single draught; that would not be difficult for me. However, my Buddha has precepts, and a śramaṇa must not drink wine. I request—"
He added arsenic and the poison of the *hin* bird to it, saying, "I shall drink this with you so that we may not be guilty of an offense. Can you drink it?
Xiao said, "Please let the śramaṇa go first. The Master took the poisoned wine in his hand, recited incantations, and drank it as if it were water.
Having finished drinking, he overturned the vessel. To show that not even a single drop remained, he immediately filled another vessel to the brim and gave it to Xiao.
Xiao, trembling with fear, did not dare to accept it. The Master said, "You have fallen below me. Yet Xiao continued to speak boastfully and act with arrogance.
The Master drew a vajra-circle on the ground and cast a spell over it; Xiao unconsciously leaped into the circle, his sweat falling like rain as he assumed a most hideous and disheveled appearance.

The registers were searched exhaustively, but he could not be found. The Emperor urged the Master to abandon his pursuit, to which the Master replied, "Were it not for Your Majesty’s presence here, I would have shattered your head with my vajra-pestle.
The Jin ruler greatly praised him and granted him ceremonial insignia to escort him back to the mountains.
By imperial decree, Wansui Temple was constructed for him to reside in.
Wuzhu of the Yuan dynasty transmitted the Dharma to Wuzhu.
His birth origins are unknown. He frequently traveled within Xihu County; he called himself Wuzhu, and people likewise addressed him as Wuzhu.
He once resided at Shousheng Temple, where he sat alone with eyes closed for ten days without eating, and wrote upon his door:
He said: "When coming, one does not know from where one comes; when departing, one does not know to where one goes. One no longer perceives the path of the wind.
A man with shaven head walks with staggering steps, not knowing whence he has come. Amidst the vast mist and waters, where shall he return?

During the Zhizheng era, while residing at Ticheng Temple, whenever he encountered someone, he would point to the sky and draw on the ground, saying that the world was about to fall into chaos. At times...

He lay prostrate in the mud like a drunken man. A crowd of children pursued him, some laughing loudly and others weeping bitterly. When people asked him about their fortune or misfortune, his predictions were invariably proven accurate.
If given money, he would not accept it; if given food, he would devour it voraciously, finishing several liters in an instant, or sometimes he would simply ignore them and depart.

Once, he was lying flat on his back in the middle of the courtyard when, at midnight, the snow reached a depth of three feet; yet there was no snow upon his body as he remained in a state of deep intoxication.

He slept for three days and then arose. One day, he suddenly vanished. A local resident encountered him in the city of Xiangyang, where he was entrusted with a message for the abbot, Master [Name], stating that his departure would coincide with the very day the letter was delivered.
Zhicheng’s Biography Zhicheng was the son of Yang [surname] of Jinshan; his father was Lin. Lin served Emperor Taizu for his bravery and talent, serving as a Grand Marshal (Duyuan-shuai).

His mother was Lady Fang, who bore two sons, of whom the Master was the elder. From an early age, he possessed the aspiration to transcend the mundane world. At the age of sixteen, his parents arranged a marriage for him.

He did not comply. They coerced him, so he cut his hair and fled to the capital. There he paid homage to the Seventh Generation Patriarch, left the household life, and received the full precepts (*mahā-śīla*).
When the master knelt to request a name, the Patriarch asked, "What is your aspiration? He replied, "Sincerity alone. The Patriarch accordingly bestowed that name upon him.

He styled himself Jikan (Silent Hermit). His practice was diligent and tireless, and his spirit was clear and vigorous; regarding the essential meanings of both Exoteric and Esoteric Buddhism, he moved with effortless mastery.

If it were false, how could he have so strictly maintained the precepts on transgressions and offenses while extensively practicing the conduct of compassionate gathering? In the *dingchou* year of the Zhizhen era (1297), he served as the Chan Registrar for the Capital Region.

In the *dinghai* year (1307), he presided over Qing’an Temple. The following year, he acquired a vacant plot in Lingzhuang Village in the capital and constructed the Guanghua Hermitage, where he resided.
There he received disciples and guided the assembly, his reputation for the Way flourishing ever more. When Chengzong ascended the throne, he bestowed an imperial seal upon him.

An imperial edict conferred upon him the title "Great Chan Master Jingzhao Miaoxing" (Still Illumination and Wondrous Practice) and appointed him as the General Superintendent of the Dharma Gate for the Dhūtas of all circuits.

Throughout his life, the Master manifested many extraordinary traces; his spiritual responses and transformations were such that they startled the ears and agitated the eyes, leaving people unable to discern whether he was an ordinary man or a sage.
Once, while dwelling in quietude, a wondrous vapor formed into fine strands, taking the shape of Sudhana with palms joined, appearing above the Master at night.
While he was sleeping, people saw a white light shining through his chest that did not dissipate for some time.

On another occasion, a flock of sparrows gathered upon the Master’s head as if perching on a withered stump. A woman of the Zou family in the capital had been possessed by a malevolent spirit for a long time;

the Master struck her with his prayer beads, and the possession ceased immediately. Once, when the Master encountered someone he recognized, he dispatched four of his disciples, including Li Chun, to go [to him].

He traveled to Jiangnan, but did not return for over a year. While the Master sat waiting, Li Zhi arrived; the Master questioned him regarding his intermediaries and matters of religious doctrine, receiving very detailed accounts.
After a short while, Li indeed arrived, and everything he said accorded perfectly with what had been reported.

On another day, Xu Shanyou was seen coming from Baoding, reporting that Master Jizhao had passed away; this proved to be true. Instances such as these were numerous. Once, there was a thief who entered the room.
"Do not capture [them]. Even if others treat you with violence or injustice, do not take it to heart.

In the autumn of the Great Virtue’s sixty-fifth year, the year Yi-si (1305), as he was about to pass away, he wrote by hand a copy of the *Bodhicittotpāda-śāstra* along with a golden-lettered version of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, and bestowed them upon his disciple Fayun. He spoke to him regarding the affairs of the Zen school, saying:
"I am about to depart. Light incense and change your robes. Then, lying on his right side with his feet crossed, he passed away. His age was sixty-five. [The funeral rites were performed.]
Wei obtained thirty-two grains of five-colored śarīra, which he enshrined in a stupa beside Qing’an Temple. From his entry into the Way until his parinirvāṇa, nearly fifty years passed.
Wearing tattered robes and eating coarse food, he maintained the various sections of secret mantras, striving tirelessly from morning till evening;

he never for a moment neglected his practice due to cold or heat. Through the power of such dedicated cultivation, he attained spiritual efficacy on his own. He was truly of the same lineage as Daorong and Kumārajīva.
Is it so? The Biography of King Uisfa (with the appended account of He Qing).
Karmā Uisfa was a person of the Tibetan region. His Way embraced the profound and vast, and his spiritual efficacy was unfathomable; his fame resounded throughout the Middle Kingdom.
In the Yongle era, our Emperor Taizong Wenhuang sent envoys to the Western regions to welcome him.

Upon his arrival in Jinling, he was granted an imperial edict that revealed the Emperor’s sagely resolve, conferring upon him the title of "Dharma King of the Great Treasure of the Tathāgata" and "Great and Virtuous Sovereign Buddha of the Western Heaven."
As the head of the Buddhist teachings throughout the empire, the Master was by nature fond of quiet seclusion and could not endure clamor or distraction.
He submitted a memorial to decline the appointment; however, His Majesty’s regard for him was most earnest, yet he could not be persuaded to remain.

Thereupon, the Emperor bestowed upon him the ceremonial insignia of a state carriage, banners, and streamers, and dispatched an imperial messenger to escort him to Daxiantong Temple on Mount Wutai. Furthermore, he issued an edict to the Inner Attendant Yang Sheng to restore the temple.
The temple also maintains the Buddha-relic stupa established by King Aśoka to adorn the abode of the Dharma King.

Previously, when the Emperor and the Dharma King visited Linggu Monastery to establish a dharma altar for the memorial rites of the late Emperor and Empress, they were moved by the auspicious omen of the stupa’s shadow and golden light.
Later, when the Dharma King entered Mount Tai, the Emperor was so filled with longing that he could not let go of him. Consequently—

Reflecting upon the previous auspicious omen, the Emperor visited Linggu Temple once again. The Emperor silently offered his prayers; on this day, he beheld auspicious signs twice as magnificent as before.
On the tenth day of the fourth month (dinghai), the Emperor dispatched an envoy to deliver a letter to the Great Dharma King of Mount Tai, the Great and Good Sovereign Buddha.
The letter read in brief: "On the fifteenth day of the fourth month, I, the Emperor, went to Linggu Temple together with the Great Master Hongji."

Observing the shadow of the stupa seen earlier, its patterns and radiance are exquisite and wondrous, manifesting in thousands of transformations and myriad forms—ten times more magnificent than before.
Though one were to employ the utmost skill of painting and the most eloquent of speech, neither could depict or describe even a ten-thousandth part of it (and so forth).
All of this is due to the Tathāgata, the Great Jewel Dharma King, the Sovereign Buddha of Great Virtue, whose Way transcends all equals and whose merit is supreme.
Peerless, he is fully endowed with the ten thousand practices and proclaims the six supernormal powers. He transforms and guides all classes of beings;
he is truly Śākyamuni Buddha appearing once more in this world, manifesting such inconceivable spiritual responses. My heart rejoices, beyond the power of words to describe.
I have briefly reported these matters; may the Tathāgata take note of them. The following year, he took his leave.

When the Emperor entered nirvana through the cremation fire, that same year, an official at the Hexi Pass saw the Dharma King departing gracefully toward the west. He presented the jade pendant bestowed by the Emperor as proof and returned to report it.
The Emperor marveled at this incessantly and issued an edict to the eunuch Yang Sheng to sculpt a statue in the Dharma Hall of Xian Tong Monastery so that it might be venerated forever.
He Qing was a native of Yunnan who maintained his clarity and was diligent in his practice; he went to see the Dharma King, who bestowed upon him the secret scriptures of the precepts and methods.
He manifested great spiritual efficacy, and during the Zhengtong era, he received an imperial decree to accompany the military expedition to Lufu, where he established an altar and performed rites.
He was posthumously granted the title Gong (Merit). In the sixth year of the Tiānshùn era, he was summoned by imperial decree for an audience;
shortly thereafter, he passed away.

The Emperor dispatched Zēng Zhuó, a Chief Clerk of the Ministry of Rites, to offer a ritual sacrifice. The *Hóngmíng tōngjì* states that he ordered the Western monk Śākya-halima to perform rites at Linggu Monastery.
At the Dharma altar, offerings were presented for the Imperial Father and the Imperial Mother.

The Master of the Sangha led the monastic community in performing the Great Ritual of Universal Salvation for fourteen days. Celestial clouds and heavenly flowers appeared; sweet rain and ambrosia fell; śarīra relics and auspicious light manifested;
and blue birds and white cranes gathered in succession day after day. One night, golden flowers grew upon the cypresses and pines, covering them entirely.
In the capital city, the Golden Immortal Arhat manifested in the clouds above, adorned with the wondrous forms of a white elephant and a blue lion.
Celestial lamps led the way, and banners and canopies circled him in an unceasing variety. Furthermore, the sounds of Brahma-chants and celestial music descended from the heavens.
The ministers presented a memorial of congratulation, and scholars such as Hu Guang offered a memorial on the auspicious omen of sacred filiality.

It should be chanted in song. From this time on, [the Emperor] devoted himself in secret to the Buddhist scriptures and composed Buddhist melodies, which were then performed by the court dancers and singers.
The masters Jingzhong and Guangneng transmitted these.
Jingzhong was a person from Qujing in Yunnan; he was of the Mian ethnic group. During the Zhengtong era, he resided in a desolate, ancient temple where he practiced asceticism for over forty years.

With nothing but an iron board and a single *pútán* (seated cushion), he did not sleep throughout the night. One night, his prayer beads were scattered in the darkness; he searched for them and reassembled them into a string.
He was as diligent and urgent as one whose hair was on fire. Someone asked the Master, "Why do you subject yourself to such hardship?"
Thus it was. The Master said, "If there is no suffering, true realization cannot be achieved; I am merely refining away the demon of sleep.
Because of this, people came to call him the Elder Zhenfeng (True Peak). One day he told his disciples, "A guest is arriving; you must prepare a vegetarian meal in advance.
That evening, a dozen or so thieves burst in. The Master said, "It is empty here; I fear my guest will come in vain. What shall we do? He then proceeded to pack their belongings with his own hands.

He provided them with food and drink, and they departed with their entire households. The thieves carried off what they had obtained and fled through the night, rejoicing that they were now very far from people.

When dawn broke and they looked back, they found themselves merely circling between the two corridors; they had not yet even left the temple gates. The bandits prostrated themselves in a circle and begged for their lives.
The Master comforted them and sent them on their way. The Master wished to build a great hall for Amitābha, and after divining the site, he found one.
At Longtan, he made a vow, saying, "You dragon must ascend the mountain; lend me this place to establish a monastery. Before long, the waters shifted to the summit.
Guangneng was a native of Guizhou who, during the Zhengtong era, planted his staff at Yuetan Temple. He observed the precepts with meticulous diligence and frequently engaged in recitation and study.

Regarding the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, he attained the power of hearing and retaining [the teachings]. Once, a tiger suddenly burst into the monastery; the monks fled in terror, but the Master remained unmoved.
When the tiger entered the hall and beheld the Master, it tucked its tail and departed. Someone asked, "Does the Master possess the Way? The Master replied, "It is the power of the *Avataṃsaka*.
Consequently, he kept this matter hidden from the assembly. In the year Jisi (1069), the Miao tribes rose in rebellion against Xinglong; an arrow entered the monastery gate.
The monastic community fled, entreating the Master to depart. The Master said, "I have labored with great diligence to construct this place and establish the Triple Gem;

I vow to share its fate and shall remain alone to guard it. When the raiders arrived, they intended to kill the Master. He said, "I pray you execute me outside; do not defile this sacred ground of the Buddha.
The bandits, moved by his righteousness, released him and further cautioned their comrades against violence and the destruction of the temple. Thus, the monastery was preserved.
When the invaders retreated, the assembly asked him about it. He replied, "This was the power of Huayan.
Master Maji and Master Qiu both received the Dharma from Master Maji.
Master Maji was a native of Huai’an in Fuzhou and was the son of the Chen family. At the beginning of the Hongwu era, he left the household life and formed a monastic community.
Mao resided on the great summit of Mount Gu, which is Mount Lishu. Monk Qiu was a native of Taizhou and was also a monk from the beginning of the dynasty.
He frequently traveled between Mount Tiantai and was addressed by people as "Monk Qiu," though it was unknown whether "Qiu" was his surname or his given name.
He possessed miraculous traces; once, while out for a stroll with a young boy, he encountered a tiger on the road, to which he calmly tucked its tail.
It remained tamed by his side. When the boy returned home and told his parents, the Master stroked the child’s head and said, "Do not speak, do not speak.

Thereupon, the boy lost his voice. Someone once gave the Master a pair of shoes; he hurriedly put them on and walked through the mud. The donor felt regret for his gift, but when the Master returned the shoes, they were seen to be completely unstained.
One day, while visiting the lay patron Zhou, he encountered Zhou’s maidservant gathering mulberry leaves.
The Master hurried forward, embraced her, and reached out his hand to stroke her neck as if to loosen her bonds. The maidservant, startled and enraged, informed her mistress.

The mistress rebuked her, saying, "How can you, one who has left the household life, be so轻薄 (qīngbó—frivolous and indecent)? The Master replied, "Seven days from now, you shall know for yourself. The mistress was astonished by these words.
When the day arrived, she placed the maidservant in a room and stationed people to guard her. At the first watch of the night, the guard...
He dozed off for a moment. Upon waking and looking at the maidservant, he found she had already died. He questioned the Master, who said, "Previously, I saw a ghost with ten ropes binding its neck;
I severed them, but not all were cut. At Huading Temple, the Master instructed the temple administrator, "Tomorrow, a fire-omen will enter the temple;
on the day after tomorrow, a fire will surely break out. On the following day, suddenly a woman appeared.

The people accompanying him with sedan chairs, horses, and servants were very numerous; those who had previously attended his assemblies and established vegetarian feasts felt their hearts rejoice at the thought that they would receive alms from the temple community.
They said to the Master, "Where is the calamity of fire? The Master replied, "The host of today's feast is it. You all only fear losing it; what can destiny do?
Suddenly, fire broke out from within, and the entire monastery was reduced to ruins. This was the Master’s manifestation of supernatural traces.
It was very much so. The elders of the mountains were still able to speak of it. Later, he manifested his passing at Mount Tiantai.

After his transformation, he spoke to a young tiger cub, who was then able to speak again. The tracks at Maji (Horse Tracks) are roughly the same as those of the Master. Whenever it was the first or fifteenth day of the month, it would invariably return home to pay respects to its parents;
the house was fifty *li* from Gushan, and the stone steps were steep and treacherous. The local people marveled at this.
The next morning, he went ahead to wait for them; yet he never once stepped down from the mountain, even though he returned home as if he had been there all along.
Guo Chen, the Regional Commander of Fuzhou Road, marveled at this and appointed him as a monk-judge, but he subsequently fled, and his final whereabouts remain unknown.
These two masters manifested themselves by the seashore, where they responded simultaneously with the celestial winds and ocean waves; truly, this is inconceivable.
Yi ren was a man of the second generation who attained perfect faith.
He was a native of Fangshan in Jingzhao. Having shaved his head at Baiyun Mountain, he took the monk Dejing as his master.
He traveled back and forth between Shangfang and Honglu for over twenty years. Wherever he went on his pilgrimage—Wulin, Huai'an, Liuan, and Zhongnan—he would stay for several years at each location.
In the Gengshen year of the Jiajing era, he arrived at Mount Tai and took up residence in the Tiger-Ear Cave (*Huer Yanxue*).
There, the howling beasts vied with one another to flee and hide. He leaned against a rock to build a dwelling, gradually clearing away its overgrowth.
He accumulated dozens of round gourds, which he stacked like hats, lining the stream as he sat upon rocks and moved in and out among the secluded flowers and beautiful bamboo.
On the cliff were two lotus ponds, each about twenty feet wide, which did not dry up even in years of drought. His thatched hut was three-sided and just large enough for his body;
whatever he obtained—a single thread or a single grain of rice—he gave entirely to the traveling monks from the ten directions. He practiced this for several years.
It eventually became a great monastic center that drew the attention of the entire land of China. Men and women came in such numbers that they wailed and wept;

yet even those who reached Tiger’s Ear Rock (*Hueriyan*) were like those who had not yet ascended the mountain peaks. Those who arrived at the rock and failed to prostrate themselves with their heads and faces touching the ground considered it a deficiency in their karmic conditions and would inevitably depart in bitter weeping.
Otherwise, they would wait vigilantly outside the door of the cave for several days until they could catch a single glimpse of him; upon seeing him, their joy would exceed all expectations.
For this reason, the fame of Mount Huer (Tiger-Ear Rock) spread throughout the world. Counting the tracks of worthy scholars and gentlemen, they arrived there daily;

the imperial gifts from the Shangfang (Palace Storehouse) and the provisions from the Yeching (Imperial Harem) arrived monthly. Since the Jia and Long reigns, among those renowned as eminent elders, none has been like this Master.
However, the Master was intent on practicing in secret and did not manifest his understanding outwardly; in responding to circumstances...
He spoke thus: "He relied primarily on filial piety and reverence, caressing [his disciples] with great warmth, like a wet-nurse toward her pampered child.
When gold and money poured in, he refused to accept them; when those who offered grain arrived, he entrusted it to the former residents to provide offerings.

For over forty years, his shadow never left the mountain. He sat cross-legged within a single niche like a withered tree stump. Even those of sharp faculties who were fond of eccentric talk and heterodox studies [could not move him]."
Whoever beheld his countenance could not help but feel a profound sense of reverence. The Master’s *śīla-vatsara* (summer retreats) were the most numerous of all;

calculating back from his birth, it would have been during the reigns of Emperors Xuan and Cheng. His disciples once attempted to question him regarding his seniority, but he did not answer. On one occasion, they searched through his chest and found an old woolen robe (*kambala*).

Hu suddenly said, "This is the seventh year of Emperor Wu; it is the robe obtained from the almsgiving held in the royal city. When struck, he again did not answer. Later, he passed away on the mountain.
Empress Cisheng retrieved gold from the imperial treasury to have a stupa constructed for the Master. Yan Pengtou was a native of Xiangyang.
He recited the name of Amitābha Buddha tens of thousands of times daily. By nature he was lofty and pure; he had accumulated a fortune of several thousand pieces of gold which he gave in charity.
He cast them aside as if they were dust; his traces were most extraordinary, such that people could not distinguish whether he was mundane or sagely.
He was a peerless and marvelous man, belonging to the lineage of those who have realized non-duality.
Minghe said: "Some say that Fubai’s surname was Xu; his family had long been of the Xiangshan lineage. Xu grew up in Shengzhang, and it was Fubai who sent him forth into the monastic life.
Fubai took his wife and entered Mount Wutai to practice. Fubai subsequently searched for his parents for many years."
Upon finding the non-dual within a heap of ice and snow, he said in great anger: "You unworthy son! Why have you come running from so far away?
You take me for your father and mother; I have already left the household life. You take me for your teacher, yet I have not yet realized the Way.
A great man appearing in this world dwells on a solitary peak at the summit of a mountain, in a single small thatched hut, having fully accomplished his own self."
"There is no leisure; you are still driven by the passions of birth and death. Have you come to this state? Depart quickly; do not fail in my affairs.
Thus, Wunni returned south and dwelt at Hueri Rock, becoming a great spiritual teacher of the age.

Although Wunni’s numinous roots had been planted long ago and his attainment was naturally so, the assistance that brought it to fruition was likewise due to his parents. They remained in harmonious union.

One Gate. Furthermore, he emerged from the region of Xiang; it cannot be known whether he was a rebirth of the Pang family. The *Biézhuan* (Separate Biography) records that the Elder transmitted the lineage of Huizong.
"Biézhuan" is his courtesy name. He was a son of the Wang clan from Yunmeng in Huguang. From birth, he was serene and still, taking no pleasure in the secular world.
At the age of seven, he entered the White Crane Monastery (*Báihè sì*) to become a monk. At nine, a layman named Wang invited him to enter Shu.
Upon reaching Shìmén Temple in Qíjiāng, Chóngqìng, he received full ordination.

In the Jiājìng *jiǎwǔ* year, while ascending the summit of Mount Éméi to pay homage to the Buddha, the clouds suddenly dispersed and the bright sun hung in the sky; there he beheld a wondrous person of golden hue traveling upon a small boat.
The bronze stupa was half-buried by the cliff. He recounted this to Dharma Master Qian Gong, who said, "You have a great affinity with this;

it is a manifestation of a Bodhisattva. From that time on, he made it his mission to uphold the mountain gate. For forty years he resided in the mountains, from the White Water [Village] to the mountain peak;
regarding the halls, pavilions, and sacred images, there were none that he did not renovate or expand, until they were as majestic as those of heaven.

He transformed the palace into a city of transformation. In the Jisi year of the Longqing era, he first left the mountains to travel to the capital, cross the South Sea to pay homage to the Great Being Avalokiteśvara, and enter Mount Wutai with the intention of remaining there for the rest of his life.
Throughout his life, the Master strictly observed the precepts and took no pleasure in producing writings on paper or ink, saying:
"Even the scriptures of the Tripiṭaka are but dregs; what is the use of further verbosity? He passed away beforehand.
On the third day, he suddenly said, "I am about to return to the West. He bathed, changed his robes, sat in the full lotus posture with a tranquil mind, and recited the Buddha’s name without ceasing.
When the appointed time arrived, he summoned his disciples and said, "I have never before left behind written words;
today, however, I cannot remain silent. He then sang this verse: "Birth is fundamentally without that which is born; Death likewise has nothing that exists. This stinking skin-sack— this very day..."
The body became mummified. His disciples struck the bell; when the tolling ceased, he suddenly opened his eyes and continued chanting (as before).

He passed away peacefully at the age of eighty-one, with seventy-five years of monastic seniority (*saṃgha-rakṣā*). His stupa is located beneath the Sihui Pavilion. Throughout his life, the Master displayed many miraculous manifestations.
Once, while at Xinghua Temple in Xintan, he was unable to complete the labor of forging a metal vessel; he first sought [instruction] from Bai Ban.

He withdrew and went to the residence of a wealthy man of the [certain] surname. He sat in the lotus posture for seven days and nights, begging for several *mǐn* of coins to provide offerings for the monks.
At first, the host was unwilling to give. When night fell, a brilliant light permeated the entire house; startled by this marvel, he followed its trace.

The light rose from the place where the Master sat, and only then did he begin to revere him. He then went to Jintang County in Hanzhou, where he struck a fish-drum to solicit alms; wherever the sound reached...

"It should not be fixed. If one strikes in the east, it is heard in the west; if one strikes in the west, it is heard in the east. One night there was heavy rain, yet the Master did not leave his room.
The sound of fish was likewise heard throughout the fields. When the villagers went to investigate, the Master was simply sitting peacefully in the shrine.
When he crossed the sea, he saw the Great Being in white robes sitting upon a golden lotus flower, slowly ascending amidst the clouds. His disciple, Zhen..."
Cang had not yet shaved his head when he was carrying [the master’s] belongings for him, becoming very exhausted. The Master asked, "Are you enduring this?
He replied, "Yes," and after walking ten or twenty li, he answered as before without showing even the slightest weariness. Thereupon, at Shuangfei Bridge, the Master shaved Cang's hair.

Pitying his simplicity, he had him light incense and kneel before the Great Being (Avalokiteśvara), while Cang held a water basin upon his head and recited the *Zhuchi Mingming* (Incantation for Bestowing Wisdom).
He recited it one hundred times. This continued for years at Baishui. One day, a fire broke out in the monastery. Wang Cang knelt down and pleaded with the Master to leave.

The Master counted [the recitations] and rebuked him. Thereupon, Wang Cang formed the visualization of entering the water and addressed the void, saying: "Since the halls and buildings are now empty..."

"May the treasury office remain unharmed. He then returned to the storehouse and sat in silence. The water on his head remained exactly as it was, and when the fire reached him, it extinguished itself.
Thus one knows that throughout his life, the Master’s cultivation of his disciples was always of this kind. Feng Siming Mengzhen said: "The Elder Biexuan’s conduct was pure and white;
he took the adornment of the Dharma hall as his Buddhist service—this was his 'one upward step'."
My son, although we have not heard whom he once met or which ancestral lineage he succeeded, in essence, he has come riding upon the wheel of his vow;
he cannot be fathomed by ordinary sentiments.
The Biography of Liaowu of An’ye (with the Appendix on Luyuan) Liaowu’s style name was Wujì;
he was also known as Cangu. A native of An’ye, he was born into the Mo family. In his youth, he worked as a laborer for Huang Youliang at Yanping Village in Dazhu County.
He was capable in ways that set him apart from other laborers; there were even occasions when others would hire him to perform their own plowing and herding.
Huang Yizhi married him to his own daughter. They sat facing each other with their knees pressed together like guests, never once showing even the slightest sign of intimacy.
All their conversation concerned the Buddha-dharma. Huang was increasingly amazed by him and consequently built a hermitage for him to dwell in so that he might fulfill his aspirations.
He provided him with food, drink, clothing, and other necessities daily without fail. One day, the daughter-in-law privately sent a pair of shoes to the Master. The Master—
Startled, he asked, "Where has this come from? He then drew his knife and shattered it. Reciting a verse to thank his host, he departed.
He shaved his hair at Luowei Temple in Dingyuan and served Elder Benzhen as his teacher. Benzhen told him, "Master Yougu is a true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) of the present age.
Thereupon, he set out on foot to visit him, whereupon he attained realization of the essential point of the mind and subsequently developed supernatural powers.

He manifested great spiritual wonders, and people from all quarters—whether noble or humble—reverently turned toward him. When he ascended the seat to preach the Dharma, celestial flowers fell like rain.
Once, while traveling through Liuhe Village in Ba County, the villagers paid him homage. The Master spoke a verse, saying: "The world suffers a great drought."
In this place, half [of the population] was gathered; the world was in great chaos, yet here there was no distress. What was said was never without its fulfillment.

From then on, those who followed him increased daily, and wherever he went, there was a tumultuous stir. Some, however, deluded the masses with demonic falsehoods and were imprisoned by the judicial inspectors.

During the day he sat upright in meditation; at night he went out to solicit funds to repair the prison buildings. To this day, there have been no rats, lice, mosquitoes, or gadflies within the prison.

The Master resided at An’ue for over forty years. During the Yongle era, he was summoned to the capital, where he was appointed as the presiding patriarch to ascend the altar and administer the precepts.
He was granted the title "Great Good Knowledge" (Dashan Zhishi). Later, he resided at Niushou Temple in Nanjing. One—

On the day he gathered the assembly, he spoke a verse: "The self and the self are fundamentally without self; the radiance is perfectly round and full. Vast and expansive, it moves freely in all directions;

everywhere there is no confinement or fetter. He passed away while sitting upright. An imperial decree granted him sacrificial offerings and a posthumous title, and his remains were returned for burial at Mumen.
A single volume of his recorded sayings (*yulu*) was circulated in the world.
The master’s successor was named Lingyuan, with the style name Fubii. He was the son of the Xue family of Fengyang. His spirit and appearance were exceptionally brilliant and refined.

He visited Wuji, who bestowed upon him the "Mu" (No-Word) kōan. After a long time, he attained realization. Delighting in the mountains and waters of Guang’an, he built a thatched hut and inscribed its name as "Snow-Bone.

At that time, the Great Emperor [Taisong] dispatched envoys to compile records throughout the empire and to seek out those among the immortals and Buddhist monks who had manifested extraordinary achievements.

The local officials neglected to record this, and Yuan composed a memorial to submit it to the throne; within it, he subtly embedded satirical admonitions. Prefect Zhu Heng detested its audacity and reported it to the court.

Yuan was summoned to the capital and brought before the legal authorities to answer for his conduct. Hardly had he reached the gate when he passed away peacefully, having attained spiritual liberation.
When the Emperor heard of this, he sighed and said, "To lose such a monk means I am devoid of the necessary karmic conditions. He granted the North Gate of the Pagoda [as his residence].
Regarding Yue Tianchuan:
Yue Tianchuan was a man of unknown origin. His eyes were both blind. During the final years of the Tian-shun era, he traveled about as a wandering youth.
Upon reaching the western side of Mount Pingding in Ye County, he suddenly sat down upon the ground and said, "An hermitage can be built here.

The local people marveled at this and collectively donated timber to construct a small hut for him to dwell in. After some time, whenever he spoke, his words were immediately fulfilled; he possessed foreknowledge of all matters.

Donations from far and near poured in every day, leading him to establish a Buddhist monastery. When the construction began, they discovered an ancient foundation, which turned out to be the ruins of a temple from a previous dynasty.
Whenever alms were about to arrive, he would invariably announce to his disciples in advance, saying, "A certain person is coming to offer such-and-such an item. It was always exactly as he had said.
He once composed verses extemporaneously and had a monk write them down; upon reading them, they were found to be deeply reasoned and elegant.

At over eighty years of age, he announced the time of his passing in advance and then died. The Yunchao Temple in Huangdian Village to the north of the present-day county is the very place where Yue Tian [resided].
A bone stupa was erected beside it.

The Chapter on the Relinquishment of the Body, composed by the Śramaṇa Minghe of Huashan Temple in Wumen during the Ming Dynasty;
including the Biography of Yu Mituo of the Song Dynasty (with the appended account of Jingzhen).
Sijing was the son of the Yu family of Qiantang. He excelled at painting Amitābha Buddha, reaching a level of sublime mastery.
Yang Wuwe called him "Yu-Mituo" (Yu-Amitābha), and by this name he became known to the world. Someone asked him, "Master, you can paint Amitābha; why do you not practice Chan meditation?
The Master replied, "Throughout my life, I have only known how to recite the name of Amitābha; as for practicing Chan, I do not know how—what can be done? I only need to..."
"The wind and moon over the Five Lakes—what need is there to brandish weapons in the Age of Great Peace?
When the Master was a child, he visited Duobao Mountain on West Lake and made a vow, saying, "In the future, I shall carve this rock into a Buddha. Later, it indeed became a statue of Maitreya.
When Minister Xue Gong asked, "Maitreya is currently preaching the Dharma in the Heavenly Palace; why carve a stone [image] here? the Master replied, "Tsk!"

"O stubborn stone! It relies entirely upon the skillful artisan to refine it. Now, as Maitreya Buddha, do not wait for his descent to seek him. His responses to those with whom he interacted were like this.
Throughout his life, the Master was dedicated to practicality and did not engage in empty ornamentation. He once rented a house near the Northern Gate to provide meals for monks;
before twenty years had passed, the total reached three million coins. He then changed the name of the establishment to Miaoxing (Wondrous Conduct) and expanded his residence into a temple.

During a period of rebellion and disorder, his monastery alone was not burned. When the master approached the rebels' camp, he vowed to sacrifice his own life in exchange for the lives of the entire city.

The rebels were struck with awe and consequently refrained from their violence for a time. Many were thus saved from death. In the winter of the seventh year of the Xiangsheng era, he passed away while sitting in the lotus posture.
The Court Gentleman Zhang Wugou (Jiucheng) inscribed his stupa. Later, during the Jiaxi era, there was one named Jingzhen who likewise sacrificed himself for the benefit of others;
he possessed the spirit of Master Jing, who built embankments to save lives. Zhen initially took Ruoping of Xingsheng Temple in Wusong as his teacher.
While traveling through lecture halls, he mastered the essential tenets of the Xianshou school. Upon reaching Qiantang, he happened upon the waters of the river.
The waters overflowed greatly; the embankments collapsed and were destroyed. The residents looked at one another, frantic and with nowhere to place their hands or feet.

Zhen presented a verse to Zhao Duanming, the Pacification Commissioner, saying: "The sea boils and the rivers and streams join together; The residents are swept away, their anxieties ever more intense."
He threw himself directly into the dragon palace, intending to quell the surging waves that lashed against the heavens.

He then cast himself into the sea and returned after three days, saying to the assembly, "I preached the Dharma in the dragon palace, and the dragon deities listened and accepted it; this embankment shall no longer collapse.

Having finished speaking, he entered the sea once more. When the matter was reported to the court, an imperial edict conferred upon him the title of State-Protecting Dharma Master (Huguo Fashi), and a shrine was established for him.
At Huiling, they established a shrine for him.
Regarding the *Huaseng zhuan* (Biographies of Transformed Monks), which includes [the accounts of] Jixiang and Ciji:

as for these "transformed monks," at first one could not discern who they were. With gray-skulled heads and dark-brown faces, they came and went with great frequency amidst the [scattered] dwellings, appearing extremely familiar.
He was frequently seen by people, yet no one ever inquired after him.

On the morning of the second day of the twelfth month in the fifth year of the Chongning era, he came from outside to beg for food in the city as usual, appearing as ever composed and expansive. When he saw that the sun was about to set, he suddenly tucked his robes into his bag as if intending to depart.
As he walked past the eastern part of the marketplace, he rested for a moment at the inn of the Ma family and asked for some gruel.
Thereupon, he adjusted his robes, sat in the full lotus posture, and passed away before the meal had even been served. His jade-like bones stood as firm as a mountain, neither leaning nor slumping.

All who gathered there gazed upon him and prostrated themselves in worship. They escorted his remains back to Beixi, where they enshrined them in a stupa. To this day, his true body remains solemn and vivid, as if alive.
Yang Tianhui of the Song dynasty composed a literary record of this event, stating: "How extraordinary! I have never seen such a thing before. This is the guidance..."

This Master did not leave behind the clamor and bustle of the marketplace, yet he demonstrated the ease of stillness; he did not disdain the filth and confusion of butchers and wine-sellers, yet he demonstrated purity and refinement;
he did not abandon the turbidity and evil of birth and death, yet he demonstrated the ultimate; he took no pleasure in the adornment of physical marks and beauty, yet he demonstrated steadfastness.
His voice was harmonious and gentle, resembling that of a common village shrine, yet no one knew his name or lineage; his skin was emaciated.

May they give rise to thoughts of admiration and cultivate the practice of pure faith, so that there may be those who follow and enter [the path].
Furthermore, there was a monk named Jixiang (Auspiciousness) who once resided at Jiemo Temple in Dongchuan; he was tall and sturdy with great strength, consuming five bowls of rice at a single meal.
Day and night, he recited five fascicles of sutras. In front of the monastery was a pond where fish were kept; Sengxiang knew their exact number and called them by name.
They all emerged from the water in succession, as if responding to Sengxiang’s words, and departed one after another.
In Yunnan there was a monk named Ciji. He once performed prostrations to Kāśyapa Buddha atop a perilous rock on Mount Qingdian, northeast of Erhai Lake.
He recited his daily liturgy with a hundred prostrations. People named that rock the "Prostration Rock. It overlooks an unfathomable abyss.

Thereafter, he immediately manifested a transformation-body upon the rock; even now, no one is able to tread upon that stone. His manifestations were inconceivable, all of them being of the same caliber as the transformed monks.

Faqing’s successor was the Chan Master Baizhi of Foguo. He once served as the secretary. Initially he resided at Puzhao Monastery in Sizhou, later moving to Shaoshi on Mount Song.
When the Bian region fell, he was captured by the barbarians and taken north to collect cattle. Only a monk who lectured on the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* recognized him.

The two masters Yuanjue Qing and De Lin transmitted [the lineage] to Jueqing.
