He was refined in the Vinaya precepts and roamed among the people with effortless ease.

Regarding any matter that could benefit things or aid others—ranging from paving streets, digging wells, providing soup and tea, to distributing medical needles and prescriptions—he would never fail to exert his courage and press forward, whether the task were great or small.
When he saw others performing such deeds, he regarded them as his own, assisting them with all his might. During the Zhizheng era, he arrived in Yunchuan.
I rejoice. I am eager to join the assembly of the Buddha Puzhao.

As the time for his entry into parinirvāṇa approached, on the twenty-third day of the first month, he composed a letter in advance to bid farewell to his dharma friends in Siming and Qu-yuan in Hangzhou, appending a verse that said:

"Throughout immeasurable kalpas there has always been a self; Yet there is no 'having a self,' nor is there even a 'self. Without self and without person, there is nowhere to be found; Vast and empty."
A brilliant light shone across the vast void. Everyone tried to stop him, but he would not listen. There was a man named Chen Yuanjian who welcomed him back to his home.
Two days later, the Master said, "The moonlight is bright; it will soon reach the third watch. How many people are there who can endure this bone-chilling cold?
Having said, "I am going back," why would he shamelessly remain? As he finished speaking, he became silent. When they searched for him, he had already passed away. The assembly rushed to his side.
They carried him to Xiyanyen Temple for cremation, yet sweat poured from his entire body; they then escorted him back. That evening, a crimson light illuminated the heavens.
After ten days had passed, his countenance remained as if alive, and his beard and hair grew of their own accord. Sengyuan and Sengjian were moved by deep faith;
they donated their own residence to establish a shrine for him and applied lacquer to it.
Dेलिन (De-lin) was a native of Dong’ou. During the Zhizheng era, he hung up his monk’s staff at a ruined temple in Zhezé, Shanghai.
Hunger and cold never troubled his mind. In the fifth month of summer, he suddenly said to people, "Who can provide me with a single niche?

On the first day of the ninth month, I shall cremate this body. People considered him a deceiver and did not believe him. When the appointed time arrived, he emptied his alms bowl and exchanged it for firewood.
Qiao turned to face him. Sitting cross-legged with palms joined, he said: "For twenty-seven years I have studied non-action;

now, as it comes to hand, I have attained it. (And so forth. Fire erupted from his body. Those who witnessed this were initially startled. They prostrated themselves and pleaded, saying, "To burn a person alive in this place is an ill omen for the region.
The Master responded from within the flames: "Once the rain has passed, there will be no harm."
Ming: The Recluse Monk (Supplement: Xue Mei), Yonglong.
A son of the Shi family of Gusu. While still in his swaddling clothes, he abstained from meat and blood; he aspired solely to the Buddha-dharma.

Having passed the age of twenty, he requested his parents for permission to leave the household life. He subsequently departed for Chongfu Temple on Mount Yin, where he shaved his head to become a monk and received full ordination.

His resolve and practice were austere and simple; his steadfast character was consistently distinct from that of ordinary people. Once, while sitting in meditation at night, he heard a celestial deity in the air announce:
"This temple was founded during the Tianjian era of the Liang dynasty and was destroyed at the end of the Yuan dynasty; it has been thirty years since then."
"I have received the Buddha’s entrustment to protect this monastery. If you, Master, can rebuild it, I shall provide my secret protection. The Master was moved by the words of the celestial deity;
he then summoned the assembly of donors and immediately pricked his finger to draw blood and wrote out the two great scriptures, the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, as a vow.
While he was writing, śarīras emerged from the tip of his pen, shining with a brilliant light. No one failed to be struck with wonder and to respond with reverent faith.
The Master gathered funds and prepared materials; he first established the Mahāvīra Hall. He traveled by boat to Sanqu to procure large timbers and crossed the Qiantang River.
A typhoon blew his raft toward the sea, and the crew on board all sighed and wept. The Master said, "What I am doing..."
All this was prompted by divine inspiration; how could the spirit truly go back on its word? In a mere moment, the wind shifted, and the raft turned to reach the riverbank.
Huang Youliang, a timber merchant, marveled at this and said to his companions, "How extraordinary! When the hall is completed, I shall commission a great Buddha statue to repay [the deity's grace].
In the eighth month of the *Xinwei* year of the *Hongwu* era, the hall was finished. In the twenty-fifth year, the *Ren-shen* year...
The imperial court was conducting a census of monks. The Master led his disciples to the capital to undergo scriptural examinations and request ordination certificates.
At that time, there were more than three thousand śrāmaṇeras among them; many were unable to memorize the scriptures yet wished to seek ordination by deception.

Consequently, the Emperor became enraged and sent them to the Jingwei Guard, where they were all registered as soldiers. The Master, moved by compassion and seeing no way to save them, went to the Fengtian Gate to petition the Emperor.

He wished to cremate his body to seek liberation. The Emperor granted his request. On the twenty-fifth day of the second month, he issued an imperial decree for palace attendants to provide a strict military guard for his reliquary shrine (*kaṅ*).
Upon reaching the Rain Flower Terrace (*Yuhua Tai*), the Master emerged from the shrine, gazed toward the palace, and prostrated in farewell.
He re-entered the shrine and requested paper, writing a verse which said: "Thirty-three years of this illusory body— The nature-fire blazes forth, revealing the Perfected Truth."

"On this day when the Buddha-Dharma flourishes under the Great Ming, may the imperial domain be blessed with ten million springs. He then took another piece of incense and inscribed upon it the four characters "Wind and rain shall be harmonious and favorable.
Addressing the inner ministers, he said, "I trouble you to report to His Majesty that if one prays for rain during a drought using this incense, it will surely be efficacious.
In an instant, he held it to a torch and burned himself; the smoke and flames soared into the air, a wondrous fragrance overwhelmed the senses, and flocks of cranes flew by.

It hovered above the top of the shrine for a long while. Afterward, the remains of the fire yielded an incalculable number of *śarīra*. Thereupon, more than three thousand people were all granted remission of their sins and issued certificates to become monks;
this was entirely due to the Master’s grace. At that time, there was a great drought, and the Emperor summoned the officials of the Office of Buddhist Records (*Senglusi*).
He received the incense left behind by the Master and went to Tianxi Temple, where he led the assembly in prayers for rain, setting a period of three days.
On the night it reached, a heavy rain fell. The Emperor was delighted and said to his ministers, "This is truly the 'Ever-Abundant Rain' (Yonglong).
He personally composed a poem titled "The Wandering Monk" to commemorate this. In the eighth month of that year, the disciples escorted the remains back for burial.
He erected a stupa on Mount Yin.
Xue Mei was a man of unknown origins who resided at Tianxi Temple; he once visited Yuhua Terrace and was by nature unrestrained and unconventional.

Her speech was unrestrained, yet her interpretations of the *Shijing* were refined and extraordinary; people vied with one another to transmit and recite them. Several years later, she walked singing through the marketplace.
She commanded a young boy to surround her and join in a rhythmic song, saying: "Old snow-melting plum, today you do not return; when will you return?
She would then immediately answer herself: "Return, return. After answering this three times, she sat upright and passed away.
**Ming: Zuoyu.** Zuoyu was a man of unknown origins who called himself a disciple of Cizhai Zhou.

He came from Jinling to Yuan’an and practiced *zhan* (seated meditation) at Falin Cave, sitting in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*). His footprints never reached the foot of the mountain, and he also subsisted on water.
He observed the fast, consuming no grain but drinking only water, continuing in this manner for forty-nine days. He followed this as his regular practice every year.

In the fifteenth year of the Chenghua era, Xue Gang, the Vice Commissioner for Education, while touring Yuan’an to supervise studies, arrived at the cave and saw that [the Master] was emaciated and appeared to be ill.
He therefore said to him: "This rocky ridge is remote and secluded; it is not a place where humans dwell. Why have you..."
"Self-inflicted suffering such as this," [the Emperor] said, "cannot lead to the attainment of Perfect Enlightenment. He asked again, "A person dies if they do not eat for seven days.
I have heard that you have been fasting on water for forty-nine days; what technique allows you to do so?
Fayü replied, "I know only how to transmit the teachings of my Master; there is no other technique. However, for the first three or five days, I was scorched by the fire of hunger."

His body was feverish and exhausted; his strength could no longer sustain him. After six or seven days had passed, he drank water that was completely clear and cool, feeling as refreshed as if he had never been ill.
Xue sighed in admiration and departed. In the eighteenth year, Xue visited the cave again and found Shang still unharmed.
He saw that the western railing of the hermitage had been destroyed by a rock fallen from the cliff, located only about ten feet from the meditation hall. Xue questioned him about this.
[The Master] said, "Could you have known beforehand that the rock would fall? And were you not afraid? He replied, "I did not know.
Xue said, "The rock has no eye of wisdom, yet you are not a golden body. If it were to fall again one night, you would surely be reduced to powder.
Sages and worthies who possess the precepts and understand destiny do not stand beneath crumbling walls; you ought to recognize this and be cautious. When encountering even a slight [danger]..."
He smiled but did not answer. On the night of the second day of the fifth month in the twentieth year, a great storm of thunder and rain broke out;
boulders fell chaotically from the cliffs, their sound shaking the earth. He was struck by a falling rock and passed away, having reached only the age of forty. Such was the firmness of his resolve.
He remained thus unchanging until death.
Minghe said, "Whether regarding worldly or world-transcending dharmas, if one’s resolve is such as this, what task will not be accomplished? Life and death are fleeting and illusory;

to those who possess the Way, they are viewed as a play and treated as if they do not exist. Xue spoke these words repeatedly and earnestly. Why? [Because he wished for him to realize that]... (text fragmentary).
It is only natural that when one tells a dream to an awakened person, they would meet it with laughter and remain silent.
Regarding Shanxin:
Shanxin, whose courtesy name was Wuyi, was a son of the Wu family from Jiading, Suzhou. At the age of twenty-nine, he shaved his head and donned the dyed robes of a monk.
The monk was illiterate, yet he devoted himself solely to *dhyāna* and entered Xuangmu Mountain to study under Master Wanfeng.
Suddenly attaining realization, he said to the assembly, "Since I left home to become a monk, my side has never touched the mat; today, at last, my task is complete.
Not long after, he manifested a slight illness. He requested a bath, entered his coffin, and in the space of a finger-snap, flames suddenly erupted, spontaneously cremating him.
This is the body of one who has attained the Way and is eager to enter extinction. Someone praised him with a verse: "A single thought-moment, once empty, and the myriad objects are forgotten;
There is no further matter left to deliberate. Turning over his body, he enters forever the fire-light samādhi; The old Bhaiṣajyarāja on Vulture Peak is startled into a fall.
Leaving saṃsāra only to re-enter it— In the ultimate sense, where has there ever been coming or going? Yesterday...
A flame erupted from within a frozen river at night, burning the void until it was reduced to a single heap of ash.
Da Yun was a native of Xiangyang. Initially, he was a monk at Jixiang Temple in Beijing; he was the younger brother of Daji and possessed a nature that was both quick-witted and grave.
He was proficient in both Buddhist and secular studies and maintained a life of austere discipline according to the Vinaya. During the Jiajing era, he resided at Guangde Temple.

He regulated his own conduct and served the community so impeccably that no one could find fault with him. Once, when two monks were quarreling incessantly, Yun prepared a vegetarian feast for them and mediated their grievances. He then said to them:
"In the past, my elder brother Daji was in the capital. One day, he joined his palms and recited: 'May I be born within the Pure Land of the West;
may the nine grades of lotus flowers be my parents. He then passed away while sitting upright. Now, as I resolve this conflict for you, I shall likewise follow my brother’s example.
Consequently, he sat in the lotus posture, joined his palms, and recited the first two lines. Having finished speaking, he passed away."
Guangyu (廣玉), whose courtesy name was Wuxia (無瑕), was a native of Honglian Chi in Zizhong, Shu. In lay life, he was known as Layman Meng.

Having observed that the phenomena of the world were devoid of permanence, he was moved by this realization and left the household life. Clad in a single robe, he entered Mount Jiufeng; at the highest point of the mountain, he established his dwelling.
At Leiyin Temple, he resided for nine years at Yugusi, practicing asceticism and tranquility until he attained a sudden realization.
In the year Jia-shen of the Wanli era, he suddenly announced to the assembly: "On the seventh day of the third month, this poor monk shall part from you all.
From that time on, he took no food or drink for over twenty days, yet his spirit and vitality flourished even more. Those who prostrated themselves daily to seek his Dharma words [increased].
He would often address several hundred people at once, responding to them all with such warmth and grace that it was like the turning of a wheel or the pouring of water—continuous and uninterrupted.
Those who heard him were without exception moved to deep emotion and resolved to awaken their minds. When the appointed time arrived, he bathed and ascended the seat;

suddenly, the sky grew dark and thunder shook the earth so violently that the roof tiles seemed about to fly away. The assembly cowered in awe, not daring to look up. After a short while, the sun cleared and the weather brightened, whereupon the Master...
With a compassionate voice, he consoled the multitude, saying, "My remains shall be as clear as white wax; place them wherever you wish.
Having spoken these words, he passed away. Initially, his remains were placed in a wooden tub. When it was opened after three months, his countenance appeared as if alive.
The officials and citizens of Peng raised ten thousand catties of copper to construct a stupa and temple at the mountain peak, where they enshrined him with lacquer.

Ningyi also assisted others. Initially, he resided at Sandui Mountain; later, while traveling as a wandering monk, he encountered a spiritual mentor who instructed him to practice the dharma-gate of asceticism.
Consequently, he subsisted on vegetables and beans, sitting upright in meditative refinement. When people mocked him, Ningyi said, "My karmic obscurations are deep and heavy;
it would not do otherwise. After a long time, he attained realization. In the *guwei* year of the Wanli era (1603), he piled up firewood and [prepared for his own end].

He was cremated; as soon as the torch was raised, his body was like a withered stump, consumed in an instant. Those who understood him remarked, "He has entered the *ābhāsvara-samādhi* (Fire-Light Samādhi). Regarding Ye Tai:
Ye Tai was a man from Western Shu who, in his youth, practiced the arts of guiding the breath and abstaining from grain. He encountered Master Dazhi at Mount Emei.

Mí shaved his head and received the precepts. Taking leave of his teacher, he traveled to Zhōngnán and Fówǔ Mountains, and subsequently to Wǔtái, where he mostly subsisted on water and observed the fasts.
By day he sat in meditation; by night he roamed the terraces. People therefore called him "Night Terrace" (Yètái). The Wǔtái range spans five hundred li in circumference;
there, violent winds howl, hurling great boulders and blowing mules and horses away like scattered leaves. The Master wore a robe and cap of *būr* (coarse fiber), and held [a staff] in his hand.

He held an iron staff; when he encountered wind, he would stop, and when the wind ceased, he would proceed. At times, in the pitch-black darkness, he fell into pits and ravines, yet his iron staff would bend down and uncoil itself, and the Master remained unhurt.
When he encountered tigers, he would cast himself toward them and say, "If you devour me, we shall form a small karmic connection.

Once, encountering bandits with mining tools, he shook his monk’s staff until it rang out in a circle; the bandits called out from afar, "The Master of Night Terrace has come; he is awe-inspiring and submissive! and they did not harm him.

He dared not move. A great snowfall covered the mountains; the assembly followed the Master through the snow with their spades, yet he was already stiff and withered, buried up to his waist and knees in the snow.
The assembly carried him back and placed him upon a heated earthen cauldron, pouring hot water over him. After a short while, he revived and again traveled at night as before.
During the night, the Master frequently saw the light of lamps and wild fires, as well as fierce beasts and ghostly apparitions, yet he personally beheld the [Buddha’s] countenance.
Shu [the master] would sometimes appear as an elderly bhikṣu, or as a beautiful woman holding an infant with her lower body bare; in an instant, he would vanish.
He traveled in this manner through the night for over twenty years. In the year of the Water-Rabbit (癸卯), he entered the capital.
Empress Dowager Cisheng bestowed upon him an alms bowl, a staff, and a set of purple-bordered *kāṣāya* robes. Previously, at Tayuan Temple, the Master had established a thousand...
He convened assemblies at Longquan Temple, establishing Dragon Flower (Nāgapuṣpa) assemblies for forty-nine days each.

Furthermore, he cast one "幽冥" (Yǒumíng, "Mysterious Darkness") bell at each of Mount Wǔtái and Mount Éméi, weighing thirteen thousand *jīn*. He also commissioned two sets of the Tripitaka at Mount Púttuó and Mount Éméi.
Moreover, he established a Shuilù (Water and Land) ritual site at Mount Jiǔhuá. As for his remaining wealth in silver and grain, he distributed it as alms to those in seclusion.

As for his quarters and those of the impoverished monks, he did not allow even a grain of weight or an inch of measurement to enter his private purse; thus, over time, both the monastic community (zī) and the laity (sù) came to trust him all the more.
As the Master traveled back and forth among the four great sacred mountains, his physical strength grew frail and exhausted. While traveling from Shu to Guangling, he suddenly fell ill.

The practitioner named [Name] cut off his finger and placed it in porridge, hoping to cure his master’s illness. His master rebuked him, saying, “One who has left the mundane world should not imitate the actions of children and women.
My time is drawing near. At that moment, the illness had already been cured.

He purchased a large vessel and established images for the Water and Land rites, performing the *yankou* (flaming-mouth) ceremony without ceasing. In the tenth month of the Gengxu year, he crossed the sea from Tongzhou and passed Mount Fu, feeling great joy.
However, wishing to remain [there], he first sent away his disciples and kept only the old man of the Way with him.

As they were about to set sail, two merchants from Xinxian earnestly requested to board the boat. The Master said, "These are people with whom I have a karmic connection," and granted their request. He raised the sails and traveled very swiftly.
When it was asked whether it was noon, he replied, "It is noon. He ordered food to be prepared and served the two guests, then took out money for travel expenses and gave it to them.
Having prostrated to the Buddhas of the ten directions, he said, "I wish to return to the sea. The assembly was startled and asked, "We are already in the midst of the sea;

where else is there to return? The Master replied, "I have heard that when the Bodhisattva of Liberation was approaching the end of his life, he instructed his disciples to divide his body into three parts:
one to give to birds and beasts, one to give to fish and turtles, and one to give to ants. I am now doing the same. The assembly was moved to grief.
The master’s sobriquet was "Qianwan" (Tugging and Pulling). He produced a sheet of paper and handed it to the guest; it was the very speech of the Bodhisattva Jie-mo (Goddess of Liberation).
While the assembly continued their mournful tugging and pulling, the master said, "Bow to the Buddha for my sake. They all prostrated themselves. The master leaped once and entered the sea.
When the crowd wished to lower the sails and rescue him, the master sat upright upon the waves and waved his hand, saying, "If you lower the sails even once, you will all be capsized. You must...
Suddenly, a yellow mist enveloped the Master and he departed. This was on the twenty-fifth day of the tenth month in the Gengxu year of the Wanli era.
An old Daoist returned and recounted this to Chen Menghong of Huating, who composed a written record of these events.
Autumn Moon (Qiuyue) was an elderly monk of Xuanmu Mountain in Suzhou. He was refined in the precepts and diligent in ritual worship and recitation.

He performed Buddhist services using tea as an offering. Those who passed by Xuanmu would invariably visit Autumn Moon; however, if they were not men of noble character, Autumn Moon would not grant them an audience, nor would he offer them tea even if they did see him.
At that time, when the periods for Chan meditation and formal lectures were held, people flocked there from all directions in great numbers. The Master—
He remained as tranquil as if he had not heard them. When some urged him to go out once to join in the celebration, he smiled but did not answer.

In the first year of the Tianqi era, he bid farewell to his fellow practitioners in the mountains and set out for the South Sea. As they traveled along the Lotus Ocean, he suddenly rose to the bow of the ship and prostrated himself.

He called out the Buddha’s name in a loud voice and immediately leaped into the water. The crowd rushed forward to pull him back, but it was already too late. At that moment, a great wind and waves arose;

the Master appeared and disappeared amidst the surging billows, yet he continued to join his palms and call upon the Buddha. As the boat gradually drifted further away, he finally vanished from sight.
The commentary says: Yetai traveled to the four great sacred mountains, his footsteps reaching throughout the land;
Qiu Yue quietly closed himself in a single room, knowing nothing of what occurred outside. Throughout their lives, the two masters were as distinct as day and night;
yet regarding that final stroke, there was not the slightest difference between them. This is because Yetai... [preserved in the] Zang [Tripitaka].

The stillness resides within movement; the autumn moon dwells in movement within stillness. Regarding the traces of these two masters—stillness and movement—they have transcended the threshold of life and death without the slightest hindrance.
As for the minds of these two masters, it is truly impossible to judge which is superior or inferior.

Chan Master Hongzhun was a native of Guilin. He had studied under Chan Master Nan for many years. By nature he was pure and sincere; he never...
He was never at odds with others. When he heard of another’s virtue, it was as if it had emerged from within himself; a radiance of joy would well up from between his brows.
When he heard of another’s evil, he would invariably join his palms and strike the air as if in repentance, causing all who saw him to smile.
Yet his sincerity remained thus, consistent from beginning to end. In his later years, he did not take charge of monastic affairs, but resided at Hanxi Temple. He lived to a ripe old age.

He was already over eighty years old. Throughout his life, from morning until night, he had no other concerns; beyond the necessities of sleep and food, he did nothing but chant *brahmā*-sounds and praise Avalokiteśvara.
At the time of his death, while his disciples and followers had all gone to visit the donors, only a single servant remained.
The Master took up his *kṣaṇḍila* and sat before the shrine of the local deity (*sthānapati*), reciting the *Mayūra-vyamsaka-sūtra* once as a final farewell. Then, immediately—
He sat upright with his eyes closed; for three days he did not lean. Villagers who came to observe him stood shoulder-to-shoulder like a wall.
The Master suddenly opened his eyes and smiled, then had them sit on the ground. After a short while, his disciples returned; the Master called them to stand at his right side.

He took their hands in his as if cooking rice for a long time, then gazed at them silently before departing. His countenance remained unchanged, and his cheeks were as rosy as if he were alive. People sculpted his likeness along the roads.
This is prior to the niche of the image.
There was one named Yu An who attained enlightenment by reading the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* with broken phrasing. He was a native of Fuzhou and resided at Shangfang on Mount Ruilü.
His virtue and character were widely renowned, and he was highly revered as a patriarch by those in his region. At the time of his death, he was liberated and composed.

He was with his master as if they were of one hand. One day, as he was about to pass into extinction, he called his disciple Yunren to stand in attendance by his side while the coffin was set down nearby.
He spoke this verse: "It was not carried away from the mountain peak; How could it have been entrusted here from Kukkuṭapāda?"
He followed them into the coffin himself, settling into it with composure and dignity. He instructed Yunren to close and nail the lid.

After three days, his disciples opened the coffin and saw the Master lying on his right side. The assembly was overcome with grief and lamentation. The Master then rose, appearing as if waking from a dream, and ordered the drum to be beaten.
He ascended the hall to preach the Dharma, rebuking them and issuing a warning, saying: "Those who open my coffin again this time are not my disciples. Having said this, he passed away.
He entered his coffin once more and passed away.

As for Dao Guang, the transmitter of the Dharma light: he was a monk who transcribed scriptures at Yongle Temple in Qizhou. Dwelling in a few thatched huts in the mountains with his elder brother, Dao...

He shared his quarters with others; morning incense and evening lamps were lit as he performed the Buddha’s work through meditation and recitation. He drew blood to mix with ink and transcribed all the sutras.
His horizontal and diagonal strokes were as even as rain falling from the sky, and as orderly as fish swimming upstream;

all were achieved through the power of his diligent exertion. Furthermore, he was pure and simple in character, loyal in his duties, and filial in serving his parents, serving as a model for the village.
He was one whom his neighbors revered and trusted, and whom his Dharma-relatives honored and esteemed. All who followed him were as solemn and respectful as if in the presence of the Buddha.
The Venerable Jiyin once visited his hermitage and stayed for several days; there he was able to see all the scriptures he had transcribed, numbering no fewer than ten or more varieties.
He held them upon his head in reverence and joy, praising him as a true bhikṣu, and composed a verse to present to him, which says: [Verse omitted per instructions]
Observe his actions: from morning until night, he engages in dialogue and exchange with the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; how could he possibly harbor any worldly thoughts?
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "To never, in every thought-moment, conjoin with worldly thoughts—this is great diligence. Guang took this as his standard.
Yuan Ru-yi. Biography of Master Ru-yi of Yi-an.
He was a native of Yongjia. Born into the Xuán clan, five days before his birth, his father dreamed that a strange monk arrived carrying a Sanskrit manuscript.
When asked where he had come from, he replied, “From Wuyun. When asked what his surname was, he said, “The surname is Yīn. When asked what his name was, he likewise replied [the same].
His surname was Yin. The man said, "I shall come again in five days; take this Sanskrit manuscript as a token of my pledge.

When the appointed day arrived, the Master was born. His skull was prominently raised, and his gaze pierced others. At the age of fifteen, he attended upon the Elder of Fangshan, shaved his head, and donned the black robes.
He began reciting the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* from memory, but upon reaching the fifth fascicle, he contracted a disease that caused him to vomit blood, whereupon he ceased his recitation.
Upon reciting [the scripture], his illness was swiftly cured. One night, he dreamed that all the scriptures he had not yet recited appeared in the air as large characters written in gold;
he read them aloud with a forceful voice. Upon waking, they still remained before him, only gradually fading after some time. He felt a sense of clarity and coolness in his mind.

Thereafter, whenever he recited, it flowed like a stream, connecting the later parts with the earlier ones, such that he never forgot them for the rest of his life. He then relied upon Master Zhu Yuan to pursue further inquiry.
Regarding the aforementioned matters, although he grasped the essential principles and held the main framework, he did not neglect this scripture. In his later years, he resided at Xijian Hermitage;
he did not concern himself with managing disciples, nor did he strictly refuse those who came to him. He lived in a state of serene detachment, possessing the spirit of Zheng Huangniu.
Xingran’s lineage was Xingran. His courtesy name was Baodeng. He was the son of the Yang family of Dong'e. For generations his family had been farmers. From birth he suffered from many ailments.

At the age of seventeen, he renounced secular life, donned monastic robes, and received the precepts. Possessing keen faculties from an early age, he suddenly gave rise to supreme vows and cultivated the practice of purity, reciting [the scriptures] while kneeling.

For nine years, he devoted himself to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, remaining within his chamber with the door bolted and never venturing out. Later, he suddenly traveled abroad to various regions, visiting Mount Pǔtuó and Mount Wǔtái;

he journeyed south through Wú and Yuè, and reached as far west as Qīn and Lǒng. He left his footprints at every famous mountain and eminent monastery. His practice was refined and austere, and his reputation for spiritual attainment grew increasingly prominent.
Upon returning to his home village, he resided at Xiāngshān Temple, where the temple’s affairs were entirely renewed. At that time, the Prefect, Lord Yīn, paid him three formal visits.

Among all his disciples, he knew that this master was his closest; thus, he served him with ever-increasing reverence. The master built a small pavilion for him as a hermitage, where he took up residence.

Furthermore, he locked the doors and practiced purification even more diligently than before. Chanting the Buddha’s name, whether eating, drinking, waking, or sleeping, he never ceased the sound of his recitation.
Through cold and heat, dusk and dawn, he never once lay upon a pillow. His shadow did not leave the mountains, and his tracks did not enter the secular world, remaining as if—

This was over sixty years ago. Lord Yu was cautious in his conduct and once questioned the Master, saying, "When those above recite the name of Amitābha orally, will they truly be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss?
The Master replied, "Who is Amitābha? What is the Land of Ultimate Bliss? It is my own mind.

If one continues this recitation sound by sound without forgetting it for a moment, the five aggregates will naturally become empty and the six sense faculties will be purified, and the lotus flower will appear."

"The Western Land of Ultimate Bliss is certainly present within a single kṣaṇa; how could it be so remote? Yu was moved by these words and remarked that he possessed a spiritual acuity not found in those who merely labor through arduous practice.
He purchased a plot of land to provide for him. The Master’s physical frame was imposing and his eyebrows were sharply defined.
Though advanced in years—his beard reaching his chin—he moved with a vigorous stride. He constructed a seated niche to the right of his couch and would frequently enter it.
He sat for a short while and smiled. Suddenly, one day, he announced that his end had come. He summoned Master Yin and instructed him on his final affairs.

Thereupon, he prostrated himself, entered the coffin, and passed away while sitting in the lotus position. He was born in the Gengshen year of the Hongzhi era and died in the Guisi year of the Wanli era, at the age of ninety-four.

Puming transmitted [the dharma] to Puming, whose courtesy name was Jizhao. He was a monk of the Jiashan Miaochang Hermitage. Having shaved his head and received full ordination, he recited the Lotus Sūtra daily without ceasing.
He paid no heed whatsoever to the myriad affairs of the world. Entering the mountains of Guhang, he shut himself in his room to engage in recitation and study.
Having finished his recitation, he would simply sit in meditation. Snakes, rats, birds, and small fowl became so familiar with him that they would frolic and play before him by day and by night.

Whenever a guest arrived and knocked at the door, they would all fly or scurry away; those that did not manage to escape, he would immediately take up in his hands and tuck them into his bosom, covering them with his robe.
Once the guest had departed, they would emerge and resume their playful intimacy as before. Once, a sick man came to visit him, and he stroked the man’s head with his hand.

His long-standing ailments were suddenly eliminated, and he consequently entrusted his body to his disciples as their teacher. One day he said to his disciples, "I shall pass away on the eighteenth day of the fifth month.
The disciples replied that the fifth month was not an auspicious time. He said, "In that case, it shall be the eighth month."
Once the date was set, he returned to Jiaxian. When the appointed time arrived, his disciples came to visit him.

Mingfang was sweeping the floor when they spoke with him, and he said to them, "If you had not come, I would have almost forgotten. He ordered the bell to be struck to assemble the congregation and wrote this verse:

"This old man has no schemes or calculations at all; He does not practice Chan, nor does he study the sutras. Throughout his life, he has been clumsy and incapable in everything; Now he hides his traces among the green pines."

At the edge of a cliff, he was as still as a massive boulder or Mount Tai, yet when he moved, he was like the crashing of thunder or a flash of lightning. He cast down his brush, sat upright, and passed away.
Upon cremation, flames of five colors illuminated the heavens, and a wondrous fragrance did not dissipate for several nights. His tongue remained intact; when struck, it produced a sound.

More than ten days after his transformation, people still saw him in ancient Hangzhou. His stillness reached its ultimate limit, his radiance permeated all things, and he possessed mastery over both departure and remaining.
These were also those who attained realization through recitation.
*Supplementary Biographies of Eminent Monks*, Scroll Twenty-one;
*Supplementary Biographies of Eminent Monks*, Scroll Twenty-two.
Written by the Śramaṇa Minghe of Huashan Temple in Wumen during the Ming Dynasty.
The Chapter on Promoting Merit:
The Biography of Master Yong of the Song Dynasty.
Master Yong was a man of unknown origins; he was a successor of Chan Master Fayun Yuantong Xiu.
Having established a karmic connection with the capital, he performed great Buddhist services, and his fame resounded throughout the four quarters. He was granted purple robes and a formal title.

At Tianxi Temple in Jiangning Prefecture, there was formerly a burial site for the true-body *śarīra* relics of Śākyamuni. Later, when the temple fell into ruin, it was restored during the Southern Tang period and again in the Song dynasty.
Initially, the temple was abandoned. During the Xiangfu era, the monk Kezheng submitted a petition and was granted permission to restore it as a monastery.
Kezheng built a pagoda at the very site where the auspicious signs had manifested and was granted the name Shengganshelibota Temple (Holy Response Śarīra Jewel Pagoda Temple).

Situated according to the geomantic features of the mountains and waters, facing south-west with its back to the north-east, it took the Terrace of King Yue as its "mountain" (an). Later, the terrain behind the pagoda sloped downward, and Kezheng’s [design] failed.
In his efforts to adapt to the circumstances, he was unable to construct the intended layout; consequently, he temporarily established a courtyard in the northern corridor as a place to settle monks.

Although the scale was barely sufficient, it was narrow, cramped, and inferior, such that the undertaking failed to meet its purpose and conditions were unfavorable; for this reason, the temple never recovered its former vitality.
In the second year of the Yuánfú era, Lǚ Shēngqīng of Wēnléng, who served as the Prefectural Administrator, remarked, "This is a great monastic community;

it is simply that no one worthy has yet been found to preside over it. He subsequently petitioned the imperial court to change the system to a ten-directional abbotship (shífāng zhùchí), and the request was immediately granted.

He immediately welcomed Master Yong to serve as the first patriarch of the founding of the monastery. Upon entering the temple, Master Yong looked around and sighed, saying, "This is truly a blessed site.
The reason it has not flourished is precisely because its foundation is not upright. He then constructed a terrace of piled earth behind the stupa;
starting from the bottom and ascending, it was accumulated to a height of two zhang and three chi, with a depth of forty chi and a horizontal span of twenty [chi].
The Master was about to construct a Dharma Hall, intending to arrange the positions in their proper order.

Shortly thereafter, the lay devotee Wei Debao of Nanchang, together with his wife, Lady Wang, saw this and said with joy, "Only through such a reorganization will the site's superior geomantic advantages be realized.
Looking at his wife, he said, "If we do not plant blessings in this place, where else shall we go? Thereupon, he alone pledged to build the hall, saying, "I shall not calculate its [costs]..."

The patrons resolved to accomplish this task. The Master immediately gathered materials and mobilized craftsmen; before long, the hall was completed. It was lofty, bright, serene, and deep, where the myriad phenomena seemed to vanish together.
Its scale was vast, its beauty magnificent, and it became the preeminent monastic center in the region. Looking down upon the former site, it was no different from before.

He illuminated what was hidden and shattered the darkness, as if emerging from beyond the clouds and mists. For the common tiles, brickwork, lacquer, and painting, he expended a total of five million coins.
Master Yong further constructed a dormitory and a *abbot’s quarters*, exhausting all the increased depth of the site and providing the necessary resources for their construction.

He also built a monks’ hall, a kitchen, and a storehouse, and moved the Tripitaka from the old temple so that it could be displayed according to its proper orientation, each element finding its correct place in a brilliant splendor.
It was entirely renewed; it was truly a great monastic center (mahāvihāra). On another occasion, when Debao arrived once more, he leaped for joy and praised him, saying:
"If it were not for the Master’s penetrating insight and transcendent power of the Way, nothing could have been undertaken.

And if it were not for my own faith and initiative in commencing the work, how could the various conditions have converged? He then invited the assembly of monks to recite the Great Canon and perform the Water and Land (shuilu) ritual feast.
The project was completed. He further said, "Now that the monastic community has been newly established, there will likely be between five and six hundred people.
How will we provide for their morning and evening meals? Yong replied, "That depends on you. Debao said, "I request that you grant me land to establish an estate for the Master."
He purchased Luzhou and collected its revenue to provide for the monastery's needs. Master Yong said, "If you truly have such a vow, then your merit shall be perfected.
From that time on, the community had a regular supply of food, and the mountain gate relied upon it. The Master’s final whereabouts were unknown.
Minghe said: "Who is this 'Virtue-Treasure' (Debao)? He is able to empty his chest and overturn his bag for the sake of Buddhist practice.

Whether it be plucking out his hair or spitting out his saliva, he does so with such detachment that it is as if it were nothing to him. Although he manifests these physical signs to stir the minds of others, they are nonetheless the result of Master Yong’s own virtue and realization;
thus, there was a reason for his inspiration. Employing a mind of empty tranquility for the sake of liberation, he fundamentally has nothing to relinquish."
The Master, too, did not accept it; on the contrary, he remarked that for a man of such family background to sink into the sea was a matter of great regret.

His precious virtue and lofty character can still be envisioned. Yet, to say that Master Yong saw through Yuan Tong implies that his single move during the Tianxi era was merely a performance put on for the occasion.
Observing his actual deeds now, one finds no trace of what he claimed—this truly belies Yong’s own intentions.
Zhaojue Yanmei was the dharma heir of Master Yong'an Deuan.

He was the son of the Du family of Pingquan in Yang’an Prefecture. Having left the household life, he received full ordination under Vinaya Master Yantong, at whose seat Zhaojue had previously studied.
Later, due to his spiritual conduct, he was appointed as the abbot. He regarded Grand Master Liaojue as his fifth [predecessor].
The founding patriarch was Liaojue, styled Xiūmèng. He studied under the various elders of Shishuang and Dongshan and attained a profound mastery of the essential teachings of Chan.

He was the very person who, during the reign of Emperor Xuānzōng’s restoration of the Buddhist teachings, received the imperial edict to shave his head before the throne. Later, he extensively propagated the Dharma at Zhaojue; the Master was a distant descendant of him.
Not only was he able to succeed to his master’s spiritual lineage, but he also extensively expanded the temple buildings of Fuye Temple.
While they were originally one hundred rooms, the Master increased them to three hundred. He renovated the hall for chanting the *Brahma* hymns and enlarged the abbot’s quarters.

He prepared the rituals for the *Shuilu* (Water-Land) assembly and established separate halls for the Arhats, the Sixth Patriarch, the *Yixian* (Assisting Goodness), and the *Dabei* (Great Compassion) Bodhisattva, each with its own section, further dividing them into a thousand units.
He constructed a hall for the *sūtras* to serve as the eastern and western niches, and further established a Hall of the Constellations and Planets, which was exceedingly magnificent.
He ensured that everything was fully provided, from the lodgings for the monastic community to the public kitchen, storehouses, offices, granaries, the dining hall, and the bathhouse.

The old site of the temple had been overgrown with weeds for a hundred years amidst crumbling walls; yet, in a single day, the Master raised the foundations and corded them together, mobilizing hundreds of laborers to restore it.

He repaired the old buildings, constructing over five hundred rooms and surrounding them with gardens and orchards. The neighboring residents, out of reverence for the Master’s virtue, yielded to one another in the hope of being first to offer their assistance.
From then on, when thousands gathered for the morning meal, they sat upon layered cushions as if entering an empty city;

not a single item was required that had to be sought from outside. People said of him: "The Master opens his mouth without employing deliberate means of transformation; he speaks not, yet the sea gulls gather."
He was easygoing, possessing a humble and open mind that responded skillfully to others; like a valley, he remained full even without seeking.

From the Wushen year of the Dazhongxiangfu era until more than thirty years had passed, his diet never included more than one flavor and his clothing no more than a single layer of silk; he lived with such simplicity and detachment.
At that same time, there was one named Deyuan, who was also refined in his religious practice.

He greatly expanded the Yongan Chan Monastery and invited Master Qin to serve as its abbot, so that the teachings and traditions might be propagated for the benefit of all. He exhorted his disciples, saying: "Exalt this precious monastery."

This is truly dependent upon the collective resources of many; it is fitting that those who come here should dwell here whenever conditions converge. Moreover, formation and destruction alternate in succession; like bubbles and illusions, things easily perish.

All conditioned phenomena are forgotten; how long is this floating life? Objects are merely given provisional names—how could they ever have a fixed master? Hereafter, my dharma-heirs should extinguish all divergent thoughts.
Do not follow private interests; do not harbor discrimination. Unite only through the Dharma; do not engage in contention or encroachment. May there be...

To violate this oath is to surely suffer secret execution. Pensioner for the Hanlin Academy Peng Cheng praised him, saying: "The Chan Master traveled far and wide with his single staff; he attained clear understanding through half a verse.
His mirror was free from the need for polishing; his banner was left to flutter as it pleased. He trod the broad highway of the Deer Park and followed the tracks beyond Tiger Creek.
His Way existed through prior awakening, and those who sought refuge in him arrived like radiant clouds. His words conformed to the Mahāyāna."
Visitors were satiated with the nectar [of his teachings]. Had it not been for his long-accumulated practice and the overflowing renown of his fame and virtue, how could he have deserved this?
—From the *Tiqian zhuan* (Biography of Tiqian).
Tiqian was a native of Yongjia. He was a monk of ascetic practice who disregarded his physical appearance and endured hunger and cold. He delighted in performing difficult tasks.

He entered Mount Lu to dwell in seclusion, where for several years he practiced "sword-plowing" and "fire-seeding. Later, he descended from the mountain to wander as a cloud-dweller and arrived at Junzhou.

There, the local faithful crowded around him, detaining him and saying, "Where will the Master go? This great karmic connection in Xinjie depends solely upon you, O Sage. Your holy mouth is like wood..."
"The tongue is the aspiration of sentient beings. The Master joyfully accepted the command, saying, "This is my task.

From a certain year he began the solicitation, and by a certain year the work was completed, whereby the New Street of Jūngzhou was established. He operated with a mind like empty space and performed deeds of extreme hardship and difficulty.
His virtue moved others as if summoned, and conditions returned like echoes. In total, he solicited one [unit] of gold and silver coins.
Ten million [workers] were summoned to quarry stone and kiln-bake brick; several tens of millions of these were obtained.

They were laid to form a great road that cuts northward to the river, while to the south and west it winds around the marketplaces for a total of several tens of thousands of *chi*. There are also horizontal channels and underground conduits.

Bridges were constructed to connect them, numbering several dozen. Among those gentlemen who joyfully made offerings, calculating by the length of the roads, they ranged from five hundred feet down to one hundred feet, totaling several dozen individuals.
Calculating by the amount of money, it ranged from three hundred thousand coins down to ten thousand, totaling several dozen individuals;
those below ten thousand are beyond counting. Not a single hair’s breadth of the funds obtained was kept for private use.

All funds were deposited in the treasury of a certain family; all expenditures and revenues were managed entirely by that family. Wearing hempen robes and grass sandals, he supervised the heavy labor.
At night he stayed in a甄 (Zhēn) shed, and when hungry, he ate at the homes of donors.

When Lord Yú Xiāng was on a southern campaign, he encountered the master at the head of his troops and recorded these events, saying: "That superior man wore tattered clothes and coarse food, making his ascetic practices his own hardship."
Beyond its own benefit, it can further inspire faith and unity of mind to achieve this welfare.
It enables those who frequent government offices or roam the marketplaces to emerge from the mire and enter the realm of purity. This is truly the service of the Buddha;
it encourages the practice of the precepts and a fondness for skillful means. To record this, I offer words free from shame.
Biography of Master Kongyin Shi.
Shi, whose courtesy name was Kongyin, received the Dharma from Fazhen of Wujiang. He was the fourth-generation descendant of Tiandi Huai.
He preached the Dharma at the foot of Mount Lu, and students flocked to him like clouds. [He served as abbot of] Miyin Chan Temple on Mount Wei and Dayuan Yu...

The Patriarch’s site where the Dharma was first opened is the preeminent monastery of the southern realm. In the third year of the Chongning era, it was destroyed by fire and reduced to ashes in a single night.

As the scale of the temple was vast and grand, the Governor of Tan, Lord Zeng Xiaoyun, consulted with the assembly, concluding that none but a world-renowned great master, fully endowed with both merit and wisdom, could shoulder such a task. "Is not Master Shi the one for this? he asked. At that time—
It was so. He received him with the fullness of ritual propriety. The Master, too, was moved by a sense of urgency and took the restoration as his own responsibility.

He expanded the foundations and structures, renovating them so that their magnificence matched the mountain’s majesty and depth. He cast a bronze bell weighing ten thousand *jin* and coated it with gold.

He established the Great Dharma-Treasury Hall (*Dafabaozang Dian*) to enshrine the words of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. Furthermore, in the following year, he expanded the Good... (or *Shan* Monastery).
Behind the Dharma Hall is the Rain of Flowers Hall (Huayu Tang). It is empty and luminous when inhaling the breeze, and vast and profound when exhaling the moonlight.

To the left of the two corridors, it is encircled by secondary buildings; there, the storehouse courtyard is established and the hall administration office is built. The monks' hall is extensively renovated, saying:

"That which is increased is the field of merit for humans and devas, the ground for the causal stage of Buddhas and Patriarchs—this is what people see. As for the remote wilderness and deep mountains, this is where the sages [dwell]."
The site of the Way is maintained by Arhats and is invisible to ordinary people. Since he has already extensively expanded what can be seen, how could he not revere that which remains unseen?
Furthermore, he carved images of five hundred venerable ones, enshrined them in a pavilion, and made offerings to them.
Another year passed, and he found a marvelous tree in a remote ravine; it was as thick as a man’s embrace and twice the length of a fathom. He cut it down...

There were three [sections]: he carved images of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the Pure Land, rendered with exquisite beauty. He established a hall to the south of the kitchen for offerings to the deities.
Furthermore, he specially constructed a pavilion in front of his private quarters to enshrine the imperial calligraphy bestowed by Emperor Shenzong.

When the pavilion was completed, it leaned toward the southeast. The Master calculated silently, saying, "Even ten thousand oxen could not pull it back. Furthermore, this is where the Imperial Edict and divine calligraphy reside;
it is the proper place for the Mountain Lord and Water King to dwell. To carefully enshrine and protect them is my duty;

if I fail to perform my office now, it would be a disgrace to the spirits. As soon as he finished speaking, wind and rain battered the building and the mountains shook. In an instant, the pavilion stood upright.
Ten thousand people raised their voices in unison. Another year passed, and the Great Triple Gate was reconstructed. The Grand Preceptor, the Duke of Chu, inscribed its nameplate.
Looking out toward the strategic landscape, the various peaks appeared as if coming to pay court; a terrace presented itself naturally before them.

Within this terrace, he enshrined the precious *dantadhātu* (sacred tooth) relic, and constructed a pagoda above it—nine stories high and one thousand feet tall, towering and brushing against the clouds and mist. All...
Everywhere, stupas for collective interment were erected facing the monasteries, at a distance no greater than the range of a cow’s lowing. Only at Mt.
Mui did the proponents of yin-yang theory insist that a burial site should not be too close to a temple;

thus, from the founding of the mountain until the present three hundred years, the stupa was built south of Huixin Bridge, ten *li* from the temple. Because of this distance, the presiding authorities [there]—
In some cases, one may be unable to attend in person. The Master said: "Regardless of whether a matter is great or small, it must be decided according to principle;
compliance or refusal cannot be handled with negligence. When a monk was cremated, the entire assembly attended together. This is because the injunctions of the former sages must not be violated.

As for the arrival of calamity or fortune, one should respond by avoiding or pursuing them through wisdom; one must not follow blindly. Consequently, he constructed a universal stupa to the west of the temple and roofed it over.
Furthermore, he renovated the Great Perfect Ancestor Pagoda and erected two pavilions to shelter its ancient and modern inscriptions.

The fields of the Sacred Stream Estate (*Seonggye-ji*) had been swallowed up by neighboring lands for several generations and nearly a century; no one dared to protest. The Master said, "To return [land] without asserting what is right is to lead a person into hell.
He dispatched his administrative officials to hold the title deeds as evidence, and the various authorities eventually restored two hundred *mun* of land.

Mu. There was a monk who was the abbot of Yuzquan; he died at Longya Mountain. The people of the mountain would not allow him to be buried there, so his disciples carried his remains to a stone site and wept.
The Master took pity on them and ordered that a plot be chosen at Weishan to construct a tomb and stupa. The monastic community approved of this.
The excellence of the Master’s hidden conduct and subtle application was frequently manifested in his acts of bestowing and withholding; yet all were rooted in benevolence.

Both monastics and laypeople were transformed by his virtue. In the sixth year of the Zhenghe era, an imperial edict appointed him to reside at Mount Jiao in Zhunjun. The Master’s sincere intention was not to go east;

he resigned from his position as abbot and earnestly declined the appointment, returning to his hermitage on the Luan River. Shortly thereafter, an imperial decree permitted him to return to Mount Mui.
From the time of his initial arrival until his final departure, eight years had passed, during which all neglected affairs were fully restored. It was no small feat.
Riding upon the power of his vows, how did he attain this? The Way of Xuedou and Tianyi reached its great zenith under this Master;
the monastic communities turned their hearts toward him. His restorations and constructions were merely his playful pastimes.
The Biography of Chan Master Haizhi of Yue-lu.
He was the son of the Wan family of Watai in Jizhou. From childhood, he was serene and focused, possessing no affinity for worldly tastes.

He left home to become a disciple of Master Jin and received full ordination before traveling to study under various masters. He relied upon Masters Donglin and Yujian for the longest period, yet he attained no realization.
Wu arrived at Yangshan later in life and remained submerged among the masses. Only Master Foyin Yuan regarded him as extraordinary.

At that time, the Master was intent on his studies and took pleasure in calligraphy and painting. Yuan rebuked him, saying, "Your original purpose is to practice the Way; why instead occupy yourself with words and brushstrokes?

Even if you were to master words and brushstrokes, what benefit would that bring to the Way? Moreover, you have not yet mastered them. Thereupon, the Master abandoned these pursuits and went into retreat at Xiang.
In the south, at Zhushan, he relied upon Dayi for ten years. The style of his teaching regarding the gate of *tathatā* (Suchness) was renowned for being as steep as a vertical cliff;

students all retreated upon seeing the precipice, yet the Master alone received his seal of approval (*kṣānti*). When Tathatā went by imperial decree to reside at Xiangguo Temple in the capital, [the Master] followed him there.
The Master’s natural inclination was not to travel west; he led the assembly of monks at Huayao Mountain in Hengyang, where he shared the teaching seat and expounded the Dharma.

In the Jīmūna year (1099) of the Yuánfú era, he began his formal dharma-transmission at Dōngmíng to the east of the city. Shortly thereafter, he moved to Yùlù on the western outskirts of the city. Not long after that—
The foot of the mountain suffered from a fire, which reduced everything to ashes in a single night. Both monastics and laypeople were struck with awe and lamented his death.
The Master smiled and said, "The formation and destruction of dreams and illusions are all but a play. Yet, by relying on the power of my vows, this temple shall not be utterly abandoned.
Thereupon, he built a hut in the forest and dwelt there alone. Together with his servants and laborers, he transported bricks and rubble, and gathered the remaining timber from the ashes.
He constructed beds, couches, floorboards, and lattices; indeed, all the utensils and implements appropriate for a monastic community were fully prepared.

He said, "The buildings have been completed, yet the lack of necessary implements is my concern; therefore, I have prepared these first. Those who heard this departed with secret laughter, but the Master remained as he was.
Before many months had passed, the wealthy offered gold and silk, the poor offered their labor, and the craftsmen offered their skill.

Through ten years of giving, the grand hall was completed. With its terraces perched upon cliffs supported by ten thousand pillars, its soaring columns and tiered galleries gilded with gold and interspersed with azure tiles, it was as if the palaces of Śakra, Brahmā, the Nāgas, and the Devas had been miraculously manifested.
To the people, they saw only the ever-renewing progress of its construction.

Yet it was unknown that this had emerged from his leisurely conversations and laughter. On the ninth day of the seventh month in the Jihai year of the Xuanhua era, he entrusted his lifelong ritual implements to his attendant and ordered him to assemble the community for an auction.
At dawn, having finished rinsing his mouth and washing his face, he sat in his chamber. Upon hearing the signal drum for the morning gruel, he summoned his disciples;
thereupon, he recounted the origins and history of his monastic life and exhorted them to propagate the Way without ceasing. He then recited a verse:

To distinguish him from others, there was one named Zhixian who stepped forward and said, "Master, could you not stay for just a little longer? The Master shook his hand to dismiss him, then cast a glance around him left and right.
After a long while, he passed away reclining on his right side. He had lived for sixty-two years and spent forty-two summers in meditation.
His stupa was erected at the foot of Shuntang on the western slope.
Chan Master Mingda (Liaoming) was a native of Xiuzhou. He was a "dragon or elephant" among the disciples of Miaoxi, known throughout the monastic community as Chan Master Mingda.
He stood eight feet tall with a girth of ten spans; wherever he went, people would inevitably gather to gaze upon him. When Miaoxi was first exiled to Meizhou...
The provincial and county authorities provided extremely strict escort; some even believed the disaster might be unforeseen.

The Master carried the cangue upon his shoulder as he traveled through the rugged terrain, enduring hardships without the slightest negligence. Once he arrived at his place of exile, disciples followed him, and those who came to inquire about the Way numbered no fewer than two or three hundred.
Because provisions for meals were insufficient and fearing further calamity, Miaoxi once urged them to depart.
The Master would invariably refuse, taking it upon himself to provide the vegetarian meals and gruel. He would often carry a *kaolao* (a large woven basket) on his shoulder to beg for alms;

by evening, dozens of people would be carrying back rice, flour, firewood, vegetables, and other provisions for food and drink, returning in a long procession. Although there were many disciples, [the Master remained steadfast].
There was nothing that was not fully provided for. In this manner, seventeen years passed as if they were a single day.

The flourishing of Miaoxi’s Dharma lineage—such that those he received while in exile accounted for half of his disciples—was due to the Master's efforts. When Miaoxi was granted imperial permission to resume his monastic robes and live at his own convenience, [the Master continued his service].

Subsequently, he received an imperial decree to go to Yuyang Monastery. The Master had previously been among the disciples under [Wuzu] Fayan. By nature, the Master was bold and unrestrained, possessing a sharp and swift faculty of response.
In Miaoxi’s quarters, he did not permit his monks to utter the "shout" (*he*). Whenever the Master entered the room, he would invariably let out a loud shout before withdrawing.
One day, Miaoxi posted a notice in front of the abbot’s quarters stating: "Those who utter the shout shall be fined one *guan*. When the Master saw this, he...
He then secretly placed a thousand coins in his sleeve and went into the hall. He first set them down on the floor, let out a loud shout, and then departed.
He did this several times, and Miaoxi could do nothing about it. A notice was posted again, stating:
"Those who shout 'down' shall be fined one portion of the day's hall provisions. When the Master saw this, he immediately hurried to the storehouse and said, "The Abbot wants ten [coins]."
The two gold coins were given to him without hesitation by the administrator. The Master then sent an attendant to follow him to the Abbot’s quarters.
Upon entering, the Master tucked the coins under his arm and set them down on the floor, letting out a loud shout. Miyō was greatly startled;
when the session in the room concluded, he asked calmly what had happened and learned the truth. He laughed and said to the Master each time, "You fat fellow! To understand Zen in such a manner!"
It was not until the year of the donkey that he even dreamed of such a thing. Nevertheless, mindful of his long-standing diligence, [the Emperor] appointed him to reside at Toudi in Shuzhou.
Previously, the cattle on the various estates of Toudi had suffered from an epidemic and nearly all had perished; furthermore, harvests for several years had been poor.

By the power of his great vows, the Master transformed two hundred oxen and brought them there to replenish the herd. Consequently, for several consecutive years, the harvests were exceptionally bountiful, more than double what they had been before.
He performed many extraordinary deeds. When he moved to reside at Changlu, disciples gathered there like spokes converging on a hub, and the monastic community was transformed.

When Miaoxi resided at Jingshan, the Master came to provide offerings and to feed the great assembly. Upon his return to Changlu, Miaoxi sent him off with a verse, which said: [Verse omitted as per instructions]
People say that filial sons emerge from the tip of the staff; I say it is out of love for one’s child that one fails to notice their ugliness.
When the Elder Changlu comes forth in this manner, Miaoxi has needlessly exhausted his mouth. Let the four seas spread these false rumors at will; even a jackal can let out a lion’s roar.
Who says there is nothing to present as a gift for your journey? With a shout, the Iron Ring Mountains run backward! Later, he was summoned by imperial decree to reside [at a monastery].

At Jingshan, his reputation for the Way grew even more prominent. Previously, Prince Yanghuo had dreamed of an extraordinary monk who was tall and large-bellied, walking slowly, saying he wished to convert a manor in Suzhou.
Upon waking, he found it strange but did not speak of it. The following day, the Master suddenly arrived on foot, carrying his staff and sandals.
The gatekeeper scolded him and would not let him pass, so he reported this to the Prince. The Prince went out to see him; from afar, he gazed upon the Master.
It was magnificent, no different from what he had seen in his dream. He immediately called his attendants to come out and view it.
The attendants all lit incense and paid their respects. After tea, the Master spoke first: "Your Majesty possesses vast estates;

you might grant one estate in Suzhou to provide for the worship of the Buddha and the feeding of monks at Mount Jing, which would be of inexhaustible benefit. King Wang had not yet given his decision when—
He was ordered to prepare a vegetarian feast for a single person. Once the master had finished his meal, he departed immediately without saying another word.

At that time, people both inside and outside the palace were in an uproar, spreading the word that the Prince of Wang had donated a manor in Suzhou to the Elder of Mount Jing. This eventually reached the ears of Emperor Xiaozong. It so happened that the Prince of Wang was entering the imperial court.
The Emperor spoke on his behalf. Upon hearing that the Minister had donated a manor in Suzhou to Mount Jing, the Emperor declared, "I shall remit the taxes for it.
Wang Hui expressed his gratitude and returned home. On the following day, he sent a letter to Mount Jing, requesting the Master to enter the city. Two days prior to this...
He had already passed away previously. From then on, whenever Prince Wang was at leisure and fell asleep, whether for a moment or when his eyes grew heavy, he would see the Master before him.
The Master would say, "Among the six perfections, the perfection of giving comes first. To begin well and end well—this is the ultimate.
Thereupon, Prince Wang donated his estate to Jing Mountain Monastery; this estate yielded one hundred thousand [units] annually, including plow oxen and boats.
His carriage was for the use of the treasury; all necessities were fully provided. The Master had a great affinity with both monastics and laypeople;

wherever he stayed, offerings poured in like clouds, and monks gathered there in great numbers. His Buddhist activities were so extraordinary that throughout Jiangxi, Zhejiang, and the two lakes, everyone proclaimed him to be the rebirth of the Bagua Monk.
The Biography of Master Xueting Yu of the Yuan Dynasty:
Master Yu, whose courtesy name was Haowen, was popularly known as Xueting (Snow Court). He was born into the Zhang clan of Wenshui in Dali.

At the age of nine, he could recite a thousand words daily. As he grew older, he encountered the upheavals of his time and was left solitary and without support. On the road, he met an elderly bhikṣu who exhorted him...
He was studying Buddhism and said, "It would suffice if one could merely recite the Lotus Sūtra. The Master asked, "Is the Buddha-dharma limited to this?
The old bhikṣu marveled at this and, taking him along, went to visit the Ancient Buddha of Xianyan, saying, "This man is of the lineage of dragons and elephants; he is destined to be a great vessel.

He immediately performed the ritual for ordination and the reception of the full precepts for him. Together with Guang of Shuangxi, he served as an attendant. Later, they traveled to Yan, where he relied upon Wansong.

The Elder was the most senior; his reputation and brilliance rose majestically, and students flocked to him. While the Emperor Shizu was still in the palace of his private residence, he summoned the Master to Shaolin to preside over a *zijie* (precept-receiving) assembly.
Shortly thereafter, he was again summoned by Emperor Taizong to reside at Helin. This was the Xingguo era, the *xinhai* year.
Emperor Xianzong summoned him to the temporary capital at Beiting, where he consulted him on the Way for many months; his words were concise and pleased the Emperor’s heart.
Upon the accession of Emperor Shizu, he was charged with overseeing all matters of the monastic community and was granted the title Guangzong Zhengfa (The Light of the Orthodox Dharma).

For his teacher, he constructed a vihāra in his native village called Ba’en (Gratitude), to which he granted land and property and appointed monks to maintain it. In the spring of the eighth year of Zhizheng, an imperial edict was issued to all Buddhist [monks] throughout the realm...

The Master was summoned to the capital for a grand assembly. His followers constituted one-third of the total congregation; they were so numerous and dignified that they were a magnificent sight to behold. The Emperor was greatly pleased.

At that time, the seat at Shaolin was vacant, and Wansong Haiyun requested the Master on his behalf. The Emperor looked at the Master and said, "In the past, you presided over the *zijie* (provisional ordination) assembly;

thus, there is a karmic affinity between us. I trouble you to lead the assembly on this journey. This occurred during the period following the ignominious destruction of Shaolin. The Master maintained a solemn and dignified demeanor.
Those who approached him flocked to him as if returning home; those who were delighted gave alms as if from a gushing spring.

The various monasteries of Mount Songyang were newly adorned in gold and green, and the sutra assemblies at Baima Monastery in Luoyang continued without interruption—all through the Master’s efforts. Yet when the Master sat in meditation with eyes closed, he appeared as if he had no part in it.
His character was broad and level, his demeanor calm and detached. For over thirty years he preached the Dharma, sounding like a drum.

Like thunder and lightning, he revealed the sun and moon; following in the footsteps of former sages, he set a standard for later students. He possessed the refined legacy of the ancient masters of wisdom.

As a dried-up pond sprang forth a spring and an ancient hall was restored to its luster, auspicious omens appeared repeatedly; yet the Master forbade others from speaking of them. At a certain time, he entered *nirvāṇa*.

At the beginning of Emperor Renzong’s reign, the Master was posthumously honored with the title of Minister of Works (*Sikong*), Grand Master for Ceremonial Rank Equal to the State Councilor (*Kaifu Yitongsi*). [He was] posthumously...
He was enfeoffed as the Duke of Jinguo. Furthermore, he commanded a court scholar to compose a commemorative inscription for his stupa. The Emperor issued an edict, saying:

"The Emperor reverently reflects that our Great Ancestor possessed divine prowess yet refrained from killing; he rooted himself in benevolence and modeled himself on righteousness to unify the realm under heaven. I desire to manifest my ancestor’s virtue."

To maintain fullness and preserve what has been achieved—this you alone are capable of inheriting. Thus, our First Ancestor will forever respond to your benevolence, thereby extending great salvation to my myriad people.
Looking back, the former sages have passed away; I am unable to see them here now, and they are far removed from us.

Although their coming and going are like dreams and illusions, beyond the reach of names, does the honor of posthumous titles and the glory of mourning not rest with me? Therefore, I shall exalt your office and augment your rank.
Entrusting this to posterity, it shall serve as an instruction for future generations and ensure eternal renown for ten thousand ages.
Thus did the sovereign of the time offer his long-lasting lamentations in remembrance.
This concludes the "Biography of Ming Zhengying."
Zhengying, styled Jie’an, was the son of the Hong family of Jinxi in Fuzhou. Having taken the tonsure in his youth, he was naturally brilliant and insightful, never acting recklessly.
As a great monk, he received full ordination at Zhaokong Temple in Hangzhou during the time of Chan Master Xunzhong.
He preached the Way at Linggu Monastery. The Master went there to visit him; his brilliance eclipsed the entire assembly, and they immediately reached a profound accord.

He was bestowed the Dharma as a true son and served as the head attendant, occupying that position without hesitation. During the Hongwu era, he received an imperial decree to take charge of Tiantai Monastery in the capital.

He did not provide bedding or curtains, remaining content with a single robe even in the cold. When the Emperor heard of this, he praised him and issued a new command for him to take charge [of another monastery].

The Kaiyuan Temple in Quanzhou. Its former name was Lianhua Temple. Since the founding by Great Master Kuanghu of the Tang dynasty, there has never been a lack of eminent monks throughout the generations.
Recently, however, due to the disturbances of the late Yuan period, successive calamities and fires broke out, [destroying] the dwellings of the monastics.
"Nothing shall be spared; let it be reported to the authorities, and thus this decree is issued. The August Founder, the Emperor, personally instructed that you be sent, saying:
'Go and serve as abbot. Today, being an abbot is difficult: if you are too lenient, you will be subjected to insults and fail to sustain the community;
if you are too strict, you will incur slander and bring ruin upon yourself. You need only purify your mind and cleanse yourself; remain reverent for a long time.'"

He was able to rectify the collapsing order himself and illuminate his ancestral seat. The Master received the imperial decree with the utmost reverence and presided over the temple to propagate the teachings.

Before long, the profound influence of the Dharma flourished greatly. He first constructed a lecture hall, inscribing its plaque with the words "Purifying the Mind and Cleansing the Self" to demonstrate that he would never forget his origins.
Next, the Amṛta Precept Platform was constructed before the Hall of Purified Self. This was intended to ensure that the arising of concentration and wisdom must be rooted in the precepts;

thus, it was considered a matter of primary importance. Once the two [platforms] were completed, all the laborers worked together, and there was no need to trouble others by soliciting public assistance.
Within a few years, they had been resplendently renovated, surpassing their former state. In the second year of the Yongle era, [he] respectfully...
An imperial edict appointed [Zhang] as the abbot of Chongsheng Temple on Mount Xuefeng, honoring the completion of its construction during the Kaiyuan era.

Chongsheng was the site of the Dharma-seat of the Patriarch Zhiju (Zhengjue). When Zhiju passed away, he left a prophecy, saying: "The stone pagoda will crack like an egg; the pine branches will sweep the ground; and bamboo shoots will sprout."

"Five hundred years hence, I shall return. It was exactly five hundred and two years since the Master ascended the mountain; thus, all the prophecies were fulfilled as if matching the notches of tally-sticks.
Moreover, the Master’s countenance was no different from that of the True Awakened One (Bodhidharma). Consequently, people all considered him to be the Patriarch returned once more.
The Master became even more diligent and courageous in his pursuit of the Way and its Virtue; his sincerity moved others so profoundly that he transformed them without even speaking.
During the autumn of Xuefeng’s decline, grain was accumulated in the granaries and timber was felled from the mountains. Tiles and bricks were fired to store for ritual implements;
once the Buddha Hall had fallen into ruin, the Dharma Hall and the three gates all collapsed. These were then reconstructed one after another, all vast, magnificent, and grand.

The statues were dignified and solemn, their gold and green glazes shining with brilliance. Those who came to gaze upon and prostrate before them rejoiced and offered praise, while those who looked on stared in awe.
His eyes were startled and his heart was moved, as if boundless forms and appearances had surged forth from the earth in the mere blink of an eye, leaving one with no time to respond.
Yet the Master gazed at them as if they were nothing and remained amidst them as if they were empty; thus, one can know the man he was.
