The Master was strict and rigorous in his observance of the precepts, regarding them as his primary concern. Once, while observing the summer retreat at Phoenix Mountain in Jianyang, he encountered a great flood;
by means of reciting the *Prātimokṣa*, he saved over a thousand men and women. While traveling through Ouning, he established Jinshan Hermitage and attracted a following of five hundred disciples.
As his years drew near to their end, like the setting sun, the Master wished to retire to Linggu Monastery, and accordingly sent a formal notification to the Registrar of Monks.
The Monastic Registrar reported this to the throne, and permission was granted. His disciple Yuanzhi succeeded him in presiding over the Dharma seat at Xuefeng. Zhi’s style name was Qiuyi.
After the Master returned to the capital, he passed away several years later. Among his writings is the *Jie’an Yulu* (Recorded Sayings of Jie’an).
The Biography of Upāsaka Xu:
Upāsaka Xu, named Kaile, was a native of Qingpu Qi. He had formerly been a fisherman on the sea. At times, there were those who committed robbery upon the fishing boats;

some even claimed that Kaile was among them. Upon hearing this, he was filled with intense indignation and subsequently shaved his head to become a monk, thereby adopting the surname [of his new order].
Xu. People called him Master Xu. Morning and evening he prostrated before the Buddha; a square inch or so rose indistinctly upon his forehead, appearing like a suspended pearl.
His speech was gentle and warm as he exhorted others to do good. At that time, the mountains and rivers were causing havoc;

he opened a path at Shajiao and leveled the bridge at Pingdong to diminish the force of the waters. He further paved Denggong Bridge. Once these great public works had commenced, the expenses required...
The situation was precarious. The public was filled with anxiety and consulted one another. "Master Xu is a man of cultivation whom all respect;

if we can get him to speak out once, the matter will be settled. We only fear that he may not consent. Hui-kai heard this and said, "If there is benefit to be gained, there is nothing that should not be undertaken.
What harm could there be in my humble service? He immediately acted as a wooden clapper, chanting the Buddha's name throughout the village. Within a few days, people flocked there like clouds.
The rains gathered. The wealthy contributed their wealth; the poor offered their labor. Before a month had passed, the bridge was completed.
The local villagers then wished to build a dragon palace, but considering the mountain’s height and the distance of the stone quarries, they found that transporting materials would be inconvenient.
They again sought the counsel of Master Xu Kai, who did not decline. He undertook the project’s management; looking about, he saw only a massive rock nearby. The Master gazed at it but said nothing.
Suddenly, an old man with white hair appeared before them and said, "Carve this stone, and it will suffice to complete the palace.
Having finished speaking, he produced several *sheng* of rice from his sleeve and placed it on the ground; then, he suddenly vanished. The assembly marveled at this.

Since the rice was too little to provide enough for a full meal, Hui-kai had gruel boiled instead, so that everyone was able to eat their fill. They immediately applied their hammers and chisels, and by the time the palace was completed, the stone was entirely exhausted.
If one were to try chipping at other stones, they would be so hard as to be unbreakable. From this, people came to know that Master Xu was no ordinary man.
*Biography of Great Wisdom Chan Master*.

Zhenrong was a native of Macheng in Chu. From childhood, he possessed a nature of wisdom. At fifteen, he became a śrāmaṇera and devoted himself to the study of the Buddhist scriptures for several years.
He traveled about with his alms bowl, visiting famous mountains and establishing karmic connections wherever he went.

In the Dingwei year of the Jiajing era, he arrived at Jiankang and entered Mount Niushou to practice asceticism. The following year, he entered the capital of Yan and took up residence at Chongguo Temple.

At the temple, he recited the Lotus Sūtra. After several months, he went to Mount Wanshou; having ascended the altar to receive the precepts, he entered Mount Wutai, where he practiced with strict discipline for five years, becoming increasingly diligent in his cultivation.
In the year Jiayin, he went to Guibeishi on Mount Funiu, where he engaged in ascetic refinement for three years, his observance of the precepts becoming even more rigorous.
In the year Dingyi, he returned from Mount Funiu to the region of Chu, staying at Longhua Temple in the provincial capital to continue his recitations.

The following year, he entered Shu and resided on the summit of Mount Emei. He restricted his movements for twelve years, gathering the assembly to cultivate practices for rebirth in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang).

He established a monastic community (*conglin*) and constructed a library pavilion named the Pure Land Hermitage (*Jingtu-an*), welcoming wandering practitioners with such earnest diligence that he felt as though he could never do enough.
In the second year of the Wanli era, he left the mountain and visited Yinguang Mountain to pay his respects; Yinguang and Emei stand like two hands joined in reverence toward one another.

Whenever he encountered the crowds of pilgrims heading toward the mountain, he observed that the eighty-li path was rugged and precipitous, with winds and rains occurring at irregular intervals, leaving no place to set foot.
He wished to establish a place for rest, yet found it difficult to secure a foundation.

Hearing that there was a pool on the mountain called the Golden Lotus Pool (*Jinlian chi*), whose upper reaches were level and expansive enough to build a *daochang* (site of practice), the Master was greatly delighted. He went to inspect it and found it was indeed so; he then leveled the rocks to prepare the ground.

Clearing the site, timber was felled for materials; the craftsmen were diligent in their efforts, and the people delighted in providing assistance. Within one or two years, a great monastery was completed, named Jinlian An (Golden Lotus Hermitage).
It truly served as a "Transformation City" for Mount Eme, upon which monks from all quarters relied. Subsequently, the Qianfo Ge (Thousand Buddhas Pavilion) was constructed.

He established it as a guardian for the Golden Lotus. Subsequently, he reflected further: "Among the three great sacred sites of the world—Wutai, Emei, and Putuo—I have already visited and paid homage at the former two.
Is it not fitting that I should also go to Putuo Mountain, the place where Avalokiteśvara manifested his transformation?

In the Gengchen year of the Wanli era, he crossed the sea and arrived at Xiaobaihua. There, he was moved by the manifestation of the Great Being’s form, which greatly fulfilled his long-held aspiration. From then on...
He said, "I have a karmic affinity with this mountain; eating porridge and vegetables will suffice for the remainder of my life.
Thereupon, to the left of Bodha Temple, at a place called Thousand-Step Sands, he traveled gradually eastward. At the end of the sands was a mountain called Guangxi Peak (Radiant Peace).

The Master built a hermitage at its base; in front was a pavilion from which one could clearly observe the rising sun over the vast ocean, and behind was a shrine for the Great Being (Avalokiteśvara).
The rest of the quarters and the Fragrant Accumulation Hall were all adorned with reverent care.

When the hermitage was completed, he named it Hai-chao (Ocean Tide), for its scenic beauty was not far removed from that of Mount Emei or Mount Wutai. As for the Master’s character, he was single-mindedly sincere.

He endured hardship with fortitude and strove to eradicate emotional consciousness. Whether people were noble or base, young or old, he regarded them all with an eye of compassion as he wandered about.
He swam through the ocean of the teachings and entered deeply into samādhi. Throughout his life, he never dwelt within the hall of pure karma by means of dualistic gates;

he remained on a single mat for his entire life, no different from the common assembly. He once said to others: "I have practiced asceticism for sixty years; how could I dare to harbor any vain aspirations?
I only wish to establish a karmic connection with the Triple Gem and attain the minor fruits of human or celestial rebirth—this alone shall fulfill my vow. Thus spoke the Master.
Mount Zhuzhai abounds in traces of divine wonders. Those who guard its secrets strictly have been forbidden from revealing them upon seeing them;

for when stillness reaches its ultimate limit, luminosity penetrates—this is simply the natural order of things. I myself am not deluded, so how could I dare to delude others? The Master’s shore of the Way is boundless.
Thus, those who travel toward the sea beheld the Great Wisdom Chan Master and regarded him as a great Bodhisattva in his current physical body. The monastic communities...
It is traditionally said that this has been passed down as a common saying. In the □□□ month of a certain year, he passed away while seated at Haichao Monastery.
Zhenlai Fuzi’s lineage was transmitted by Fudeng, whose courtesy name was Miaofeng. He was a native of Pingyang in Shanxi; his secular surname was Xu, and he resided at the place known as Xujiju.
Later, at the age of seven, his parents died during a year of famine; he had no means for burial, possessing only a mat to serve as a shroud.
Having no one to rely upon, the Master worked as a shepherd for a wealthy man in the village. At twelve, he left the household life; at eighteen, carrying his alms bowl, he arrived at Pufan.
Previously, King Shanyin had constructed the Wenchang Pavilion on the eastern mountain of the commandery and invited the monk Senglang to reside there. The Master [proceeded to...]
He arrived and went about begging in the marketplace. In the evening, he sought lodging within the pavilion. Just then, the King was out on an excursion;

seeing him, he questioned Daolang. Daolang informed him of the circumstances. The King said, "You must look after this youth well; in the future, he will surely become a vessel of great capacity. Daolang then accepted him as his disciple.
It happened that the earth shook violently, and the Master was buried under the ruins but did not die. When the King heard of this, he marveled at it and said to the Master: "You..."

Having narrowly escaped this great peril, why do you not feel deep anguish over the momentous matter of birth and death? Thereupon, he entered Mount Zhongtiao, closed himself within his retreat, and practiced the contemplation of the *Avataṃsaka*.
He took thorns and brambles and affixed them to the four walls; he provided no bed or seat, standing like a crane day and night amidst the thorns.

In this manner, three years passed. He had begun to show some signs of awakening, so he composed a verse and presented it to Shanyin. Shanyin sighed and said, "The extent of this youth's insight is already like this;
if I do not break him now, he may become mad in the future. Thereupon, she took a worn-out shoe from one of the palace ladies.
He cut out the sole of the shoe, washed it clean, and sent it sealed to him. Attached was a verse which said: "This piece of stinking shoe sole / Is sealed and sent to you;
/ It is not for any other purpose, / But solely to strike at the mouth of the poet. When the Master saw it, he immediately prostrated himself before the Buddha.
He tied a cord upon his head and thereafter remained silent, uttering not a single word. After three years, he broke through the barrier to go and see the King;
the King saw that he possessed the marks of a great man and was greatly pleased. The King then said, "Although you know your own fundamental duty, you have not yet heard the Buddha-dharma;
I fear you may fall into false views. At that time, there was a Dharma Master in Mount Jiehou who was lecturing on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. The King urged the Master [to go and study].
He went to listen to the teachings and received full ordination; he attended while performing his duties at the age of twenty-seven.

At that time, the King deeply revered the Triple Gem and often regretted that he could not travel afar with a water gourd and a monk’s hat. One day he said to the Master, "To be a monk and not travel to various regions is like being a frog in a well.
There are many spiritual friends in the South; you should go there to consult them. Upon your return, you may act as a traveling mendicant for this old man."

The Master then set out on his travels, visiting various monasteries until he reached Tianjie Monastery in Nanjing. There, under the guidance of Old Man Wuji, he served as the *jingtou* (sanitation officer), sweeping away filth and washing the counting sticks (*zhoutang*).
The assembly marveled at how exceptionally clean his quarters were compared to others and realized that this sanitation officer must be a man of the Way, though they did not know who he was.
At that time, Master Han was serving as the Vice Lecturer; after observing him for several days, he finally...
He found him and established a friendship with him, agreeing to travel together on a pilgrimage. Before ten days had passed, he searched for him and found that he had already departed in secret.
When the Master returned and saw the King, the King asked joyfully whom he had visited. The Master described it in detail; his intention was to dwell in the mountains.

He entered once more into the deepest recesses of Mount Zhongtiao. There he cleared away the weeds and dwelt alone like a solitary shadow, abstaining from grain and subsisting only on water for three years.

He attained great awakening and came to revere the Triple Gem with ever-increasing devotion. When the Great Brahma Monastery was completed on South Mountain, he was compelled to leave his retreat and reside there.

Furthermore, wishing to seek out the *Beizang* (Northern Collection) scriptures, he desired that the Master go in person. However, as the Master had lived in the mountains for a long time, his hair had grown long and remained uncut; thus, he appeared like a layman.

He disguised himself and entered the capital, where the printing blocks were stored within the Imperial Palace; they could not be obtained without an imperial edict, and moreover, they had long remained sealed and unreleased.
When the Master acquired them, it was as easy as picking something up. At that time, Master Han had already arrived in the capital and was listening to Dharma Master Zhong lecture on the Dharma.
The Master recognized him while on horseback; dismounting, he greeted him with a wry smile and said to Han, "Look at me—how am I?
Han replied, "My original face is ever-present. Thereupon, the Master took Han along with Zang and departed from the capital, saying, "This is merely the fulfillment of your long-cherished vow."
He then entered the Five Terraces (Wutai) at Longfan Stone. Amidst piles of ice and snow, he found several rafters of an old house and took up residence there.

At night, the Master traveled to the five peaks to dispel the darkness and confusion; by day, he pricked his tongue with a needle to draw blood and transcribed the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Upon completing the scripture, he convened an unrestricted assembly (*amogha-mahāpariṣad*).
He established the karmic conditions for ten thousand sages of Mañjuśrī at Tanyuan Temple for one hundred and twenty days. Nine times...

The eight provinces sent both monastics and laypeople, and those who arrived for the assembly followed one another along the roads in succession. The grandeur of this Dharma assembly was unprecedented.
The two Palaces repeatedly bestowed gracious edicts upon the virtuous masters; yet I privately reflected that it is difficult to remain long under such great fame.
Consequently, he entered the Luya (Reed-Sprout) Valley and constructed a hermitage, intending to spend the remainder of his life there. The Holy Mother sought out a master and found him;
she built the Great Huayan Temple at the summit of Luya for him and commanded the master to reside therein. She further commissioned the construction of seven ten-thousand-Buddha iron pagodas.
The Venerable Zibo had personally transcribed a copy of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* and enshrined it within [the stupa].

Subsequently, in accordance with the compassionate decree of Empress Cisheng, he was sent to Mount Jizu to deposit it in the treasury. On his way, he passed through Mount Emei, where he paid homage to the Silver-Colored Light (Yinsèguāng) and secretly vowed to build a copper temple, though no one knew of this.
Upon returning from Yunnan to Shanyin, he requested the restoration of the main hall of Wangu Temple; the hall was lofty.
It was thirteen *zhang* long and nine *zhang* wide. The Wei River was difficult to cross, causing great hardship for travelers. Grand Councilor Li petitioned to construct a bridge over it.
The Master resided there for two years and repaired thirteen arches of the bridge. He further accepted an invitation to build a double-tiered bridge over the Great River at Xuānfǔ;
the upper tier had thirty-two arches. This Great River flows from the lands of the Hu into China, its current surging with great force.
The task of carving the gushing [fountain] was the most difficult to accomplish. The Master ultimately completed it, as if by divine assistance.

For the two bridges and the hall, the expenses amounted to several million gold pieces; yet the Master truly had no single coin in his hands. Offerings from the faithful gathered like clouds and fell like rain, their source unknown.
The fulfillment of such meritorious conditions is almost inconceivable. Having returned to Luya, he excavated a stone cave.

At Ninghua County, there was a cave three zhang and five chi deep, wide, and high. Within it, he carved a diagram of the worlds of the Buddhas of the ten directions from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, along with images of ten thousand Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
The work was so exquisite, intricate, and detailed that it became a great site of practice (*mahā-maṇḍala*).

Upon seeing this, the Prince of Shen remarked with joy, "A supreme cause has been accomplished; this is a fine place for one to dwell as a mountain recluse seeking to still the mind. The Master replied, "I have not yet finished my work at Mount Emei."
The King then presented ten thousand *kin* of gold to the Master and took the plank road into Shu. It happened that Vice-Censor Wang Xiangqian was the regional commander (*zongzhi*) of that area;
he welcomed the Master and inquired about the essentials of the mind. Thereupon, he said to the Master with a smile: "The three Great Beings are brothers in practice.
You treat Samantabhadra in this way, yet you do not take into account Avalokiteśvara and Mañjuśrī—would you call this partiality?"
The Master said, "This poor monk does nothing more than offer empty fists to follow in your footsteps. If it were as you say, there would naturally be powerful great men like yourselves.
The King replied, "Indeed, indeed. With a single word from the Master, the three bronze temples stood majestic once more.
Each temple contained various statues gilded with refined gold; one each was placed at Mount Wutai and Mount Emei, while the attempt to go to Putuo failed, and thus [the statue] remained in An.
It was enshrined at Mount Hua in Nanjing. The two imperial palaces issued edicts to provide protection for the Three Mountains.
Furthermore, the seven sites and nine assemblies of the *dōjō* were celebrated with rites of praise at Yongming Temple on Mount Tai. Subsequently, a pagoda was constructed in Taiyuan.
He repaired the bridge at Xiufuping and established the Chayao Hermitage at Longlong Pass, for which His Majesty personally inscribed the plaque.
He also repaired the Great Bridge over the Hutuo River, five li in length, and restored the Dasi Temple in the provincial capital.

Subsequently, he returned to Mount Tai to manage the upper and lower monasteries he had founded, establishing them as *shifang conglin* (public monasteries for the ten directions) and leaving behind no members of his own dharma lineage.

In the eighth month of the Gengshen year of the Wanli era, he was bestowed with a golden Buddha statue, an embroidered crown, a *kaṣāya* of ground hemp from the Thousand Buddhas, purple robes, and the title "True Coming Son of the Buddha.
In the twelfth month of that same winter, he manifested slight illness; flocks of birds cried out in sorrow and extraordinary light enveloped the earth.
The Master then gathered the assembly and finished his final instructions, after which he passed away sitting upright at the age of seventy-three and fifty years since his ordination.
1. Upon the announcement of his death, the two palaces dispatched eunuchs to offer sacrifices and granted him burial on the western ridge of Yongming, where a stupa was erected.
The Empress Dowager separately provided the funds for his funeral. The Master’s physical frame could not support his robes, and his speech did not issue from his mouth;
yet he began by assisting the Way as a minor official and ultimately brought about the patronage of the Sage Emperor, the Sage Mother, and the various princes.
Whenever he undertook construction projects, they would arise like clouds at his mere thought. Wherever he set foot, it was immediately transformed into a jeweled monastery (*ratnavihāra*).
Although the expenses often amounted to tens of thousands, he entrusted all matters entirely to those of proven capability and genuine practice.

The Master remained aloof and self-contained; beyond his single robe, he possessed no superfluous belongings. He drifted like the gathering and dispersing of floating clouds, coming and going like a solitary crane. Had he not been...

Profoundly realizing Mind-Only, he took whatever circumstances he encountered as the very essence of his teaching—how could it be otherwise? Su Yunpu, a Palace Attendant, once sought the Way from the Master;

having attained deep resonance in his heart, he remarked: "People regard Master Miao as a field of merit and a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), yet they do not truly know the depth of his transcendent awakening.
Wang Boyu, the Grand Marshal, once said of Master Han: "In the present day..."

There was no one who could serve as a teacher to the Master; only Miaofeng was such a person. Thus, Master Han devoted his heart to him and served him with reverence, and there were not two [different] men in this regard.

Wúbiàn (Boundless) was the son of the Cáo family of Dàizhōu. From his youth, he aspired to leave the household life. He first sought instruction from Wúxiàng (Formless), who did not grant him permission, saying, "If you can merely awaken to the Way, what need have you for the complications of home?
Thereupon, he visited Mù'ài Yuán (Unobstructed Origin) and received the tonsure. He then went to see Fén...

The Elder An of Zhuzhou instructed [Zhaozhou] to investigate the koan, "The myriad dharmas return to One. One day, An raised the dialogue concerning King Prasenajit’s observation of the river and questioned the Master.
The Master was unable to provide an answer and earnestly requested instruction. An said, "I am not unwilling to explain it to you."

"You must awaken to this yourself before you can attain it. Thereupon, he stood upright and did not lie down. He then entered the fire-pit at Mount Niu and visited various elders, yet found no entry into the Way.
Returning once more to serve An, he exerted himself to grasp a single word until he forgot both sleep and food.
One day, while sweeping the ground, he heard someone reciting the *Amitābha Sūtra*: "In that land there is a Buddha named Amitābha, who is currently present."
He was preaching the Dharma when the Master suddenly let out a cry. Seeing An, he said, "I have recognized one. An asked, "Where is it?

He replied, "It is currently here, preaching the Dharma. An pressed him on this, and he was left utterly bewildered. An suddenly struck him with his palm and said, "You are merely a follower of empty words.

The Master withdrew and wept, saying, "I certainly understood it clearly; alas, how can I fall back into confusion when confronted with the actual situation? He then went to visit the two masters, Yufeng and Baoshan.
Later, he visited Longshu at Mount Chu. There, he heard a woodcutter say, "People suffer because they do not let their minds rest.

Upon hearing this, the Master was suddenly liberated and remarked, "The myriad dharmas are fundamentally tranquil; it is only people who create their own clamor. He presented a verse to Master Chu-feng, who approved it.

From then on, he concealed his brilliance and hid his traces, such that no one could fathom his limits. After some time, disciples gathered from all directions, vying with one another to build meditation huts for him. It was there—
The present Dayuanbo Hermitage on Mount Wutai is this very place. When the Master resided on the mountain, he maintained himself with austere simplicity;
he always shared his meals with the assembly, possessing the style of the ancients. For thirty years, it was as if it were but a single day. Far and near, all vied to praise him.

In the *wuzi* year of the Wanli era, the two venerable masters Miza and Hanyu entered the mountain to seek a dwelling. [The Master] then stored the Tripitaka in bound volumes. The Master... [text ends]
Wen said: "The Monastery of the Monks (Seng'an) was formerly occupied by Shi-fang; now everyone treats it as their own private property. I have always considered this a source of shame.

Now that I am fortunate enough to encounter such a superior cause, I shall give away this monastery and all its contents to Master Zang, so that the Great Canon in its written form may circulate throughout Jambudvīpa one day sooner—this would be for me one day’s turning of the Wheel of Dharma. Thereupon...

He summoned all the senior monks of the mountain to serve as witnesses and established a covenant, saying: "If any member of this assembly uses even a single bowl or a single set of chopsticks for private gain, they shall be expelled.
Initially, Master Zang was still hesitant and did not dare to accept; however, seeing that the Master’s intention was most earnest, he finally consented.
He went to listen to him. Shortly thereafter, the Master manifested illness; three months later, he passed away.

During his period of suffering from illness, he spent day and night with Master Zang investigating and resolving matters concerning the primary truth (*paramārtha-satya*), never showing even the slightest frown due to his physical ailment. Some have said:

The Master was truly resolute in his intent to shatter the realm of existence (*bhava*). When presented with a single measure of rice and a bowl of bean soup, an ordinary person cannot help but show a look of reluctance;
yet the Master offered up all that he had accumulated throughout his life in a single day to bestow upon others—this was already an act difficult for anyone else to perform.

Furthermore, when the four elements (*catvāri mahābhūtāni*) were about to separate and the winds and fires of dissolution pressed in upon him—a time when an ordinary person would cry out in terror and have no leisure to attend to reason—the Master remained earnest and persistent.
To resolve matters solely by means of the mark of the primary truth (*paramārtha*)—is this not exceedingly difficult? This is precisely what enables one to cast away the body.
Because one is able to cast away the body, one can cast away even this hermitage as if it were a worn-out sandal. Could this not serve as a banner of light for the Dharma of the Final Age?
The Master cannot be fathomed by ordinary sentiments; those with the true eye will naturally discern him for themselves.

Compiled by the Śramaṇa Minghe of Huashan Temple in Wumen, Ming Dynasty.
**Biography of Huiquan** from the *Za ke pian* (Miscellaneous Section) of the Later Zhou:

Huiquan was a great virtuous master (*dàdé*) of Kaiyuan Temple in Shangdang. He was thoroughly versed in the sutras and devoted to the Vinaya, yet he remained indifferent to worldly affairs and manifested his virtue [in seclusion].
During the reign of Emperor Shizong, the policies of the Huichang era were implemented; the monastic ranks were strictly regulated and the Buddhist teachings were extinguished.
Daotian, carrying his scriptures and images, moved to dwell among the mountain crags and valleys. A bandit planned to go there to plunder him, yet Daotian was unaware of it.

Suddenly, a man riding a horse came down from the mountain peak and said to him, "There are thieves tonight; you should flee at once. Daotian, knowing this was a deity, joined his palms and addressed him:
"The state has fallen and my teachings are left solitary and destitute; therefore, I have come to seek refuge with you, the donor, looking up to you for protection.
Otherwise, I shall simply wait for death; where else could I flee? That night it snowed heavily, and the bandits were unable to advance.

When the weather cleared, the robbers plotted to go again, but as long as someone was there to guard him, they ultimately could not commit their offense. Because of this, Tan remained safe. Many people living near the mountain provided him with offerings.
He was raised [in this manner]. Afterwards, nothing was known of his ultimate end.
Regarding the *Biography of Shanhui* from the Song dynasty:
Shanhui was the son of the Huo family in Guo County. From childhood, he was intelligent and wise, possessing a divine luster. He enjoyed playing with mud to fashion images of the Buddha.
He was a butcher by trade. Once, he gathered flowers to offer as a plaything. Seeing this, his father sighed and said, "This boy is a son of the Śākya clan; I have lost all hope for him.

When he grew up, his parents feared he would stray from the path, so they forcibly arranged a marriage for him. After three years, however, he remained untainted by sensual contact. His parents then rebuked him.
The Master sighed and said, "The wheel of karma within birth and death has desire as its foundation; the weary life within the three realms has craving as its root.
Immersed in this state since beginningless time, how could I ever again perpetuate such faults? His parents, knowing that his resolve could not be thwarted, permitted him to leave the household life.
He paid homage at Qingliang Temple and took Cheng Dade as his preceptor. Cheng said, "This is a 'qilin' child of our house."
He was instructed in the sutras and attained mastery through a single reading; he applied himself diligently to his studies without ever becoming lax.
After some time, Cheng assigned his disciples to oversee the construction and repair of the three gates. The Master said, "Illusions are like fleeting light, vanishing in an instant.

Since I have not yet settled the matters pertaining to my own person, how can I engage in such idle affairs for others? It would only increase my ignorance. I pray that you, Master, will exclude me from these duties."
This was appropriate. During the Qiandao era, he became renowned for his virtuous conduct, and the authorities conferred upon him the title of Great Master Xuansi (宣秘大師).

He was appointed to oversee the administrative seals and manage the affairs of the religious community. When the decree arrived, he could not decline; he accepted the post with diligence. Monastics and laypeople flocked to him, and the Dharma-grove was harmonious and solemn.
On his deathbed, he said to his disciples: "In the past, Boyi and Shuqi starved to death on the slopes of Mount Shouyang.

It was not that they held life in low regard or delighted in death; rather, they knew that righteousness was more important than their own bodies. For twenty years now, my own practice has not yet been pure."
"To be burdened by monastic affairs is to sacrifice the light for the sake of the heavy; thus one's virtue is impaired. You all must strive diligently;
do not follow my humble example. Having finished speaking, he passed away.
The Biography of Master Māyī:
As for Master Māyī, it is unknown where he was from. During the period of the Five Dynasties, he wore only hempen garments.
He traveled between Ze, Lu, Guan, and Shan provinces, attaining profound mastery of the *Yi* (Book of Changes) and unlocking the secrets of the *Hetu* (River Chart), which he then transmitted to Hua.
The Mountain Hermit Chen Zhuo first obtained this [text] and composed the *Jue* (Instructions) to transmit it to Zhong Fang. Zhong Fang transmitted it to Li Kai; Li Kai transmitted it to Xu Jian;
Xu Jian transmitted it to Fan Echang; and Fan Echang transmitted it to Liu Mu, who then composed the *Gouyin Tu* (Diagram of the Hidden Hook) to expound upon it.

The truth is fundamentally based on the Master. As for the title [of this work], it means that the Master’s exposition of the *Yì* was more subtle than it had been two thousand years after [the Buddha’s passing];
it was surely a divine endowment. Before passing the civil service examinations, Qián Ruoshuǐ visited Fǎtuó in the mountains and saw an elderly monk wrapped in a *nà* robe huddling by a fire.
When Ruo-shui bowed to him, the monk merely opened his eyes. After sitting for a long time, Zhuo asked, "How is it? The monk replied, "You lack the bones of an immortal. Ruo-shui withdrew.
Zhuo cautioned him, saying, "You may come again after three days. He went as scheduled, and Zhuo said, "At first, when I saw you, your spirit and appearance were pure and refined;
I thought you could learn the way of the immortals, which is why I requested a decision from this old monk. This old monk said—"
"You lack the bone of an immortal; you can only become a worthy high official, but you must withdraw with courage from the swift current.

He asked who the monk was. Zhibo replied, "My master is the Wayman Māyī (Máiyī Dàozhě). When Your Majesty served under the Zhou dynasty, you once visited my master and asked, 'The current Emperor is destroying the Buddha-dharma;
this is most certainly not a blessing for the longevity of the state. My master said, 'This is why the three Wu emperors left no legacy.'"
[The account] concludes. He asked again, "When will the world be settled? The Master replied, "The signs of the 'red qi' have already appeared; between the hours of the Dragon (7–9 a.m.
and the Monkey (3–5 p.m.), a true lord shall emerge, and the Buddha-dharma will also flourish greatly. When he received the abdication [of the throne], it indeed accorded with what had been said.

In the fourth year of the Kaibao era, he personally led an expedition against Taiyuan. Passing through Luzhou on his way, he visited the Master’s monastery and prayed personally before the Buddha, saying: "This journey is for the purpose of offering condolences..."

He made the eradication [of evil] his primary concern, vowing never to kill a single person indiscriminately; this was likely because he did not forget the instructions given by his teacher during the time of the "Dragon’s Latency.
Huiquan succeeded to Huiquan.
A native of Pengcheng, he resided at the Gezhi Monastery on Mount Nantai. By nature solitary and pure, he did not casually associate with others. He possessed great wisdom...
Many scholars came to visit him. When he spoke with them, his discourse was expansive and delightful. Yet, the more they sought his intimacy, the more he would reject them and remain unresponsive.

Furthermore, his mastery of the doctrinal studies was profound and comprehensive; he was skilled in poetry and possessed a world-transcending aesthetic sensibility. This was during the final years of the Taiping Xingguo era.
Cáo Bīn was sent out to assume command due to the slander of Mǐ Dèchāo; he closed his gate and declined visitors.

Sūn Hé came from the capital and, having been unable to see him for a long time, composed a poem in self-reproach, saying: "I wish to visit the Commander-in-Chief but lack an introduction; Xué Néng’s poetic plaque remains in the Eagle Hall.
Later, when Dēng Nán tái heard of Quán Gāi, he knocked at his door, and upon seeing him once, [they felt as if they had known each other for a long time].

They were old acquaintances. He was hosted at his hermitage, where he was provided with exceptionally generous provisions and hospitality. Upon his departure, [the host] presented him with furs and horses as parting gifts.
Two years later, He became the head of the Jinshi (Metropolitan Graduate) examination. His fellow graduate, Lu Zhen, was serving as an official in Pengmen.

He highly praised Quen’s profound commitment to righteousness and his refusal to seek recognition from others. When Lu Zhen took up his post, he brought his subordinates and guests to visit him. His disciples said, "Our Master has heard of your honor..."
When he arrived, [Huì]quán had already departed for Zhejiang. Zhèn sighed with admiration and left a poem on the wall, saying:

"Master Hán once spoke of Master Huìquán, who could explain the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* and compose poetry. Today I have come, but the Master has already gone; I stand amidst the wind and rain at the thatched hall for a long time.
Huìquán’s resolve may truly be called "practicing what one learns," and he did no shame to our school.
The Biography of Chan Master Xiaoshou of Xingjiao, Hangzhou.
As for Chan Master Xiaoshou, it is unknown where he was from or whose son he was. He was known as "Xiaoshou" because there was another contemporary named Yongming Shou.
Therefore, they were referred to as "Short-lived" to distinguish them from one another. Both masters were true disciples of National Teacher Shao of Tiantai.

When the Master [Zhili] heard a piece of firewood fall, he attained enlightenment and composed a verse, saying: "It falls, yet it is not something else; Lying crosswise or lengthwise, it is no mere dust.

Mountains, rivers, and the great earth— The entire body of the Dharma King is revealed. The National Teacher nodded in approval. When he began to propagate the Dharma, the monks vied to honor him as their master. Heaven...
During the Xì era, Wáng Gōng Suí, the Minister of the Court of Judicial Review, was dispatched to govern Qiántáng. He went to visit the Master at Húshàng;

leaving behind his attendants, he walked alone up to the master’s quarters. The Master was just then basking in the sun, wrapped in a coarse woolen garment, appearing entirely unperturbed. Upon suddenly seeing him, the Master asked:

The official asked, "What is your surname? The Master replied, "My name follows my surname, which is Wang. The official then bowed to him. The Master pushed aside his meditation cushion and sat directly on the ground.
They conversed and laughed for the entire day before the official departed. His disciples remonstrated with him, saying, "That was a royal minister who came; why did you not pay him due respect?
This concerns the entire community and is no small matter. The Master merely said, "Yes, yes. On another day, when the official arrived again, the assembly...
He struck the great bell with a horizontal blow. The entire monastery came out to welcome him, but the Master hurried forward and stood beneath a pine tree.

When the Prince saw him from afar, he stepped out of his carriage, took the Master’s hand, and said, "Why do you not greet me as you did on the previous day? Why have you suddenly adopted such formal etiquette?"
The Master looked to his left and right; walking along as he spoke, he said, "If the Vice Minister were to obtain it, what would we do about the Warden’s resentment?
Such was the purity and excellence of his natural character.

Wéizhōng. Wényīng’s biography states that Wéizhōng, whose courtesy name was Huìyǎ, was a monk of Kāiyuán Monastery in Péngzhōu. Having traveled to Chéngdū, he did not return to his hometown for forty years.
By nature solitary and pure, he did not casually associate with others. He was refined in the study of Chan and the Vinaya, and was skilled in versification.
His poetry was characterized by a refined and meticulous style, ranking him as a peer to Li Ke and Liang Youpeng; contemporaries hailed him as the "Poet Patriarch.

Furthermore, he was well-versed in Confucian classics, and students flocked to his feet daily to inquire about their meanings. Though his appearance was emaciated, his face soiled, and his clothes tattered and shoes worn out, those who saw him could not fathom what lay within.
In the fifth month of the fifth year of the Qingli era, he passed away at Daci Gan Monastery.
Ludaochang was sixty-nine years old at the time. He emptied the entirety of his purse, obtaining eighty thousand coins, and entrusted them to those with whom he had previously traveled.
The practitioner of the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, Jishu, said, "I am about to depart;
this is all that remains from my entire life. For my sake, commission a skilled artisan to paint an image of the Sixth Patriarch in the Śākyamuni Hall of your monastery."
"Your Excellency, I have been subjected to such reproach for this; I dare not decline. Rather, I wish to cause those who come here to see this and thereby recognize this mind.
Through such knowledge and vision, one can cleanse away all delusions, dissolve appearances, and extinguish the mind.
This is my intention regarding this meritorious work. [The Emperor] granted his request. Liu Yunchen was commissioned to name it, and Wen Tong of Zizhou was commissioned to paint it. He once...
I asked my teacher about this matter and recorded its events.
Wenying, surnamed Su, was a native of Quanzhou. He traveled for trade to Chengdu and amassed a fortune of tens of thousands of units.

Taking an interest in the joy of Chan, he suddenly attained a realization. He then relinquished all his wealth and sent a letter to bid farewell to his wife and children. He shaved his head at Jiayou Monastery. His wife...
Zi Wanli traveled to Shu to visit him, but the Master would not see him at all. Zi sat resolutely in a single room for three days amidst total silence and the absence of human sound.
His wife and children, realizing that the Master’s resolve could not be swayed, abandoned him and departed; consequently, the Master’s reputation grew even higher.
He presided over four monastic centers (*daochang*), remaining longest at Chaowu, which was one of the three great monasteries of Daci.

Truly inheriting the remains of the ashes, the Master gathered craftsmen and laborers to construct a Zen monastery. He built a total of one thousand pillars, opening up a dragon palace and housing the *palm-leaf* scriptures;
its scale was vast and its appearance magnificent. As soon as it was completed, a fire broke out in an adjacent courtyard, threatening to spread.
The Master immediately informed the local government and ordered the destruction of the three gates of the main temple to cut off the flames. He then requested that...
After the construction was completed, the fires were extinguished and the three gates were renovated. Originally, the monastery had no fields;
the Master collected monetary donations from benefactors and petitioned the government for the lands of an abolished temple, acquiring three hundred *mu* to provide for the kitchen.
Thus, Chaowu became a magnificent great monastic center, all through the Master’s efforts.
The practitioner of the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* named Ji was distinguished by his lofty conduct; he was granted the title of Great Master Jueji.

He was a friend beyond the secular world with Wen Yuke, and they were on very cordial terms. [Wen] composed a poem to present to him, and the Great Master Jueji also inscribed a eulogy upon his portrait.
He praised him most highly, saying:
"The Great Master Bao Yue transmitted [the teachings] to the Great Master Bao Yue.
Wei Jian, courtesy name Zonggu, was surnamed Su and was a native of Meishan. He was a non-affinal relative (wufu) to Dongpo."
The elder brother left home at the age of nine and received full ordination at nineteen. At twenty-nine, he was granted the purple robe; at thirty-six, he was conferred a title.
The Master was pure, bright, and quick-witted, thoroughly proficient in all affairs. He disciplined himself with integrity, exhausting his own labor to enrich others.

All people held his talent in high esteem and were moved by his sincerity; whatever he desired to accomplish, they hastened to bring to fruition. He renovated the vihāra located in... (the text ends here).

In Chengdu and [郫-卑+((白-日+田)/廾)], there were a total of one hundred and seventy-three structures. There was one canon of scriptures, four images of Vairocana, Amitābha, Maitreya, and Mahākāruṇika, and twenty-seven brick bridges;
all were completed with ease and laughter. Their solidity and craftsmanship could sustain the world for a generation.
Although the Master’s Buddhist activities appeared to be conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), they were like a farmer tilling the soil and sowing seeds in his plots.
He waited for things to develop naturally, rather than acting repeatedly or forcefully. He delighted in distributing medicine, saving lives beyond count.
The provincial governors and imperial envoys were all eminent officials of the time, and each was on friendly terms with the Master;

yet the Master rarely saw them and spoke little, striving to keep himself aloof, such that it was impossible to distinguish him as either intimate or distant. In his youth, he was close friends with Zhang Yin Shaoyu, a native of Shu.
Laoquan (Su Shi) held him in high esteem, saying: "This youth’s talent and capacity are no less than those of Chengguan;
if he enters official service, he will surely achieve distinction in the world, and even as a monk, none shall surpass him. It was just as he had predicted.

On the ninth day of the sixth month in the second year of the Shaosheng era, he began to suffer from a slight illness and immediately wrote a letter to inform his acquaintances, instructing his descendants that all matters should be in accordance with the Buddha-dharma.
A man of great affairs, he never uttered a single word for his own private benefit. On the twenty-second day, he assembled his disciples and asked them about the time of day;
when it was mid-morning, he said, "I am going," and then passed away. He was eighty-four years old.
On the twenty-sixth day of this month, his remains were returned to the Sū-t'a (Longevity Stupa) at Chibokwon Temple to the east of the city.
Furthermore, there was the Great Master Baoyue (Jewel Moon). His courtesy name was Shuwei, his secular surname was Wang, and he was a native of Qiantang in Hangzhou.

He entered the monastic order at the age of nine and received full ordination at eleven. In the second year of the Jingyou era, he was granted the purple robe; in the first year of the Baoyuan era, he was bestowed the title of Great Master Baoyue.

During the Zhiping era, the provincial authorities requested that he serve as the *Sengzheng* (Monastic Rectifier) for the jurisdiction. The Master was by nature easygoing, kind, and compassionate. He possessed...
His wisdom and discernment were such that he showed no sign of joy or anger. Having read the Five Classics, he understood their great principles;
he took particular pleasure in composing poetry. From his youth, he was frail and frequently ill; he first studied medicine, and once he had mastered it, many who were sick turned to him for help.

Regardless of whether they were noble or humble, rich or poor, he applied his skills to them all without exception, never showing partiality. To those in extreme poverty, he would even provide clothing.
Because of this, from the capital to the four quarters, and from the high officials and ministers down to the scholars and gentlemen, many knew his name;
upon meeting him, they all delighted in following him as a companion.

As for the people of the local districts, even down to the sojourners and travelers, there were none among those who sought refuge with him who did not find their hearts satisfied. In his manner of receiving others, though he was weary, he never showed it.

He was free from weariness and showed no expression of reluctance. Regarding his basic necessities—medicines, clothing, and food—even when they were exhausted, he never once harbored thoughts of calculation or stinginess.
His outward conduct was thus. Yet, when he withdrew to dwell amidst the vicissitudes of poverty and wealth, or death and life, there was nothing that could burden his mind.
Thus, even when he reached a point where he could not provide for himself, he never once let his intention waver. As for...
He was on the verge of death, yet he never once altered his countenance or changed his expression. In the tenth month of the first year of the Xining era, he contracted an illness.

When his disciples and those with whom he had previously associated for the study of Buddhism gathered around him, he informed them that his end was near; he then composedly took his seat and passed away.

Chongshou transmitted [the Dharma] to Dayi County. Chan Master Chongshou was a native of Putun in Qiong Prefecture, the son of the Qi family. From the time he lost his baby teeth, his inclinations were lofty and far-reaching.
Whenever his family performed Buddhist rites, he would sweep the area and present offerings with such reverence, diligence, and sincerity that no instruction was required.
He disciplined himself accordingly, yet he often feared that he might not be able to conform to the Dharma.

His parents, perceiving his exceptional nature, enrolled him in the monastic register of Jinglin Monastery in Dayi, making Renpu his teacher. At the age of sixteen, he shaved his head; at twenty, he received full ordination.
He came to Daci Monastery in Chengdu to listen to lectures on various Mahāyāna sūtras and thoroughly mastered their profound meanings. Seven years later, he returned to his former residence;
everything there had fallen into ruin and was neglected, consisting of only a few dilapidated rooms with rotting rafters, broken walls, slanting roofs, and leaking eaves.
The Master remained serene and contented upon a single mat within that place, showing no sign of weariness. This was the result of his meditative realization.
In his leisure time, he also composed verses that were profound yet simple and pure. His speech was harmonious and gentle;

he never clashed with others, harboring neither love nor hatred in his heart, and showing neither joy nor anger on his face. Furthermore, he was robust and seldom ill. His physical appearance was tall and dignified, and his nature was compassionate, forgiving, and warm.
Regardless of age, everyone wished to see him; upon seeing him, they would invariably prostrate themselves in joy, lingering for a long time, unable to bear to depart.
One day, he suddenly summoned his disciples, including Muan and others, and said to them: "Since humans are born, it is natural that they must die.
Death is not an extraordinary matter. Furthermore, I have long been free from birth and death. You should realize the reason why I am without birth and death;
be careful not to grieve like the common crowd, so as not to burden me with my final entrustment. My spiritual radiance—"
He remained in this state for countless moments. "You must uphold the precepts I have taught: do not commit evil, and do not fail to practice the good.
Having spoken these words, he drew up his legs into the full lotus posture, folded his hands, closed his eyes, and passed away. Though shaken and pulled, he could not be moved;
he sat as motionless as a carved statue. His worldly age was eighty-six. This was the twenty-third day of the tenth month in the first year of the Zhìpíng era. Thus it was with the Master.
The Master’s true body remained undecayed; the wind-gods were serene and appeared no different than on ordinary days. His disciples subsequently enshrined it within a stūpa.

Wen Yuke served as an official in the prefectural administration and visited him from time to time. Later, when he was appointed to the position of Acting Governor, the Master had already passed away.
He took a detour through the county, went beneath the Master’s stūpa, circumambulated it in worship, and with deep sorrow and lamentation, said: "The Master..."

The master’s countenance appeared as if alive, yet his voice could no longer be heard. Consequently, [the author] composed an inscription for his stupa so that it might be transmitted for a long time (appended is the record of Qingshun).
Qikou, style name Yilao, was a native of Qiantang. At the beginning of the Tiānshèng era, he received the full precepts and studied the teachings under Jingjue. There was nothing further to add.
Shizhi delighted in composing ancient-style regulated verse. His residence at Xiangfu on West Lake was a solitary room in which he lived in complete seclusion;

pure and upright, he maintained his poverty without ever showing a trace of distress. When Dongpo was the governor of Qiantang, during the Lantern Festival of the Yuanxi month, he went to view the lanterns at Jiuqu.

Leaving his attendants behind, he walked alone into the Master’s quarters, where there was no light at all, yet he could still smell the lingering fragrance of *campaka* flowers. In admiration, he composed a poem.
There was the Buddha Not Grasping Lapis Lazuli Radiance, who first realized that "the inexhaustible is fundamentally not a lamp.

Pu Zongmeng compiled a collection of ancient and modern poetry from Qiantang and requested the master’s draft manuscript. The master said, "I take it as I get it and depart; I have never kept anything."
Those who heard of this held him in high esteem. In his later years, he shut himself within his door; when seeing off guests, he would not cross the threshold.

He abstained from grain, sat in tranquil composure, and engaged in the cultivation of contemplative practice for over ten years. Outside his window there were only a few stalks of red banana and a hundred shoots of green bamboo—how serene it was!
One day he said to people, "When I die, the banana tree will also die, and Master Zhai Ying will also die. Before long, all of these came true.
People sighed in wonder at this.
The master’s friend, Qingshun, was also a native of Qiantang; his courtesy name was Yiran. His poetry was renowned as being equal to that of the master, and his conduct was likewise identical.
Ye Mengde of Shilin remarked: "During the Xining era, there were two men, Qingshun and Kejiu.

The places where they resided were both among the most excellent scenic spots of the lakes and mountains. Yet they were pure, frugal, upright, and serene, never engaging in frivolous socializing with others, nor visiting anyone except on matters of great importance."
Many officials and gentlemen went to visit him. At that time, there were those who sent him rice; he would accept no more than several *sheng*.
He stored it in a jar on a small table and consumed two or three *he* per day. Even though his diet consisted of vegetables, he never once tasted them with relish.
Consequently, people held him in even greater esteem.
The Biography of Chan Master Weidi. Weidi was a man of unknown origins.
He inherited the Dharma from Yunmen and his guidance was clear and penetrating. Once, he answered a questioner regarding the Buddha, saying:
"The sun rises in the east at the hour of Mao. When asked again to point out the Way, the Master said: "Look after three days. [He further remarked: "The wealthy loathe even a thousand mouths."

"Little. Poverty makes one regret having too many bodies. These were all words spoken by the Master according to the capacity of his audience. He also spoke in the manner of guest and host, saying: "The guest within the guest:
the sun and moon have no old or new. The host within the guest: the staff is three or five feet long. The guest within the host: who is this person engaged in question and answer?
The host within the host: with the true eye, who would dare to look? The general outline of his teachings was thus. During the Xining era, [the monk] Pu of Shu...

A monk from Tōzan-in presented himself at the provincial government, expressing his wish to invite an elder of eminent practice to propagate the school’s tradition and restore the former achievements of the Qingzhou lineage.
The Provincial Governor, Grand Councilor Nanyang Gong, approved this and ordered the relevant authorities to carefully select a suitable candidate, appointing the Master for the position.
Upon the Master’s arrival, the people of the capital were moved with enthusiasm and inspired to emulation; thus, the teachings were widely propagated once again.
Dàoyóu lived his entire life in austere simplicity. He presided over three meditation halls in succession, yet his chamber remained desolate;

a single rain hat hung upon the wall, which he would carry with him when traveling, appearing ever serene and composed. What was most extraordinary was that wherever he went, he was accompanied by the true bodies of ancient masters.
When he first resided at Mǎxī, there was the Venerable Shuǐguàn; later, at Wúwéi, there was Huìkuān.
The Venerable Master, while residing at Pǔtōng Monastery, also [enshrined] the true body of the Venerable Master of Qīngzhōu;
both are seated in the full-lotus position with knees bound, their dignified features remaining solemn. Could this be a mere coincidence of human affairs? Or must there be some underlying cause?

(During the Wáng Shǔ period, there was the Chan Master Hónggǎo, who came from Qīngzhōu and settled at Dōngchán Monastery. At that time, the two assemblies resided together. The Ruler of Shǔ, admiring and respecting the Master’s virtue, appointed two palace attendants named Dào Zhēn and Dào Fěn to serve him. Later, there was a courtesan named Dàoyù, who was a provincial courtesan...)

In particular, upon hearing the Master preach the Dharma, he attained realization beneath the words and subsequently shaved his head to serve him. Thereupon, public opinion clamored; the Ruler of Shu was incensed and ordered an investigation. However, knowing the Master to be pure, steadfast, precise, and authentic, the Ruler treated him with even greater reverence.

Consequently, the Master bestowed his residence upon Guànxiū and chose to dwell at Pǔtōng Mountain to the southeast of the capital’s outskirts. He later entered *nirvāṇa* there, and thus his true body remains. The people of Shu called him "The Stork" (*jílíng*) because of the seven dots joined together [in his name].

The hermit Tián Xiāoyáo of Huáyáng visited the Master in the mountains and, upon seeing him, asked: "What is 'the seven dots joined together'? The Master replied: "Counting on one's fingers does not reach it; there are no tracks upon the ground. Dìgōng once brought this up to address the assembly. Some have doubted that Dì was the Master’s subsequent incarnation. This concludes the record.
The cycle of principle is likewise unknowable).
Zhilin’s Biography:
Zhilin’s surname was Keng. His ancestors were from Panyu. Having received full ordination, he took the Venerable Qing as his preceptor and transmitted [the teachings].
The Secret Teaching (Guhyamantra). For forty years, he applied himself with right effort, not wasting a single day. Emperor Renzong delighted in Buddhist affairs;

he selected the northwest corner of Kaibosi Temple and renovated a vihāra there, purifying the site and personally inscribing the plaque for the hall. The images and their settings were magnificently adorned, all provided from the imperial treasury.
He was granted the name Baosheng Yuan and appointed as its abbot, charged with presiding over the affairs of the Gate of the Teachings. [He was] granted...
He was titled the Great Master Xuanchao. He served as the head of the monastic registers throughout the realm. Regarding the gates of *dhāraṇī*, he maintained them with meticulous precision;

whenever the state offered prayers, there were none that did not receive a response. From the inner palace and government offices down to the imperial clan and noble relatives, all treated him with great courtesy.
Both clergy and laity looked toward him with devotion, and the scholar-officials held him in high esteem. By Zhang Wen Ding, An... (the text ends).

Zhang Qian devoted himself deeply to the inner scriptures (Buddhist texts). He once questioned his teacher regarding the study of the *vaṃśa* (Sanskrit) language. The teacher elucidated for him the hidden and profound mysteries, categorizing and explaining them with clarity and fluency.
Upon hearing this, Zhang attained a lucid understanding and consequently deepened his reverence and service toward the teacher. Zhang further asked:

"The various sections of the *pāśa* (noose-mantras), the rituals of the maṇḍala, and the various forms of adornment do not depart from worldly truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). As for the seal of the mind of the Buddhas of Unsurpassed Perfect Enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), its..."
"How is it used? The Master said: "The altar has many names; the wisdom of emptiness is supreme. A single thought, pure and perfect, is identical to the nature of the Dharma-realm.
Abiding in non-abiding, it is like space, having no dependence. One who reaches the height of such sincerity can even move heaven and earth."
Thus he moves spirits and deities; his wondrous, profound, and all-encompassing samādhi of the single mark possesses supernatural powers that are beyond the reach of thought.
It is for the sake of this great causal matter that the Buddha appears in the world; there is no second dharma, only the path of the One Vehicle.

As for establishing teachings in accordance with conditions and benefiting sentient beings by responding to their needs, the hundreds of thousands of *dharmaparyāyas* are all equally its wondrous function.

As for what is called "the wisdom of emptiness," it is the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*). Zhang Zhi sighed and said: "This is like clarified butter and sweet nectar—something I have never heard before.

I already knew that you, Master, had deeply realized the mark of the ultimate emptiness of phenomena through *prajñā*; it is not merely that you strictly purified the *vinaya* and were single-mindedly diligent."
He remained solely in meditative practice. On the twelfth day of the fourth month in the fourth year of the Xīníng era, his physical condition was as usual;

suddenly he spoke, saying, "Is my karmic retribution to end this very evening? At dusk, he returned to stillness. His disciples buried him on the eastern plain of Kāifēng County, where Lord Zhāng inscribed a stele for him.
The Elder Shitai transmitted the lineage of Shitai to the Elder Jie.
The Elder resided at Shitai Monastery in Yangzhou. When Dongpo was traveling to Dengzhou, the Master went there to welcome him.
Sūshun said, "I wished to see the stone pagoda, but because my journey was so swift, I did not have time. The Master stood up and said, "Is this merely a brick stupa?
Sūshun replied, "If there are seams, what can be done? The Master said, "If there were no seams, how could it contain the ants of the entire dharma-realm?
Later, when Sūshun was stationed in Weiyang, the Master sent an attendant to submit a petition for his release from the monastery. Sūshun asked, "The Elder..."
When asked where he wished to go in his old age, he replied that he intended to return to his former hermitage by West Lake.

Su Shi, together with his subordinates, went to Shitai Temple and struck the drum to assemble the congregation. From his sleeve, he produced a memorial and had Chao Wujiu read it aloud; the text said:
"The Elder Master Jie has opened the gate of non-duality and bestowed the treasury of the inexhaustible. His long absence from West Lake was merely a matter of circumstance."

If Dongpo had stayed for a little longer, there would have been nothing that could not have been accomplished. For a time, all bowed their heads in reverence as the mallet was struck again for the assembly.

As the boat returned from the ferry crossing, the colors of the clouds and mountains remained as before; yet with the arrival of autumn and the passing rain, the sounds of the bells and drums were entirely renewed.

Such was the deep affection and longing of the worthies of the age. The Elder must surely have been a man of renowned virtue at the time; it is only a pity that we cannot know the full details of his life’s beginning and end.
Zhitiān (also known as Yuánpǔ).

Zhitiān was born into the Chén clan of Quanzhou; he was the elder brother of the former Tongzhí (Court Gentleman) Jiān. Initially, he resided at Yúnhuá Yán in Nán'ān, later traveling to the capital where his reputation for the Way became widespread.
In the first year of the Yuánhòu era, an imperial edict summoned him into the palace to serve as a preceptor to Prince Suíníng.
On his birthday, he was granted the title Great Master Zhijue (True Awakening), along with a coarse cotton robe (*kāṣāya*), golden rings, a waist-belt, and a monk’s staff.

Emperor Zhezong personally wrote an imperial edict to present to him, granting permission for him to ordain monks every year and allowing him to reside at will in famous mountains and auspicious lands throughout the realm.
Initially, he resided at Fushan; subsequently, he stayed at Fuyan in Xiuzhou. Huang Tingjian, Assistant Director of the Court of Imperial Scribes, once presented him with a poem that said:
The rush mat and wooden bench are entrusted to the Zen master; the tea kettle and incense burner are shared with guests. Myriad households, scattered and uneven, reflect the bright moon;
a single family, solitary and sparse, shares the pure breeze. Furthermore, the eulogy says: "When stone emerges from the mountain, its resonance is like a lute;
when a pine does not wither, its skeletal form stands firm amidst frost and ice. Now, having obtained Yunmen’s hanging board, he has shattered the ghost cave and the spirit bed."
This rock is capable of producing clouds and rain across ten thousand *li*; these pines have long provided shade and coolness for the three realms.
This appears to be like the men of old, yet they are not the men of old; let my old friends in the mountains deliberate upon this. Minister Chen Xuan also presented him with a poem, which says:
"Wheel-ruts and hoofprints race through dust and smoke, All vying to watch the ten thousand torches burn in Chengdu. Only I tread open..."
Snow at the Pavilion. Master Bān sat together with Yuánpǔ in a single meditation hut. It is unknown from whom he received the Dharma;
he resided at Lèshān and named his hut Hǎihú (Sea Lake). He remained in seclusion, sitting upright for twenty years.

Jīng Gōngwàng, the Censor-in-Chief, composed a song to invite him, setting forth three questions to which [the Master] gave no reply. Whenever Gōngwàng sat upon the Fǎnyuǎn Terrace overlooking the district seat...
He bowed from afar toward the hermitage; such was the reverence he received from the worthies of his time.

After Fayun had departed, Duke Wang (Wang Gongwang) commemorated him with a poem and also composed the "Record of the Duoxia Pavilion," praising him as a recluse of Western Shu—this was because Fayun was indeed a native of Shu.
Both masters were renowned monks of Quan; people still speak of them to this day.
Baiyun Kong Qingjue’s lineage was transmitted by Qingjue, whose style name was Benran. He was the son of the Kong family of Dengfeng in Luojing and the fifty-third descendant of Confucius.
His father, Yin, was a jinshi graduate who possessed hidden virtue. His mother was Lady Cui. From childhood, Shi was exceptionally intelligent; he studied the Confucian classics.
In the second year of the Xining era, while reading the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, he attained a profound realization and sought ordination.

His parents granted him permission. He followed Great Master Haihui of Longmen in Ruzhou for tonsure and full ordination. Master Hai recognized his potential and instructed him to travel south to seek instruction. He first visited Qian at Mount Emei.
Master Suì received instructions from [his teacher] and traveled to Fushan in Shuzhou, where he built a hermitage at Taishouyan.

He sat in meditation there for twenty years until a realization dawned within him. In the eighth year of the Yuanyou era, he went to Hangzhou and entered Lingyin Monastery, where he lived among the assembly.
There were two practitioners, Wang and Luo, who sought the essential teachings of the Master. A single word from him struck the mark, and his influence resonated across a thousand li.

Those who came to inquire and receive instruction arrived like wind and rain. The abbot of the temple provided the Baiyun Mountain Hermitage behind the temple for them to reside in and propagate the Dharma.

He established his own school of thought and authored the *Zhèngzōnglùn* (Treatise on Proving the School), the *Sānjiàobiān* (Compilation of the Three Teachings), and the *Shídìgē* (Song of the Ten Stages), all of which were modeled after Buddhist scriptures.
People referred to his school as the Báiyún Zōng (White Cloud School). In the first year of the Daguān era, he pitched a hut at Qīnjiān Market in Húzhou.

He then traveled again to Jīngshān in Wūchéng, where he struck the ground with his monk’s staff and obtained a spring; he built a hermitage there to dwell, naming it Chūchén (Transcending the World). His disciples once again...

He was invited to return to Zhengji Temple. Zhengji was the site where Huiguang had formerly lectured on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Huiguang established his teachings specifically to denounce the Chan school.
Chan Master Yuhai of Fuyuan vigorously argued that Huiguang’s views were erroneous, leading to Huiguang’s imprisonment and banishment to Enzhou.

In the second year of the Xuanhua era, his disciples Zhengbu and others submitted a petition, and by imperial decree he was released and returned home. In the eighth month of the following year, he composed a verse and presented it to the Prefect, You.
The Duke requested leave, bidding farewell on the twenty-sixth day of the ninth month. When the appointed time arrived, he passed away.
His sacred remains and śarīra relics were returned for interment on the Southern Mountain of Yuhang.
The Way of the White Clouds is not pure; it is only fitting that criticism should be directed toward it.
To go so far as to equate it with the White Lotus Society, differing from them only in their lack of wives and children, is indeed excessive.

Nevertheless, his observance of the precepts was refined and meticulous, and in the face of suffering and death, he was liberated and unimpeded. He was far removed from ordinary people; therefore, I have adopted his conduct.
Later, he regretted having spoken those words.
As for Master Quan:

the state granted him the honorary title of Great Master Wenzhao. He was a native of Huating. His physical constitution was pure and frail; he devoted himself to practicing stillness by closing his door.

As for his affairs, he did not engage in casual socializing; only Liu Fa, the Assistant Administrator, would frequently visit him. [Fa] was skilled at playing the *qin* and possessed a fine instrument called "Resonant Spring" (*xiangquan*).

On fair winds and bright moons, [Zhao] would play it with refined incense, saying, "This is to be offered to the Buddha. His neighbors, being noble and envious of this, built a pavilion outside the wall to listen during the night.
When they learned of this, [Zhao] moved his window to the north. Liu Fa, relying on the teacher's recognition of him, occasionally invited a guest.
Tong Jianquan was just then tuning his strings for the introductory notes when a guest suddenly praised him as excellent. Jianquan immediately stopped; the guest departed displeased.
Jianquan looked back at Tanfa and said, "How could you have led a worldly person into my seat? Fa apologized in shame.

The master’s residence was called Miaoyin Pavilion (Tower of Wondrous Sound), for which Fa composed a record and presented a poem, saying: "What was obtained regarding the precious lute? That which was obtained..."
It is profoundly subtle and profound; I borrow briefly the resonance of the zither and lute to transcend the workings of wisdom. The frosty wind mourns the jade bridge-pins;
the river moon enters the pearl inlays. When all such conditions are exhausted here, who among men can judge right from wrong? Quan and Fa were both contemporaries of the Yuanyou era.

Chan Master Qianjian, whose name was Chuyan and courtesy name was Bowei, was the son of the Jia family of Leqing, Wenzhou. His mother was surnamed Wan. While she was pregnant, one night she dreamed that a black dragon leaped down from the sky;
it suddenly transformed into a Daoist immortal who entered her home. When he was born, there were extraordinary signs that alerted [the world].

His realization was extraordinary. Whenever he glanced at the classics and histories, he could recite them from memory. From his youth until adulthood, he abstained from eating meat; though his mother urged him otherwise, he ultimately did not comply.
One day, while visiting a monastery, he returned and said to his mother: "As for my vegetarian diet, living in the secular world is not suitable for me.

I wish to leave the household life to study the Buddha-dharma. He received the tonsure at Mingqing Monastery. Initially, he practiced the exegesis of the teachings, elucidating the doctrines of his masters. He attained full understanding.

He was free from doubt and hesitation. His peers were still engaged in compiling records and devoted themselves to mutual refutation; the Master, however, rejected this with his own mind and consequently abandoned the teachings to venerate Chan.
He traveled extensively to visit senior masters and elder practitioners, inquiring after and striking at the profound essence of the Dharma, attaining many points of realization.

When some offered him the position of head monk, the Master disregarded it and departed. Beyond his own spiritual realization, the Master was widely learned and capable in poetry and prose; he was pure, dignified, and profound.

He was elegant and skilled in calligraphy, possessing the stylistic methods of the Jin and Song dynasties. At that time, the two masters Daohan and Sincong were close associates of Dongpo (Suzhou Dongpo), and their reputations were widely renowned.

Someone once encouraged him to present his works to the gentry to seek a patron, but the Master laughed and said, "In antiquity, when śramaṇas associated with scholar-officials, it was not for the sake of seeking them out;
rather, the Way naturally brought them together. Thus, he never did so throughout his life.

He sought an audience with [the Emperor] using a single character; those who recognized his worth held him in high esteem. During the Yuanyou era, he returned to Yongjia and resided at various monasteries, including Jingguang, Dayun, and Kaiyuan.
His disciples followed him in great numbers as their master, and those who came to knock at his door to request instruction did so in continuous succession.

The Master instructed them in their fundamental studies, while additionally guiding them through poetry, the *Book of Documents*, the *Book of Songs*, and the histories of the *Zi* and *Shi*. All those who received his guidance attained realization.

Toujiao. At the beginning of the Yuánfú era, he returned to his former mountain. There he cleared away the weeds and built a thatched hut; he diverted the runoff and collected the flowing water, calling himself Qiánjiàn (Hidden Ravine).
He amused himself by composing poetry and playing the *qín*, possessing the "rustic air beneath the trees" of the ancients. The Master possessed eloquence and was skilled at lecturing and exegesis.

When the great families of the local district wished to entice him to lecture on the sutras, they were unable to bring him there. Consequently, they prepared a formal Dharma assembly and gathered a vast multitude.

A high seat was prepared in anticipation; once the Master arrived, the assembly urged him to take it. He hurriedly ascended the seat and expounded upon the profound essence [of the teachings], adorning his discourse with elegant literature.
His voice was resonant and clear, leaving the listeners both amazed and delighted. Governor Zhang Gongping received the great meaning of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* from the Master.
Initially, he had been appointed as the Head of the Sangha (*Sengzheng*), and later appointed to preside over the Chan seat; in both instances, the Master declined resolutely and would not accept.

Every time he went to the prefectural office, he carried a straw hat in his hand. Furthermore, because the Master was held in high esteem by the Prefect, the latter would entrust him with various matters.

The Master, however, would sternly refuse with a grave expression. Whenever there were administrative policies in the prefecture that were inconvenient for the people, the Master would explain them in detail; the Governor would then change his demeanor and listen attentively. When the Magistrate of Ruian, Mr.
Lü Qín, encountered the Master, he was overjoyed and accompanied him back to the county seat, where they built a hermitage on the grounds of the magistrate’s hall.

He repaired the rear garden and invited the Master to reside there. After staying for three nights, the Master departed. In his later years, he withdrew from all worldly affairs and diligently cultivated pure practices.
He recited the *Śūraṅgama*, *Awakening of Faith*, *Vimalakīrti*, *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, and *Lotus Sūtras* until they flowed from him with perfect fluency and mastery.
Sitting alone on a quiet night, he burned incense and recited [the scriptures] in silence; the clear, resonant sound issued forth beyond the forest canopy.

He once transcribed by hand the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Prabhāsa-sūtra* to repay his mother’s kindness, and further copied eighty fascicles of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, remaining diligent from beginning to end without slackening.

His calligraphy was exceptionally skillful. On the twentieth day of the first month of the Renchen year of the Zhenghe era, he manifested parinirvāṇa at the age of fifty-four and with thirty-nine years of monastic seniority (*bhikṣu-vaṃśa*).
Upon cremation, several hundred *śarīra* relics were obtained, as brilliant and lustrous as pearls.
A stupa was erected behind his former residence, where his remains and the *śarīra* were interred. Regarding Buddhist studies, there was nothing the Master did not thoroughly understand.

He was particularly profound in Chan, yet he engaged with sentient beings through formal instruction; thus, he became renowned as a *śrāmaṇera*. Throughout his life, he produced a great many writings, but his manuscripts were mostly destroyed and lost.
After his parinirvāṇa, his disciples collected his surviving works and compiled them into two volumes titled the *Qianjian ji* (Collected Works from the Hidden Stream).
Whenever anyone obtained even a fragment of paper or a single character of his writing, they treasured it as a hidden jewel. His literary style was held in high esteem by...
