People say this: (The mother of Wang Meixi Shi-peng was pregnant. On the day she gave birth, she dreamed that the Master came to bestow upon her a golden ring. When she awoke from the dream, the Master had just passed away while sitting in meditation.

The next day, Meixi was born. Everyone considered him to be the Master’s reincarnation. Thus, in the preface to the inscription he wrote for the Master, it says: "In the year the Master passed away, I was first born. The Master had previously written the stele for Shiqiao Temple. When Meixi, serving as a Vice Commissioner in Shaoxing, traveled through the temple on his way, the monks there had previously dreamed of welcoming the Venerable Yan.

The next day, Meixi arrived. The monks informed him of their dream, and he composed a poem which said: "People call me the Venerable Head Seat Yan; in a former life, I once wrote the Shiqiao Stele. Zhen Longyou, in his poem matching Gong’s "Shuangfeng," said: "The Poet-Old Man [Gong]... )
His physical appearance was dignified and majestic (this refers precisely to this matter).
Biography of Chan Master Canliao (appended by Dingzhu):
Daoqian, styled Canliao, was the son of the He family from Yushan in Hangzhou. In his youth, he underwent ordination after reciting the *Lotus Sūtra*. Regarding books, he had no...

He was one whom none could fathom. He was capable in the composition of prose and, in particular, took great delight in writing poetry. He maintained a relationship of "external friendship" with Qin Taixu and Su Changgong (Su Shi).
Su Shi held him in high esteem and wrote to Wen Yukai, stating that his poetic lines were pure and exquisite, ranking equal to those of Lin Bu, and that he thoroughly understood the Great Meaning;
upon seeing him, one was struck with a sense of solemn reverence. When Su Shi was exiled to Qian’an, he... [the master]... served him.
He traveled more than two thousand *li* to visit [the Master], remaining for a full year. They moved to Ruhu Sea and traveled together to Mount Lu. Later, they returned to the mountains of Quanzhen.
When Su [Shunqin] governed Qiantang, he selected a site at Zhiguo Monastery on Mount Shan and led sixteen of his guests, each composing a poem to see him off as he entered the monastery.
Subsequently, the Master intended to travel south by sea to visit him; Su [Shunqin] sent a letter.
Su Guozhi suppressed him. The authorities also collected the Master’s poems and sayings, claiming they contained satirical criticism; consequently, he was disgraced and returned to lay life.

At the beginning of the Jianzhong Jinggu era, when Zeng Zhao served in the Hanlin Academy, he declared that [the accusations against] him were unjust. By imperial decree, he was restored to the monastic order and granted the title of Grand Master Miaozong.
Toward the end of the Chongning era, he retired to live out his final years at Mount Qian. His *Collected Works of Chanliaozi* circulated in the world; people said—
The Master’s poetry is refined, simple, and sincere; it aspires to emulate Tao Qian and Bai Juyi, while on a lower level it forms a "wild goose flight" with Su Shi and Huang Tingjian.
Although he has not yet entirely escaped the "smoke and fire" of Zizhan (Su Shi), he does not delight in sharing that same "smoke and fire" with Song dynasty poets.
As for Canliao, he remains true to himself as Canliao; he is not esteemed merely because of his connection to Zizhan. These words are definitive and certain. He was a native of Jinjiang.

He was capable of composing poetry; his diction was clear and remote, devoid of any vulgar or worldly air. He associated with various eminent figures such as Zeng Hui, and those who discussed him remarked that his poems were of the same tonal register as those of Chanliao.
His inscription for a painted water-screen reads: "Where there are no waves, waves arise;
it grieves the solitary wanderer crossing the sea. He had a collection titled *Yùhuá jí* (Gathering of Fallen Flowers), which was roughly of this character.
Song Jingliao composed the inscription for the Yewangshan Monastery, stating:

"On one day, Dajue Liaoyi, along with Jiufeng Shaogong, Foguo Baigong, and Chanliao Qiangong, discussed the Way in a single room which they named 'The Hall of Obscurity' (Mengtang); the monastic community took this as a model.
(This may be included in the biographical records.)
The Head Seat Huìyuǎn transmitted [the Dharma] to the Head Seat Huìyuǎn.
A native of the north, he was solitary and firm in his self-reliance. Having studied under Huìtáng and Zhēnjìng, he truly attained a state of realization;
yet he lived inconspicuously among the community, such that no one recognized him. At Huì'ān Yù in Fēngxīn, Hóngzhōu, his quarters faced the gate.
To the left of the road, monks passed back and forth; there was no one who did not travel by way of Huanglong, Ledu Tan, Dongshan, and Huangbo.
By chance, the Dharma seat had been vacant for a long time, and the Prefect sent a letter to Zhenjing, ordering him to select someone to preside over it.
The head monks, administrators, and senior elders all dreaded the task. When the Master heard of this, he said to Zhenjing, "Would Huiyuan be able to go? Zhenjing replied, "You..."

He departed. He then sent a reply letter recommending the Master. Upon receiving the official document, the Master took his leave immediately. At that time, Zhantang was the Head Seat (Zuoyuan). He asked the Master, "How will you manage the abbacy once you have gone?
The Master replied, "I have no merit; I shall simply cultivate karmic connections with all people.

I shall carry a wicker basket on my back and go through the streets to provide for the assembly. Zhantang said, "You must indeed be an elder brother like this to succeed. He then composed a verse to see him off.

The Master resided at Huian Temple and provided daily offerings. Whenever someone arrived briefly, he would invite them back to the temple to rest, saying, "Please allow me to return once I have finished preparing the offerings.
He maintained this practice for thirty years without wavering even in wind or rain. He subsequently renovated and newly constructed the Buddha Hall.
The Wheel Repository (Lun-zang) and the Hall of Arhats—whatever is traditionally required for a monastic community—were all fully prepared there.
When Chan Master Sisi of Huanglong visited him, the Master said, "New Elder, you have always loved to employ that one 'point' of hidden intelligence to sweep away people.
Tonight, stay here for a while so that we may discuss some subtle and great Dharma gates together. The New [Elder] was intimidated by this.
He said to his attendant, "This man truly understands; I cannot match him in wordplay or debate.
It is better to leave and stop here. Without staying overnight, he departed. The Master passed away at Huian. During his cremation, three of his sense organs remained unburnt.

Countless śarīra relics were obtained, and a wondrous fragrance filled the hall, continuing for many months without ceasing. When the new army arrived, everything was reduced to ruins with nothing remaining;
yet the various halls of Huian alone stood firm and survived. Is this not the fulfillment of his vow-power and the protection of divine beings?

The Biography of Juexin (with the appended biographies of his successors Zhiyong and Zuoshao) Juexin, whose courtesy name was Xujing, was the son of a wealthy farming family in Jiajiang, Jiazhou. In his youth, he was fond of hunting;

one day, however, he released his hawks and dogs, abandoned his wife and children, and left home to study the Way. He traveled extensively through the clouds and waters, appearing to have attained some realization. By nature, he was fond of...
He was skilled at painting grasshoppers and insects; people called him "Heart-Grass-Insect" (Xin Caocong).

He traveled through the Central Plains and composed the *Tongdu Tu* (Diagram of the Following Calf) and its accompanying poem, which caused a sensation throughout the age. Scholars and officials alike unanimously revered him as their master.
Kong Nanming and Cui Defu invited him to Linru, where he resided at three major monasteries: Danchan in Ye County, Tianning, and Xiangshan in the prefecture. Later, due to the military upheavals...
He returned to Shu during the period of turmoil. The two Shangshu Lang, Shao Zemin and Liu Zhongyuan, appreciated his work and invited him to reside at Bili Monastery.
Chen Jian praised him, saying: "What the Master Xu Jing has realized is the Way. He expresses himself freely in poetry and plays with ease in painting;
like mist, clouds, water, and moon, he appears and disappears within the Great Void. Is this not what is called 'the wind blowing over the water, naturally forming patterns and textures'?"
Later, he passed away at his residence.

There was also Zhi Yong (智永), who followed his lineage; both of them expressed their intent through poetry and painting. Zhi Yong once painted a "Night Rain over Xiao and Xiang" (*Xiāngxiāng yèyǔ tú*) and presented it to Shao Xishan.
Shao inscribed upon it: "I once envisioned a light boat on the western waters of the Xiang; by the window of my thatched hut, I trimmed the candle and counted..."
"Period of Return. At the place where Master Hui wielded his brush for this poem, I am reminded instead of that night of the heavy rain.
Suspecting this, he asked Yong: "Have any of the seniors ever composed such a verse? Yong then recited Yi-shan’s "Inquiry on Returning Home.

Seeing this, Xi-shan was startled and subsequently revised the work. Yong was by nature filial; when Yu Wen-jimon, the Dragon-Tu Official, praised Yong for his mastery of Chan principles and his skill in... [the text ends here].

They conversed and invited him to reside at the monastery. Zongyong declined, saying, "My parents are still living; I cannot do so yet. Thereupon, he sold his own skills to provide for his parents' sustenance.
As for his poetry and painting, Zongfu modeled himself after Zhou Wangji, yet his spirit and resonance were exceptionally transcendent.

During the Zhenghe era, when the imperial decree was issued to change monks to "De-shi" (Virtuous Men), Zongfu sighed and said, "In my life, I have never turned my back on the Buddha; would I now follow a heterodox path? He then took... [the text ends here].
He burned his *sibu* (Bureau of Sacrifices) certificate and returned to lay life, wearing a cap and headcloth. He observed the precepts for the remainder of his life.
Master Yuan of Qian’an inherited the lineage of Qingyuan; he was styled Qian’an.

He was the son of the Deng family of Xinjian in Hongzhou. His family had been farmers for generations. From childhood, he was exceptionally outstanding; though small in stature, he was of great spirit.
He was vigorous and incisive. He went to rely on Hongya Fazhi as a novice. At the age of twenty-one, he shaved his head and received full ordination.
At that time, Wuquan Chang, Baofeng Yue, and Yunju Shun possessed a reputation for the Way that eclipsed the entire monastic community; the Master frequented the company of these three elders.

He was accepted by all as a worthy vessel, yet his doubts remained unresolved. Later, he met Master Huanglong Nan publicly; whenever Nan entered the room for instruction, he would have him sit beside him.
Together with Yun’an, he went to Jicui, where the Master served as attendant for seven years. After Nan passed away, he lived in seclusion at Xishan. At Xishan there was Huiyan Monastery;
when a monk died, the hall was without images or ritual furnishings, and the monks sat in the open air. Upon seeing this, the Master...

He sighed, saying: "The ancients cleared mountains to establish their foundations and attained the state of non-action; how could one who possesses such forbearance fail to bring it forth? He then sought a dwelling to repair and complete it.
Within five years, the halls and pavilions were magnificently finished and all things were renewed. He then departed to travel to Mount Lu.
Hearing of the Master’s reputation, Xu Gong, the Governor of Nankang, invited him to reside at Qingyin Temple on South Mountain. The temple was located...
To the north of the Great River, facing Mount Lu, the Master’s teaching style was solitary and austere; students all retreated upon merely beholding his precipitous presence.

Consequently, he dwelt alone on the mountain for eighteen years. Morning incense and evening lamps, ascending the hall to preach the Dharma as if before a thousand-fold assembly, he possessed every requisite for a monastic community.
From time to time, he would dig the earth with a hoe to arrange his surroundings, once saying: [The text ends here.]

The former master first served Xián Qīxián and Lètán Chéng for twenty years; there was nothing among the marvelous mysteries of the Chan school or the essential subtleties of the sutras and śāstras that he did not thoroughly penetrate.
However, when he encountered Címíng through Wényuè, not a single word remained of use.

Címíng established three barriers to test the Chan practitioners of the world, yet those practitioners were like Yè Gōng’s painted dragons: as soon as the dragon appeared, they were struck with terror.

Sentient beings act as obstacles to liberation; Bodhisattvas have not yet transcended conceptualization. Even Mañjuśrī, possessed of great wisdom, when wishing to inquire about the meaning of the Dharma from the Buddha Śūnyatā-rāja, was immediately expelled.
This was because he had fallen into difficulties, and thus his active afflictions (*saṃmukhībhūta-kleśa*) arose.

There was a monk who studied under a teacher for twelve years, and the teacher sent him to stay at Jingzhong Temple. As he was taking his leave, the teacher said to him: "Although you have been here..."
He spent months and years [in study], yet truly did not understand the affairs of our house. Had he succeeded to the Dharma, he ought not to have made worldly deception his concern.
That man, however, inherited the lineage of Cuiyan. The reclusive gentleman of Nanchang, Pan Yanzhi, became a fellow traveler with him beyond the secular world.
He invited the Master to return to Xishan, but various local officials vied for his presence; consequently, by imperial decree, he was appointed to reside at Tianning. Disciples such as Fangyun...

He hurried to his seat below. At that time, renowned scholars came, adjusting their robes and seeking instruction. Because the Master suffered from eye disease, he lived in seclusion within the quarters of Longxing Temple;

yet the shoes outside his door were already piled high. Zhonggong of Shanglan was his Dharma-nephew; he invited the Master to reside in the East Hall of the temple and served him just as he had served his own teacher.
When the Master reached the age of eighty and lost his sight, students flocked to him with even greater devotion. There was...

Wishing to have his words carved onto wooden blocks for wide circulation, the Master threw them away in refusal, saying, "If my words are in deep accord with the Buddhas and Patriarchs, they shall become clear again within one hundred days from now;
only then will I grant your request. As the period ended, the illness was indeed cured.

Previously, when Master Juefan Hong had been imprisoned in Taiyuan, he was bound and confined in a guesthouse; people avoided seeing him, but the Master alone braved the rain and walked there on foot to offer him comfort.
It was his final parting from death. The following year, when he returned south and saw the Master again, the Master laughed heartily and said, "I did not expect to see you again.
Thus Juefan wrote in his preface: "Alas! As the Buddha-dharma gradually recedes, those who wear tattered robes and use earthenware vessels..."

There were also those who harbored extravagant desires. Those who served as teachers vied with one another to admire grand buildings and seek comfort and warmth; you alone raised up what was dilapidated and renovated it.
They vied with one another to attract disciples, regardless of whether they were wise or foolish, desiring them to enter their schools; you alone distinguished between the refined and the coarse.
They vied with one another to sit at the head of the eight-lane thoroughfares to sell their own doctrines; you alone dwelt in remote and desolate places.
He cherished this [teaching] for himself. While others vied for power and profit and loathed what was base and ugly, he alone defied these common evils;

trusting in his own convictions, he practiced them with vigor. He often said to his disciples: "There is no principle outside of phenomena, nor any phenomenon outside of principle. Observe how he applied this in every action.
Could this truly be so? When the Master passed away, he was nearly a hundred years old.
Biography of Chan Master Chongjue Kong:
Chan Master Chongjue Kong was a native of Gushu. By nature, he was headstrong. Having attended Sishi for a long time, one day he took his leave.
Ququ said, "Your merit is meager; you should nourish yourself. Master Qing of Caotang sent him off with this verse: "Ten years we gathered at Longfeng Temple;
A single awakening to the void left all realms at rest. Go henceforth as circumstances lead, and remain in lofty seclusion; Do not let your name fall among the common folk of the world.
Later, he accepted an invitation to take charge of the world at Nandang in Hangzhou. Before many months had passed, the monastery was consumed by fire.
Nothing was left out. He sighed and said, "I have contravened the words of my former teacher, and thus I suffer this present affliction.

There was a wealthy man who resolved to build a monastery, wishing for the Master to visit his home once to receive offerings. The Master declined, saying, "The public bestows wealth to seek merit; it is not for an Elder to personally accept such gifts.
If you were to instruct me to eat apart from the assembly, that has always been something I have not desired. Thus he practiced with diligent resolve.
Throughout his life, he never engaged in the labor of building temples or monuments. The Master offered this verse on the "Wild Fox" kōan:
"Sputting blood at others first soils one’s own mouth; Baizhang’s wild fox lost its head and ran madly away. Suddenly called back, it performed a somersault."
Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks,
Volume Twenty-three and Volume Twenty-four.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Minghe of Huashan Temple in Wumen, Ming Dynasty.
*Zakepian* (Miscellaneous Section on Doctrines) Biography of Master Yuanjue Yan Yan was a native of Enzhou in Hebei.
His secular surname was Cui. He was a disciple of Chan Master Man of the Yuanfeng era and propagated the Yunmen school.

He was one who embodied the Way. His appearance was dignified and orderly, and his observance of the precepts was strict and meticulous. During the Xuanhong era, Emperor Huizong summoned him into the inner court to preach the Dharma and bestowed upon him a purple cassock.
He possessed great karmic affinity at that time and resided in a total of thirteen monasteries over the course of his career.

He ordained more than one thousand two hundred disciples. While he was residing at Yongfuk Nengren Temple, there was previously a temple monk who had captured a macaque, bound it alive, and molded it with clay, calling it the "Monkey King.
As years passed, it eventually became a malevolent spirit haunting the local residents.
Those who encountered it would first suffer from severe chills and fever, gradually falling into madness and losing their appetite; they would then climb over fences and ascend [into trees].
The wooden [image] would suddenly cast itself to the ground, often causing death; children were especially victimized. Consequently, those who worshipped it increased in number.

When sacrifices failed to cure the affliction, they summoned shamans and sorcerers who arrived before the temple at nightfall, sounding gongs and blowing horns, which they called "summoning the structure.
The monks of the temple also struck bells and drums in response to them, claiming to assist the deity. This practice grew more frequent day by day and month by month.
"No one has corrected you. When the Master arrived and moved his residence to this temple, he heard of this and sighed, saying: "You may be said to suffer to the utmost.
Those who killed you have already received their retribution, yet your lust extends even to other men; as your accumulated karma deepens further, when will you ever be liberated?"

He recited the Great Compassion Mantra for her benefit and deliverance. That night, while sitting in meditation, the Master saw a woman with a human body and monkey feet, her left armpit stained with blood.
Beside her was a small monkey whose two hands were bound by an iron chain around its waist. It held a young girl in its arms and bowed twice before him, saying:
"I am a monkey king. For a long time I have suffered the pain of deep grievance, but through the power of the Dharma, I have now attained liberation."

He ascended, and thus came to offer his thanks. He further requested that the master untie the rope binding the little monkey. The master complied and spoke this verse: "The Monkey King has long endured the suffering of confinement;
Through the secret aid of the Dharma-power, he has attained the heavens. One must believe that one's own mind is originally the Buddha."
The numinous light shone through with penetrating brilliance, leaving no distinction between center and periphery. Having heard the verse, he prostrated twice and departed.

The next day, when he opened the hall, he found it secured by three layers of locks; this was because, some years prior, a sorcerer had shot an arrow that struck his left armpit, and for this reason he had always kept it tightly closed.
A monkey carried off a small girl exactly as he had seen her, and he then smashed the statue. Furthermore, more than thirty of its attendants were likewise reduced to fragments by crows and vultures.

This was the doing of the kindred of owls and nightjars. When he threw them into the mountain stream, the monsters were finally extinguished. Later, the Master returned to Xuefeng, where he spent the remainder of his life.
(Recorded by Zhenbao of the Song dynasty, based on the account of Qingyu.)

Zhenbao was a monk of Mount Wutai who, in his practice of the Way, had mastered the transcendence of life and death. During the disturbances of the Jingkang era, he trained in martial arts with his disciples within the mountains.
Emperor Qinzhong summoned him for an audience in the private hall; moved by this honor, Bao returned to the mountain and further gathered a multitude to practice martial skills.

When the prefectural seat could no longer be held and enemy forces arrived in great numbers, Bao exerted all his strength to resist them, but they were not matched. The monasteries were burned to the ground.
The monks fled and dispersed. The chieftain issued an order to capture Zhenbao alive. When Bao arrived, he spoke with firm resolve and remained undisturbed.

The prefect Liu Tai employed a hundred methods of persuasion to entice him, but in the end, he paid no heed. He further declared, "The Buddha has established the precepts; I have already pledged my life to the Emperor of Song.
How could I, through the exhaustion of my strength, betray my word? Simply execute me quickly. Thereupon, he accepted his execution with a serene countenance.
Among the northerners who heard of this, there were none who did not marvel and express their admiration.
Qingyu was the son of the Hu family from Jinshan in Nanjing; he sought the Way from Master Furong Kai and grasped its essential principles. He resided at Dahong Mountain.

When the bandits rose during the Jingkang era, the surrounding regions were thrown into turmoil, yet Qingyu remained composed and leisurely in his daily conduct while outwardly preparing for a firm defense.

Internally, he remained tranquil and focused, diligently practicing meditation and recitation to stabilize the resolve of the assembly. After several years of this, he sustained more than ten thousand people;

among the families of the scholar-officials, those who relied on him for their livelihood numbered seventeen or eighteen out of ten. When the situation had somewhat stabilized, he moved to Xingguo Temple on the south side of the river.

Upon learning of this, the local governor memorialized the throne, and he was granted the honorary title Huizhao (Wisdom Illumination). During the Shaoxing era, he traveled to Mount Kuang and entered the region of the Eight Min, where he took a liking to the snow.
Fengshen was profound and beautiful. He remained in seclusion for over ten years. When he was about to pass away, he addressed the assembly and wrote a verse, saying:
"The final phrase is most difficult to clarify; To turn back and look around involves thousands of miles. Except for my own true son, Who else would dare to tread within?
He threw down his brush, smiled, and passed into stillness.
Song Dynasty: Biography of Zhirong of Laoniuzhuang.
Zhirong’s secular surname was Xing; his original name was Cheng. His family had resided in the capital for generations. He entered government service as a physician.

After the southward migration, he settled on Wansong Ridge in Lin’an, where he styled himself "Ca'ān" (The Hermitage). He served as the official Xing Langzhong until the Chenghe era, during which time he frequently entered and exited the imperial palace to receive honors.
He was granted exceptional imperial favor. At the age of fifty, he resigned his office and took leave of his wife and children; shaving his head, he entered Lingyin Monastery.

Although various officials and nobles sought to dissuade him, they could not prevail. Thus, while remaining no great distance from the secular world, he traveled extensively through various regions, including Mount Jing and Mount Lu.
Having traveled almost everywhere, he heard of the excellence of Xuedou and consequently settled there, intending to spend the remainder of his life.

He sat deeply within a single room, his physical form appearing as mere wood and earth, so utterly detached that he resembled a wooden puppet. Occasionally he would go out leaning on a staff; if anyone wished to follow him, he would decline and dismiss them.
In the secluded and sublime locations of the mountains, he wandered or sat alone, sometimes remaining there for hours until no one else was present.
He peered into its depths and found it was a master of painting, yet he never gave his works to others. In the deep mountains there were many snakes;
he suddenly depicted two strange ghosts on a wall—one blowing fire toward the sky, the other leaping upon a snake and seizing its tail—whereupon the plague of snakes was finally eliminated.

Later, when there were frequent alarms of fire, he again depicted the cry of an earth-owl at the tip of a flame, and the danger was thereby averted. He once painted the head of a dragon, leaving it half-finished.
Whenever he offered prayers for rain during a drought, it would invariably respond; this was somewhat bordering on the miraculous. Yet the Master did not take pride in this himself.

Someone once asked about painting, and when the conversation turned to human figures, the Master said, "I am too old to paint them anymore; my eyesight has grown dim and I cannot bring myself to lay down two brushstrokes. He said:
"Those two strokes—could they not be within 'this' (the sphere of the spirit)? The Master said, "Although this is an ancient saying, it is close but not quite right.
What I mean by 'two strokes' is that when one wishes to depict a person, one must first paint the upper eyelid.
If these two strokes capture the person's intent, then everything else follows from those strokes and the spirit becomes complete. This is why it is so difficult. Or he added:
Regarding matters of status and profit, he avoided them all the more deeply; yet if his mind was in accord with another’s, he would immediately grant his favor without stint.
Lou Gonggui sought [his calligraphy] for a long time without success, until he urged him with a poem in the "Ancient Style" (gufeng), which said: "The ancients valued ink as they valued gold;
the old Rong valued ink as he valued his life. He composed few poems and used few words; his paintings likewise lacked vulgar airs. Initially, he himself had said: "If..."

He became a monk and closed his eyes in meditation for thirty autumns; with no words, all affairs came to rest. He passed away in the fifth month of the fourth year of the Shaohui era at the age of eighty;
his years as a monk matched what he had previously predicted. He was particularly fond of acting like an ox and styled himself "The Old Ox Zhirong."

Minghe said: "How profound! This is indeed a discourse on painting that fuses [the art of] oxen-slaughter with its principles. I have heard the words of Cook Ding and thereby attained the way of nourishing life.
Translated by Song Chun, Custodian of the Repository.
Zhangshu Jingchun was a disciple who received his full ordination at Huadu Monastery in Fuzhou. He had long studied under Master Bao Fengxiang and emerged as an outstanding figure among the assembly.
His character was refined and noble, as fully evidenced by his own poems on mountain dwelling. When Master Xiang saw them, he cautioned Chün, saying:
"These poems are no inferior to those of Guankui; I fear that the world will regard you for your literary skill rather than your Way, and thus the Dharma will not be truly believed in by others."
There are several dozen poems in total; I now record ten chapters here to ensure their transmission. I am naturally coarse and straightforward, knowing myself to be far removed from worldly ways;
dull and foolish, I have managed to dwell deep within the mountains. For my livelihood in this life, I possess nothing else but a weathered staff of one *zhen* (approx.
2.3 meters). My cottage, with its few rafters, overlooks the water and rocks; a single path leads to my gate, where climbing vines and creepers hang. It is because of this place that—

It is fitting to cast my old age here; may I have enough to enjoy the mountain streams and clouds passing by morning and evening. I smile at myself for being as reckless as Shidde, yet who would know that my dullness is like Nanquan’s?
Several times I have grown weary from wandering the mountains after a full meal; thus, I simply sleep wherever I am, in my clothes. Where the earthen cauldron is heated, pure smoke mists the air;
when the iron chime is struck, its dawn melody is cold. My single string of prayer beads is coarse and heavy; I pick them up—
Come, let us not deceive one another with the hundred and eight worldly concerns. Yanzi’s single ladle was no mere pursuit of pleasure; Sima Xiangru’s four walls were not the height of nobility.
How can these compare to the true livelihood of a mountain dweller? Above the eaves, the pine notes resonate like the autumn tides. A few lines of large characters upon *bēṭā* leaves;

a single stick of coarse incense at the roots of ancient cypresses. In the stillness of the stone chamber, spring days are drawn out long; the cries of the cuckoo on its staff break through the falling petals.
Flower Village. The Fisherman Father and Son sing the Song of Ambrosia, imitating the *Hanshan* verses on the Lamp of Dharma.

Do not say there is no one to hear you amidst the deep clouds; the myriad phenomena are all clearly known. Sitting upon the rock, one already feels the marrow and bones grow cold; rinsing the mouth at the spring, one perceives the teeth and gums becoming clear.
Within this there is a flavor that causes the thought of returning home to be forgotten; with nothing remaining in body or world, one accords with this sentiment. Deep Crags.
Sitting in stillness, I come to tame the tigers; walking along the ancient stream, I naturally grow intimate with the gulls. This is not because I have forgotten my faculties or severed all thoughts;

it is simply that, having reached old age, I have found the rest of the mind. Afraid of the cold, I am too lazy to shave my tangled hair; loving the warmth, I frequently add more firewood to the hearth.
"Brown robes hang in disarray; who could labor so hard to arrange them? This verse expresses a state of leisure and ease with such perfection that it is truly unsurpassed.
Were it not for what was nurtured within his heart, who could have achieved this? Alas, as the Way of the Dharma did not take hold, he spent his life in indolence until old age.
In the end, he fulfilled the words of Master Xiang and left the expectations of those from all quarters in vain.
Biography of Chan Master Jian of Beijian, Song Dynasty.

Jian, whose courtesy name was Jingsou, was the son of the Wang family of Tongchuan. His natural disposition was exceptionally sharp and extraordinary. Whenever he first encountered Buddhist scriptures, he would invariably sit upright in silent contemplation as if they were familiar from a previous life.
He received the full precepts at Guangfu Monastery in his hometown under the guidance of Tuche. He subsequently went to visit Biefeng Xuyun.

At Jingshan, he immersed himself in silent contemplation. One day, while reading the records of Wan’an, he attained a realization. He immediately went to Yuyang to see Fozhao; their spiritual faculties were in accord.

From then on, he came and went at his gate for fifteen years. Among the eminent elders of the community at that time, there was none who did not treat him as an equal, setting aside age differences to become his friend.
He traveled to Jiangxi to visit the sites associated with the various patriarchs. Ying Zhongwen once served as his attendant.
Dahui’s record [states]: "An-yuan Lake compiled what he had heard into a book to elucidate the ancestral Way. The Master found his discussions with the teacher most extraordinary.
After a long time, Dahui, who was residing at the Yangyu Hermitage, entrusted the bamboo cane to the Master, Xun. Long thereafter...

The *Prajñā* [monastery] of Chuzhu Tai was moved to Baoen, where eminent monks vied to join him as disciples. The great scholars Qian Zhuyan and Ye Shuixin both humbled themselves to seek the Way from his feet.
When Zhen Xishan, the Grand Councilor, served as the Imperial Commissioner for Jiangdong, he offered the position of Abbot at Donglin to him;
however, he declined on the grounds of illness and instead cleared a site at Beijian on Feilai Peak.
He resided in his quarters for ten years; people did not dare address him by his courtesy name, instead referring to him as "The Man of the Northern Gorge.
He was invited to serve at Tiefo Temple in Xiya, Zhejiang; Xianqing and Biyun Temples in Changzhou; Huiri Temple in Suzhou; and Daochang Temple on Mount Hu.

By imperial decree, he was transferred to Jingci Temple. Wherever he went, his spiritual transformation and teachings flourished greatly. The Master emerged from the lineage of Fozhao and was among the most eminent of the Dharma-yanas.

He was like a divine steed or a fragrant elephant; his spiritual capacity and character were transcendent and peerless, most difficult to emulate or approach. His verse on the story of the World-Honored One’s birth says:

"A single cry, *kili*, and the earth shook; Suddenly emerged such a great *icchantika*. From this land and the Western Heaven, calamity and harm arise; Majestically, he washes the soil until it is no longer mud.
Furthermore, his verse on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*’s "six functions dissolve and one perishes" says: "The six functions..."
Without merit, faith does not penetrate; all at once, it is entrusted to the spring breeze. A single curl of incense smoke lingers idly through the clear day;
though no birds come, the flowers are naturally red. He cleared a room for his dwelling and named it the "Garlic Room" (*xièshì*), composing a rhapsody to express himself.

Its summary says: Advancing, one faces a wall; retreating, one sits in a well. The pillar suddenly fails to support, and the wall is about to collapse. Suddenly it becomes empty and vast, desolate yet luminous.
It is like striking a veil of mist, like being startled by a thunderclap. It is like an inexhaustible treasury, like a great round mirror.
The front mountain presents its greenness, as if a strong man were pushing open a gate; the back mountain turns to peer back, like a skilled artisan at work.
He drives his swift steed, strokes the great swans and cranes as he gazes afar at twilight. He enters the profound darkness and draws far away, laughing at the light departure of clouds and mist.
Wandering aimlessly and without fixed destination, he halts the setting sun upon the western peaks and extends the first crescent moon over the eastern ridges;
all these are what he attains within. There is the *Beijian ji* (North Gully Collection) in nineteen fascicles. Zhang Gongchengzi wrote its preface, saying: "Having read..."

As for his writings, Zongmi did not know which of the two brothers was superior; yet when he recited his poetry, it could not be matched by the combined efforts of Canliao and Juefan as a single person.
Beijian did not readily seek conformity with others, nor did he readily diverge from them;

in matters of acceptance and rejection, or advancement and withdrawal, he remained pure and unblemished. Ye Shuixin’s poem says: "Master Jian’s poetic diction is truly startling; six times he has overturned [the conventions]."
Teng remained motionless in his body and spoke to the young son and daughter of the eastern neighbor: "Coated in blue and dyed in green, spring cannot yet be restrained.

While the Master resided at Weiyu on Mount Tiantai, two families were contending over a bamboo mountain; they exhausted their resources yet would not desist. Wang Junyi, the Magistrate of Xianju, petitioned the Master on their behalf.
The Master composed a "Rhapsody on Planting Bamboo" and presented it to the two families, whereupon the litigation ceased. Such was his virtue.
His spiritual influence was thus transformative. When the position at Lingyin Monastery became vacant, Zhao Jiezhai memorialized the throne to appoint the Master to fill it.

The Master smiled and said, "My time is drawing near. He then nominated Chijue Chong of Tiantong. On the twenty-eighth day of the third month in the spring of the *Chunyou* cycle year (1266), he requested paper and wrote a verse.
At the bottom of the paper, he further inscribed the six characters: "The first day of the fourth month—take care."
He summoned his disciples and exhorted them, saying, "Time does not wait for man; let this serve as my own admonition. My worldly ties remain for only two days more.
When the appointed time arrived at dawn, he requested a bath. After bathing, he took a short nap; yet when they looked upon him, he had already passed away.

He was eighty-three years of age and sixty-two years since his ordination (*śrāmaṇera*). His entire body was interred beside the stupa of Master Chang of Yuetang, in accordance with his final instructions.
The two masters Jiān and Níng of Gǔshān transmitted [the Dharma] to Míjiān, whose style name was Shìshì.
He was the son of the Chén family of Míngqīng. Possessing sharp and keen faculties, he visited various monastic seats;
finally, upon meeting Mǎogōng Xiù, their minds met like a lid fitting its box, and he subsequently received the robe of Dòngshān.
Zhengning was from the Li family of Ta Hu in Shu Zhou. He was a fellow disciple of Jian, and both had attained the Way of Master Xiu.

Fa Lin relied upon him as a pillar of strength. Ning possessed a robust and dignified appearance; wherever he went, crowds gathered to gaze upon him, and offerings were bestowed in mountain-like heaps.

At the beginning of the Jiaxi era, he entered Min, where the provincial governor invited him to reside at Guqiao. His reputation for integrity and conduct spread far and wide, and the fourfold assembly looked up to him with deep admiration, as if seeing the Buddha manifest before them.
During his time at Rulai [Temple], he accepted offerings from the faithful numbering in the tens of millions, all of which he used entirely for the maintenance of the resident community.

For over thirty years, he wore plain clothes and slept upon paper quilts, never once changing his attire until the end of his life. By renouncing worldly pleasures, the character of what he preserved can be generally understood. He passed away during the Xianchun era.
Upon cremation, his prayer beads remained unburnt, and the *śarīra* relics within his teeth were like a pile of bricks—so firm that they persisted. Thus it was with Jie.

Ning was a *zhuchi* (abbot) whose pure aura overwhelmed all who encountered him. Although his fortune and conditions were slightly inferior to those of Ning, his opening of the gate of wisdom and his capacity for reception surpassed him.

Daily he wore the robes of Mount Dongshan while preaching the Dharma; the sound of his teaching spread far and wide. At the place where he kept his robes, there was once a light that was as white as day at night.
Two thieves entered the room to steal them, but they were bound to the ground by a deity. Upon looking [at them], they saw...

He could not rise; he remained steadfast in his repentance and apology. Only then did he revive and depart. During the Deyou era, when the court intended to move southward, an imperial decree was issued to expand the city walls and ramparts.
He requested that Jian be appointed as the supervisor for the eastern gate, whereupon he joyfully rushed to the task, saying, "Where could there be anything other than the work of the Buddha?
With his own hands, he oversaw the construction of sixty *zhang*. The following year it was completed, and he subsequently passed away. He left behind these instructions:
Fayi remained at the mountain gate. Before long, the two kings fled and the army of Guang reached the foot of the mountain. Public sentiment was in turmoil, and everyone thought of plundering;
however, Fayi frequently manifested supernatural wonders, and the temple was thereby preserved intact. Alas! Fayi was a Dharma-holding person sent by the Tathāgata.
He performed the deeds of a Tathāgata; his power of aspiration was vast and firm.

Because he had entrusted it to him, even a single color or a single fragrance could all communicate with the spirit and manifest the subtle and wondrous—how much more so this golden robe? When he entered the Yuan dynasty, the robe remained intact. During the Zhizheng era, it suddenly disappeared without a trace.
Song: Sishou. Sishou’s courtesy name was Yongtang.

He was the son of the Yang family of Huangyan, Taizhou. At the age of fourteen, he entered Xiangji Temple on Mount Santong and took the venerable Shangren as his teacher, where he received full ordination (*upasampadā*).
He traveled through various regions, consulting and inquiring of senior masters until he attained realization of the Mind.
Regarding the essentials of his study: after returning from Lingyin during an illness, San Tong daily practiced the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*.

He harbored doubts regarding the statement, "Transcending the conditions of seeing and hearing, one enters the Buddha-ground," yet despite his diligent investigation, he found no entry point. Suddenly, he heard the sound of a pestle pounding grain.
Suddenly, he had a profound realization of himself. He spoke in verse: "The Sixth Patriarch in his day did not recite sutras; He set down his firewood and immediately transmitted the lamp.

Who would have known that after a thousand years, it still endures today? Under the autumn moon, the sound of pounding rice in the long corridor. From then on, his practice and conduct progressed daily.
He was skilled in calligraphy. Using gold as ink, he transcribed the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, *Avataṃsaka*, *Śūraṅgama*, *Vajracchedikā*, and various other Vaipulya sutras.
Furthermore, upon silk, he inscribed a single *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* stupa in gold, which was so exquisitely refined that it was hailed at the time as a rare wonder.
When his end approached, he sat upon his couch reciting the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*; he passed away before he had even finished a single scroll.
Taichuan’s Biography:
Taichuan was a monk from Shu. While residing among the assembly, he once lamented that the Buddha-dharma was muddled and confused, with heterodox views arising like swarms of bees.
He then said, "I shall practice Chan; if I attain true and correct insight, I will not spare my verbal karma. He subsequently made a vow to pay homage to Mazu.
He worked on the pagoda for many years without ceasing. Suddenly, one day, the pagoda emitted a white light, which moved him to a profound realization.
Later, wherever he went among the monasteries, he would test the veteran masters. Passing before Mount Xuedou, he remarked, "This old fellow’s mouth is dripping with water."
When Xuedou heard these words, he seemed somewhat displeased. When the Master came to see him, Xuedou said, "Do you not approve of me, old monk?
The Master replied, "This old fellow, as expected, has his mouth dripping with water. He then struck his sitting mat once and departed.
The steward was resentful and, while on the road, had someone beat the Master, injuring one of his feet. The Master said, "This was sent by the old man Xuedou;
one day he must break a leg to repay me. Later, it indeed came to pass as he had said. Subsequently, when the Master arrived in the capital, he behaved unrestrainedly among the market stalls.
There was a palace lady who invited him home to provide for him. Although the Master repeatedly declined, the palace official...
He detained him firmly, treating him with even greater reverence. He frequently sent his handmaidens to present food before the master. One day, an official arrived;
the master intentionally flirted with the handmaidens, whereupon the official changed his attitude toward him and was eventually able to take his leave.
Not many days later, the master sat upright in the midst of a bustling marketplace and passed away. His name was Taiyin; he had a goiter on his neck, so people called him "Tai-liu" (The Great Tumor).
In the Song dynasty, there was a man named Nanchuan Younan.
A native of Min, he was by nature wise and perceptive, finding delight in poetry. He remained indifferent to worldly tastes.

While traveling through Kaiyuan and Chengtian in Quanzhou, every time he passed through marketplaces or shops where trade was conducted, he would obtain double the profit from his lodging expenses. People began to find this extraordinary. Upon arriving at...
Those coming from the market scramble for the shortcut, fearing only that they will not arrive in time. Upon arrival, people vie with one another to leave money behind;

they tuck it into their robes or sleeves, and when the amount reaches several hundred coins, they toss it onto the ground. Children compete to pick it up, laughing heartily for pleasure as they treat this as a novelty.
The Imperial Secretary Jiang [Name] held this practice in the highest regard. One day, he suddenly said to his disciples: "Tomorrow..."
"I am about to part from the assembly. The assembly took this to be a jest. At dawn, he indeed sat cross-legged and passed away suddenly.
Someone reported this to the Attendant (Jigshi), who came to inquire after him. Thereupon, while still upon his seat, he slightly opened his eyes and eyelashes and called out to Master Jiang.

He bestowed upon him a verse, saying: "In the eastern provinces, letters and inquiries have come in frequent succession; the Buddha-sun and its robe and bowl have been transmitted from one to another.
If we ask what matters come and go, a single orb of river moon spans the sky. With this, he raised his hand and passed away into stillness. For ten years, his true body remained undecayed;
his disciples then erected a stupa over his remains and enshrined them therein.
Song Ziyong. Ziyong was a native of Min.
He constructed a thatched hut at Moxie Cliff and sat in meditation to cultivate stillness. Suddenly, a dragon appeared at the tip of a tree;

he remained serene, reciting sutras without looking back. After a long while, the dragon emerged from the mountain again, and as its claws and talons struck the rock, they made a sound. Ziyong said to it—

The layman said, "The dragon has come again. Upon looking, it was indeed so. One day, as he was returning home carrying his water jar, a tiger followed behind him and went down to drink from his water.
Yong turned back and said slowly, "Where have you just come from? You are so thirsty.
Furthermore, once at night, he passed by some thieves outside their hut and said to them with a smile, "Do you wish to empty my bags and pouches? You shall obtain a *sheng* [of grain]."
He poured out a jar of rice and gave it to them, saying, "I am ashamed that it is so meager. The thieves thanked him and departed. At over eighty years of age, he passed away;
his body did not decay, and his complexion remained as if alive. Alas! Yong was truly one who possessed the Way.

Otherwise, how could he have reached such a state of non-differentiation from things? He felt no trepidation when climbing heights and no alarm when entering water; though ten thousand transformations were arrayed before him, he remained unmoved. Only then...
One may discuss with him the cycle of birth and death and the transcendence thereof; yet to abandon this and claim to be "studying the Way" is something I do not know to be possible.
Therefore, I deeply regret my inability to provide a thorough and enduring account, and I append these few words to await future sages who shall continue them.
Song Dynasty: Fachai.

Fachai was a virtuous monk (*dàdé*) of Changqing Temple in Shangyu. In his daily life, he lived in seclusion and rarely went abroad. He swept and cleaned a single room and sat in meditation within it.
The courtyard was adorned with flowers, bamboo, springs, and rocks, possessing an air of profound serenity; many scholar-officials frequented this place for recreation.
Cí was quite skilled at chess and excelled at discussing philosophy and logic. He would burn incense and brew tea, welcoming guests without ever growing weary.

At the beginning of the Jiatai era, he suddenly declined visitors and shut his door; yet, though advanced in years, his spirit remained sharp and clear, with no apparent cause for such a change. People initially did not consider it strange.
It happened that one of his novice attendants was about to depart for the imperial court to request a monastic certificate (*sengjie*), and Cí spoke to him:
He said, "Go now, and you should return quickly. After a long time had passed without news, he inquired daily about him. Once he returned, Cixi said, "It is very good that you have come back.
Since it was the height of summer, she immediately ordered her attendants to prepare a bath. When he had finished bathing and changed into clean clothes, he sat upright;
then, as if about to close his eyes, he entered stillness. His disciples called out urgently, saying, "Master, you have fortunately attained such a state of excellence!"
"Why do you not leave behind a single verse for posterity? He replied, "You did not speak earlier; I cannot write it now.
If you take up the brush for me, it may be done. Then he said: "Since beginningless kalpas, I have never been born; today on this very stage, who is there to die? Who is there to die?
Throughout ten thousand miles of a scorching sky, one seeks a falling snowflake. As soon as these words left his mouth, he passed away.
**The Biography of Qingyinzzi of the Song Dynasty** Qingyinzzi was a person of unknown origins. He claimed his surname was Yang and his given name was Daoheng.

Toward the end of the Song dynasty, he led a macaque from Jinling to the region of Songjiang, settling it among the mugwort and pepper fields north of the prefectural city. The macaque was as large as a human and could serve as a domestic attendant.

When Qingyinzi sat in meditation at midnight, light emanated from him. The people of Song vied with one another to offer him food; whether the offerings were abundant or meager, he did not express gratitude, merely saying that such things are determined by destiny.
Consequently, people regarded him with even greater wonder, and their offerings increased daily. He therefore constructed a hermitage for his residence, naming it "The Great Ancient" (Dagu).
He waited expectantly for guests from the four quarters who were like clouds or water. He once walked barefoot through the marketplace, begging for alms to provide for the assembly;
he further styled himself the "Barefoot Immortal" (Chijiao Daoren). After some time, a soldier playfully cooked one of his monkeys and ate it.
Qingyinzzi sighed in lamentation and immediately took leave of the assembly. He wrote a verse by hand which said: "For eighty-one years I have been loquacious; at last—"

His daily manifestations of spiritual causes never ceased. On the Double Ninth festival, he returned home; along the way, amidst pure breezes and bright moonlight, he sat cross-legged and passed away.
— Recorded by Jin Da Han, Registrar of Monks.

The Great Han Senglu (Chief Registrar of Monks) was surnamed Nie. He stood nine chi tall and possessed physical strength that surpassed ordinary men. Having shaved his head to follow the Buddha, he upheld the Vinaya and recited the sutras;
he possessed profound insight into the nature of reality, and his speech was unfathomable. It seemed as though he had attained deep realization within the Dharma.

Furthermore, he was capable of reciting mantras to expel malevolent spirits, and was thus known as the "Buddha Monk who Destroys Demons. When Emperor Xizong heard of him, he summoned him for an audience, granted him a meal, and appointed him to the position of Palace Attendant.

The General firmly declined, saying, "I wish to serve the Buddha from beginning to end; I do not wish to hold office. He did not accept the command, but instead served as the *Senglü* (Monastic Registrar) of Jiaocheng County, leading the community in that region.
He was granted the "Dragon-Phoenix Mountain-River Robe," a garment manufactured in the imperial palace, which the *Senglü* was ordered to wear to convert others.
Consequently, he was also known as the "Great Robe Chan Master" (*Dàyī Chánbó*), and his fame resounded throughout the age. Those who were transformed by his influence...

The assembly later witnessed his passing into nirvana. During the cremation, there was the extraordinary phenomenon of red light emanating from the śarīra. To this day, the people of Jiaocheng can still speak of it;
yet, it is regrettable that no detailed records exist for verification, leaving his great deeds largely obscure.
Jin Hongzhao’s Biography:
Hongzhao, whose courtesy name was Xuanning, was originally from Xiagui in Huazhou. His family had pursued the occupations of farming and sericulture for generations.

At the age of eighteen, he entered the Way and practiced the dhūta austerities, never flagging day or night. He devoted himself to the profound study of the Sūtra teachings. After his tonsure, he redoubled his efforts.

He strove with vigor to seek liberation and received the seal of approval from Chan Master Daming Pingkong. He traveled extensively through Henei, where he discovered the ruins of an ancient abandoned temple.
Lush green cliffs leaned askew, elegant trees grew densely alongside, and a clear spring flowed beneath them. Beholding this, Zhanguo looked upon it with joy and said:
"This is the place of peace for those who walk the true path. Upon inquiring with the local people, he learned that it was the Tang-era Chan monastery of Juelin.
Zhaofang constructed a thatched hut and dwelt there, subsisting on coarse food and simple fare. After some time, the fourfold assembly responded to his call and gathered together;
they began construction and excavation, discovering an inscribed stele, a bronze statue, and over a hundred oil lamps and pure offering bowls. Once the monastic complex was completed, the world...
The Emperor honored Zhaoxing by bestowing upon him the title of Chan Master Yuantong and granted the monastery the plaque name "Xiangyan. Zhaoxing possessed lofty insight and profound discernment;

his intelligence was transcendent and his eloquence penetrating. From his initial entry into the Way and the Dharma-treasury, he investigated the meaning according to the words, and through the meaning, he clarified the underlying principle.
He deployed the great compassion of conditioned salvation and entered the subtlety of attaining the unconditioned truth, skillfully alternating between relaxation and tension in his practice.
He abandoned [worldly concerns]. Whether opening or closing his eyes, speaking or remaining silent, he always attained mastery within the illumination of awakening.

To uplift the style of the school and enlighten future students, whenever there was a patriarchal teaching contained within a chapter or a sentence, he would invariably quote it and elaborate upon it.
Whether scholars sought its depths or followed its currents, all found therein a place to wander and rest; according to their respective capacities, they all received [his instruction].
Thus, for a time, the Buddha-dharma took illumination as its compass. He dwelt in the mountains for thirty years without ever crossing the threshold of a donor’s gate.
Whatever he required for daily sustenance was provided through the offerings of officials and lay devotees; he accepted these with joy and never grew weary of them.
Although gold and silk were piled up before him, not a single coin remained in his pouch. In the twenty-sixth year of the Dading era, as he was about to pass away, he bathed and changed his robes.
When asked about the time, he replied, "It is late afternoon. He spoke a verse and passed away peacefully. He was seventy-two years of age.
He was buried at Yufeng Peak to the west of the monastery.
Yuanjun received the transmission from Yuanzhi of Gaoyang.

Yuanzhi, whose courtesy name was Tianyin, was the son of Yao [surname] of Gaoyang. His younger uncle Mian, his father Wen, and his elder brother Yun all passed the civil service examinations and served as renowned ministers of the Song dynasty.
As the Master examined the phenomena of the world, he experienced a profound awakening within himself during the Xianping era.
Chun left the household life in the year Jiaxu. At the age of nineteen, he shaved his head under the guidance of Chan Master Hui-lang (styled Qīn) of Mount Yang.

He devoted himself to quiet reclusion and kept few acquaintances, cherishing the flavor of the Way with serene joy. He delighted in composing literary works, intending to propagate and protect the Dharma.
It was not to flaunt his knowledge and views for self-promotion. Thus, his writings progressed day by day.

When he said, "I am a sage," and styled himself "Wénfó" (Cultivated Buddha), it was because he wished to preserve his Way for eternity; nothing but writing could achieve this. Hence there are the *jīng* (sūtras) and the *lùn* (śāstras).

All these are merely material things. Only the masters of China, wishing to guide those of middling and inferior capacities, all manifested themselves as possessing innate superior wisdom while appearing outwardly simple and lacking in literary refinement, engaging in the same activities as the ignorant.
This was the hidden skillful means (*upāya*) of the Sage, not his true nature.
The ignorant were led by these traces and simply claimed that the Sage’s Way was subtle and wondrous, yet could be understood through vulgar and mundane approaches.
He overstepped [the bounds], treating the sutras and śāstras as shallow teachings and disparaging written words as heterodox. Is this not delusion?

Regarding those who discuss our school’s literature, he alone granted his approval to the one person, Song Mingjiao; his capacity for synthesizing and transcending views and knowledge, and his resolve to uphold the school and rectify the Way, are truly worthy of contemplation.
During the Yuanzhen era of the Zhizheng period, he resided at Nengren Monastery in Jianchang and preached...
Fayi received his precepts from Qinqi, but after less than two years, he departed. The Master’s movements were not constant; this was simply the longest period he resided in one place.
In the second year of the Dade era (Wuxu), he passed away on Mount Lu at the age of forty-three.

It is a pity that there is no record of the duration of his cultivation to investigate where his Way ultimately led or the extent of his transformative influence; this is truly lamentable. He left behind one volume of collected writings.

It was preserved by the monk Kuishang of Qisha at Wumen. He presented it to Fang Xugu of Ziyang, who, upon reading it, became intoxicated with admiration and composed a preface for it, which was subsequently carved into woodblocks.
Dexi Wuzhao (得喜無照) inherited the Dharma from Xuanzhen (玄真).
He was the son of the Qian family. During his childhood, he followed Master Quan of Xingsheng Monastery to receive the tonsure. Upon reaching adulthood, he came to admire the Chan school.

He ascended Mount Tianmu and called upon the elder Huanzhu, with whom he attained a profound spiritual resonance. Upon returning to his native village, a lay devotee of pure faith offered him a plot of land in a garden;
the Master accepted it and established a hermitage there. While excavating the foundation, he discovered an ancient stone engraved with the two characters "Xi" (Joy) and "Jian" (Seeing).

The assembly marveled at this. Once the hermitage was completed, offerings of Zen staffs arrived in abundance. Huanzhu wrote the two characters "Xijian" (Joyful Seeing) in large calligraphy and inscribed them above the door.

From this time on, the local people called the Master "Bodhisattva Xi" (Joy). The Master held that one who studies the Buddha must take liberation as his core intention and universal compassion as his practice.
Moved by the influence of his Way, a single alms-bowl was inexhaustible; beyond providing the four requisites for the assembly, his relief and benefit were profound and vast.
Those who came for clothing in the cold or medicine for illness returned as if to their own homes. For those who were starving while alive, he nurtured them like a father; for those who had died...
As for those who were violent, he buried them like the sons of men, doing so with singular sincerity, faith, and truthfulness, never growing weary.
He once preached the Dharma at the home of Cheng Linzhong in Wujiang; there was a divine being wearing a white cap and golden armor who listened with palms joined.

Later, the entire assembly saw him. Whenever the great families sought to avert calamities or pray for blessings, it was considered a great fortune if the Master visited even once. During the Zhishun era...
He moved his monk’s staff to Panlongtang. Before long, it became a great monastery. After his passing, śarīra relics were found in abundance;
wherever the ground was dug up where he had been cremated, they were all obtained. Both the masters Jianwu Zhao and Jianwu Ai had once served Huanzhu.

Wuzhao was a native of Nanzhao. Initially, he studied the Exoteric Teachings (Shengjiao), becoming erudite, brilliant, and outstanding. He often said, "I have heard that there is a Chan school in the Middle Kingdom.
If it proves to be authentic, I shall follow its teachings; if it is not correct, I shall replace its fundamental tenets."
Having traveled ten thousand *li* from his own country, he attained a thorough realization of the source of the Dharma through a single word.
Just as he was planning to return home to propagate the Way, he passed away in Zhongwu at the mere age of thirty-seven. Huanzhu offered a sacrifice and wept for him, composing this inscription:
"I say that Wuzhao had attained realization regarding our Way; the true mechanism was within the palm of his hand—who would dare deceive? I say..."
Non-illumination. Having no awakening within my Way, the Great Square (Dafang) extends before my eyes; how could one not be deluded?

I laugh at Deshan’s burning of his commentaries—what frantic pursuit of acceptance and rejection! I despise Liangsu’s returning from his lecture hall—merely asserting "this is right" and "that is wrong.
Only my non-illumination is entirely otherwise: it is such that names and reality interpenetrate.
He interfaced with all things without deficiency. As he entered and emerged from the gates of the great masters of both schools, who did not sigh in admiration and marvel at his excellence?
For eight years we followed one another, never differing by so much as a hair’s breadth. Having encountered many people, I have sought someone like Wuzhao;
not only is such a person rare today, but even in antiquity they were scarce. I do not grieve for the lack [of others].
"Zhaowei has perished; alas, the Way of the Ancestors has already crumbled. From this day forward, who will support the tottering and sustain the precarious?
Facing the incense burner this evening, I share with the mountains, rivers, plants, and trees a grief that transcends this world. Reading these words, my nose stings with sorrow.
If the man were not truly one of great surpassing virtue, it would not have been enough to move Laozi to such regret.
It reached this point. However, the presence of the Chan school in Nanzhao actually began with Wuzhao.
Wugai was a native of Yongjia who studied under Huanzhu for a long time without gaining realization. Huanzhu directed him to see Longyuan;

one day, upon smelling the fragrance of lotuses, he attained entry [into awakening]. He composed a verse which said: "The message within this is fundamentally ordinary; how many times have I needlessly [struggled]?"
Measuring it out: today the mass of doubts shatters into a hundred fragments. A gust of west wind brings the fragrance of white lotuses.
One knows not where it ends. *Miaoen Chuan* (Appended: Daguī, Qizu, and Jiedaozhě).
Miaoen was born into the Ni clan and was a native of Quan. He maintained the Vinaya with such rigorous austerity that his side did not touch the mat for over forty years.
Having traveled extensively to consult renowned masters, he subsequently entered Xuefeng to pay his respects to Master Xiang, receiving his seal of approval.

His reputation rose daily until, during the Zhizhi era of the Yuan dynasty, the Monastic Registrar Jianyi petitioned the Provincial Administration to merge the one hundred and twenty monasteries of Kaiyuan into a single institution.
A great *kṣetra* (monastery) invited the Master to serve as its first patriarch. His wisdom and understanding were perfectly integrated; he did not allow Chan to supersede the teachings.

He once composed a commentary on the *Maitreya’s Rebirth Above Sūtra* to manifest his intent. When the Nanshan Lohan Hall in Wulin was destroyed by fire, the Master dreamed that five hundred monks sought his protection.
Before long, the news arrived, coinciding exactly with the night of the dream. Consequently, he established the Lohan Hall.
The Han Hall is located in the eastern wing of the temple; its magnificent and resplendent appearance follows the model of the former capital of Wulin.
Thus, by taking the mind of emptiness as the mark of merit and virtue, one further perceives the immeasurable nature of the gate of wisdom. Its dharma heir, Daguī, composed this eulogy:
"With azure eyes and a bushy brow, you are one who dispels nightmares. Seeking but a single measure, your smile is joyful and expansive. In a single day, you have added five."
The Hundred Idlers. A great hall opens wide under purple clouds. When the Master was about to pass into extinction, he spoke this verse:

"There is no need to shave the head; there is no need for bathing. A single mass of red flames—ten thousand feet, a hundred thousand feet. Once the cremation fire had subsided, śarīras fell like rain.

Guī also possessed both practice and realization. Having read extensively across the Confucian classics, he once said: "If one does not read the Analects of the East, one will not know the meaning that came from the West.
His prose was concise, rigorous, and elegant; his poetry was particularly imbued with refined charm.

He styled himself the Dream-Contemplation Recluse (*Mèngguān Dàorén*) and authored the *Mèngguān jí* (Collected Works of Dream-Contemplation) as well as the *Zǐyún Kāishì Zhuàn* (Biography of the Purple Cloud Bodhisattva), which were in great demand at the time. Qìzǔ was born into the Zhāng family of Tóng'ān.
He also transmitted the Dharma to his disciple, instructing him to succeed to the lineage and serve as a teacher in Xiang. This successor was skilled in expounding the essentials of the Dharma;

his realization was complete and natural, and he was granted the title Chan Master Foxin Zhengwu. There was a man named Jie Dao who was eccentric and unrestrained, constantly sweeping the streets and markets.
Wherever he went, people would mock and laugh at him. His clothes were so filthy that they seemed beyond cleaning, yet suddenly he took up a washbasin and said, "It is clear."
The day passed. When the next morning came, he asked for the monks' gruel, but it was not given to him. Jie said, "I shall not ask a second time; please give it to me.

Having received the gruel, he returned and placed it upon a small table. Sitting upright and composed, he passed away. Master Zu lit the funeral pyre and said, "Throughout his life, Jie was a formidable fighter who practiced Zen with relentless intensity.
He roamed through streets and alleys, acting like one driven mad by the wind. Had he not reached this ultimate end, he would not have been worth half a cent."
As for the Way: who would believe that cold ashes could harbor warm smoke?
Yuan Ruofen’s biography states:

Ruofen, styled Zhongshi, was the son of the Cao family of Wuzhou. He shaved his head and received full ordination, after which he traveled extensively among the lecture halls of the monasteries. He was quite...
Having received the Master’s teachings, his peers urged him to propagate them. Zhi Fen said, "I am not capable of this. Fen was a man of pure withdrawal and was skilled in literary composition.
He served as the administrative secretary (*shuji*) of Upper Zhu Mountain, where he extolled Buddhist affairs and indulged in the art of calligraphy, earning the highest praise of his time.
He was also skilled in painting; he often depicted clouds and mountains to convey his inner meaning. When someone came to request his work, at first he would not...
He was extremely stingy. Although he responded with only a few sparse strokes, people treasured them as much as the "linked cities" of jade.

Later, those who sought them became too numerous to count. Fen laughed and declined them, saying: "The August tide at Qiantang and the peaks of West Lake after the snow are the most magnificent sights under heaven.
You, my friends, have passed these right before your faces; instead, you seek to play with a monk’s few remaining dabs of ink."

Why was this? From that time on, he retired from worldly affairs and returned to the deep mountains. He constructed a hermitage among the ancient streams and verdant cliffs, naming it "Jade Stream" (Yùjiàn), and adopted this as his style name.
He further built a pavilion facing Mount Fúróng (Lotus Peak) and styled himself the "Master of Fúróng Peak.
He once inscribed a painting of bamboo, saying: "If it were not written by the old monk himself, who would report all is well at dawn? His spirit and intent were thus.
It is as one might imagine: those who possess a refined quality still retain their original character and are not entirely obscured by superficial skills.
When compared to those of the present day with shaven heads who take pride in their calligraphy and inkwork, the difference is more than merely that between heaven and earth.
Yuejiang Jinggong transmitted the lineage to Jing.

His courtesy name was Yuejiang; he was a native of Wuyi. He was a Dharma heir of Zheng’an Yungong. Tall of stature and imposing in appearance, his roots of virtue were planted early, and his awakening arose from his innate nature.
He constantly used the seal of the Buddha-vehicle to examine the Confucian classics; he was able to integrate them in silence and to harmonize them through eloquence.
He was not unrestrained. The poetry and prose he authored are all worthy of study. He took it as his personal responsibility to engage with sentient beings and benefit their lives;

in his practice, he was never indolent. Even regarding minor precepts—such as treading on green grass or breaking off a sprout, or the rules for washing one's hands and arranging the seating mats—he never allowed his mind to wander from them.
When Master Wang Shiyuan, a Palace Attendant and Lecturer, was compiling works at the Secretariat, the Junior Tutor Yao [Chong] personally...
He oversaw these affairs and deliberated with the two masters and the renowned monks of the southeast, among whom the Master was one.

When the General Administrator heard of his virtue, he recommended him for the position of abbot of Mount Jing. At that time, eminent officials and high-ranking ministers all joyfully issued petitions to invite him to restore the spiritual majesty of the mountain.
During the Master’s tenure at this mountain, he did not establish grand gateways or paths, nor did he gather a vast assembly of disciples.
Furthermore, he was simple and unpretentious, striving for substance. He once told people: "The body is a single scroll of a living sutra that never ceases to turn;
the mouth is two pieces of dead skin that move whenever there is speech. True knowledge and actual error do not reside in words.

When the Master employed written characters, he did so only to assist in the Buddha’s work; once his purpose was served, he cast them aside like dust, dross, or chaff, without lingering attachment to them at all. Up to this point...
In managing the affairs of the mountain gate, whether great or small, he ensured they were carried out with necessity;

he was able to establish his residence and settle all matters in an instant, without the delay of hesitation or lingering doubt. He was truly an eminent hero of the Dharma-gate. Some have offered praise for his portrait, saying:
His spirit was settled and his breath was pure; his speech was majestic and his countenance was grand. With a single strike of his whisk, the great ocean’s currents were severed;
with a single cough or sneeze, Mount Sumeru was pulverized. He was the model for the patch-robed monks and the very marrow of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.

This is what is called the direct transmission of Master Zheng’an, a scion of the seventh generation of Miaoxi. Later, he passed away while reciting the Buddha’s name and was interred at his home mountain.
The Biography of Yuan Huiming.
Huiming was a native of Lingqiu in Weizhou. His mother dreamed that a strange man riding a white horse and dressed in white robes came to stay with her, and she subsequently conceived.

He was born as a child of extraordinary character; he studied the *Shi* and *Shu* classics and mastered the teachings of the hundred schools of thought. Later, he renounced these studies to seek out Haoyun Jian.
The Chan Master realized his place upon hearing these words. Haiyun praised him with a verse. He returned to reside at Quanhui Temple in Lingqiu.
Just then, the Great Huayan Monastery in the Western Capital had its seat vacant and invited Haiyun; Haiyun recommended the Master to serve as his successor.

The former abbot of Huayan had lost the administrative order, and the monastery was in ruins and desolate, having long ceased to function as a monastic community. The Master governed his subordinates with broad clarity and maintained himself with integrity.

With the utmost reverence: His reputation for the Way resounded far and wide. Throughout the palace corridors, the abbot’s quarters, the kitchen, the storehouse, and the various monastic halls—whatever was required for a great monastic assembly—he transformed the decayed into the new, restored what had fallen into ruin, and completed what was unfinished.

In the year of Renzi, while the Emperor Shizu was still in the state of concealment, he honored the Master’s fame and virtue, invited him to ascend the hall to preach the Dharma, and bestowed upon him an honorary title. Subsequently, the Master moved to Qingshou Monastery.

The officials of Yanjing submitted a formal invitation to Haoyun. Emperor Shizu and the Crown Prince frequently attended his Dharma assemblies, providing funds from the imperial treasury to host great acts of charity.
The Master grew weary of his proselytizing duties and requested to retire, returning to his private quarters.

For several years, he lived in tranquil seclusion at his quiet desk within the secluded courtyard. Yet, the summons for the Avatamsaka Sūtra recitation was issued once again. By nature, the Master was pure and prudent; his capacity...

His demeanor was serene and joyful; he remained steadfast and unbending when facing affairs, and was humble and harmonious in his dealings with others. Whenever he ascended the hall to expound the Dharma, ten thousand fingers surrounded him.
The Master delivered several pointed remarks, enabling every listener to grasp the meaning beyond words and forms, possessing the spirit of the ancient honored elders.
Although he encountered the noble and eminent daily, he treated them all with equanimity, never compromising his Way to conform to worldly trends.
In the second month of the seventh year of the Zhizhi era, he manifested a slight ailment. He said to his disciples, "The sun is setting.
He requested a brush and wrote a verse, then said, "Go straight ahead," before casting down the brush and lying down as if in deep sleep. When shaken, he had already passed away.
His secular age was seventy-two; he had spent forty-five summer retreats. After his cremation, relics of five colors shone brilliantly.
They were divided and enshrined at the two monasteries of Huayan and Quhui, where they were marked by stone monuments.

Yuanzuzheng (元祖英), styled Shishi (石室), was the son of the Chen family of Wujiang. Having left the secular life at the age of seven, he immediately took up his staff and traveled through various regions.
Initially, he followed Xuguleng (虗谷陵) at Yangshan; hearing of the spiritual transformation of Huiji (晦機) at Jingshan, he hurriedly came to join him there.
At their first meeting, they were in perfect accord. [Wuzu] appointed him as the head of the secretarial office (*zhishi*). From then on, his reputation for learning grew daily.
He served at the prominent monasteries of Mingzhou—Wanshou, Xuedou, and Yuwang. Later, while he was ill at Tiantong, Tianxiu Di and Pingshi Wen went to inquire after him.
He answered in verse, saying: "This body is without self, its sickness deep-rooted; Out of shame and remorse, Mañjuśrī has come to visit from afar.

There are naturally the mountain flowers to discourse on non-duality; Facing each other by the blue lamp, we laugh and chant. Later, he constructed a small shrine called "Wooden Cage" (*moku-tō*) and sat within it daily, no longer engaging with worldly affairs.
