In the third month of the *kaimu* year of the Zhizheng era (1363), he saw a decrepit woman bowing her head before him.
"I request that you, Master, manifest yourself as a king. The Master replied, "I do not wish to be born into the family of a celestial king.
Seventeen days later, he passed away while sitting in the lotus posture. Yuan Yuju.
Like jade, from Mount Kuanglu to the Double Creek at Mount Jing, he beheld the lush and majestic mountain slopes at the spring of Lu Yu.

Thereupon, he settled in a thatched hut to dwell in seclusion, holding his alms bowl to beg for food and guiding others according to their conditions. He styled himself "The Patchwork Robe of Double Creek. After a long time had passed...
Supporting his staff, he ascended to the Lingxiao Peak; relying on its foothills, he constructed a dwelling. For three years he did not descend the mountain.

One day, gazing from afar at the Jixiang Peak, he remarked upon the five-colored auspicious clouds, saying, "There must surely be spiritual energy within these peaks. He then sought out the slope on the leeward side of the peak and built a temple there, which became a flourishing monastic center.
Later, by imperial decree, it was granted the name Da'an. One day, Chan Master Miaosong composed a poem in jest to lament this event:
[The Master] said: "Jizu shall succeed me in my place; his karmic conditions and conduct are worthy of emulation. Throughout his life he has remained on the Path;
recognizing his ailment, he was too indolent to seek a physician. His appearance is ancient and difficult to capture in brushstrokes; his lofty spirit is unknown to the world.

Wherever the clouds of compassion spread, the solitary moon is naturally in harmony. Having finished reading this, the Master took up his brush and replied: "Who else in my entire life shares such affinity with the Way? In my leisure, I find solace in you."
He knew it most deeply in his heart. Initially, he did not wish to complete the poem on parting, fearing he might err regarding his fellow practitioner. He set down his brush and sat away.
Sixty years later, the door of the stupa opened of its own accord, and the true likeness was there, solemn and vivid.
Yuan Aonao was known as Aonao.
He was a native of Qiantang and a hired laborer who sold vegetables. Every morning he would shoulder his load of vegetables and enter the market.

One day, he went out too early and returned home briefly to rest. He sensed something unusual within the room; peering through a crack in the wall to listen, he discovered that his wife was having an illicit affair with another man.
Someone said, "How does he compare to me? His wife replied, "He is crooked and restless; you are steady and composed. She then recited a poem:
"The bamboo rattles and the crows cry out; The gates of Qiantang have not yet opened. As soon as the crooked one goes out, The steady one comes in."

He subsequently abandoned his home and went to Yuewangtai in Xiaoshan, where he took up residence. From then on, he devoted himself wholeheartedly to the joy of *dhyāna*, attaining profound realization and verification.

Later, he passed away while seated in meditation; his countenance remained as if alive, and his entire body was light and supple. Every month his hair grew, so his sister would shave it for several years.
His sister said, "I am old now; from this point forward, there need be no more growth. After another few years, she used clay...

Its body was fashioned in clay, with only the face left exposed. Those fond of such matters would regularly welcome the image into the city during the spring season to plant seeds of cause and effect;
this practice continues unabated to this day.

The Biography of Dharma Master Fuzhongyou from the Ming Dynasty, from the *Zakepian* (Miscellaneous Chapters).
Dharma Master Fuzhongyou, whose alternative name was Fuan, was the son of the [surname] family of Haichang in Hangzhou. He relied upon the Elder Yuweng as his preceptor.

Having shaved his head, he studied the essential meanings of the teachings with great diligence and came to realize that there was a matter beyond the gates of the school (the Chan/Zen tradition). His writings were like spring flowers and autumn moons:

their brilliance required no adornment, and their clarity did not need the cold to enhance it. The subtlety of his literary blossoms shone across both past and present. He used this literature to elucidate our Way;
yet when praised for it, the Master received such acclaim as if it were spittle. During the Hongwu era, he presided over the seat [of the monastery].
At Mount Wu Great Vehicle Monastery in Qiantang, his spiritual influence was greatly renowned. In the Gengzi year of the Yongle era, he succeeded to the abbacy of East Pagoda Monastery in Jiahe.
This monastery had once been the former residence of Zhu Maichen of the Han dynasty; Emperor Xiaozong of the Song dynasty had once visited there on a pleasure tour.
Having suffered repeatedly from the ravages of war, its halls and buildings were dilapidated and in ruins. Former abbots such as Canghai Shen and Yungu Xiang all [sought to restore it].

His resolve to restore [the temple] remained unfulfilled. When the Master arrived, he was moved by a profound sense of resonance. He then emptied his robes, his alms bowl, and whatever was in his possession, as well as the offerings of those who contributed.
He selected timber and gathered craftsmen; they cleared away the thorns and brambles and hauled away the tiles and rubble.

Beginning in that year and concluding in the winter of the Wushen year of the Xuande era, he devoted his entire essence for ten years, until what had once collapsed a hundredfold rose up again. Monastics and laypeople from all quarters alike regarded the Master as...

Auspicious stars and celebratory clouds appeared; those who gazed upon them and sought refuge in him were beyond counting. The Master, weary of the burden, declined their requests and retired to a separate chamber.
In the year Wumu of the Zhengtong era, the lecture seat at Huíyīn Monastery on South Mountain in Hangzhou had long remained vacant.

The monastic communities of all mountains unanimously declared that Huíyīn was the preeminent among the foremost Buddhist establishments of China, and that none but one of profound virtue was worthy to occupy it. Only...
The Master was such a man that he could not refuse despite repeated entreaties. At that time, Huiyin’s temple was also in ruins.

Upon the Master’s arrival, his merit in restoring what was abandoned and reviving what was decayed was no less than it had been during his time at the East Pagoda. Moreover, both mountains were Huayan lecture temples; indeed, as for the Huayan school—
It began with Xianshou, was perfected by Qingliang, and established by Guifeng; all these flourished and propagated the teaching in the north. When it reached Jinshui, it entered Hangzhou.

In Hangzhou, the Huayan school became the dominant tradition, making it difficult for others to exert their influence. Yet this Master twice established great monasteries and once again revitalized a declining lineage.
Since the time of Jinshui, such instances have generally been rare. That he could operate with solitary strength and singular resolve is truly praiseworthy and magnificent. [End of] brush.
A brief biography has been composed here to show future generations.
The Biography of Dharma Master Nanzhou Puchaya:

The master’s name was Puchaya; his courtesy name was Nanzhou. In his later years, he styled himself Yugou (The Recluse of the Meandering Path) and was also called Yiyu Weng (The Old Man of the Single Rain). His surname was Lu. He was of the Song dynasty.
He was a descendant of You, the Grand Master for Special Counsel of Baizhang Pavilion. His family had resided for generations in Shanyin, Kuaiji.

His grandfather, [name], served as the Magistrate of Yuyang County in Raoyang Prefecture. His father, Renfu, settled there because of that appointment. His mother was Lady Zhou. He was born in the Bingxu year of the Zhizheng era.
From childhood, he was bright, cheerful, and exceptionally gifted. When his father instructed him in the *Shijing* and *Shujing*, his understanding and realization progressed daily.

Before even reaching the age of seven, he had already set his mind upon the supramundane Dharma (*lokottara-dharma*). An elderly man once teased him, saying, "Immortals are originally made from mountain men.

The Master responded immediately, "The phoenix is ultimately no ordinary bird. This struck everyone with wonder. Whenever he entered a monastery (*caitika*) to gaze upon Buddhist images, he was filled with devotion.
He would immediately pay his respects by prostrating himself. His parents, knowing they could not restrain him, sent him to Puzi Temple in the prefecture to take Xueting Xiang as his teacher.
He received full ordination at Shang Tianzhu and went to visit Dongming Ri; upon seeing him, the latter regarded him with great esteem.

He was appointed to oversee the reception of guests; his deportment was composed and his proceedings were orderly. Many veteran elders of the monastic community (conglin) highly esteemed and submitted to him, considering such conduct difficult to achieve.
Furthermore, he extensively investigated the scriptural canons, never flagging whether in cold or heat, morning or night.

Subsequently, he followed Master Ji of Ju’an at Pufu Temple to seek out the essential meanings of the teachings. Regarding all the various scriptures and texts, there were no principles—whether refined or coarse, small or large—that he did not master.
He mastered the Buddhist scriptures while also gaining a comprehensive understanding of Confucian texts; in his leisure time, he composed poetry and prose with great proficiency.

Master Xi commissioned him to lead the ritual practices of the Samādhi of Repentance, through which he advanced in the path of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calm abiding and clear insight) and luminous stillness.

In the Xinhai year of the Hongwu era, he entered the public life to reside at Manao Jangsi on Mount Gu, and subsequently served as the abbot of Beichen Monastery in Suzhou, where his disciples gathered.

The assembly gathered like clouds. The Master expounded for them the Five Periods and Eight Teachings—the manner in which the Tathāgata bestowed his transformative teachings throughout his entire life.
Whether they were wise or ignorant, noble or lowly, everyone departed with their desires fulfilled.

At that time, eminent masters of the school, such as Master Jiugao Sheng and Master Qizong You, all marveled at and praised him, declaring him the foremost in the Dharma assemblies of the Wu region. Six years later, he arrived at...

In the lower Tianzhu district of Hangzhou, he followed the precedent of Ciyun by establishing a Golden Light Dharma-Assembly for the Protection of the State, vowing to perform repentance rituals for seven days and nights.

He lectured on the scriptures for the assembly without a single day of idleness. When Emperor Taizong heard of his virtue, he summoned him to serve as the Right Lecturer of the Office of Monastic Records.

The Emperor’s own voice offered praise and exhortation, noting that he had mastered the teachings of the East (Confucianism) while possessing a profound understanding of the meaning of the West (Buddhism).
Yu resided in the western *vimala-śālā* (chamber) of Changgan for three years. At that time, he dreamed of Guan Zhu Tianxi.
One of his disciples, Gao, had a dream one night in which he went to the Master’s quarters; upon reaching the door, two divine beings wearing helmets and golden armor stood guard with great severity.
They rebuked Gao, saying, "The Abbot of this temple is here. Upon waking, Gao went to the Master and told him of his dream, adding, "May you take my place."

Master, within a month after his passing, there was a dream-vision. An imperial decree was issued appointing the Master to preside over Tianxi Monastery. Three years later, he was promoted to the rank of Left Shanshi (Left Superior Worldly One).
When Emperor Taizong launched the "Jingnan" campaign, the Master—then known as Master Daoyan—performed meritorious service by assisting in the defense of the capital.

Upon the Emperor’s accession to the throne, he summoned Daoyan from Beijing and commanded him to preside over the affairs of the monastic community; however, the Master declined the position out of deference to his seniority as Left Shanshi.
Yan himself sat on the right. The Emperor praised his compliance. In the fourth year of the Yongle era, an imperial edict was issued to repair the pagoda of Tianxi Temple.
On the day of its completion, the imperial carriage visited the site, and the Master was commanded to perform the rites of celebration. Auspicious light shone brilliantly.

A multitude of ten thousand people gathered to gaze upon him, and the Emperor’s countenance was joyful and serene. At that time, there was one named Ren Jueyi, who envied the Master’s favor and fabricated words to create discord between them.
Consequently, Ren Jueyi was demoted to the position of Right Jueyi and issued a formal reprimand. The Master did not defend himself, remaining composed and at ease.

Subsequently, the Emperor perceived his true intentions and restored him to the position of Right Shan-shi. During the reign of Emperor Renzong, as the Master was an elder of long standing who had frequently been...
The Emperor summoned him for an audience and treated him with exceptional courtesy. He was ordered to reside at the Songyin Hermitage in Qingshou Monastery to enjoy his leisure;

meanwhile, the Emperor ascended the private hall and summoned the Master to an audience, offering him the most profound consolation. Thereupon, the Master petitioned to return to Dabaoen Monastery in the Southern Capital to spend his final years, and this request was granted.
The Emperor bestowed upon him several *mǐn* of Buddhist statues, scriptures, and cash, and provided an official post station for his travel.
He boarded a boat. An imperial official was dispatched to escort his escape. Once he arrived, the following year was the first year of the Xuande era.
On the twenty-eighth day of the seventh month, he suffered from a slight illness. He summoned the abbot of the temple, Weishi, to entrust him with his final affairs and left behind a verse.
He bid farewell to his disciples, saying: "I dwell in pure and sovereign freedom. Thereupon, he passed away. He was eighty-one years of age and had been a monk for sixty-nine years.

His entire body was enshrined in a stupa on Fengling. Over ten thousand people escorted him there. Upon hearing the news of his passing, His Majesty dispatched the envoy Wang Lin to preside over the sacrificial rites.

Throughout his service under successive sovereigns, the Master was consistently guided by utmost sincerity; his speech and conduct were invariably respectful of ritual propriety. He lived in harmony with others and governed the assembly with broad magnanimity.
Whenever he encountered scholars in scholar’s robes, he delighted in discussing literary and scholarly matters. This continued for thirty or forty years.
Among the great, dark-robed elders who possessed reputations for literary talent, there were none but the Master and Master Yan.

Among the Master’s writings are two fascicles of the *Commentary and Appendices to the Diamond Sūtra*, several fascicles of poems composed for imperial commissions and in response to the verses of renowned figures,
and all the liturgical texts for the national Buddhist assemblies established by the State, which he codified to serve as a model for posterity.
He ordained several disciples, including Wonwu Dajeon and others. His dharma heirs included Wonjeong, Hongui, Hwiraeng, and others.
In the autumn of the first year of the Xuande era, he passed away at Nanjing.
His disciples enshrined his remains in a stupa on the sunny side of Fengling Hill to the southwest of Changgan. Furthermore, they constructed a meditation hut before the stupa.
Resident: Zhou Chen of Luling, Right Vice-Minister of the Ministry of Works, composed this record, saying:

"The refinement of the Master’s conduct and the loftiness of his talent and reputation have already been fully detailed in the Stele Inscription for the Junior Tutor Yang Gong; thus, a record such as this might seem superfluous.
Nevertheless, regarding the construction of this temple, I alone feel a profound resonance. Long ago, after the passing of Confucius, his disciples all—"
He raised a mound at the grave and observed the rite of mourning in spirit for three years. When the mourning period ended, he prepared his belongings to return home.
Upon entering and bowing to Zi Gong, they faced one another and wept until their voices failed. Zi Gong returned to dwell in a mourning hut atop the grave for another three years before departing.
Indeed, the relationship between teacher and disciple, through which the Way is transmitted and the teachings are bestowed, possesses an affection akin to that between father and son.
Alas! In later generations, this Way has not been clarified. While their teachers were still alive, there were those who acted contrary to the Way and departed from it in opposition.
How many people are there capable of observing the rite of mourning by heart (*hsin-sang*)?
If they cannot even observe the rite of mourning by heart, how much less can one hope for them to dwell in a hut at the grave for as long as three or six years? This is what I have heard.
During the Yongle era, Master Qiā was once estranged from his colleagues. Emperor Taizong, wishing to test his observance of the precepts, imprisoned him in the Jinyi Prison.
At that time, most of his disciples dispersed like clouds and birds;

only Master Zhù remained, enduring hardship with a burning heart and parched bones, following his teacher through this adversity and performing menial labor such as fetching water and wood, never for a single day.

He departed from worldly entanglements and ultimately enabled his religious practice to remain intact. Having received the grace of the state, he caused his teachings to flourish greatly in the latter part of his life.

Observing how he devoted himself to his vocation, never altering his resolve regardless of life or death, or success or failure, this is something difficult even for scholar-officials to achieve, yet Master Zu was able to do so; at this, I am moved once again.
For this reason, I have written this as a record, so that those who observe it in the future may, through Master Zhu (Zhugong), find some cause for inspiration and exhortation. [There is a saying:

When the troops of the "Pacification of the Rebellion" rose, the Master performed the Yakushi Lamp Rite and a curse against Changling for the sake of the Jianwen Emperor. When the Golden Gate opened, he again shaved his hair for the Jianwen Emperor. Upon the accession of Changling to the throne, he heard a rumor of these matters.

He remained imprisoned for over ten years. When the Duke of Rong was on his deathbed, Emperor Changling sent someone to inquire what he wished to say. He replied, "I wish to be released from the prison of Tuan Jia. Changling granted this request and set him free. At that time, his white hair grew several inches long, covering his forehead.
The Biography of Chan Master Muran Jik:
Master Muran Jik was a native of Wuyi. He received the Dharma from Master Xugu Ling. He occupied three monastic seats, each of which has its own recorded sayings (*yulu*).
Lord Wang Wenzhong Hui wrote a preface for them, stating: "During the final years of the Song dynasty, among the venerable elders of the Zen school..."
One after another, they passed away and vanished; only Master Qin remained steadfast and resolute, taking it upon himself that this Way was of great importance.
He who received his transmission was Master Ling of Xugu. Having encountered a sagely age and been favored by imperial grace, the Master’s Way became even more radiant and prominent.
His foremost disciple was none other than our Chan Master Mukan Jishin.

When the Master entered his room, he not only resolved the essentials of the mind through inquiry, but also received the transmission of the seal of the literary tradition; thus, in his practice of the Way, there was nothing that did not accord with that of the Master.
Initially, the Master appeared in the world at Xifeng in Ningbo, and subsequently arrived at Yangshan in Yuanzhou.

Mount [Shan]. Now, having moved his residence to Huiyun in Hangzhou, his disciples have collected the words he spoke during three assemblies concerning the activities of daily life and recorded them according to their chronological order.
They maintain that although the Master’s Way does not reside exclusively within the realm of language, one may nevertheless come to know the extent of his Way through what his words reach.
I respectfully observe that the Master’s words possess a sharp and precipitous edge, which is truly sufficient to awaken a student’s preliminary understanding.
As for the thoroughness of his expositions and the severity of his admonitions, the Way of the teachings and the precepts (*śāsana-vinaya*) does not lie beyond these.
Alas, the decline of Chan studies in recent times has led its followers to concern themselves solely with mere words and oral transmission, merely following...
They take up the words of men of old and, following one another as teachers, use them to deceive themselves and delude others.
They neglect skillful means and invert the truth, yet none of them reflect upon this. If such is the case, what indeed do they have to do with the One Great Matter?
Students, if you can regard the words of your teachers as mere traps and snares, then perhaps you may perceive the Way through direct observation.
Lord Ling and the Master were both my fellow countrymen. Having been born later, I was unable to enter Lord Ling’s gate;

however, I have the good fortune to share the refined intimacy of a close friendship with the Master. I shall briefly describe the origins of their spiritual lineage to serve as a preface to this record of his teachings.
As for Lord Zhongwen, his literary brilliance and meritorious achievements set a standard for his era, ranking him among the foremost figures of the founding generation.

When a person records even a single character or a single word to be taken as credible by the world and posterity, how could they grant such permission to others recklessly while showing private favoritism only toward their own local community?
It is for this reason that I know the virtue of the man from Muran must surely be great enough to be observed in the *Zhongwen*.
Thus, although Zhongwen wished to avoid mentioning Muran and not speak of the Wood Hermitage (*Mukan*), he could not help but do so.
Regretting that his life’s traces have vanished, I shall briefly cite the preface as a substitute for a short biography, as recorded by Mukan:
"Xiaoshan Liang was transmitted from Yuangliang.
His courtesy name was Xiaoshan. He was the son of the Xiao family of Xinyang in Henan. On the night of his birth, there was light in the room like daylight. Just as he was born...
He had long observed the vegetarian precepts and recited the Buddha’s name, never engaging in worldly affairs. His father took him on an official tour to Tang, where he eventually settled.

There, he encountered the monk Zhifu of Baolin Temple in Tang, whose realization of the Way was unsurpassed in his time. The Master paid his respects and had his hair shaved; Zhifu instructed him in the essentials of Chan, leading to a profound awakening.

Furthermore, Zhifu directed him to visit Chan Master Yougu of Guyu in ancient Yuzhou. Upon entering the master’s room for instruction, their accord was like the meeting of a needle and its eye; the defilements of worldly toil were instantly cast off.

A single insight dissolves doubts and obstructions with but a few words. In the *Renzi* year of the Hongwu era, he returned to Tang and established Baoding Monastery, where he widely propagated the Dharma.

At that time, as the authorities were selecting men of renowned virtue and eminent character, they reported the Master’s name; by imperial decree, he was appointed to reside at Ba’en, later moving to Daci.
Imperial edicts were repeatedly bestowed upon him, including one that read: "The orchid has long been hidden beneath the Tang forest; it did not realize its subtle fragrance..."

The phrase "fragrance leaking through the nine heavens" was inscribed [upon his robe]. The Master earnestly sought to retire from the monastery; after a long time, he was granted permission to return to the mountains.

Initially, the Prince of Shu invited the Master into the inner court to preach the Dharma and presented him with a golden-embroidered robe, a monk’s staff, an alms bowl, and other items, along with the various gifts bestowed by the Emperor.
The Master accepted these and preserved them for the sake of the ten directions and all monasteries, never using them for himself from beginning to end. He once composed a verse...
The Master recited these verses: "How could a turtle ever escape from within a jar? A shrimp may leap, but it never leaves the measure.

If one lacks a firm and resolute mind for transcending the world, One will wander in vain through the six realms of rebirth. On the thirteenth day of the tenth month in the year of Gengchen, he suddenly requested a bath, changed his robes, and sat upright.
At that time, the sky was clear and cloudless, and the sun stood at its zenith. Suddenly, the sound of three peals of thunder was heard.
A halo appeared in the sky, its number equal to that [of the previous master]. He then vanished. His body was cremated, and the *śarīra* relics fell like pouring water.
De’ang transmitted the lineage to De’ang, whose alternative name was Fuyan. He was the son of Wu Shouzhen of Kuaiji. When the wars broke out at the end of the Yuan dynasty, Shouzhen sought refuge.
At Dishimen, he quelled the rebellion of the Miao soldiers. His mother, née Yu, threw herself into the water and died.

When Fang was twelve years old, he followed Shi Shouzheng back to Yue. Before long, Shouzheng also died in battle. Having no one to rely upon, Fang departed for the mountains of Jinhua, where he shaved his head and donned the robes of a monk.
He cultivated himself with rigorous discipline and soon became a venerable elder; people looked upon him with respect. When the weapons of war had just...
He traveled to Qiantang to visit his mother’s grave. The Imperial Scholar Song Lian wrote a preface to see him off, praising his supreme filial piety and Confucian conduct.
Coinciding with the compilation of the *History of Yuan*, Xu Ang went to the capital and informed the historians of his mother’s death; consequently, she was included in the biographies.

Upon returning, he tended to his mother’s grave and named his residence "White Clouds" (*Báiyún*). He also erected a monument at the ancestral cemetery for the people of the town, inscribing it as the "Hall of the True Mother" (*Zhēnmǔxián*).
Wang Ang. His ultimate end was unknown thereafter.

Form does not arise apart from its parents; nature finds no lodging apart from form. For those who perceive their nature and clarify their minds, there is sincere devotion to repaying their origins and returning to the source.
To seek liberation apart from this is to distance oneself further and further from the Way. This was Wang Ang’s perception of his nature and clarification of his mind.
I do not know what to say of it. It is simply this one thought of sorrowful compassion, so diligent and sincere, that is sufficient to serve as a rebuttal for my Way.
Even though Master Dahui established a successor for his parents, he was merely extending this very mind;
how could there be even a hair’s breadth added to the principle of *ang* (filiality)?
Biographies of the Two Masters Tianyuan Jun and Jifang Lian.

Jun, whose courtesy name was Tianyuan, was a native of Huangyan in Taizhou. Having received full ordination, he traveled to study under Master Guding Ming, through whom he attained significant realization.
He was subsequently appointed to serve as the internal secretary. He preached the Dharma at Wanshou Monastery in Siming, but before long, he abandoned the assembly to return to seclusion.
Within the Pure Thunder Peak, the gentry and scholars attempted to detain him, but they could not prevail. Master Song Lian composed a farewell essay for him, the gist of which says:

"I had not yet been able to know Tianyuan personally; however, upon seeing the map of the empire he had drafted, where the vertical and horizontal dimensions were barely more than a foot, yet the mountains, rivers, provinces, and prefectures were all clearly arrayed therein, I already marveled at his character."
I did not yet know that he was capable of composing poetry. Later, however, there were those who transmitted his works;

their flavor was pure and serene, yet their spirit was rich and full, capturing the subtle resonance beyond the literal words of the ancients. I already knew then that he was capable of poetry, but I still did not know that he was capable of prose.
This spring, I happened to meet Tianyuan in Jianye, and we discussed literary theory together; his arguments were both profound and extensive.
It is brilliant and swift; the treasure-trove is opened, and its pearls and jade shine resplendently. The Milky Way forms its patterns, and the sun and stars blaze forth.
The Long River stretches ten thousand li; with favorable winds and rapid currents, the dragon-sprung vessel rides upon them to gallop.
Having requested several of his recent compositions to read, I find they are all as round as pearls and pure as jade, their formal structure being most meticulous and rigorous. I am further—
I marveled at his character and transmitted [his writings] to the Imperial Library (Jinlin). Many of the gentlemen of the Library sighed in admiration of him.
I privately believe that Tianyuan’s talent was not necessarily inferior to that of Miyuan or Haochu;

the reason he remained hidden along the shores of the Eastern Sea and failed to achieve great renown was simply because the world lacked a Minister of Rites and a Lesser Master (the respective patrons of those two). People often say that regarding literary composition—
Those who are truly excellent are indeed rare. Alas! Is it not truly rare?
Now that the four seas are unified and the governance through culture has flourished, there will surely be those like these two gentlemen who shall shoulder the responsibility for this literature.

If they were to see what Tianyuan has composed, they would certainly praise it with great enthusiasm. Haochu and Biyan shall not alone possess the excellence of the past. Some, however, say: "Tianyuan..."
This is the teaching of the Buddha. According to the Dharma of the Buddha, heaven, earth, and the myriad things are regarded as illusory transformations;

how much more so, then, are what are called poetry and prose? This is certainly the case. Within the single nature (ekaprakṛti), there is not a single thing that is not encompassed, nor a single matter that is not governed.
It is so vast that it has no exterior, and so minute that it has no interior. Truly, it cannot be divided into two. If it were as you say, [then this would be impossible].
Thus, there would be something remaining outside of nature. People take Tianyuan to be a manifestation of the dragon; this is not the way to speak of him.
As Tianyuan was about to return to the East, many officials and gentlemen sought to detain him, but they could not prevail.
They sang songs to bid him farewell, for my acquaintance with Tianyuan was especially deep. I request that you write a preface to accompany his departure.

Daolian, whose courtesy name was Jifang, was a native of Ningbo. In his youth, he studied Confucian texts and exhausted himself in the learning of investigating principle (*li*) and the mandate of destiny (*ming*).

Upon reaching adulthood, he relied upon his venerable father, Master Xi, to cultivate the conduct of a śramaṇa. He subsequently served as an internal recorder at the Great Tianjie Monastery and eventually inherited the Dharma from Chan Master Jingjue.
His demeanor was dignified and composed, and his every advance and retreat followed constant rules of propriety; indeed, he was warm and radiant like jade.

Within the monastic communities, all held him in high esteem. Whenever anyone urged him to accept the position of abbot, he would demurely decline, saying, "My study of the mind has not yet reached full clarity;
nor have I fully mastered the teachings of the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the scriptures.
I shall return to the mountains of Siming to seek the truth within myself alone. Thus spoke Master Song.
I composed this preface and sent it with them. Both gentlemen were renowned for their understanding of the Way, yet they remained humble and did not dwell upon their own achievements;
they possessed a spirit of lofty integrity. It is only fitting, therefore, that they are praised by those of long standing.
Shi Ying was his courtesy name;
Bao Tan was his pen-name. His ancestors had migrated from Bian to Wu and were descendants of the Song Prime Minister, Lord Wang Wenmu.
Among them, those residing in Wuxing all practiced hidden virtue without seeking fame, with the sole exception of [his father], who was devoted to the Buddhist faith.

Her father was a man of the world, while her mother, Lady Zhu, was exceptionally devout in her service to the Buddha. One night, she dreamed of a monk knocking at her door, and subsequently became pregnant.
Shortly thereafter, a monk arrived from Mount Tiantu, informing them that Chan Master Duānyá had passed away; this coincided exactly with the time of her dream.

From then on, everyone said that the Master was Duānyá incarnate in a second lifetime. While still in her swaddling clothes, she would invariably smile with joy upon encountering monks and knew how to perform prostrations before the Buddha.

He sat with his legs crossed. Wherever he went, monks and laypeople followed him like a shadow; all addressed him as "Upādhyāya. Even when venerable masters of long-standing virtue paid their respects, he remained composed and did not decline them.
People vied with one another to offer gold and silk; upon receiving these, he used them to establish monasteries and cast Buddha images in various places.
What remained, he distributed as alms to the poor and destitute. When Emperor Gao (Emperor Taizong) ascended the throne, he sought him out in the mountain forests.

Among those who had been left behind were scholars of the Way and practitioners of virtuous conduct. When Master [Yuan] was summoned, his responses accorded with the Imperial will, and he was granted a meal as a token of imperial favor and consolation.
After some time, he was ordered to reside at Tianjie Monastery on Longhe.

In the eleventh year of the Hongwu era, the Emperor, noting that Mount Emei was the site where Samantabhadra manifested his transformations and that it had long lacked a master to lead the liturgical services, remarked, "None is better suited than Ying," and summoned him for an audience.

He consoled them and sent them away. After eight years had passed, the people of Shu were all transformed by his influence. At that time, princes, nobles, officials, and commoners from various noble households came daily to offer donations.
Consequently, at the summit of Mount Jue, he cast a large image of the Bodhisattva in bronze at Guangxiang Temple and constructed a multi-tiered wooden pavilion to house it.
In the twenty-fourth year, monks were assigned to manage and purify the Buddhist teachings; the Emperor issued an edict to the monks.

The Recorder was appointed. Baotan resided in Shu, where the people submitted to his transformative influence. He was commissioned to manage local affairs; having completed his duties, he came to court.
In the sixth month of the following year, he returned to the capital with his report. His arrangements were conducted according to protocol and deeply satisfied the Sovereign’s mind.

The Emperor’s countenance was greatly pleased. Consequently, [Baotan] memorialized that the three *āraṇyakas*—Jiyun, Miaoyin, and Dayun—where he had previously resided in Wumen, should be treated as one.
The foundation [of this work] was originally divided into three parts; I now request that they be merged into one. The above constitutes his words.

He had been granted the imperial plaque inscribed with "Nanchan Jiyun" (Southern Zen Cloud-Gathering) and was scheduled to take his leave of the Emperor in the tenth month before returning home, but he fell ill.

On the ninth day of the sixth month, he passed away while sitting in the lotus posture with eyes closed. Although it was the height of summer, his countenance did not change, and a fragrant aroma permeated those nearby. Thus it was obtained.
He lived to the age of fifty-nine, and his years of monastic seniority were the same. When the Emperor heard of this, he was moved to grief and lamentation;
he subsequently dispatched an official to offer a ceremonial sacrifice and provided a meal for three thousand monks. His body was cremated, and those who gathered numbered in the tens of thousands.

His disciples divided his remains, returning them to Gusu and Emei respectively, where they each erected stupas to enshrine them. The lay devotee Li Zheng, having attended him for a long time, [recorded] all matters concerning his conduct and movements.

He arrived before being invited, and in subsequent matters he applied himself with even greater devotion. Throughout his life, the Master never engaged in ostentatious conduct, yet the world held him in universal esteem;
he never uttered words of excessive praise, yet people came to trust him all the more. He repeatedly undertook the construction of Buddhist monasteries.

He did not dwell upon his own achievements, treating them as if they were cast away. Could one who has not thoroughly realized that birth and death are all like illusions and dreams be capable of such a thing?
[This concludes] the biographies of the two masters, Shouren and Dexiang.
Shouren, whose courtesy name was Yichu, was a *śrāmaṇera* at Miaozhi Temple in Fuchun. His poetry and prose were as virtuous as his character.
You Dediang, whose courtesy name was Zhian, was a native of Renhe. During the final years of the Yuan dynasty, these two gentlemen were intent on practicing the Way;

however, because the times were perilous and chaotic, they felt stifled and discontented, and thus devoted themselves wholeheartedly to poetry. Both gained renown during their era. Yichu once said: "We of our generation..."
Dealing with literary matters was not for the sake of abandoning the Way to purchase fame; rather, it was because there was no other alternative. Zhizan said, "Is poetry my business?
It is merely for the purpose of providing embroidery and adornment. By observing this, one can know the minds of these two masters. This is the first poem.
Pure and simple, with a far-reaching spirit, Yang Lianfu praised him most highly. He was also skilled in calligraphy; his brushwork was vigorous and powerful.

During our dynasty, he was summoned and appointed as the Right Supervisor of the Sangha Registry (Senglu Youshan Shi). At that time, emerald-feathered birds were being presented from Nan Yue; Yichu composed a poem on them which said:
"I have heard it said that the 'Crimson Robes' are being sent from the Land of Fire; in a single day, nets are cast throughout the east and west. Even their feathers are sufficient..."
"Bound by the burdens of this body, how could you fly through the quiet places of the autumn forest? When the Taizu saw this, he said in anger, "Do you not wish to serve me?
Do you say my Dharma-net is too dense? Zhi'an resided at Mount Jing and propagated the Way, becoming the patriarch revered by Chan practitioners.

The transformation of customs was harmonious and pervasive. Furthermore, both masters incurred the Emperor’s displeasure due to their verses concerning the Western Garden; both brought about their own misfortune through poetry, nearly escaping with their lives.
Yet, Zhi’an was extremely strict in governing himself and possessed a disciplined method for presiding over the assembly; his demeanor was majestic and imposing.

Yichu, however, felt listless at the end of each day and tended toward unrestrained behavior, such that he could not be received into the Dharma-gate. From this, one can see the difference between the two masters.
Regarding their relative merits: thus, Zhi’an was able to fulfill his original aspirations to some extent, whereas Yichu ultimately failed to achieve any resurgence.

When Zhi’an reached the end of his life, he sat upon his meditation seat to address the assembly; if one does not harbor thoughts regarding birth and death, one becomes liberated and free from all attachments—the radiance of such a state is truly worth contemplating and beholding.
Minghe said: "It is not that Zhuangzi and Laozi do not practice the teachings of the Six Dynasties; it is not that poetry and prose do not greatly expand upon the Chan of the Song and Yuan.

As one gradually distances oneself from antiquity, such a state of affairs—consisting of lingering waves and peripheral currents—is bound to arrive at this point. Nevertheless, as for the authenticity or falsehood of the Way,"
As for the discussion of right and wrong, I am still able to examine it by looking at their words; but nowadays, this is largely not the case.

Those who are blunt and unrefined take "the staff and the shout" (zhui-hang) to be Chan, and treat the pointing to scriptures and questioning of characters as something to be shunned—how could they have leisure for poetry and prose?
Those who are frivolous, fickle, and ambitious cling to sectarian gateways as their teaching; just when...
"Entering the room to wield the enemy's halberd"—what could one hope to find in Zhuangzi and Laozi? The more one pursues them, the lower one sinks.

One realizes that during the Six Dynasties, the Song, and the Yuan periods, although the Way of the Dharma had changed from antiquity, it was still worth observing. Thus, I record several words from these two masters;
my sighs over the times can find no better expression than in the present moment.
The Biography of Master Xue’an.

Master Xue’an’s name was Ji; his surname is unknown. During the period of dynastic transition, when Emperor Wen entered the capital, the Master had just reached the prime of his youth and received the tonsure.
He traveled to Dazhu County in Shanqing Township of Chongqing Prefecture in the southwest, where the mountains and waters were extraordinary.
He was determined to stop it. Du Jingxian, a recluse from that village, recognized that the Master was no ordinary man and subsequently became his companion.

They traveled between Bailong and various other mountains; seeing a pine and cypress grove by a rapid stream where creepers and bamboos grew in lush profusion, the Master wished to establish a temple there.
Jingxian was wealthy and influential, so he promptly built the temple for him. The Master then led...
A mere handful of people entered and resided there. At dawn and dusk, they recited the *Qian* hexagram of the *I Ching*. The mountain dwellers, however, insisted it was a Buddhist scripture.

Jingxian knew this, but could not bear to inquire further, fearing he might disturb the Master’s peace. The Master, likewise perceiving Jingxian’s intention, changed his recitation to the *Guanyin Sutra*.
Consequently, the temple was named Guanyin Temple. The Master also enjoyed reading the *Chuci* (Songs of Chu) and would occasionally purchase a copy.
He rolled up his sleeves and boarded a small boat, rowing swiftly toward the middle of the stream. He recited the "One Leaf" poem aloud, casting one leaf into the water with each verse.
Having cast it, he would weep; having wept, he would read again. When the leaves were exhausted, he returned, while no one among the crowd knew what was happening.

Jingxian felt an increasing sense of pity and reverence for him, yet he never questioned the Master. The Master enjoyed drinking and did not observe the precepts; every day he set aside a jar of wine, waiting [for him].

Guests: whenever guests arrived, he would drink with them; if there were none, he would drag in woodcutters or herd boys to join him in drinking. When they were half-intoxicated, he would call for the boys to sing along with him.
Once the singing ended, he would close his eyes and fall asleep. The Master was tall and elegant, with slender, soft, and white fingers.
His compositions flowed from his pen without much effort, yet his spirit was effusive and capable of moving others to deep emotion. Some said that the Master had built... [text ends].
During the Wén period, he served as an *yushi* (Censor). On the day of his death, his disciples asked, "The Master has passed away; for whom should we compose an inscription?
The *Heshang* opened his eyes and said, "Sōngyáng. When they asked for his name, he did not answer. He left behind several dozen poems.
If Xue’an had encountered a true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) at the moment he was weeping bitterly, I see that his doubts would have been completely resolved like ice melting away.
When one’s will is undivided, the spirit becomes concentrated. If one turns this very state toward the study of the Way, what Way could not be mastered?
Therefore it is said: "If Deshan and Linji had not left home to study the Buddha-dharma, they would certainly have become Cao Cao and Sun Quan."
There is no doubt that Zhongmou [Liu Bei] was like this; the mundane and supramundane teachings are of one principle.
What a pity that Xue’an did not encounter someone like Linji or Deshan to receive a single point of transformation!
The Great and Virtuous State Preceptor, Trishalibhadra, was the second son of King Tsakgama of Eastern India.
He was born after his parents had experienced wondrous dreams; while still in the stage of childhood, he was exceptionally intelligent and extraordinary, yet remained free from all worldly desires.

Seeing only the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, he gave rise to profound reverence and faith. At the age of sixteen, he requested permission to leave the household life. He was sent to pay homage to Guṇamati as his preceptor;
having shaved his head and received full ordination, he supported himself by studying the academic curriculum and mastered the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*).
Because the preceptor’s ethical conduct was so rigorous and his wisdom so clear, all the ministers and commoners of the entire kingdom honored him with the title "Master of the Five Sciences."
Pantāla (Bantada). The Master’s footprints spread throughout the Five Indias, and those who were converted and attained liberation through his teachings were exceedingly numerous.

Whenever he passed by a site of practice, a stupa, or a temple, he would invariably pay his respects in person with the utmost reverence. Upon reaching the Earth-Sprung Stupa, he performed his devotions and planted his mendicant’s staff there;

however, as the Meditation Stupa had long been in ruins, he exhorted the King to restore it. He extracted a central bamboo shaft from within, beneath which was inscribed the Master’s name and title. All present were filled with wonder.
In the Jia-wu year of the Yongle era, he entered China and had an audience with Emperor Wen at the Fengtian Hall.
His responses were in accord with the Emperor’s wishes, and he was ordered to reside at Haiyin Temple. In the Ding-you year, by imperial command, he traveled to Mount Qingliang;

upon his return to the capital, he was summoned to the Wuying Hall, where the Emperor spoke words of warm consolation and bestowed generous rewards. He was appointed as the *Senglu* (Monastic Registrar) of the Chanjiao rank and ordered to reside at Nengren Temple.
At the temple, in the year Jiachen (1424), Emperor Renzong Zhao raised the grand rite of recommendation and promotion;

the Master presided over its execution and was specially conferred the title of State Preceptor for Great Goodness, Great National Preceptor, with the posthumous name Yuanjue Miaoying Cihui Puzhi Fuguo Guangfan Hongjiao Guanding.
He was granted a golden seal, a jeweled crown, ritual implements, and ceremonial insignia. In the year Yisi (1425), Emperor Xuanzong Zhang...

He was recommended [for office], and the Emperor further commanded the Master to take charge of the administration. Throughout his life, the Master did not boast of his reputation nor did he pursue profit.

Outwardly, he appeared as a *śrāvaka*; inwardly, he cultivated the Great Practice (*mahācaryā*). When encountering imperial favor, his resolve became even more humble; when encountering various conditions, his observance of the precepts became increasingly firm.
While in the capital, he ordained several thousand disciples, guiding and encouraging each according to their individual capacities, gradually leading them forward.
Next, he ascended. He did not stand upon narrow, treacherous paths that would cause people to gaze at the precipice and dare not proceed.
As he was about to pass away, he said to his disciples, including Droṇācārya and others: "I have traveled from the Western Heaven to convert beings here.
Now my karmic conditions for conversion are exhausted, and I am about to depart. You must each well protect the Great Dharma of the Tathāgata; do not be even slightly lax."
"Be diligent. Having spoken these words, he passed away in solemn stillness. This was the thirteenth day of the first month in the third year of the Shixuande era (1386).

Upon hearing the news of his passing, the Emperor expressed deep sorrow and lamentation, and commanded the relevant authorities to prepare the funeral rites. After cremation, the śarīra were collected at Xiangshanxiang.
He enshrined [the relics] in a stupa and, according to his final instructions, they were divided and stored at Mount Qingliang; a stupa was likewise constructed at Yuanzhao Monastery.
Regarding Decong’s biography:
Decong’s surname was Du, and he was a descendant of Du Shimei, the Tang Dynasty *shiyi*. He entered the monastic order at Chongshan and supported himself by...

He ploughed with oxen and sowed by fire; both his thighs bore scars from being scorched by the sun. He was profoundly versed in both Buddhist and secular classics, yet he rarely left the mountains to teach, so few people knew of him.
When the Chengzu Emperor sent an eunuch to Kaifeng, the official investigated and learned of his reputation. Upon returning to court, he reported this to the throne.

It happened that a monk from the Western Regions had arrived as an offering, who claimed to have a thorough mastery of the Three Teachings and the Nine Schools of thought, and was deemed worthy [of imperial favor].
He served as the preceptor to the sovereign of China. The Emperor was displeased and said, "In this magnificent imperial court, how could there not be a single person capable of matching him?
He issued an edict summoning Decong to the capital. Upon his arrival, the Emperor bestowed upon him a golden-embroidered *kāṣāya* robe and a silver alms bowl.

The following morning, he summoned all the monks and had them sit upon high stools; he then engaged them in debate. Decong’s discourse flowed forth like a gushing torrent, encompassing the nine classics with ease.
Daocong was slow in his verbal responses, and the assembly initially doubted him. After a short while, he suddenly asked a Western monk, "What is the meaning of the character *di* (諦)?
The Western monk’s reply was somewhat delayed, whereupon Daocong spoke loudly to explain and interpret it. He had studied the Great Tripitaka and explored Confucian texts;

he then demonstrated the principles of philology (*zi-xue*) one by one, saying, "If you do not know this, what use is it to call yourself a scholar? The Western monk was filled with shame and resentment, yet he prostrated himself in worship and sighed in admiration.
He took his leave. The Emperor was pleased and summoned him back, granting him a seat. On that very day, he was appointed as the Left Shanshi (Director of the Buddhist Registry).
An abode was constructed for him at Mount Jikō to serve as a repository for the Tripitaka. At the age of fifty-seven, he recited a verse and passed away.
By imperial decree, a stupa was erected on the northern slope of the mountain, and he was granted three imperial sacrifices.
Master Xian Guan’s lineage transmits Huiguan.
His alternative style name is Xian’an. He is a descendant of the eminent official Hu Zhongjian (Huang Quan). He relied upon Master Qingyuan Xubai Jing as a śrāmaṇera.
In the deep mountains of Qingyuan, the scholar Chen Zongsun would frequently come to stay in seclusion; the Master [served] him.

He was extremely diligent in his affairs. At sunset, he received instruction; from this, he became widely proficient in literature. Having grown up, he shaved his head and traveled to various regions, seeking enlightenment from those of renowned virtue.
His realization was profound and expansive. The traces of his staff covered almost the entire world, though he resided in Shu for the longest time.
The Prince of Shu provided him with offerings, once saying, "This is a true man of the Way. Many of the provincial officials were elderly.
He became a renowned master, and all paid him their respects with humble etiquette. In the first year of the Zhengtong era, he first arrived in Beijing.

Those who held him in deep faith joined forces to establish a monastery in the northeastern corner of the city, where he resided. Those who came to pay their respects and inquire about the Way filled the space outside his door.
One day, Yang Dongli visited his quarters and saw that offerings of incense and provisions were being presented in continuous succession; he therefore teased him.
It was said: "What of eating but one meal at midday and staying but one night under a tree? The Master replied slowly, "The student uses these as a means to cultivate sincerity;
I cannot refuse him. Why would you find this strange? Upon entering to inspect the room, it was desolate and devoid of any superfluous belongings.
Only the portraits of four former officials were present: Lord Zhongjian, Yang Zhongxiang, Yang Wenjie, and Hu Gangjian. To the east...
Li further remarked, "Is this not still lingering in the realm of appearances? The Master replied, "These several gentlemen were of eminent virtue and high reputation;

they were all spirits nurtured by the mountains and rivers, the vital essence of the state. Moreover, how could I part with these four scrolls, which have been cherished by my ancestors for generations?
How could I dare to treat them with indifference? Dongli sighed and said, "If the Master’s love for the worthy and respect for virtue is such as this, how could it ever be considered ordinary?"

Setting himself apart from all peers and transcending the common species, he falsely claimed to deceive the world, considering himself among the ranks of the lofty. Before long, he passed away while seated;
the faithful enshrined him in a stupa and provided it with a roofed hall. There is a single volume of his recorded sayings (*yulu*), for which Dongli wrote the preface.
Biography of Deren (with Dao’an attached).
Deren, styled Weian, was the son of the Zhang family of Huating. From birth he possessed extraordinary features; there was a mole beneath the sole of his left foot.
His mouth could hold a fist, and his tongue could lick his nose. At the age of seven, he recited the *Lotus Sūtra* at Tiantong Temple in Hangzhou.
Moved by a sense of urgency, he conceived the aspiration to travel widely. He first met Master Shiwu Gong and later studied under Chan Master Qianyan Chang.

There was a profound spiritual resonance between them. Xuyun told Hong that his karmic conditions lay in the Wusong region; he then wrote the two characters "Songyin" (Pine Shadow) for him. He further instructed him, saying:
"Suzhou Shouzuo lacked the merit to leave the mundane world and benefit others. You must follow in the footsteps of Master Su."
He then returned to his native village south of the city, where he constructed a hermitage to dwell in. He hung up the calligraphy of Xuegong as the plaque for the hall.

For several years, he did not step beyond its threshold. He once sliced his own finger to provide blood, commissioning the eminent monk Daoxian to transcribe the eighty-one fascicles of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
At the beginning of the Hongwu era, he was summoned on account of his possession of the Way. Not long after, he returned home due to illness. He once said:

"Those who study the Dharma must not rely solely upon their level of insight or their fragmentary understanding; what can such things accomplish? It depends entirely upon how one applies oneself through practice. Thereupon, he became even more diligent and earnest.
At times, he would compose verses in regulated meter, but he did not engage in poetic exchanges with others, composing only for his own personal satisfaction. He possessed a boat...
He composed ten poems, which were pure and sublime, worthy of recitation. He also constructed a seven-story pagoda to enshrine the Dharma-treasure written in his own blood.
On the fourteenth day of the fourth month in the twenty-first year, he took leave of the assembly and passed away in serene stillness. His entire body was interred in a pagoda at Songyin Hermitage.
His dharma son was Dao’an, who maintained his integrity and sharpened his conduct, possessing the character of his father; he frequently practiced the Pratyutpanna Samādhi.

In the *Pingshen* year of the Yongle era, at the age of seventy-seven, he passed away. His final verse says: "I do not understand digging the earth to measure the heavens, yet I also know how to drive a wedge into empty space.
Startled, Mount Sumeru dances upside down; the toad at the bottom of the sea swallows the moon.
Having trampled over the great ocean of birth and death, what need is there to speak of the arising and ceasing of bubbles?"
The two masters Miaozhi and Mingxuan both transmitted the teachings to Miaozhi, whose style name was Baiyou.
He was the son of the Yang family from eastern Zhejiang. From his childhood, whenever he was fed meat or pungent foods, he would immediately vomit; from that time on, he maintained a vegetarian diet.
The Yang family had long been devoted believers in the Buddha-vehicle. One day, while reciting the *Lotus Sūtra* with his father, they reached the passage on the "Burning House."
He sought the Dharma. His father regarded him as extraordinary. At fourteen, he left the household life and relied upon the Elder of the East Forest at Lingjiu Temple.

The Elder, noting his brilliance and refinement, wished to test him. Just as the moon rose, the Elder went outside and said, "The sun has set; come look at the moon at the edge of the sky. What trouble is there with 'ignorance' (avidyā)?

The Master pointed to the lamp in the Buddha niche and replied instantly, "The candle is spent; let us trim it and light the lamp before the Buddha. The Elder praised him, saying, "I shall see to your instruction."
Xu Yan said with joy, "This child is one who has returned for a second birth. What I possess is insufficient to sustain him.
He therefore urged him to travel extensively to seek instruction from various masters. Consequently, he traveled south to Xuefeng, west to Emei, and visited Tiantai and Yandang.

He called upon and studied under various teachers, gaining a profound realization of the meaning beyond words. He once sighed, saying, "The Buddha-dharma has no depth or shallowness; it simply depends on one's effort."
He traveled about. If one fails to attain realization and merely plunders empty words, then even if one’s reputation surpasses that of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, what benefit is there for oneself?

Later, he entered Mount Lu and repaired a thatched hut at the former site of Tianchi (Heavenly Lake), where he resided. His mother, Lady Chen, who was over seventy years old, suddenly died one day and then revived.
She said to her family members: "Yesterday I arrived at a certain place; the palaces were solemn and profound. I knocked on the gate, but the gatekeeper would not [open it]."
He granted him entry and pointed out the way back home, further bestowing upon him this verse: "For eighty-four years, a lioness mother, Suddenly, through wind and candlelight, realized impermanence.
How wonderful is Yuxi’s diligent recitation of the Buddha’s name! The celestial breeze carries the fragrance of lotus flowers.
At that time, the Master was at Mount Lu, where he styled himself Ganchi (Sensing Creek). Later, the mother indeed passed away at the age of eighty-four, in the Wuzi year of the Yongle era.
On an autumn night, the Master and several attendants, including the head monk, were gazing at the moon when they suddenly recited a poem by Wang Dingxin: "The hermitage has no one to guard it.
On the night of the Gengshen day, lotuses bloomed in the pond with flowers facing both north and south (zi-wu). When the assembly asked what this signified, he smiled but did not answer.
At dawn ten days later, he rose, bathed, and sat upright. Addressing the assembly, he said, "Today is the Gengwu day. He then spoke this verse: "Within, there is neither inner nor outer."

There was no external [distraction]. At seventy-two years of age, he moved unhindered according to circumstances. Casting off his "stinking skin bag," he remained silent for a long while and said, "I am free.

Thereupon, he passed away. Mingxuan was a native of Jiangjin in Shu. He maintained strict observance of the precepts and was naturally filial. Once, while lying down at night, his heart stirred, and he said, "This must surely be..."

"Because she was my own mother," he said. He then galloped two hundred li through the night and arrived home. His mother was indeed ill; he cut flesh from his thigh to offer her, and she soon recovered.
She experienced the auspicious omen of a miraculous cloud enveloping the room. There was a thief in the village who dreamed that the Master led a general.
The executioner raised his axe to strike him down, but he was spared through a plea for mercy. The next day, he went to the master to seek absolution.

The master said, "My dream was exactly like this. You must quickly repent and reform; otherwise, disaster will befall you beyond remedy. Yet the thief remained as deluded as before. One day, he fell gravely ill.
He cried out repeatedly, "Master Xuan, save me! Save me! Before long, he died. The Master passed away at the age of eighty.
Those living at the foot of the mountain saw him within five-colored clouds, holding his mendicant’s staff and departing with graceful ease.

Qi Dongbai, whose courtesy name was Dongbai and whose style name was Xiaonan, was surnamed Yang. He was a native of Changzhou in Suzhou. The Yang family had long held official rank and for generations resided on Zhisheng Mountain in Wu;
they moved to the Northern Ward during the disturbances of the military era. His father was named Yongnian, and his mother was of the Lu clan.
The Master was barely able to speak when he already mastered the Buddhist scriptures; his parents marveled at this and sent him to enter the Wuliangshou Monastery.

There, he took the tonsure under the preceptor Yongmao. Upon reaching maturity, he withdrew to Longshan Mountain, where he devoted himself day and night to the study of the classics, histories, and the works of the hundred schools of thought without ceasing.
His reputation rose in secret, and such great masters as the Junior Preceptor Yao Guangxiao, Shan-shi Chao Nanzhou, and others all esteemed him.
He was held in high esteem. He served as the administrative head (*diǎnjì*) at Qiāngōng for a considerable time. In the first year of the Yǒnglè era, he presided over Yongdìng in Sū;
in the sixth year, he presided over Yánqìng in Sōng. After more than a year, he was promoted to Vice-Administrator (*fùdūgāng*) of that prefecture and resided at Nánchán Temple.
Subsequently, he responded to the imperial summons to compile the *Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn* and participated in the collation of the *Dàzàngjīng*, for which he was bestowed a golden-threaded *kāṣāya*.

One day, a fire broke out in the three palaces. An imperial edict was issued seeking candid counsel, and the Master submitted a memorial detailing the benefits and maladies [of the state], but no reply was received.
At that time, renowned figures such as Shen Minwang, Wang Xifan, Wang Ruyu, Chen Sishu, Qian Pu, and Zhao Zongwen were all his "square-and-circular" (non-sectarian) friends outside the monastic fold.
Once, when peonies were in full bloom, they invited one another to gather for appreciation and composition; it took place in Qiantang.
Qu Zongji was preeminent in the composition of *ci* and *fu*. When he and the Master engaged in literary duels, they would often exchange a hundred verses using a single rhyme;

his verbal acumen became increasingly sharp, and this was transmitted throughout the realm. This was merely the Master’s surplus talent. He passed away on the eighth day of the eleventh month in the eighth year of the Zhengtong era.
From the fifteenth day of the eleventh month in the third year of the Hongwu era until his death, his worldly lifespan was seventy-five years.

At sixty years of monastic seniority (*saṃgha-lakṣa*), in the very year he manifested *parinirvāṇa*, his disciples escorted his coffin back for burial at his former retreat on Longshan Mountain, in accordance with his final instructions.
Lord Qian Wéntōng Pǔ inscribed the epitaph for his stupa, stating in his preface: "Generally, those whose friendship is deep possess a knowledge that reaches its ultimate;
those whose words are numerous possess an affection that is surely profound. Formerly, during the Xuāndé era, the Minister of the Court of Judicial Review..."
Hu Gonggai was the Provincial Governor of Eastern Wu; his prestige and reputation were greatly renowned, and he alone showed the Master exceptional respect.

At that time, Shi Pu had recently reached the age of capping and wished to seek admission to the provincial examination. When he went to pay his respects to the Governor, the Master suddenly saw him and took a liking to him.

He then entered and informed the Governor, who allowed Pu to participate in the provincial examination. Furthermore, Pu began to listen to the Master’s discourses and observe his deportment, finding him to be a resolute Confucian scholar. From this point on...

Their coming and going was harmonious and frequent; if one did not see them for several days, he would invariably send a short note to summon them. These notes were written in the style of Ou-yang Xiu, with characters arranged according to the principles of calligraphic composition.

Upon seeing such a note, he would invariably straighten his robes, burn incense, and sip tea, sitting in conversation for a long time. When the guest departed, he would continue to talk while seeing him off.

Sometimes he would close his door and open a chest, bringing out ancient calligraphic masterpieces; he would examine and critique them together, yet in both poetry and prose, he never sought to produce novelty by imitating others.

When discussing the distinctions between Confucianism and Buddhism, he said: "Furthermore, each serves its own teaching. He also said: "The Way was transmitted from East Lu (Confucius), while the realization of nature was taught in West India (the Buddha);

in neither case does anything take precedence over honoring one's roots. Therefore, even though they parted from their parents, [they still performed] the rites of nourishing life and sending off the dead..."

He died. Throughout his life, he was single-mindedly devoted to propriety and generosity. He was an intimate friend to his brothers and doted upon his nephews, providing them with both instruction and care that reached its highest mark.

In his dealings with the eminent scholars and renowned monks of the four quarters, he was invariably sincere; he never once displayed a look of indolence. Yet, if a person was not of the right character, he would never associate with them.
As the Master of Han said, he was one who bore the name of a Mohist but practiced the conduct of a Confucian. Since I, Pu, had already been entrusted by my teacher with high expectations...
For a long time. If, with my remaining teeth, I can remain unfailing toward this world, then I shall also remain unfailing toward all that I have known.

(The *He Shi Cong Shuo* states: When Qian Wentong was young, he already enjoyed a reputation for his literary talent. In the prefecture there was a monk named Shanqi, styled Xiaohan; he was renowned for his poetry and calligraphy, ranking among the ranks of the ten great eminent monks.

During the Yongle era, he was summoned to the capital to assist in compiling the *Da Dian*. Later, he served as a monastic official and resided at Nanchan Temple. When Lord Zhou Wenxiang served as the Provincial Governor, he held him in high esteem. Whenever he had a moment’s leisure from public affairs, he would go to Nanchan to converse with Master Qi.)

[The Master] said: "At that time, Qian Wentong was a *xiucai*. He was also on intimate terms with Master Qi. One day, while in the *sansiang* (dispersal hall) of the academy, he went to visit Master Qi and placed his indigo scholar’s robe (*lanshan*) upon the crossbeams of the railing.

Shortly thereafter, Wenxiang arrived; there was no time to clear it away. When Wenxiang questioned him about it, Master Qi praised Wentong’s talent. Wenxiang immediately requested an audience and asked for his previous compositions. Upon reading them, he highly esteemed them and they subsequently became close friends.
[Regarding the titles: The *Heshi* says the Provincial Governor was Zhou, while Qian himself says it was Hu. These must have been two different occasions; Hu was earlier and Zhou was later.
Qiyuan Zhuan:
Qiyuan’s surname was Zhang, and his courtesy name was Taichu. He was a native of Japan. At the age of nine, he shaved his head and began studying the teachings of the Buddhist vehicle (*śāsana*).
He was diligent in the Vinaya and took delight in observing Chinese characters, being able to point out their strengths and weaknesses. Furthermore, in his heart, he admired the fame of China.
The flourishing state of the mountain Chan masters further resolved his ambition to travel and observe the world.

In the first year of the Ruyi era (1368), he sailed across the sea and traveled until his footsteps had nearly spanned the entire realm, seeking and receiving the seal of approval from various Chan masters. In the Bingyin year of the Hongwu era (1386), he entered Meigong Cave in Angu;

seeing the four surrounding mountains lush with greenery and two rocks overlapping so that the space between them was hollow like a Chan meditation cell, he stood facing it with a sense of profound longing.
He said: "When Zen practitioners meet, they merely snap their fingers; how many can truly know this mind? This place may serve to rest my feet.

For a long time this mountain has been a den for tigers and pythons; the axes of woodcutters could not enter, and thorns covered the heavens. Since the Master resided here, all evils have been silenced.
The residents at the foot of the mountain occasionally saw light upon the peak; as they gradually approached to draw near, [they found peace]."
Within a few years, it had become a flourishing monastic center. Those who heard of his reputation and came to seek the Way numbered several hundred at any given time.

In the *Pingxu* year of the *Yongle* era (1406), he erected a living stupa to the south of the monastery as a place for his final retreat and awaiting death, saying, "I am old; I shall do this myself so as not to trouble my successors.
On the morning of the first day of the third month of the following year, after completing his prostrations before the Buddha, he entered the stupa and sat upright.
The multitude rushed to look, but he had already passed away. During the Xuande era, when the stupa was opened, his hair was seen hanging down and his fingernails were curled back.

Upon hearing the roar of wind and thunder, they closed it again. The Master had three volumes of recorded sayings (*yulu*) which harmonized Confucianism and Buddhism, demonstrating that his discourse on the Way was unimpeded.
Furthermore, there was Jixian (如筏來復), whose courtesy name was Jixian.
He was the son of Wang Shi of Fengcheng in Yuzhang. Because he was born on the winter solstice, his name was derived from the terminology of the *Yijing* hexagram to signify his character.
Possessing the will to practice pure conduct and desiring to transcend the mundane world and stand alone, he eventually returned to the Śākya clan. Together with... [text continues]

His fellow practitioner, Gongxu Weng, vowed to eliminate all external conditions and directly clarify the wondrous purport of *nirvāṇa*. After some time, he perceived the unimpeded nature of the whole;
yet, not considering this to be ultimate, he traveled to Shuangjing to pay his respects to Chan Master Yue of Nanchu.

He recounted his own circumstances, and as their minds met, they struck one another like a hawk swooping down and a rabbit fleeing—without a hair’s breadth of interval between them. Yue deeply approved and retained him in his service.

An internal record: Three years later, he again made an agreement with the scholar Zhan to cultivate the Western Pure Land at Mount Tianping in Wu, setting a fixed date for breaking through his obstacles;

he applied himself even more diligently than during his meditative contemplations. When the Right Chancellor of the Zhejiang Province, Duke Da Jiucheng, admired the Master’s spiritual progress and invited him to reside at Tiger Hill in Suzhou, he declined and did not go.
Subsequently, as the military uprising broke out, he took refuge in the mountains of Kuaiji.
Cixi borders on Yuezhi. Within it lies Dingshui Monastery, situated directly on the shore of the Eastern Sea. It is secluded, remote, and vast, a place well-suited for binding oneself in meditation.
The Master was further invited to emerge and take charge of it; he restored its former glory and established the ritual protocols of the Chan school.

The ceremonies were performed in succession. Monks arrived one after another with their alms bowls and staffs; he sustained them by begging for food, and together they vigorously expounded the primary truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Soon thereafter, as war drums resounded along the roads, he was unable to see his mother.

He built a hut by the eastern stream of the temple and named it "Bamboo Hut" (*Pú-ān*), following the precedent of the Venerable Master Chen, thereby manifesting his longing for his parent. From that time forward, the people of Ningbo requested the Master to reside there.

At Tianning Temple, the monastery was at that time being used as a military garrison camp. Men and women were intermingled in disorderly fashion, and the defilement within the pavilions was especially severe.

The Master petitioned the regional commander to relocate the troops and expel the various servants. He then swept and cleansed the site, repairing what was dilapidated and restoring everything to its former state.
The Master’s reputation grew day by day. High officials and scholars repeatedly sent letters of recommendation, urging him to take charge of Lingyin Monastery on Hangzhou.

Coincidentally, an imperial edict was issued summoning monks of eminent conduct; the Master traveled twice to the Southern Capital, where he was granted a meal in the inner court and received generous expressions of imperial favor.

Subsequently, when the Great Memorial Service for the Dead was established, the Master ascended the seat to preach the Dharma by imperial command. His words were poignant and earnest, and all who heard them were deeply awakened.
It is said that Master Minlang was profound and resolute; he not only excelled in internal studies but also expressed them through poetry and prose.
His spirit was magnificent and his diction archaic, such that many learned scholars considered themselves his inferiors. Among those who extolled him, Li Wen-hao, the Imperial Tutor, remarked:
"He took the Way and its Virtue as his abiding practice, and employed literature as a form of play. Thus spoke Chen Zuzhen, the Metropolitan Graduate.
Renzi said: "His profound realization of the source of Chan and his meticulous exploration of the scriptural divisions have filled him within and extended him without;
he is a guiding compass among the clergy. As for his arrival in the state of Chu, such figures as Ou-yang Wen-gong Xuan and Zhang Gongzhu of Lu praised him most highly in their writings.
Furthermore, the Academician Song Gong Lian even extolled his prose, comparing its preciousness to that of the *muka* and coral."
The high ministers, dukes, and great officers all praised his virtue.

His Majesty commanded his attendants to take it up for inspection and commended it without ceasing, saying that among the present-day practitioners in monastic robes and the followers of the Confucian gowns, few have surpassed him.
In the twenty-fourth year of the Hongwu era, he consequently met with disaster. Alas, this too was but destiny (at that time, the authorities in Taiyuan, Shanxi, captured members of the Hu faction;

the monk Zhicong confessed that when Hu Weiyong plotted to stage a rebellion, he had gone back and forth to Hu’s residence with Le Jitan, Fu Jianxin, and others; both masters were thereby implicated and punished, while Le was sentenced to forced labor at the construction of a temple, and the Master could not avoid the same fate).
When the Master was in the waters of meditative concentration, he ordained a disciple, saying, "He is like a raft. His conduct was upright and prudent;
he was proficient in both Buddhist and secular classics, skilled in calligraphy, and capable of poetic composition. He was truly a preeminent figure among the monastic community.

During the Yongle era, he was summoned twice by imperial decree and successively resided at Yuelin in Fenghua and Cuiyun in Fuzhou. He authored the *Cuiyun Gao* (Drafts from Cuiyun). He lived to the age of eighty-five.
He returned to Yongming and passed away there.
His biography is like that of [Ba]ru.
He was styled Mian. He was the son of Jiang of Jiahe; his mother was of the Yin clan. She conceived after being moved by an auspicious dream, and the Master was born.
He was exceptionally gifted and did not delight in remaining within the mundane world. He took Master Ji of Mount Heng as his teacher; Ji was the foremost talent among the masters of the *Yiyuan*.
The Master attained profound mastery of the inner sanctum of the teachings. Later, he realized that written characters were not the ultimate Dharma. In the year of Jingtai Gengwu (1450),...
