He arrived in Hangzhou and visited Master Long of Konggu at Xiujishan. He asked about the karmic conditions regarding the "exposed pillar" (lu-zhu). After a long silence, Long said, "This is something that cannot be explained;
you must realize it for yourself. A long time passed, and Long passed away. He felt as though he had lost his protector and began to focus his mind exclusively on the Pure Land dharma-gate.
Both for his own benefit and for the benefit of others, he dedicated himself entirely to this path, even to the point of encouraging others to recite the Buddha's name many times.

He struck a gong once for every grain of rice, accumulating two hundred hu (approx. 24,000 liters) to cook as meals for the assembly and distribute as alms to various monasteries by the tens of thousands.

He continued this practice for many years. The Master had long felt that the *Wudeng huiyuan* (Compendium of the Five Lamps) was voluminous and unwieldy, failing to capture its essential meaning for practitioners;
he therefore resolved to transcribe and abridge it, intending to ensure that readers could grasp the core and understand the ultimate goal without being burdened by excessive detail.
The work was completed and titled *The True Lineage of the Chan School*. This proved convenient for students.

While reading through it, upon reaching the section concerning Du Hongjian’s visit to Chan Master Wuzhu at the place where the crows were calling in the courtyard trees, he experienced a realization and said, "It is indeed as they say: that which cannot be spoken.
The Master had long possessed a refined and tranquil practice, free from the habit of superficiality; though advanced in years, his progress toward the Way continued to increase.
He possessed great power. He did not allow himself to rest simply because he had gained some slight insight; the Way is inexhaustible, and he could not seek it as something finite.
In his later years, he exhausted his robes and bowl to carve the *Jingxun* (Warnings for the Black Robes), which he shared with those of a similar age. His intention was clearly evident in this.
Later, he passed away at his native mountain.

Tianyin Chihong was a native of Yanping in Min who succeeded Nengchi. He entered the monastic order at Tianning Guangxiao Temple, where he practiced the recitation of scriptures; as his eyes passed over the text, he could recite it from memory.
Since Tianning was not a center for Chan practitioners and its administration was lax and mediocre, the Master abandoned it to travel abroad, eventually visiting almost all the famous [monasteries].
Shan approached various renowned masters. Later, while on a sea vessel, he attained realization through the words of Master Ci.

Having no intention to leave the mundane world, he soon returned to his hometown, where he built a hermitage among the pines to retire in seclusion. His cultivation progressed daily and deeply; people could not fathom the source of his attainment.
Disciples from all quarters gathered around him, and the Master could no longer withhold his teachings. His junior disciples recorded his words as they were spoken, and the work was titled *Tian*.

The *Yin Yulu* (Recorded Sayings of Yin). "Tianyin" (Heavenly Seal) was the master’s title. He also authored the *Chekong Neiji* (Inner Collection of Penetrating Emptiness) and the *Dongyun Waiji* (Outer Collection of Cavernous Clouds);
both directly penetrate the profound and subtle without revealing any bypaths. People said that the Master was skilled at proclaiming the Way, yet he acted as if he heard nothing.
At the age of eighty-one, he gathered the assembly and announced his passing, saying: "Father and son ascend the mountain; each must exert himself. As for this matter, how is it? Tian.

The rain made the ground damp. He then said, "When I die, let there be no burial for me. On such-and-such a day three years from now, when a great star passes from the east to the west, that shall be the time to bury me.
After he had passed away, his disciples placed his remains in a bamboo sedan chair within the thatched hall; he sat upright as if alive.
Even in the height of summer, flies and gnats did not intrude, nor was there any foul odor. When that appointed time arrived, the assembly said, "As previously..."
These were words of illusion. Before he had finished speaking, a star as large as a bushel appeared from the east and moved toward the west; with a thunderous roar, it vanished.
The assembly was greatly startled. They subsequently buried him and conferred upon him the title of Chan Master Tianyin.
Liaoyong, Dechao, and Wuai—these three masters transmitted the lineage to Liaoyong.
His style name was Xueji; his secular surname was Zhang, and he was a native of Suining.

Initially serving as a ritual assistant (*yingjiao*), he happened to go out one day and encountered Master Tianyuan, who said to him, "Observing your temperament, you are fit for the monastic life. The Master replied, "Am I still a layman? Yuan...
He said, "To practice worldly affairs is to be a worldly person; how does it depend on whether one has hair or not? Thereupon, he was enlightened and abandoned his former occupation.

Wearing a single robe, he followed Master Yuan to study Chan. After a long time, he attained realization. When people wished to urge him to emerge into the world as a teacher, the Master shook his hand and said, "I will not enter this 'sleeve-society' (the monastic community).
Consequently, he built a hermitage and lived in seclusion. He composed a poem which says: "Beside the trees I have repaired my hut, leaning against the emerald peaks. Smoke..."

Mist winds around as white clouds deepen; for one as ignorant and dull-witted as I, it is only fitting to dwell among springs and ravines. In my failing years, what prevents me from discoursing on the past and present?
By the stream, strange rocks mark the traces of my departure; beneath the crags, drifting mists sever all sound of coming and going.
In this world of Great Peace, there was originally nothing to do; yet I have needlessly exhausted myself seeking outwardly. At seventy-two years of age, he passed away in his mountain hermitage.
Dechao, styled Puguang, was surnamed Chen. His ancestors were from Zhejiang. At the beginning of the dynasty, he followed his father, who held office, and settled in Shu.

From birth, the Master displayed many extraordinary signs. He left secular life to study under Chan Master Wuji of Zhuyushan for three years, at which time he received the master’s first nod of approval.
Thereupon, he entered Yongxing Mountain, where he erected a hermitage to dwell in seclusion, wearing clothes of grass and subsisting on wood and water. He proceeded to...
He went to Nanliang. The mountain was steep and high, and it was difficult to find water. The Master entered meditative concentration (*samādhi*), perceiving a cool, gurgling sound within a rock.

Following the sound, he struck it with his staff, and a spring gushed forth; this is the present-day Erquan (Ear Spring). Furthermore, he possessed foreknowledge of future events, and his miraculous feats were numerous.
However, the Master kept them strictly secret, so that people could not transmit them. He passed away at the age of eighty-nine.
Wu’ai was a native of Xinyang who possessed supreme conduct. Carrying a single alms bowl, he entered the Lion Cliff on Mount Tiangzhu at Nan Yue.
The cliff was so narrow it could barely accommodate a wooden bench; Wu’ai sat upon this wooden bench, eating wild vegetables, and for seven years he did not consume grain.

The local people heard of this and went to see him; upon seeing him, they were so struck with awe that their tongues hung out. They then deliberated on a place for him to dwell and collectively labored to renovate Nan Tai Temple to house him.

During the Hongzhi era, the official Li Taoyai visited Mount Heng and spoke of a monk who lived as a recluse on a cliff, eating raw vegetables and wearing a hundred-patched robe like a stalk of millet.
When he saw people, he remained silent and unresponsive; this was indeed the one known as Wu Ai (Unobstructed). He lived in the wilds.
Like a solitary crane amidst the clouds, he drifted serenely, having no concern for this world. Many eminent figures of the time held him in high regard;
Governor Qiao Ying of Daonan, Censor Liu Yang, and various other dignitaries all composed poems in his honor.
With a straight spine and steady footing, the lofty character of these three masters can truly be envisioned through their example.
Biography of Zonglin (with Zhichun).

Zonglin’s courtesy name was Dafeng, and Xuan’an was his dharma name. He was a native of Hangzhou. Orphaned at a young age, his mother feared he would be unable to support himself, so she sent him to Puning Monastery to serve as a novice under Master [Name] and attend to his needs.
He recited the scriptures and performed his duties with such diligence that he was able to win the master’s favor.
His mind grew expansive, and he cultivated his refined precepts and conduct with utmost care. He was cautious in initiating friendships and would only associate with others according to the Way.
He was capable in poetry and prose, yet he did not compose frivolously; whenever he did write, it was invariably startling. By nature, he was profoundly filial;

though he had left the household life, he remained diligent in his thoughts for his mother, saying, "The precepts do not require one to forget their kin. From this point on, his reputation spread until it reached the imperial hearing. During the Hongzhi era, he was...
He was summoned to the capital and appointed as the presiding master for the Great Precepts ceremony on the altar, serving as a teacher to those studying the Buddha-dharma.
Furthermore, he was commanded to supervise Mount Wutai and to revise the *Qingliang Tongchuan* for inclusion in the Tripitaka.

In the first year of the Zhengde era, he was granted purple robes, a jade belt, and the title of "Great Master. He established the Office of the Master at Daxiangshan Temple outside the Xizhimen Gate to reside there.

Although he reached the height of glory and prosperity, he regarded it as if it were nothing, remaining as serene and detached as ever. A poem of his says: "The imperial mandate has been transmitted while the ink is still wet;

Braving wind and rain, I ascended to Chang'an. I bow my head with reluctance to accept the rank of the Three Ducal Ministers; I wash my feet with shame to ascend the Altar of Ten-Thousand-Year Longevity.
Having heard the precepts, I have kept many of them; Though it is easy to receive the Emperor's grace, repaying that grace is difficult. How can I..."

As if dwelling only within the mountains, where pines and bamboos rustle through the year’s cold. The Master grew weary of serving as a bridge across the waters and submitted a petition to return south.
Upon receiving his request, he was filled with joy and composed a poem: I prostrate twice before the vermilion palace; The fragrance of the robes lingers on the imperial road anew.
Rain falls upon the nine gates in the third month; A lone traveler returns from a thousand li away. Horses tread upon paths of fading blossoms; Orioles sing amidst the fine grasses.

In the spring of the Willow year, he thought of his mother whose hair had turned white, and the fire in his heart burned as if consumed by flames. These two poems allow one to imagine Lin’s character.
Previously, there was one named Zhichun in Hangzhou who was also renowned for his observance of the precepts; he once recited the *Prātimokṣa* at Lingzhi Temple.

Shou was of distinguished lineage. During the Zhengtong era, he was summoned to serve as the Grand Master of the Platform. In the sixth year of the Jingtai era, he bathed and passed away while seated in meditation.
The Emperor dispatched Zhao Xu of the Ministry of Rites to deliver a decree for a sacrificial offering. The stele stone remains extant within Lingzhi Temple.

Compiled by the Śramaṇa Minghe of Huashan Temple in the Wu Gate region during the Ming Dynasty.
Section on Miscellaneous Subjects, Part on Clarifying: The Biography of Deshan.
Deshan was a native of Ningbo. In his youth, he traveled by sea and was falsely accused by fishermen; he was imprisoned for theft for seventeen years.
At the age of [blank] years, he attained the white robe and became a monk. He encountered Master Tianyan, who transmitted the Dharma to him; he achieved considerable realization.

He traveled as a wandering mendicant until he arrived at Longshou Peak south of the city of Piling, where he took up residence. He made it his daily practice to provide meals for the Sangha and cultivate merit, persevering with untiring diligence.
He lived in extreme austerity, eating only one meal a day, consisting solely of coarse grain and bran. Throughout both winter and summer, he wore only the garments provided by the prison.
If something was broken, he would repair it rather than replace it; yet his spirit was radiant and his wit was swift and agile.
Tang Zhongcheng Shunzhi held him in high esteem, and their friendship was very close. He often remarked: "To pluck the bright moon from a cauldron of boiling water;
to perform a somersault atop a hundred-foot pole. Thus did Tang praise him. He once cast bronze to fashion a Buddha statue and sent it to Putuo Mountain. Furthermore, at that mountain...
He constructed a hall without beams, but passed away before it was completed. His disciples enshrined his remains for burial within the temple;
because his appearance was so strange and ancient, people called him the "Lama Monk."
Dà'ān Chuan was the son of the Hao family of Xiāngyáng. In his youth, he paid respects to the Chan master Gǔzōng, who shaved his head at Mèilín.
Gǔzōng, recognizing that he possessed wisdom from past lives, sent him to Gǔyán to study. Both of these "Gus" were disciples of Tiānqí.
Among the gatekeepers, Yan was the preeminent leader. Residing on Mount Zhongnan, he was followed by a multitude of eminent disciples like dragons and elephants.

When a student arrived, if a single word met with his spiritual resonance, he would immediately bestow upon them the robe and bowl. He lived as a hermit on Mount Lu for thirty years, and the people of Chu served him with the utmost reverence.
Mr. Wang Boyu of Xindu once followed the Master to resolve his doubts, receiving many enlightening instructions. He once remarked, "I have heard what Master Da'an said..."

"Seeing one's nature" is a profound accord with what Confucius called "embodiment of benevolence" (*tǐ rén*). Not only have worldly scholars failed to understand this, even Dà'ān himself was unaware of it.
This is because the Master once discussed "seeing one's nature" with Wáng. On the fifteenth day of the fifth month of such-and-such a year, he passed away.
Prior to this, he had foretold the date of his departure to his disciples, saying: "None of you should wear mourning garments or weep."
For his funeral, he instructed: "Do not背离 (contradict) my family’s dharma. When his disciples asked for the reason, he showed them a verse.
When the period of mourning had concluded, he bathed and sat upright. His disciples requested his final instructions, whereupon he again showed them a verse.
From his birth in the year Dingmao until his passing at the age of seventy-three, his disciples built a stupa beside his former hermitage to enshrine his remains.
Lì. Biography of Dàchǎn. Dàchǎn was the son of a prominent family in Dōnghé.
He was profoundly insightful regarding the principles of nature and attained realization of the "empty flowers" at an early age. He relied upon [Master] Hè of Yùxī.
Shang then shaved his head and devoted himself with all his might to the supramundane path. He visited every Zen monastery and lecture hall to seek instruction, yet found no entry.
Consequently, he established a hermitage at Yantou and remained there for ten years, closing the gate. At the moment he touched his chest and pointed to his forehead, he suddenly grasped it;
the relief from his long-standing itch was beyond description. He then went directly to the Venerable Huizhong of Tianjie Monastery in Hezhou to seek definitive resolution.

They met and simply smiled at one another. Thereupon, they attended each other morning and evening; their karmic conditions were in harmony, like the notch and the arrowhead of a crossbow fitting together.
Having received this seal of approval, he took up his staff and departed from the Min Pass; traveling through Ze and across the Huai River, he encountered many wise masters until he reached Jintai.

He stayed at Dàbǎo Chán Temple, where his reputation for the Way spread widely. When the two officials, Huang and Gao of the Court of Ceremonial, heard the Master’s name, they came to visit him with incense tucked in their sleeves.

Their words and spiritual resonance were in perfect accord, and they regretted that they had encountered him so late; they wished to recommend him to the Emperor, but the Master firmly declined, and they desisted.

From then on, those who came to inquire and pay their respects followed one after another outside his door. The Master taught them according to their capacities, striving to cause each person to awaken.
He departed with a joyful heart, and I felt that my discourse had not been in vain. Yet another day passed, and I began to feel somewhat vexed and distracted.
One day, while casually reading "Return of the Hermit" (Guiqulai Ci), I sighed in contemplation and said: "Tao Yuanming would not have stooped to bend his waist for five bushels of rice."
He abandoned his official post and departed. As a śramaṇa and son of the Śākya, he instead used a single bowl of rice to sustain himself and sought stillness beneath the trees;

his seat was merely a single mat of woven grass as large as the earth. How much of the green mountains did he need to achieve his transformation? In the eighth month of the Wuxu year, he drifted southward in return.
The following year, he resided at Ba’en Monastery in Jinling. He sent a letter to the two Grand Secretaries of the Imperial Household, who merely marveled at it.
Later, a lay devotee from Shaozhou established a temple and invited the Master to dwell there. For over twenty years, his style of pure detachment inspired many to follow his teachings.
On the seventeenth day of the second month in the spring of the Xinyou year, he adjusted his robes and passed away. His disciple Jingyuan...

He compiled these dialogues and utterances into an upper and lower volume, which were subsequently carved into woodblocks and published. The Master delighted in composing poems about his mountain retreat;

they expressed his aspirations for proclaiming the Way and are worthy of recitation for their serene quality. Among them, a verse written while passing through Mount Jinshan reads: "The moon reveals the shadow of the hidden dragon;
the clouds enshroud the cry of the aged crane. This truly manifests the spirit of Chan.
The one who transmitted the Way of the School was a native of Guancheng whom people called Wukong. His physical frame was like that of wood or earth, and he could not recognize a single character;

he could only recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and the *Heart Sūtra* from memory. Yet, he was pure, prudent, sincere, and trustworthy, such that none could fathom his inner nature. He served...

Tiemo was originally a disciple of Master Yuanming, serving him with tasks such as providing firewood and water. He would recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* with a clear, resonant voice, never ceasing.
At the age of twenty-six or twenty-seven, he departed from Yuanming to travel as a wandering monk.

He journeyed extensively through the regions of Jin, Song, Jing, Chu, Guan, Shan, He, and Luo, seeking teachers and choosing companions with an urgency like that of one parched by thirst. He eventually settled in Kaocheng, where he resided for ten years.
In the year Xunwei of the Zhengde era, there was an uprising of bandits that caused turmoil throughout the north and south. The Master returned to his hometown and resided at Yuanjue Temple.
Subsequently, he stayed with the Ma family to the north of the city, and later moved to the Southern Garden of Zhang Taichang.

He would not settle anywhere unless it were for a period of ten years or more; once he did reside there, people came to revere him as a Buddha. While he was at Zhang’s garden, he had already reached the age of one... [text fragment].
He was one hundred and eight years old, yet his vigor and alertness were unlike those of ordinary men. To behold him was like looking upon ancient pines or strange rocks;

he walked and stopped without leaning on a staff, and his hearing and sight were as sharp as those of a youth. At first, he appeared dull and slow-witted, but later he became quite conversant with affairs and understood them clearly.
He usually did nothing at all, remaining only in a state of profound stillness while sitting upright. When questioned about the nature of his cultivation, he would not utter a single word.
They corroborated one another’s accounts, yet he simply did not know that people were harboring sexual desires. Some mocked him, saying, "What is there to value in this drowsy monk?
In response, Beishan Yaoshi offered this defense: "To sit upright in profound stillness, unaware of human desire—what other dharma-gate could there possibly be beyond this?
Later, his final whereabouts remained unknown.
A withered tree leaning against a cold cliff—throughout the three winters there is no warmth. This is truly the mechanism of a dead man.
Were he to encounter one with clear eyes, he would surely be cast out and his hut burned. For the Way, in general, lies in its application; and application lies in the state of death.
Those who study the Way today never seek death; where, then, is there life? They will inevitably end up deceiving and misleading themselves. If...
I encountered one with clear eyes, yet I did not know how to dispatch him. Thus, even for a dead man, a great deal of effort was required;
however, because his mental light did not shine forth, he was subjected to scrutiny. It takes a true "old fellow" (a master) to be able to pass such an examination.
I cannot simply brush him aside.
Liaoran Guanzhu transmitted the teachings to Nenghong.
He was titled Liaoran Guanzhu because he frequently secluded himself in retreat (yanguan) wherever he went due to his chronic illness; hence he received this appellation.
He was, in fact, the tonsure master of Master Kaiming. The Master was long on friendly terms with the Venerable Zibo. Kaiming...

Because of his teacher, he was able to serve the Venerable Zibai. In the *wuli* year of the *Guiwei* cycle (1623), when the Master closed the meditation hall at Dongta, Zibai was residing there at that time.
Together they investigated the matter beyond the ordinary, and after a long period of development, Zibai traveled north.
The Master then instructed Master Kai to follow him, entrusting him with these words: "Serve this elder well; if you should attain a foothold..."

It is our great fortune to hear of your reputation; we consider this a blessing for our school. It so happens that the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* has been newly restored, and we have invited you, Master, to occupy the Eastern Quiet Chamber—the former residence of Zibo.
Your physical appearance is slender and delicate, yet your spirit is harmonious and refined; you take the greatest delight in encouraging and welcoming others.

In his youth, he studied the subtleties of the doctrinal teachings with great diligence. After some time, however, he abandoned them and went to attend upon Master Yungu, where he investigated the "Mu" (No) koan.
Although there were occasional insights, he did not yet accept them as his own. Nevertheless, from that point on, his understanding of the doctrinal teachings became even more profound.

Whenever he presented the essential purport of the sutras and treatises to others, it was direct, lucid, and penetrating; those who heard him could not help but applaud his mastery. Later, he delved into the matter of Deshan’s bowl.
Regarding the circumstances, Zibai showed him a verse which said: "The conditions for begging for alms are not particularly difficult; a secret whispering by the ear is the profound barrier.

The Master’s doubts increased even further. When he reached Mount Wutai, where Gong was observing the *jinzu* (foot-binding) retreat at Longfansi, one night he dreamed that five teeth fell into his palm, leaving bloodstains clearly visible.
After several days had passed, he received a letter from the Master, which contained thorough and earnest instructions that struck directly at the core of his concerns.
Furthermore, regarding the matters discussed previously, Master Kai requested the seal of approval from Zibo.

Master Kai felt that his own realization was "the head has passed through, but the tail has not," and thus he did not grant his consent. Once the reply reached him, the Master (Zibo) subsequently passed away.
When Master Kai heard the news of the obituary at Dongchang, Zibo was observing the summer retreat at Lingyan. He dreamed of two banners, one falling to the south and the other falling to the north.
The following day, Gong arrived and informed him of the Master’s passing as well as the news of the death of the venerable elder Wubian at Mount Tai.
When the Master passed away, he joined his palms and called out, "Master Daguan, let your light descend and gather me in. This continued until the twenty-fourth day; Wubian did the same.

A single thought resonates in response; ten thousand miles are not a barrier. Water and moon reflect each other’s light; needle and magnet attract one another. How could these be considered different?
The Master’s secular surname was [Name]; he was a native of Wangdian in Jiaxing. He was born in the *jiǎmǎo* year of the Jiājìng era and passed away in the *wùzǐ* year of the Wànlì era.

His worldly age was forty-six, and his monastic seniority (*sēnglà*) was thirty. In his later years, he was honored by the Empress Dowager with the gift of a *kāṣāya* robe from the Thousand Buddhas. He opened...
The Duke enshrined the sacred remains in a stupa behind the abbot’s quarters of Lengyan Monastery.
*Record of Chan Master Nyechon (attached is Hyesim)* Chisun, style name Nyechon, was the son of the Chen family of Yongjia.
His mother was a devout follower of the Buddha who observed the precepts with great care. She once dreamed of a monk wearing...
Her halo was like the shape of the full moon. She traveled upstream against the river current, saying, "I shall become your daughter.
Upon waking, she became pregnant. Once born, her excellent qualities were formed from an early age; from childhood, she took no pleasure in keeping her hair long, cutting it as it grew.

Her parents, understanding the causes from her past lives, permitted her to leave the household life. She received full ordination at Tianning Temple and recited the Lotus Sūtra, following the text word by word.

Through his lectures, he gained a profound mastery of the scriptures' essential meaning. Subsequently, he remarked, "Study values extensive learning, but how can this alone resolve the matter of birth and death?
He then changed his robes and entered into meditation, departing for Tianbao Mountain in Min to visit Master Tieguan Shu.

Desiring to dwell under the master's guidance, the master rebuked him, saying, "A man of spirit in this world should not merely vie with others within the great monastic forests; you are confining yourself within this narrow shell."
"Yes. He brushed out his sleeves and entered. The Master went down to the guest quarters and wept bitterly. When the official heard of this, he said with joy, "I knew he was a vessel of the Dharma;
I was merely testing him. He then invited the Master into the Sangha hall, where the Master stood as immovable as a cliff ten thousand fathoms high.

He was unable to move or turn his body; though day and night alternated between light and dark, he could not distinguish them. After more than a month had passed, while returning from the latrine, he beheld a gourd vine in the inner garden.
This triggered a wondrous realization, and his four limbs became light and pure. He knew that he had emerged from bathing and left the room, and from every single pore, radiant light issued forth.
The great earth before his eyes suddenly sank level. To the utmost limit of joy and fortune, he hurried upward toward the [upper story].

When Chang requested certification [of his realization], Master Shitong happened to have entered the provincial city; the Master did not go to see him, remaining instead at ease and unconfined by the riverside and beneath the forest.

Subsequently, he visited various masters one after another, but none accorded with him. He then paid his respects to Chan Master Qianyan Chang, but seeing that all the master’s responses were entangled in intellectual reasoning, he returned to the East with a light step.
Nevertheless, he composed a vow-text, vowing that he would not rest until he had realized the Way.
Thereupon, he reflected again to himself: "No one but you is worthy to be relied upon. He traveled repeatedly to Min Province to see him. It happened that the Master was out on an excursion;

seeing the teacher from afar, the Master said with joy, "My disciple has come at last! He urged the teacher to abandon his former interpretations and engage in actual practice. After five months of diligent effort, [the teacher] attained great enlightenment.
The Master finally granted him formal certification (*kanna*) and ordered him to take charge of the library. Shortly thereafter, he was appointed to share the teaching seat and preach the Dharma.

Upon the Master’s passing, the Abbot succeeded him in presiding over the affairs of the monastery. Having grasped the heart-seal of the patriarchs and Buddhas, the Master ascended the seat to preach the Dharma and deliver sentient beings;
yet he often exerted his surplus energy to adorn pagodas and temples, leading people toward the path of avoiding evil and transforming toward goodness.
In the two regions of Zhejiang and Fujian, the Master established more than ten great sites for the Way, while others were renovated.

The master restored many ancient sites; indeed, they are too numerous to list. Possessing great talent, whenever he undertook a project, he spent gold as if it were soil, yet one never knew its source.
When he was restoring the Jingguang Pagoda in Wencheng, Chancellor Fang had previously garrisoned that region and wished to levy funds from the common people to repair it.
He appointed the master to oversee the matter. The master said, "The people's strength is exhausted and their resources depleted. Fire... [text fragment ends]
"The flames blaze ever higher, adding fuel to the fire. How could I bear to do such a thing? If you must have me employed, do not interfere with my affairs within the official precincts;
it would be best if you heard nothing of them. Only then did he grant his consent. The Master then devised a plan regarding the households within the city.
An additional twenty thousand households contributed one *sheng* of rice per month, resulting in a monthly yield of two hundred *shi* of grain.

As for the firing of tiles and the selection of timber, it was as if spirits were transporting them; they gathered from all four directions in great abundance. A pillar intended to stabilize the foundation, measured in cubits, was one hundred and fifty feet long;
it was the most difficult to procure, yet the Master settled upon its procurement with a smile. Once seven-tenths of the structure was roughly completed, he continued to build beneath it.

The stupa hall was vast, spacious, and magnificent; its nine-tiered pinnacle appeared even more imposing. One day, a typhoon arose, and a single tier was caught up by it and swept into the ocean waves.
Everyone lamented this, saying, "Can the stupa never be completed? The Master replied, "The stupa can ultimately not be finished."
His resolve became even more firm. He dispatched his disciples to Min to cast a dew-dish (*lupan*), a wheel-sign (*cakra*), and various flaming pearl ornaments (*jvālāmaṇi*).
Before long, each was completed; their gold and azure were so brilliant as to seem as if they had descended from heaven or surged forth from the earth.

When Yanzhi Buhua was stationed in Min, he wished to inspect the Great Canon of the Honored Sutras in his private residence. Some, however, raised the objection that it would be difficult to provide sufficient seating, mats, and ritual vessels.
The Master ordered one hundred and seventy Buddhist monks to be divided into groups of ten to attend to their respective stations, each marked with a designated title.
They assembled all at once, and he further had them depicted in a diagram so that they might follow the sequence according to the chart.

Those assigned to serve during the meals also proceeded in rotation, with the ringing of bells and drums serving as the signal for each shift; thus, the order of precedence remained unconfused. He distinguished and regulated [the proceedings].
Yue said, "If my master were to command the army as supreme commander, there would be no fear of defeat. At that time, there was an alarm on the East Sea.
The Supreme Commander, Duke Da Zhongjie, stationed his troops at the provincial seat and dispatched an envoy to invite the Master to enter the mobile headquarters.

The Master declined the invitation and did not meet with him, as he felt Duke Da was currently preoccupied with the affairs of war. Duke Da’s admiration for the Master remained undiminished; he inscribed the two characters "Ni Chuan" (Flowing Against the Current) for him.
He was released. The Master then provided food for the prisoners and exhorted them not to harbor any thoughts of escape;
they were soon restored to the light of day. Before long, the imperial pardon arrived. The two prisoners, Zhou and Wu, regarded the Master as a deity.

Later, when mountain bandits broke out and set fire to everything in their path, the two monasteries of Guiyuan and Baoen were spared from total destruction solely because of the Master. The Imperial Court...

To reduce the number of monastic quarters, the Emperor bestowed upon him the honorary title "Buddha-nature Perfect Eloquence" (Fóxìng Yuánbiàn) and a golden-embroidered dharma robe. The Master did not consider these honors a cause for joy;

he distributed all his accumulated robes and alms bowls and retired to a single room. There, he dug the earth to make a hearth and broke bamboo to make chopsticks, remaining as serene and detached as ever.
Later, he was selected from among the monks of Mount Zhong, and when the Imperial Carriage arrived in person, the Emperor offered him full consolation and inquiry.
Upon completion of his duties, he returned to Qiantang. At that time, Master Wei Qingyuan was presiding over Jingci Temple;

he proposed the Master to serve as his successor. Following the war, Jingci Temple was in a state of extreme decay. The Master summoned craftsmen and calculated the wages required, exhausting the contents of his own storehouses with the intent to carry out extensive renovations.
However, many monks who were in arrears with government taxes were imprisoned and crowded the courtyard; the Master wept for them and paid their debts in full.
He repaid [the debt]. It happened that the imperial court summoned a monk of realized virtue to serve as a counselor. The assembly all recommended the Master.
Upon arriving in Nanjing, he had been there for only four months when he bathed, wrote a verse, and passed away. He was cremated at Mount Jubaoshan, where countless *śarīra* relics were obtained.
The Master’s *Wuhui yulu* (Recorded Sayings in Five Assemblies) and his *Shancai wushisan can ji* (Verses on the Fifty-three Pilgrimages of Sudhana) are both transmitted.
The monk Huixin once sought the Way from his teacher. Later, he was also summoned to enter the Wenyuan Pavilion to assist in the compilation of the *Da Dian* (Great Canon).
After his death, he was cremated, and countless śarīras of five colors were obtained. His heart was named Jiankong; he was from Leqing.
Fangshi. Master Jixiang’s lineage was passed to Jixiang, whose surname was Zhou.
He was the younger brother of Empress Xiaosu. As a child, he enjoyed wandering about; he once went out...
He no longer returned home, and his family did not know where he was. Later, even before he had entered the palace, his family had already lost all contact with him.
After a long time, he shaved his head at Dajue Temple; however, he would often wander through the marketplace.
That night, she went to Kōkoku-ji Temple and stayed overnight in the temple hall. The Empress’s mind, however, remained as if she had forgotten the matter.
Suddenly, she dreamed at night that the guardian deity of the temple came to her and said, "The Empress’s younger brother is currently in my care. Emperor Ying also had a dream at the same time.
Their words matched perfectly. At dawn, he dispatched a eunuch of the Yellow Gate to seek him out at the temple as he had dreamed.

Upon finding the Master in the hall of the monastery, they seized him and brought him away. He was led before the Emperor for an audience and questioned regarding his reasons for wandering abroad and becoming a monk.
At that time, both the Emperor and the Empress wept; the Emperor then said, "How could it be better than being a member of the Imperial clan today? The Master shook his head and did not answer.
She wished to return to the temple; the Empress could not dissuade her and bestowed generous gifts upon her. When Emperor Ying died, the Empress became the Empress Dowager.
She drew from the Inner Treasury to construct Daci'en Temple for her residence. During the reign of Emperor Xiaozong, the Empress Dowager became the Grand Empress Dowager.
A protective imperial edict stele was erected for her; the stele recorded that she had been granted some several hundred *qīng* of farmland.
The Master entered parinirvāṇa at Zuoshanshi, whereupon the Emperor dispatched an official to present offerings. During the Master’s tenure, the monastic community often numbered several hundred;
their practice of Chan meditation and recitation was flourishing and orderly. Later, when Qingshou Monastery was destroyed by fire, the monks also came to reside here.

Both the new and old communities relied on the provisions from the imperial granted fields, ensuring that the two daily meals were never lacking. Observers remarked that the Master had cast aside his status as a royal nephew.
Noble, yet he delighted in the seclusion of the supramundane. While the Two Sages were in the Palace of Compassion, their filial devotion was profound;
what imperial favors were not bestowed upon him? Yet the Master remained as serene and detached as ever. Since the reign of King Yeong, among the royal kinsmen—

Those who hold the rank of Enze Hou (Marquis by Grace) cannot endure for more than a few generations; yet the temple bestowed upon Master [Dao]zhuang still preserves several hundred people living there for food and clothing.
This serves as evidence that the wealth and nobility of a single moment cannot last long, whereas those who dwell in the profound stillness of night endure forever.
Manqi (Mǎnqǐ) was a successor in the lineage of Zhēnchán (Zhēnchán Chuán).
He was known at the time as Báiyún Shàngren (Master White Cloud). A native of the Niu family from Ānzhōu, he received the tonsure at Yǒng’ān Temple.

During the Zhèngdé era, he traveled south to the various mountains of Fúniú, where he met the Venerable Xīzōng, who transmitted the essentials of Chan to him. He subsequently lived in seclusion on Jièlǐng.
At Chanlin, he fulfilled his vow to protect the pearl; subsequently, he entered Maoping at Mount Funiu, where disciples from the four quarters gathered around him.
The Master then departed to travel to Wutai Mountain and entered the Divine Capital (Beijing), residing at Tianqing Temple. There, the two gentlemen Guo Jiang and Jia [invited him].
He served as the master of offerings. His teacher was strict regarding the precepts, and he practiced them with arduous cultivation.

He delighted in performing meritorious deeds, carving thirteen volumes of the *Lóngzàng* (Dragon Canon) and enshrining them in famous mountains and great monasteries. Other acts, such as providing meals for the Sangha and casting statues, were merely minor matters undertaken according to circumstances.
One day, he said to his followers: "I have a karmic debt to repay; I must withdraw in quietude for several days."
He then closed the door and said, "Do not enter unless you are summoned. The assembly peered through a crack and saw the Master lying face down;
the flesh on his back was a dark purple-black color, and the swelling was immense. It did not subside until seven days had passed. When the Master rose, he summoned the assembly to enter.
He said, "I have just returned and completed my life's task; now I am free from suffering. My Master had many karmic connections, and wherever he traveled, his followers always numbered five hundred.
Throughout the city and its outskirts, people vied with one another to offer him support; the appearance of the Jetavana Grove grew increasingly magnificent day by day.
Thereupon, he sighed deeply and said, "Is it truly fitting for it to be like this beneath the imperial capital? He then took up his alms bowl and departed.
He retired to Mount Funiu, declined all social engagements, and no longer left the mountain. In the ninth month of the Renxu year of the Jiajing era, he passed away while seated.
Zhenchan, whose style name was Wuwe, was a native of Jiangling in Chu. His surname was Liu; from childhood, he was intelligent and wise, delighting in goodness and fond of practicing charity.

He lived in harmony with all things and devoted himself to the study of the *juzi* (civil service examination) curriculum, gaining a widespread reputation within the literary circles. In his leisure time from studying the classics and histories, he delighted in discussing Buddhist scriptures.
Later, he encountered an elderly monk who marveled at him, saying, "You are truly a vessel for the Mahāyāna Dharma; the carriages and robes of the secular world are but a dream and an illusion.

Thereupon, he suddenly underwent a transformation of awakening. Hardly having reached the age of twenty, he took leave of his parents to enter the monastic life. His parents sought to thwart his resolve.
Unable to attain [his goal], he went to Mount Yuquan and served the Elder Wubian as his teacher. He shaved his head and received full ordination, vowing his heart to investigate the Way.

On three occasions, he burned off his fingers as a sign of his unwavering faith and resolve. After a long time, he attained deep realization; wherever he went, both monastics and laypeople turned to him for refuge.
Later, while traveling to the capital, the fourfold assembly at Guanyin Temple welcomed him and invited him to reside there. His reputation for the Way spread widely.
The Imperial Court heard of this and bestowed offerings of vegetarian food upon him without a single day’s interval. Later, weary of such distractions, he retired to hide away at Mount Funiu.
As he was about to pass away, he said to his disciples, "This mundane world is but a true dream;

I am about to depart. You all must exert yourselves and do not fall under the weight of the monastic robe. Having finished speaking, he passed away. Wang Yuanchun, the Inspector of Shaanxi, composed [a memorial] for him.
A stone was erected there to commemorate his deeds.

Chunggyeongdang (Hall of Loyalty and Reverence) refers to Chŏngmuk, whose style name was Gyŏngdang. He was the son of the Cho family of Sinan. From the age of seven, he delighted in sitting upright in meditation; at nineteen, he traveled to Ch’ŏn.
At Lingyin Temple in Tang, he was inspired by meeting monks from all quarters; he subsequently shaved his head and received full ordination.

After studying at a lecture hall for several years, he traveled on foot to Shaolin, where he met Master Dajian Run. He then proceeded to Chang’an to attend upon the two venerable masters Bianrong and Xiaoyan.
He was instructed in the essentials of the mind and attained a slight degree of awakening. He subsequently entered the fire-field of Niu Mountain to refine his three karmas.
Later, he returned to Mount Kuanglu, where he admired the lofty excellence of Tianping; there he lived alone, planting over one hundred thousand pine trees with his own hands.
After some time, disciples gathered around him, and Tianping thus became a great monastic community. The Master was by nature simple and straightforward, devoid of artificial ornamentation.

In leading the assembly, he did not rely on formal regulations; he shared equally in both their hardships and their joys. Even a grain of rice or a stalk of vegetable, he would only eat after it had been shared with the community.
He always placed himself at the forefront of all laborious tasks. He did not establish separate gates for meditation or lecturing, but revealed the truth to others in its entirety.

Those who relied upon him—whether foolish or wise—were gradually transformed through silent influence over time, without even realizing it themselves. Thus, those who came to him felt as though they were returning home to serve their kin.
He was like a parent to all. Moreover, he had a method for instructing people and a measure for employing them. His speech was earnest and poignant, reaching the very core of human feeling;

those who heard him were struck with awe, and there were none who did not grasp his meaning in their hearts and realize it through their spirits. The entire assembly sat in solemn order, as if before a great furnace and bellows.
He taught by example rather than through words; he was truly a man of substance who dwelt among the mountains. The Grand Historian Liu Yunqiao visited him...
The Master saw him once and their minds were in accord; he then gave the temple its name, "Yunzhong" (Clouds Amidst).

The Elder Han wrote a commemorative record for it, and the Grand Secretary Zhang Hongyang inscribed the three characters "Gao Lushan" (High Mount Lu) as a gift to honor his aspirations. In the autumn of the Gengshen year, he manifested a slight illness and said to his disciples:
"I see the red sun suspended in the sky and golden lotuses covering the earth; it is time for me to depart. Having spoken thus, he passed away.
Having finished speaking, he passed away in profound stillness. The Elder Han further composed an inscription for his stupa, saying:
"The Master resided in Yunzhong for over twenty years as if it were a single day. He regarded the monastics of the ten directions as he did himself.

He applied his mind with devotion for the sake of the assembly, never harboring divergent thoughts or allowing distinctions between self and others to weigh upon his heart. These few words are indeed a factual record; the Master would bear them without shame.
Minglong transmitted [the Dharma] to Minglong. He was the son of the Yao family in Suzhuan, Huainan; his secular name was Dongyang. He had formerly been a local scholar (*zhusheng*) of that county.

Throughout his life he delighted in cultivation, and for over twenty years he did not inquire after his family’s worldly affairs. He regularly associated with virtuous spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).

In the first year of the Longqing era, he shaved his head and resided at Xiufeng Hermitage on Mount Yang. His reputation for virtue rose daily, and many high-ranking eunuchs among the imperial guards provided him with offerings.
Yet the Master remained as he was, clad in tattered rags; his single robe was no more than a "hanging porcupine" (a metaphor for extreme poverty), and he wore no vest, nor tunic, nor shoes.
Nevertheless, he settled at Mount Yang and established a site for a thousand-day assembly, gathering seventy-two followers. Day after day, the Master...
The Great Assembly expounds the sutras, and the Great Assembly also delights in being its listeners.

At that time, when Emperor Shenzong first ascended the throne, the Imperial Commissioner for Border Affairs, Lord Dao Kunwang, traveled through the various imperial mausoleums and went to visit the Master to inquire about the Way;
he held him in particularly high esteem. He then asked, "When the thousand-day period concludes, will you be able to reside at Yangshan? The Master replied, "There is no 'tasting' (no abiding)."
There was no fixed abode. Fifteen days later, on the day the Grand Astrologer was due to pay his respects, Mount Yang emitted a light on the day of the commencement of winter.
Seven days after that, as the year was drawing to a close, the Master gathered the great assembly and said: "On the first day of the first month of the first year, I shall depart.
You who dwell here, those of you who can read, recite the Buddha’s name with a focused mind; those of you who cannot read, recite the Buddha’s name with a focused mind. Strive for wisdom!"
"Make wisdom your primary task and cultivate a universal mind; this itself is the Buddha. You all must exert yourselves.

On the night of the New Year’s eve, when it was already past midnight, he commanded his disciples to observe the midheaven star, asking, "Is it midnight? They replied, "It is midnight. The Master said, "Not yet. He departed only at noon on the first day of the month.
When the sun was nearly at its zenith, Mount Yang emitted light just as it had before. Shortly thereafter, he passed away while sitting in meditation; this was likely at noon. Seven days later...
At noon, it again emitted light as it had before. All the nobles from the various mausoleums were present;
leading the great multitude, they prostrated themselves in rows to honor the construction of the stupa and the enshrinement of the śarīra.

Nanyue Dou'er Fo, whose dharma name was Ruixiang, was the son of the Zhou family from Sheng County in Yuezhou. Possessing the aspiration for world-transcending enlightenment, he followed his paternal uncle on official travels to the capital, where he met Xiangyan in Liuxiang.
Xiangyan examined his spiritual capacity and instructed him in the Dharma-door of Buddha-recitation. The Master...
He nodded in agreement. After a short while, he returned south; he abandoned his wife and children, shaved his head, and went to Qixia to pay his respects to Dharma Master Suan.
Although he resided at a lecture hall, he practiced mindfulness of the Buddha without interruption. He also studied under Bianrong, whose instructions were identical to those of Xiaoyan.
From Wutai Shan, he entered Funiu Shan, where he attained realization under Master Bosong. He remained in a stone grotto, casting off his shadow among the trees.

He remained in this state for three years. One day, while sitting in *paryaṅka* (full lotus posture), snow accumulated until it filled the forest; the fire was extinguished and his robes were soaked with moisture.

Shilong went to observe him and struck a *ghaṇṭā* (bell) to bring him out of his meditative absorption. He then instructed him, saying: "This light ease and minor tranquility are not the final destination.

If you become attached to this state, you will fall into one-sided emptiness (*ekānta-śūnyatā*). Go forth on your travels; when you encounter the South, stop there. Thereupon, he departed with a carefree air and traveled everywhere.

He traveled through the regions of Chu and Shu, where he eliminated all intellectual views and preserved only solitary clarity. Later, while traveling to Mount Nanyue, he suddenly recalled the words Mañjuśrī had spoken at the time of their parting;
he then resolved to remain there for the rest of his life. At that moment, a monk offered him the hermitage on Peak of the Slanting Blade.
From then on, he set aside his body and mind and focused his will single-mindedly on the Buddha.

He solicited forty-eight *shí* of beans, with each bean representing one Buddha, maintaining pure mindfulness continuously until the end of his life; he did not know how many times forty-eight *shí* had passed.
Consequently, those from all quarters called him "Bean-Buddha. Monks from the ten directions vied to return to him, and Side-Knife Peak (Zhedao Feng) thus became a center of activity.

Renowned throughout the realm as a great assembly, he constantly admonished his disciples, saying: "You have shaved off your hair and beards, yet you do not realize the greatness of the matter of birth and death.
Merely leaning against walls and resting by the eaves, your karmic consciousness is vast and indistinct—what can this be called?
Is this not precisely what our Buddha rebuked? Wearing the patched robe in seclusion, falsely claiming to be an *āraṇyaka*, yet failing to concentrate on pure karma, when the great limit arrives..."
"Having arrived here, with what shall you answer Old Man Yan? Those who heard this were moved to tears without exception.
Although the Master had severed all ties to the human world, the gentlemen of his time who heard of his character could not help but look up to him in admiration.
Such was the case for Provincial Governor Liu Gong, Censor-in-Chief Shi Gong, Academician Wu Gong, Minister of Rites Zeng Gong, Minister of Revenue Cai Gong, and Grand Guardian Guo.
The Duke and the Great Official, the Duke of Song, both inclined their hearts toward him and sought the Master’s guidance; yet when summoned by them, he would not go.
When County Governor Lu held a temple sacrifice, he fined those who arrived late with over thirty *shí* of rice and sent it to the Master.

The Master said, "How could an old monk like me gather such resentment from the masses for the sake of a single bowl of rice? He ultimately refused to accept it. Those who heard this sighed in admiration of the Master.
He received visitors and travelers without discriminating between the good and the bad, treating all with a single flavor of impartial compassion.
Seven men, including the great bandits of Jingzhou and Xiangyang, Jia Er and Tang Jiu, were being pursued by authorities; they threw themselves upon the Master seeking to live.

Moved by their sincerity, the Master accepted them, placed the monastic cap upon their heads, and ordered them to perform manual labor alongside the assembly. When the pursuing officers arrived, although they recognized these men as thieves, they saw only the Master’s compassionate heart.
He was full of serene dignity. Hearing that [the Master] had been moved by the practice of *nienfo*, he untied three pieces of gold from his waistband, made offerings, and departed;
even that thief was transformed and became an ascetic monk. The Master resided on Side-Dao Peak for over thirty years. He did not seek out patrons for alms, nor did he form external alliances.
He established no *fangzhang* (abbot’s quarters) and employed no attendants. In a single small shrine to the left of the Buddha hall, he sat upright in meditation, reciting the Buddha’s name.

The Buddha resided among them. He did not maintain a storehouse, and his chest contained no superfluous items. On the day of his passing, when it was examined, there was only a single jar of black pepper and several pieces of old cloth.
He had often sustained himself on meals of grain-cake mixed with chaff. If anyone threw such food on the ground, the Master would pick it up, roast it over a fire, and eat it.
When traveling, he always carried a hoe; whenever he saw discarded filth, he would surely cover it with earth. As he was about to pass away—

He instructed the head seat to lead the assembly in seated meditation while reciting the Buddha’s name. He admonished the assembly, saying, "Do not engage in empty pretenses or fabricate wonders to deceive the people of the world;
simply and single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name with sincerity. Having spoken these words, he joined his palms and passed away.

This was on the sixth day of the second month in the Gengxu year of the Wanli era. He had lived seventy-nine years and held forty-three years of monastic seniority. His remains were kept in the coffin for seven days.
On that day, his complexion remained unchanged. His disciples enshrined his entire body and erected a stupa on the right side of the peak.
Master Sanzang was a dharma successor of Benrong;
he was a native of Meixian in Shaanxi. Having undergone tonsure, he studied under Venerable Songgu of Huaiqing and later visited Yian.

At the Great Buddha Mountain (Dafoshan), he was among the assembly at Shaolin, the seat of the Lord of the Great Thousand Worlds. Carrying only a single alms bowl with him, he lived without causing any disturbance.
Master Qian marveled at this and offered him a ceremonial silk scarf (*pā*), which he did not accept. He resided in the Dharma Cave for over forty years.

In the *dinghai* year of the Wanli era, he traveled to the capital and stayed at the mountain gate of Longhua Temple, remaining unperturbed by wind, rain, heat, or cold. He later resided at Jixian Temple.
In the temple, the Elder of the Corridor Hall, seeing that the Master was diligent and toiling day and night without ceasing, specially constructed a niche for him and invited him to reside there.
He subsequently established a "Ten Directions" (śāṃsārika) hall to serve the Master, receiving wandering monks for thirteen years; offerings from the faithful arrived like gathering clouds.

Between cause and effect, there was not the slightest discrepancy. In the final years of his life, he remained in the world for an ocean of *kalpas*, receiving and guiding the masses according to conditions.
He made the recitation of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* his daily practice; his secret conduct was so profound that throughout his life he never let his side touch the mat, nor did he eat past noon.
He would not take meals at his permanent residence, but instead went from village to market with his alms bowl to beg for food. Once he had obtained food, the bowl would [overflow].
When he was about to go out, he would turn his alms bowl outward so that people could observe whether the Master had eaten and thus distribute their offerings.

Every time he finished his meal, he would immediately chew a willow twig, close the door, and sit in meditation. Even if he had not yet received his midday meal, he would likewise beg for a cup of water from the well to rinse his teeth before entering his room to sit;
he never failed to finish his meal before noon. If a donor provided an offering or gave him gold, he would certainly...

He would only grant permission if the entire assembly was equally provided for; otherwise, he would firmly refuse and not accept. When someone requested that he recite the scriptures, the Master said, "The virtuous ones in my hall are not practiced in chanting.
Whenever there were those who came to the temple to provide a meal for the monks, he would entrust them with the funds and immediately arrange for rice, salt, vegetables, and fruit.

He would set up the offerings without delay. In his labors, he took the lead of the community with his own body; as for food and drink, whether fine or coarse, he partook according to what was available.

He never forced anyone to do anything against their will. Throughout his life, he never troubled others with requests for construction or repairs. He said: "This life is but a weary journey and a temporary lodging;
when one stays, it is according to conditions, and when one departs, it is forgotten. Why concern oneself with ornate beauty to burden body and mind?

Once, when Empress Cisheng was providing a vegetarian feast for various senior monks, she offered each monk five taels of gold, one roll of silk, and a full jin of sandalwood. The Master firmly [refused these offerings].
He was unwilling to go. The eunuch official, having no other choice, carried him to the monastery. The Master then ate his meal together with the assembly.

At the beginning of the first month of winter in the *Ren-yin* year of the Wanli era, the Master manifested a slight illness. When the Imperial Censor Mr. Xiao questioned him, the Master raised one finger.

That very day at noon, he sat upright and passed away. Upon cremation, his cranial bone was as large as a jujube fruit (*qianshi*). Where the smoke had entered the ground, they dug and found [relics].
He obtained śarīra relics. At first, the two eunuchs Zhang and Liu jointly donated their residence to establish it as a world-monastery.
The Master resided there, and the number of his disciples often exceeded one thousand.

At that time, Cao Lang Guo Jiazhen, Wang Xuemu, Xiao Dingtai, Bao Ying’ao, and Geshi Duanyan all admired the Master’s spiritual influence, holding him in profound reverence and esteem. Lord Duan once visited the Master.
The Master said, "Layman, you have sat for a long time and must be hungry; I shall cook some noodles as an offering. Duan said, "I have long admired the Great Teacher.
I have come specifically for the great noodles to taste their flavor. The Master said in a stern voice, "I allow you to eat the noodles, but I fear you will not be able to swallow them.
Duan stuck out his tongue at this. Such was the loftiness of his school's style. The people of the capital called the Master "The Tripitaka."
"Master" (*shi*) was likely his title.
As for the "Blue Ox" (*qingniu*):
we do not know where he was from. He shaved his head as a youth to become a monk and dwelt in a place of profound stillness at the highest peak of Mount Lu.
In his cell, he recited sutras and mantras by day, and at night he circumambulated the mountain chanting the Buddha’s name. His robes were made of patched quail-feather cloth with a hundred seams;
his sandals weighed ten *jin* and had teeth hardened with yellow wax and white oil, appearing as if cast from raw iron.

When people heard the sound of his sandals in the cold hemp robes within his quiet chamber at night, they vied with one another to bring pine resin as an offering, calling him the "Ancestral Master of the Blue Ox. On the mountain...
The tiger saw him approaching, so it crouched by the side of the road to wait for him. This continued for fifty years.

In the spring of the Renyin year, Hu Jishi Zhengji was traveling to Mount Kuanglu on official business; he took a liking to [the Master’s] countenance and stayed in his room for five nights. In the Guiyou year...
The official Yuan Yi went to visit Master Shi. He saw nothing but a nest of purple pine branches, a water jar, a brazier, and a staff.
Occasional visitors who were lovers of the arts would occasionally offer cotton thread, rice, or millet—only once or twice a year.
When they arrived, these items were left exposed on the ground for the master to take out; there was no door to lock, yet no one ever stole them. When guests arrived, he would not ask their names.

[The Master] was named [Name]. He did not bow or offer worship, appearing entirely ignorant of human affairs. When the Duke encountered him, he found him extraordinary and questioned him, but the Master remained silent.
The Duke then composed a poem for him as an expression of admiration. Someone asked the Master, "When you were out walking at night and encountered a tiger, did your mind feel any agitation?

He replied, "People often harbor thoughts of harming tigers, but tigers have no intention of harming people. When questioned about his spiritual practice, he simply said, "I recite the Buddha’s name. (Jihyou)
In the autumn of that year, he entered Chang’an. His countenance and physical features were such that there was not a single aspect that did not inspire profound reverence in those who beheld him.

Before long, word of his presence reached Empress Dowager Cisheng, who bestowed upon him the title Qingrong and provided him with gold coins, incense, and fruit for his sustenance within Yongan Temple.

A high-ranking eunuch who had studied Buddhism was about to petition for the master’s title and purple robe. When the Master heard of this, he loathed it and fled to conceal himself at Long’an Temple to the east of the city.
One night, he passed away while sitting in meditation. Empress Cisheng provided treasury funds to perform rites of repentance and to escort his remains.
Guyue Chuan was a person from the north; his native place, clan, and surname are unknown. While traveling south on a pilgrimage, he entered Zhongnan Mountain.
Beholding the mountain’s undulating and towering majesty, he thought that there must be sages dwelling in seclusion within its depths, saying, "I shall find my home here."
Relying upon and inheriting the secret truth, he was fortunate indeed. He then packed his provisions and set out, traveling over a hundred li each day.

Wherever he went, he had to clear away brambles and tread upon stones until his feet became cracked like tortoise shells. After ten days of travel, he encountered a hunter with a falcon on his arm and hounds in tow;

he was a dashing young man. The hunter asked him, "Moon, why have you come to this place? He replied, "I am seeking a master and inquiring after the Way, traveling no less than a thousand li. I do not know [where you are going]."
"Is there any eminent monk here whom one might rely upon? The hunter replied, "This is the lair of great boars, long snakes, bears, and mountain ghosts.
Where else would you seek a monk? Desist! Ahead is a stone cave where a white bear sits glaring with fierce intent;
none who pass by escape being ground to powder. Do not put your body to such a trial. Yet Yue-xin was not afraid; he rose.
He thanked the hunter and traveled another several dozen *li* until the sun set upon the Fine Willow Forest (*Siyi-liu*). There he saw a rocky cave and felt a sense of great wonder.
As soon as he peered into the cave, a white bear was crouching there, its eyes flashing like lightning. The bear opened its eyes and gazed at the moon, who said:

"I have journeyed ten thousand *li* in search of this place, hoping to find someone who has heard the Way. Now that I have encountered you, will you allow me to dwell here? Otherwise, it is but fate."
He stood there without fear, staring at the bear for a long time before it wagged its tail and departed. The moonlight then entered the cave, where he stayed overnight.
Three days later, a hunter arrived and exclaimed in astonishment, "You are truly a divine man to have escaped from the bear's mouth.

Yue replied, "I was fortunate enough to escape the bear's jaws, but during the night there were two great men with black caps and long legs standing by my side. What kind of specter was that? The hunter...

The man said, "Before the cliff stands an ancient tree described in two verses. Previously, it was cut down for firewood; could this not be a manifestation of a mountain deity? I request that you clear away its roots.

Yue said, "I cannot bear to sever the life-force of the tree," and he stopped them from clearing it. That night, the two men did not appear. Yue thought, "My compassion has moved even the plants and trees.
The hunter then restrained Yue, who again took his leave. Upon reaching the mountain peak, a monk was sitting in meditation.

The thatched hut was his dwelling. The moonlight delightedly entered the thatched hut. The monk sat in meditation with eyes closed; his five limbs were as firm as a mountain, and from afar he resembled a wooden rooster.
[The Master] opened and inspected his cooking pot; the pot was covered entirely in green moss. He prostrated himself before the monk.

For three days, the monk remained motionless and steadfast. [The Master] then supported him from behind the waist, whereupon he finally regained consciousness. The Moon said, "I pray to receive your instruction. The monk—
"It should not be so," the monk replied. "However, you have no karmic connection with Zhongnan Mountain. Yet you, Yue, have sought instruction with such earnestness.
He said, "When we meet a mountain, we shall stop; when we encounter a hermitage, we shall hide. Having finished speaking, he pointed toward the path of return with his staff to show Yue the way.
Yue saw from afar a blue bird fluttering toward them as if to guide them. After traveling for several days, they crossed Zhongnan Mountain to the west and suddenly beheld a city. This was—
He was also from Shu. When he questioned the people of Shu, he learned that Mount Lu existed in Jiangxi;
he then traveled south by boat from Jingzhou and planted his monk’s staff at Wulao Peak. Forty years later, he passed away.
Gūyuè braved danger to seek out wonders, hoping to gain some insight; yet what he saw was as follows.
He was able to stand tall before the mouth of a bear without succumbing to fear, and below, he paid his respects to the monk Dìng with deep sincerity.

Although what he heard did not reach the essential core of the matter, he nonetheless cannot be considered anything but a person of spiritual resolve. My only regret is that the name of the monk Dìng has not been recorded.
"O humans! Alas! He truly regarded the human realm as an illusion; why, then, would he use a name?
The Biography of Chan Master Baozang:

His courtesy name was Nengxuan, and his secular surname was Liu. A native of Xian County in Hejian, he lost his father at a young age. He went to the Ordination Platform to follow a Great [Master]..."
When Qian Zhen received full ordination, a monk came from Mount Founiu to request instructions on the precepts and matters concerning the subduing of demons.
Qian was filled with joy and immediately set out on foot. Upon encountering a great river, he was granted the Dharma-door of Buddha-recitation;
thereupon, he established a term of practice for the Pratyutpanna Samādhi. After seven summer retreats, he crossed the Qianhe Gou and visited the Elder Tongtian, where he remained to pass the year.
He stood alone throughout the night until dawn; in the time it takes to snap one's fingers, he heard the sound of a wooden board, and his mind was suddenly enlightened.

He composed a verse which he presented to Tōngtiān. Tōngtiān urgently forbade him, saying, "Do not allow yourself to be seized by a mad demon. Later, upon hearing the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, he attained understanding at the passage concerning the investigation of the mind.
He entered the "field for refining demons" once more, practicing walking and sitting meditation for ninety days, during which he clearly attained the signs of meditative concentration.
He then traveled to Mount Zhongnan, where he stayed with Chan Master Guyue for four years. While wandering in the mountains, he happened upon a small chamber and settled there.
Each day he dug up wild mountain vegetables to sustain himself, dedicating his mind entirely to meditative stillness.
Guyue exhorted him, saying, "Do not become intoxicated by the wine of samādhi; do not fall into this deep pit. Following this advice, he went to Yan to visit [Master] Long.
Master Xiu of Chongshou, the lecturer Hua Tong, had attained much insight and understanding. He sighed and said: "How profoundly intimate is the solitary moon to me!
Nevertheless, to indulge in stillness alone is not right; how could it be appropriate to rush toward the clamor of the world?

After the ancients realized the essential meaning, they willingly accepted the bland and endured the bitter by the crags and beneath the trees. How could there be anyone like those today who easily exchange their thatched huts for crimson gates?"

Regarding those who maintain the purity of giving as their worldly occupation, I feel ashamed that my virtue and Way are insufficient; thus, I have been unable to lower my hands to enter the marketplace.

With but a single thatch roof over my head, I shall ultimately remain untouched by the dust of the world. Nevertheless, the fourfold assembly earnestly requested that I reside at Guangji Temple; having no choice, I consented.

Yet, with my corded robes and coarse fare, I regarded this as no different from dwelling in the mountains. When the karmic conditions for my departure were about to end, I first [prepared] the three...

On that day, he gathered followers from all directions. When the appointed day arrived, he recited the names of the Buddhas three thousand times and passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture.
His worldly age was eighty-four, and he had spent seventy-three summer retreats in the monastic life. He was interred in a stupa behind the Avalokiteśvara Hermitage outside Desheng Gate.
Biography of the Tiantang Monk Wulin.

When young, the Tiantang monk was sold by his parents to a merchant from Huizhou to serve as a kitchen boy at a private school. By nature he was simple and sincere; he served his fellow students with devotion.

He was like his master; he usually remained in silent stillness, and no one could fathom his actions. Suddenly, one day, his mind opened and his discourse became extraordinary, leaving all those in the house struck with awe.
When some questioned him regarding difficult points in the scriptures, he explained them according to his own inclination, far surpassing the realm of ordinary intellect.

Those who were fond of such matters approached him to inquire about the great principles of the Buddha-dharma; everything he responded to accorded perfectly with the profound truth, even though he had not [actually studied them].
He had never recognized a single word [of the teachings]. When asked, "What is meant by the Way? he replied, "A single mind is the Way.
When asked, "What is meant by the mind? he replied, "A single person is the mind. Someone heard this and questioned him further, saying, "What you said yesterday was merely one corner of the matter;

you may explain it again. He then asked, "What is meant by the Way? [The master] replied, "A mindless state is the Way. When asked, "What is meant by the mind? he replied, "A personless state is the mind."
The listeners were further struck with profound awe. They all sighed and said, "For a long time, we have been what is called 'bodhisattvas in human form' for others.
Thereupon, they requested that he ordain them, but he declined, saying, "My body has its master; how could I act according to my own convenience? I wish to continue serving as before.
Please redeem me with 'righteous money' (yi-qian). They replied, "Very well. Thus, they collected the funds and returned them to the owner.
He then took his leave to become a monk, and his final whereabouts remained unknown.
A bhikṣu from Wulin (of whose native place no details are known), he traveled through Wulin and once mingled among the marketplace crowds.
He enjoyed associating with scholars of letters and was indiscriminate in what he ate and drank; people called him eccentric or deranged. Suddenly, he said to those he encountered: "I, [Name]..."
"I shall depart on such-and-such a day; I would be honored if you would come to see me off. When the appointed time arrived and the assembly had gathered, the bhikṣu went out to welcome his guests.

He greeted them with his usual joking laughter, saying, "I have troubled you all to come from afar like clouds; why do you wish to provide a farewell banquet for me? They all asked, "Would it not be appropriate to chant the Buddha’s name?
He replied, "Do not trouble yourselves with that. Simply compose a fine poem for me. They asked which poem would be best, and he said, "Cui's 'Yellow Crane Tower.'"
The poem was excellent, and the guest sang it aloud. The bhikṣu clapped his hands in harmony with the song;
when they reached the third line, he passed away before the clapping had even finished.
The Monk Yuet-tam (Yue-tan) transmitted [the Dharma] to Yuet-tam.
The monk did not know his origins; he said himself that his surname was Yang and that he was born in the Jiawu year of the Chenghua era.
He received the full precepts at Mount Wutai. In the Wuyin year of the Jiajing era, he began his travels.

Throughout the realm, [his fame] was perhaps greatest in Shu, where he resided for the longest time among the mountains of Qiong[-liu]. In the *Xinwei* year of the Longqing era, he came to Jiangnan carrying his monk’s staff;
upon reaching Loudong, the two masters Wang Fengzhou and Lin Zhou built a dwelling for him.
He remained there for seventy years, passing away in the winter of the *Bingxu* year of the Wanli era. His secular age was one hundred and thirteen, and his monastic seniority (*senglà*) was ninety.
8. The King inscribed this upon his stupa and wrote in praise:
