They were brilliant in their time and their luster reflected throughout the world. If there were no records to describe them, how could future generations be informed?
For this reason, authors have appeared in successive eras to establish biographies for them, categorizing them into ten sections to synthesize their deeds and reality.

From the High Tang and the Five Dynasties, through the Song and Yuan, and into the Great Ming—spanning over a millennium—therein were those who were like divine dragons and embroidered tigers, who expounded the teachings and propagated the school. And yet...
Those who uphold the ocean of the Dharma did not yield to their predecessors, yet they merely relied on oral tradition, lacking a written record.
Thereupon, Master Heshan Hua rose to concern himself with this matter; having entered the ranks of the monastic community, he took it upon himself to continue the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*.
He desired to encompass all traces of the past; nothing was more reliable than taking faith in inscriptions on metal and stone.

Thus, undaunted by the clouds and mountains of a thousand *li*, carrying only a single calabash and a walking staff (*zhuli*), whenever he encountered a ruined stele or broken monument lying prostrate amidst the smoke and weeds, he would invariably go himself to brush off the dust and copy the characters.
In examining these historical remains, I have searched far and wide and probed the obscure depths, enduring both cold and heat and braving wind and rain;
I have spared no effort. Alas! How bitter was the toil of my heart. Having accumulated over many years, I have compiled them into a volume.

During the intervals of my meditative contemplation, I have arranged them chronologically and set forth their biographical outlines, providing a separate biography for each individual to record their transformative deeds. This process has undergone several revisions.

The draft was completed. A total of several individuals were involved, resulting in several volumes collectively titled the *Supplementary and Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Buxu gaoseng zhuan*).

This work serves to transmit the bright lamp as it nears extinction and to continue the life of wisdom that has not yet been severed; its merit is indeed vast. Yet, before the work could be formally announced as complete, his life’s conditions had reached their end.
He reflected on the need to entrust this task to a worthy successor, yet he found such a person difficult to find and exercised the utmost caution. Gold... [text fragment].

The River’s final testament regarding the illumination of the eastern sun was truly bestowed upon the Venerable Master Huǐguāng. He then produced the complete text and entrusted it to him for its completion.
As for the gift of the incense burner and the *ruyi* scepter, there shall be even more added to this. The Venerable Master Huǐguāng accepted this bequest.

Bearing this immense responsibility, I hoped to draw from the waves of the Dharma to fill the ocean of my vows. Unforeseen, I have encountered times of adversity; war and famine have arrived in succession.
My spirit remains unsettled by these calamities, and though I have traveled to the four quarters with feet blistered by the road, I have achieved nothing at all.
My heart burns with anxiety, fearing I shall fail to repay the mandate I have received. Therefore, I have brought this draft to Mount Yu to consult with the Master Jigu.

Master Zijin’s original aspiration was profound and far-reaching; he manifested his body in accordance with his vows, harmonizing with his long-standing karmic affinity and joyfully pledging his heart.

At that time, I was also present in the assembly and likewise rejoiced in and supported this endeavor. We immediately entrusted it to the woodblock carvers, and the work was completed within the appointed timeframe.

This undertaking has served as the means by which the "dragons and elephants" (great masters) of successive dynasties have emerged. Had it not been for Master He, its spiritual essence could not have been transmitted; had it not been for Master Jiong, who would have succeeded to his will?

It was not Ziji (Zhouyi) who could have announced its completion. These three individuals responded to the call for Buddhist service, alternating as host and guest, their achievements forming the three legs of a tripod.
That this oceanic treasury has been made to circulate—truly, one cannot help but rejoice. Because of this undertaking, I was privileged to participate in the editorial collation;
beholding its final accomplishment, a great joy pervaded my entire being, beyond all description. Thus, at the end of this volume...
I have briefly recorded these circumstantial origins to mark the years and months. Thus it is said.

On the first day of the moon in the early summer of the year *Chóngguāng Zuòè* (the 24th year of the sexagenary cycle), the disciple Mǎ Hóngdào, who has retired from the mountain, respectfully composed this record.
